nodes.misconception: Students may think that 'eyewitness' accounts produce a more reliable picture of historical events.
nodes.response: Although 'eyewitness' accounts are valuable, they were produced for a particular purpose which may distort their contents.

nodes.misconception: King John signed the Magna Carta.
nodes.response: A modern misconception is that King John signed Magna Carta, this is untrue, royal documents were not signed but sealed.

nodes.misconception: Always use 'zu' to mean 'to'.
nodes.response: 'To' is expressed in different ways in German. 'In' and 'nach' also mean 'to'. 'Zu' can also mean 'shut', 'closed' or 'off'.

nodes.misconception: Hyperinflation affected everyone equally.
nodes.response: Some people, like businessmen who hoarded essentials to sell at inflated prices, profited during the crisis. Meanwhile, many middle-class Germans saw their savings wiped out and were forced to barter for survival.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that Elizabeth was always going to be an heir.
nodes.response: The abdication had to happen in order for Elizabeth to be an heir.

nodes.misconception: That the sole turning point of the Second World War was due to America being brought into the conflict.
nodes.response: America's entry into the conflict was an important turning point, however, another significant turning point occurred with the first defeat of the Nazi army in the Soviet Union.

nodes.misconception: Enid doesn't think England is racist.
nodes.response: Enid is very private about her views: we see only her reaction to the discrimination she faces. Consider if her dialogue reveals more.

nodes.misconception: Development of the smallpox vaccine helped scientists to develop vaccines for other diseases.
nodes.response: It was not understood why the smallpox vaccine worked, so no new vaccines were developed until the last decades of the 19th century.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is only one way to refer to 'they' in French.
nodes.response: In French there are in fact two ways to say they: ils and elles. Use ils when referring to a group of boys, or a group of boys and girls (masculine form). Use elles when referring to a group of girls (feminine form).

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that swimming fast is most important.
nodes.response: Slow, steady and energy efficient swimming is best for longer distance swimming.

nodes.misconception: Arrays and lists behave in the same way.
nodes.response: An array has a predefined fixed size. A list can vary in size throughout program execution.

nodes.misconception: 2D drawings cannot be transformed into 3D forms.
nodes.response: 2D drawings are like a blueprint for 3D forms. By imagining how shapes in a drawing could extend into space, students can add depth, volume, and perspective to give their designs a 3D appearance.

nodes.misconception: You cannot print a game board or table layout neatly in Python.
nodes.response: You can added spaces and | to format a game board or table in Python.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often try to hit the ball too hard when batting. Often pupils hit the ball in the same space every time they bat which is usually around 2nd and 3rd base.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on accuracy and control rather than power. Encourage pupils to change the angle of their hips, front foot and backswing to help them hit the ball in different directions.

nodes.misconception: Sculptures must take a long time to create.
nodes.response: Some sculptural works can be quick responsive works.

nodes.misconception: A sketch is always needed to be able to use the Extrude command in Fusion.
nodes.response: Users can extrude from component faces and existing solid bodies.

nodes.misconception: CAD applicatons like Tinkercad just allow you to recreate an idea or design as a digital version.
nodes.response: CAD applications like Tinkercad are great for creating ideas and designs in a digital 3D world. They can also help you test your design and even simulate how it could work.

nodes.misconception: It is perfectly possible for pupils to be highly numerate but struggle with the spatial awareness needed to visualise / imagine whether a 2D net will fold together to form a 2D shape.
nodes.response: As part of the lesson design process you may wish to incorporate manipulatives such as construction materials for those pupils whose learning needs scaffolding. As with all scaffolding, aim to move pupils away from this when you can.

nodes.misconception: I'm not flexible so I can't do yoga.
nodes.response: Flexibility develops over time with consistent practice. Yoga also improves strength, balance and mindfulness. Many poses can be modified to suit all levels, so anyone can start, no matter their current flexibility.

nodes.misconception: Surgery continually improved during the 19th century.
nodes.response: Improvements in anaesthetics led to more invasive surgeries which actually made infection a greater problem in the mid-19th century.

nodes.misconception: There are many misconceptions about diet, such as the need to cut out carbohydrates or fat because they are seen as responsible for weight gain.
nodes.response: A balanced diet requires all macronutrients because each has its own benefits to the body and health. Cutting any of them out completely will negatively impact overall health and performance in sport and phyiscal activity.

nodes.misconception: There are many misconceptions about diet, such as, the need to cut out carbohydrates or fat because they are seen as responsible for weight gain.
nodes.response: A balanced diet requires all nutrients because each has its own benefits to the body and health. Cutting any of them out completely will negatively impact overall health and performance in sport and physical activity.

nodes.misconception: Verbs ending in -a are feminine.
nodes.response: Unlike nouns, verbs in Spanish are not masculine or feminine. 3rd person singular verbs ending in -a can refer to he or she.

nodes.misconception: l' is only for feminine nouns.
nodes.response: l' is the article for all nouns starting with a vowel sound.

nodes.misconception: That Hortense is simply ungrateful.
nodes.response: Think about the promises and expectations that were used to encourage migration. View Hortense's and Gilbert's interaction in light of this betrayal.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils approach many fitness tasks as a race/competition and often give up as opposed to slowing down and maintaining movement until the end.
nodes.response: Reassure that a finishing position is irrelevant and instead focus on personal performance and improvement to their own fitness.

nodes.misconception: It is acceptable to copy the work of others in dance.
nodes.response: Copying the work of others and passing it off as your own is known as plagiarism. However, identifying features that are common to a dance style and applying it to your choreography is different, but should remain respectful to the original source.

nodes.misconception: The police force we have today is the one society has always had.
nodes.response: Explain that the police force was a new concept to Victorians and thus civilians had a lot of anxiety around crime.

nodes.misconception: German verbs always stress the same syllable.
nodes.response: Generally German infinitive verbs stress the first syllable; however, words starting with inseparable prefixes be-, er-, ge-, ver-, ent- stress the 2nd syllable, which includes most past participles; -ieren verbs stress the 'ie' in present and past.

nodes.misconception: When we speak, the pitch of our voice rises and falls in the same way in German and English.
nodes.response: The rise and fall of our voice is similar in German and English sentences, but more marked in German and more noticeable with one-syllable words. Note the larger fall when saying 'gut' in German compared to 'good' in English.

nodes.misconception: Dickens aims to shame his wealthy readers into showing compassion by demonstrating that poor people cannot enjoy Christmas because of the poverty they are forced to live in.
nodes.response: While Dickens does use the novella to encourage his readers to show compassion, his depictions of poor people do show them enjoying Christmas. In fact, we could argue poorer characters seem happier because they are able to enjoy simple pleasures.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that Scrooge is evil.
nodes.response: Scrooge is not evil - he is immoral. A distinction between the two needs to be clarified.

nodes.misconception: Workhouses were a positive form of social reform; instead of being sent to prison, poor people were offered the chance to work off any debts they had.
nodes.response: Workhouses were an alternative to debtor's prison but they were not positive places; inmates were separated from their families, lived in squalid conditions and forced to do hard labour for 10-12 hours a day.

nodes.misconception: People who work hard enough can escape poverty.
nodes.response: This was a common belief in Victorian times when people in poverty faced much social stigma. Unfortunately, poverty was not easy to escape; many poor people were uneducated, had no access to healthcare and lived in cramped conditions.

nodes.misconception: The Industrial Revolution brought great prosperity to the Britain; factories helped to provide wealth equality because it provided jobs to help poor people out of poverty.
nodes.response: The Industrial Revolution did bring great prosperity but unfortunately the wealth was not shared across all social classes. Industrial wealth improved the lives of business owners but poor people suffered due to low wages and overcrowding.

nodes.misconception: Wealthy Victorians did feel bad about those living in poverty but had no power to do anything about it.
nodes.response: Many wealthy Victorians felt little sympathy for the poor, believing instead that people in poverty were lazy or morally inferior.

nodes.misconception: Wealth alone guaranteed a high social status in Victorian society.
nodes.response: While wealth was important to securing high social status, reputation was extremely important to wealthy Victorians. Arranged marriages and inheritance were key levers to ensure a good family reputation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils create sequences and motifs that include long stops between actions as pupils fail or forget to use additional actions to aid transition.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that in order to create a sequence that flows well, we need to include addtional actions to support the transition from action to action.

nodes.misconception: Poppies is a poem about a mother whose son died during WWI.
nodes.response: Although Poppies are a symbol of remembrance for those who died in WWI, Weir uses her poem to draw attention to the many conflicts that have occurred throughout history. It isn't clear which conflict the son is heading off to fight in.

nodes.misconception: Del hates the education system and school.
nodes.response: Whilst Del did not have a positive school experience, she knows the value of education, hence her extreme reaction to Viv skipping an exam.

nodes.misconception: When revisiting vocabulary using the Leitner system, we need to revise all the words in the different boxes every day.
nodes.response: When learning vocabulary using the Leitner system, we use 4 boxes with words: words that need to be revised daily, words that need to be revised every 3 days, weekly and monthly.

nodes.misconception: Shakespeare was a misogynist or, conversely, Shakespeare was a feminist.
nodes.response: We don't know about Shakespeare's political or social beliefs. The text is there for us to interpret, not define Shakespeare's views.

nodes.misconception: All plural nouns are formed the same way in German.
nodes.response: Nouns can form their plural in different ways in German. There are rules to help you learn this.

nodes.misconception: Add -s to make all nouns plural in French.
nodes.response: Many nouns do need an -s in the plural form but masculine nouns ending in -eau or -eu need -x adding in the plural form, and there are other exceptions.

nodes.misconception: I know from the sound if a Spanish word starts with 'h'.
nodes.response: The letter 'h' is a silent letter in Spanish. We need to learn the spelling of words that start with 'h' by practising vocabulary regularly.

nodes.misconception: There are no strategies I can use to understand words in a text; I either know them or I don't.
nodes.response: I can use several strategies to help me understand a text: I can use the surrounding words that I do know, I can use my knowledge of patterns, e.g. for adjectives, and I can use cognates.

nodes.misconception: Only syllables in words with written accents should be stressed.
nodes.response: Any vowel with a written accent is stressed. For words ending in vowels, -n  and -s, the penultimate syllable is stressed. For all other words, the final syllable is stressed.

nodes.misconception: To say 'you' in German, we just use 'du'.
nodes.response: 'Du' is 'you' when talking to one person you address by first name.  When talking to more than one person you know this well, use 'ihr'. The verb ending is -t.

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the person who possesses the noun.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the noun they describe, not the person who possesses it!

nodes.misconception: That all families were the same 140 years ago and life was the same for everyone.
nodes.response: Explain that while the photograph gives us some clues to life in the past, just like now, all families were different.

nodes.misconception: 'The' is always 'le'.
nodes.response: There are three ways to say 'the' in French in the singular. 'Le' is used in front of masculine singular nouns. 'La' is used in front of feminine singular nouns. 'L'' is used in front of singular nouns starting with a vowel.

nodes.misconception: As long as I am comparing the key points of two sources that is enough.
nodes.response: Using both comparative and correlative conjunctions will ensure there is nuance in your comparisons. They will also help keep your comparisons succinct.

nodes.misconception: The stem of the 'I, you, she/he/it' form of the verb 'poder' is spelt exactly the same as the infinitive.
nodes.response: The infinitive is 'poder' but when we conjugate the verb, the spelling changes for the 'I, you, she/he/it' form. 'Puedo' means 'I can', 'puedes' means 'you can' and 'puede' means 'she/he/it can.'

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that the fighting in the Second World War only happened in Europe.
nodes.response: Discuss how the fighting was global and happened across three different continents with millions of people worldwide involved.

nodes.misconception: The molecules of a substance change when a substance melts or break down into individual atoms when it boils.
nodes.response: Provide opportunity for pupils to describe, in their own words, the effect on particles of the melting and boiling processes.

nodes.misconception: That the English language developed quickly.
nodes.response: The English that we speak today was shaped across many hundreds of years by lots of significant events in our history.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, adjectives go before the noun in French: a fast car.
nodes.response: Unlike in English, most adjectives go after the noun in French: une voiture rapide.

nodes.misconception: All German words that look or sound similar to words in English are cognates.
nodes.response: Similar looking and sounding words are only cognates if they share the same meaning in both languages. When the meaning is different, similar words are called false friends.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have perceptions of Vikings as only fierce fighters.
nodes.response: Evidence shows that the Vikings who settled in York were peaceful; they farmed the land and were known for being great craftsmen, traders, artists, engineers and ship builders.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand how the objects prove the trade links around the world.
nodes.response: Particular objects during this time could only come from certain places. For example, silk was only made in China and travelled via the Silk Road to the Middle East and onto Europe.

nodes.misconception: In French, there is a separate word for 'would' that is used with an infinitive to express what someone 'would' do.
nodes.response: The conditional form of verbs expresses 'would' + verb e.g. je visiterais - I would visit. There is no word for 'would' in French.

nodes.misconception: To make nouns plurals in Spanish, add -s or -es as in English.
nodes.response: To make nouns plurals in Spanish, add -s if the noun ends in a vowel, add -es if the noun ends in a consonant and add -ces if the noun ends in z.

nodes.misconception: Infinitive verbs are only used when they follow a conjugated verb.
nodes.response: When an infinitive is used at the start of a clause, it becomes a noun, e.g. 'Étudier est un bon moyen de trouver un meilleur emploi.'. ('Studying is a good way to find a better job.')

nodes.misconception: Infinitive verbs are only used when they follow a conjugated verb.
nodes.response: When an infinitive is used at the start of a clause, it becomes a noun, e.g. 'Étudier est un bon moyen de trouver un meilleur emploi.'. ('Studying is a good way to find a better job.')

nodes.misconception: That Queenie and Bernard's relationship is only a marriage of convenience.
nodes.response: How do Queenie and Bernard interact with each other? Can you find any clues where love or affection might be present?

nodes.misconception: Reflexive verbs are just for routine activities.
nodes.response: In Spanish there are many reflexive verbs and they are not just used to describe routine activities. This lesson includes the verb 'acordar' ('to agree') compared with the reflexive verb 'acordarse' ('to remember').

nodes.misconception: That only people born in Britain were part of the British Army that fought in WWII.
nodes.response: The British Army contained a huge number of soldiers from different countries. For example, over two and a half million men from the Indian subcontinent volunteered for service, producing the largest volunteer army in history.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that populations of organisms stay the same forever.
nodes.response: This model clearly demonstrates that populations change over time due to natural selection, with advantageous traits (e.g. camouflage) becoming more common in the population.

nodes.misconception: The genetic code and DNA are the same thing.
nodes.response: The DNA is a long chemical molecule made of four different types of chemical units (A, T, C, G). These units make up the genetic code.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to explain why a motion is not effective.
nodes.response: Explain thoroughly the criteria of an 'effective motion': it should be clear and easy to understand; both sides must  have an opportunity to make a fair point; it must be relatable, important and respectful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that it's ok to stop and stand mid-court.
nodes.response: It is essential to return to the middle of the court and split step as your opponent hits the ball to load elastic energy in your legs to be able to move quickly. Don't get caught standing between the baseline and non-volley line on approach to net.

nodes.misconception: You can add the suffix -los to any German noun to make an adjective.
nodes.response: You can't just add -los to any noun to form an adjective. It only works if the result makes real sense - usually where there’s a natural English -less equivalent (like 'hairless', 'hopeless', 'windowless').

nodes.misconception: Adjectives only change their spelling according to the gender of the noun they describe.
nodes.response: Adjectives change their spelling to match both the gender of the noun and the case, e.g., 'das ist ein lustiger Hund', 'ich habe einen lustigen Hund'.

nodes.misconception: When addressing questions to someone, I can just use 'du'.
nodes.response: Questions often need to be asked using 'Sie', in situations where respect should be shown, such as when asking a teacher or an unknown adult.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense only describes what used to happen.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense describes what was happening and what used to happen and can be used with the perfect tense and a conjunction like 'quand' or 'pendant que'.

nodes.misconception: Bernard completely rejects Queenie's baby due to his racial prejudices.
nodes.response: What does the baby symbolise? How does Edmundson use Benard's behaviour to hint at the potential for reparation and change.

nodes.misconception: It is only the verb in a sentence that can tell us whether the action of the verb implies movement towards a destination or a static location.
nodes.response: The case (form of the article 'the' or 'a') used after prepositions 'in' and 'auf' tells us whether movement or location are implied, e.g., when the article is in the accusative case ('in den', 'in die', 'ins') it means 'into' and indicates movement.

nodes.misconception: Prepositions with the verbs 'depend' and 'reply' in English work the same way as prepositions with 'dépendre' and 'répondre' in French.
nodes.response: 'Depend' is followed by 'on' in English and 'dépendre' by a form of 'de' in French. 'Répondre' is always followed by a form of 'à' in French whereas in English it can be translated as 'reply to' but also with 'answer', where there is no preposition.

nodes.misconception: German word order is just like English - it's always subject-verb-object.
nodes.response: In English, word order is usually fixed: subject-verb-object, e.g., 'she eats an apple'. In German, the word order is more flexible because in main clauses the verb must be in second position. Any element can start a German sentence for emphasis.

nodes.misconception: After all prepositions, the case used depends on whether the verb describes 'location in' or 'movement to'.
nodes.response: Some prepositions always require dative endings regardless of the verb meaning; e.g., 'aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu'; other prepositions are only ever used with the accusative, e.g., 'durch, für'.

nodes.misconception: 'Information' is used in French like it is in English.
nodes.response: 'Information' is a cognate but it is usually in the plural form in French ('des informations'). When used in the singular form, it means 'a piece of information'.

nodes.misconception: German [v] is always pronounced like English [f].
nodes.response: In many words, German [v] sounds like English [f]. However, in German words of foreign origin, [v] usually sounds the same as English [v], e.g., 'Universität', 'November', 'Aktivität'.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is used in written, but not usually in spoken German.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense forms of 'sein', 'haben' and 'es gibt' are widely used in spoken German, along with imperfect modal verbs which, combined with a 2nd (infinitive) verb, are used to say what you and others wanted, were able or had to do.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may suggest ideas for main or non-finite clauses that cannot be done simultaneously.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to imagine the two actions and consider whether they can be done at the same time.

nodes.misconception: Children may be unsure which noun or noun phrase the relative clause should be placed after.
nodes.response: The relative clause is placed after whichever noun or noun phrase it provides extra, relevant information about.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any sentence beginning with an -ing word contains a non-finite clause.
nodes.response: Emphasise that a non-finite clause is a subordinate clause so cannot make complete sense - 'Singing is great!' is not a non-finite clause.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe relative clauses can only be placed in the middle of sentences.
nodes.response: Relative clauses follow nouns/noun phrases; although we focus on the middle position in Y4, it can vary.

nodes.misconception: The idea that atoms can be created or destroyed when new products are formed.
nodes.response: Matter cannot be created or destroyed, only arranged differently to be formed into new products.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, adjectives come before the noun just like in English.
nodes.response: In English, adjectives come before the noun.  In Spanish, many adjectives follow the noun. Practice in first identifying the object and then what it is like helps to embed the Spanish noun-adjective pattern.

nodes.misconception: All Spanish sound-symbol correspondences are pronounced the same everywhere Spanish is spoken.
nodes.response: [z] and [c] are pronounced differently in different Spanish-speaking countries. In Latin America and the Canary islands, [z] sounds the same as [s].

nodes.misconception: Spanish -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the present tense.
nodes.response: The verbs endings for Spanish -er and -ir verbs are the same for 'I', 'you (singular)', 'she', 'he', 'it' and 'they'. The 1st person plural ‘we’ ending for -er verbs is -emos, and for -ir verbs is -imos.

nodes.misconception: The simple present tense in Spanish is only for habitual actions, e.g. 'every week I do my homework'.
nodes.response: The simple present in Spanish is used for habitual actions and immediate plans. '¿Qué haces hoy?' translates as 'What are you doing today?' - 'Hoy hago mis deberes.' 'Today I'm doing my homework'. English uses the present continuous here instead.

nodes.misconception: All Spanish verb forms for -ar verbs end in -ar.
nodes.response: Spanish -ar verbs end in o-, -as, -a, -amos depending on who they refer to. -o for 'I', -as for 'you', -a for 'she, he, it' and -amos for 'we'

nodes.misconception: Light from a lamp moves in parallel rays in a preferred direction towards the observer.
nodes.response: Overtly discuss the direction light rays move from a lamp by considering where light from a lamp can be seen from.

nodes.misconception: Reference resources, like dictionaries, only provide the definition of a word.
nodes.response: Reference resources, like dictionaries, also indicate word class and gender.

nodes.misconception: There is one word for 'the' in Spanish as in English.
nodes.response: 'El' is the word for 'the' for masculine nouns; 'la' is the word for 'the' for feminine nouns.

nodes.misconception: When conducting the ruler drop test, the partner or assistant will countdown so the performer knows when the ruler is going to be dropped.
nodes.response: Remind students that they need to drop the ruler randomly, rather than when the performer knows they will drop it, to really ensure validity to test reaction time.

nodes.misconception: That rest is not incorporated into these types of training.
nodes.response: All of these can be performed as a type of interval training and rest after each exercise / session is important to avoid the body getting injured.

nodes.misconception: That rest is not incorporated into these types of training.
nodes.response: All of these can be performed as a type of interval training and rest is important after each exercise / session to avoid the body getting injured.

nodes.misconception: That rest is not incorporated into these types of training.
nodes.response: All of these can be performed as a type of interval training and rest after each exercise/session is important to avoid the body getting injured.

nodes.misconception: Running is the only type of interval training.
nodes.response: Interval training can be done with any activity as long as it involves high intesity work followed by a rest period.

nodes.misconception: Running is the only type of interval training.
nodes.response: Interval training can be done with any activity, as long as it involves high intensity work followed by a rest period.

nodes.misconception: Running is the only type of interval training.
nodes.response: Interval training can be done with any activity as long as it involves high intesity work followed by a rest period.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may measure their heart rate incorrectly after completing the 150 steps for the Harvard step test.
nodes.response: Before starting the Harvard step test, allow pupils an opportunity to practice finding and measuring their heart rate.

nodes.misconception: Starting the multi-stage fitness test too quickly.
nodes.response: It can be beneficial to start the multi-stage fitness test at fast walking pace to conserve energy for the faster levels.

nodes.misconception: When conducting the ruler drop test, the partner or assistant will countdown so the performer knows when the ruler is going to be dropped.
nodes.response: Remind students that they need to drop the ruler randomly, rather than when the performer knows they will drop it, to really ensure validity to test reaction time.

nodes.misconception: Starting the multi stage fitness test too quickly.
nodes.response: It can be beneficial to start the multi stage fitness test at fast walking pace to conserve energy for the faster levels.

nodes.misconception: Raising the knees in the sit and reach test.
nodes.response: When performing the sit and reach test the knees should. be flat along the floor to give an accurate reading of flexibility.

nodes.misconception: A proper cool down speeds up reduction in heart rate after exercise and prevents muscle soreness.
nodes.response: An active cool down actually prolongs the elevated heart and breathing rate after exercise to help flush fresh oxygen through the muscles and improve recovery. However, DOMS may still occur due to microtears in muscles if training was intense.

nodes.misconception: All of the oxygen we breathe in is used by the muscles.
nodes.response: The body only extracts a small percentage of the oxygen in each breath so it is important we keep breathing during and after exercise. You can only moves gases to an area of lower concentration so once that is equal diffusion stops.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not stand straight against the wall with their arm touching the wall to gain the initial mark for the vertical jump test.
nodes.response: It is important for reliable results when measuring power that the arm is against the wall and outreached as high as possible, when taking the initial measurement.

nodes.misconception: Raising the knees in the sit and reach test.
nodes.response: When performing the sit and reach test, the knees should be flat along the floor to give an accurate reading of flexibility.

nodes.misconception: Raising the knees in the sit and reach test.
nodes.response: When performing the sit and reach test, the knees should be flat along the floor to give an accurate reading of flexibility.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think deoxygenated blood at the muscle tissue goes straight to the lungs rather than via the heart first (i.e. they forget they need to go through the heart twice).
nodes.response: Remind pupils the heart is a double circulatory pump consisting of a pulmonary and a systemic loop. Without this, blood pressure would be too low on return from the legs to efficiently get blood to the lungs for oxygenation.

nodes.misconception: I can describe a photo using single words.
nodes.response: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to use full sentences with verbs. To make the description even more interesting and complex add justifications and contrasts.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to say please to a person in French: 's'il vous plait'.
nodes.response: There are two ways to say please in French: 'sil vous plait' for someone you don't know very well or someone in a position of responsibility like your teacher. But for friends and family you use 's'il te plait'.

nodes.misconception: The 3rd person plural 'they' form of the verb 'sortir' is 'sorent' and of the verb 'venir' is 'vienent'.
nodes.response: The verb 'sortir' keeps its 't' to become 'sortent' and the verb 'venir' doubles its 'n' to become 'viennent'.

nodes.misconception: The pronoun 'on' only means 'people in general'.
nodes.response: The pronoun 'on' does mean 'people in general' but it is often used to mean 'we' in informal conversations, like when you are talking to friends. You will have seen this meaning before in the phrase 'on y va !' which means 'let's go!'.

nodes.misconception: The direct object precedes the indirect object in a German sentence.
nodes.response: If there are two objects in a sentence and one is a pronoun, the pronoun will precede the noun, regardless of whether it is the direct or indirect object. However, if both objects are nouns, the indirect object is first.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, 'sans' is followed by the -ing form of a verb in French.
nodes.response: In French, 'sans' is followed by the infinitive form of a verb, e.g. 'elle part sans dire un mot' - 'she leaves without saying a word'.

nodes.misconception: English verbs use the same prepositions as in German.
nodes.response: German verbs often use different prepositions from those used with English verbs; for example 'ich hoffe auf' - 'I'm hoping for' (not 'hoping on').

nodes.misconception: The prepositions 'auf' and 'an' are always followed by the accusative case.
nodes.response: 'Auf' and 'an' are followed by the accusative case when there is movement. They are followed by the dative case when a location is being described.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'c' in Spanish is always pronounced in the same way.
nodes.response: The pronunciation of the letter 'c' changes depending on the following vowel. [ci] and [ce] have soft 'c' sounds and [ca], [co], [cu] have hard 'c' sounds.

nodes.misconception: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender. If a word is feminine we think of it as a girl if it is masculine we think of it as a boy.
nodes.response: Grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender. Spelling clues help to identify Spanish grammatical gender: nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, nouns ending in -a are usually feminine.

nodes.misconception: With gustar-type verbs, the verb agrees with the person who likes something.
nodes.response: In gustar-type verbs, the verb agrees with the subject - the thing liked, literally, the thing that pleases - not the person, e.g. 'Me gusta la música.' Since 'música' is singular, the correct form is 'gusta'.

nodes.misconception: If a word looks the same in French and English, it will always be a cognate.
nodes.response: There are lots of cognates, where English and French words are the same or similar. However, there are some words, known as 'false friends'. These are words whose meanings are not what they look like e.g. 'attendre' meaning 'to wait' not 'to attend'.

nodes.misconception: The 3rd persons singular and plural with verbs like 'entendre' have different spellings but the same pronunciation.
nodes.response: The 'd' at the end of the 3rd person singular is a silent final consonant but the 'd' in the 3rd person plural is pronounced, whilst the -ent is silent.

nodes.misconception: Every child has their own bedroom.
nodes.response: It’s a common misconception that every child has their own bedroom. In reality, many children share rooms, sleep in a living area or move around different homes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to combine inequalities.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use a number line and draw on the potential solutions. In order for a solution set to be valid for all the stated inequalities, it must include values that satisfy all potential solution restrictions.

nodes.misconception: All the tests run on GM crops have found that they create no health issues.
nodes.response: Most major scientific bodies find no conclusive evidence of harm from approved GM foods, which have all been tested. However, some animal studies raise questions, and critics argue that long-term human studies are limited.

nodes.misconception: To form a negative in Spanish, you need to translate the word 'any' in plural sentences as well as making the verb negative, as in 'there are not any beaches'.
nodes.response: There is no Spanish word for 'any' in plural sentences. The word 'no' is used before the verb to form a negative.

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [o], [au] and [eau] are spelt differently so they must be different sounds.
nodes.response: There are three different ways to spell the same [o] sound. You have to be careful and learn the spelling of words in French,  as well as being able to read them aloud correctly.

nodes.misconception: Children only use one method of transport to get to school everyday.
nodes.response: Depending on the circumstances on that day, e.g. weather, parent's work schedule, public transport delays etc. you might travel to school in different ways on different days of the week. We are looking at the most frequent way you travel on average.

nodes.misconception: That the government of the DRC is only concerned with the military and defence and not with other important matters that affect the people.
nodes.response: The government of the DRC has many departments focussed on a variety of areas from energy and industries to farming and conservation. The government makes policies and pledges in a number of contexts, not only in defence and military matters.

nodes.misconception: The pronouns 'y' and 'en' go after the verb, as 'there' and 'of it/them' do in English.
nodes.response: 'Y' and 'en' go before the verb in a present tense sentence e.g. 'elle y va' and 'elle en boit'.

nodes.misconception: Use subject pronouns after prepositions to link nouns/pronouns.
nodes.response: Use the emphatic pronouns 'moi' and 'toi' instead of subject pronouns to link and emphasise nouns/pronouns.

nodes.misconception: Learning genders is not as important as learning the noun itself.
nodes.response: Leaning the genders of words is essential because it affects other parts of the sentence such as which form of 'à/de' to use before a noun.

nodes.misconception: When performing in a group formation, this should always be in unison.
nodes.response: Unison can be highly effective in clear formations as this also communicates unity and power, but other choreographic relationships such as canon, mirroring or contact work also add interest and are visually exciting to watch.

nodes.misconception: Difficulties in using digital mapping tools.
nodes.response: Provide additional teaching input to support learners in using digital mapping tools.

nodes.misconception: Individual objects can't be used to make art.
nodes.response: If we collect a range of materials in contrasting colours and various textures, we can combine them to produce a nice composition.

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter which Spanish translation of the verb 'to be' we use, as they both mean 'to be, being'.
nodes.response: The verb 'ser' is for permanent traits, and the verb 'estar' is for temporary states/moods and location. It sounds as odd to a Spanish person if we use the wrong verb 'to be' as it does when someone says 'I make sport' or 'I do a cake' in English.

nodes.misconception: 'Estar' can be followed by 'en' or 'a'.
nodes.response: The preposition 'en' is generally used with 'estar' and can mean 'in', 'on' or 'at'. The preposition 'a' is generally used with the verb 'ir'.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that the novel is Gothic in the typical sense.
nodes.response: Be clear about subversion and how it works in the novella. Although Stevenson uses some Gothic elements they are not always used in the typical way for the genre.

nodes.misconception: Ne ... pas goes around the main verb (the past participle) in perfect tense sentences.
nodes.response: Just like in other double verb sentences, ne...pas goes around the first verb; in the perfect tense, that's the conjugated form of 'avoir'.

nodes.misconception: Only change your main verb into a past verb in French like we can do in English to form the past tense, e.g. I do → I did.
nodes.response: In French you need two verbs in the perfect tense for it to make sense; the correct part of 'avoir' and the past participle.

nodes.misconception: Students often don't realise that Dickens' deliberately capitalised on a popular genre.
nodes.response: Dickens wanted the novella to become a bestseller, as this would give his message the best chance of reaching as many people as possible.

nodes.misconception: Speaking doesn't require rehearsal or practice.
nodes.response: To develop fluency, it is important to rehearse speaking and practise reading aloud. This helps you improve pronunciation, speed and intonation so you convey a clear message with confidence and without too many hesitations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that a spike is performed with the hand in a fist shape.
nodes.response: A spike is performed with an open hand with the fingers together and the ball contacting the centre of the palm.

nodes.misconception: Students often simply 'method spot' in analytical responses.
nodes.response: The writer's intention should form part of students' analysis of the text, as they should be outlining why the writer has used the method.

nodes.misconception: Analysis can only include a language focus, especially single word analysis.
nodes.response: You should analyse a range of writer's methods; this analysis should support your thesis or topic sentence.

nodes.misconception: Students think that the first version of their work is the finished piece.
nodes.response: Redrafting work improves its quality, depth and coherence. Students should be encouraged to appreciate, and embrace the value of redrafting their work.

nodes.misconception: 'Können' and 'dürfen' both mean 'can' in English.
nodes.response: Whilst we often use 'can' to translate both verbs in English, they are different in meaning.  'Dürfen' refers to permission - 'may I/am I allowed to?'. 'Können' refers to the ability to do something - 'can I/am I able to?'.

nodes.misconception: Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not change when forming their past participle.
nodes.response: Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not add 'ge-' when forming their past participle, but many do have vowel changes, e.g., 'vermeiden' becomes 'vermieden', 'empfehlen' becomes 'empfohlen'.

nodes.misconception: The subject and verb in a 'zu' clause must match the subject and tense of the linked clause.
nodes.response: We always use the infinitive and never a subject and finite verb in constructions with 'zu'. This applies to all tenses.

nodes.misconception: Abolition of slavery in Britain and its colonies was a response to a single event.
nodes.response: Abolition of slavery in Britain and its colonies was a response to a number of events and an ever-growing public demand for change.

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials, pupils may rely purely on observation, rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities to test different materials and observe what happens.

nodes.misconception: Infrared radiation is visible and is seen when objects glow.
nodes.response: Distinguish clearly between light radiation and infrared radiation in terms of what is visible and what is not visible.

nodes.misconception: That the blood and circulatory system are synonyms.
nodes.response: Blood and circulatory system are key words and introduced as specific concepts.

nodes.misconception: You should only add layers to a painting with paint.
nodes.response: Dry materials can be used in a variety of ways to add detail and shading to an art work. Dry materials can be layered over the top of wet materials once dried. Examples include pastel over watercolour or pen over dried ink washes.

nodes.misconception: Abstract art is easy to create.
nodes.response: Abstract art does not try to show things as they look in real life. Instead, it focuses on expressing emotions, ideas, or movement which is not an easy task.

nodes.misconception: We use the term 'multiplicative relationship' when talking about direct proportion.  Pupils may need reminding that division is equivalent to multiplying by the reciprocal.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities to explore division of a number and multiplication of its reciprocal.  Remind pupils that any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal is equal to 1.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all art is still and that it doesn't show movement.
nodes.response: Artists have lots of ways to show change or movement such as using lines, colours, and even how they arrange things in the picture.

nodes.misconception: For all direct and inverse proportions, the multiplicative relationship is with x and y.
nodes.response: The multiplicative relationship whether direct or inverse can be shown as y and x^n. Show a ratio table of y and 1/x^2 and  a table of y and 1/x. The inverse multiplicative relationship is seen with y and 1/x^2 and not with 1/x.

nodes.misconception: Mark-making is only needed in abstract work.
nodes.response: Artists use different marks to express emotions, create mood, and bring their artwork to life.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to use the correct technique for running fast. Pupils are slow to react.
nodes.response: Model the correct technique for running. Reiterate the importance of acceleration and give pupils another pupil to race against.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that if velocity or speed is increasing, then acceleration must also be increasing. Pupils often don't associate a change in direction at a constant speed with an acceleration.
nodes.response: Before teaching acceleration, consolidate an understanding of the differences between velocity and changes in velocity. Discuss how an object can be accelerating AND travelling at a constant speed (circular motion).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that if velocity or speed is increasing, then acceleration must also be increasing. Pupils often don't associate a change in direction at a constant speed with an acceleration.
nodes.response: Before teaching acceleration, consolidate an understanding of the differences between velocity and changes in velocity. Discuss how an object can be accelerating AND travelling at a constant speed (circular motion).

nodes.misconception: Working collaboratively is always positive and has an impact on productivity.
nodes.response: There are some disadvantages to collaborative working, for example complex decision making with multiple people can become a lengthy process and coordination of resources can be difficult.

nodes.misconception: Prototypes are finished pieces that cannot be adapted.
nodes.response: Prototypes can help identify problems and prototypes made from card can be adapted easily.

nodes.misconception: All fasteners are accessible to everyone.
nodes.response: The user needs should be considered when choosing fasteners so they are accesible to the individual.

nodes.misconception: Textile products are only designed for fashion.
nodes.response: Textile products can also serve functional and practical purposes, such as accessibility and user needs.

nodes.misconception: 'S' always sounds the same in French.
nodes.response: The 's' at the beginning of words and double 's' is a soft sound but 's' between two consonants is [s], pronounced as in 'maison'.

nodes.misconception: The only translation of 'iba' is 'I used to go'.
nodes.response: 'iba' can means 'I used to go' or 'she, he, it used to go'. As 'iba' has several meanings, it’s important to consider to context of the sentence to work out who it refers to.

nodes.misconception: Accents are present in several forms of 'ir' and -ar verbs in the imperfect tense.
nodes.response: Accents are only present in the 1st person singular (we) form of 'ir' ('íbamos') and -ar verbs (-ábamos) in the imperfect tense.

nodes.misconception: When describing photos in speech and writing, a one-word answer will suffice.
nodes.response: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to use full sentences and convey a range of information.

nodes.misconception: Surds are any number with a root symbol.
nodes.response: √4 is not a surd as it is equivalent to 2.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to tuck their head when performing forward and backward rolls causing a rough landing or strain on their neck.
nodes.response: The chin should be tucked gently into the chest looking at their stomach. This will protect the neck and keep the head aligned.

nodes.misconception: Students may use sentence fragments in their work
nodes.response: Showing exactly how sentence fragments obscure meaning and explaining why they should not be used

nodes.misconception: Children may write 'four-quarters' instead of 'one' or 'one and eight-eighths' instead of '2'. Children may also confuse 'part' and 'marks' when determining the unit that we are working with.
nodes.response: One is composed of four-quarters, but we write '1'. Two is composed of one and eight-eighths but we write '2'. We need to count the equal parts in between the intervals, not the marks.

nodes.misconception: Pupils hit the ball with both the flat side and the curved side of their stick.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they can only use the flat side of the stick and they lose possession if they break this rule.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think they will only be successful if they can achieve all the activities at the most challenging level.
nodes.response: Everybody is different and success is different for everyone. Anyone who tries their best and gives maximum effort should feel successful, regardless of the level of challenge they completed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that acids 'eat' away at substances, e.g. acid rain and limestone, rather than understanding that this is a chemical reaction.
nodes.response: Using familiar reactions between acids and bases, e.g. hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide or calcium carbonate, will provide evidence that a reaction has taken place (i.e. a change in temperature or producing a gas).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that acids 'eat' away at substances, e.g. acid rain and limestone, rather than understanding that this is a chemical reaction.
nodes.response: Using familiar reactions between acids and bases, e.g. hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide or calcium carbonate, will provide evidence that a reaction has taken place (i.e. a change in temperature or producing a gas).

nodes.misconception: Acid rain is immediately harmful to human skin. Acid rain's effects are quick and devastating.
nodes.response: Educate that acid rain is less acidic than household acids. Discuss the long-term ecological and structural impacts of acid rain.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can get confused by the litmus paper test and presume that a change has to take place for it to be a positive result.
nodes.response: Use the phrases, stay red, stay blue, turn red, turn blue to help them understand that sometimes a positive test is no colour change.

nodes.misconception: Shakespearean tragic heroes are often nobility who command respect from all before their fall.
nodes.response: Othello, the tragic hero, is not respected by Iago and Roderigo because of his race.

nodes.misconception: Othello will live up to others' expectations and opinions of him.
nodes.response: Othello is completely different to other's perceptions of him. Indeed, he must be worthy of sympathy if he is to be a tragic hero.

nodes.misconception: The storm in Othello is just a device that means the Turkish army is defeated and the war is over.
nodes.response: The storm in Othello is a device that is symbolic of chaos and disorder to come.

nodes.misconception: You can't compare one scene to another. You must focus on one at a time.
nodes.response: A play is not a sequence of unconnected scenes and characters. They all work together to present and explore particular ideas. You should compare characters and scenes in order to understand a play, its characters and ideas more deeply.

nodes.misconception: Iago is similar to many other Shakespeare villains.
nodes.response: Iago stands out because of his diabolical nature.

nodes.misconception: Othello's downfall is solely due to his own faults.
nodes.response: Shakespeare carefully crafts Iago as someone who plays a huge role in Othello's downfall - acting like the serpent in the Garden of Eden.

nodes.misconception: The audience will perceive the tragic hero to be at complete fault for their downfall.
nodes.response: In Othello, due to the amount of time we spend getting to know Iago, we can see the huge role Iago plays in Othello's character change.

nodes.misconception: Iago is an evil villain, completely in control the whole play.
nodes.response: Iago begins to show his fallibility in 5.1.

nodes.misconception: Othello is the only character that suffers a tragic fate
nodes.response: Desdemona, Emilia and Othello all suffer a tragic fate

nodes.misconception: Music for films is always recorded and played through speakers.
nodes.response: Before technology existed to do this, film music was played live by performers in the room. It would often be a solo piano/organ player, who would improvise along with the film. Sometimes, ensembles such as orchestras would play music live instead.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that when replicating Newtons Cradle, when we make contact with others, we have to bump or push them away.
nodes.response: The actions don’t have to be bumps or pushes when making contact with a partner, but instead could be any action such as a lean, a step, a jump etc.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, French has two present tenses.
nodes.response: There is no 'be -ing' in French. There is only one present tense for both the simple present and continuous present.

nodes.misconception: When you perform a canon, you have to perform the same action as each other.
nodes.response: Whilst this is often true, the actions can vary, e.g., pupils may jump apart one at a time, yet each pupil may perform a different jump, or pupils may change shape. It is the staggered timing that is the essential element.

nodes.misconception: It's fine to adapt or mitigate, we don't need to do both.
nodes.response: Adaptation helps us cope with climate change, but it doesn’t stop the problem from getting worse. Mitigation helps slow down climate change. The best approach is to use both mitigation and adaptation.

nodes.misconception: It is possible to leave 'que' out in French like it is in English.
nodes.response: Even if we would not translate 'que' (that) in English, in French we always need to put it when we mean 'think that'.

nodes.misconception: When making contact you always use your hands
nodes.response: Making contact can involve different body parts, e.g. foot to foot, elbow to shoulder, back to back. Using more unusual connections can make a dance appear more interesting to the audience.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to make a certain shape (e.g. a wide star-shaped stretch for the letter 'X').
nodes.response: There are many possible responses - the shapes can be recreated using just part of the body or all of it. Changing between sitting, lying and standing is also an option as well as incorporating balances or jumps.

nodes.misconception: Travelling is only a whole-body movement and involves moving around the space available.
nodes.response: Travelling can be either a whole body action or be performed by isolated body parts. As well as moving around the space it can also involve going up and down as well as turning on the spot.

nodes.misconception: Children might think these results will be permanent.
nodes.response: If time allowed you could repeat the fieldwork on a different day, or send groups out a different times then compare the results.

nodes.misconception: 'I am reading' and 'I read' both translate as 'leo'.
nodes.response: 'I am reading' is the present continuous and therefore it translates as 'estoy leyendo'. 'I read' is the present simple and it translates as 'leo'. We need to use context and time markers to know when to use each.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense only has one translation e.g. 'used to'.
nodes.response: Students must be aware that the imperfect tense can be translated differently according to context and intended meaning e.g. 'used to', 'was doing' or 'did'.

nodes.misconception: Infinitives in Spanish can only be translated as 'to + verb'.
nodes.response: Infinitives in Spanish can be translated as 'to + verb' or '...ing'.

nodes.misconception: 'Cuánto' is used to ask about one thing and 'cuántos' for several things.
nodes.response: 'Cuánto' is used for uncountable nouns, not for one thing.

nodes.misconception: Spanish verbs follow the same pattern as English verbs. The 'I', 'you', 'we' and 'they' forms are all the same and the only change happens in the 'she, he, it' form.
nodes.response: In Spanish, each subject has its own special ending. For -ar verbs, this is '-o' for 'I', '-as' for 'you', '-a' for 'she, he, it', '-amos' for 'we' and '-an' for 'they'.

nodes.misconception: Word order is the same in German and English.
nodes.response: German sentences containing adverbs have a different word order to English.

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' means 'to do, doing' in French.
nodes.response: The verb 'faire' means 'to do, doing' and 'to make, making' in French. 'Je fais le lit. ' (I make the bed). 'Je fais du sport.' (I do sport).

nodes.misconception: To make sentences negative in French, you need to put the equivalent of 'don't' before the main verb.
nodes.response: To make sentences negative in French, you 'sandwich' the main verb between 'ne' and 'pas'. There are two elements which need to be in place. For example: 'je fais le ménage' (positive) 'je ne fais pas le ménage' (negative).

nodes.misconception: I have to pronounce every syllable of 'qu'est-ce que'.
nodes.response: When you say it slowly there are five separate syllables in 'qu'est-ce que' but in conversation we should naturally speed up the pronunciation and pronounce four syllables, we leave out the 'ce'.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'c' is always soft (like the 's' in English) in French.
nodes.response: The letter 'c' is naturally soft before 'e' and 'i'  e.g. 'c'est', but hard before 'a', 'o' and 'u' e.g. 'carte'. The cedilla 'ç' is used to soften it before 'a', 'o' and 'u', e.g. 'français'.

nodes.misconception: Word order is the same in German and English.
nodes.response: Word order is not always the same in German and English. Pay close attention to the position of different sentence parts (subject, verb, nouns, adverbs).

nodes.misconception: The SSC [-tion] makes a 'sh' sound, like in English.
nodes.response: The SSC [-tion] makes a 's' sound in French.

nodes.misconception: The Spanish [h] is always silent, no matter which letter it appears next to.
nodes.response: The Spanish [h] is not pronounced, but [ch] is always pronounced like the [ch] in 'churros' and 'chocolate'.

nodes.misconception: The feminine plural always refers to girls/women only and the masculine plural, to boys/men only.
nodes.response: The masculine plural is used to refer to groups of women and men too.

nodes.misconception: A sentence such as 'puedo participo' is correct and it means 'I can participate'. Both verbs are in the 'I' form.
nodes.response: The sentence 'Puedo participo' is not correct because the verb 'poder' is always followed by an infinitive. To say 'I can participate' we must say 'Puedo participar.'

nodes.misconception: There is just one word for ‘we’ and one word for ‘they’ in Spanish.
nodes.response: Spanish has two words each for ‘we’ and ‘they’. The plural pronoun ‘we’ is ‘nosotros’ for boys/men or mixed gender groups, ‘nosotras’ for girls/women; ‘they’ also has two forms, 'ellos' and 'ellas'.

nodes.misconception: Subject pronouns, e.g. 'I', 'she', 'we', 'they', are used in the same way in Spanish and English.
nodes.response: English always uses subject pronouns. Spanish often relies on verb endings alone to indicate the 'doer'. However, Spanish has subject pronouns, e.g. 'yo' (I), 'tú' (you), 'él' (he), 'ella' (she), which are used for emphasis and clarity, as needed.

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to predict outcomes for random events such as radioactive decay.
nodes.response: Use analogies to show that random nuclear decay can lead to predictable outcomes, such as the randomness in the order popcorn kernels pop, but the predictability of how quickly all the popcorn takes to cook.

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to predict outcomes for random events such as radioactive decay.
nodes.response: Use analogies to show that random nuclear decay can lead to predictable outcomes, such as the randomness in the order popcorn kernels pop, but the predictability of how quickly all the popcorn takes to cook.

nodes.misconception: Ada Lovelace invented the first computer.
nodes.response: While Ada Lovelace wrote the first algorithm, she did not invent the first computer. Micro:bits demonstate the principles that Ada Lovelace worked on.

nodes.misconception: The creation story in Genesis is unique to Christianity.
nodes.response: All Abrahamic faiths share this story, with Adam as the first human.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe they can maintain their shorter distance pace over the longer distance, without needing to adjust.
nodes.response: Longer distances require more controlled pacing. Running a 1500m at 800m pace or a 200m at 100m pace will almost always lead to early fatigue and poor performance. Learning to distribute your effort is key to completing longer events effectively.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think being adaptable as a leader is when there is a forced change.
nodes.response: Adaptability for an effective leader is when it is always happening and the leader is responding to how the needs of the group are being met and if the environment is working or not.

nodes.misconception: That animals can only exist within the biomes they are native to.
nodes.response: Animals do thrive best in their natural habitats, however in countries all around the world there are zoos and animal centres that recreate natural conditions to allow animals to live and survive in a different biome or climate zone.

nodes.misconception: Not appreciating the links between form and function in biological structures.
nodes.response: This lesson develops a key cross-cutting idea in biology: the shapes and forms of biological structures are adapted for specific functions.

nodes.misconception: Organisms are able to adapt to the place where they live.
nodes.response: Referring to inheritance, explain that changes to organisms take time to evolve - responses to any environmental change is not instant.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often refer to the walls of the alveoli as "cell walls".
nodes.response: This lesson makes the scale of different parts of the gas exchange system clear (e.g. whether a structure is a tissue or cell).

nodes.misconception: As students struggle to remember that plants are alive, they don't think of plants as being adapted to their surroundings.
nodes.response: This lesson gives many examples of the adaptations plants have which help them to thrive in their environments.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can sometimes mistake the excess base for the salt formed as it is a solid.
nodes.response: Emphasise at the beginning of the experiment what soluble means and that the salt will be initially obtained dissolved in water.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will sometimes remove or add ones or tens to one addend and forget to amend the other addend so that the calculation has been transformed but doesn't give the same sum as the original.
nodes.response: Encourage buddy checking of jottings as the children practise so that they can help each other to be reminded.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may refer to adding numbers in the tens as 3 + 6 rather than 30 + 60
nodes.response: Encourage them to refer to the tens numbers as tens, and use the language appropriately. In 34 + 44, we add 4 and 4 together and then we add 30 and 40 together. This will support their reasoning as they progress in this unit.

nodes.misconception: If children partition both addends when addition involves bridging 10, they may forget to add the extra 10 made when combining the ones.
nodes.response: Encourage children to consider whether an addition will bridge 10 before solving and if so, partition only one addend to reduce the number of steps required, increasing efficiency.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not use zero to show that there are no tens or ones number in a 3-digit number. They may also use a zero to show that there are no hundreds when adding a 2-digit to a 3-digit number.
nodes.response: Emphasise with pupils that they need to use a zero only when needed. The number 75 would not be written as 075, so should not be written like this in column addition.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be confident in representing addition problems using bar models.
nodes.response: Make connections between bar models, tens frames and 'first...then...then...now' representations. Take time to model examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not understand that addition is commutative and are unable to 'swap' addends around.
nodes.response: Use practical equipment and small numbers to show pupils that a sum is still the same even if values are added in different orders.

nodes.misconception: Simple eletrical systems are not dangerous.
nodes.response: All exposed electrical wires need to be covered to prevent injury or fire.

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty finding one less than a multiple of ten saying, for example, one less than 60 is 69.
nodes.response: Refer to the order of the decades counting forwards and backwards and encourage visualisation of the decades on number lines and one hundred squares to support this. Help children to generalise about the number before a decade number ending in 9

nodes.misconception: Children may focus on the ones digit rather than the tens digits. They may calculate inefficiently by counting on/back in ones rather than using the pattern in the tens digits.
nodes.response: Use Base 10 equipment alongside one hundred squares to support with understanding the structure of adding or subtracting ten and difference. Encourage children to notice what changes and what stays the same.

nodes.misconception: Children might still try to add or subtract the denominators as well due to a misunderstanding about the denominator showing what unit-fraction is being used for calculation.
nodes.response: By this stage, buddy checking can be useful. Get the children to check each other periodically but ensure that children can also explain why this is incorrect.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that only one digit will change when adding two numbers where one addend has only one non-zero digit.
nodes.response: This is usually correct but what would happen if the digit changed to a value of 10 or greater? Then we would need to regroup (another lesson).

nodes.misconception: Children may not see the link between adding or subtracting ones and adding or subtracting tens. They may not know how to use known facts to help work out equations using multiples of ten.
nodes.response: Reinforce understanding of unitising by describing groups of objects in ones or tens. Make the link between known facts and equations using multiples of ten explicit. Show it with equipment such as base ten blocks and represent on place value charts.

nodes.misconception: When adding or subtracting fractions with different denominators, you just add or subtract the denominators from each other.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to use prior generalisations such as when the numerators are the same, the fraction with the largest denominator is the smallest, to help them reason about the above misconception.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count on from, or back from, a given number.
nodes.response: Encourage automaticity with the counting sequence through regular practice. At times, pause so that children need to predict the number that is one more/less. Initially, you may need to model silently counting from one through to the given number.

nodes.misconception: The language of one more or one less than can confuse children, so 55 is one more than ? may be interpreted as 55 plus 1
nodes.response: Encourage children to articulate and explain in full sentences alongside number lines to support the understanding of the different ways to articulate the concept. Use stem sentences to support with this and display them around the classroom.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may partition numbers incorrectly when adding or subtracting across a 100s boundary.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add or subtract to first the 100s number, using number pairs that total 10 or 100.

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly identify the even number 'before' or 'after' the one given.
nodes.response: Provide practice in the form of missing number problems where children must identify the even numbers before or after one given. Do this until fluent. Initially, allow children to use a number line. Remove this scaffold once feeling more confident.

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly identify the odd number 'before' or 'after' the one given.
nodes.response: Provide practice in the form of missing number problems where children must identify the odd numbers before or after one given. Do this until fluent. Initially, allow children to use a number line. Remove this scaffold once feeling more confident.

nodes.misconception: Children may make mistakes when adopting more mental strategies.
nodes.response: Leave scaffolds in place until showing confidence in verbal explanation. For example, once confident visualising 'making 10' using the ten frame, remove the scaffold of the ten frame and counters.

nodes.misconception: Children may partition the second addend in a way that does not allow them to make use of the multiple of ten and use their number bonds to calculate efficiently.
nodes.response: Use ten frames and number lines to support children in finding the multiple of ten and partition the addend in different ways to compare the efficiency of different ways of partitioning.

nodes.misconception: In the addition of fractions, many children will try to add together both the numerator and denominator.
nodes.response: Show the children many completed examples using representations alongside the fraction notation. Encourage them to make generalisations and spot that the denominator remains the same because it is the unit.

nodes.misconception: Typically, many children add both the numerators and denominators together to get the sum.
nodes.response: Pupils need to grasp units and unitising. Get them to move around the classroom/school performing simple additions with different sets of objects. Revisit fractions explaining that they're using unit fractions and this is shown by the denominator.

nodes.misconception: Adding the fractional part of a mixed number to a proper fraction may result in an improper fraction, which may be recombined with the whole number part of the mixed number and left as improper.
nodes.response: In a mixed number, the numerator of the fractional part must always be smaller than the denominator. If it is greater, a final conversion is needed.

nodes.misconception: Children may automatically count on in tens to add a multiple of ten.
nodes.response: Discuss efficiency and compare different methods. Use practical equipment to draw attention to the relationship between adding multiples of ten in two-digit numbers and the known facts they already possess.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with the language of unitising.
nodes.response: Encourage children to read aloud and spot what they notice - which known fact can they see - what is the same/different?

nodes.misconception: When adding fractions with the same denominator many children may try and add both the numerator and denominator.
nodes.response: This is a misunderstanding of the unitisation. Practise counting in different set of objects such as cubes, counters, children. Move children on to counting in fractions and explain that this is simply a different unit, shown by the denominator.

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty when the sum is presented on the left of the equal sign.
nodes.response: Ensure that equations are arranged with the sum both on the left and the right of equal sign. Use term 'is equal to' to stress equality.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe a pair to 10 only exists if the addends are next to one another in an equation.
nodes.response: Addition is commutative. Model the use of tens frames to show efficient addition of calculations containing number pairs to 10.

nodes.misconception: If children record incorrectly, they could re-add an addend that has already been used to make a pair to 10
nodes.response: Carefully model how to record thinking, rewriting the new equation inclusive of 10 underneath.

nodes.misconception: Children rely on one strategy for adding to find a sum and do not consider the values.
nodes.response: Discuss when it is most efficient to use doubles, near doubles, number pairs to 10. Model efficient approaches.

nodes.misconception: Children unable to understand that addends can be swapped but the sum will remain the same.
nodes.response: Use a number line to explore commutativity in a situation where it looks less obvious as this will show children the different structures but also different starting pints but the end pint will remain the same.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make the connection between the concrete, pictorial and abstract representations.
nodes.response: When using the part–part–whole representation, make sure you explicitly connect each number with what it represents. Ask the children to describe what they can see using the full stem sentences. 'The ___ represents the __________.'

nodes.misconception: Shadow appears all around the object in a single, dark tone. Pupils may also draw shadows as a solid, dark shape.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to draw an arrow to show where the light is coming from. Remind pupils to look carefully at their object and consider where the shadow is darkest and where the shadow fades.

nodes.misconception: Many pupils will want to use a written method/algorithm immediately such as column method. This lesson is to support mental addition strategies.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to forget about using written procedures because they are inefficient when the addends are suited to adjustment. As class teacher, use adjustment and race the children desperate to use columns to see who is fastest!

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that a tens counter has a value of ten. For example, they may think that 14 tens and 11 tens make 25 altogether, forgetting to convert 25 tens into 250.
nodes.response: Encourage counting in tens using counters to begin with. Move onto modelling questions using base ten so the children can count the tens blocks.

nodes.misconception: Children may transpose digits in the numbers, so add tens as ones and vice versa. They may also use inefficient counting strategies to count on in tens, then ones.
nodes.response: Ensure that the numbers are partitioned into tens and ones, so their place value is clear and the link to known facts can be easily seen. Refer back to known facts using the stem sentence 'I know that..., so I know that ...'

nodes.misconception: Children use ten frames but use them to ‘count all’ or ‘count on’ without making 10
nodes.response: Ten frames can provide a great scaffold for all in this lesson when used to 'make 10'. Stress that we partition an addend to make 10 and that once the ten frame is full, it shows one ten so we do not need to count them all.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly aligning 3-digit and 4-digit numbers resulting in an incorrect sum.
nodes.response: Practise partitioning 3 and 4-digit numbers into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones to support when placing in columns. This will also support in understanding the relationship between the columns when regrouping.

nodes.misconception: Adding more features always makes a product better.
nodes.response: Adding features should be done carefully, focusing on usefulness and how well they work together to solve a problem.

nodes.misconception: Pupils misinterpret the score and think the accompaniment is the second line of the melody.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to follow the score through when listening to the music and reinforce that both lines are part of the same system.

nodes.misconception: Backspace removes a whole sentence.
nodes.response: Backspace removes one character at a time so that minormistakes can be corrected quickly.

nodes.misconception: One instrument can only make one type of sound.
nodes.response: Our body is an instrument and we can create many different sounds, all with different timbre.

nodes.misconception: To solve circuits you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.

nodes.misconception: When choosing images, pupils should select the ones they like best rather than the most appropriate images.
nodes.response: When choosing an image, it’s important to select one that best fits the purpose and message of the work, rather than just picking one based on personal preference.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all nouns can be made plural by adding an 's'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that there are some other ways to show more than one, such as one goose, two geese or one child, two children.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume the rule applies to all verbs with no exceptions.
nodes.response: Remind children that rules are for most spellings, but not all. There are exceptions to the taught rule such as I play - She plays.

nodes.misconception: Pen up and erase all do the same thing.
nodes.response: Pen up stops the sprite from drawing a line, erase all clears all lines already drawn. Pen up stops new marks being drawn on the screen but keeps what is already there whilst erase all clears everything that already exists.

nodes.misconception: Decorations used are to make it look pretty.
nodes.response: As well as appearance, we need to consider usability and safety when choosing finishing touches.

nodes.misconception: Images are stored inside HTML files as one document that is downloaded and displayed.
nodes.response: HTML only references image files, which are stored separately. When a web page is downloaded, the linked images are downloaded separately.

nodes.misconception: When you make a mistake in video editing software, you have to start again.
nodes.response: There are lots of ways to fix a mistake. You could change the order, undo, or delete.

nodes.misconception: There is a hierarchy in notation - stave notation is always best.
nodes.response: Notation is only effective when it can be read easily. We can notate in many different ways.

nodes.misconception: When adding numbers in standard form, pupils can also add the exponents of 10.
