nodes.response: The use of the place value chart shows how the magnitude does not change to the sum of the powers of 10. The place value chart can support pupils to make the correct addition or subtraction of large or small numbers.

nodes.misconception: One iteration of the tresillo and habanera has to last for two beats.
nodes.response: The tresillo and habanera can be played in 2/4 or 4/4. The important thing is the relationship of the notes to each other. Practise clapping the rhythms twice as fast or slow to the same beat to help pupils grasp this concept.

nodes.misconception: Each sound in a rhythm is a beat.
nodes.response: Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations. Rhythmic notes can have a duration of one beat, more than one beat, or less than one beat.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they need to include all the explanation for their opinion in their point.
nodes.response: A point is just the speaker saying what they think or believe and giving one short reason to justify that opinion using the word because.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can mix up the representations of 'l' and forget the representations which are most likely.
nodes.response: Frame the new learning on -al in the context of prior knowledge around representations of 'l', highlighting the most common representations.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the difference on where you can and cannot find a root word.
nodes.response: Show examples of where an obvious root word can support spelling. Words without an obvious root word need to be practised.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know the meaning of words encountered in the lesson.
nodes.response: Ensure to gloss the meaning of all vocabulary used in the lesson and say in full sentences to help embed the meaning.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that all verbs ending in 'y' follow the rule remove the 'y' and add -ied.
nodes.response: Look at examples that add -ed and remove the 'y' and add -ied. Focus on the sound the 'y' is making and see if it is part of a digraph.

nodes.misconception: Children may spell words with the suffix -en as they sound with 'in' or 'n'.
nodes.response: Explicitly draw comparisons to how words encountered are spelt and how they sound, particularly when there are differences.

nodes.misconception: Children may think words such as 'feathery' have the -ery suffix.
nodes.response: Reinforce that most words ending in -ery have a root word. Encourage children to spot the root word before the -ery.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be used to the 'ck' representing the 'c' phoneme when at the end of the word.
nodes.response: Explain that in most words where the 'c' is at the end, it is represented as 'ck'. As this is a suffix, it doesn't follow usual rules.

nodes.misconception: Children cannot remember the dictated sentence because it is too abstract.
nodes.response: Give context to the sentence, such as imagine someone is applying to be part of a netball team. This is what the coach asks. Add images.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think 'y' is removed and replaced with an 'i', like with the suffix -ed e.g. carry
nodes.response: Show that we end up with two 'i's in a row if this happens: fly becoming fliing, so we keep the 'y'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the spelling 'ize' to represent the -ise suffix.
nodes.response: Explicitly reference the difference between how the word is spelt and how it is pronounced. In American English, the spelling -ize is used.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to spell the root word or stem.
nodes.response: Ensure to focus on all the difficult elements of the words presented, not only the -ous ending that demonstrates the spelling rule.

nodes.misconception: When adding chords to a bass line, the chord has to be the same as the note in the bass.
nodes.response: In most cases the bass note should be one of the notes in the chord, but doesn't always have to be the lowest note of the chord. For a balanced chord sequence most notes in the bass lines should be the root, but not all have to be.

nodes.misconception: An interval of a 3rd is three tones higher or lower than the first note.
nodes.response: In C major (where pupils are counting the white keys), they should count the starting note and final note, plus any in between. So an interval of a 3rd is actually two tones higher or lower than the first note. An octave would be seven notes higher.

nodes.misconception: Axle holders can be placed at any angle.
nodes.response: Clarify that axles need to be parallel to ensure proper wheel function.

nodes.misconception: Without correct representation, children may struggle to know what to calculate.
nodes.response: If needed, provide support at this stage so that the structure of the mathematics is clear to children.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that adding or subtracting zero gives zero. For example, 6 + 0 = 0 or 4 - 0 = 0
nodes.response: Use manipulatives to help children see that adding or subtracting zero will not change the starting amount. Model this alongside the written equation so that they can see what each part is representing.

nodes.misconception: Children may misrepresent a given problem meaning they are led to calculate the solution incorrectly.
nodes.response: Children may identify the solution quickly when working with smaller numbers, but it is still important they are encouraged to visualise and represent each problem so that they know how to reveal the structure of the maths in more complex problems.

nodes.misconception: Pupils partition one of the addends incorrectly to help them bridge ten.
nodes.response: Pupils use number pairs that total ten to help them partition the addend. They consider what they have to add to make ten.

nodes.misconception: That addition will always make the result bigger.
nodes.response: If pupils are struggling with the concept that adding can make an integer smaller encourage them to use counters and form zero pairs.

nodes.misconception: Not including the bonds at the end of a repeating unit.
nodes.response: The slide deck states the need for open bonds to show how repeating units are bonded to each other.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think like surds need both the radicand and the coefficient to be the same.
nodes.response: Remind them of the distributive law: a(b+c) = ab + ac.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway; using highlighters can help to visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: Rearranging equations means you can just swap where terms are.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that subtraction and division are not commutative so swapping the order will matter.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think expanded noun phrases are full sentences.
nodes.response: Clearly highlight that these groups of words are called phrases. Provide lots of exposure to phrases not sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to think of adjectives to compare two nouns.
nodes.response: Make use of physical objects, images and word banks to support them with generating vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might struggle to identify adjectives within a sentence and confuse them with other words.
nodes.response: They will only be exposed to adjectives that come before nouns initially so that they become confident in identifying and using them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think if they are struggling to achieve the guided training in the app, they have failed and have to stop.
nodes.response: The app is flexible and can be adapted to individual needs and fitness levels. Even though it is set over 9 weeks you can complete it at your own pace and revisit weeks / runs if needed.

nodes.misconception: As long as I say something about the topic, it doesn't matter what tense I use.
nodes.response: You must respond to the bullet point using the correct tense (e.g. past, present, future) to fully address it. Other tenses can add depth, but they don't replace the need to respond directly in the specified tense.

nodes.misconception: [ce], [ci] and [z] always sound like the 'th' in 'think' in Spain, the Canary Islands and Latin America.
nodes.response: [ce], [ci] and [z] sound like the 'th' in 'think' in most of Spain, and 's' in Latin America and the Canary Islands.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any piece of first person writing is internal monologue.
nodes.response: Internal monologue is first person writing that focuses on the inner thoughts of the person.

nodes.misconception: Negative feedback only works to reverse high levels back to normal.
nodes.response: The slide deck has several slides where changes are described as being high and low and there is a CFU question in the final learning cycle that specifically assesses this misconception.

nodes.misconception: Negative feedback only works to reverse high levels back to normal.
nodes.response: The slide deck has several slides where changes are described as being high and low and there is a CFU question in the final learning cycle that specifically assesses this misconception.

nodes.misconception: Rendering is just adding tone.
nodes.response: Rendering should consider tone and depth but also the texture of the material the product is made out of.

nodes.misconception: The fake is too subtle and not performed at a fast enough pace. Pupils make fake too early so it is easy to read.
nodes.response: Use clear and exaggerated movements when faking and shift your weight explosively. Wait until the defender is close before performing your faked movement.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the only way to defend is to mark 1 player on the opposite team.
nodes.response: Sometimes moving as a unit, where you shift together, can prevent any of the attackers from making a break and getting the ball up the court.

nodes.misconception: Pupils wait until their opponent hits the shuttle before starting to initiate movement to retrieve it.
nodes.response: If you wait until you know where the shuttle is going before starting to move, you will often be too late to get to it. Instead, pre-load your legs with a split step to trigger an explosive lunge to reach the shuttle faster.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often place their foot too low on the wall which affects their ability absorb and redirect impact. Pupils sometimes jump straight at the wall.
nodes.response: Pupils should aim to plant their foot around knee/waist height and remind pupils to push off the wall, not into it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the only movement that is important is the movement with the ball.
nodes.response: Movement off the ball is just as important, it helps create space and supports the player in possession.

nodes.misconception: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
nodes.response: Pupils should finish every problem by substituting their solutions back into the original problem. This will help them check their answers but also make them think about whether their solutions are valid in context.

nodes.misconception: E.g 4.5 hours is 4 hours and 50 minutes
nodes.response: Encouraging pupils to use ratio tables to represent proportional relationships using minutes allows them to appreciate the multiplier of 60 when converting hours to minutes, or minutes to seconds

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only one type of diagram/table can be used to solve each probability problem, or be unsure which representation to use when it is not provided to them.
nodes.response: Probability problems can often be modelled using multiple types of representation. The one you choose may depend on the information that you are trying to organise and what you then intend to do with that information.

nodes.misconception: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%
nodes.response: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 30%

nodes.misconception: When questions are in context, the length may be described as the depth or height and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from the area of a cross section multiplied by the height or depth. They may need to evaluate a perpendicular length from other given information, using trigonometry or Pythagoras' theorem.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to describe what has happened to an object to create its image.
nodes.response: There may be multiple transformations or combinations of transformations that map the object to the image.

nodes.misconception: P is a point such that AP : PB is in the ratio of 1 : 3 means that point P is a third of the distance of AB from A.
nodes.response: There are 4 equal parts in total, meaning that point P is a quarter of the distance of AB from A.

nodes.misconception: We are only interested in points that are in the region satisfied by all inequalities.
nodes.response: With practical contexts, such as project management, it is useful to know when one constraint is not being met as it can suggest where additional resources (if available) should be allocated.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may give an angle rather than a bearing.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a bearing is an angle, measured clockwise from North and given as three figures.

nodes.misconception: A graph drawn on axes with no scale shown means nothing is known about the graph.
nodes.response: Understanding the shape of a parabola, cubic curve, and reciprocal graph and then applying key features like positive/negative coefficients and $$y$$-intercepts enables pupils to infer much about the equation without needing actual coordinate values.

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.

nodes.misconception: The intersection of two different graphs on a speed-time graph is the point where the faster particle overtakes the slower moving particle.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that this is a speed-time graph and ask, "How do we find the distance travelled on a speed-time graph?". Then, ask pupils to calculate how far each particle has travelled at the point of intersection.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be confident in knowing whether to apply Pythagoras' theorem or a trigonometric ratio.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to label the diagram with all the information they have and then consider what they can deduce.

nodes.misconception: Truncating the numbers rather than rounding when considering the suitable degree of accuracy.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the numbers are being rounded and therefore the digit in the next decimal place must be considered.

nodes.misconception: Biased samples are always bad.
nodes.response: A biased sample is sometimes useful if the sample is proportional to the population and/or it focuses on a section of the population relevant to the investigation.

nodes.misconception: Using the laws of indices, when dividing by a number with a negative exponent pupils can incorrectly subtract the negative exponent.
nodes.response: When the bases of all the numbers are the same, forming an equation with the exponents can reduce errors.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway, sometimes using highlighters can help visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: Testing is a one-off activity that only happens at the end of designing.
nodes.response: Testing is an iterative process - it happens throughout development. Each round of testing reveals new insights and informs further refinement.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that plastic food packaging only has disadvantages, due to its effects as a pollutant in oceans and land ecosystems.
nodes.response: This lesson explores the advantages of plastic packaging in reducing food waste, alongside the risks it can pose to biodiversity.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not recognise that an adverbial clause is one type of subordinate clause.
nodes.response: "Subordinate clause" is an umbrella term. Any subordinate clause is a group of words that contains a verb and does not make complete sense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not grasp that the different types of subordinate clause are all subordinate clauses.
nodes.response: Reinforce the point that these are sub-types of subordinate clause.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse adverbs with adjectives.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils are exposed to both throughout the lesson so that you can discuss the differences. Only focus on -ly adverbs to begin with.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are unsure about situations when the body works aerobically and when it works anaerobically.
nodes.response: Aerobic exercise requires oxygen from the air we breathe to totally break down glucose to release energy for exercise. This is the most efficient mechanism but requires exercise to be at a low/ moderate intensity, whereas high intensity is anaerobic.

nodes.misconception: Students frequently write in exams that respiration "creates" energy.
nodes.response: This lesson contains checks and practice tasks that address this misconception.

nodes.misconception: Students frequently write in exams that respiration "creates" energy.
nodes.response: This lesson contains checks and practice tasks that address this misconception.

nodes.misconception: Aerobic cellular respiration is a single chemical reaction.
nodes.response: This lesson uses the terms 'chemical process' and 'series of chemical reactions'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think aerobic training is only relevant for endurance athletes like long distance runners.
nodes.response: Aerobic training is useful for any athletes that play sports that last longer than 20 minutes, e.g. rugby, netball football, hockey.

nodes.misconception: The shape of a vehicle has no effect on its speed.
nodes.response: Vehicle shape is considered in order to reduce air resistance (less drag).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise the significant leading role Aethelflaed had during this time.
nodes.response: Aethelflaed was thought to have been a strong, independent and well-educated woman. She had learnt a great deal about military leadership and strategy by watching her father King Alfred.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that it was a combination of factors that led to laying the foundations of England.
nodes.response: Aethelflaed and Edward were able to lay the foundations for England by establishing strongholds to protect their towns and cities, combining their forces and leading campaigns together.

nodes.misconception: The names Aethelflaed and Aethelred are very similar and may be mistaken for the same person.
nodes.response: Highlight that the two names are very similar but that Aethelflaed was the daughter of Alfred the Great and became Lady of Mercia, whereas Aethelred was the king of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia.

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxons only had one king in Britain.
nodes.response: The Anglo-Saxons had different kingdoms in Britain, each with its own king.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all leaders are recorded in history.
nodes.response: Female leaders, like Aethelflaed, are often written out of history as there was prejudice towards women. Despite Aethelflaed's success and the respect she gained, she was likely erased from history so it did not undermine male leaders at the time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that the Viking army was so large it was able to split its forces which led to its success across Britain.
nodes.response: The Viking army was so large, it could split into different sections and fight in different parts of Britain at the same time. The army could also send reinforcements from one section to support another section in need.

nodes.misconception: A response is successful if it includes relevant quotes.
nodes.response: We should aim high in our language analysis. That means going a step further to use the most meaningful evidence as well as looking for patterns in the text that help us gather a collection of evidence.

nodes.misconception: Students may find it difficult to harmonise their perspective choice with appropriate metaphors.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing less effective pairings e.g. a tree would would not perceive people in a city as 'ants' but an airplane might.

nodes.misconception: You use the verb 'être' in French to say your age, as you use the verb 'to be' in English.
nodes.response: In French you 'are' not an age, you 'have' an age. Use the verb 'avoir': j'ai neuf ans.

nodes.misconception: The verb 'tener' has one meaning, 'to have, having'.
nodes.response: The verb 'tener' means 'to have, having' and with certain nouns, it also means 'to be, being'.

nodes.misconception: All acts of aggression involve violence and are the result of anger.
nodes.response: Some aggressive acts are controlled and are used to gain a performance advantage in sport. They are also within the rules of sports such as rugby and the combat sports.

nodes.misconception: Many young batters fail to move their feet when batting, instead they try to contort their bodies to deal with all sorts of line and length deliveries with little success.
nodes.response: Through practice, pupils can learn how to move their feet in response to different pitches of delivery. With short deliveries moving weight on to the back foot and changing foot position allows for pull, hook and cut shots.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that balance is not important for games players and only useful in gymnastics.
nodes.response: Provide examples of when games players would need balance, e.g. a rugby player will need balance when kicking a conversion to provide greater accuracy.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that flexibility is only useful for gymnasts or dancers.
nodes.response: Discuss wider examples such as hurdlers, footballers and swimmers that will also benefit from high levels of flexibility.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that working on our muscles means lifting heavy weights to make them big and bulging.
nodes.response: Healthy muscles don't need to be bulging muscles. They need to stay supple so they work well; they need rest so they don't get injured; they need to be used regularly so they don't become stiff.  This can all be achieved without lifting weights.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that flexibility is only useful for gymnasts or dancers.
nodes.response: Discuss wider examples such as hurdlers, footballers and swimmers that will also benefit from high levels of flexibility.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that being able to sprint fast will always make them successful in a game or activity.
nodes.response: Being agile involves more than running quickly in one direction. Being on the balls of our feet, rotating our hips and using different footwork can help us to move quickly, react appropriately, and change direction so that we are successful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to think of a counter-argument.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think of one strong point. When thinking of a counter-argument, pupils should consider the opposite idea to their point.

nodes.misconception: The factors mentioned in the lesson are the only factors to consider when considering costs/profits of livestock.
nodes.response: There are many more factors to consider. Pupils could research these or brainstorm with a partner. An example could be selling the wool from any sheep owned.

nodes.misconception: Confusing unfamiliar units of measure.
nodes.response: Pupils may benefit from having two lists of metric and imperial measures to reference should they need to.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that agriculture just means growing crops.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the idea that agriculture also includes using land to rear animals, and that this has destroyed more habitat than using land to grow crops.

nodes.misconception: All artificial intelligence systems use machine learning.
nodes.response: No, some AI systems, such as rule-based expert systems or symbolic AI, use predefined logic and heuristics rather than learning from data.

nodes.misconception: AI can think and make decisions like humans.
nodes.response: AI systems have no awareness or emotions and do not think or understand in the way humans do. AI systems process data and follow patterns or rules based on training data.

nodes.misconception: Using AI when designing is cheating.
nodes.response: AI can be used to help inspire us and is used to develop our own ideas. We must just be open and honest in our use of it.

nodes.misconception: A writer's attitude will remain the same throughout a non-fiction text.
nodes.response: If a writer is recounting an experience then their attitude may change from the beginning to the end of their text.

nodes.misconception: Gaseous exchange only involves oxygen.
nodes.response: Gaseous exchange is when oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between the lungs and the blood, and then between the blood and muscle tissues.

nodes.misconception: Air resistance does not exist or it only works vertically.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching including diagrams and examples of air resistance working in all directions.

nodes.misconception: All objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of their size or shape.
nodes.response: Discussion and practical exploration will address this misconception.

nodes.misconception: Akbar is remembered as a strong military leader because he only used violence to expand the Mughal Empire.
nodes.response: Akbar used a variety of methods to expand the Mughal Empire. In some cases, such as to gain control over the Rajput states, diplomacy was more important for expansion under Akbar than violence.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly writing the molecular formula of alcohols.
nodes.response: Help pupils understand the difference between structural formula, e.g C₂H₅OH, and molecular formula, e.g C₂H₆O.

nodes.misconception: Alexandria is a city in Greece.
nodes.response: Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria in Egypt, not on the mainland or any island of Ancient Greece. There is still a city called Alexandria on the original site in Egypt today; some ruins of the ancient city can be visited by tourists.

nodes.misconception: That only Egyptian people who were related by blood to the previous pharaoh could become a pharaoh.
nodes.response: Alexander was an ancient Greek. He was not Egyptian by birth or by blood but the Egyptian people still made him a pharaoh after Alexander drove the Persians out of Egypt.

nodes.misconception: That the Kingdom of Macedon and the modern republic of North Macedonia are the same place.
nodes.response: Although North Macedonia's name stems from Macedon, they are not exactly the same location. Most of North Macedonia was part of Macedon, but Macedon also covered large parts of what is now northern Greece, southern Bulgaria and eastern Albania.

nodes.misconception: When variables are used in diagrams, pupils may be unsure whether it represents a probability, frequency or a particular outcomes.
nodes.response: Variables can be used to represent either of these pieces of information. It can be helpful to start a problem by writing down what the variables represent (e.g. "Let x = the total number of marbles).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write a3 instead of 3a to represent multiplication of a and 3.
nodes.response: Use algebra tiles to show a x 3 gives 3 lots of a. Highlight that conventions make mathematics clearer to read and avoids miscommunication.

nodes.misconception: When $$x : y$$ are in the ratio 1 : 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$
nodes.response: Show that the equation $$x = 2y$$ in a ratio table would mean the multiplier from $$y$$ to $$x$$ would be times by 2, this would mean when $$y=1 x=2$$ which is 2 : 1 not 1 : 2

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the coefficient of b in a-2b is 2 instead of -2 .
nodes.response: Show subtraction as addition of a negative value. This can be done with negative algebra tiles.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors,
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway: using highlighters can help to visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: Algorithmic bias can be completely eliminated.
nodes.response: It is extremely difficult, maybe impossible, for complex algorithms to be completely free from bias.  By aiming to understand sources of bias, actively working to reduce it, and being transparent, algorithmic bias can be reduced as much as possible.

nodes.misconception: 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugé'.
nodes.response: 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugué'. An extra 'u' is added after the 'g' to preserve the hard [g] sound.

nodes.misconception: Students may not be accustomed to forming an opinion on a narrator, typically seeing them as a neutral figure in a story.
nodes.response: First person narrators are often protagonists of their stories and they can retell the events in any way they want to. This allows us to be critical of a narrator.

nodes.misconception: That 'South Africa' refers to the southern half of the continent of Africa.
nodes.response: 'South Africa' is one single African country, which is located in the south of the continent of Africa. The south of africa (the part that sits in the southern hemisphere) covers a much larger area and includes 15 other individual African countries.

nodes.misconception: A non-living thing is something that is dead.
nodes.response: Examples demonstrating that non-living things have never been alive.

nodes.misconception: The shortest alkene is one containing only one carbon atom.
nodes.response: Teach that alkenes contain the C=C bond and therefore the shortest alkene is ethene.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, adjectives go before the noun in French: a grey bike.
nodes.response: Unlike in English, most adjectives go after the noun in French, these are postnominal adjectives: un vélo gris.

nodes.misconception: We use the verb 'je suis' ('I am') with ages in French.
nodes.response: When giving ages in French, we in fact use the verb 'j'ai' ('I have'), e.g. 'j'ai neuf ans' ('I have nine years').

nodes.misconception: [g] and [j] always have the same sound in Spanish, like [b] and [v] do.
nodes.response: [g] sounds different when followed by a, o, u, when it sounds just like g + a, o, u in English.

nodes.misconception: Hindus have cared for the Earth only recently.
nodes.response: Ancient scriptures show that this has always been important to Hindus.

nodes.misconception: Children may not know the meaning of some words reviewed, such a 'precision' or 'beautician'.
nodes.response: Explain the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary by giving a simple definition and applying in the context of a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Muslims might follow rules within Islam without a deeper understanding of God.
nodes.response: Most Muslims follow obligations or rules to bring a sense of submission and harmony with God.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Sunni Muslims do not believe in the justice of Allah (Adalat) because it is not mentioned in the six articles of faith.
nodes.response: Al Adl (the just) is one of the 99 Names of Allah and is important to Sunni Muslims as well as Shia, but it isn't in the six articles of faith and may be seen as part of a believe in Tawhid - the oneness of God.

nodes.misconception: A dominant condition is 'stronger' and that only the strongest characteristic is inherited from one parent.
nodes.response: Two genes are inherited, so both alleles contribute to the genotype. In some cases one is dominant and therefore will always be expressed (through protein structure) in the phenotype, the recessive allele is still present.

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter if you address a stranger in France as 'tu' or as 'vous'.
nodes.response: Using the correct register of address is very important for students. Practising role-plays in both formal and informal settings allows students to understand when to use the appropriate form of 'you'.

nodes.misconception: The imperative can only be used in the 'tu' and 'vous' forms in French, to instruct others to do something.
nodes.response: The imperative can be used in the 'nous' form in French. In this case, the imperative is suggesting what we should do, and is translated as let's in English.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often find it difficult to apply what they have learnt about alloys when asked about an unfamiliar one, or when provided with a table of data.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a range of different examples of alloys. Give them plenty of practice of comparing the properties of the alloy with those of the pure metal.

nodes.misconception: Students might try to draw parallels between Jack and the snake from the Garden of Eden.
nodes.response: Arguably, the temptation is not Jack himself, but the savagery and evil that resides within him. It is the "beast" within him that tempts him to evil.

nodes.misconception: Referring to alternate angles as 'Z' angles because of the arrangement of the lines.
nodes.response: Modelling the justification correctly through every example and using exterior alternate angles to highlight the limitations of 'Z' angles.

nodes.misconception: Renewable energy is always expensive to set up.
nodes.response: Small-scale renewable energy projects such as micro-hydro plants can be fairly cheap and help communities in lower income countries.

nodes.misconception: Students struggle to distinguish between phytoextraction and bioleaching.
nodes.response: Reinforce that the term 'phyto' is a combining form meaning 'plant'.

nodes.misconception: Students struggle to distinguish between phytomining and bioleaching.
nodes.response: Reinforce that the term 'phyto' is a combining form meaning 'plant'.

nodes.misconception: Training at high altitude leads to permanent change in the body to support performance of an endurance athlete.
nodes.response: Adaptations to altitude are lost very quickly when returning to sea level. Therefore, an endurance athlete needs to plan carefully when to access altitude to be at optimal performance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might instinctively believe that midnight is 12 pm. There is often confusion about the use of am and pm with midnight and midday.
nodes.response: Utilise opportunities for quickfire counting outside the Maths lesson, from different starting points. For example, 10 am, 11 am, 12 pm, 1 pm, 2pm, or 9 pm, 10 pm, 11 pm, 12 am. 1 am.

nodes.misconception: Students may overuse exclamation marks because they think it adds sophistication
nodes.response: Show pupils that exclamation marks are best used for dramatic effect

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense in German is only used in writing.
nodes.response: Whilst the imperfect is largely used in writing, modal verbs are also used in speaking, along with verbs like 'war', 'hatte' and 'gab'.

nodes.misconception: Line dancing must use the feet.
nodes.response: Whilst it is typically performed with an emphasis on footwork, this can easily be adapted to use the arms or any other body part. The emphasis is on the use of a repeating pattern, with a change of direction through 90'.

nodes.misconception: All Native American were the same and part of a single society.
nodes.response: There was a wide range of indigenous nations in the Americas, with many differences between their sizes, social structure and cultures.

nodes.misconception: America and Britain won the war by defeating the Nazis in Berlin.
nodes.response: The Soviets had pushed the Nazi army back across eastern Europe; four out of five German soldiers killed in WW2 were killed on the Eastern Front.

nodes.misconception: Ammonia and ammonium are the same thing.
nodes.response: Carefully compare the different chemical formulae, structures, and distinct uses in fertilisers vs. industrial applications. Use visual aids to reinforce these differences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a ‘balanced’ diet should include equal-sized proportions of the different food groups (rather than appropriate amounts of each food group).
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need to eat different amounts of foods and that the Eatwell plate shows us the amounts of each food that we should eat.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only birds lay eggs.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to make it clear that other animals, including amphibians, lay eggs and these can look different to bird eggs.

nodes.misconception: A thesis statement is just a rewording of the essay question.
nodes.response: The essay question is useful in formulating a thesis, however try using key question vocabulary and using it to form your own argument.

nodes.misconception: The characters are referred to as real people. For example "Old Major describes himself as ..."
nodes.response: Think about the purpose of the characters and why Orwell has constructed them the way he has.

nodes.misconception: That context refers just to historical facts.
nodes.response: Think about the 'big ideas' in the text and what has influenced and informed these. This all comes under the umbrella of context.

nodes.misconception: Art is only made from traditional art materials.
nodes.response: Art can be made from almost anything, including plastic waste, as in the case of Mandy Barker.

nodes.misconception: Always use 'werden' and a 2nd verb in the infinitive to express future ideas.
nodes.response: In German future ideas can be expressed by the present tense with a future time phrase. They can also be expressed by 'werden' plus a 2nd verb, or by 'möcht-' to say what you would like to do in the future.

nodes.misconception: Always use 'werden' and a 2nd verb in the infinitive to express future ideas.
nodes.response: In German future ideas can be expressed by the present tense with a future time phrase. They can also be expressed by 'werden' plus a 2nd verb, or by 'möcht-' to say what you would like to do in the future.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle with their release point when bowling underarm which results in an illegal bowling action. Pupils are too slow to throw from backstop to first base when trying to run the batter out.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on a smooth pendulum action when bowling to ensure that the ball is bowled between knee and head height and to the side of the batter. When backstop has the ball, focus on a flat, hard throw to first base to run the batter out.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it challenging to think about how current flows through the connections and around the coil in the motor.
nodes.response: Take pupils step–by–step through the building of a motor from a motor kit and provide an opportunity for pupils to build their own working motor to help them to consolidate their understanding.

nodes.misconception: A magnetic field is the same as the electric field around a charged object.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that an electromagnet does not attract small pieces of tissue paper, as a balloon with a static charge can do.

nodes.misconception: People only come to Eryri National Park in order to climb Wales' highest mountain.
nodes.response: People do come to climb mountains but also enjoy other enjoy outdoor activities and the historical and cultural attractions in North Wales.

nodes.misconception: Weather hazards don't badly affect the UK population .
nodes.response: The UK experiences weather hazards that have serious social, economic and environmental impacts, the Beast from the East killed 10 people and cost the UK £1 billion per day.

nodes.misconception: Glaciated landscapes are only found in polar regions
nodes.response: Glaciated landscapes can be found in many mountainous regions around the world, including Snowdonia in North Wales, not just in polar areas.

nodes.misconception: Sustainable development is all about the environment.
nodes.response: One pillar of sustainable development is the environment but sustainable development is only achieved when social and economic aspects are also considered.

nodes.misconception: The earthquake caused most of the destruction in the 2011 Tohuku disaster.
nodes.response: While the magnitude 9.0 earthquake was powerful, Japan’s strict building regulations meant that most modern buildings withstood the shaking. It was the 10-metre-high tsunami that caused the majory of the destruction.

nodes.misconception: The extreme destruction in Haiti was the result of the earthquake magnitude being unusually powerful.
nodes.response: The earthquake had a magnitude of 7.0, which is not unusually powerful. The high death toll and destruction were due to Haiti’s poor infrastructure, weak building regulations and lack of preparedness, not just the earthquake’s strength.

nodes.misconception: 'Sie' always means 'she'.
nodes.response: 'Sie' can mean 'she', 'they' or 'you (formal)'. Check the verb endings used alongside the pronoun and the spelling of 'sie' to determine the correct translation. Formal 'Sie' is always written with a capital letter.

nodes.misconception: We always use ‘du’ to mean ‘you’ in German.
nodes.response: 'Du' is informal 'you'. You should use 'Sie' (formal 'you') when speaking with adults that you address by surname. Use 'du' with friends, family, other people you know very well and other children.

nodes.misconception: We have to translate the word 'do' into French to ask the question 'do you have?'
nodes.response: There is no word for 'do' in French. We use intonation to change the statement 'you have' into the question 'do you have?'

nodes.misconception: Macbeth is a Jacobean.
nodes.response: 'Macbeth' is set in 11th century Scotland. However, it was first performed in 1606 in front of a Jacobean audience.

nodes.misconception: The Macbeths invite Duncan to their castle so they can kill him.
nodes.response: King Duncan is honouring the Macbeths by staying with them; he is honouring them because of Macbeth's performance in the recent battle.

nodes.misconception: Macbeth actually sees a dagger.
nodes.response: Shakespeare signals the dagger is a hallucination, and that Macbeth is aware it is a hallucination too: 'a dagger of the mind'.

nodes.misconception: Macbeth is solely worried about Banquo and Fleance in this scene.
nodes.response: Macbeth's focus is Banquo and his son, but his language reveals his worries about the regicide, his soul and his immediate future.

nodes.misconception: Macbeth is a tyrannical ruler, and enjoys his tyranny.
nodes.response: Macbeth is a tyrant, but doesn't enjoy his reign. He is also self-aware: "I am in blood Stepp'd so far" or calling the witches "the worst".

nodes.misconception: Malcolm is an immoral person.
nodes.response: Malcolm pretends he is filled with lust and greed, but this is to test Macduff's loyalty.

nodes.misconception: The imaginary blood on Lady Macbeth's hands could symbolise Duncan's blood.
nodes.response: Symbols represent an idea that doesn't have a physical existence. Guilt is not a physical thing so the object, blood, is used.

nodes.misconception: A theme is any moment or idea in a text.
nodes.response: A theme is an idea that is explored in multiple different ways - it has to come up more than once in a text.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the island in the novel is like a tropical paradise.
nodes.response: Draw their attention to the suggestion of danger in the language used.

nodes.misconception: Students may think the boys all feel the same about the killing of Simon.
nodes.response: Focus on words used: Some talk about "murder," some call the killing an "accident" or pretend that they left "early".

nodes.misconception: Students may think that Piggy's death is an accident, similar in kind to Simon's, an example of boys getting carried away.
nodes.response: Draw pupils' attention to the fact that Roger is compared to a hangman. A hangman kills intentionally.

nodes.misconception: Students may see the rescue as wholly positive.
nodes.response: Draw your pupils' attention to the lack of understanding of their ordeal. Also, to the fact rescue comes on a warship and the officer is carrying a revolver.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often judge Piggy by the critical standards employed by the other boys.
nodes.response: Pick out examples of how sensible and intelligent Piggy is and how his judgement is usually sound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the rift in the novel is only between Ralph and Jack.
nodes.response: Draw attention to how the boys are increasingly living separately: Piggy is on his own, the "littluns" are a group by themselves and Simon sneaks away to be alone.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that Golding's reference to a world order in "ruins" refers to the damaged sandcastles and their ruined life on the island.
nodes.response: Remind students of Golding's wartime experiences and the events of WWII.  Golding is referring to the world the boys left behind as well as the world on the island.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that Ralph doesn't blow the conch to summon the boys back because he is afraid of Jack.
nodes.response: Ralph is not afraid of Jack. He is afraid that if he blows the conch and the boys don't return, he will have lost his authority.

nodes.misconception: Students may not understand that Sam and Eric have not actually seen the parachutist.
nodes.response: Unpick the description given by Sam and Eric. Were we (the reader) actually shown the different aspects of the beast?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be puzzled by Ralph's seemingly sudden descent into the violence and savagery that seems to have captured the other boys.
nodes.response: Point out how Jack's more aggressive behaviour appeals to the boys.

nodes.misconception: Students may be confused about what is actually happening in the encounter between the beast and Simon.
nodes.response: Remind them that Simon has a tendency to lose consciousness. They need to be able to interpret this encounter on multiple levels.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think that only Jack's hunters are involved in the killing of Simon.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the one sentence where Golding says that Ralph and Piggy want to be part of the group.

nodes.misconception: That the process of amelioration and pejoration mean a word completely changes its meaning.
nodes.response: Pejoration and amelioration refer to a word becoming more negative/positive and this does not mean the word completely changes its meaning.

nodes.misconception: The play is set over a series of days so Del's character development is rapid.
nodes.response: The stage directions at the beginning of each scene show that sometimes a few days have past, and sometimes much longer.

nodes.misconception: Del is as rude as ever about obeah.
nodes.response: Del is rude in this scene, but she also asks questions and watches Mai's practices.

nodes.misconception: Enid's husband never loved her. They had a terrible relationship.
nodes.response: Whilst there are descriptions of conflict in their relationship, the description of their moving to England shows their initial devotion.

nodes.misconception: Brod's drinking is appropriate and meant to be funny.
nodes.response: Both Enid and Del challenge Brod's drinking, and his scenes expose his unhappiness, isolation and vulnerability.

nodes.misconception: Mai's son emigrated with her.
nodes.response: Mai's son was born in Britain, but his cultural identity is important to him and he doesn't feel at home in Britain.

nodes.misconception: Brod is not religious.
nodes.response: Consider the admiration Brod has for Pastor Chully Johnson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel unprepared for the debate as the tasks leading up to Task C are verbal discussions.
nodes.response: Plan an additional lesson where pupils prepare their speech using the PEPS structure and give them time to rehearse and write down their ideas. Then, conduct the debate in a separate lesson.

nodes.misconception: Texts can only be compared to others from the same time period or literary movement.
nodes.response: In reality, comparing texts across different periods or movements can enrich understanding, as themes, ideas, and literary techniques often transcend time.

nodes.misconception: The play is definitely Brechtian or purely social realism.
nodes.response: The ideas behind Brechtian theatre and social realism were part of the cultural landscape when Priestley was writing. Instead of fitting it into one category, it’s better to consider how Priestley may have been influenced by these forms.

nodes.misconception: Rewording or summarising the main points of a question will lead to a developed response.
nodes.response: A nuanced response goes beyond rewording the question. It requires you to engage deeply with the text, offering detailed analysis and considering multiple layers of meaning.

nodes.misconception: On a network, servers, clients and routers have the same purpose.
nodes.response: Servers, clients and routers have distinct roles and functionalities in a network. They are not interchangeable and serve different purposes.

nodes.misconception: Students panic about unseen activities and think that there is a 'right' or 'wrong' answer.
nodes.response: The text is unseen - students are not supposed to be experts on it. They just need to read the text and give their opinions about it - any well-evidenced opinion is the 'right' answer.

nodes.misconception: Brod is Enid's husband.
nodes.response: Brod is a family friend. Enid's husband is mentioned in the play, but he left her and his two children when they were little.

nodes.misconception: When pupils think about the role of rules in society, they tend to focus on the role of more punitive rules and argue that rules are restrictive.
nodes.response: Try to get pupils to understand the necessity for rules and laws - particularly those that ban harming others. Get students to imagine what life would be like if harming others was not prohibited.

nodes.misconception: 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me' is saying that life isn't scary.
nodes.response: The poem lists many scary and frightening things. It presents some of the world's dangers. The speaker, however, is not frightened of life despite these dangers.

nodes.misconception: A natural hazard is the same thing as a natural disaster.
nodes.response: A natural hazard is a potentially harmful event, a natural disaster is when a natural hazard event significantly affects humans.

nodes.misconception: Slam poetry doesn't have any rules or conventions, so anything goes. It's just speaking to an audience.
nodes.response: While slam poetry encourages creativity and self-expression, it does follow certain conventions, like using sound techniques, imagery and themes. These conventions help poets effectively communicate their messages and engage the audience.

nodes.misconception: The Anthropocene is the period of Earth’s history from when homosapiens first evolved.
nodes.response: The Anthropocene is a proposed geological epoch that marks the period in Earth’s history during which human activity has had a significant impact on Earth.

nodes.misconception: Music from the Romantic period is all about love and romance.
nodes.response: The word Romantic in the musical sense has nothing to do with love or romance, this was just the name given to the period. The music was often intense, emotive and dramatic, and might sometimes link to ideas of love, but it was very varied.

nodes.misconception: Students can often confuse the word summaries for the different types of cellular respiration.
nodes.response: This lesson directly compares the different word summaries for anaerobic cellular respiration to help understand the differences between them.

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that plants don't respire, and that they (only) photosynthesise instead.
nodes.response: This lesson contains examples of plants respiring.

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that plants don't respire, and that they (only) photosynthesise instead.
nodes.response: This lesson contains examples of plants respiring.

nodes.misconception: Learners often assume there is only one type of cellular respiration (aerobic).
nodes.response: This lesson explores aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration in humans.

nodes.misconception: Anaerobic exercise is only useful for improving your ability to run fast.
nodes.response: Anaerobic training can also build muscular strength, power, endurance and improve body composition. All of these can benefit your performance in many different sports not just running.

nodes.misconception: All types of smile indicate happiness in a person.
nodes.response: There are many nuances in smiles, such as a polite smile versus a genuine smile, which can convey different feelings.

nodes.misconception: In nature, patterns are perfectly repeated.
nodes.response: Remind children that in nature, patterns sometimes repeat but the shapes, colours or lines are slightly different.

nodes.misconception: That spotting lots of different features makes a good analysis.
nodes.response: Simply spotting a feature is too superficial. The best analysis will say a lot about little. Being able to develop multiple comments on a single feature, creates a much better more in-depth analysis.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify visual, narrative and contextual elements in Task A.
nodes.response: Task A could be done in pairs or small groups, with adults supporting with modelled examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify visual, narrative and contextual elements in Task A.
nodes.response: Task A could be done in pairs or small groups, with adults supporting with modelled examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find the concept of 'manipulation' difficult to understand.
nodes.response: You could provide pupils with a context that they might understand, for example, imagine a friend doesn't want to take someone else's packed lunch, but you want them to. How could you manipulate them? What could you say to convince them?

nodes.misconception: Students are quick to identify a poem's rhyme scheme, but they often fail to explain its effect or why it has been used.
nodes.response: In this poem, Hardy arguably uses the same rhyme scheme throughout to reflect the inevitability of death and grief as a result of war. The rhyme scheme becomes a pattern in the same way that death and devastation becomes a pattern in war.

nodes.misconception: Students often want to be told the 'right' answer in English and think there is a right answer for every question.
nodes.response: There are no 'right' answers in this lesson - this lesson asks students to consider different possibilities and interpretations and to make up their own minds about the poem.

nodes.misconception: That you don't need to use quotes in your essay.
nodes.response: Quotes act as textual evidence and are needed to write a successful analytical essay.

nodes.misconception: Context is required in every paragraph of a comparative analytical response.
nodes.response: Context is important to include in your response but it isn't necessary in every paragraph. In order to avoid 'bolt-on' context, it should only be used when it is relevant to the point you're making in that paragraph.

nodes.misconception: Adding "bang" or "crash" to the end of a line or stanza is an effective way to use onomatopoeia.
nodes.response: Although onomatopoeia might seem like an easy device to use, it still needs careful consderation and crafting to be used effectively and creatively.

nodes.misconception: All range references in a spreadsheet needs to be the same as cell references in the format of column letter followed by row number (e.g. A1:A4).
nodes.response: If you want to reference the whole column you can remove the row numbers (e.g. A:A). Note that this is the only case where cell references do not have to follow the column:row convention.

nodes.misconception: Planning can often be seen as a waste of time.
nodes.response: You must take time to make notes and gather ideas so the analysis you write is strong.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may wish to directly replicate the language, style and vocabulary used in the poem.
nodes.response: The process of generating vocabulary from another poem is a source of inspiration to expand one's own vocabulary in a meaningful manner.

nodes.misconception: That magic in stories always happens in a make-believe, faraway world.
nodes.response: Magical-realist stories are set in the real world but magic and fantastical events happen.

nodes.misconception: Ambivalence means you do not care either way (similar to indifference).
nodes.response: Ambivalence is when someone has mixed or conflicting feelings about something or someone.

nodes.misconception: The speaker feels as though her cousin Kate has ruined her life completely.
nodes.response: While the speaker does feel that Kate has stolen the life she deserved/desired, she also feels that she can have the 'last laugh' since she has given birth to the nobleman's son.

nodes.misconception: Students may fail to recognise that arguably, this poem is a series of stories instead of one 'big' story.
nodes.response: Dove arguably tells several small stories which all contribute to our understanding of the depth of love between her and her husband - Fred.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise the value of representing data on graphs or charts and might view it as just another task to complete.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources, clearly explain the value of presenting data in a chart or graph and how it makes information easier to understand.

nodes.misconception: Data collected by a data logger can only be used in the data logging software.
nodes.response: You can export the data from the data logging software into a spreadsheet that then allows you to perform lots of operations on the data.

nodes.misconception: The mean and median will always be close to the most frequent values (or peaks) in a dataset.
nodes.response: The mean and median may be at the lower or lowest frequency parts of a distribution. This is especially likely if the data is bimodal.

nodes.misconception: Connotation is the definition of a word.
nodes.response: Connotation is a feeling that a word gives .

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes fail to recognise that the tense shifts as the poem progresses.
nodes.response: Owen includes three tenses in his poem, perhaps to illustrate that the impact of war has, is and will be felt in his past, present and future.

nodes.misconception: You should decide on one main interpretation of text and focus on that in your analytical writing.
nodes.response: Effective analytical writing often includes multiple interpretations of a text and careful consideration of the wider context.

nodes.misconception: That the ending of a text isn't as important as the story itself.
nodes.response: The ending of a text defines the story - it offers resolution or poses questions and can impact the way we see characters and the way we interpret the overall meaning of a story.

nodes.misconception: That the unknown is always scary.
nodes.response: While we typically think of the unknown as something scary and overwhelming, it can also be something exciting and refreshing.

nodes.misconception: Comparative paragraphs should only focus on differences.
nodes.response: The most effective comparisons look for subtle differences within larger similarities.

nodes.misconception: That personal responses involve making guesses about the writer's context and state of mind.
nodes.response: Personal responses consider how and why a poem might create a certain emotion in the reader or what they say about society in general.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify informal language.
nodes.response: Spend some time examining different ways informal language appears in the model diary entry (e.g. exaggeration, contractions, capitalised words, informal vocabulary).

nodes.misconception: Students may think that in the last two lines of the poem, the father now follows behind the son while he is out ploughing a field.
nodes.response: Although their roles have reversed, there is no indication that the last two lines involve the father and son ploughing. The echoes in the language merely symbolise that their roles have reversed as the son has grown up.

nodes.misconception: A geographer has to be good at maths to successfully analyse quantitative data.
nodes.response: Successful analysis in geography means correctly understanding what numerical values mean, not necessarily being able to process and manipulate data.

nodes.misconception: Students recognise that the hawk is powerful and don't explore this any further.
nodes.response: The significant question in the poem is arguably what makes the hawk powerful? Is it nature? Instinct? His physical strength? His intelligence?

nodes.misconception: It's important to include a contextual link in every analytical paragraph.
nodes.response: Although it is important to include links to wider context in your overall response, it isn't necessary to include a contextual link in every analytical paragraph. In fact, 'bolt-on' contextual links should be avoided.

nodes.misconception: Comparative responses are just a list of similarities and differences.
nodes.response: While identifying similarities and differences is essential, your comparative response should also articulate a clear argument that ties these observations together.

nodes.misconception: Analysis should be led by identification of the writer's methods.
nodes.response: Effective comparative analysis should be led by key ideas and then supported by textual evidence and identification of the writer's methods and intentions.

nodes.misconception: Analytical paragraphs should be led by identification of writer's methods.
nodes.response: An effective analytical response avoids 'feature-spotting'. Paragraphs should be led with a comparison of key ideas in each poem, followed by a detailed analysis of how the writers use methods to convey these ideas.

nodes.misconception: Every analysis paragraph should link to the wider context.
nodes.response: Effective analysis links to context only when relevant to the discussion of key ideas/methods and avoids 'bolt-on' sentences.

nodes.misconception: You should ignore any parts of the poem that don't fit with your overall interpretation.
nodes.response: To create a nuanced argument, you want to think about why the poet may have chosen not to present a cohesive whole to the poem.

nodes.misconception: There is only one valid interpretation of a method.
nodes.response: There might be several different ways of interpreting a method.

nodes.misconception: The final word of a poem is an unimportant detail.
nodes.response: The final word of the poem offers us the lasting impression of the poem's message.

nodes.misconception: That material possessions don't matter.
nodes.response: While material possessions can be replaced, nevertheless they do provide a sense of safety and comfort for us.

nodes.misconception: That refugees come from places that have always been war torn and a disaster zone.
nodes.response: Refugees can come from anywhere - places that used to be beautiful but have changed through war, regime change or natural disaster.

nodes.misconception: That men were supposed to be the 'bigger man' and act rationally in the face of a challenge to their honour.
nodes.response: In Elizabethan England, men were expected to defend their honour.

nodes.misconception: That natural imagery is only designed to help paint a picture to the reader.
nodes.response: Natural imagery can also be used to suggest a concept is natural or make a comment about the relationship between humans and nature.

nodes.misconception: The poem 'Island Man' only tells the story of someone that misses the Caribbean.
nodes.response: The poem 'Island Man' can help to tell the story of any migrant who experiences nostalgia for their home country.

nodes.misconception: Some students think that villains are one dimensional.
nodes.response: Villains have their own struggles.

nodes.misconception: You can only compare methods that both writers use when comparing non-fiction texts.
nodes.response: It can be very effective to compare why one writer might choose to use a certain method while another writer may choose not to use it.

nodes.misconception: The speaker of the poem has unrequited romantic feelings for the man and yearns to be with him.
nodes.response: This is only one interpretation of the poem. Alternatively, the reference to "romance" in L.5 could imply that the speaker romanticises the natural world that she is so distanced from in her urban landscape and yearns to return to nature.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Dharker is critical of the structures in the slums.
nodes.response: Though Dharker portrays how dangerous these buildings are, she also shows great admiration of the slum community's resourcefulness in building these structures - she celebrates their fortitude and resilience in the face of adversity.

nodes.misconception: Students fail to recognise that the poem itself is a kind of memorial for the 38th division in the Battle of Mametz Wood.
nodes.response: The poem immortalises the Welsh soldiers in the 38th division, who lay undiscovered for decades, their stories untold. In this sense, the poem itself has become these soldiers' legacy.

nodes.misconception: Students often use context as a 'bolt-on'.
nodes.response: Context is a valuable additional source of evidence for your argument. Context should be relevant, specific and support your argument. It should be 'peppered' throughout your essay and not 'bolted-on' at the end.

nodes.misconception: A poem has to follow a similar rhythm the whole way through.
nodes.response: By creating two different rhythms, we can juxtapose two places.

nodes.misconception: The speaker mourns the growing distance between him and his mother.
nodes.response: This is just one interpretation of the text; we could also infer that the speaker has felt stifled by their mother's involvement in their life until now and yearns for their independence.

nodes.misconception: When describing music, just describing each element is enough.
nodes.response: For some questions, it may be appropriate just to describe each element. However, often we should give a more sophisticated response that links each element to the compositional purpose - why did the composer use that and why is it suitable?

nodes.misconception: You need to include a reference to the wider context in every analytical paragraph.
nodes.response: The best analytical responses only include relevant pieces of context and weave it subtly throughout. It is important to include context in your answer but it isn't necessary to include it in every paragraph.

nodes.misconception: To solve circuit problems you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.

nodes.misconception: To solve circuit problems you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.

nodes.misconception: All of the world is equally interconnected.
nodes.response: Some parts of the world are more interconnected than others. It is influenced by many factors including wealth and size.

nodes.misconception: All throwing events have the same technique.
nodes.response: While there is a common core technique across all throwing events, each event has a unique set of technical elements that range from the grip, stance, release and recovery phases.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often make slow decisions when covering each other due to lack of confidence. They also panic when they are under pressure in a game situation.
nodes.response: Encourage quick and clear communication using captains and coaches to help players make good decisions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not notice the significance of the textile imagery.
nodes.response: The textile imagery was carefully chosen for the poem, Jane Weir would have been very conscious of putting this in as she was a textile designer.

nodes.misconception: You should only analyse one quotation per paragraph.
nodes.response: Analysing multiple quotations, and exploring the connections between them, makes for the most powerful analysis.

nodes.misconception: Students may misconceive what the phrase "my tongue" means initially.
nodes.response: Explain the figurative language involved in the phrase "my tongue" and the link to language.

nodes.misconception: To solve circuits, you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.

nodes.misconception: To solve circuits, you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.

nodes.misconception: Students do not think that they can analyse the poem's title.
nodes.response: In analytical responses, students can absolutely analyse the poem's title!  This can be a great way to start a response or comparison.

nodes.misconception: The extended metaphor of trees and vines represent her absent lover.
nodes.response: The extended metaphor of a tree symbolises her absent lover whereas the extended metaphor of the vines symbolises her fantastical thoughts of her lover while he is away from her.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often fail to notice or appreciate how defiant this poem is at the end.
nodes.response: In saying that she will love her future husband "better" after death, Barrett Browning defies her father and any cosmic force which may try to prevent the couple from being together. Barrett Browning's passion and commitment to Browning is evident.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the vocabulary, particularly in stanza six.
nodes.response: Give explicit definitions for any unfamiliar language, using visuals to support the explanations, to help pupils' understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to understand some of the vocabulary in stanzas one and two.
nodes.response: Reading and listening to unfamiliar vocabulary should not put us off studying poetry or texts that contain it!

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up different poetic devices.
nodes.response: The tasks in learning cycles one and two explicitly model how each poetic device is used in each stanza.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that there is no description in non-fiction texts.
nodes.response: In narrative non-fiction texts authors use literary devices such as imagery, similes and metaphors to enhance a reader's understanding.

nodes.misconception: Students may be confused about when the extract is taking place or what war the extract is about as it references multiple moments of time.
nodes.response: The novel opening takes place during the siege of Sarajevo in the 1990s. However, the reference to the aftermath of WW2 is significant in universalising the themes and messages of the novel.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise the significance of Scrooge's transformation in the ending.
nodes.response: Remind pupils in lots of detail how Scrooge behaved and treated others in Chapter 1. Re-reading Chapter 1 would be helpful.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify informal language.
nodes.response: Spend some time examining different ways informal language appears in the model diary entry (e.g. exaggeration, contractions, capitalised words, informal vocabulary).

nodes.misconception: Children might struggle to understand how the structure can appear different visually.
nodes.response: Differentiate between structure and layout. Journalistic reports should follow the same structure but may be laid out differently.

nodes.misconception: Children might think that an advert is always to sell a product.
nodes.response: Expose children to a variety of adverts that have different purposes, e.g. to change behaviour (environment, diet, health, etc.).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify informal language.
nodes.response: Spend some time examining different ways that informal language appears in the model diary entry (e.g. exaggeration, contractions, capitalised words, informal vocabulary).

nodes.misconception: Children find the difference between an index and a contents page confusing.
nodes.response: Clearly explain the key differences and look at examples of contents and index pages from a range of non-fiction texts to highlight this.

nodes.misconception: That you cannot analyse words in structural analysis.
nodes.response: Analysis of where certain words appear in a poem is a valuable structural analysis.

nodes.misconception: That the persona is the same as the writer.
nodes.response: Emphasise the difference. Draw attention to the different personas in 'The Haunted Palace' and 'The Raven'. Same writer, different personas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that non-chronological reports can be written in an informal way.
nodes.response: Reports should be formal and not use language that is too closely associated with fiction writing.

nodes.misconception: In Task A, pupils might need support in identifying what each still from the animation is showing.
nodes.response: Look at each image and prompt pupils with questions such as 'Who is this character?'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with some of the complex character trait vocabulary.
nodes.response: Use the vocabulary pictures to tell a very short story about how what the character is doing reflects the word - or choose your own images which do this in another way if you prefer.

nodes.misconception: Students think that the entire poem is in rhyming couplets.
nodes.response: Only the beginning of the poem is written in rhyming couplets. The couplets fade to pararhymes and then to non-rhyming couplets by the end of the poem, possibly to reflect the soldier's pain fading and the healing process.

nodes.misconception: The mother feels a loss of her her beauty, confidence and independence after having a child.
nodes.response: It's important to remember that the 'voice' we hear this from is the speaker's (the daughter). In this way, the negative connotations associated with motherhood could be interpreted as the speaker's guilt for taking her mother's freedom.

nodes.misconception: That idyllic settings stay the same forever.
nodes.response: Arguably, Landon's 'Captain Cook (To My Brother)' suggests that an idyllic place does not last forever.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to read a poem aloud.
nodes.response: Reading poetry aloud invites the reader to inject their own emotions, personal interpretation and expression into it.

nodes.misconception: Lines 9-16 of the poem use abstract imagery to convey the moment of the birth in the hospital room.
nodes.response: While this is one way of interpreting these lines, others have argued the abstract images could reflect society's unfair expectations of mothers and the nature of the developing maternal relationship.

nodes.misconception: Sibilance is only used to create a sinister atmosphere.
nodes.response: The repetition of 's' sound could also create a calming, soothing sound.

nodes.misconception: That analysing punctuation isn't an effective way to approaching a poem.
nodes.response: Punctuation can affect a reader's journey through the poem as well as their emotional response.

nodes.misconception: That imagery has one set meaning and connotations.
nodes.response: The connotations of an image can change depending on the language used in relation to it.

nodes.misconception: That there is one accepted interpretation of a poem.
nodes.response: People may interpret and respond to poetry differently because poetry is, at its core, about emotion and we all have different emotion responses to stimuli.

nodes.misconception: The structure of the poem is entirely predictable.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that Blake does break his rigid structure e.g. iambic tetrameter at times.

nodes.misconception: This poem is only about a Romantic view of love (from an abstract, philosophical perspective).
nodes.response: This poem appears to have an ulterior motive. Shelley uses language, form and structure to subtly persuade the listener to enter into a romantic relationship with him.

nodes.misconception: That the Romantics only wrote about nature.
nodes.response: Often Romantic writers also wrote about a nostalgia for the past.

nodes.misconception: The form of poem an author might choose means little to the message
nodes.response: Poets pick their forms carefully, as we can see in 'Ozymandias' even the slight tweaking of form can impact the reading of the poem and its meaning.

nodes.misconception: That the form of a poem doesn't influence our analysis.
