nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens with two spots alongside 2 p coins to start with to deepen the understanding of one coin representing a value of . Discuss deliberate errors, articulating thinking around why these cannot be correct.

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully understand the concept of unitising and may confuse the number of coins with the total value. They may also count sets of coins containing 10 p coins and other coins in tens.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens with ten spots alongside 10 p coins to start with to deepen the understanding of one coin representing a value of 1. Discuss deliberate errors, articulating thinking around why these cannot be correct.

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully understand the concept of unitising and may confuse the number of coins with the total value. They may also count sets of coins containing 5 p coins and other coins in fives.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens with five spots alongside 5 p coins to start with to deepen the understanding of one coin representing a value of . Discuss deliberate errors, articulating thinking around why these cannot be correct.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make connections between division and the value of a part.
nodes.response: Support children to understand and describe what they know from the information given, for example, the whole, the size of a part, or the number of parts. Also, what it is that they are trying to find. Encourage representation as a bar model.

nodes.misconception: Trigonometry always involves rounding.
nodes.response: Try evaluating sin(0) on your calculator. What answer do you get?

nodes.misconception: Trigonometry always involves rounding.
nodes.response: Try evaluating sin(30) on your calculator. What answer do you get?

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that if velocity or speed is increasing, then acceleration must also be increasing. Pupils often don't associate a change in direction at a constant speed with an acceleration.
nodes.response: Before teaching acceleration, consolidate an understanding of the differences between velocity and changes in velocity. Discuss how an object can be accelerating AND travelling at a constant speed (circular motion).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that if velocity or speed is increasing, then acceleration must also be increasing. Pupils often don't associate a change in direction at a constant speed with an acceleration.
nodes.response: Before teaching acceleration, consolidate an understanding of the differences between velocity and changes in velocity. Discuss how an object can be accelerating AND travelling at a constant speed (circular motion).

nodes.misconception: That the sequence $$3n+2$$ starts with 3 and adds 2, or starts with 2 and adds 3.
nodes.response: Calculate the first few terms. Ask, "When $$n = 1$$ what is the term value?" This is the first value for our sequence.

nodes.misconception: "When finding the perimeter of a sector, I need to multiply the radius by a fraction of a full circle, just like I did with the circumference to find the arc length."
nodes.response: Reminder that only part (the arc length) of the formula for perimeter of a sector varies with the angle. A desmos or geogebra model can help to show this.

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease.
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the mass or weight of an object with density.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a range of objects of varying sizes they are going to measure the density of and, before starting to do so, ask the pupils to rank the objects in order of density with explanations. Compare results to the list after measurements.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that energy transfers usually result in the heating of the surroundings and therefore some energy ends up in a thermal store.
nodes.response: Pupils should have opportunity to identify and describe places in a system where energy is dissipated and transferred into a thermal store.

nodes.misconception: Energy can be lost or created in physical processes.
nodes.response: Always discuss how energy is dissipated to the surroundings when discussing energy transformations, even when dealing with ‘ideal situations’ in which there is no dissipation.

nodes.misconception: A pair of coordinates on a s-t graph can be used to calculate the instantaneous speed or velocity at that point, but that only works for a straight line graph through the origin.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to calculate the velocity of a graph that represents a steady velocity on a line that does not go through the origin, and to check to see if dividing the values at any point on the line gives the right value for velocity.

nodes.response: Emphasise the need for pupils to always read the axes of a graph first, before they start to think about any lines drawn on it.

nodes.response: Emphasise the need for pupils to always read the axes of a graph first, before they start to think about any lines drawn on it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse displacement–time graphs with velocity–time graphs.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need for pupils to always read the axes of a graph first, before they start to think about any lines drawn on it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse displacement–time graphs with velocity–time graphs.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need for pupils to always read the axes of a graph first, before they start to think about any lines drawn on it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often consider time in the acceleration equation to be moment in time (perhaps read from a graph) rather than a change in time.
nodes.response: Label the value of t in the acceleration as a change of time rather than just time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often consider time in the acceleration equation to be moment in time (perhaps read from a graph) rather than a change in time.
nodes.response: Label the value of t in the acceleration as a change of time rather than just time.

nodes.misconception: Identifying if integer is a multiple when its given in its prime factor form.
nodes.response: Only the bases need to be considered, not the exponents.  e.g if it is a multiple of 3 it must be a multiple of 3^2, 3^3, etc.

nodes.misconception: Calculating area by counting squares rather than looking at the scales.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that often on speed-time graphs the scales on the axes will be different. Check the scales before calculating distance. Check the final answer is realistic in context.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to think of a different context to apply to finding the perimeter.
nodes.response: An alternative context could be: putting a ribbon around a cake and leaving space for decoration.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to divide by 2 when calculating the area of a trapezium.
nodes.response: The area of a trapezium is half of the area of the parallelogram formed from two identical trapeziums.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to combine lengths that are not parallel to a known side length.
nodes.response: For two sets of side lengths to be equal, one set must be parallel to the other and none of the lengths can overlap.

nodes.misconception: Often, after teaching, pupils often do not understand what specific heat capacity means.
nodes.response: Discuss the size of a substance’s specific heat capacity in terms of how hard it is to heat up a certain mass of the substance and of how much energy needs to be transferred to heat it up.

nodes.misconception: Often, after teaching, pupils often do not understand what specific heat capacity means.
nodes.response: Discuss the size of a substance’s specific heat capacity in terms of how hard it is to heat up a certain mass of the substance and how much energy needs to be transferred to heat it up.

nodes.misconception: "Constant speed" can be interpreted as "moving all the time", and "steady speed" as "not too fast".
nodes.response: Use the terms with care, qualifying them with examples when they are used, e.g. "a constant speed of 4 m/s" or "a steady speed of 100 m/s".

nodes.misconception: That the interval widths need to be constant, or conversely that they can be anything.
nodes.response: If interested in people's ages it may be that decades makes sense once over 30 but that significant ages such as 16, 18 and 21 should form boundaries, depending on context. Encourage critical thinking for data with unequal intervals.

nodes.misconception: You can only find the median class from a stem-and-leaf diagram.
nodes.response: The data is organised into intervals based on place value. However the full data is still available so the middle value(s) can still be found. The diagram is a form of an ordered list so previous methods for finding the median still apply.

nodes.misconception: Using any two side lengths for the sine formula.
nodes.response: It must be two side lengths and the angle between them. So any two side lengths of the triangle can be used so long as you also use the angle between them.

nodes.misconception: When calculating energy in the kinetic store, pupils often work out ½ mv and then square everything, rather than just the speed.
nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how kinetic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how kinetic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how kinetic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.misconception: When calculating energy in the elastic store, pupils often work out (½ times spring constant tmes extension) and then square everything, rather than just the extension.
nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how elastic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how elastic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how kinetic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how elastic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.misconception: When calculating energy in the elastic store, pupils often work out (½ times spring constant tmes extension) and then square everything, rather than just the extension.
nodes.response: Scaffold calculations to show how elastic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that direction matters when determining the distance between two points.
nodes.response: Direction matters when dealing with displacement, not distance.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway, sometimes using highlighters can help visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: That estimation is guessing.
nodes.response: Estimation is a process with each step being logical. In this case the estimation is necessary because some of the detail is lost in a grouped frequency table.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may divide by how many groups/bars there are, instead of the total frequency.
nodes.response: By reminding students frequently that averages need to give a 'typical' value of the data set, ask them to sense check their mean value.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may choose the middle bar on the bar chart or the middle value on the x-axis as their median.
nodes.response: Pull off the data from the bar chart or line graph to show where the median value is.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistakenly choose the bars which have the same heights to be the mode.
nodes.response: By reminding the pupils of the definition of the mode and asking the question in the context of the data, this should support students.

nodes.misconception: Gradient is change in $$y$$ divided by change in $$x$$.
nodes.response: The gradient is calculated by considering the change in $$y$$ when moving one unit in the positive $$x$$ direction.

nodes.misconception: When finding the probability of an outcome based on a frequency table, pupils may use the number of different categories as the denominator rather than the total frequency.
nodes.response: When strawberry flavoured sweets have a frequency of 11, it means that 11 of the sweets in the box are strawberry flavoured. The box of sweets could be visually represented with each sweet being shown by the first letter of its flavour.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that theoretical probabilities can be also found in cases where individual outcomes are not equally likely (e.g. picking a sweet out of a box where the sweets are different shapes).
nodes.response: If the sweets in a box are different shapes then picking a sweet out of the box is not necessarily random. Someone could find their favourite flavour sweet by feeling the different shapes.

nodes.misconception: A probability tree can only have two branches.
nodes.response: A probability tree can have any number of branches on a layer, but the more branches you want to include, the trickier and less practical the probability tree is to draw and use.

nodes.misconception: When I see a probability tree, I always multiply the probabilities.
nodes.response: If a probability tree shows a two-stage trial, then the probability of an outcome is the product of the probabilities of the outcomes at each stage. The probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of each outcome in the event.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with finding the probability of A or B, and may count the outcomes that belong to A and B twice.
nodes.response: If you use an example, such as visiting particular countries, ask the pupils how someone would respond to the question 'have you visited X or Y' if they have in fact visited both countries.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may count the number of outcomes and state this as the probability.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the probability scale is between 0 and 1, so an answer of 3 is not correct.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with finding the probability of A or B, and may count the outcomes that belong to A and B twice.
nodes.response: If you use an example, such as visiting particular countries, ask the pupils how someone would respond to the question 'have you visited X or Y' if they have in fact visited both countries.

nodes.misconception: Understanding electrical circuits is about memorising equations and procedures.
nodes.response: Give pupils the opportunity to discuss what happens in a circuit before they attempt to answer questions about it.

nodes.misconception: Understanding electrical circuits is about memorising equations and procedures.
nodes.response: Give pupils the opportunity to discuss what happens in a circuit before they attempt to answer questions about it.

nodes.misconception: Any sound that is digitised is going to be noticeably different to the original sound.
nodes.response: When sound is turned into digital form with a high enough sampling rate and sample resolution, the difference from the original sound is too small for human ears to notice.

nodes.misconception: Any sound that is digitised is going to be noticeably different to the original sound.
nodes.response: When sound is turned into digital form with a high enough sampling rate and sample bit depth, the difference from the original sound is too small for human ears to notice.

nodes.misconception: That an argument needs to present a balanced viewpoint for both sides of the argument.
nodes.response: An argument needs to give your reasons behind your answer to the question.

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is difficult and only professional musicians can do it well.
nodes.response: Improvisation is about exploring new musical ideas. Even young pupils can improvise in a fun and playful way using familiar material as a starting point.

nodes.misconception: Echo and call and response are the same thing.
nodes.response: An echo is an exact match of a phrase. A call and response is a question and answer structure in which the response can be different from the call.

nodes.misconception: Sea shanties were only sung on-board ships.
nodes.response: This unit features working songs of the sea that were sung on different types of boats, not just ships. For example, Tongo is a canoe song. It was sung to keep fisherfolk in time as they rowed in their canoes along rivers.

nodes.misconception: Calligraphy is just pretty writing.
nodes.response: Calligraphy is an art form that communicates meaning.

nodes.misconception: Most campaigners for reform like the BPU wanted all adults in Britain to be enfranchised.
nodes.response: The BPU campaigned for tax-paying males to be enfranchised, which would have continued to exclude many poor workers as well as women.

nodes.misconception: Calypso, mento and soca are different versions of the same musical style.
nodes.response: Although they have superficial similarities, these are all distinct styles with different features and histories. Soca is strongly linked to calypso and can be seen as an offshoot of that style, but mento is a completely separate tradition.

nodes.misconception: Laser cutters burn or melt the materials they are cutting.
nodes.response: Laser cutters actually vaporise the material with high precision.

nodes.misconception: All cams create the same movement.
nodes.response: The size, shape and position of a cam will create different types of movement.

nodes.misconception: The suffrage movement always involved violent or illegal tactics as well as peaceful and legal ones.
nodes.response: The early suffragist movement was committed to peaceful tactics, even among the so-called 'radical suffragists'.

nodes.misconception: The larger the diameter of a pulley wheel, the higher the output speed.
nodes.response: The smaller the pulley wheel, the quicker it will complete a rotation, therefore increasing the output speed.

nodes.misconception: All automata create the same up and down linear output.
nodes.response: The position of the follower and the size, shape and number of cams can create a range of movements.

nodes.misconception: Diversity and unity are opposing ideas and cannot coexist.
nodes.response: A diverse society can be united through shared values, inclusion, and respect, which help build strong, cohesive communities.

nodes.misconception: The infinitive comes directly after the form of 'können', as in English: 'I can play guitar'.
nodes.response: The infinitive comes at the end of the sentence in German when used with a modal verb such as 'können', as in 'Ich kann Gitarre spielen'.

nodes.misconception: Always use the word 'nicht' to negate a statement.
nodes.response: Use the correct form of 'kein' to translate 'not a/any' with nouns. Use 'nicht' with verbs and adjectives.

nodes.misconception: Citizens have no power to influence the law in the UK.
nodes.response: Citizens in the UK do have the power to influence the law. They can use methods like online petitions, surveys, lobbying politicians and working with the media or charities to bring attention to issues and encourage lawmakers to make changes.

nodes.misconception: Select committees are just for criticising the Government.
nodes.response: Select committees gather evidence and make recommendations to improve decision-making.

nodes.misconception: Identity is fixed and based only on things like nationality or ethnicity.
nodes.response: Identity is complex and fluid, made up of many parts including culture, experiences and beliefs, and can change over time.

nodes.misconception: Social media is just for fun and entertainment.
nodes.response: Social media is also used for serious things like political campaigns, protests, and sharing important issues.

nodes.misconception: All governments charge their citizens Income Tax.
nodes.response: There are many countries that do not pay Income Tax at all; their governments get their income elsewhere like from VAT or natural resources.

nodes.misconception: Digital democracy means it is easier for everyone to get involved.
nodes.response: Digital democracy can help reduce barriers. However, not everyone has equal access to technology or the internet. Some people may struggle with digital skills or lack internet access, creating barriers to participation.

nodes.misconception: I use 'à' for 'to' with cities and 'en' for countries.
nodes.response: We use 'en' to say 'to' for feminine countries e.g. Je vais en France. If a country is masculine however we use 'au' e.g. Je vais au Portugal.

nodes.misconception: Directions in French use lower case letters like in English.
nodes.response: Directions in French use capital letters: 'le Nord, l'Est, le Sud et l'Ouest'.

nodes.misconception: Just add 'ne ... jamais' around the verb to say 'never'; the rest of the sentence stays the same.
nodes.response: Add 'ne ... jamais' around the conjugated verb, but in addition, change any indefinite/partitive articles to de/d' after a negative.

nodes.misconception: Conjugate 'mettre' and 'remettre' exactly like 'entendre'.
nodes.response: 'Mettre' and 'remettre' do take the same verb endings as 'entendre'; however, they also drop a 't' in the singular present tense forms.

nodes.misconception: There is nothing a person can do to decreases their risk of getting cancer.
nodes.response: Although we can't change inherited genetic risk factors for cancer, it does also have many associated lifestyle risk factors such as obesity and smoking.

nodes.misconception: Candomblé always embraces Catholic elements.
nodes.response: Candomblé is an ancient African faith shaped by enslavement. While some include Catholic elements for tradition or protection, many focus purely on African roots. It’s a living, evolving religion adapting to each generation’s needs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that moving in canon means one person moves, then there is a pause before the next person moves, so the sequence becomes disjointed.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we need to ensure that one pupil is always moving or balancing to ensure the sequence flows.

nodes.misconception: Getting the correct position and angle for the diagonal lines on the letters A and K can be challenging at first.
nodes.response: Give the children extra tracing opportunities for these letters to support their spatial awareness.

nodes.misconception: The height of the vertical line is sometimes too short or too tall.
nodes.response: Emphasise starting the vertical line on the ascender line and finishing on the baseline.

nodes.misconception: Children may revert to forming the letters between the baseline and the x-height line.
nodes.response: This is a good opportunity to show the children how supportive the tramlines are. Remind them to ensure all of their capital letters are sitting on the baseline, reaching up to the ascender line and are straight.

nodes.misconception: The formation of the Y and the Z can be challenging for children at first, particularly finding the correct position for the diagonal lines and forming the zig-zag.
nodes.response: Giving the children lots of opportunities to trace these letters will help them to become familiar with the formation and the sizing.

nodes.misconception: In Capoeira you use pre-recorded music.
nodes.response: In Capoeira the music is played live and the tempo and style of the music dictates the style of the game that will be played.

nodes.misconception: Capoeira is based on fighting.
nodes.response: Capoeira is based on challenging your opponent, but in a game-like scenario. This is why performers are called 'players'.

nodes.misconception: Medals were only awarded to leaders who fought in WWI.
nodes.response: Medals were awarded for acts of bravery across all ranks of soldiers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to rearrange the equivalent fractions.
nodes.response: A ratio table may be easier for pupils to use instead.

nodes.misconception: All players are desperate to get the opposition's treasure so they have a high risk of getting caught and neglecting the protection of their own treasure.
nodes.response: Let pupils do it however they like first but then give time to regroup and plan a smarter team strategy.

nodes.misconception: Data capture forms are only electronic.
nodes.response: A data capture form can be designed and used on paper and data can be collected in person.

nodes.misconception: Eco-anxiety can be caused by news coverage of rising greenhouse gases and global temperatures, and pupils may feel like little is being done to prevent this.
nodes.response: Use the slides to look at the many ways that scientists and engineers are working to create new technologies to capture, remove and reduce the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

nodes.misconception: Plants can absorb all of the carbon dioxide that human activity adds to the atmosphere.
nodes.response: Talk to the pupils about what happens to the carbon dioxide absorbed by plants so that they understand how the size and number of plants determine the maximum amount of carbon dioxide they can store.

nodes.misconception: Children may have heard about the ozone layer and think this is the main cause of climate change.
nodes.response: Whilst ozone depletion and climate change are linked, it is not a major cause of climate change.

nodes.misconception: Confusing the concentration and strength of acids.
nodes.response: Clearly define a strong and weak acid.

nodes.misconception: Glue is the only way to join card sections.
nodes.response: Pupils might think that glue is the only joining technique. This lesson will explore other methods.

nodes.misconception: Packaging has always been the same.
nodes.response: Packaging has developed over time. The rise in plastic use has seen plastic replacing glass, increased use of recycled paper/card, less use of wooden crates used in the past.

nodes.misconception: A lever is just a seesaw mechanism and only moves up and down.
nodes.response: Levers move up and down and the end of the lever moves in a curved direction. Levers can be turned for different effects.

nodes.misconception: Card and paper are the same.
nodes.response: Card is thicker and more durable than paper. Explain the differences in characteristics and uses.

nodes.misconception: Slider mechanisms have a pivot points.
nodes.response: Slider mechanisms do not have pivot points and therefore do not use split pins. Slider mechanisms use a guide and a slot. They move in a straight line, rather than turning or pivoting.

nodes.misconception: Cardboard is a weak material that is not suitable for modeling.
nodes.response: Cardboard has a fluted layer that increases its strength and rigidity. Modelling techniques, such as layering, can be used to increase its strength further, making it a versatile and very good material to model with.

nodes.misconception: That commuters all drive cars to work.
nodes.response: Many people do drive their car to work, but commuters are all the people that travel to a place for work using any mode of transport.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all parks have playgrounds and play equipment like swings and climbing frames.
nodes.response: Some parks do have places to play, but not all of them. Parks are natural open spaces often with grass or woodlands that we can enjoy.

nodes.misconception: That taking journeys is only about getting from one place to another in an efficient way.
nodes.response: Travelling between locations may be about getting there quickly for commuters, but journeys can also be taken in free time for pleasure. For example, taking long walks in natural places, or bike rides in the countryside are very enjoyable journeys.

nodes.misconception: The heart does not have its own blood vessels. Students often believe the heart gets oxygen and glucose from the blood circulating through it.
nodes.response: The heart has its own blood supply through the coronary arteries.

nodes.misconception: Speed is just about running fast.
nodes.response: An example of speed is moving quickly across the ground but also includes other body parts too such as the speed of arms in table tennis.

nodes.misconception: Speed is just about running fast.
nodes.response: An example of speed is moving quickly across the ground but also includes other body parts too such as speed of arms in table tennis.

nodes.misconception: Speed is just about running fast.
nodes.response: An example of speed is moving quickly across the ground but also includes other body parts too, such as, the speed of arms in table tennis.

nodes.misconception: Rest is not good for the body as it is the opposite of being active.
nodes.response: Rest is really important to help the body recover, grow, repair and get stronger.  However too much time not moving can cause the body to reduce fitness and strength.

nodes.misconception: Cybersecurity jobs are only for highly technical people who know how to code or hack.
nodes.response: Cybersecurity careers are diverse, and many roles value communication, analytical thinking, problem solving and ethical judgment just as much as technical skills.

nodes.misconception: There is only one correct solution to a problem when programming.
nodes.response: There are lots of different approaches to solving a problem in programming. Some solutions can work better than others but the first stage in getting a solution is ensuring that it provides the expected outputs that are required.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals are classified according to their habitat, for example aquatic animals, or by their method of movement, for example creeping animals.
nodes.response: Explain that Aristotle classified animals into water, air and land groups, but there are problems with this method, e.g. this would put birds, bees and bats in the same group. Use the examples in the lesson to make clear the correct groupings.

nodes.misconception: There is one way to ask 'how many' like in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the words for 'how many' agree with the gender of the noun.

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that all animals' teeth are the same. They may also think that all herbivores only have molars, and all carnivores only have canines and incisors.
nodes.response: By showing images of the teeth of carnivores and herbivores, children will see how animals have different types of teeth, depending on their diet.

nodes.misconception: Formulas can only be used on cells within one worksheet in a spreadsheet.
nodes.response: Formulas can work across multiple worksheets in a spreadsheet.

nodes.misconception: It is better to check that hyperlinks work each time you add a link instead of checking them at the end.
nodes.response: You should check the hyperlinks as you go to fix errors immediately but also check the whole product is working once you have finished. This will ensure that the product meets the brief and works in its entirety.

nodes.misconception: Christian Aid only helps Christians.
nodes.response: Christian Aid helps people of all faiths. For example, during the Rohingya crisis, it provided aid to Muslim refugees, offering food, shelter and support.

nodes.misconception: That AI is soleley used to create and spread disinformation, often via deepfakes.
nodes.response: AI can also be used to identify and delete disinfomation.

nodes.misconception: Christians should always obey the law
nodes.response: While Christians are generally taught to respect the law, many also believe they must put God’s will first. Some believe that when laws are unjust or cause harm, faith may require civil disobedience

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, adjectives always end in -o.
nodes.response: In Spanish, adjectives must agree with the noun they describe in gender and number. If the noun is feminine, the adjective will end in -a, but if it is masculine, it will end in -o. If the adjective already ends in -e, it will stay the same.

nodes.misconception: Catalysts increase the amount of product formed.
nodes.response: Catalysts do not affect the quantity of products formed. They increase the rate at which the products are formed.

nodes.misconception: The catalyst is one of the reactants and gets used up during the reaction.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the chemical reaction will take place without the catalyst but at a very slow rate.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often throw with a stiff arm and do not step into their pass with the opposite foot, resulting in inaccurate and unbalanced throws.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils can throw with the correct technique from a static position before adding any movement.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the mathematical conventions for rounding should apply.
nodes.response: This is rounding in a practical context and pupils should consider what the effects of rounding up and down are and how they affect the answer.

nodes.misconception: All wildfires in the taiga are harmful and should be prevented.
nodes.response: Some wildfires are natural and necessary for ecosystem renewal, as they clear old vegetation and help new trees grow. However, climate change has made fires more intense and frequent.

nodes.misconception: Climate change is entirely caused by humans.
nodes.response: Students will recognise that our climate changes naturally and there are physical causes of this. Humans have intensified the process in recent years.

nodes.misconception: The changes in the UK economy affected all regions equally and at the same time.
nodes.response: Some areas, such as the north east, continued to rely on traditional industries until the 1980s and 1990s. Other areas, like London, moved into tertiary industries long before others.

nodes.misconception: That the physical environment is the key cause of global inequalities.
nodes.response: Physical geography is a cause of inequality but human factors, past and present, are as influential in affecting the pattern of trade and development.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that as the focus of the lesson is about migration, that inflows and outflows are responsible for all population change.
nodes.response: Migration is important to understand when addressing population change but changes to birth and death rates must also be considered alongside for complete understanding.

nodes.misconception: There was only significant tension between members of the Grand Alliance at the Potsdam Conference when the war had ended and Roosevelt had been replaced by Truman as US President.
nodes.response: Although tensions increased significantly by the Potsdam Conference, there was a high level of mistrust between the members of the Grand Alliance from early on. This is illustrated by Stalin's concern about the delays in opening a second front.

nodes.misconception: Only the present tense is required when performing the photo description task.
nodes.response: The present tense will mostly be used to describe a photo; however, other tenses are required for the follow-up questions based on the topic of the photo. Students should be able to use future and conditional verbs to discuss future plans.

nodes.misconception: The subject pronoun 'il' always means 'he'.
nodes.response: There are a number of impersonal verbs such as 'il faut', 'il neige' and 'il pleut'. Verbs such as 'il fait' and 'il est' can also be used in an impersonal sense. In these cases, the English meaning is 'it' or impersonal 'you', 'we' as appropriate.

nodes.misconception: Cecil Rhodes was Prime Minister of South Africa.
nodes.response: Cecil Rhodes was Prime Minister of the Cape Colony - the British colony in the region of southern Africa.

nodes.misconception: All Christians celebrate Christmas on the 25th of December.
nodes.response: Some Christians, such as many Eastern Orthodox Christians, celebrate Christmas on the 7th of January.

nodes.misconception: Christians only go to church on Easter Sunday to mark Easter.
nodes.response: Some Churches will hold services throughout Holy Week and Christians may go to a number of services.

nodes.misconception: Only men take part in the Seder and that women don’t have a role.
nodes.response: Women are an important part of the Seder. Some families even change the Seder to include stories and voices of women, so everyone feels included.

nodes.misconception: No one celebrates Winter Solstice anymore.
nodes.response: Pagans today still celebrate Winter Solstice.

nodes.misconception: Changing dynamics when we sing is mainly so the listener hears a variety.
nodes.response: Whilst a range of dynamics keep a song or piece of music interesting, the benefits of changing dynamics can invoke an emotional response in both the listener and the singer.

nodes.misconception: When I am forming information questions with 'est-ce que' I put the question word after it.
nodes.response: When forming information questions with 'est-ce que', the question word must come before it, e.g example: 'Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire demain ?' 'What are you going to do tomorrow?'.

nodes.misconception: Combination numbers in French are written like this: 'dix sept', 'vingt deux'.
nodes.response: French numbers which are made up of a combination of more than one number must be hyphenated, e.g. 'dix-sept' (17), 'vingt-deux' (22), and 'trente-et-un' (31).

nodes.misconception: Wesak only celebrates the birth of the Buddha.
nodes.response: Wesak also commemorates the Buddha's enlightenment and final attainment of Nirvana (Nibbana).

nodes.misconception: All -re and -ir verbs follow the same pattern.
nodes.response: There are different groups of -ir and -re verbs that follow slightly different patterns. It's good to revisit these regularly in their own right and because they can help with other tenses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all animals and plant are multicellular and that all unicellular organisms are bacteria.
nodes.response: Lesson explicitly addresses this misconception and the questions in Task A are designed to expose the misconception.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that only animals respire, and that plants only photosynthesise (and do not respire).
nodes.response: This lesson uses examples of plants respiring in order to address this misconception.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all of our knowledge of the Iron Age is definitely correct.
nodes.response: Explain that archaeologists use artefacts to learn about the past, they get ideas and clues from the artefacts and build up a picture of what they think the past was like. There is very little written evidence about the Celts.

nodes.misconception: Religious freedom means Christians never face challenges or restrictions today.
nodes.response: Religious freedom is protected by law in the UK, but in the worldwide community and the UK Christians can still face censorship, legal cases, or public pressure.

nodes.misconception: A good cake-inspired sculpture must look realistic.
nodes.response: Cake-inspired sculptures can be creative, experiment with textures, colours and other ideas, not just realistic depictions. Great art can be a combination of interpretation and imagination.

nodes.misconception: The Buddhist belief in rebirth teaches that after death, a persons 'soul' is reborn in to another living being.
nodes.response: The Buddha taught that nothing is permenent, everything changes (anicca) and there is no fixed self or soul (anatta). Rebirth may be described as a person's ‘energy’ being reborn, rather than a fixed soul.

nodes.misconception: The only way to form the singular of a feminine noun is to add -e. The only way to form the plural of a noun is to add -s.
nodes.response: There are 4 ways to form feminine nouns which need careful practice. Similarly, there is more than one way to form plural nouns depending upon the final letter of the singular noun.

nodes.misconception: In French the idea of 'best' and 'worst' is translated as 'plus bon' or 'plus mauvais'.
nodes.response: Just as in English, the French for 'best' and 'worst' are irregular adjectives and need to be learned carefully to avoid misunderstanding.

nodes.misconception: In French, the stress is placed on the first syllable of a word, like in English.
nodes.response: In French, the stress is ususally placed on the final syllable of a word, although stress is not as strong in French as it is in English.

nodes.misconception: Marbling was invented in Britain.
nodes.response: Art historians are not exactly sure where marbling was invented, but it was certainly popular in places such as Japan a long time before it was brought to Britain.

nodes.misconception: Most air pollution in Jakarta comes from industries.
nodes.response: While factories contribute, the main source of air pollution in Jakarta is traffic, particularly from motorbikes and older diesel vehicles.

nodes.misconception: Most homes in Jakarta have piped water and are connected to city sewage infrastructure.
nodes.response: Only 65% of Jakarta has piped water. In kampungs, many homes lack running water and toilets, relying on public wells and pumps and shared toilet facilities, which can spread disease.

nodes.misconception: As a global megacity in an NEE, Jakarta is too developed to have serious problems with providing clean water and sanitation.
nodes.response: Despite being a global megacity, large parts of Jakarta (especially kampungs) lack piped water and sewage systems. Many people rely on groundwater, and open drains are still common in some areas.

nodes.misconception: All people in Jakarta have equal access to safe housing with running water.
nodes.response: Not all people in Jakarta have equal access to safe housing with running water. Poorer communities, especially in informal settlements, often lack basic services, while wealthier areas have more reliable infrastructure.

nodes.misconception: Most people in Jakarta can easily access good healthcare and education, no matter what income level they have.
nodes.response: In poorer parts of Jakarta, schools often lack teachers, books, and resources. Although Jakarta has about 1 doctor for every 350 people, hospitals are still overcrowded, and poor families struggle to get care.

nodes.misconception: Greenfield sites are quicker and cheaper to develop as they have not been built on before.
nodes.response: Greenfield sites may take longer to develop and be more costly as everything has to be built from scratch including raod networks.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can make sweeping statements about people that live in places.
nodes.response: It is important that data is used as an average and not the characteristics of every individual. The word stereotype is useful to use in this instance.

nodes.misconception: Inequality is just about the difference in how much money people have.
nodes.response: There are many different inequalities between people’s lives such as access to education and health care, quality of housing, job opportunities and how people are treated.

nodes.misconception: Inequality is just about the difference in how much money people have.
nodes.response: There are many different inequalities between people’s lives such as access to education and health care, quality of housing, job opportunities and how people are treated.

nodes.misconception: Services grow at the same pace as population in cities.
nodes.response: When the population of a city grows rapidly, often the growth of services is slower. In the twenty-first century this is particularly the case in rapidly developing countries, where lots of people arrive into cities each year.

nodes.misconception: The rank on the Index of Multiple Deprivation tells you everything about the deprivation of an area.
nodes.response: The Index of Multiple Deprivation is calculated by combining seven indicators. The overall rank is therefore an average and can mask significant variation in different aspects of deprivation.

nodes.misconception: The successor states completely ignored the Mughal Emperor's authority.
nodes.response: Successor states took a lot of power for themselves but still claimed to be loyal to the Mughals.

nodes.misconception: The verbs 'traduire', 'conduire', 'interdire' and 'dire' follow exactly the same pattern as 'lire' in the present tense.
nodes.response: The verbs 'traduire', 'conduire', 'interdire' and 'dire' follow exactly the same pattern as 'lire' in the present tense with one important exception. The 2nd person plural form of 'dire' is 'dites'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils give up when training gets tough rather than pushing themselves closer to exhaustion.
nodes.response: To get a fitness benefit, it is essential to work your body harder than it is used to and hence a little discomfort is necessary to improve. This is often referred to as no pain, no gain.

nodes.misconception: It can be difficult for young learners to grasp how long 3000 years actually is and therefore appreciate just how long standing and important the Ancient Egyptian civilisation was.
nodes.response: Draw a timeline with 1AD in the middle, 2086 BCE on the left end and 2024 on the right end. Use this to demonstrate that the Ancient Egyptians existed for even longer than the time that has passed since 1 AD to today.

nodes.misconception: That the Normans destroyed all Anglo-Saxon government.
nodes.response: Anglo-Saxon government systems were sophisticated, perhaps more developed than Normandy’s. The Normans retained and built on the existing Anglo-Saxon governmental institutions.

nodes.misconception: Children need to understand that evidence can become dated - especially mapping and media evidence.
nodes.response: You could present some media reports of an issue which has been resolved (e.g. a new road crossing).

nodes.misconception: Coastal management always positively impacts coastlines.
nodes.response: Coastal management can sometimes harm coastlines by causing erosion in nearby areas. For example, building groynes may protect one section but increase erosion further down the coast.

nodes.misconception: Some children might assume any photograph in black and white is from a very long time ago.
nodes.response: Show children a black and white photo of their local settlement today.

nodes.misconception: All added calcium hydroxide dissolves completely, and the pH readings are accurate without consistent mixing.
nodes.response: Calcium hydroxide has low solubility in water, so not all of it dissolves readily. Consistent mixing ensures uniform pH readings. Without proper mixing, pH readings can be inaccurate, leading to incorrect conclusions about the neutralisation point.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that everyone goes through, or should go through puberty, at the same time.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that everybody is different and will go through puberty at different times.

nodes.misconception: That certain jobs are for men only or women only.
nodes.response: Just like during the war, anyone should be able to and can do any job.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that height is dependent on age, so taller adults must be older than shorter ones.
nodes.response: Explain that by the time humans reach adulthood they have stopped growing. At this point, their height is not related to their age. Use examples of familiar adults such as staff members to make this clear.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all offspring resemble their parents.
nodes.response: Show examples of offspring that resemble their parents and of those who do not.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they grow on their birthday, rather than growth being gradual and continuous.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain to children that during childhood they are slowly and continuously changing and growing.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not recognise the floor as a piece of apparatus.
nodes.response: The floor is a very demanding piece of apparatus because many different skills are required such as leaps, spins, splits, dance and acrobatics. In rhythmic gymnastics, additional apparatus is also used such as clubs, ribbons, hoops and balls.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might suggest that rolling or cartwheeling is a turn to change direction.
nodes.response: Although a body rotates during a roll or cartwheel, it moves along one course, facing the same direction at the start and finish. This lesson focusses on changing the course that we are moving along which is achieved through turns and spins.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the words and pictures in a food chain represent an individual plant or animal rather than populations of living things within a habitat.
nodes.response: It is made explicit within the examples in this lesson that each living thing named in a food chain represents a population of that type, or species, of plant or animal within a habitat.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the baby grows inside its mother's stomach.
nodes.response: Using the resources, explain that babies develop in an organ called a womb.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that having the most skillful gymnasts in their group will make it easier to create a group sequence.
nodes.response: Creating sequences in groups needs lots of different skills which are just as important as physical skills. Groups will need to make thoughtful decisions, will need to rehearse responsibly and will need to work cooperatively.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may suggest jumping to mount and dismount apparatus as a change in level during their sequence.
nodes.response: This lesson guide focuses on a change in level in relation to the surface of the apparatus i.e closer or further away. For example, from stomach, push into a plank. Jumping off changes levels in relation to the ground which is not the intended focus.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that performing with flow means performing with speed.
nodes.response: Sequences need control and smoothly linked movements. This creates a steady pace that feels fluid and not rushed. Balances create stillness and are held for a least 4 seconds; flow can still be achieved even with still moments and steady movements.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all elders are like their grandparents or other older people they know, whether they are fit and active or more frail and sedentary.
nodes.response: Using the resources to support, explain that all humans are different and so there'll be differences in how they age. Also make it clear that old age can span up to 40 years so there'll be differences between someone who is 65 and someone who is 95.

nodes.misconception: River valleys remain V-shaped from source to mouth.
nodes.response: A river valley changes from a V-shape to a U-shape as they flow towards the mouth due to processes like lateral erosion and deposition.

nodes.misconception: Changes that affect ecosystems are always created by people.
nodes.response: Naturally-occurring events such as storms also affect ecosystems. For example, a storm could fell trees which may have been a habitat for other species.

nodes.misconception: Limited understanding of the difference between unprocessed and processed or ultra-processed foods.
nodes.response: Sort some different foods into categories according to their level of processing.

nodes.misconception: The quality of life of people around the world is getting worse.
nodes.response: In most places around the world, social indicators such as life expectancy and the average expected years of schooling, have increased.

nodes.misconception: Pressure is a weight or a force; pressure has a preferred downwards direction in a liquid or gas.
nodes.response: Use the particle model to provide opportunities for pupils to explain the causes of pressure in a gas that is in a container, and to explain how the difference in pressure between inside and outside causes an outward force.

nodes.misconception: Evaporation only occurs above the boiling point of a substance.
nodes.response: Give examples of substances other than water.

nodes.misconception: Averages (mean, median, mode) will always change if a data point needs to be added, removed, edited.
nodes.response: The mean, median, or mode will remain invariant if a data point is added with the same value as that average.

nodes.misconception: Farmers in the Iron Age had the same tools farmers have today such as tractors.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that farming was done by hand with a few iron tools to help. New tools such as the ard plough and iron sickle made a huge impact on farming.

nodes.misconception: Carbon footprints and ecological footprints measure the same thing.
nodes.response: Although carbon footprints and ecological footprints both provide comparable measures of human impacts on the environment, carbon footprints measure greenhouse gas emissions while ecological footprints measure the total demand on Earth’s resources.

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.

nodes.misconception: People from different worldviews are only found in certain places.
nodes.response: People from different worldviews can be found in a variety of different places. Some localities have historical populations of people from a particular worldview. But the census shows that people are moving to different areas as well.

nodes.misconception: The digital image we see is always the originial version.
nodes.response: Digital images are often edited for a variety of purposes so we should never assume an image is an exact representation of reality.

nodes.misconception: Everyone responds to music in the same way.
nodes.response: Loud music might be exciting, but it might also be a bit scary.

nodes.misconception: We should perform loudly and confidently so that the audience can hear us.
nodes.response: Changing dynamics can actually help an audience to feel more engaged in the singing because their ears are given more variation, and they can interpret the feeling of a song more easily.

nodes.misconception: All forms of primary and secondary industry have declined in all areas.
nodes.response: While the general trend has been one of decline, some aspects of primary and secondary industries have become more successful such as organic farming.

nodes.misconception: Changes in the environment will not directly affect us.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to become aware of many different habitats and start to see how they are all interconnected and how when one thing is changed, it can impact other living things.

nodes.misconception: Children can lack awareness of the way in which living things within an environment depend upon each other. They may think that they are dependent on humans to supply them with their needs.
nodes.response: Through the lesson, children will see examples of how nature reserves and the animals and plants within it support each other.

nodes.misconception: Children sometimes don't realise plants can be in danger as well as animals.
nodes.response: Share the examples in the slide deck and give pupils time to research other plants to discover there are lots of different plants in different environments that are in danger. If time, find out if any plants in your local area are in danger.

nodes.misconception: All effects of human impact on the environment are negative.
nodes.response: Examples of positive effects of human impact on the environment.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not understand the impact of an increased human population on plants and animals.
nodes.response: Discuss, using examples on the slide deck, all the repercussions of increased population. If possible, include an example relevant to their location to help them see it first hand.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that all dance formations involve facing forwards, side by side.
nodes.response: In traditional dances, the performers typically look straight ahead, but the formations may involve people being side by side, one behind the other, in a circle or sometimes something different such as a star, a square or a double circle.

nodes.misconception: When we refer to the A section of a piece of music (in relation to structure) they have to be exactly the same.
nodes.response: Letters are used to describe sections overall but quite often there are slight differences. Use some common examples of songs pupils will know of where sections might be labelled the same piece of music, but where there are small differences.

nodes.misconception: Science understanding is similar to politics and we can all have different opinions about what is correct.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to see that scientific understanding is built up on evidence, and the best model we have fits with the evidence and can explain observations.

nodes.misconception: As Indonesia is not an HIC, most people there will still work in agriculture.
nodes.response: Agriculture was once Indonesia’s economic backbone, but its share of the workforce has declined since the 1990s. Today, industry and services dominate Indonesia's economy, with manufacturing, finance, tourism and digital sectors growing.

nodes.misconception: Biodiversity loss is not about losing half of the UK's plants and animals, but half the variety.
nodes.response: A loss of variety could be demonstrated to children using coloured cubes. Rather than taking half of each colour, remove whole colour sets.

nodes.misconception: That forest in Norman England always meant land covered by trees.
nodes.response: Forest in Norman England meant an area that was reserved for hunting and so could include open land, village land, even towns, as well as woodland.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the terms force and momentum.
nodes.response: Make explicit the understanding that forces change the motion of an object, and that the motion of an object  (that a force can change) can be described by its momentum.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to change the letter 'f' to 'v' and may just add the suffix -es.
nodes.response: Share lots of examples and give pupils the chance to say the plurals aloud so that they can hear the different sounds e.g. wolfs, wolves.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the ending is spelt how it sounds: 'iz'.
nodes.response: Show pupils that the ending is spelt with the suffix -es, even though it can sound different.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all nouns can be made plural by adding an 's'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that there are some other ways to show more than one, such as one mouse, two mice or one child, two children.

nodes.misconception: If demand for oil decreases then oil prices will always decrease too.
nodes.response: Although oil prices may decrease if demand decreases, oil-producing countries can increase the price of oil by reducing the amount of oil they supply. This requires oil-producing countries to work together to reduce supply.

nodes.misconception: Treating the ratio as the total amount. For example sweets : chocolates in the ratio 6 : 7 and 2 chocolates are eaten, thinking the ratio must now be 6 : 5
nodes.response: Looking at how these problems are formed in learning cycle 1 will help and getting pupils to explore how the ratio changes when things are added or removed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think Ethelred's reign was completely unsuccessful.
nodes.response: Although Ethelred made some poor decisions during his reign, evidence from his charters and coins suggest that Ethelred’s government was more effective than was once believed.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand that the Iron Age coins were not just different to modern day coins but the first coins ever used in Britain.
nodes.response: Explain that during the Iron Age was the first time coins and the concept of money was used in Britain. Previously, people would have traded by swapping different goods.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all objects that can be squashed, bent, twisted or stretched may return to their previous shape (elasticity).
nodes.response: Opportunities to explore the impact of squashing, bending, twisting and stretching different materials.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all objects that can be squashed, bent, twisted or stretched will return to their previous shape.
nodes.response: Opportunities to explore the impact of squashing, bending, twisting and stretching different materials.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that change in speed is instantaneous due to forces, not over a period of time.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that objects continue to accelerate while the force is acting. Make the force easy to understand (e.g. a pulling string).

nodes.misconception: Water cannot exist in a gas form. Condensation is the same as rain or only occurs during cold weather. Dew is formed by liquid escaping from plants.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that water can exist as gaseous water vapour and how condensation forms.

nodes.misconception: Water cannot exist in a gas form.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that water can exist as gaseous water vapour and the process of evaporation.

nodes.misconception: Children think that materials can only change from a liquid to solid state at temperatures below 0°C. They also believe that the change is irreversible.
nodes.response: Teaching slides give examples of materials which change from their liquid to solid state at temperatures higher than room temperature. Through investigation, children will observe that the change between solid state and liquid state is reversible.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that materials can only be heated by being placed on a warm radiator or on a stove or over a candle and don’t think of being “in the room’ as being heated.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and observations show that items which have been stored below room temperature are “being heated” when moved to room temperature. Defrosting is explained in teaching slides.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the temperature of larger ice cubes is colder than smaller ones because they take longer to melt.
nodes.response: Emphasise that both a small and large ice cube are at the same temperature when they are in the same freezer.

nodes.misconception: Light can only reflect off shiny surface;  light does not always travel in straight lines when it bounces off a mirror.
nodes.response: Diagrams and investigations will be used to address the misconceptions.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the volume of sound and the pitch of sound is the same thing, or that high sounds are loud and low sounds are quiet.
nodes.response: It is important to expose children to a wide range of high and low pitched sounds. Continue to make the distinction between volume and pitch throughout this lesson.

nodes.misconception: Video of skydiving may lead pupils to think opening a parachute makes a skydiver 'shoot upwards'.
nodes.response: Explain that this 'upwards motion' is relative motion to a cameraman. Discuss what a sudden upwards motion would do to a falling skydiver.

nodes.misconception: That the gradient of a line given the equation of the line is always just the coefficient of the x term.
nodes.response: Using graphing software to explore this could help.

nodes.misconception: Not fully isolating the required variable by leaving other terms containing the variable in the expression.
nodes.response: To make a variable the subject, it must be expressed in terms of other variables only. Factorising helps isolate a variable if it is in multiple terms.

nodes.misconception: The subject of a formula is just the first term in the formula.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the variety of equations and formulae used in the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the reciprocal of $$\\frac{1}{a} + \\frac{1}{b}$$ is $$a + b$$
nodes.response: $$\\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{1}{4} = \\frac{3}{4}$$ which is not the reciprocal of 2 + 4 = 6. To find the reciprocal, it helps for the expression to be written as a single fraction.

nodes.misconception: The subject of a formula is just the first term in the formula.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the variety of equations and formulae used in the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes we exaggerate tempo changes, interpreting singing fast as singing 'as fast as we can'.
nodes.response: Subtle tempo changes can affect the character of the music as well as big ones.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand how variables interact within a circuit and how changes in one variable can affect others.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will relate the need to control variables in a fair test to the need to do so with circuits in order to be able to relate a given variable to a measured outcome.

nodes.misconception: Nixon was the only president who wanted to remove US troops from Vietnam.
nodes.response: Kennedy and Johnson wanted the same, but, like Nixon, found themselves getting more involved in order to prop up the South Vietnamese govt.

nodes.misconception: The value is always how many times the command should run.
nodes.response: Different values cause different effects depending on the underlying command. These might not always be numerical values either.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse voltage and current, thinking voltage is part of the current, and struggle to apply their understanding to unfamiliar situations.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think of voltage as an ‘electric push’ and current as the flow of electric charge. Have them consider how current flows through a bulb and its effects, with voltage pushing the current and current being the movement of charge.

nodes.misconception: Because Christianity is declining according to census data, there are no new churches being built in the UK.
nodes.response: New churches are still being built or converted from other buildings in the UK today.

nodes.misconception: We can always hear the pulse in music.
nodes.response: Sometimes the pulse is sounded (beat), but not always. The pulse is something we can feel.

nodes.misconception: Call and response is a singing structure.
nodes.response: The call and response structure can be found in songs, chants and instrumental music in musical styles all around the world.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that "third person limited" means the narrative is limited in scope or detail.
nodes.response: "Third person limited" means insight into one character's thoughts, not a story's limited scope.

nodes.misconception: That the animals are always equal, even from the very start.
nodes.response: Focus on the positioning of the animals and how they enter the barn. Orwell is already beginning to make distinctions between the animals.

nodes.misconception: The story takes place in a dark, gloomy and traditionally Gothic setting.
nodes.response: Stevenson deliberately juxtaposes the building Hyde enters with the pleasant and well-to-do neighbourhood.

nodes.misconception: That the revolution is a complete failure.
nodes.response: Explore the quote "the farm was more prosperous now, and better organised". Who has benefitted? Would some consider this a success?

nodes.misconception: The end of Chapter 8 implies Jekyll regretted creating Hyde.
nodes.response: Jekyll is a very complex character, his actions need to be explored with nuance. The best responses will consider Jekyll's joy and regret.

nodes.misconception: Henry Jekyll is responsible for the death of Mr. Hyde. Jekyll is the 'self-destroyer.'
nodes.response: Hyde uses Jekyll as his protection from the gallows. When Jekyll is no more, it is Hyde who chooses death over punishment.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the emotions that often exist beneath anger. They may also find it difficult to distinguish between 'feeling' anger and 'responding with' anger.
nodes.response: Ask the children to consider a time they have felt angry and what emotions may have triggered the anger. E.g. loneliness or sadness. Explain that anger is a normal emotion to feel but understanding the cause of it can help us respond differently.

nodes.misconception: Old Major invents Animalism.
nodes.response: The three pigs invent Animalism in response to Old Major's speech. What might Orwell be commenting on here or trying to reveal?

nodes.misconception: Students might think Stevenson's ambiguity about Hyde's appearance is due to insufficient detail.
nodes.response: Stevenson keeps Hyde's description vague to engage readers' imaginations, amplifying the character's eeriness.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused about whether to put their ideas about Hogarth on the inside or the outside of the character outline.
nodes.response: Model completing the activity as a class and allow children to work in pairs or small groups using big sugar paper.

nodes.misconception: The pigs immediately set about taking control of the farm.
nodes.response: The pigs' increasing power and control is a gradual process, relying on incremental changes in the commandments to gain overall control.

nodes.misconception: All animals were equally responsible for the defence of Animal Farm.
nodes.response: Snowball and Boxer were instrumental in the victory. Mollie deliberately shied away and Napoleon was curiously unmentioned.

nodes.misconception: Character is more important than setting when trying to solve mystery.
nodes.response: Jekyll tells Utterson there is nothing he should worry about - this is not true. Ask pupils how the setting indicates that Jekyll is lying.

nodes.misconception: Napoleon's move towards autocracy is a sudden process.
nodes.response: It is gradual. Each chapter sees the spirit of the revolution and 'Animalism' further degraded by the actions of Napoleon and the pigs.

nodes.misconception: Utterson, as a lawyer, is a man of great curiosity and honour.
nodes.response: Utterson is both curious for the truth, but cautious about ruining the reputation of his peers. This leads to important clues being missed.

nodes.misconception: That the animals are happy in the work and with the sacrifices they are making.
nodes.response: Link back to Orwell's purpose about manipulation and propaganda. Their reality does not match the promises of the revolution.

nodes.misconception: That Snowball really is responsible for the windmill collapsing and other events on the farm.
nodes.response: Explore the question, how do you know if propaganda is working effectively? When there is unwavering belief in its messages.

nodes.misconception: Liminal spaces are things that are unnerving in a mysterious way.
nodes.response: Liminal spaces often do create a unnerving tone, but this is due to them being the boundary to two opposing states.

nodes.misconception: The animals' apparent support for the pigs is genuine loyalty.
nodes.response: The reality is that this is manipulation, fear, and the pigs' gradual control over them. Examine the pigs' tactics.

nodes.misconception: The case is over now Hyde has been found dead.
nodes.response: Get students enthused about the final mystery - how has Jekyll disappeared from a room locked from the inside?

nodes.misconception: That the animals could not have stopped the revolution.
nodes.response: How does Orwell describe Boxer? He is physically powerful and commands respect. If he had intelligence could he have made a difference?

nodes.misconception: Chapter 9 takes place after the events in Chapter 8.
nodes.response: Ask pupils if they were going to put the chapters in chronological order, how would this chapter be numbered? (Answer: Chapter 6)

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the genre of this novella is solely Gothic fiction.
nodes.response: Even without the presence of a detective character, the use of concealment and a carefully crafted mystery make this detective fiction too.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume 'evolution' refers to an internal or physical change in the Iron Man.
nodes.response: Ask the children to consider whether they think the Iron Man always had the positive qualities we witness at the end. This is a great opportunity to explore the concept of 'perception'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain about how to write their verb e.g. dances or hugs.
nodes.response: Provide children with a verbs word bank in the form they will use them e.g. jumps, hops, skip, hugs etc. to make sense within the sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to generate appearance words and may use words like 'curious' to describe his appearance as well.
nodes.response: Provide images to support them with generating ideas and explain that they can describe the appearance of specific parts of Jack e.g. 'yellow wellies', 'brown eyes', 'wavy hair', 'long legs' etc.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recognise that an idea must make sense on its own.
nodes.response: Support pupils using a sentence scaffold that guides them to join another complete simple sentence with 'and' rather than using 'and' followed by another phrase or expanded noun phrase.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what constitutes 'one single idea' to effectively create a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Use the sentence scaffolds as much as possible, so that pupils are only adding their own adjectives. The purpose of this lesson is initial introduction to joining two ideas, rather than expecting them to be secure, so model as much as is needed.

nodes.misconception: There is only one verb to say 'I am' and 'you are' in Spanish.
nodes.response: In Spanish, there are two ways to say 'I am' and 'you are'. 'I am in general' is 'soy' and 'I am now' is 'estoy'. 'You are in general' is 'eres' and 'you are now' is 'estás'.

nodes.misconception: Children might think that a narrative fiction is always a completely made up story.
nodes.response: Explain that authors often taken inspiration from real life events to develop narrative fiction texts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unfamiliar with some elements of the story, such as 'yams' and names of the Cousins.
nodes.response: When reading the story, gloss over key vocabulary and supplement with images or use of the illustrations where necessary. You can also use some of the explanation and check slides as you are reading to support their understanding further.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that there can only be one setting in a story.
nodes.response: Explain that the setting may change in a story and talk through the different settings in 'Grandad's Island'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to think of reasons they like the dark.
nodes.response: Brainstorm ideas beforehand as a class and if possible use two adults to model hot-seating before the children start the task.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand important vocabulary within the story, e.g. "preserve" or why pickling items in a jar is a way to protect them.
nodes.response: Offering a simple explanation of the word "preserve" will support the children's understanding. Vocabulary and the meaning behind word choices will be explored in greater detail in the next lesson in the unit.

nodes.misconception: The word 'woe' is repeated at several points by all characters in the story. Children may be unfamiliar with the meaning of this word or have questions around why it is repeated.
nodes.response: Provide the definition of 'woe' (great sorrow or distress). Ask the children to consider the different points at which the characters say the word and the impact this has on them as the reader, (e.g. not knowing the fate of each character).

nodes.misconception: Once on stage, it is common to focus more on the singing and drop some of the physicality.
nodes.response: We can avoid this by melding the two. How we move and how we sing can be described in similar ways. For example, legato, or smooth singing, may happen whilst we are moving in a smooth manner.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the concept of characterisation.
nodes.response: Explain that the author is trying make us feel certain things about the characters; characterisation is just the process of doing that. If the author wants us to think Grendel is scary, they have to make that happen through their descriptions.

nodes.misconception: Rocks do not change once they are formed.
nodes.response: Metamorphic rocks are created by heat and pressure acting on sedimentary and igneous rocks.

nodes.misconception: House prices will decrease the further one gets from the CBD.
nodes.response: The price per square metre may decrease as one moves further from the CBD, but as homes get larger with that distance, one cannot say that they get cheaper overall.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not understand chemical reactions as changes, they considered them to be ‘events’. They focus on observable features e.g. colour change rather than formation of a new substance.
nodes.response: Use questioning to encourage pupils to make links between their observations as evidence that a new substance is formed when substances undergo chemical reactions.

nodes.misconception: Folk music all sounds the same.
nodes.response: Many folk traditions have shared characteristics, primarily because of the way that the music was passed between generations, but folk music is incredibly diverse, and covers lots of different types of music from different cultures and times.

nodes.misconception: Performance in sport is entirely down to physiological capabilities such as speed, strength and technique.
nodes.response: Psychological factors such as confidence, motivation and learned behaviours from similar experiences in the past have as much impact on performance sport as the level of skill players have.

nodes.misconception: It is always raining in the tropical rainforest.
nodes.response: Although it will often rain every day in a tropical rainforest, the rain is often short and intense rather than continual. Some rainforests have drier and wetter seasons also.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to link their own knowledge of the world to the texts to support their predictions.
nodes.response: Link the titles of the texts to what you have done in school, e.g. 'We drew symbols in our science experiment', 'A president is someone who leads something like our headteacher or the pupil council' etc.
