nodes.response: Draw pupils attention to the tome scales on the evolutionary trees to show that evolution takes place slowly over long periods of time.

nodes.misconception: Grouping organisms based on similarities in their names (e.g. fish and jellyfish) or habitat.
nodes.response: The lesson makes clear that scientists classify organisms into groups using similarities and differences in their features (e.g. backbone).

nodes.misconception: Organisms are classified only according to their visible (macroscopic) features.
nodes.response: This lesson explores the classification of organisms into kingdoms based on the features of their cells.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the modern classification system that we use today is complete.
nodes.response: Remind pupils why new data from experiments or observations leads to changes in models or theories.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with some of the vocabulary needed for animal classification that is not used in everyday language. They may try to use an animal's habitat as an observable characteristic.
nodes.response: Model the correct classification language throughout the lesson using animals they are confident with. Although there sometimes are observable clues, you cannot be certain of an animal's habitat by looking at it out of context.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to identify plants using the habitat they are found in as opposed to their observable features.
nodes.response: Reinforce that where a plant lives is not an observable characteristic and cannot be used to identify it.

nodes.misconception: Children may ask questions that don't have a yes or no answer.
nodes.response: Keep reminding the children that their questions need to have a yes/no answer and that this is how a classification key works to help us to group and identify unknown objects.

nodes.misconception: Little bones in the hand and foot are not considered long bones.
nodes.response: Bones are classified based on their shape, if the shaft is longer than than the width and depth of a bone, it is referred to as a long bone even if it is small in size.

nodes.misconception: Little bones in the hand and foot are not considered long bones.
nodes.response: Bones are classified based on their shape, if the shaft is longer than than the width and depth of a bone it is referred to as a long bone even if it is small in size.

nodes.misconception: Recyclable energy is the same as renewable energy.
nodes.response: Renewable energy comes from natural processes that are constantly renewed, so they never run out. Recyclable energy comes from resources that are often finite (they can run out) but which can be reprocessed or reused to extend their use.

nodes.misconception: There can be confusion between the role of ligaments and tendons.
nodes.response: Ligaments connect bone to bone to stabilise a joint whereas tendons attach muscle to bone to enable movement.

nodes.misconception: A very common mistake made when classifying skills is to name a sport without the skill. For example, trying to classify 'rugby' rather than one of the many different skills within rugby.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that specific skills are required and that they can name multiple examples of skills from different sports.

nodes.misconception: A very common mistake made when classifying skills is to name a sport without the skill. For example, trying to classify 'rugby' rather than one of the many different skills within rugby.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that specific skills are required and that they can name multiple examples of skills from different sports.

nodes.misconception: A classifier can be improved by providing more training data.
nodes.response: More data doesn't always mean improved predictions. The quality of data provided to a classifier is as important as the quantity.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that all eukaryotic cells have the same cell components.
nodes.response: Draw pupils' attention to the differences between the different types of eukaryotic cells. Focus on the presence of a nucleus, mitochondria, and, in plant cells, chloroplasts, as identifying characteristics of eukaryotic cells.

nodes.misconception: Animals are misclassified based on features that have been incorrectly interpreted, such as wings.
nodes.response: Animals which are often misclassified are included as explicit examples, such as bat, whale and penguin.

nodes.misconception: 'J' is pronounced the same in both English and German.
nodes.response: In German, 'j' is pronounced like 'yot' and sounds like the English 'y'. The German letter 'y' is called  'oopsilon'. It sounds like the German 'j' at the start of borrowed words, e.g., 'Yoga', but like a short ü 'oo' in others, e.g. 'das System'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that any group of words that is not a main clause is a subordinate clause.
nodes.response: Emphasise that knowing the difference between clauses (groups of words that contain verbs) and phrases (groups of words that do not) is key.

nodes.misconception: Beads are just for decoration.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that beads can tell stories, show who someone is, or carry messages. In many cultures around the world, beads are worn to remember, to celebrate, or to show strength. The patterns and shapes often have deep meanings.

nodes.misconception: Once a sculpture is built, it should always stay the same.
nodes.response: Some sculptures are meant to change over time. Artists might add to them, reuse parts or let nature affect them. Change can tell new stories and show that art is alive.

nodes.misconception: Only men were important in history and trade.
nodes.response: Women played key roles such as making silk, running markets and sharing stories. Artists invite us to think about this through their work.

nodes.misconception: To make an adjective plural in French we add an -s like in English.
nodes.response: In French there are various ways to make an adjective plural, including adding an -s, an -x or changing -al to -aux.

nodes.misconception: That places which experience rain, particularly heavy rain as in the DRC, musn't experience water scarcity or drought.
nodes.response: Heavy rainfall is experienced in some parts of the DRC such as rainforests whilst other parts such as savanna are very dry. Furthermore rainforests are depleting and savanna is expanding as global temperatures are rising, increasing risks of drought.

nodes.misconception: The Middle East is all desert.
nodes.response: The Middle East is so vast that it contains a number of different biomes.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly thinking that we can use and damage forests and oceans without negative consequences for the planet and our own survival.
nodes.response: This lesson explores the crucial role of forests and oceans as global carbon sinks that offset human carbon emissions, and the impacts of deforestation, global warming and ocean acidification.

nodes.misconception: The Middle East is already hot and dry, so climate change won’t really affect it.
nodes.response: Climate change will continue to make the region hotter and drier, which will have consequences such as desertification, water scarcity and food shortages.

nodes.misconception: All species will be able to evolve to cope with climate change.
nodes.response: The lesson explores why not all species will be able to evolve fast enough to adapt to the pace of climate change.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that what we eat has no impact on climate change, or that all foods have roughly the same impact.
nodes.response: This lesson explores in detail the impacts of different foods and dietary choices in terms of their carbon footprint of greenhouse gas emissions.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that individual weather events are evidence for or against climate change.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the correct idea that an increase in the frequency of extreme weather events is evidence of climate change and we have to look at the long term pattern of weather events as evidence.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that climate change affects the weather, but not human health.
nodes.response: This lesson explores direct and indirect impacts of climate change on human health.

nodes.misconception: Everyone in Nigeria is impacted by climate change equally.
nodes.response: Some people in Nigeria are impacted by climate change more than than others. Many different overlapping factors make some people more vulnerable to climate change impacts than others.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that an increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide will be beneficial by increasing photosynthesis and producing more food.
nodes.response: The lesson explores why the negative effects of increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide outweigh any benefits from increased rate of photosynthesis.

nodes.misconception: Russia will benefit from climate change because it will make the country warmer, allowing for more agriculture and economic opportunities.
nodes.response: While warming may open up some land for agriculture, the negative impacts will outweigh potential benefits. For example, flooding and unpredictable weather patterns will harm crops and water supplies.

nodes.misconception: That the most important rainforest to protect is the Amazon and that other rainforests are smaller so they don't matter as much.
nodes.response: Tropical rainforests are rich in biodiversity and play a crucial role in regulating Earth's climate as carbon sinks. Rainforests in Africa or Asia are as important as the Amazon in South America, so global climate action is needed to protect them.

nodes.misconception: The greenhouse effect has a negative impact.
nodes.response: The greenhouse effect is a natural process that is essential for life on Earth. Without it, our planet would be too cold to sustain most life forms.

nodes.misconception: Everyone in China and around the world is equally responsible for climate change.
nodes.response: Although everyone has a carbon footprint, some people and places contribute more to climate change than others.

nodes.misconception: Everyone is impacted by climate change equally.
nodes.response: Although everyone is affected by climate change, some people and places are impacted more than others.

nodes.misconception: Melting sea ice does not impact ocean currents.
nodes.response: Melting ice alters the balance of freshwater and saltwater in the ocean, which can disrupt major ocean currents like the Gulf Stream.

nodes.misconception: That greenhouse gases come from greenhouses or are caused by greenhouses. This often happens when pupils don't know what a greenhouse is or how it is used.
nodes.response: Explain what a greenhouse is, where we can find them and how they work. Greenhouses provide artificially warmer conditions to make plants grow quicker and healthier. The are often made from glass, which traps heat from the sun inside the greenhouse.

nodes.misconception: In early work with graphs and charts, pupils can easily mix up the axes and try to put the values in the wrong places on graphs like climate graphs.
nodes.response: On graphs that show change over time, like climate graphs, the horizontal axis shows time (months of the year on a climate graph). The vertical axes are for numerical values representing measurements (rainfall and temperature on a climate graph).

nodes.misconception: China produces the most greenhouse gases per capita in the world.
nodes.response: China produces the most greenhouse gases in the world, but with a population of over 1.4 billion people, their per capita emissions are significantly lower than many other countries.

nodes.misconception: Earth is significantly closer to the Sun at the Equator.
nodes.response: Revisit pupils’ prior learning about the Earth and space in science.

nodes.misconception: Stamping is something we do when we are frustrated; it's not a dance action.
nodes.response: All actions can be used in dance. Stamping could be used to communicate frustration or could be used to add emphasis, make rhythmic sounds or show strength.

nodes.misconception: Using a cloning tool will always make invisible changes to an image.
nodes.response: The cloning tool needs to be used carefully and precisely to make changes look realistic.

nodes.misconception: The cloud ensures everyone can access software and resources.
nodes.response: There are many different devices that can be used to access cloud services, and the functionality of each device will have an impact on the quality of service users will experience when using cloud based services.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that the co-interior angles are equal, like alternate and corresponding angles.
nodes.response: Have pupils draw a pair of parallel lines and a transversal line themselves, identify the co-interior angles, are they equal?

nodes.misconception: Pupils might struggle to know whether 'and', 'but' or 'or' is best in a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Share and discuss many examples and non-examples where 'and', 'but' or 'or' works best in a sentence in comparison with the other options.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that 'and', 'but' or 'or' in sentences always make a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that to be a compound sentence, each idea on either side of 'and', 'but' or 'or' must have equal weight.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recognise that an idea must make sense on its own.
nodes.response: Model identifying the two ideas lots of times throughout the lesson before challenging pupils to do this themselves.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that waves are cause by tides.
nodes.response: Tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the moon . Waves are caused by wind blowing over the sea.

nodes.misconception: Enquiries that focus on coastal management have to discuss effectiveness.
nodes.response: While many coastal enquiries focus on how effective management strategies are, the concept of effectiveness is far broader. Enquiries could study how coastal defences look, if they prevent access to the beach, or how sustainable it is to build them.

nodes.misconception: Nature reserves or world heritage sites only apply to places on land.
nodes.response: Many coasts and underwater ecosystems are classed as Marine Protected Areas and are protected in the same way as nature reserves.

nodes.misconception: Everyone will have the same views and opinions about the importance of protecting the Sundarbans.
nodes.response: Role play could be used to investgate the perspectives of different stakeholders in the Sundarbans such as fishing communities, farmers, government officials, tourism operators and conservationists.

nodes.misconception: That everyone involved or invested in a plan must want said coastal management project to happen to protect the coastline of an area.
nodes.response: In almost all cases, there are a wide range of opinions about coastal management projects, some in support of the plans and others not in favour for various reasons that they feel are important.

nodes.misconception: The melting of sea ice will contribute to rising sea levels.
nodes.response: There are some great videos of experiments used to demonstrate that only the melting of land ice (e.g. glaciers, ice sheets on Greenland and Antarctica) will exacerbate sea level rise.

nodes.misconception: When planning a round-the-world cruise children may not understand that the western edge of the map in task A matches up to the eastern edge of the map.
nodes.response: Use a globe to demonstrate the passage of cruise ships across the Pacific and how this relates to their world maps.

nodes.misconception: A light dependant resistor (LDR) only senses light levels.
nodes.response: An LDR's resistance changes depending on the amount of light it is exposed to. As the light level increases, the resistance decreases. This change in resistance can create a voltage change, which can be used as a signal to control an output.

nodes.misconception: Who finds it first, wins.
nodes.response: Accuracy and teamwork so we find the correct outcomes is more important than being first.

nodes.misconception: Bubble sort is a fast and efficient sorting algorithm.
nodes.response: Bubble sort is considered inefficient for large data sets, but it can be made more efficient by using a flag to indicate when a swap is made in a single pass.

nodes.misconception: Bubble sort is a fast and efficient sorting algorithm.
nodes.response: Bubble sort is considered inefficient for large data sets, but it can be made more efficient by using a flag to indicate when a swap is made in a single pass.

nodes.misconception: There was only one Cold War crisis involving Berlin: the USSR's blockade of Berlin in 1948 and the Berlin Airlift launched by the Western powers in response to this.
nodes.response: Berlin was a source of conflict between the USA and the USSR from the start of the Cold War. The crisis that took place between 1958 and 1963 and resulted in the construction of the Berlin Wall is sometimes referred to as the Second Berlin Crisis.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that teams are only successful if they score the most points or win against their opposition.
nodes.response: Scoring the most points or goals is one way you can measure success. Including all team members, playing fairly and improving are all equally important ways of being successful when competing.

nodes.misconception: When working in pairs, one pupil who is naturally faster moves ahead quickly from point to point, leaving their partner behind.
nodes.response: Both partners need to stay together so they can support each other with navigation and decision-making. If one person moves ahead alone, they miss the chance to communicate, plan effectively and succeed as a team.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that good aim is a fixed skill that you either have or do not.
nodes.response: Accuracy and aim is closely linked to balance and technique, i.e. when a pupil can hold a steady position and perform an accurate technique, often their aim improves.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that teams are only successful if they score the most points or beat their opposition when they compete.
nodes.response: Competing successfully can be measured in different ways. Scoring the most points or goals is one measure. Including all team members, playing fairly or bringing positivity are all equally important ways of being successful when competing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils should design individually, and time should be taken when creating and thinking about design ideas.
nodes.response: Designers work in teams and collaborate to create design ideas. Working quickly when generating design ideas can prevent overthinking and allows freedom and creativity to lead the way.

nodes.misconception: All abstract symbols need to be explained to others.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that some abstract symbols hold personal or cultural meanings that don’t have to be explained. The West African Adinkra symbol Sankofa, literally means “go back and fetch it” and suggests that we carry our past with us.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that texture is only about how something feels when touched.
nodes.response: Remind children that in art, texture can also be shown visually, like drawing rough bark or smooth leaves, even if you can’t physically feel it.

nodes.misconception: Data and information are the same thing.
nodes.response: Data and information are realted but are different. Data is raw facts and figures whilst information is data that has been processed to have meaning.

nodes.misconception: When data is being recorded, if the person recording knows what each value represents, column labels are not needed.
nodes.response: Column labels are important to make the data clear and easy to understand for everyone, even if the person recording it knows what it means.

nodes.misconception: Each piece of evidence can be looked at in isolation when thinking about the crime.
nodes.response: Question your students' explanations to help them acknowledge where they have failed to consider certain pieces of evidence.

nodes.misconception: Secondary data has to be collected by geographical experts.
nodes.response: Secondary data is often collected by experts or professional geographers but it can also be the data collected by other students in a different time frame.

nodes.misconception: Numerical data is more valuable to geographers than text data.
nodes.response: All data is valuable to geographers, providing it is fair and unbiased.

nodes.misconception: Systematic and stratified sampling are 'better' than a random sampling strategy.
nodes.response: There is no hierarchy of effectiveness in sampling strategies. The best strategy to use depends on the dynamics of the location, the size of the overall population of data, and what geographical conclusions one hopes to be able to make from the data.

nodes.misconception: The subject pronoun is used with the verb to make an imperative.
nodes.response: Imperative instructions do not include the subject pronoun e.g. Écoute ! Écoutez !

nodes.misconception: That every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction.
nodes.response: The slide deck addresses that not every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction. The particles must collide with the activation energy in order for the collision to be successful and a new product be formed.

nodes.misconception: That countries are always the same shape and size, with the same borders and the same name throughout their history and that these aspects will never change.
nodes.response: History has shown that in many countries borders move, countries expand or shrink and the name of any given country is not fixed and permanent. These things are often the result of conflict or warfare which causes significant political change.

nodes.misconception: That countries are always the same shape and size, with the same borders and the same name throughout their history and that these aspects will never change.
nodes.response: History has shown that in many countries borders move, countries expand or shrink and the name of any given country is not fixed and permanent. These things are often the result of conflict or warfare which causes significant political change.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not place a main clause before the colon.
nodes.response: Emphasise that for questions and lists, we always have a main clause before the colon; for questions, we also have one after the colon.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may give a consequence instead of an explanation after the colon.
nodes.response: Ask the question 'why?' about the part of the sentence before the colon - the answer should be an explanation not a consequence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the correct punctuation for bullet points.
nodes.response: There are very few hard-and-fast rules; the key is to select consistent punctuation throughout the list.

nodes.misconception: Artists can always match colours on the first attempt.
nodes.response: Remind children that it can take an artist several tries to make the correct colour. By practicing colour mixing, artists can improve over time.

nodes.misconception: When describing the movement of vectors, "across" is used to describe a horizontal movement.
nodes.response: Embed the understanding that "across" refers to the horizontal component, but the direction must be described concisely as a vector has direction and magnitude.

nodes.misconception: When using the product rule, pupils may be unsure whether they should divide the product by 2.
nodes.response: Pay extra attention to the context of the problem. If the order of the two outcomes is irrelevant, then you should divide by two. If each of the two outcomes is allocated to a separate event (e.g. 1st and 2nd) then do not divide by 2.

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty understanding partitioning of the whole group where one part is zero.
nodes.response: Include contexts with zero, so children can discuss and clarify their thinking.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to relate to some of the negative emotions explored in the lesson and therefore don't see the benefit of practising the mime and meditative balance sequences.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it is important to practise and understand the benefits so that we are prepared for future challenges in our lives.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may spend their practice time adding more actions onto the sequence instead of repeating and refining a shorter sequence.
nodes.response: Practice time can be used to repeat a skill and improve the quality of a performance, or it can be used to make changes to a sequence to improve the flow or increase the range of movements for more interest.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to identify the dividends and confuse these with the divisor.
nodes.response: For each problem, ask the children what each number represents and help them to describe this. For example,  'the number of sweets before they were shared and the number they are sharing between' alongside the terms dividend and divisor.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils neglect the value of, and need for teamwork, opting to try and dribble the ball each time they receive it.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make the correct decisions as when to pass and when to dribble. Also ensure to implement rules where all pupils must touch the ball before scoring.

nodes.misconception: The petals of a flower are flat.
nodes.response: Remind children that the petals of a flower curve and bend, so are not flat shapes. They are a three-dimensional form.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils forget to follow through and stop their racket immediately after hitting the ball.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that a proper follow through, towards the target, is crucial for both power and accuracy. Remind them if you see the racket stopping too early or ending up pointing to the sky or to the ground.

nodes.misconception: Children will solve an equation by working from left to right and forget that multiplication needs to be completed before addition or subtraction.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities for children to practise solving equations that cannot be solved working from left to right. You could highlight the operation symbols to draw children's attention to these before they begin to solve them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mistake dribbling fast and dribbling with control, which causes them to lose control of the ball. Often pupils won't catch the ball but just move straight into a dribble.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that dribbling fast is good but dribbling with control is essential. The better control they have, the faster they will be able to dribble. Remind them that they should receive the ball and assess the best option before dribbling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils recieve the ball and automatically try to shoot, regardless of their position on the pitch/court.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that their shots will not be successful if they don't give careful consideration to the position they are in before shooting.

nodes.misconception: Pupils stand behind defenders when waiting to receive the ball. Pupils keep moving into space but don't look at the player with the ball to acknowledge they are ready to receive a pass.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to move to the side of the defender creating an angle for the pass. Support pupils to communicate (verbal and non verbal) when they are ready in a space.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to take their time to pass and move and instead panic, rushing their passes and shooting far from the target.
nodes.response: Pupils need to have patience to support each other to pass and move towards the target, and shoot when in a suitable position.

nodes.misconception: Children may rely on the order of the addends rather than their place value when calculating. They may also default to counting on rather than using known facts.
nodes.response: Refer back to known facts and efficient strategies and model their use throughout, discussing the best strategy to use at each point and why. Model errors that can be made when not adding ones then tens for example, or in counting on in ones.

nodes.misconception: Children might record that numbers can only be partitioned in one way.
nodes.response: Children here have the chance to explore how numbers can be partitioned in many different ways. Narrate when exploring these different ways throughout, using  ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part.

nodes.misconception: Performers have to smile all the time.
nodes.response: Performers use facial expression to communicate the mood or feelings of their character. This range can include smiling if happy, weeping if sad, a furrowed brow if worried, a cleanched jaw if angry or eye-rolling if annoyed.

nodes.misconception: Counterbalances are always symmetrical.
nodes.response: Counterbalances can involve the same action as a partner but these can be varied by level, direction of size. Counterbalances can also use contrasting body parts to connect, e.g. the hand of one dancer pressing against the shoulder of their partner.

nodes.misconception: In Salsa you have to apply tension to your whole body.
nodes.response: In Salsa it is the torso that is firmly held maintaining an upright stance, the arms are also fixed when in hold but change to some degree when moving between holds or when moving independently. The legs largely remain soft and fluid.

nodes.misconception: Audio tracks have a set volume, meaning they might not be usuable for certain projects.
nodes.response: Even if the volume of a track isn't suitable for your project, audio editing software can adjust the volume so that it plays at an appropriate level.

nodes.misconception: A sprite can only use one type of code block in a sequence.
nodes.response: A sprite can have sequences made up from multiple types of code block. For example, sound and motion code blocks can be combined.

nodes.misconception: Pupils understand they multiply by 100 when converting m to cm, but when converting m^3 to cm^3, fail to recognise the need to multiply by 100^3.
nodes.response: Illustrate a 1m^2 square and the equivalent 100cm^2 square, calculating the area and allowing pupils to see the equivalence of 1 m^2 = 10 000 cm^2. Also apply this to a 1m^3 and 100cm^3, thus allowing students to see 1m^2 = 100 000 cm^3.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes can be made when subtracting negative values. E.g. thinking that 5 - - 2 = 3.
nodes.response: Consider additive inverses, subtracting a negative is the same as adding the additive inverse. Pupils should be able to spot mistakes in learning cycle 1 by checking their new equation is still true.

nodes.misconception: There is only way to select part of an image.
nodes.response: There are multiple ways to select parts of an image.

nodes.misconception: A melody must be completely conjunct.
nodes.response: This is not true - great melodies often use disjunct movement. However, when learning to compose melodies, sticking to mostly conjunct movement and small intervals helps them to sound melodic.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often stop between movements resulting in poor flow and continuity. This may be due to hesitancy or lack of confidence in their technique.
nodes.response: Pupils should repeat short sequences of movements until they are performed with flow. For example, focus on linking 2-3 movements together before adding more. Focus on flow before looking at speed routes.

nodes.misconception: The motor must be wired in one specific way to work.
nodes.response: It will work in both directions, but reversing connections changes spin direction.

nodes.misconception: Combining ratios without using equivalent ratios to equate the common part.
nodes.response: Pupils may need to spend extra time finding equivalent ratios and looking at when it is ok to combine ratios or not.

nodes.misconception: Instruments can only create one sound or represent one animal.
nodes.response: There is no right or wrong when choosing instruments for their timbre.

nodes.misconception: The average speed is found by adding the speeds and dividing by how many average speeds are given.
nodes.response: The common misconception is calculating an average of an average. Show how the answers when calculating the average of the average speeds is not the same as calculating the average speed using the total distance and total time of the average speeds.

nodes.misconception: The taal and raag begin and end at the same time.
nodes.response: A raag can start and end at any point in the rhythm cycle.

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to measure the initial mass of the burner and initial temperature of the water.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance in remembering to measure this data when writing a method for this practical.

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to measure the initial mass of the burner and initial temperature of the water.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance in remembering to measure this data when writing a method for this practical.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that commas are only used to demarcate clauses or for 'pauses'.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about the specific rules for comma use, including for clauses, in lists and between adjectives in ENPs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that commas indicate a 'pause' in sentences, or 'taking a breath'.
nodes.response: Commas have a number of specific functions, several of which are covered in this lesson.

nodes.misconception: Travelling around the room means you run in a circle. Pausing and balancing are always star shapes.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that travelling involves a wide range of actions including skipping, shuffling, marching, jumping, creeping. Also ensure pupils understand that we can balance on a range of body parts in a variety of shapes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use a comma to separate any main and subordinate clause.
nodes.response: When an adverbial subordinate clause comes after a main clause, no comma is needed; relative subordinate clauses don't always need commas.

nodes.misconception: Historians have finished debating the legacy of the British Empire.
nodes.response: Historians continue to debate the legacy of the British Empire as new information emerges.

nodes.misconception: The letter x in the words 'sixième' and 'dixième' is pronounced the same as in English.
nodes.response: The letter x is pronounced as z due to liaison in these words and should be carefully practised to develop an authentic pronunciation.

nodes.misconception: Commercial viability only relates to how well a product works.
nodes.response: A product can work well or be aesthetically pleasing, but if it’s too expensive to make, doesn’t meet market demand, or won’t sell at a profit, it isn’t commercially viable.

nodes.misconception: Students often struggle to understand the concept of having a common ancestor and confuse it with one species being descended from another.
nodes.response: This lesson uses evolutionary trees to help students visualise the relationships between groups of organisms.

nodes.misconception: Ciphers and encryption are the same thing.
nodes.response: Ciphers are one type of encryption method. Encryption includes ciphers but also involves algorithms, keys, and protocols used in modern digital security systems.

nodes.misconception: The order of instructions in a program doesn't really matter, as long as all the instructions are there.
nodes.response: Computers execute code line by line, in the order it's written. If you change the sequence, you're changing the steps the computer takes, and that will change the output.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes with the defects and treatments in vision caused by long- and short-sightedness (e.g. getting the symptoms or the type of lenses mixed up) or how lenses actually correct vision are common.
nodes.response: The conditions are dealt with separately with clear and concise information conveyed and supported with diagrams and reinforced with questions that focus on these mistakes and misconceptions.

nodes.misconception: Elements cannot have metal and non-metal properties.
nodes.response: Introduction of the metalloids and discussion of their properties.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants have flowers all year round and that all flowers look the same.
nodes.response: Use examples of plants at different times of the year, both with and without flowers, as well as examples of plants with flowers of various colours, shapes, and sizes.

nodes.misconception: All bacterial cells looks like the bacterial cell model.
nodes.response: Bacteria can come in different shapes and sizes, this will be outlined within the slide deck.

nodes.misconception: Sketching is the only way to iterate design ideas.
nodes.response: Design ideas and iterations can be communicated using various techniques, such as sketching, CAD, prototyping, and AI.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe talking loudly or shouting is how they should communicate as a leader.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that shouting instructions isn’t the same as giving clear, helpful directions. As well as this, good communication works both ways and leaders should allow their teammates opportunities to speak too.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that all effective forms of communication are verbal.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that there are many different ways they can communicate through both verbal and non-verbal communication.

nodes.misconception: The main role of graphic designers is to make work that is pleasing to the viewer’s eye.
nodes.response: Many graphic designers push traditional boundaries and shift the focus from creating purely aesthetically pleasing works to communicating messages about social justice.

nodes.misconception: Messages sent online are always private.
nodes.response: Some tools store messages or share them with others.

nodes.misconception: Pupils disregard their tactics once they start playing the game, getting distracted by everything else that is going on in the game.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand their tactics and make an effort to use them during the game. Highlight and praise pupils that manage this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think leading is just about giving instructions.
nodes.response: A ledaer also requires active listening and the time and confidence to provide feedback on what has been completed well and how things can be improved.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that effective communication only involves speaking clearly to someone.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that communication works two ways. Speaking clearly is important, however listening attentively is equally important to ensure the information is received.

nodes.misconception: To describe a language, where something or someone is from, use exactly the same word in French, as we do in English, e.g. 'I learn Spanish,' 'he is Spanish'.
nodes.response: When used as a noun for a language, the word needs a definite article. When used as an adjective to describe nationality of a person or thing, the word agrees with the noun it describes. When used for nationality, the word needs a capital letter.

nodes.misconception: The only translation of 'fue' is 'she, he, it was'.
nodes.response: 'Fue' can mean 'she, he, it was' or 'she, he, it went' depending on the context. The verbs 'ser' and 'ir' are identical in the preterite tense.

nodes.misconception: The only meaning of 'por' is 'for'.
nodes.response: 'Por' can mean several things in Spanish. For example, in addition to 'for', it can also mean 'by' and 'in' in certain contexts.

nodes.misconception: You should select one quotation from each text in a comparative paragraph.
nodes.response: Like in a powerful analytical paragraph, selecting multiple quotations from each text will help strengthen your argument. Selecting these quotations in the planning stage is key.

nodes.misconception: You can't talk about two different texts in the same paragraph.
nodes.response: It can be tricky to talk about two texts in one paragraph, but it often makes for a stronger comparison. A good way to start is to consider one aspect of the texts you wish to compare, and then draw out the differences in your analysis.

nodes.misconception: We have two different presentations of Achilles. One of them must be right, and one must be wrong.
nodes.response: What Miller and Barker do with their novels is show how important perspective is. For Patroclus, Achilles is awe inspiring and innocent. For Briseis, he is quite the opposite. Their perspectives are based on their relationship with him.

nodes.misconception: As long as I am comparing the key points of two sources that is enough.
nodes.response: Using both comparative and correlative conjunctions will ensure there is nuance in your comparisons. They will aslo help keep your comparisons succinct.

nodes.misconception: Compound nouns take the gender of their first noun.
nodes.response: Compound nouns take the gender of their final noun.

nodes.misconception: Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase and so may not accept that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: When we multiply by a unit fraction, it is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. This results in a decrease in length.

nodes.misconception: Children may say, 'Times longer' but this is imprecise.
nodes.response: We say 'Times the length' because this is more precise.

nodes.misconception: Children may say 'ten times heavier' which is imprecise. Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: We say, 'ten times the original mass' because this is more precise, especially when the scale factor is fractional. When we multiply by a unit fraction, it is the same as dividing the whole by the number of equal parts in it, resulting in a decrease.

nodes.misconception: Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: When we multiply an integer by a unit fraction, the effect is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. It results in a decrease.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils do not realise that it is not always necessary to consider all of the digits when comparing or ordering numbers. For example, when comparing 3,974 and 7,832, the thousands are different.
nodes.response: Develop a systematic approach, such that pupils always begin by checking to see if the thousands are the same, then if necessary the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones. Counters and place value grids can really help to exemplify this.

nodes.misconception: A number with more digits after the decimal point is greater than a number with fewer digits.
nodes.response: Create the numbers using place value counters or base 10 blocks and re-iterate the magnitude of each digit within the number.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that because a representation has more images/items then it is a larger number.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider the value of each image/item and say this verbally as ___ wholes and ___ tenths.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the comparative language of taller, tallest, longer and longest.
nodes.response: Talk about the difference between longest and tallest. Collect examples together and label each object as tallest or longest to support children's understanding.

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that the size of the item relates to its mass and that a larger item will always be heavier than a smaller item.
nodes.response: Explore examples where the larger item is lighter and the smaller item is heavier to address this misconception. For example, compare the mass of an inflated balloon with a stone, or an empty box with a small bag full of coins.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a taller container always has a larger capacity.
nodes.response: Choose tall narrow containers alongside short, wide containers and compare the capacities in different ways, such as recording a measurement for each capacity as well as pouring from one container into another to see which has the greater capacity.

nodes.misconception: Children may count the marks rather than the equal parts between integers and  may compare the fractional part of the mixed number first rather than the more significant whole number part.
nodes.response: Count the equal parts in between the given integers, not the marks to determine the unit that we are working with. When comparing and ordering, consider the whole number part first - this determines which integers the mixed number sits between.

nodes.misconception: Pupils mistake numbers with more digits after the decimal point to be the larger number.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to build numbers with base 10 blocks, enabling them to see the magnitude of the numbers they compare.

nodes.misconception: Children will often fall into the trap of thinking that a greater denominator creates a bigger fraction.
nodes.response: Ensure the children have good access to fraction walls to reinforce the fact that the greater the denominator the smaller the fraction. Fraction walls that can be dismantled and arranged are very useful for this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to compare two time intervals when they are presented in different formats, such as five minutes to a quarter of an hour.
nodes.response: The lesson encourages converting time into minutes. Develop automaticity in recalling facts such as 15 minutes = quarter of an hour, 30 minutes = half an hour, 45 minutes = three quarters of an hour and 60 minutes = one hour.

nodes.misconception: When a number is higher, its value is greater. Pupils may struggle to understand that as the denominator gets larger / greater, the size of the parts get smaller.
nodes.response: Show pupils lots of images, comparing fractions with the same numerator (e.g. one-fifth and one-third and then two-fifths and two-thirds). Highlight that even though the number of parts we have is the same, the size of those parts is different.

nodes.misconception: There are no rules to help you learn which verbs are strong and have a vowel change in their stem.
nodes.response: Only verbs with an 'a' or 'e' in their stem can be strong.

nodes.misconception: Children may compare the fractional part of the mixed number first rather than the more significant whole number part.
nodes.response: What do you notice? If the whole number is the same, we need to look at the fractional part. If the numerators are the same, we need to compare the denominators - the smaller the denominator the greater the fraction.

nodes.misconception: Children may compare the fractional part of the mixed number first rather than the more significant whole number part.
nodes.response: What do you notice? If the whole number is the same, we need to look at the fractional part. If the denominators are the same, we need to compare the numerators - the smaller the numerator the smaller the fraction.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to compare fractions with the same numerator or denominator.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use fraction representations to help them visualise. Reference the size of the parts (same numerator, greater denominator means smaller parts) or how many there are (same denominator, greater numerator means more parts).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to compare fractions where the wholes are not the same.
nodes.response: It's important that pupils understand that for comparison of fractions the wholes must be the same. This lesson uses one example of comparing distances in miles versus distance in kilometres as well as comparing pizzas of different shape and size.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the greater value number is the one that starts with the greater value digit even if the number has fewer digits overall.
nodes.response: When comparing numbers, compare the value of the digits not the digits themselves. If both numbers have the same amount of digits, so we need to compare the largest place value digit that is different.

nodes.misconception: There is only one word in German for 'our' and 'their', just like in English.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives like 'unser' and 'ihr' change the spelling according to the gender of the noun and the case that is needed e.g.  'unser Hund', 'unsere Katze'; 'ihr Vater', 'ihre Mutter'.

nodes.misconception: Children may understand the value of each set of coins but incorrectly use a symbol ( < > = ) in comparing them.
nodes.response: Encourage reading from left to right e.g. ___ is less than / greater than ___. Ensure children have opportunities to place the coins within the symbols to understand the correct orientation of them.

nodes.misconception: Using less and fewer incorrectly when describing and comparing.
nodes.response: Reinforce 'fewer' is used for things we can count (not as many) and 'less' is used for things we cannot count (not as much). Explore a range of examples of this together.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to understand how to represent the number rods to show the difference when trying to find the missing rod.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils spend time representing each question with an equation then match this with the number rods. This may help them to visualise the missing part as well.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that they must see both the tens and ones in a two-digit number to compare them. They may also reverse the tens and ones and compare the ones first.
nodes.response: Ensure that numbers with the ones digit hidden are given to compare so that children can appreciate the relative size of the numbers. Use practical equipment and stem sentences to consolidate understanding of the structure of two-digit numbers.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the inequality symbols and use them the incorrect way around.
nodes.response: Take time to practise using the symbols with hand signals or using manipulatives. Emphasise the shape of the symbols reflecting their use i.e. more cubes 'fit' into the wider end of the symbol.

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that the greater the denominator the bigger the fraction.
nodes.response: Reinforce this using the fraction wall. Constantly refer back to it and ensure that the children become experts at using it as a tool for comparison.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate their own adverbs.
nodes.response: The focus of the lesson is using adverbs within a sentence, so provide as many as children may need. You can use word banks to support as well as lots of oral rehearsal.

nodes.misconception: Algorithms and computer programs are actually the same thing.
nodes.response: A computer program is a specific implementation of an algorithm's logic. A clearly written algorithm provides instructions that can be implemented in various ways including, but not limited to, computer programs.

nodes.misconception: The changes between the Bronze Age and the Iron Age happened instantly.
nodes.response: Explain that the changes between the Bronze Age and Iron Age happened gradually over time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may discuss other similarities and differences between the songs (such as song structure, genre).
nodes.response: Verbally model examples based on themes and imagery used.

nodes.misconception: Larger objects have a greater mass. Taller containers have a greater capacity and/or volume.
nodes.response: The size of something does not determine how much mass an object has; taller containers may be narrower and so may not hold as much liquid.

nodes.misconception: You can't compare different text types to each other. For example, an article to a memoir.
nodes.response: By comparing different forms, we can often come to understand why a writer chose a particular text type more deeply - what this particular text type allowed them to do or convey to the reader.

nodes.misconception: Some solids can be poured and take the shape of their containers and therefore are liquids. A material is not the same material after it has been crushed.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and investigation will help children consider the difference between one solid particle of a material and a pile of particles which behaves together like a liquid.

nodes.misconception: You can compare numbers that are more than one apart and say which numbers are one more or one less.
nodes.response: Make it clear whether pupils are comparing numbers or whether they are giving the values that are one more and one less.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging when comparing numbers made from the same digits (e.g. 245 and 254).
nodes.response: Base ten blocks, place value grids and number lines can all be used so pupils can see the size of numbers and see which is larger.

nodes.misconception: You have to be writing in the C18th to use Romantic conventions in your writing.
nodes.response: While Romanticism was a predominant movement in the C18th and C19th, more modern poets can also adhere to Romantic conventions and present a Romantic view of the world.

nodes.misconception: Vector images are better than bitmap images in every situation.
nodes.response: Vector and bitmap images are suited to different tasks. Vectors are best for simple, scalable designs like logos, while bitmaps are better for detailed images like photos.

nodes.misconception: Not referring to the context of the question when comparing the data.
nodes.response: Highlight that just saying the median or the middle 50% of data is bigger is of little use unless you know what the data was about. Check that pupils understand the context of the question.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only consider animals' characteristics to be observable if we can see them in a photo, rather than us also being able to observe their behaviour over time.
nodes.response: Explain that when scientists classify living things they make many observations of how that living thing moves, behaves and reproduces, as these are all characteristics we can observe to help us identify and classify things.

nodes.misconception: That society has always considered childhood as a space for play and exploration.
nodes.response: Before the Enlightenment, children were generally considered small versions of adults.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that 'Coming to England' is a fictional book as it is presented as a story and is being directly compared to Paddington, a fictional story.
nodes.response: From the beginning, explain that the story is based on real events, supplementing the slides with photos of Floella Benjamin. When comparing, discuss the difference of fiction and non-fiction explicitly.

nodes.misconception: The best compression method is the one that makes files the smallest.
nodes.response: Smaller isn’t always better, sometimes important details are lost. The best method depends on the file type, quality needs, and purpose.

nodes.misconception: When giving commands, you should make them as long as possible so that it is really clear what needs to be done.
nodes.response: Commands are easier to understand when they are short. The more details you add, the more chance there is for misunderstanding. Commands need to be clear and to the point, leaving out any detail that would not be helpful in understanding them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the chemistry meaning of strong/weak and concentrated/dilute due to the use of these words in everyday conversation.
nodes.response: Clear definitions of the words are required with practice opportunities to recognise/describe whether the substances are strong or weak acids and if concentrated or dilute.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel that one statistical summary is enough to compare two data sets.
nodes.response: Highlight to pupils that the more information you know, the better your understanding of a data set and therefore a more comprehensive comparison can take place. Compare the means of {-120, -100, -50, 0, 1000} and {145, 145, 146, 147, 147}.

nodes.misconception: All charts made from the same data are equally useful.
nodes.response: Some charts might not help answer a specific question, even if they are accurate. Choosing the right chart type and structure matters.

nodes.misconception: Attributes always relate to physical objects.
nodes.response: Attributes can also be hidden, such as peoples' jobs or preferences. They exist but in order to determine what they are you have to ask people.

nodes.misconception: The British Empire was different from other European empires because Britain willingly relinquished control of its colonies and decolonisation was mostly a peaceful process.
nodes.response: While it was a peaceful process in some British colonies, decolonisation involved significant violence in other colonies. Even in colonies where decolonisation was relatively peaceful there was some violence (e.g., Accra Riots in the Gold Coast).

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a plant or animal can only be part of one food chain.
nodes.response: This lesson shows a number of examples of how plants and animals can be part of many different food chains. Children are encouraged to research and create different food chains for the same plant or animal.

nodes.misconception: Computers are always better than paper.
nodes.response: Both digital and paper can be better for different tasks. You should choose the one that better suits what you need to do.

nodes.misconception: Dystopian voices have to fit the archetype (e.g. rebellious, overly critical) in order to be compelling.
nodes.response: Ishiguro subtly crafts his voices to allow the reader to reflect on their own world.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate their own adjectives.
nodes.response: Refer back to any adjectives generated in the previous lesson and have them available for children. When describing Paddington's emotions, clarify definitions of any key adjectives and repeat them using 'my turn, your turn'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the main theme in a story.
nodes.response: Talk about the themes in well-known fairy tales and link these to the lesson learnt at the end of the story. For example, the theme in 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff' is courage. The goats' courage helps them get to the other side of the river.

nodes.misconception: A food chain shows the full detail and is a true representation of what organisms eat.
nodes.response: Include explanations that animals have a varied diet and eat many different foods. A food chain only shows one food source at a time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils get easily confused between variables and how to ensure a fair test.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand the independent variable is the type of fuel, the dependent variable is the temperature increase and control variables are mass of fuel and volume of water.

nodes.misconception: That comparing language is the best way to compare poems.
nodes.response: As well as comparing the language, you can also compare the use of form, structure and voice in poems.

nodes.misconception: Students think that they can only discuss the similarities OR the differences between poems.
nodes.response: Though they should approach the comparison by identifying key or significant similarities or difference, within that, they can also explore the subtle variations between poems too.

nodes.misconception: All war poems from the anthology are equally comparable.
nodes.response: Some war poems are more suitable for comparison, depending on which question you are asked. You should make your decision based on which ideas and themes you want to discuss.

nodes.misconception: That the idea of life being temporary must always be a sad notion.
nodes.response: The idea of life being temporary might inspire us to live life to the fullest.

nodes.misconception: Taking a photograph of someone's suffering is an effective way of showing their suffering to others.
nodes.response: Arguably, both Duffy and Ghose reveal the futility of using art as a means of showing their suffering to others.

nodes.misconception: That all types of negative feelings are the same.
nodes.response: There are nuances within negativity - some negative emotions might stem from fear, anger, jealousy or uncertainty.

nodes.misconception: There is a set of rules to follow when comparing poems.
nodes.response: Comparing poems often involves exploring similarities and differences, but remind pupils that it is a subjective process.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that all poems must include rhyming words.
nodes.response: Use 'Teetering Towers' to exemplify that not all poems include rhyming words, but they can still follow a pattern and have a rythmic, musical quality.

nodes.misconception: When comparing objects, children may think that one is longer or taller because they have not aligned them to start at the same point.
nodes.response: Encourage children to place objects on a flat surface such as a table when comparing height, or against a wall when comparing length to make sure that they have the same start point.

nodes.misconception: Students often think: all glass types have the same properties and uses; polyethene types are identical in structure and use; and composites are simple mixtures (not engineered materials).
nodes.response: Clarify that soda-lime and borosilicate glass differ in production and use. Explain the distinct processes and uses of LDPE and HDPE. Describe how composites are engineered to achieve specific properties.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only one type of diagram/table can be used to represent each probability problem and worry about choosing the correct one.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the same probability problem can often be represented using multiple diagrams or tables. In many cases, they will be able to find what they are looking for in any representation but it may be clearer to see in some more than others.

nodes.misconception: The probability of an event is the product of the probability of each outcome in the event.
nodes.response: The probability of an event is the sum of the probability of each outcome in the event seen in the sample space of a diagram. For example, in the sample space at the end of a probability tree, or by adding the outcomes in the sample space of a table.

nodes.misconception: Venn diagrams are useful when generating a complete list of outcomes and showing the probabilities of that list.
nodes.response: Venn diagrams can be very useful when categorising already known outcomes into events. The Venn diagram can then be used to calculate probabilities. However, Venn diagrams are not as useful when generating a list of outcomes.

nodes.misconception: Limited understanding of what misconceptions and stereotypes are and the possible impacts of these.
nodes.response: Discuss examples of misconceptions and stereotypes that learners have encountered in their own lives.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that every poem in the anthology is equally suitable for every potential question.
nodes.response: While there are common links between the poems, some have more tenuous connections than others.

nodes.misconception: Linking one more or one less than a number to the number after or before in the count.
nodes.response: Use objects to model one more being added or one being removed to show one less or fewer.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that Emily Davison and Paul Stephenson were fighting for the same thing.
nodes.response: Emily Davison and Paul Stephenson were fighting for different change to happen in Britain at different times, around 50 years apart.

nodes.misconception: That considering which poem you have a stronger emotional reaction to is not worthwhile.
nodes.response: Comparing your personal responses to poems can help you to see how the poet has managed to create meaning and mood through their writing.

nodes.misconception: Students may not at first understand that they must use a parallel sentence structure when using correlative conjunctions e.g. Both 'Island Man' uses imagery as well as 'Search for My Tongue'.
nodes.response: Model a few sentences with correlative conjunctions to show that parallel structures are needed. e.g. Both 'Island Man' and 'Search for My Tongue' use imagery.

nodes.misconception: Prayer and reflection has no value today.
nodes.response: People find it useful to pray and reflect to gain balance in their busy lives.

nodes.misconception: I can use outcome tables to categorise outcomes into as many events as I want.
nodes.response: Outcome tables are limited to categorising outcomes into only two events. You can use more tables to categorise outcomes into three or more events, but the number of tables you need quickly becomes massive!

nodes.misconception: An outcome tree doesn't have a sample space.
nodes.response: Each representation of the outcomes of a trial have a sample space as a part of it. For an outcome table, the table itself is the sample space. For an outcome tree, a sample space must always be constructed after drawing the two layers of branches.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is only one type of salt and that it all comes from the sea.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain how salt is produced and introduce pupils to rock salt and table salt.  Pupils make a comparison of the two.

nodes.misconception: Juliet was Romeo's only love in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet'.
nodes.response: Before Juliet, Romeo believes himself to be in love with Rosaline.

nodes.misconception: A linear search algorithm and binary search algorithm are equally complex to write.
nodes.response: Binary search algorithms are more complex to write due to the different paths that the algorithm can take rather than stepping through the search data in order.

nodes.misconception: The battery produces a fixed sized current that splits between each branch of a parallel circuit.
nodes.response: Consider each branch of a parallel circuit as a separate series circuit connected to an identical battery, in which the total current through the battery is determined by the current it can push through each of the branches  added together.

nodes.misconception: Pie charts but not bar charts can show what proportion of a dataset a particular subgroup represents
nodes.response: You can figure out proportion from a bar chart by comparing the frequency of one subgroup to the total frequency, by adding heights of bars.

nodes.misconception: If two datasets have the same mean, then the distribution of data points will look similar.
nodes.response: Even with the same mean, two datasets could have vastly different ranges. One dataset could be bimodal, whilst the other could be unimodal.

nodes.misconception: All the different persons of the -ar verbs in the preterite tense have the same endings, as in the English simple past, e.g. 'did', 'ate', 'went', 'learned'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the endings for -ar verbs in the preterite tense differ depending on the grammatical person. The 'I' form ends in -é and the 'you' form ends in -aste.

nodes.misconception: That different translations of the Lord's Prayer over time have been purely literal.
nodes.response: When new translations are made, writers change both the language and the content to suit modern audiences.

nodes.misconception: Nomadic lifestyles no longer exist.
nodes.response: Discuss the fact that many people in different parts of the world still live a nomadic lifestyle, some through choice and others as part of a continuing and ancient tradition.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that metamorphosis of an animal is the result of evolution.
nodes.response: Explain that metamorphosis is the change in form of a single animal; it’s still the same animal after metamorphosis.

nodes.misconception: All animal life cycles have the same stages; anything different to mammals is not an 'animal'.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the slide deck to make it clear that different types of animals have different life cycles.

nodes.misconception: That there are "good" pigs and "bad" pigs.
nodes.response: For Orwell, all are susceptible to power and corruption. Orwell uses the pigs to critique the subtle and overt ways that this can be done.

nodes.misconception: Students thinking they need to  find big differences in the poems.
nodes.response: It's often better to choose similarities and then explain and explore the subtle differences.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that all objects fall at the same rate (this is only true in a vacuum).
nodes.response: Use force diagrams to discuss the effect of different sized drag on the parachutes, linking this to resultant force and acceleration.

nodes.misconception: All victim profiles are similar.
nodes.response: Conan Doyle manipulates his presentation of victims depending on how he wants the reader to view them.

nodes.misconception: When used, rhetorical devices have only one possible effect or outcome.
nodes.response: Writers can craft rhetorical devices to create different tones and match their purpose, audience and form. For example, direct address can be used to sound confrontational or it can create an intimate and personal tone.

nodes.misconception: Rhetorical devices always have the same effect.
nodes.response: Although we can make some assumptions about the effect of devices, considering specific information like the writer's intention and form will give a much more detailed and nuanced explanation.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe all toothpastes are the same.
nodes.response: By investigating the effectiveness of a variety of toothpastes, children will realise there are a range of different toothpastes for different jobs.

nodes.misconception: You can't compare different text types to each other. For example, a short story to a memoir.
nodes.response: By comparing different forms, we can often come to understand why a writer chose a particular text type more deeply - what this particular text type allowed them to do or convey to the reader.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to visualise the two settings being described by the poets.
nodes.response: Additional photographs could be provided to develop understanding of the two locations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes struggle to understand how using different mobile and/or stationary phases affects the resulting chromatograms.
nodes.response: Perform chromatography of the same mixture using different mobile phases/stationary phases and discuss the pros/cons of each combination.

nodes.misconception: That comparison involves spotting the differences between poems.
nodes.response: Arguably, the best comparisons are where there is an exploration of subtle differences within similarities.

nodes.misconception: The mode is the most useful average as it can be calculated from bar charts, pie charts and frequency tables.
nodes.response: Although it is often the easiest of the averages to calculate, this does not make it the most useful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants need exactly the same things, in the same quantities, in order to survive and grow.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain how plant requirements differ from plant to plant.

nodes.misconception: We no longer experience gender inequality in today's society.
nodes.response: Although today's society is much more progressive than Victorian society, there are still areas where gender inequality is experienced, although it is usually much more subtle and institutionalised.

nodes.misconception: That perspectives are simply positive or negative.
nodes.response: Positive and negative can be useful words to initially consider a perspective, but then you must become more nuanced and use specific adjectives to identify feelings and perspectives.

nodes.misconception: There is an equivalent way to add -er onto adjectives to make comparisons like in English.
nodes.response: We cannot change adjectives to make comparisons in French. To compare two people or things, we instead have to say that one is more or less 'something' than another. For example: 'Elle est plus grande que son frère.' She is taller than her brother.

nodes.misconception: The preposition 'a' stays the same regardless of the noun it precedes.
nodes.response: In English the preposition 'to' stays the same. In Spanish, the word 'a' changes to 'al' before masculine nouns and to 'a la' before feminine nouns.

nodes.misconception: Compassion (karuna) and loving-kindness (metta) are the same thing.
nodes.response: Loving-kindness is a pure love, selfless and not possessive. For example, wanting your friend to be happy without wanting anything in return. Compassion might arise if your friend is suffering and you want to help them and reduce their suffering.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe only performers participate in competitive events.
nodes.response: Competitions depend on various roles to run safely and efficiently. Performers can only participate if officials and organisers set up the event correctly.

nodes.misconception: That organisms are able to quickly adapt to the place where they live.
nodes.response: Referring to inheritance, explain that changes to organisms take time to evolve - responses to any environmental change is not instant. In some organisms, where reproduction is slow, responses can be too slow to avoid extinction.

nodes.misconception: Many learners think that the only way animals compete for resources is through physical aggression.
nodes.response: This lessons contains many examples of how animals and other organisms compete for resources.

nodes.misconception: Colouring everything in neatly makes a finished artwork.
nodes.response: Finishing an artwork isn’t just about colouring - it’s about choosing colours and adding details that help tell the story more clearly and powerfully.

nodes.misconception: Children might spot the unit of repeat and draw a repeating pattern rather than a symmetrical pattern.
nodes.response: Allow children to fold and unfold painted patterns on the mirror line to see where each part of the pattern would be reflected. Printing is a great tool to create symmetrical patterns.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not correctly identify the type of polygon (e.g., rectangle, square, parallelogram), leading to errors in determining the missing coordinate.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to first identify the polygon by examining the given vertices. Review the properties of common polygons (e.g., opposite sides of a rectangle are equal and parallel). Use visual aids or models to reinforce these properties.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils will not want to perform to a large audience.
nodes.response: Some pupils practise performing for a small group, and if they still feel they can't perform for a larger audience, they don't have to.

nodes.misconception: Success means performing actions perfectly.  Pupils land a jump, and their hands touch the floor.
nodes.response: Success refers to progress relative to a starting point. Any improvements to actions should be viewed as successful. Remind pupils to land with straight backs (not rounded) to help them 'land and stand' when they land a jump.

nodes.misconception: Mirror is the same as rotate.
nodes.response: Rotating complex or compound shapes will not always have the same outcome as when mirroring a shape.

nodes.misconception: 3D models are all made up of simple shapes that are scaled, moved and rotated.
nodes.response: Having only previously used object mode, learners may be unaware that geometry such as vertices, edges and faces can all be directly modified in edit mode. Working in edit mode gives a modeller greater freedom to create more complex models.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that complex sentences are superior to other sentences.
nodes.response: Show the effect of all sentences working in harmony via a model.

nodes.misconception: Electricity is stored within a cell or battery.
nodes.response: Children will model and learn that the battery provides the push to start the flow of electricity rather than being the store of it.

nodes.misconception: Some words have different meanings in day-to-day life compared to their meaning in science (cell, battery and circuit).
nodes.response: Teachings slides will discuss confusion with words circuit, cell and battery.

nodes.misconception: There are many misconceptions about diet, such as the need to cut out carbohydrates or fat because they are seen as responsible for weight gain.
nodes.response: A balanced diet requires all nutrients because each has its own benefits to the body and health. Cutting any of them out completely will negatively impact overall health and performance in sport and physical activity.

nodes.misconception: Varying the population size of an organism will not affect an ecosystem.
nodes.response: All organisms are important within an ecosystem. If one organism's population size changes, either as a result of a biotic factor (predation / disease) or an abiotic factor, it will affect all organisms within the ecosystem (to varying degrees).

nodes.misconception: Certain sports only need one type of component of fitness to be successful, e.g. 100m sprinter just needs speed.
nodes.response: Identify all the components of fitness that are useful for each athlete, determining why they are beneficial and justifying which is most important.

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused about how to write mixed numbers. Children may say 'five and one-eight, rather than five and one-eighth.
nodes.response: As a school, establish how mixed numbers will be recorded so that you have consistency. Ensure children are accurately expressing the fraction part.

nodes.misconception: Children might not notice that the two small and two large triangles are the same size.
nodes.response: Lay the tangram pieces on top of each other to physically explore and compare the size of each piece.

nodes.misconception: Chord sequences have to follow fixed rules exactly.
nodes.response: We use parameters as a guide to give a musical starting point for composing, but sometimes you might find other chords work. Always encourage pupils to try out a few ideas and perform their ideas so they can hear what they sound like.

nodes.misconception: Secondary chords shouldn't be used.
nodes.response: Secondary chords are important for interesting harmony and using them is a good idea. As you become a more experienced composer, you'll learn how to effectively use them. For now, a good rule of thumb is to use them sparingly.

nodes.misconception: For musical ideas, such as a riff or melody to contrast, they have to be totally different.
