nodes.response: Songs should have to have some continuity between the different sections. Highlight ways in which two melodically different ideas might still have some similarities ie. same rhythm, same shape, same number of notes, same initial motif.

nodes.misconception: Rhythm and beat are the same thing.
nodes.response: The beat is the playing or showing of the steady pulse, like the ticking of a clock. The rhythm is the pattern of sounds we play and sing over the steady beat.

nodes.misconception: Changing the tonality from major to minor will automatically make the music sound sad.
nodes.response: This is an oversimplification. All of the musical elements work together to create the character or mood of a piece of music.

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing isn't important. We can just do it if we have time.
nodes.response: Rehearsing helps us to practise and prepare, so our performance can be successful.

nodes.misconception: Embellishing a theme to create a variation makes a totally new composition
nodes.response: Although each variation is different, each is based on the initial theme, and pupils will be able to recognise aspects of the original theme.

nodes.misconception: You can fit any lyrics to a melody.
nodes.response: Lyrics or melody often have to be adjusted to fit each other. This can be because there are too many or too few words to fit in a phrase, or there are too many or too few notes to fit with the words. Trial and error is the best way to address this.

nodes.misconception: Pulse, beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Pulse is the underlying feeling of uniformed beats - it is the heartbeat of the music. When organised into metres, we then feel it as beats e.g. counting 1,2,3 1,2,3. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations.

nodes.misconception: Rhythms with shorter duration notes means the music is faster.
nodes.response: The speed of music is determined by the tempo.  A complicated rhythm with shorter notes can be played at a fast or slow tempo

nodes.misconception: Bigger or longer instruments usually create a higher pitched sound. Shorter or smaller instruments usually create a lower pitched sound.
nodes.response: Usually, the bigger the instrument, the lower the sound.

nodes.misconception: When composing, to make a melody interesting, it should be complicated with lots of different notes.
nodes.response: A simple melody with lots of repetition and stepwise movement often makes a more memorable melody.

nodes.misconception: When composing, choosing a wide variety of complicated rhythms is more exciting than using simpler ones.
nodes.response: When starting composing it's often good to use mostly simpler rhythms, and to make use of repetition.

nodes.misconception: The more complicated rhythms we use when we compose, the better our music will sound.
nodes.response: Successful music is repetitive, playable and memorable!

nodes.misconception: Bhangra is a traditional style of music that doesn't use music technology extensively.
nodes.response: Modern bhangra uses many of the tools that are available to musicians now, including different applications of music technology. It uses these to enhance the music, while still having its roots embedded in the traditional features of Punjabi bhangra.

nodes.misconception: Only 3rds, 5ths and octaves work as disjunct intervals in a melody.
nodes.response: This is not true: all intervals (except sevenths) can work effectively, as long as they jump between chord tones. If intervals jump to or from non-chord tones, the melody will sound ineffective.

nodes.misconception: Different voice types cannot sing any of the same notes.
nodes.response: The ranges of voices overlap, so there are some notes that can be sung by different voice types. For example, many notes that a bass can sing are also possible for tenor voices to sing.

nodes.misconception: A soundtrack should have music all the way through.
nodes.response: Careful use of silence can heighten the tension and help to emphasise the dialogue. There is a balance and silence can be used sparingly to elevate other parts of the music and the story, particularly after a musical build up.

nodes.misconception: Using all the white notes is C major will sound cheerful
nodes.response: It's important that the home note (in this case C) is used appropriately to reinforce the notes sounding like they are in C major.

nodes.misconception: May not identify which pattern block will fill the shape of a space.
nodes.response: Model filling spaces using trial and error, each time describing why it does / does not fit.

nodes.misconception: To compose a rhythm we need to consider notation first.
nodes.response: It is important to encourage pupils not to be restricted by only rhythms they can notate and for them to experiment with rhythmic patterns that they like musically. Highlight that individual note durations such as a crotchet are not rhythms.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not identify that ten tens are equal to 100 and cannot decompose 100 in this way.
nodes.response: Base ten blocks or a bead string are useful tools to allow pupils to compose and decompose 100 into equal groups of ten.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe only multiples of 10 can compose 100 and therefore do not see four groups of 25.
nodes.response: Focus on practical representations e.g. bead strings and base 10 blocks where 100 can be composed and decomposed.

nodes.misconception: Any group of objects can be counted in tens.
nodes.response: Identify groups that do and do not have 10 objects, drawing attention to the fact that colour, orientation and size are not relevant.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to use unitising to make connections between the composition of 1,000 or 10,000 and one million or ten million.
nodes.response: Use the suggested stem sentences e.g. '250 is one quarter of 1,000, so one-quarter of 1,000 thousands must be 250 thousand' to support developing the unitising concept.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to comprehend that e.g. 1,200,000 may have a digit '2' in the one hundred thousands place but is actually composed of 12 hundred thousands.
nodes.response: Even though the digit in the 100,000s place is a 2, the number 1,200,000 is composed of 12 hundred thousands because one million is composed of 10 hundred thousands.

nodes.misconception: The arrangement of the elements has no effect on the overall effectiveness of the composition.
nodes.response: A successful composition creates structure and activates the visual language to convey meaning.

nodes.misconception: Every shape must be moved on its own once on the workplane, so it is better to not make changes.
nodes.response: By grouping shapes that designers are happy with together, it makes it easier to move, rotate or scale them and make changes to the design.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are confused with when to use a comma and when not to use a comma.
nodes.response: A comma is used before "but" and "or" co-ordinating conjunctions. A comma is used after the adverbial clause if it is first in the sentence.

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3. This error continues when increasing amounts e.g increase 40 by 3% has a multiplier of 1.3
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to covert a percentage into a decimal we divide by 100. This applies with increase too e.g 120% has a multiplier of 1.2

nodes.misconception: Failing to understand the difference between simple and compound interest.  And, therefore finding the interest for one time period and multiplying it by the number of time periods.
nodes.response: Pupils can forget to transfer the year end balance as the starting balance of the next year.  Using repeated language can help.  E.g. "At the end of year 2 there was ... in the account, so, at the beginning of year 3 there was ... in the account."

nodes.misconception: Giving a density answer in the wrong units.
nodes.response: Read the question carefully and check the units of the mass and the volume.  It may be necessary to convert between metric units.

nodes.misconception: Using the total surface area of the solid rather than the area of the solid that is in contact with the floor/table.
nodes.response: Refer back to the high-heeled shoe and elephants foot example.  This should clarify that it is the area in contact with the foot that increases or decreases the pressure.

nodes.misconception: E.g 4.5 hours is 4 hours and 50 minutes
nodes.response: Encouraging pupils to use ratio tables to represent proportional relationships using minutes allows them to appreciate the multiplier of 60 when converting hours to minutes, or minutes to seconds.

nodes.misconception: Compound sentences are better than simple sentences all of the time.
nodes.response: Make it explicit to students that sometimes simple sentences can be more suitable in their writing; long does not equal better.

nodes.misconception: Compounds will have the same properties as the elements from which they are made.
nodes.response: Compounds usually have completely different properties from the elements from which they are made.

nodes.misconception: A higher compression ratio always means better quality.
nodes.response: A higher compression ratio actually means the file size has been reduced more. This often results in lower quality, especially with lossy compression.

nodes.misconception: Computational thinking techniques are only related to solving problems with computers.
nodes.response: The underlying principles of computational thinking can be applied in various aspects of life, even without any digital technology.

nodes.misconception: The CPU is the only important part of a computer.
nodes.response: The CPU is an important part of a computer system but a computer also needs memory, input, output, and storage to work properly. All parts must work together as a system.

nodes.misconception: You must look through every record individually to find an answer.
nodes.response: Sorting a computer database by fields allows you to quickly find answers without checking each record one at a time.

nodes.misconception: Increasing cores and clock speed improves performance.
nodes.response: It can improve performance but not always, as other hardware components may not be able to work that way.

nodes.misconception: Humans have no involvement in computer systems. They are run by computers and don't need humans.
nodes.response: Humans are still required for some elements of computer systems otherwise they are not providing anything useful that humans can use.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that as the concentration of a solution in excess changes, so does the volume of gas produced.
nodes.response: The slide deck uses graphical data to show that the same volume of gas is produced when different concentrations are used, so long as the reacting solution is in excess.

nodes.misconception: The reaction stops when the 'X' is no longer visible.
nodes.response: The disappearance of the cross only indicates that the sulfur precipitate has formed sufficiently to obscure the cross. The reaction itself continues beyond this point until all reactants are consumed.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that as the concentration of a solution in excess changes, so does the volume of gas produced.
nodes.response: The slide deck uses graphical data to show that the same volume of gas is produced when different concentrations are used, so long as the reacting solution is in excess.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the chemical definitions for 'concentration' and 'strength'.
nodes.response: Stress that concentration is a measure of particles interspersed throughout a specific volume of liquid.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the chemical definitions for 'concentration' and 'strength'.
nodes.response: Stress that concentration is a measure of particles interspersed throughout a specific volume of liquid.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the chemical definitions for 'concentration' and 'strength'.
nodes.response: Stress that concentration is a measure of particles interspersed throughout a specific volume of liquid.

nodes.misconception: Students think they should present lots of different ideas in an essay.
nodes.response: Whilst you should present lots of different knowledge, the knowledge should all form part of the same idea or argument.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only recognise the destructive force of ambition in the play.
nodes.response: It is also possible to consider the destructive force of guilt as central to the play.

nodes.misconception: Some people might think that letter writing has no place in modern society.
nodes.response: While other forms of communication have overtaken letter writing in popularity, letter writing is still necessary for many professional purposes.

nodes.misconception: A narrative written in the first person perspective conveys the writer's voice.
nodes.response: A narrative written in the first person perspective does not necessarily reflect the writer's voice but a construct.

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think they need to include as much as possible in their argument and support their ideas with overly long quotations.
nodes.response: Encourage students to select short and precise quotations to keep their writing concise.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that finishing a piece of writing is the end of the writing process.
nodes.response: When adults model enthusiasm for editing and improving, pupils will follow. Giving pupils a real outcome and audience for their writing also hugely increases the motivation to edit and improve.

nodes.misconception: The tail functions as a summary of the events.
nodes.response: Although a conclusion in any other form of writing would contain a summary, an article summary usually goes at the beginning.

nodes.misconception: Conclusions should include quotations.
nodes.response: Conclusions are about summing up your overall argument (your thesis) rather than continuing to develop it via analysis of new quotations.

nodes.misconception: Words with [tion] are cognates, therefore pronounced the same in English and French.
nodes.response: Although [tion] words are usually cognates, the sound is different and useful to revisit regularly.

nodes.misconception: All -ir verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense.
nodes.response: There are different groups of -ir verbs. Learn which verbs act like 'sortir', 'choisir' and 'venir' in the present tense.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that all polymers are only made up of one monomer. Also, confusing condensation reactions to think that it means to condense and take up less space.
nodes.response: Examples are shown where more than one monomer is used to make condensation polymers. Discuss what condensation is, and how condensation polymerisation produces water or other small molecules depending on the monomers used.

nodes.misconception: When pupils construct probability trees for scenarios where two marbles are removed from a bag, they may mistakenly subtract 2 from the denominators of the probabilities instead of 1.
nodes.response: Even though two marbles are removed from the bag at once, you can think of it at choosing one marble and then immediately choosing a second marble. At the end of the process, two marbles have been removed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may conflate the meaning of mutually exclusive with the meaning of independent.
nodes.response: Emphasise the word 'exclusive' in 'mutually exclusive' to suggest that one event excludes the other. Also, emphasise that the opposite of independent is dependent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the probability of event A given B, P(A|B), with the probability of event A and B occurring.
nodes.response: Use the context of the question to make a judgement about what probability is to be calculated. Try to avoid using, or draw attention to, potentially ambiguous language/notation. E.g. Is P(AB) referring to P(A given B) or P(B given A) or P(A and B)?

nodes.misconception: The order of conditions in an if/else if chain doesn't matter.
nodes.response: Conditions are checked in order, so earlier ones take priority.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may round the wrong way when finding the term number for a particular term value.
nodes.response: By calculating the terms either side of the non-integer value of $$n$$, pupils can easily determine what the rounded value of $$n$$ should be.

nodes.misconception: A condition only needs to be checked once.
nodes.response: Conditions need to be constantly checked to make sure the program reacts when the rule is met.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly assume that sportsmanship and gamemanship are the same thing.
nodes.response: Sportsmanship is positively conforming to the rules and etiquette of the sport, whereas gamesmanship is more negative because a performer may bend the rules to gain advantage.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that this book describes what life is like for the majority of people who live in Malawi.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the fact that the book is an autobiography and, therefore, is about the writer's own experiences.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that they should show or tell the key details of a story immediately.
nodes.response: Encourage them to think about mysteries and thrillers which keep the identify of the villain secret.

nodes.misconception: Students may assume that they need to identify and name specific structural devices in their structural analysis.
nodes.response: An answer simply referencing 'the beginning, middle and end' can make for a successful structural analysis.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that they have to tell a story chronologically.
nodes.response: Encourage them to consider how many books and films start with an exciting event and then go back to explain the exposition of the story.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think conflict is negative and should always be avoided.
nodes.response: In reality, resolving conflict is an important lifeskill that can also be the catalyst for creativity and innovation. It can challenge assumptions but does need to be managed constructively.

nodes.misconception: The only issue in protecting or exploiting the taiga is economic growth versus environmental conservation, without considering the social, cultural, and long-term ecological impacts.
nodes.response: The debate also involves factors such as the rights of indigenous communities, the potential long-term damage to ecosystems, and the need for sustainable management practices that balance both conservation and resource use.

nodes.misconception: Reading and re-reading a text is always an effective way to read for understanding and get the right answers to comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Simply reading and re-reading a text isn't always the most effective way to read for understanding. Using active reading strategies such as reading the title and reading and annotating the questions can boost comprehension and accuracy in responses.

nodes.misconception: Reflexive pronouns always come before the conjugated verb.
nodes.response: Reflexive pronouns can go in two plaes: before the conjugated verb or or after the infinitive, attached to it, with 2-verb modal structures.

nodes.misconception: Land use conflicts in glacial areas only concern conservationists and developers.
nodes.response: Land use conflicts are much more complex. While conservation groups and developers often have opposing views, there are other stakeholders involved, such as local communities, local governments, farmers, and tourism operators.

nodes.misconception: The verbs refuser, demander, essayer, laisser and éviter, are followed directly by an infinitive e.g. éviter faire (to avoid doing), refuser faire (to refuse to do).
nodes.response: These verbs are followed by 'de' plus an infinitive e.g. éviter de faire (to avoid doing), refuser de faire (to refuse to do).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they do not have enough information about a shape to determine whether it is congruent to another shape, when in fact they do.
nodes.response: Pupils could attempt the draw the shape based on the information that they have. They can then consider whether there are multiple way that the shape can be drawn while still satisfying all the given information.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up the meanings of congruence and similarity or struggle with the hierarchy of their nested sets (e.g. thinking that all similar shapes are congruent rather than the other way around).
nodes.response: Frequently refer to a Venn diagram showing the set of congruence shapes inside the set of similar shapes when examining pairs of shapes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spot congruent triangles if they only look for ASA.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add any further information to diagrams, like the third angle, before starting to prove congruence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make assumptions about diagrams containing a right angle incorrectly.
nodes.response: Remind pupils, that they cannot assume there is a right angle, just because it may look like the two edges are perpendicular to each other.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that the angle doesn't need to be in between the two known sides.
nodes.response: Use the Geogebra files to demonstrate that more than one triangle can be formed at times, and therefore it does not guarantee congruence between two triangles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that as the sides fix the angles, that this implies it is true conversely.
nodes.response: Use any regular polygon to highlight that the angles will always be the same, but the edge lengths are not always the same length. Regular polygons are always similar but not necessarily congruent.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make the connection between division and finding a fraction of a quantity.
nodes.response: Support children to see that the denominator of a unit fraction tells us how many equal parts the whole has been divided into and that that is the same as the divisor.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about paint pouring is that it’s purely random and anyone can do it without skill.
nodes.response: In reality, while paint pouring involves chance, artists use technique, colour theory and control to create intentional and successful compositions. It’s both creative and technical.

nodes.misconception: Circuits in the classroom are always safe to use.
nodes.response: Electricity is dangerous and needs to be carefully worked with. It can't always be seen and hazards need to be identified.

nodes.misconception: All devices on a network are connected directly to each other.
nodes.response: Devices are connected through a central switch. The switch makes sure messages go to the right device, without needing every device to connect to every other one.

nodes.misconception: Sending and receiving radio signals broadcasts to all devices that have radio capability.
nodes.response: A radio channel can be set which means that only devices on that same channel will receive those broadcasts.

nodes.misconception: Because a computer is connected to a network, it will be connected to the internet.
nodes.response: Not necessarily, it still needs a connection to the internet through a router. Networks can be created and used for many different purposes and that does not always have to involve being connected to the internet.

nodes.misconception: Any wire can connect any component and the circuit will work.
nodes.response: Specific pads must be connected correctly to complete a circuit. Circuits that are not complete will not work as charge will not be able to flow.

nodes.misconception: You always have to take a photograph from the front.
nodes.response: You can experiment with angles and frames to make your photographs more interesting.

nodes.misconception: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
nodes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

nodes.misconception: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
nodes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

nodes.misconception: The more times I read the text, the better I'll understand it.
nodes.response: Simply re-reading without purpose doesn't necessarily lead to better comprehension. Strategies such as reading through the text and questions, using each question to find the relevant part of the text, avoiding distractors, etc. are more effective.

nodes.misconception: I can use my knowledge of sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs) to successfully complete a read-aloud task.
nodes.response: Simply re-reading without purpose doesn't necessarily lead to better comprehension. Strategies such as reading through the text and questions, using each question to find the relevant part of the text, avoiding distractors, etc., are more effective.

nodes.misconception: To give an order or command to 'tú' (you, informal), you should use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
nodes.response: When talking to somebody familiar to you ('tú') with the affirmative imperative of an -ar verb, use the ending -a, and for an -er or -ir verb, use the ending -e. Irregular imperative verbs include: 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven', 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'.

nodes.misconception: To give an order or command to 'tú' (you, informal), you should use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
nodes.response: When talking to somebody familiar to you ('tú') with the affirmative imperative of an -ar verb, use the ending -a, and for an -er or -ir verb, use the ending -e. Irregular imperative verbs include: 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven', 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'.

nodes.misconception: Believing that a sedentary lifestyle only affects physical health through weight gain.
nodes.response: A sedentary lifestyle can have a negative impact on social and emotional health too.

nodes.misconception: That the benefits of international migration are limited to the country of origin (such as remittances).
nodes.response: Destination countries experience a wide range of social and economic benefits as a result of immigration.

nodes.misconception: Urban areas have more facilities and services than rural areas. As a result, rural areas can offer cities little in return.
nodes.response: Rural areas can offer the residents of urban areas a source of labour and produce. They can provide jobs in industries such as agriculture and opportunities for recreation and leisure.

nodes.misconception: The Cuban Missile Crisis made war more likely between the superpowers.
nodes.response: Both the US and USSR were shocked at how close they had come to war and were relieved to have avoided it. Further steps were agreed between both countries after the crisis had ended to make war less likely in future.

nodes.misconception: The USSR only experienced benefits from the Korean War.
nodes.response: Some new strains were created in Sino-Soviet relations due to limits on assistance from the USSR which were intended to avoid a direct conflict between the Soviets and Americans.

nodes.misconception: That poaching only involves 'trophy' animals like elephants and wild cats.
nodes.response: Poaching happens on a daily basis all around the world as a means of organised illegal activity (but in some cases for survival). It can include any animal species, large or small, that has a perceived value in its meat, skin, or another biproduct.

nodes.misconception: Pupils get confused with what numbers can be changed, many of them try to change the subscript numbers in formulae to balance equations.
nodes.response: Use the layout modelled in the slides to go through the examples using the 'circled method' and tell pupils that when adding more of a substance they must add all elements in the substance, e.g. 2MgO = (MgO)(MgO).

nodes.misconception: Pupils can struggle to link chemical formulae to what is happening on the atomic level and to what they observe during a chemical reaction.
nodes.response: Reinforce via demonstrations, modelling and diagrams via Johnstone's triangle.  One simple demo (e.g. magnesium + oxygen) = one model, one diagram and one chemical reaction equation.  Use progressively more complicated demos and build up from there.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that being able to complete calculations by substituting numbers into an equation is the same as fully understanding the relationship.
nodes.response: Include questions for which pupils are required to explain their understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not think that species of plants can become extinct in the same way that animals can.
nodes.response: Explain that if all of a particular species of plant, and its seeds, were destroyed then that plant would be extinct and none would ever live or reproduce again in the future.

nodes.misconception: If using slides, not recognising objects have been rearranged and counting all again.
nodes.response: Gather objects to manipulate (either under a visualiser with the whole class, or in front of a small group) so that children can clearly see that none have been added or taken away.

nodes.misconception: Biodiversity conservation can only take place in large natural habitats such as forests.
nodes.response: Biodiversity conservation can take place on a small scale, for example, by providing habitats in gardens and in urban areas. On a smaller scale still, seeds and embryos can be stored to help conserve gene pools.

nodes.misconception: If a prototype works, it can definitely be manufactured successfully.
nodes.response: Functionality doesn’t guarantee feasibility or success. A design might work in one-off form but fail in cost, scale, or sustainability when made commercially.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may add together costs that are expressed in different units (e.g. the cost of petrol in pence and the cost of a car park in pounds) without considering the implications on place value.
nodes.response: Writing units on your answers to each stage of working can help you to double check whether numbers in subsequent calculations are expressed in the same units.

nodes.misconception: Only soldiers on the front line had direct experiences of conflict.
nodes.response: Who does war impact? Besides being a soldier, what other roles do people have in war?

nodes.misconception: Priestley wrote 'An Inspector Calls' solely to change the views of his audience.
nodes.response: While it may seem that Priestley wrote 'An Inspector Calls' solely to change the views of his audience, it could also be argued that a 1945 audience would lean towards socialist ideals and therefore his play aimed to solidify these views.

nodes.misconception: That cliffhangers are only designed to make the reader carry on reading.
nodes.response: Cliffhangers can entice the reader to continue reading, but they can also create tension and subvert the reader's expectations.

nodes.misconception: That you should always use words with high modality (must, need, have to) to make your writing seem persuasive.
nodes.response: Exclusively using words with high modality can make your tone seem too direct and, therefore, make the reader feel defensive.

nodes.misconception: That the connection between the subject and object of a sentence doesn't matter in persuasive writing.
nodes.response: Using active or passive voice can affect the tone of your writing and how the reader responds to it.

nodes.misconception: Any use of personification will be effective in your writing.
nodes.response: In order to be effective, personification has to evoke a response that will make the reader feel persuaded by your argument.

nodes.misconception: That we should only consider the image that a simile offers us.
nodes.response: While the image may be particularly evocative, it's also useful to analyse the connotations of the comparative image as that can reveal layers to what the writer is trying to portray to the reader.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel that the Windrush experience was overly negative. Many people from the Caribbean experienced racial discrimination and found themselves in very challenging circumstances.
nodes.response: There were some positives that occurred as a result, including the setting up of the Notting Hill Carnival. Pupils may wish to explore this further.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be hesitant to start the problems due to uncertainty.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to try an approach and then reflect on whether there has been progress towards a solution. Deducing something you didn't already know if progress even if it does not seem like it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might consider the sole purpose of a non-fiction text is to inform.
nodes.response: Explore a range of reasons as to why the text might have been written. If possible, provide other non-fiction texts to allow comparison.

nodes.misconception: Students may think George The Poet's attitude towards his city is wholly negative.
nodes.response: George The Poet critiques certain aspects of London, particularly inequality and the way in which people often do not acknowledge the poverty in London.

nodes.misconception: That dialogue is a superfluous part of a text and can't be analysed in the same way as other structural or language features.
nodes.response: We can analyse dialogue by considering how it's structured, how the conversation is divided up, the use of punctuation and through the use of body language.

nodes.misconception: That a recurring image happens by accident - especially if it's an everyday object then it's likely to be meaningless.
nodes.response: Images are often symbols for deeper meaning in literature - especially everyday, domestic objects and then can represent ideas about the central theme of a text.

nodes.misconception: It’s OK if your background or characters move quite a bit between frames.
nodes.response: Even small changes can make the animation look jumpy. Keeping things still is key to making it look real.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget previously learnt rules and skills, leading them to chase after the ball instead of maintaining positions and structure.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that teamwork, communication, positioning and tactics can all lead to creating better chances, conceding less tries and scoring more tries.

nodes.misconception: That people didn't believe in magic in Shakespeare's time.
nodes.response: In Shakespeare's time, most people believed in magic and thought it could bring ill luck and misfortune.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the relics of St Columba were valuable.
nodes.response: The relics of St Columba were an important symbol of the Christian faith throughout the kingdom of Alba.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think revenge always involves killing people.
nodes.response: Revenge is the act of getting back at someone for something they did to you. This may involve stealing something or destroying something like property.

nodes.misconception: Constantine forced everyone in the Roman Empire to be Christian during his rule.
nodes.response: Constantine issued a law, the Edict of Milan, that protected all faiths from religious persecution so that everyone in the Roman Empire could practise the religion they wanted.

nodes.misconception: Students may not consider how materials are joined together.
nodes.response: When constructing a structure, we must think carefully about how they are joined together.

nodes.misconception: Children might think that any shape they draw around or use is a whole and the new shapes they create represent lots of wholes joined together.
nodes.response: Ensure the children understand that a whole can be anything and can change as you add parts to it. A piggy bank is a good analogy for this as you are constantly adding money to the whole and it is made up of many parts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that line graphs are only used for continuous data, where the points between those that are plotted have meaning.
nodes.response: Show children examples of graphs where there is no meaning between divisions on the x-axis (e.g. heights of children). Here, the points cannot be joined to make a line graph.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify specific quadrilaterals e.g. trapeziums when making them out of construction sticks as it can be harder to see the properties.
nodes.response: Using a ruler to draw the shape, using the inside of the construction sticks, can support pupils in seeing and identifying the key properties to help them classify a quadrilateral.

nodes.misconception: Plotting the midpoint of the class against the cumulative frequency.
nodes.response: Ensure that the pupils are clear that each cumulative frequency includes all values up to the upper boundary of each group.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use a protractor to draw a right angle.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they need to construct the right angle with a pair of compasses and a ruler, using appropriate construction techniques.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to draw the triangle using only a pencil and ruler, rather than construct it using a pair of compasses.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that if the task is to 'construct' then they must use their geometry equipment.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spot congruent triangles if they only look for ASA (angle-side-angle).
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add any further information to diagrams, like the third angle, before starting to prove congruence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not use a pair of compasses to find the two positions of the third vertex and instead just try to use their ruler.
nodes.response: You could encourage them to draw the circle before the angle each time.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not recognise that they have constructed congruent triangles to one and another.
nodes.response: Use a piece of tracing paper to show that the triangles are congruent to each other.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to construct the whole from a given part. They may misunderstand the total number of parts needed as this includes the original part.
nodes.response: Emphasise the denominator as the number of equal parts and ensure the learner sees the part they have as one of ___ equal parts. Take time to construct and deconstruct wholes from and into equal parts so learners know what to include in the count.

nodes.misconception: Thesis and topic sentences are the same thing.
nodes.response: A thesis must be overarching. A topic sentence can be much more specific.

nodes.misconception: An essay can contain random ideas about a theme/character as long as they link to the question.
nodes.response: Points in an essay should be planned tightly to expand upon and demonstrate the thesis statement.

nodes.misconception: Students try to include as much knowledge as possible in their responses.
nodes.response: Encourage students to be selective in their choice of ideas and to explain their choices.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use a protractor rather than a pair of compasses.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a construction is done using a pair of compasses and ruler.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may select additional cells which will cause their chart to look strange.
nodes.response: They can edit the data selected or delete the chart and start again.

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to order the list of data before finding the 5 key pieces of information.
nodes.response: Ask some pupils to stand at the front of the classroom.  Find the person in the middle, and pose the question "is they the median sized person?" Repeat with quartiles. This should highlight the importance of putting the numbers in order first.

nodes.misconception: Any form of data presentation can be applied to any data set.
nodes.response: There are many different types of data. Accurate data presentation means that appropriate graphical data presentation techniques are matched with the particular characteristics of a data set.

nodes.misconception: When using Desmos, incorrect brackets () are used to input raw data as elements.
nodes.response: [] are used to denote a set of data elements or elements. Encourage pupils to think about set notation when using Venn diagrams. Desmos will reject the use of () as they do not denote a set of elements.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the locus of a line is a rectangle.
nodes.response: Choose the vertices of their rectangle and ask if they are the same distance from the line as another point. Link to Pythagoras' theorem if necessary to highlight that the diagonal length will be longer.

nodes.misconception: 1) = not necessary to put into function, 2) students type in number to calculate, not click the cell
nodes.response: 1) the = at the start tells the spreadsheet to start a calculation, 2) clicking the cell means if input data chances, outputs auto-update

nodes.misconception: The frequencies on the frequency table are the angles you plot onto the pie chart.
nodes.response: Challenge the misconception by using an example with frequencies that clearly add to more or less than 360 e.g. {90, 90, 180, 90, 60)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may avoid using the pair of compasses and opt for a ruler instead.
nodes.response: Emphasise the efficiency and accuracy of using compasses instead of a ruler in the construction of their triangles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to assign the correct variable to the y-axis when graphing on a spreadsheet.
nodes.response: Explain that the word "series" is used to mean the y-axis in this software.

nodes.misconception: Task B Q2 - Pupils may choose to go up in 100s on the vertical axis.
nodes.response: Highlight that all of their data points will be in the bottom half of the graph and suggest going up in 50s.

nodes.misconception: That the stem always has to have the same number of digits.
nodes.response: Data with a range between 93 cm and 147 cm, draw the stem-and-leaf diagram but how do they write a key for it? Stress the leaf is the final single digit (all truncated so final digits have same place value), and all other digits form the stem.

nodes.misconception: There is often a lot of information to process, in order to complete a three event Venn diagram accurately. Pupils may confuse which region to complete.
nodes.response: A three event Venn diagram is easier to complete if information from intersecting events is completed first.

nodes.misconception: Time series graphs always use years as the time interval.
nodes.response: The time interval used in a time series graph depends on what the graph is intended to show.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may avoid using the pair of compasses and opt for a ruler instead.
nodes.response: Emphasise the efficiency and accuracy of using compasses instead of a ruler in the construction of their triangles.

nodes.misconception: The USA fought to prevent the construction of the Berlin Wall.
nodes.response: The USA believed that the construction of the wall meant they would no longer be threatened in West Berlin and used it as a valuable propaganda symbol.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may substitute incorrectly.
nodes.response: Each variable in a formula represents something. Substituting for one variable at a time may help ensure that values are in the correct places.

nodes.misconception: 'Es' + adjective + 'que' is always followed by the subjunctive.
nodes.response: The subjunctive is used after 'es' + adjective + 'que' when the action is uncertain, desired or not a fact. When the verb before 'que' expresses certainty, the action after 'que' is more a statement of fact and does not require the subjunctive.

nodes.misconception: 'Quiero', espero', 'deseo', 'prefiero' are always followed by infinitives.
nodes.response: Use 'quiero' + infinitive when you want to do something yourself. Use 'quiero' + 'que' + subjunctive when you want someone else to do something. Both forms often talk about the future, but the change of subject triggers the use of subjunctive.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the consumers in a food chain are organised in order of importance.
nodes.response: This lesson focuses on food chains showing how living things depend on each other for food. Individual living things in a food chain are just as important as each other.

nodes.misconception: Methane from cow flatulence causes global warming.
nodes.response: Ruminant animals (like cows and sheep) produce methane during digestion, 90–95% of this is released through eructation (burping). Methane is a greenhouse gas, which insulates our planet.

nodes.misconception: Kicks/throws and catches are not pushes and pulls.
nodes.response: Explicit explanation that kicks and throws are pushes, and catches are pulls; that pushes and pulls can involve short term contact.

nodes.misconception: Telling a story in dance (narrative dance) should include talking.
nodes.response: Whilst some dances include dialogue, in dance a story is usually communicated solely through actions and the performers are usually silent.

nodes.misconception: Counter balances should always involve pushing against our partner's hands.
nodes.response: We often start by connecting using our hands. Once skilled at countering our partner, we can find different points of connection or use different levels or directions to make our combined shapes more interesting and creative.

nodes.misconception: When being supported by someone you don't have to do anything.
nodes.response: It helps the 'supporter' if the 'supported' person is still, but they need to remain alert and actively hold their body firm, which makes it much easier for the 'supporter' to absorb their weight and return them to an upright position.

nodes.misconception: Foreign aid support packages, for instance Marshall Aid, are made up of just money.
nodes.response: Equipment such as heavy machinery or weapons, natural resources such as coal, as well as money, make up foreign aid support packages.

nodes.misconception: Polygamy is only done because men want lots of wives.
nodes.response: There are different types of polygamy (polygyny and polyandry) and there are different reasons why it might be practised.

nodes.misconception: Only certain 'qualified' people can add content to websites/create websites.
nodes.response: Anyone can add content to websites or create their own website. Services have developed that make it easy for anyone to upload content that can be shared across the world.

nodes.misconception: You must use the given rhythms.
nodes.response: The rhythms used are variations on traditional accompaniments that are passed down orally across generations. At this stage, any rhythm can be used as a starting point for getting pupils making music but this example covers the required techniques.

nodes.misconception: Taiko is the name of the style.
nodes.response: Taiko is Japanese for 'drum' and the drums make up kumi daiko which is ensemble drumming.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse site and situation.
nodes.response: The site of a settlement is its exact point on the surface of Earth and the situation describes it in relation to other human and physical features.

nodes.misconception: Priestley suggests that all gender roles have been successfully challenged by the end of the play.
nodes.response: A more nuanced view is that argaubly Priestley shows both progress and resistance, suggesting that while some characters challenge gender roles, societal change is slow and not fully realised.

nodes.misconception: As conquerors, the Normans could make any changes they wanted to.
nodes.response: The Normans were greatly outnumbered in England and William hoped to convince most English people that his was going to rule in the same way as King Edward the Confessor.

nodes.misconception: All types of variation can be measured in the same way.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the differences between discontinuous and continuous variation and how they can be measured.

nodes.misconception: Using a bar chart to plot continuous data. Features with continuous variation are only due to genetic factors.
nodes.response: The lesson explores why a histogram or line graph is the correct choice for plotting discontinuous data, and the idea that continuous variation is usually  influenced by many factors, including genetics, the environment and lifestyle.

nodes.misconception: All types of contraception work in the same way.
nodes.response: Different types of contraception use different methods, e.g., barrier, hormonal, surgical, intrauterine.

nodes.misconception: Harmonic rhythm means the rhythm that each chord plays.
nodes.response: Harmonic rhythm means how often the chords change, not the actual rhythm that the chords play. Show examples of the same harmonic rhythm different rhythms in the chords. Changing the harmonic rhythm is a useful tool to alter the feel of music.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that using contrast and juxtaposition in character descriptions means simply listing opposing traits without showing how they interact or affect each other.
nodes.response: It's important to show how the contrasting traits of characters impact each other. For example, instead of just stating that one character is kind and the other is cruel, describe a scene where their actions and behaviors directly conflict.

nodes.misconception: Not fully appreciating the huge size and diversity of Asia and the variations in climate and climate zones.
nodes.response: Use a globe/world map to highlight the size of the continent and the wide range of latitudes it covers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that contrast just means doing the opposite of someone else.
nodes.response: Contrast in dance means that you are doing something distinctly different, for example, performing different directions, levels and pathways to each other.

nodes.misconception: The physical geography of Nigeria is very similar everywhere in the country.
nodes.response: Nigeria has a range of physical features. These include rivers, plateaux, mountains, savannas, deserts and coastlines.

nodes.misconception: Christians and Muslims do not think about conduct in war.
nodes.response: Both Christianity and Islam think about possible limits and boundaries for war. Both religions aim for peace but accept war in limited conditions.

nodes.misconception: Creative writing is more effective when it focuses on something extraordinary.
nodes.response: Describing something very well known to you can be more effective as you're able to spend the time focusing on the little details.

nodes.misconception: Those in informal employment are unskilled.
nodes.response: Just because work is unregulated it does not mean that the workers are unskilled. While some workers may not have official certification of skills, they still possess expertise.

nodes.misconception: Abortion debates are always clearly pro-life vs. pro-choice.
nodes.response: Many positions are more nuanced, e.g., some people who identify as pro-life accept abortion in certain circumstances, and some who are pro-choice may personally oppose abortion but support the legal right to choose.

nodes.misconception: All Christians completely oppose euthanasia.
nodes.response: While many Christians strongly oppose euthanasia, some take a more compassionate approach, considering quality of life and situation ethics. Some may support assisted dying in certain circumstances, though this remains a minority view.

nodes.misconception: Christian worship only happens in a church and Muslims can only pray in a mosque.
nodes.response: Christians and Muslims can pray and worship at home and in other places as well as in congregational, communal services.

nodes.misconception: The UK is a safe and equal country, so Muslims do not suffer prejudice.
nodes.response: Many Muslims experience prejudice. Incidents of Islamophobia have increased in recent years.

nodes.misconception: The word 'actuellement' means 'actually'.
nodes.response: The word 'actuellement' means 'currently'.

nodes.misconception: The word 'actuellement' means 'actually'.
nodes.response: The word 'actuellement' means 'currently'.

nodes.misconception: I should start transcribing as soon as the dictation begins.
nodes.response: It is useful to listen to the full sentence once before transcribing to get an idea of its meaning. This will help you write the sentence down and check it during the second and third times that the audio is played.

nodes.misconception: I should start transcribing as soon as the dictation begins.
nodes.response: It is useful to listen to the full sentence once before transcribing to get an idea of its meaning. This will help you write the sentence down and check it during the second and third times that the audio is played.

nodes.misconception: Answers in listening comprehension questions are usually obvious.
nodes.response: Listening comprehension passages do not always make answers obvious, often containing synonyms and distractors to test your attention to detail.

nodes.misconception: Answers in listening comprehension questions are usually obvious.
nodes.response: Listening comprehension passages do not always make answers obvious, often containing synonyms and distractors to test your attention to detail.

nodes.misconception: When describing the photo in the writing exam, I should develop my sentences with justified opinions and a range of verb tenses.
nodes.response: You should keep photo description sentences short and simple in the writing exam.

nodes.misconception: When describing the photo in the writing exam, I should develop my sentences with justified opinions and a range of verb tenses.
nodes.response: You should keep photo description sentences short and simple in the writing exam.

nodes.misconception: I can choose which bullet points I answer for the essay questions in the writing paper.
nodes.response: You must answer all bullet points for the essay questions in the writing paper.

nodes.misconception: I can choose which bullet points I answer for the essay questions in the writing paper.
nodes.response: You must answer all bullet points for the essay questions in the writing paper.

nodes.misconception: I should develop my answers as much as possible for all parts of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to develop your answers extensively for all parts of the speaking exam. Remember to keep your answers short and succinct in the role-play section.

nodes.misconception: I should develop my answers as much as possible for all parts of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to develop your answers extensively for all parts of the speaking exam. Remember to keep your answers short and succinct in the role-play section.

nodes.misconception: We sing a song at the same dynamics all the way through.
nodes.response: We can help to convey the meaning of a song by varying the dynamics within a song. Singing with a range of dynamics also provides the listener with a broader range of sound to feel engaged with.

nodes.misconception: If we don't read music fluently, there's no point in looking at the written music of a song. We should just use the lyrics.
nodes.response: We can build on our understanding of pitch by identifying 'melodic shapes' or 'melodic contours' in the music. We can also find clues in the music to help us know how to sing each part of the song.

nodes.misconception: All sprites share the same program so the commands should all be placed in the same place in the programming area.
nodes.response: Each sprite has its own programming area. Sprites have different programs and the commands for each one are separated to allow them to be followed independently.

nodes.misconception: Medieval queens had little influence.
nodes.response: Eleanor was an intelligent and powerful queen, acted as regent, and was a key conspirator of the revolt.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often look directly down at their feet which shifts their head forward and throws them off their centre of gravity. Pupils are often overly tense when balancing.
nodes.response: For safety in parkour, pupils should focus just in front/ahead of their feet. Pupils should stay relaxed especially in their arms and shoulders.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often take-off flat footed or leaning backwards and look down during their jumps.
nodes.response: Pupils should take-off from the balls of the feet with knees and hips engaged, swinging their arms for more momentum. Pupils should ensure they keep their eyes locked on the landing spot from take-off to landing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to make contact with the shuttlecock when serving. Pupils may struggle to serve to the back of the court. Pupils may struggle to serve diagonally across the court or over the net.
nodes.response: Pupils could revert to serving by throwing the shuttlecock. Remind pupils to be side on with a wide stance to help generate more power. Make sure pupils feet are positioned correctly to serve diagonally. You can lower the net or use cones.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to co-ordinate, letting the ball bounce before serving underarm. Pupils struggle to aim diagonally across the court into the service box.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils are bouncing the ball in front and to the side of their body and that they are stood side on to help them make contact with the serve. Pupils need to make sure their feet are lined up correctly to help them aim diagonally.

nodes.misconception: Misconceptions about the roles of the kidneys, bladder and how the blood is 'cleaned' exist. Students often conflate/confuse these roles, muddle key terms or offer weak descriptions or explanations.
nodes.response: The roles of the kidney and bladder are clearly described, and diagrams and flowcharts are used to support the detailed explanations. Tasks that reinforce understanding and check for clarity and correct use of key words are included too.

nodes.misconception: Misconceptions about the roles of the kidneys, bladder and how the blood is 'cleaned' exist. Students often conflate/confuse these roles, muddle key terms or offer weak descriptions or explanations.
nodes.response: The roles of the kidney and bladder are clearly described, and diagrams and flowcharts are used to support the detailed explanations. Tasks that reinforce understanding and check for clarity and correct use of key words are included too.

nodes.misconception: Misconceptions about the roles of the kidneys, bladder and how the blood is 'cleaned' exist. Students often conflate/confuse these roles, muddle key terms or offer weak descriptions or explanations.
nodes.response: The roles of the kidney and nephron are clearly described, and diagrams and flowcharts are used to support the detailed explanations. Tasks that reinforce understanding and check for clarity and correct use of key words are included too.

nodes.misconception: A condition can have multiple possible answers.
nodes.response: A condition must always be either True or False in a program.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think there is only one ray of light for each point of light on the image.
nodes.response: Many rays of light pass through the lens from each point on the object, but all the rays from a single point arrive at a single point at the image distance. The rays from each point on the object arrive at corresponding points at the same distance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that you can only reply or respond when asked a question.
nodes.response: Give examples of how to respond to statements as well as questions. For example, how could you respond if someone said 'I love your coat'?

nodes.misconception: Pronouns are necessary to understand who the subject of a verb is in Spanish.
nodes.response: Pronouns are not necessary to understand who the subject of a verb is in Spanish. Verb endings tell us who the subject is.

nodes.misconception: Spanish needs a word for 'do' in questions: 'Do you have?' and 'What do you have?'
nodes.response: Spanish questions are easy to form. Yes/no questions have the same words as statements; to make a question you raise the pitch of your voice.  Information questions just add a question word, e.g. 'qué?' in front of the verb.

nodes.misconception: The verbs 'dire' and 'prendre' have the same verb endings.
nodes.response: ‘Dire’ and ‘prendre’ are high frequency -re verbs that have slightly different endings from each other, and from the most common -re pattern of endings.

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully convert and may leave the fractional part of the mixed number as an improper fraction e.g. 13/5 = 1 and 8/5
nodes.response: Support via questioning: How many fifths make one whole? How many full groups of five fifths can you make?

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully convert and may leave the fractional part of the mixed number as an improper fraction e.g. 13/4 = 2 and 5/4
nodes.response: Support via questioning: How many quarters make one whole? How many full groups of four quarters can you make? Emphasise the fractional part needs to have a numerator smaller than the denominator and take time to discuss why.

nodes.misconception: Lots of practice has taken place for pupils to convert between kilometres and metres. Pupils may expect kilometres and miles to have a similar relationship and expect one mile to equal 1,000 metres.
nodes.response: Bar models and double number lines are excellent visual representations of the relationship and should help pupils to form a more concrete understanding of the equivalence between units. Displaying these will provide a prompt for pupils.

nodes.misconception: It is tempting to say that we need to add 12 hours to any pm times to turn them into 24 hour times. However, it is a slight over-generalisation and does not apply to 12:00 pm up to 12:59 pm.
nodes.response: A teaching point is made of this and opportunities to apply the knowledge are given in the Practice tasks. It is worth really focusing on this as it comes up and paying attention to it while pupils are engaged with the Practice tasks.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will need to be able to count in steps of 7 and 12 to succeed in this lesson and have a good recall of the 7 and 12 times tables. Calculation errors will occur frequently if not.
nodes.response: Consider pre-teaching pupils still insecure with this, and / or providing scaffolding such as a times tables grid.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will need to be able to count in steps of 6 to succeed in this lesson and have a good recall of the 6 times table. Calculation errors will occur frequently if there in insecurity in this area.
nodes.response: Consider pre-teaching pupils still insecure with this, and / or providing scaffolding such as a times tables grid.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may see the prefix 'milli' and think it is related to 'million'.
nodes.response: Part of the lesson focuses on the etymology of the words and the fact that the prefix 'milli' means 'thousandth'; a millimetre is a thousandth of a litre and a millilitre is one thousandth of a litre. Consider displaying this in your environment.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not remember whether a certain larger unit is comprised of 10, 100 or 1,000 smaller units - all of these are explored at some point in this sequence of lessons.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing the etymology of the words, and have these displayed in your environment. The prefix 'kilo' means 'one thousand' while the prefix 'milli' means 'one thousandth'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils incorrectly multiply and divide by 100 when converting, or multiply and divide by 10 instead.
nodes.response: Continue to emphasise the relationship between one pound and 100 pence and encourage pupils to spot patterns e.g. £2 = 200 p, £3 = 300 p

nodes.misconception: Pupils see values like 0.25 l and convert it to 25 ml.
nodes.response: The lesson presents fractions and decimals as parts of whole circles. As long as pupils know that 1 l = 1,000 ml, they should see from the representation that 0.25 l = 250 ml as 250 + 250 + 250 + 250 = 1,000

nodes.misconception: Assuming that the decimal part of the number will entirely disappear in the subtraction step.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils line up the decimal points and use squares in their books for each digit.  This should allow pupils to see the parts that cancel each other out and what is left when finding the difference.

nodes.misconception: E.g. 30 mm is not equivalent to 3 cm because 30 is a larger number.
nodes.response: 10 mm are equivalent to 1 cm. Millimetres are smaller than centimetres and 10 mm are needed to make an equivalent length to 1 cm.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use an incorrect mathematical relationship to calculate the number of moles in a sample.
nodes.response: Depending on the type of substance (solid, solution or gas) a specific mathematical relationship for moles must be used. Challenge pupils to classify substances as (s), (aq), or (g) and apply correct mathematical relationship.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use an incorrect mathematical relationship to calculate the number of moles in a sample.
nodes.response: Depending on the type of substance (solid, solution or gas) a specific mathematical relationship for moles must be used. Challenge pupils to classify substances as (s), (aq), or (g) and apply correct mathematical relationship.

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that 300 cm is bigger than 3 m because 300 is a bigger number than 3.
nodes.response: 1 m is equivalent to 100 cm. So 3 m is equivalent to 300 cm. 3 m and 300 cm are equal in length or height.

nodes.misconception: E.g 4.5 hours is 4 hours and 50 minutes
nodes.response: Encouraging pupils to use ratio tables to represent proportional relationships using minutes allows them to appreciate the multiplier of 60 when converting hours to minutes, or minutes to seconds.

nodes.misconception: E.g 4.5 hours is 4 hours and 50 minutes
nodes.response: Encouraging pupils to use ratio tables to represent proportional relationships using minutes allows them to appreciate the multiplier of 60 when converting hours to minutes, or minutes to seconds.

nodes.misconception: Pupils understand they multiply by 100 when converting m to cm, but when converting m^2 to cm^2, fail to recognise the need to multiply by 100^2. This is also the same with volume conversions.
nodes.response: Illustrate a 1m^2 square and the equivalent 100cm^2 square, calculating the area and allowing pupils to see the equivalence of 1 m^2 = 10 000 cm^2. Also apply this to a 1m^3 and 100cm^3, thus allowing students to see 1m^2 = 100 000 cm^3.

nodes.misconception: Converting a fraction to a recurring decimal and then rounding the decimal, gives an accurate answer
nodes.response: The use of fractions is more preferred for accuracy than decimals. e.g 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 is not 0.3 + 0.3 + 0.3

nodes.misconception: Denominators that are multiples of 10 will give a terminating decimal.
nodes.response: Investigate the difference between powers of 10 and multiples of 10. e.g 7/30 and 7/100

nodes.misconception: The calculator rounds recurring/non-terminating decimals to 10 d.p. and it is not terminating.
nodes.response: The fractional form will give a clearer idea if the decimal equivalent is terminating or not.

nodes.misconception: The more decimal places there are, the greater the number.
nodes.response: Pupils can investigate this by looking at the numbers 0.23 and 0.1237 and using a common denominator or 10000.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse when to multiply or when to divide.
nodes.response: Encourage children to think about which unit of measure is larger e.g. km are larger than m. In a given amount, there will be fewer of the larger unit so we need to divide.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse when to multiply or when to divide when converting between units of measure.
nodes.response: Encourage children to think about which unit of measure is greater e.g. kg are greater than g. In a given amount, there will be fewer of the greater unit so we need to divide.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think there is only one ray of light for each point of light on the image.
nodes.response: Many rays of light pass through the lens from each point on the object, but all the rays from a single point arrive at a single point at the image distance. The rays from each point on the object arrive at corresponding points at the same distance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think there is only one ray of light for each point of light on the image.
nodes.response: Teach explicitly about many rays of light from each point on an object being brought together to form a bright spot on the image.

nodes.misconception: All reasons to support an opinion are equally convincing.
nodes.response: Pupils should know that some reasons are more convincing than others and the one used should be the most convincing.

nodes.misconception: All substances freeze when really cold, like water.
nodes.response: Show state changes using particle diagrams / kinetic energy model.  Challenge pupils to identify state given real world temperature data.

nodes.misconception: The energy of hot objects disappears (is destroyed) as they cool.
nodes.response: Placing a cup of hot water into a surrounding bowl of cold water that is warmed without the waters mixing demonstrates how surroundings are heated as energy is dissipated.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often stand behind the ball and hit up at it rather than moving their body to get into a better position.
nodes.response: You need to move your feet quickly to get to the side of the ball to use a smooth U shaped swing on the forehand or backhand and hit through the ball towards the net.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that when they are working in a team, everyone should stay together and do the same thing.
nodes.response: Sometimes, a good tactic to quickly complete a challenge is to split the challenge into smaller tasks and share them out amongst the team. A team can still be working towards the same goal, even if everyone is working separately on different tasks.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that coordination relates only to movement of their own body.
nodes.response: Coordination requires many different elements to work in combination. Improving balance, timing, ball tracking and the way we grip equipment can all contribute to improved coordination.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that being successful in sport relies on being able to run fast.
nodes.response: In many sports, having good coordination can be more valuable than speed or strength. Swimming, rowing, golf, skiing, rhythmic gymnastics, bowling and clay shooting all require coordination, but don't rely on speed.

nodes.misconception: Christianity spread from the Middle East to Europe and that is where the most ancient forms of Christianity began.
nodes.response: The Coptic church shows that Christianity had spread to the continent of Africa many centuries before the impact of colonialism.

nodes.misconception: Children might not identify the whole unit of repeat.
nodes.response: Describe the pattern aloud to hear the part that is repeated.

nodes.misconception: You can download and copy any images you find on the interent.
nodes.response: Some images on the internet are covered by copyright, which means they are not free to copy and use. You should check before you use any images you find online.

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that all medieval Islamic states must have been identical to one another.
nodes.response: Islamic states had similarities and differences (i.e. Cordoba had many Mediterranean influences; Persian influence was stronger in Baghdad).

nodes.misconception: Jehovah's Witnesses have the same beliefs as all other Christians.
nodes.response: Beliefs differ across the different Christian denominations. Jehovah's Witnesses hold some beliefs that make them a unique and distinct Christian denominiation, such as their rejection of the Trinity.

nodes.misconception: Correlation always means that one of the variables is affecting the other variable.
nodes.response: Correlation only suggests variables may be related somehow. Show examples where variables correlate because they both depend on population.

nodes.misconception: Transversals must intersect a pair of parallel lines.
nodes.response: Transversals can intersect any set of lines or line segments, no matter whether any of those lines or line segments are parallel or not.

nodes.misconception: Students often believe rusting refers to the oxidation of any metal, and that corrosion is linked to the hazard 'corrosive'.
nodes.response: Highlight the conditions required for rusting, and the general description of corrosion.

nodes.misconception: Students often believe rusting refers to the oxidation of any metal, and that corrosion is linked to the hazard 'corrosive'.
nodes.response: Highlight the conditions required for rusting, and the general description of corrosion.

nodes.misconception: The cost of a product only concerns raw materials.
nodes.response: Other factors like labour, overhead, distribution, and economies of scale affect the cost of a product.

nodes.misconception: Foreign companies always take profits back home and give nothing to locals.
nodes.response: Many TNCs invest in local jobs, training, and infrastructure, though some profits do return to the home country.

nodes.misconception: Managed retreat is when the land is allowed to erode without any direction.
nodes.response: Managed retreat allows for certain areas to erode or flood in a controlled manner. This approach is often chosen for low value land, where it can create natural habitats and reduce long term maintenance costs.

nodes.misconception: Hard engineering is always better than soft engineering.
nodes.response: While hard engineering can be effective, it is not always the best choice due to cost and environmental impact. Soft engineering can be more sustainable and less intrusive.

nodes.misconception: If you got your electricity from 100% renewable energy sources, then your carbon footprint would be zero.
nodes.response: Even if all your electricity comes from renewables, other parts of your lifestyle (like the manufacture of the clothes you wear, the food you eat, the technology you use) still produce carbon emissions elsewhere — often in other countries.

nodes.misconception: Children may continue counting in tens when they reach the ones, e.g. count 2 tens and 3 ones completely in tens. They may think arrangement of tens and ones affects how to count them.
nodes.response: Make deliberate errors to prompt discussion and refer back to previous stem sentences, e.g. 'The objects are in ones, so I can count them in ones.' Present tens and ones in non-standard arrangements, so children practise always counting tens first.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be secure with the principles of counting.
nodes.response: Encourage any and all opportunities to count small collections of objects considering ways in which to count efficiently. Model counting using one-to-one principles and strategies such as organising collections to support counting all.

nodes.misconception: When objects are moved or rearranged, children may re-count them to find 'how many'.
nodes.response: Setting this lesson up practically will help reinforce that there is no need to re-count the set of objects - show they have just moved.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle crossing over the hundreds boundary (99 to 100, and back from 100 to 99).
nodes.response: It may help pupils to understand that 100 is ten lots of ten. This is the lesson focus and pupils will have lots of practise opportunities.

nodes.misconception: Iteration means a program will repeat something a set number of times.
nodes.response: Count-controlled iteration will repeat a sequence of commands a set number of times. Condition-controlled iteration will repeat a sequence of commands until a condition is met and so the number of times it will repeat can never be predicted.

nodes.misconception: A loop with a high number always makes a big shape.
nodes.response: The number in the loop affects the number of sides, not the size. The fd value controls the size.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the number of groups with the total, so 3 groups of 5 may be counted as 3 and not 15
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for children to identify both the number of groups as well as the total throughout. Encourage the use of the stem sentences to support their articulation of this.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the number of groups with the amount altogether, for example, they may count 4 groups of 10 as 4 not 40  They may also confuse the number of groups with the group size.
nodes.response: Draw a ring around each group of 10 whilst using the stem sentence to help describe what you are seeing as you identify each group.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be sure which unit to count in. They may confuse the size of the group with the number of groups, for example saying 5 groups of 2 instead of 2 groups of 5.
nodes.response: Encourage children to draw a ring around each group as they count the groups and display and use the stem sentence to help them describe this.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the number of groups with the amount altogether, for example, they may count 3 groups of 2 as 3 not 6  They may also confuse the number of groups with the group size.
nodes.response: Draw a ring around each group of 2 whilst using the stem sentence to help describe what you are seeing as you identify each group.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes with counting, particularly when crossing a 100s boundary.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the pattern to help them count accurately, using this to predict the next number in the count.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to count over the boundaries for multiples of ten thousand and one hundred thousand.
nodes.response: Ensure children focus on the number of thousands they have within the number. This should effectively be the same as counting in ones over tens and hundreds boundaries, with the exception of the unit changing from ones to thousands.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to cross 100s boundaries when adding 10s.
nodes.response: Base ten blocks can help with this concept. It also helps if children's attention is drawn towards the patterns in the number system.

nodes.misconception: When objects are in 10s, children may count the number of tens rather than the amount altogether.
nodes.response: Introduce errors involving confusion between the number of tens and the amount altogether for children to reason about.

nodes.misconception: Children may only think of 'ones' in terms of the extra ones after the tens have been grouped, so may fail to see 45, for example, as 45 ones as well as 4 tens and 5 ones.
