nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to define a product that they wish to design and make at this point. They become fixated on a design.
nodes.response: Pupils need to keep their design brief open so that it does not create design fixation.

nodes.misconception: A specification is written after research and then referred to once the product is manufactured.
nodes.response: Design requirements should be used throughout the iterative journey (not just at the end!) to test concepts and make effective design decisions to creatively develop the product into a successful design.

nodes.misconception: Design is about making things that have never been made before.
nodes.response: Design is about planning and making something.  It doesn’t need to be something that has never been done before, it can be to improve an existing object to make it work or look better.

nodes.misconception: That a single image can help us to understand how quality of life is different in distant places.
nodes.response: While images can be of use they can not depict all aspects of life, moreover each image can only ever show a single place or group of people. Within any country there is a diversity of lived experience.

nodes.misconception: The arithmetic sequence 5n+2 starts at 7 so the linear equation y=5x+2 'starts' somewhere.
nodes.response: y=5x+2 has no start and no end; it goes on infinitely. However, all linear equations have a y-intercept and this helps define them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the domain and the range.
nodes.response: Drawing the graph of the function and labelling the axes correctly will help pupils connect domain and range.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that we can chop down and destroy forests without affecting ecosystems.
nodes.response: The lessons explores how deforestation disrupts key processes in the carbon cycle and the water cycle, and how this can increase climate change, flooding, and put our food security at risk.

nodes.misconception: Indonesia is a large island with a small population.
nodes.response: Indonesia is not one island: it is an archipelago, a group of over 17 000 islands. Nor does it have a small population: it’s population is over 270 million people.

nodes.misconception: Deforestation is primarily caused by small-scale farmers cutting down forests for subsistence farming.
nodes.response: Deforestation is driven by large-scale commercial activities, such as industrial agriculture (like palm oil and soy), logging, and cattle ranching, which are often linked to global demand.

nodes.misconception: The same tools and methods are used for both small-scale and industrial manufacturing.
nodes.response: The scale of production heavily influences tool choice, speed, accuracy and repeatability.

nodes.misconception: Laminating is when paper or card are covered in clear polymer.
nodes.response: Laminating means sticking several layers of material together, the clear polymer coated paper or card process is encapsulation.

nodes.misconception: Rounding prematurely during multi-step calculations.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of fractions (where possible) or the use of the 'ANS' button.

nodes.misconception: Ordinary citizens don't really have any power or impact in the legal system.
nodes.response: Citizens can play key roles, like serving as jurors, becoming magistrates or special constables, and even push for legal reforms, as shown by trade unions helping pass the Minimum Wage Act.

nodes.misconception: That to do well in a discussion or debate you must shout the loudest and interupt others.
nodes.response: A successful deliberative discussion involves consideration, weighing different viewpoints and respect.

nodes.misconception: That identity only refers to personal characteristics like gender, race, or ethnicity.
nodes.response: Identity can also include factors like socioeconomic background, religion, sexual orientation, disability, nationality, or even personal experiences.

nodes.misconception: The UN is always effective in the actions it takes.
nodes.response: The UN has been a powerful force for good in the world and has secured many victories. However, there have also been actions taken by the UN which have not been fully effective or only made marginal gains.

nodes.misconception: The age of criminal responsibility is the same worldwide.
nodes.response: The age of criminal responsibility varies across countries. For example, in Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago it’s seven, while in Spain it’s 14.

nodes.misconception: That memorising the speech, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
nodes.response: An effective speech will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing speech.

nodes.misconception: The role of an audience member isn't particularly important.
nodes.response: Emphasise the power of a supportive and respectful audience. Being an encouraging audience member can help peers succeed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: The teacher says a word or phrase in a loud, clear voice, and the children have to echo it back as loudly and clearly as they can.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: The teacher says a word or phrase in a loud, clear voice and the children have to echo it back as loudly and clearly as they can.

nodes.misconception: Pupils speak too fast.
nodes.response: Pupils can use note cards to remind them when to pause for emphasis and to control speed.

nodes.misconception: That students should constantly be changing the pitch of their voice when speaking.
nodes.response: Pitch is an effective tool when delivering speeches. It should be used to make a speech more engaging and shouldn't be used arbitrarily.

nodes.misconception: That memorising the speech, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
nodes.response: An effective speech will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing speech.

nodes.misconception: Clear and confident delivery of speeches requires a consistent pace of delivery throughout.
nodes.response: Model the delivery of a sentence which starts at pace, but slows down to draw attention to particular vocabulary choices.

nodes.misconception: Liberation is not always about escaping suffering.
nodes.response: Many Black women find strength in their faith and ability to survive hardship, not because God removes their suffering, but because His liberating presence sustains them.

nodes.misconception: You can't analyse stage directions in depth.
nodes.response: The closing stage directions of 'Leave Taking' are integral in understanding Pinnock's final messages about the characters and themes.

nodes.misconception: Del is uninterested in obeah until Mai realises it is her calling.
nodes.response: Del's interest in obeah is foreshadowed from Scene One onwards.

nodes.misconception: Dance music is usually in 4/4.
nodes.response: While the majority of modern Western dance music is in 4/4, dance music around the world (and throughout history) often uses different time signatures, including 3/.4, 6/8 and 12/8, as well as others.

nodes.misconception: Pythagoras' theorem is just a relationship between the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
nodes.response: Whilst this is true, Pythagoras' theorem can more visually be represented as three squares whose sides are equal in length to the three sides of the triangle. The sum of the areas of the two smaller squares is equal to the area of the larger square.

nodes.misconception: If we see a reflexive pronoun, e.g., 'uns' or 'sich', this always means that the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the verb are the same.
nodes.response: Some plural reflexive verbs are reciprocal, meaning the action of the verb is done 'to each other' rather than 'to oneself'. The word 'gegenseitig' can be used to emphasise reciprocal use. Otherwise, use context to work out which meaning is intended.

nodes.misconception: When defending and marking, pupils focus too much on the ball instead of watching their opponent.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to always be aware of the player they are marking by constantly checking where they are. Discourage pupils chasing after the ball when their teamate is closer to it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush in towards the player with the ball when defending. Often two pupils move towards the same attacker.
nodes.response: Pupils need to stay on their toes ready to react and avoid diving in. Communication will prevent players from marking the same player and risk leaving other players open.

nodes.misconception: Kant's deontology means that actions such as killing are always wrong.
nodes.response: The categorical imperative doesn’t mean the same in every situation because it takes the context into account, e.g., killing is generally wrong it can be justified where the intention is to protect life.

nodes.misconception: Artists will always depict the texture of water in the same way.
nodes.response: Remind children that although water itself always feels wet and smooth, artists might use their materials to show the water being bubbly, smooth or rough. Artists can describe this as the texture of the water.

nodes.misconception: That the direction of the prevailing wind is the direction that the wind is blowing in at any particular time.
nodes.response: The prevailing wind is wind from a particular direction that is most frequently experienced in a location. Winds can come from other directions, especially in stormy conditions, but they are not the same as the prevailing wind.

nodes.misconception: The weather associated with an anticyclone stays the same all year around.
nodes.response: Students will analyse images to identify how anticyclones may bring different weather in the summer and winter.

nodes.misconception: 'Aber' and 'sondern' mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use 'aber' to contradict a preceding statement that does not contain a negative. Use 'sondern' to mean 'but' or 'rather' following a negative statement.

nodes.misconception: The only versions of Grimm brothers' fairy tales that exist are written in the imperfect tense.
nodes.response: There are many versions of the Grimm brothers' fairy tales. Many are written in the imperfect tense but there are also simpler, modern adaptations written in the present or perfect tenses, especially in children's books.

nodes.misconception: Interior angles always sum to 180 times the number of component triangles it is split into.
nodes.response: If line segments drawn make new vertices in the polygon, its angles won't contribute to the sum of interior angles in the initial polygon.

nodes.misconception: Verbs never change their spelling to agree for gender or number.
nodes.response: Past participles with 'être' verbs do agree for gender and number. Embedding this knowledge requires practice, a component of which can be practice of sound-symbol correspondences [i], [u], [é], [SFC], and [SFE].

nodes.misconception: French adjectives always come after the noun they are describing.
nodes.response: There are five categories of adjectives which come before the noun: beauty, rank, age, good/bad, size/quantity. Practise using these before the noun alongside other adjectives which come after the noun.

nodes.misconception: Always use the infinitive to translate the '-ing' verb form into French.
nodes.response: The infinitive used as a noun in French translates the idea of 'doing' something, e.g. 'fumer est mauvais' ('smoking is bad'). The present participle translates the present continuous in English, e.g. 'étant célèbre' ('being famous').

nodes.misconception: Always use the infinitive to translate the '-ing' verb form into French.
nodes.response: The infinitive used as a noun in French translates the idea of 'doing' something, e.g. 'fumer est mauvais' ('smoking is bad'). The present participle translates the present continuous in English, e.g. 'étant célèbre' ('being famous').

nodes.misconception: Words will stick in my memory if I read them enough times.
nodes.response: It is the act of reaching for words that roots them deeper in memory, so testing oneself or working in pairs to try to recall words from memory is the most effective learning strategy for holding onto words in your long term memory.

nodes.misconception: Words will stick in my memory if I read them enough times.
nodes.response: It is the act of reaching for words that roots them deeper in memory, so testing oneself or working in pairs to try to recall words from memory is the most effective learning strategy for holding onto words in your long term memory.

nodes.misconception: It is better to give long answers in the role-play task than short responses.
nodes.response: The role-play task is a short exercise requiring relevant answers to each bullet point that contain a verb. Longer answers are not appropriate to this task.

nodes.misconception: It is better to give long answers in the role-play task than short responses.
nodes.response: The role-play task is a short exercise requiring relevant answers to each bullet point that contain a verb. Longer answers are not appropriate to this task.

nodes.misconception: When using 'depuis' (for, since), sentences are framed in the past in French.
nodes.response: In French, when using 'depuis' to describe an action that started in the past but continues today, frame the sentence in the present tense.

nodes.misconception: 'Que' can be used in a subject-relative clause, e.g. 'le prof que s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.'.
nodes.response: 'Que' introduces an object-relative clause where a new subject and verb is used, e.g. 'la voiture que je voudrais est très chère'. 'Que' shortens to 'qu'' in front of a vowel.

nodes.misconception: 'à' is always translated as 'to' or 'at'.
nodes.response: 'à' can be translated as 'to', 'at', 'in', 'on' or 'about', depending on the context. Particular care should be taken with verbs followed by 'à', e.g., 'réfléchir à' could be translated as 'to think about' or 'to reflect on'.

nodes.misconception: 'Il y a' always means 'there is'.
nodes.response: 'Il y a' can mean 'there is' or 'there are' and can be used with singular or plural nouns.

nodes.misconception: In the perfect tense, the pronouns y and en go before the past participle.
nodes.response: Both y and en go before the auxiliary verb in the perfect tense e.g. il y est allé, il en a mangé.

nodes.misconception: 'Elle' meaning she is pronounced with an [i] sound at the start.
nodes.response: 'Elle' is pronounced with a hard e sound like in egg.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives in French have only one form that can be used to describe any noun, like English.
nodes.response: In French, adjectives may change their spelling and/or sound when describing a woman, girl or feminine noun. This is called the feminine form.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to name the shape of the faces that cannot be seen in drawings of 3D shapes.
nodes.response: Provide 3D shapes for children to handle alongside the drawings. Encourage them to visualise the shape rotating to help them identify and describe each face of the shape.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a curved surface is a face, or the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is an edge.
nodes.response: Handle the shapes and discuss how faces and edges feel. Write these descriptions down and use them to help the children distinguish between faces and curved surfaces, or curved lines and edges.

nodes.misconception: Children may mistake a 'triangle-like' shape for a triangle.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities to explore and handle cut-outs of triangles and triangle-like shapes. Describe and compare how the sides and corners feel. Touch the part of the shape that shows that it is not a triangle and explain how you know.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may record two-digit hundredth values incorrectly. For example 12 hundredths as 0.012
nodes.response: Use place value counters to represent the number and demonstrate the regrouping of ten hundredths.

nodes.misconception: Pupils put a digit in the ones column instead of the tenths column to represent a number of tenths.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents, linking back to the place value chart and the role of the decimal point.

nodes.misconception: When crossing the tenth boundary, pupils count ten hundredths as 'zero point zero ten'.
nodes.response: Use cardinal representations to guide the pupil's counting so ten hundredths and one tenth equivalence can be discussed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils write whole numbers as tenths incorrectly, for example as eight tenths not eighty tenths.
nodes.response: Reiterate that ten tenths are equal to one whole so twenty tenths are equal to two wholes. Continue this to build generalisation.

nodes.misconception: Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase, and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: When we multiply an integer by a unit fraction, the effect is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. It results in a decrease.

nodes.misconception: 'Es' and 'son' mean the same.
nodes.response: 'Es' means 'she, he, it is' and 'son' means 'they are'.

nodes.misconception: To say 'my mum is a teacher', it's 'mi madre es una profesora.'
nodes.response: In Spanish, we do not need the indefinite article ('un', 'una') when referring to jobs, so we would just say 'mi madre es profesora.'

nodes.misconception: To talk about completed events in the past with -ar verbs you always take off the -ar ending and add -é in the 1st person singular ('I').
nodes.response: For -ar verbs ending in -car, you remove the -car and add -qué in the 1st person singular, for example; 'sacar' - 'saqué' - 'I took out'.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse groups with number of items.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling of groups, demarcating groups and physically placing items into groups e.g. a bundle of straws with an elastic band.

nodes.misconception: Children may say that they do not know the name of a polygon when it is an irregular and it does not look familiar to them.
nodes.response: Show children a wide range of pentagons and count the sides and vertices of each shape. Agree that these shapes are all pentagons even though they all look different. Repeat with hexagons and octagons.

nodes.misconception: The [r] sound in German is always the same, regardless of where it appears within the word.
nodes.response: German [r] can be pronounced in different ways. [r] is a gentle ‘rolling’ vibration pronounced from the back of the throat, if [r] is at a syllable start, after a consonant or between two vowels. [r] is a gentle ‘ah’ sound after a long vowel.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'c' makes a soft sound in front of 'a', 'o' and 'u'.
nodes.response: The letter 'c' makes a hard sound in front of 'a', 'o' and 'u'. We use the cedilla 'ç' to make a soft sound in front of 'a', 'o' and 'u': français.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives do not change spelling based on gender or number, as in English.
nodes.response: Adjectives do change spelling based on gender or number, for example: 'un chien amusant', 'deux tortues amusantes'.

nodes.misconception: There is just one way of referring to 'they' in French, as in English.
nodes.response: There is both a masculine and feminine form of the pronoun 'they'. Use 'ils' when referring to a group of boys or a group of boys and girls, and use 'elles' when referring to a group of girls.

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go after the noun in French, the opposite to the word order of nouns and adjectives in English.
nodes.response: Most adjectives do go after the noun in French, however some adjectives go before the noun, these are pre-nominal adjectives. They refer to age, beauty, goodness and size (BAGS).

nodes.misconception: Objects rotate only either less than a full turn or more than a full turn.
nodes.response: Take time to discuss the purpose of the object in question and clarify the difference between what an object should do and could do.

nodes.misconception: Once a word is learnt, it stays in the memory forever.
nodes.response: Words need revisiting from time to time in order to not disappear from the memory.

nodes.misconception: 90 degrees is classified as an acute angle and 180 degrees is classified as an obtuse angle.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to classify angle sizes and build towards understanding that acute angles are between 0-89 degrees and obtuse angles are between 91-179 degrees. Classifying multiples of right angles as a separate group may help.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may remember to scale one of the sides (or pairs of sides) of a shape but forget to scale the others.
nodes.response: Focus attention on what it means when a shape is similar, drawing on examples and non-examples to support learners to understand how scaling affects all side lengths.

nodes.misconception: Using addition and subtraction to connect the parts and whole in a ratio context.
nodes.response: Model all relationships at this stage using the language and notation of multiplication and division.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may record different volumes for objects if they measure with inconsistent units (for example: different sized cubes).
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to compare the volume of the same object measured with two different units. Discuss what you notice and draw out the importance for a consistent unit of measure.

nodes.misconception: 'Nicht' is always used to negate.
nodes.response: You can use 'nicht' or 'kein(e)' to negate a sentence. 'Nicht' is used with adjectives whereas 'kein, keine' is used with nouns.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might miscount the number of squares moved horizontally or vertically, resulting in an inaccurate translation.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to count the number of squares carefully from the original position, possibly using a ruler or finger to help guide their counting. Practice with simpler shapes before moving to more complex polygons.

nodes.misconception: Some children can struggle to identify which direction a turn is in when it does not start from a 12 o'clock position on a clock.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities to explore making clockwise and anticlockwise turns that start from many different positions and not always facing up or at the 12 o'clock position.

nodes.misconception: 'Il a' and 'il y a' sound similar and can be confused.
nodes.response: 'Il a' and 'il y a', despite sounding similar, are in fact different and have different meanings. 'Il a' means 'he has', 'il y a' means 'there is' or 'there are'.

nodes.misconception: The adjective 'cher' simply adds an -e in the feminine form.
nodes.response: The adjective 'cher' does add an -e in the feminine form, but there is an additional change as the first e changes to è in the feminine form: 'chère'.

nodes.misconception: The verb 'ir' is a regular verb so I can apply the regular conjugation rules for -ir verbs.
nodes.response: The verb 'ir' is irregular, therefore, it does not follow the normal conjugation rules. To say 'I go' we say 'voy', 'you go' - 'vas' and 'she, he, it goes' - 'va'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to write the transformation as two transformations, a rotation of 180° followed by an enlargement by a positive scale factor, rather than a single transformation.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a single transformation is more efficient than multiple transformations.

nodes.misconception: Line segments connecting corresponding points on an image and object can intersect each other.
nodes.response: Corresponding point line segments after a reflection never intersect. If they do, then corresponding points have not been paired correctly.

nodes.misconception: "Right means clockwise" and "left means anti-clockwise"
nodes.response: This is only true when referencing the top of the object being rotated. Rotating "left" and "right" is incorrect for all other vertices.

nodes.misconception: Students may count between the closest two vertices rather than corresponding points.
nodes.response: Remind frequently that it needs to be between corresponding vertices, labelling may help for this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use division instead of fractional scale factors.
nodes.response: Dividing by 2 gives the same result as multiplying by a half. However, the scale factor is defined as a multiplier, not a divisor.

nodes.misconception: The best place I've ever been to has to be in another country.
nodes.response: The best place you have been to can be abroad but it doesn't have to be, it can be somewhere you have visited with family or to see family like another town or can be a place you went to on a day trip like a theme park, museum or zoo.

nodes.misconception: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts.

nodes.misconception: White space on a map means there is nothing there.
nodes.response: White space means that the land cover there is grassland or farmland.

nodes.misconception: Maps show how to get from one place to another.
nodes.response: A map can show a small area in detail. We use maps as representations of places. We can study an area in detail using a map.

nodes.misconception: Harmony and tonality are the same thing.
nodes.response: They are related, though not the same. Tonality refers to the set of notes that a piece is based on (e.g. the D minor scale) and refers to a whole piece or section of a piece. Harmony explores individual chords, chord sequences and harmonic devices.

nodes.misconception: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts.

nodes.misconception: A description of timbre should only describe the sound qualities heard.
nodes.response: While this should be included, it is also important to remember to describe the instruments that have been used, and if they from a particular ensemble. Remember that one instrument can also create multiple timbres.

nodes.misconception: Pupils regularly think that neutralisation produces a neutral (i.e. pH 7) solution.
nodes.response: Stress that neutralisation occurs from a complete reaction between an acid and base, which usually occurs between strong acids and strong bases.  If a weak acid or weak base is used, the salt solution produced may be alkaline or acidic respectively.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that descriptions of setting only serve as background and do not contribute to character development or tone of a piece of writing.
nodes.response: Settings are integral to storytelling as they can reflect and enhance a character's emotions, personality, and the overall tone of the scene. For example, a gloomy, rainy setting can mirror a character's sadness or create a foreboding atmosphere.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might be able to think of adjectives, but they may not be specific to the character of the goats.
nodes.response: Share examples and non-examples of adjectives that can be used to describe the goats. Read extracts of the story to help pupils to understand that a character can be described in a certain way because of their actions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistake an expanded noun phrase as a sentence.
nodes.response: Discuss what is missing from the expanded noun phrase to show it is not a sentence (a verb and a capital letter or punctuation mark to end a sentence). In the subsequent lessons, pupils will build their expanded noun phrases into sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start describing the details of the Clock home in the frst paragraph.
nodes.response: Clearly remind pupils that paragraph one should be describing where the Clock family home is located in relation to the main house. Paragraph two will give details of their home.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only refer to nouns modelled to them.
nodes.response: Make use of the illustrations in the book as well as other visuals of London to help pupils become more familiar and generate their own ideas. Videos can assist with creating a more sensory experience.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to join more than two ideas using "and".
nodes.response: Remind pupils that "and" only likes to be used once in a sentence, joining only two ideas.

nodes.misconception: Timbre alone creates a musical story.
nodes.response: All the musical elements need to work together to create a musical story. A glockenspiel can be many things depending on how it is played - not just a polar bear.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to generate appearance words and may use words like 'scary' to describe his appearance as well.
nodes.response: Provide images to support them with generating ideas and explain that they can describe the appearance of specific parts of the troll e.g. 'bushy hair', 'sharp teeth', 'jagged claws', 'green skin' etc.

nodes.misconception: The main thing I need to remember for long-form answers is the elements acronym (e.g. MAD T SHIRTT).
nodes.response: These acronyms do help us to remember what the elements are, but it is much more important in these longer descriptions to ensure answers are clearly structured, thorough and concise, and that correct technical vocabulary is used for each element.

nodes.misconception: Students often do not use descriptions in functional writing frequently enough.
nodes.response: Descriptive language massively enhances functional writing. Anecdotes are a brilliant example of how descriptive writing can be used to connect to the reader/audience.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to describe themselves.
nodes.response: Before describing themselves, model sentences by describing your pupils providing them with vocabulary, 'You are...'.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is one way of referring to a group of people: they.
nodes.response: In French, there are two different ways of saying 'they': masculine 'ils' or feminine 'elles'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unable to spell some of the adjectives you generate to describe the houses.
nodes.response: As you are generating, create a class word bank for the adjectives. This will help pupils to recall them when they are writing and help to spell them correctly.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives follow the same order and punctuation as in English.
nodes.response: If there is more than one adjective in a sentence, adjectives after the noun are separated by ‘et’. BRAGS adjectives go before the noun and do not need ‘et’. In some sentences, there are adjectives surrounding the noun.

nodes.misconception: In descriptive writing, students often just describe what their protagonist can see. They often neglect the other senses.
nodes.response: To create the most vivid description possible, students should focus their description on the five sense, subtly moving between exploring how the scene feels, smells, looks, tastes and sounds.

nodes.misconception: You should use an adjective to describe every noun.
nodes.response: Adjectives can help add interest and atmosphere to your writing. But not every noun needs an adjective. This can become overwhelming for the reader.

nodes.misconception: Desertification only occurs in existing deserts.
nodes.response: Desertification can occur in any fertile land that becomes increasingly arid, not just in deserts.

nodes.misconception: Photographic images always reflect reality.
nodes.response: Remind children that photographic images can be digitally manipulated using a computer or digital software, they do not always reflect reality.

nodes.misconception: I want to start coding my game right away! Why do I need to draw pictures and write descriptions first?
nodes.response: By designing first, you're planning out exactly what you want your game to do and how it will work before you write any code.

nodes.misconception: Artists can only take inspiration from the same features of a landmark.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can look at the same landmark, but choose to take inspiration from different features. Finding different things inspiring is an important part of being an artist.

nodes.misconception: Sources should be copied from exactly to create a good design.
nodes.response: Sources are for inspiration, not replication. Great designs mix ideas from multiple sources and add personal creativity.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the shapes they use need to be perfect or uniform when sketching.
nodes.response: Remind children of the difference between organic and geometric shapes. Organic shapes do not need to be uniform or perfect.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume robots have only one job, not understanding how versatile robots can be when designed for different tasks such as cleaning, farming, or saving resources.
nodes.response: Remind children that robots can have many different purposes! Show images of robots used in various ways, like cleaning oceans, planting trees, or sorting recyclables.

nodes.misconception: Golf etiquette is just about being polite.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that golf etiquette is about courtesy, consideration and respect for other players, the course and the game itself.

nodes.misconception: Wild animals don’t belong in cities and can’t survive there.
nodes.response: While some wild animals struggle in cities, others adapt well if we design spaces with them in mind. Urban environments can become important habitats with thoughtful planning.

nodes.misconception: Urban design is only about buildings and roads.
nodes.response: Urban design includes public spaces, such as parks, playgrounds, and recreational areas. Urban design is about how people use and experience space, not just what gets built.

nodes.misconception: Digital tools are not necessary for street art; real street art has to be done with spray paint on walls.
nodes.response: While spray paint is common in street art, digital tools are increasingly used in the design and creation process. Digital art allows artists to experiment, refine, and plan their murals before transferring them to large-scale physical surfaces.

nodes.misconception: Sustainable transport is just about electric vehicles.
nodes.response: Sustainability includes more than just power sources - it also involves materials, passenger capacity, energy use, and reducing pollution across a whole system.

nodes.misconception: An action plan is a list of instructions.
nodes.response: An action plan is more than a list of insructions; it provides a list of stages of making, sometimes in order but can also list the materials and tools needed.

nodes.misconception: Stitches are just used to join materials together.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that, while stitches can be used to join materials together, they are also used in a skilled and decorative way through embroidery.

nodes.misconception: Ony artistic people can produce art.
nodes.response: All people can produce art that represents their beliefs and values. This art can take many forms.

nodes.misconception: To create an expressive letterform you must have neat handwriting skills.
nodes.response: Expressive letterforms use drawing and designing skills to convey emotions and ideas.

nodes.misconception: Once  a design has been created, it cannot be adapted or changed.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can change their ideas as they go, making changes to their design as they continue through the design and making process.

nodes.misconception: Any shape can make a strong building.
nodes.response: Architects select specific shapes and structures to make homes stable.

nodes.misconception: Engineers only design buildings or fix things that are broken.
nodes.response: A range of examples of how and where engineers work will be given.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that intricate designs are necessary, however simple shapes with clear details often work best for creating patterns.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch a few different simple shapes and test how they repeat in a pattern. You can also cut out your motif and arrange multiple copies to see how they fit together.

nodes.misconception: All models can be simulated successfully in Sim Lab.
nodes.response: Before being simulated in Sim Lab, models need to be well-designed and stable, considering static and moving parts.

nodes.misconception: Design briefs are only used in creative fields like product or graphic design.
nodes.response: Design briefs are crucial across many industries, including engineering, architecture, and product development.

nodes.misconception: Modelling only takes place with physical materials.
nodes.response: Virtual modelling using 3D drawing software can help to see ideas in 3D and enables quick and easy iteration.

nodes.misconception: 3D printing is sustainable because it is an additive manufacturing process with minimal waste.
nodes.response: 3D printing filament is a thermopolymer.  As with all manufacturing processes, there needs to be consideration of the materials used, their sources and disposal.

nodes.misconception: Once a design has been decided upon, it cannot be altered.
nodes.response: A design can continue to be altered, even when at the manufacturing stage.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think they they need to know what they are designing and making straight away.
nodes.response: Pupils need to explore the context fully first to identify lots of possible design problems to solve before narrowing it down.

nodes.misconception: Design optimisation is the same as design development.
nodes.response: Design development is the bigger process of taking an idea and turning it into a final product. Optimisation is the specific part of development where you focus on preparing the design for making, creating the best version of your existing design.

nodes.misconception: Selection is only used for turning things on and off.
nodes.response: Selection can be used for different actions, such as changing speed, colour, or sound.

nodes.misconception: Patents and trademarks are the same thing.
nodes.response: Trademarks protect brand names and logos whilst patents protect inventions and new technologies.

nodes.misconception: Teams don't discuss tactics properly and instead focus on just wanting to play a game.
nodes.response: Forming a number of predetermined plans can be an effective way to capitalise on set play situations and being aware of which team members are the biggest threat to the opposition can leave other players more open.

nodes.misconception: Fabric and fasteners are chosen for aesthetic qualities alone.
nodes.response: Fabric and fasteners need to be selected carefully for their function and application.

nodes.misconception: An axle must hold two wheels.
nodes.response: The axle might hold one or two wheels. The axle can turn with the wheel.

nodes.misconception: Design specifications and technical specifications are the same.
nodes.response: Design specifications focus on the overall concept, user needs, and appearance. Technical specifications detail the materials and measurement requirements needed to build a product.

nodes.misconception: Sustainability decisions happen after the product has been designed.
nodes.response: At the design stage, designers have a huge responsibility to influence many other stages of a product's life cycle through their design decisions.

nodes.misconception: A variable can hold lots of different scores at the same time, like all the scores from a whole football match.
nodes.response: A variable can only hold one value at any one time. Variables are always changeable, meaning their value can be updated.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that improving at a physical activity requires them to perform the event in full repeatedly.
nodes.response: Help pupils to understand that training drills which overload the body are much more effective when training to achieve a goal, rather than simply repeating the full performance.

nodes.misconception: Sustainability decisions happen after the product has been designed.
nodes.response: At the design stage, designers have a huge responsibility to influence many other stages of a product's life cycle through their design decisions.

nodes.misconception: A digital device has to have exactly one input and one output.
nodes.response: Digital devices can have more than one input and more than one output. They use different devices for different tasks at different times. For some tasks, input or output devices might not be required but they might be for different uses.

nodes.misconception: You only need to program one loop for a whole game.
nodes.response: Each sprite needs its own loop so it can repeat its actions independently.

nodes.misconception: When performing divisions to calculate the maximum number of plants that fit into a space, pupils may round decimal answers up to the nearest integer (e.g. round 4.5 plants up to 5 plants).
nodes.response: The context would suggest that it may be more appropriate to truncate decimal answers to an integer rather than rounding them up to the nearest integer (e.g. there is not enough space available to fit the 5th plant).

nodes.misconception: Sustainability is just to do with the environment.
nodes.response: Sustainability takes into account the long term needs of people, the economy and the environment.

nodes.misconception: Planning a physical computing project slows you down and does not need to be thought of before starting what you want to make.
nodes.response: A plan helps you think through the steps, figure out what you need, and make sure your project turns out how you want it to. If you don't plan, you could end up making mistakes that will mean your project doesn't turn out how you would like.

nodes.misconception: Designing is just extra work.
nodes.response: Planning reduces how much you have to think about when you are actually coding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may add a capital letter and full stop to their caption e.g. 'Fresh cucumber.'.
nodes.response: When modelling, explain a caption is not a sentence. Model mistakes for children to discuss and check.

nodes.misconception: You should write your program before designing it.
nodes.response: Designing first helps you plan what the program needs to do.

nodes.misconception: All vehicles are made from the same materials.
nodes.response: Discuss the diversity of materials used in vehicle construction and why different vehicles require different materials.

nodes.misconception: Planning on paper is a waste of time and will slow a project down because extra work needs to be completed.
nodes.response: Planning on paper will make a project better because ideas can be made clear and possible problems later can be avoided.

nodes.misconception: The design process is not important; you should start coding without one.
nodes.response: Without a clear design, the program might not match the intended purpose. Whilst it might seem like time well spent at the start it will save time in the long run.

nodes.misconception: New games are often hindered by preexisting rules and scoring systems which remain the basis and stunt creativity.
nodes.response: Pupils must think outside the box and forget about pre-existing activities when creating their own games. It is important to instil the confidence to try something new even if it doesn't work.

nodes.misconception: Designers plan and follow their planning in the making stage.
nodes.response: Designers use their design brief to create a plan. This plan is important but changable depending on success of the project, alongside tools, skills and testing points along the way.

nodes.misconception: Printmaking requires the use of specialist equipment to be successful.
nodes.response: High quality printing making can be achieved using a range of domestic materials and equipment.

nodes.misconception: Exception handling fixes the error in the code or stops it from happening.
nodes.response: Exception handling does not prevent errors but allows the program to detect them and continue running by managing the error appropriately.

nodes.misconception: All the singular persons of -ar, -er, and -ir verbs in the preterite have an accent.
nodes.response: Only the 'I' and 'she, he, it' forms have an accent. For -ar verbs, the endings are -é and -ó; for -er and -ir verbs the endings are -í and -ió.

nodes.misconception: As long as I get the gist of the meaning of a Spanish question, I can answer successfully.
nodes.response: In conversation it is important to listen carefully to the tense of questions before answering. Otherwise your answers might not be relevant.  For example, 'What did you do after school yesterday?' 'I usually do my homework.'

nodes.misconception: That Dr. Jekyll enjoys the experience of being Mr. Hyde.
nodes.response: Encourage students to notice the different ways that Dr. Jekyll has declined.

nodes.misconception: Students may not immediately understand the title if they have never come across 'colonialism' before.
nodes.response: Take some time unpicking why Clarke equates colonisation to stealing.

nodes.misconception: SALT 1 represented an end to the Cold War.
nodes.response: SALT 1 helped to moderate some elements of the Cold War such as the arms race but did not bring a complete stop to this. US and Soviet rivalry continued after 1972 and so did the Cold War.

nodes.misconception: The period of Détente in the 1970s did not mark the beginning of the end of the Cold War.
nodes.response: Although there was a reduction in tensions between the USA and the USSR during the early 1970s, tensions had increased again by the end of the decade.

nodes.misconception: When using place value counters, children may misread a number if one of the digits is a zero and hence not represented with a counter.
nodes.response: Remember that the digits in numbers are organised into groups of three with ones, tens and hundreds in each group.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to connect the determiner to the noun when adjectives are in between.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that adjectives describe nouns - can they spot the noun the adjectives describe to help them find the determiner?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not spot a determiner if adjectives are used between the determiner and the noun.
nodes.response: Emphasise that adjectives can be placed between the determiner and the noun.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that determiners always come directly in front of a noun.
nodes.response: Adjectives may be placed between the determiner and the noun to provide description.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that whenever we use 'those' or 'this', we are using a determiner.
nodes.response: Demonstratives are only determiners if they are introducing a noun in a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes struggle to understand that 'heating to constant mass' takes time and multiple measurements.
nodes.response: Link the idea that atoms rearrange during a reaction and that for all atoms of a substance to be oxidised, enough oxygen must be present. If the product measurements show a 'constant mass' we can be confident that complete oxidation has occurred.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes struggle to understand that 'heating to constant mass' takes time and multiple measurements.
nodes.response: Link the idea that atoms rearrange during a reaction and that for all atoms of a substance to be oxidised, enough oxygen must be present.  If the product measurements show a 'constant mass' we can be confident that complete oxidation has occurred.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the mass of the crucible and contents will not change during the reaction because the lid is closed, believing that all gases produced remain inside.
nodes.response: Explain that even with the crucible lid on, gases like carbon dioxide & water vapour formed during decomposition can escape around the edges. This leads to a decrease in mass, which is crucial for calculating the stoichiometry based on the mass loss.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the mass of the crucible and contents will not change during the reaction because the lid is closed, believing that all gases produced remain inside.
nodes.response: Explain that even with the crucible lid on, gases like carbon dioxide & water vapour formed during decomposition can escape around the edges. This leads to a decrease in mass, which is crucial for calculating the stoichiometry based on the mass loss.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils incorrectly interpret subscript and stoichiometric values in a balanced symbol equation.
nodes.response: Both subscript and stoichiometric values represent ratios. Subscripts indicate ratios within substances; stoichiometry. Molar ratios between substances in a reaction. Much practice distinguishing between/interpreting these is time well spent.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils incorrectly interpret subscript and stoichiometric values in a balanced symbol equation.
nodes.response: Both subscript and stoichiometric values represent ratios.  Subscripts indicate ratios *within* substances; stoichiometry. Molar ratios *between* substances in a reaction.  Much practice distinguishing between/ interpreting these is time well spent.

nodes.misconception: Using ionic charges to determine the empirical formulae, especially with polyatomic ions. Standard notation is difficult and confusing, e.g. when to use superscripts, subscripts or brackets.
nodes.response: At this stage, pupils will need to just learn the the formulae of the polyatomic ions and accept that a full explanation will come later in their chemistry learning. Provide pupils with plenty of practice of writing and using ionic formulae.

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models, ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models, ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.

nodes.misconception: I can only use Pythagoras' theorem to find the length of a side of a right-angled triangle when the right-angle marker is labelled, so I know which side is the hypotenuse.
nodes.response: The right-angle marker doesn't need to be explicitly labelled in order to be able to identify the right-angle. You can use knowledge of "interior angles in a triangle sum to 180°" to find the right angle, given two other angles.

nodes.misconception: Compound nouns are completely different words that cannot be understood or pronounced unless they have been met before.
nodes.response: Compound nouns are made up of two (or more) nouns, one or more of which pupils may already know. Knowledge of formation and read aloud can promote recognition as can activities where pupils produce compounds from known words.

nodes.misconception: There is one set of adjective endings in German.
nodes.response: Adjective endings agree in case, gender and number with nouns, and there are different sets of adjective endings, depending on what word comes before the adjective. There are useful tables that can be learned to support correct usage.

nodes.misconception: Always use the imperfect tense to translate the English simple past, e.g., 'I chatted online.'
nodes.response: The perfect tense is far more common in German, used for past events in speaking and informal writing. The imperfect is used mainly to narrate past events in more formal writing. However, 'hatte', 'war' and 'es gab' are used in speaking too.

nodes.misconception: Intonation doesn't make much difference when reading aloud.
nodes.response: Using correct intonation can also help you correctly pronounce German sounds and help you communicate clearly, such as pausing briefly when you see commas or full stops, or the rising pitch of your voice when asking questions.

nodes.misconception: German forms comparatives in the same way as English.
nodes.response: Use 'als' to compare things that are different and 'so ... wie' to compare things that are the same.

nodes.misconception: German forms comparatives in the same way as English.
nodes.response: To form the comparative in German, add '-er' to the adjective. This applies in English, but only for short adjectives. For longer adjectives, we add 'more' before the adjective. This is never the case in German.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.

nodes.misconception: Group work means I only do one small part and don’t need to help with the rest.
nodes.response: While roles may be shared, everyone in the group should contribute ideas and help make decisions together to ensure the final design feels like a team effort.

nodes.misconception: Arpilleras generally avoid themes related to daily life or social issues.
nodes.response: Remind children that arpilleras are typically appliquéd textile scenes, showing everyday life, rural culture, or times of conflict. Arpilleras are sometimes used as activist art, especially in the context of human rights or social justice.

nodes.misconception: Additional features need to be finished and functional.
nodes.response: Additional features on prototypes can be shown using mock-ups made from mixed materials.

nodes.misconception: Once an idea has been drawn, it is finished.
nodes.response: Artists often revisit and refine their ideas. A first sketch is just the starting point - you can improve your work by trying different layouts, materials, and colour choices.

nodes.misconception: The environment can be anywhere; the most important clues for a story are from the characters and objects.
nodes.response: The setting is an important device for communicating a story. It shows where the story happens and adds clues about mood, time, or place.

nodes.misconception: All bridges look the same.
nodes.response: All bridges are different. They use different materials, look unique (look different) and made by different designers and engineers.

nodes.misconception: All fabric decorative techniques involve stitching.
nodes.response: Fabrics can be decorated using other techniques such as appliqué, fabric pens and paints.

nodes.misconception: Iterations are only needed when a system doesn't work.
nodes.response: Systems are iterated to modify, fix, develop and improve.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that hitting the ball into the channel is all they have to do to score a point, and they stay still after their shot.
nodes.response: Pupils aim for channels to create space to try win the overall point and hitting the channel doesn't instantly result in a point being scored. After each shot, pupils should try to return to the ready position.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are gaining points when they hit the ball into channels. This is only to practice creating space and pupils may think they score points in a game of tennis if they hit the ball into a channel.
nodes.response: It is important to provide pupils with the context of why they are aiming for channels to try and create space within the rally so they attempt to aim for one channel and then the other to move their opponent.

nodes.misconception: Design drawings must be technical and include detail.
nodes.response: Simple drawings can be annotated to add the extra information and detail needed to understand the design.

nodes.misconception: All cross-section diagrams show the vertical plane.
nodes.response: Cross-sections diagrams can show the horizontal or vertical planes and these can provide very different views.

nodes.misconception: You don't need to record failures as it will lower your GCSE grade.
nodes.response: Record all of your experiments, but make it clear in your work that you know which ones were successful and take these forward in your creative journey. This is evidence of your informed and insightful approach. This will attract a higher mark.

nodes.misconception: User feedback is just opinions, it’s not useful when developing designs.
nodes.response: Feedback is largely based on opinions. However, it provides real world insight into how people interact see, understand and would use a design.

nodes.misconception: Pupils rely heavily on using just one part of their foot, neglecting the need to use both the inside and the outside for better control.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need to alternate between both parts of the foot for greater skill and control.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that bowling should always be at the same length to be consistent. The phrase 'good length' might be part of the confusion.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand that as long as it is a legal ball, the length can vary. This is a good way to outwit the batter as different lengths create different challenges and keeps them guessing.

nodes.misconception: It is unsafe to be blindfolded.
nodes.response: While there is an increased risk in getting injured, listening carefully to friends, trusting their guidance and being sensible will all help to reduce the risk level.

nodes.misconception: Any object can be used as it doesn’t have to mean anything.
nodes.response: Objects can be used to help tell stories and add depth and meaning through what they symbolise.

nodes.misconception: The bass line must have a different rhythm from the chords and percussion parts.
nodes.response: It can be appropriate for the bass line to use the same rhythm as another part. If it sounds effective then it is fine.

nodes.misconception: Some of the vocabulary used to describe Alina's connection to nature and the moon dragons may be unfamiliar, e.g. 'intuitive'.
nodes.response: Explore the word 'intuitive' and its definition. Ask the children to consider moments that they feel a sense of intuitiveness and how this guides them to make decisions.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the nuanced difference between feelings and character traits.
nodes.response: Distinguish between a temporary feeling and a character trait. Explain that feelings become character traits if they are persistently displayed. E.g. Lila does not always feel frustrated but she has always shown determination.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the difference between feelings and character traits.
nodes.response: Distinguish between a temporary feeling and a character trait. E.g. Mulan does not always experience worry, this is a result of circumstances. However, the worry is a symptom of her consistent care for others, so we can infer that she is thoughtful.

nodes.misconception: Using chord inversions for every chord will make the chord sequence more interesting.
nodes.response: Using some inversions can make the chord sequence more interesting, but too many can sound unusual. Starting and finishing with a root position chord can help to reinforce the key.

nodes.misconception: To create a contrasting version of a leitmotif, you should change lots of features of it.
nodes.response: You must be careful to not change it too much. If you do, it becomes unrecognisable and will just sound like a different leitmotif. A leitmotif represents a character, place, or idea, so we need to be able to recognise it to link it to that thing.

nodes.misconception: A melody must feature a motif.
nodes.response: This is not necessarily true - great melodies do not have to use motifs. However, they are a useful feature to understand when learning to write melodies, because they encourage composers to balance repetition anc contrast effectively.

nodes.misconception: Confusion between the models and the order in which they were conceived. Also, pupils often mix up which subatomic particles are present in each model.
nodes.response: Practise is required listing the key features of each model and the subatomic particles present. A timeline with the key features present helps pupils to understand the process of discovery and how long this can take.

nodes.misconception: You can only change the 3rd or the 6th of the scale to change the mood of the music.
nodes.response: In the lesson task any suitable chromatic movement can be used to change the feel of the motif, so pupils don't explicitly have to change the 3rd and the 6th. Play a range of motifs in the major key and change different notes so pupils can see this.

nodes.misconception: That your feelings about a poem are irrelevant.
nodes.response: How you respond to a poem forms the basis of your argument about a poem - it helps you to understand how a poet has created meaning.

nodes.misconception: Children might think there is only one right answer to what message a story is trying to convey.
nodes.response: Authors understand that readers infer different meaning from their stories and are able to develop their own responses and opinions to them.

nodes.misconception: Building a physical computing project is just about putting the parts together. The code is not that important.
nodes.response: The code tells the hardware what to do and how to interact with the world, without the code it wouldn't move or do anything interesting!

nodes.misconception: Thinking that a metal and acid react together to produce salt and water.
nodes.response: Use symbol equations to show how hydrogen is produced, rather than water, due to the absence of oxygen atoms.

nodes.misconception: Only musical instruments (and voices) produce pitched sound.
nodes.response: Pitched sounds are everywhere. In fact, most sounds have a pitch, it is often just hard to hear it. You can probably hear a pitched sound now if you listen closely - electrical buzzing, distant speech, weather or animals all produce subtle pitches.

nodes.misconception: Retrograding breaks the rules of serialism because it changes the order of the notes.
nodes.response: Serialist composers don't consider retrograding breaking the rules. It does change the order, but the new order is still closely linked to the original tone row (by being reversed). It is therefore an acceptable and musically interesting technique.

nodes.misconception: Choosing vocabulary and ideas is the most important part of the writing process.
nodes.response: Structural features can really elevate your writing, making it more cohesive and impactful so that your reader doesn't lose interest.

nodes.misconception: A concept is entirely fixed.
nodes.response: A concept can develop and evolve but it should not completely change without very good reason.

nodes.misconception: You don’t need a plan before starting a vector design — you can just make it up as you go.
nodes.response: Planning helps you focus your design and choose the right tools and shapes before you start. Without a plan, it's easy to miss the goal or waste time making unnecessary changes.

nodes.misconception: Complex music sounds most exciting and energetic.
nodes.response: Not necessarily - sometimes the most energetic music is that which emphasises the pulse and uses driving rhythms. Sometimes if music is too complex, with many busy layers of sound, it can sound chaotic and messy rather than energetic.

nodes.misconception: In persuasive writing, I just need to include a range of rhetorical devices and sophisticated vocabulary.
nodes.response: Whilst it is important to use rhetorical devices and choose interesting language, you must also consider the structure of your writing. This ensures that your argument has a clear progression and your message doesn't get lost.

nodes.misconception: As long as I am being quiet, I am listening.
nodes.response: Although being quiet is an effective way to show you are listening, there are many other things to consider to ensure you are 'actively listening'.

nodes.misconception: A countermelody is just a type of accompaniment.
nodes.response: It is actually quite different from an accompaniment, because it should be equally as prominent as the main melody, whereas an accompaniment is not. An accompaniment is usually also based on repeating patterns, whereas a melody does not have to be.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect all experiences with deafness and the Deaf community to reflect this text.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that the text explores an individual’s recount of their experiences; it is not reflective of every experience within the Deaf community. Pupils could read additional texts to develop greater awareness and empathy.

nodes.misconception: Everyone is treated fairly and equally.
nodes.response: By exploring the text and reading the author's note, it is clear that not everyone has equal rights. Pupils could explore charities like Amnesty International who campaign for equality.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to distinguish which features within the story are modern or traditional.
nodes.response: The illustrations within the story are a powerful tool for guiding students to identify modern versus traditional mythical features.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that pollution of rivers only affects the animals and plants that inhabit it.
nodes.response: Model examples of how food chains are broken for other animals and humans if living things in rivers are destroyed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that there are multiple answers to open-ended or personal reflection questions.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to refer to the text as they discuss the questions. If a pupils' perspective can be justified by evidence in the text, it is a valid response.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that illustrations always depict exactly what is mentioned in the words the author writes.
nodes.response: Show examples throughout the illustrated chapter book where the illustrations add in additional details, such as the double page spread on 158 and 159 where Roz is switched off.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that illustrations always depict exactly what is mentioned in the words the author writes.
nodes.response: Show examples throughout the illustrated chapter book where the illustrations add in additional details, for example, the depiction of a car on pages 90 and 91.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that disability and deformity are interchangeable.
nodes.response: August's facial deformity does not directly impair his physical abilities or cognitive functions. The email conversation between Julian's mother and Mr. Tushman explores this on pages 162 and 163.

nodes.misconception: As long as I can back up my answer, I can put forward any interpretation of the text.
nodes.response: Using tentative language can lead to a more exploratory approach, rather than presenting 'right' or 'wrong' interpretations.

nodes.misconception: Collage is a set process that cannot be modified or refined.
nodes.response: Collage is a flexible process. Rearranging elements helps refine ideas and create a stronger final piece. Professional artists often make changes mid-process to improve composition and meaning.

nodes.misconception: There is archaic and unfamiliar language that pupils will not recognise or understand in the poem.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it is normal to not understand all the language in an archaic text, especially when we first read it.  That is OK.  There will be lots of opportunities to build our understanding.

nodes.misconception: A pedal note is just a long, low note.
nodes.response: A pedal note is a consistent pitch usually in the bass whilst the chords change. Encourage pupils to listen to and experiment with the pitch they choose for a pedal to hear the effect it has on the harmony.

nodes.misconception: The append() method will replace the existing contents of a list.
nodes.response: The append() method will add an item to the end of an existing list but it will not replace or overwrite any existing items in a list.

nodes.misconception: Children might confuse inference with prediction. While a good prediction relies on inference skills, inference does not always involve predicting.
nodes.response: Rehearse the definition of inference a number of times and accompany with as many relevant examples as necessary (like the example on slide 19).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may place character traits both on the inside and outside of the character outline.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that inner emotions and feelings remain inside, attributes that other characters can see go on the outside.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think you can only know how a character is feeling by an explicit feelings word.
nodes.response: We can understand a character's feelings by inferring meaning through the character's actions, their words and their experiences.

nodes.misconception: If you find oil or gas underground, it is always worth extracting it.
nodes.response: In fact, just because a reserve exists doesn't mean that it will be technically or economically viable. Reserves that are in remote locations or in challenging conditions may have high development costs, especially if oil prices fall.

nodes.misconception: That the reader will automatically be able to follow your train of thought.
nodes.response: We all have different connotations from words; you need to clearly explain how you have reached your idea in order for the reader to be able to understand your argument.

nodes.misconception: The accompaniment patterns for section A and section B are the same and the best way to practise is to play from the start to the end of the piece repeatedly.
nodes.response: The accompaniment pattern changes slightly in section B. Highlight the difference so pupils are sure of this when practising hands together. It's more efficient to identify and practise the difficult bars in isolation first.

nodes.misconception: Graffiti art is only about using spray paint on walls.
nodes.response: Graffiti can be done using many mediums, including digital media, and digital tools allow us to explore and refine our designs without needing physical walls. Graffiti is about expression, regardless of the medium.

nodes.misconception: Reimagining work means simply copying the original in a slightly different way.
nodes.response: Reimagining is about transforming the original work, changing materials, scale, techniques, or context to create something new that still connects back to the starting point.

nodes.misconception: Using inspiration from artists means copying their work exactly.
nodes.response: The goal is not to copy an artist's work but to adapt their techniques, mark-making, or approach to develop your own creative style and ideas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to imagine the scene without having seen anything like it before.
nodes.response: Whilst it might be difficult to imagine it perfectly, we can use our imagination to create ideas that paint a vivid picture.

nodes.misconception: A poet will always make choices with a clear intention or meaning.
nodes.response: Armitage reveals that poetic choices can be deliberately ambiguous, allowing for multiple interpretations and personal responses.

nodes.misconception: Most poems are deeply personal or emotional and written spontaneously from the heart.
nodes.response: Armitage suggests that writing poetry about traumatic events can be a methodical process. He states that keeping some emotional distance can be helpful.

nodes.misconception: The genre of the music tells us exactly what kind of film it is.
nodes.response: This is not always true. Sometimes composers deliberately use genres that go against expectations. This might be for humour, or to create a strange clash. A good example would be A Knight's Tale, which uses modern genres in a medieval film.

nodes.misconception: When creating a motif to represent ideas from a painting, you must use the same action over and over again.
nodes.response: When creating a motif, you can demonstrate an action then repeat it by changing the size, level, direction, speed, force, using a different body part, adding an extra action, reversing the action or coordinating another action at the same time.

nodes.misconception: Labeling literary features like "metaphor" or "imagery" is enough to demonstrate analysis.
nodes.response: Feature spotting is not analysis. You need to explain how the writer's choices create different meanings and link to the writer's intention and wider themes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils must work through the text chronologically when selecting supporting evidence.
nodes.response: Pupils need to think of the logical order they should analyse evidence from the text - which section of the novella is strongest at proving their topic sentence?

nodes.misconception: I should sing louder so my part can be heard over the others.
nodes.response: When we all sing louder, the music becomes unbalanced. If we listen and balance each layer, our music sounds clear and beautiful.

nodes.misconception: Working out the notes of a whole melody by ear is a very difficult musical skill.
nodes.response: While it seems challenging, if you break it down into small steps - individual intervals - it is no more difficult than working out one interval. Take it one step at a time in small chunks and it is completely achievable.

nodes.misconception: As long as all the necessary lines of code are present, the program will work, regardless of their order.
nodes.response: Computers run code line by line, in the order it's written. If you change the sequence, you're changing the steps the computer takes, and that will change the output.

nodes.misconception: The beat is the same as the rhythm of the words.
nodes.response: The pulse is like a steady beat that stays the same, even when the rhythm of the words changes. Clap the beat whilst saying words to show how they are different.

nodes.misconception: Every text must have a subtext.
nodes.response: Some texts are more straightforward and may focus on conveying their message or story in a more direct and explicit manner.

nodes.misconception: Graphic novels and comics share many similar features. Pupils might use the term interchangeably.
nodes.response: Graphic novels have a clear beginning, middle and end, unlike comics which are usually released weekly in shorter comic strips.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may begin writing about a character in a standalone text, rather than a series.
nodes.response: If a pupil has not encountered series fiction before, they will develop greater awareness through discussion with their peers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that only certain types of literature are valid such as novels.
nodes.response: Help pupils to celebrate a wide range of text types.

nodes.misconception: Text recommendations might be quite short in length, initially.
nodes.response: Develop pupils' awareness of reasons and possible responses they could include to develop recommendations further.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that non-fiction is a form not a genre.
nodes.response: Non-fiction is a genre of text. It can be presented in many different forms. Provide pupils with examples to read.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume a hero only portrays positive traits, an anti-hero only negative traits.
nodes.response: Discuss a range of protagonists and reflect on their traits and characterisation. Not all characters will be heroes or anti-heroes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think reading is restricted to a book.
nodes.response: By completing a reading treasure hunt, pupils can explore reading in a range of forms.

nodes.misconception: Text curation might focus solely on personal preference.
nodes.response: Identify a range of ways that pupils might curate, linking especially to any theme weeks or real-world events.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that inspirational characters are only found in two genres of texts.
nodes.response: Characters can inspire children regardless of the genre they are written in.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all poetry has to rhyme.
nodes.response: Have a wide range of different poetic forms available. Perhaps encourage pupils to discover more about the fixed verse forms at home.

nodes.misconception: Researching an author will automatically improve a reader's experience with a text.
nodes.response: Researching an author can support readers in making connections, understanding influences and exploring how a text is created.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may just think a recommendation comes from a peer or teacher.
nodes.response: Recommendations can come from a wide range of people and places.

nodes.misconception: Picture books are not suitable for older readers to choose to read for pleasure.
nodes.response: Picture books can contain a range of complex themes and emotions. Display a range of texts for pupils to explore independently.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that texts can only have emotional or intellectual connections to readers.
nodes.response: Explain that texts can connect both intellectually and emotionally. Provide examples from members of staff.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume translations offer exact word-for-word equivalence to the original.
