nodes.response: Translators make choices to convey meaning in the target language, not always aligning precisely with the source text.

nodes.misconception: The friendship between Sam and Davey is wholly positive or negative.
nodes.response: The relationship between both boys is complex. You may wish to explore the theme of bullying in a separate lesson (e.g. PSHE) to acknowledge the traits that Sam exhibits and what could be done to resolve or address the behaviour.

nodes.misconception: Friendships within texts are always positive throughout.
nodes.response: The friendships and relationships within 'Danny Chung Does Not Do Maths' are complex. They could be explored during a PHSE lesson - looking at how some friendships are not equal or balanced.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may list emotions when referring to a character trait.
nodes.response: Emotions are temporary. Explain that character traits are linked to characterisation. They are relatively stable over time. Examples of common character traits could be shared with the children prior to Task A.

nodes.misconception: A favourite character is always someone who embodies positive character traits.
nodes.response: Favourite characters can be characters involved in key moments in the text; characters who change the most in the story; or, characters who remind readers of someone they know.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make a wish for themselves personally in Task A.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to consider the impact that they could have on their local community and wider world when discussing their wishes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that character traits remain fixed throughout a narrative.
nodes.response: The characters in 'The Girl of Ink and Stars' are complex. Governor Adori's decision in the climax of the story is very different to decisions he made at the beginning of the text.

nodes.misconception: Edward isn't a likeable protagonist.
nodes.response: Edward Tulane is an anti-hero. An anti-hero is a flawed protagonist, often with ambiguous morals.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to provide two contrasting impressions of a character.
nodes.response: It may be helpful to visually mind map how readers might describe a character (using adjectives). Impressions can also be modelled verbally to develop pupils' understanding of character.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all relationships within the text remain fixed or static.
nodes.response: It may be beneficial to verbally model an example for Task A to support pupils in their understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that how a character looks determines whether they are friend or foe.
nodes.response: When discussing the character of Sally Bones, focus on character traits that intimidate Varjak, not solely her appearance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is one correct answer in relation to the question posed in Task A.
nodes.response: Explain that texts can offer us philosophical questions, which ask readers to reflect on their own opinions. Links could be made to the author's note and afterword to deepen understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a favourite character should always be someone who embodies positive character traits.
nodes.response: Explain that favourite characters can be characters involved in key moments in the text; characters who change the most in the story; or, characters who remind readers of someone they know.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only want to use vocabulary from the original story.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we are retelling our own version of the story and therefore we can include our own precise and descriptive vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Having lots of layers of music playing simultaneously is effective use of texture.
nodes.response: It is easy to create a texture that is too thick and too busy. Encourage students to experiment with both thin and thick textures and reiterate that adding too many layers simultaneously can make music sound ineffective.

nodes.misconception: Fracking only uses water which means its environmental impacts are harmless.
nodes.response: In fact fracking fluid includes toxic chemicals and sand as well as water, which can have serious environmental impacts if they get into groundwater or are spilled. The wastewater left over from fracking also needs to be stored carefully.

nodes.misconception: A verse novel has to be fixed or free verse. It cannot contain both.
nodes.response: 'Cloud Busting' has fixed and free verse poetry. The text includes a range of forms, including haikus, concrete poems and limericks.

nodes.misconception: A stereotype always has to link to someone's race or cultural background.
nodes.response: Stereotypes do not always relate to race or cultural background. Stereotypes can also be based on various other factors such as gender, age, religion, physical appearance and other protected characteristics.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all forms of poetry must have to rhyme.
nodes.response: Before the lesson, you might share examples of a range of poems in both fixed verse and free verse.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that characters' traits and behaviours remain fixed within a narrative.
nodes.response: Discuss that several characters evolve emotionally over the narrative. Governor Adori begins the text very commanding, authoritative and selfish - he ends up redeeming himself by giving his daughter and Isabella time to escape.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to remember the order of Edward's owners.
nodes.response: You may want to note down the order of owners. This could be represented visually as a timeline within the classroom.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may consider the text as telling Omar's story in one continuous narrative.
nodes.response: The graphic novel has two significant jumps in time, page 114 (two years later) and page 221 (four years later). The afterword and author's note both describe what happened to Omar after arriving in the United States.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to agree on where each word should be placed on the scale of 'angry to angriest'.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that this is subjective and some people may think 'grumpy' is more angry than 'annoyed'. Encourage pupils to justify their point using the conjunction,' because'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused by the adjective 'included' and use it as a verb.
nodes.response: Model using 'included' in sentences as a verb and also as an adjective. This is a good opportunity to recap word classes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to differentiate the use of 'euphoric' and 'cheerful' in sentences.
nodes.response: 'Euphoric' means extreme happiness. Share examples with pupils of when you may feel 'euphoric' compared to when you may feel 'cheerful'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to know what or who inspires them.
nodes.response: When introducing 'inspired', talk about pupils' different sources of inspiration and how this impacts them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to use 'sulky' as an adjective and 'sulking' as a verb in sentences.
nodes.response: Model sentences using both 'sulky' and 'sulking'. Use this an opportunity to recap word classes.

nodes.misconception: A designer's style is fixed and remains constant.
nodes.response: A designer will grow and develop and so their distinctive style will evolve over time as they experiment more and engage with new ideas.

nodes.misconception: That we will all have the same response to certain words.
nodes.response: Our response to words depends on our own individual experiences and memories and therefore we are likely to all get different connotations from words.

nodes.misconception: Lots of automation changes make the dynamics effective.
nodes.response: Doing lots of dynamic changes can sound chaotic and messy. Try to limit your use of automation so that changes are gradual and slowly change the dynamics.

nodes.misconception: That there are few people who live to 65 years and beyond in LICs and NEEs.
nodes.response: It is the proportion of the population that is small not the actual number of people. Some LICs and NEEs have large populations so there are millions of people who reach the age of 65 years plus.

nodes.misconception: Science and engineering careers are male jobs. Females cannot work in science or engineering.
nodes.response: Examples of women working in science and explanations that science jobs are for everybody.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not realise that drugs are tested on healthy individuals first.
nodes.response: Healthy individuals are used as they will not have symptoms that interfere with the side effects from the drug.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that the when the periodic table was devised, scientists knew about the subatomic particles.
nodes.response: Emphasise when the subatomic particles were discovered in comparison to when Mendeleev devised his periodic table.

nodes.misconception: Hot deserts are barren, lifeless areas with no real economic potential.
nodes.response: Deserts can have significant opportunities for economic development, for example mineral extraction, solar energy, tourism and irrigated farming.

nodes.misconception: A website will look the same on any device that it is accessed from.
nodes.response: A website will look different on different devices. This is because they have different screen sizes. Checking a website is compatible for multiple devices is important.

nodes.misconception: Traditionally, all cultures use paintbrushes to paint.
nodes.response: Remind children that although paintbrushes are a popular artistic tool, they are not traditional for every community or culture.

nodes.misconception: Chanting and mantras in Buddhism bring instant blessings or results just by saying the words.
nodes.response: Chanting and mantras help Buddhists to focus the mind, develop qualities like compassion and evoke enlightenment.

nodes.misconception: The five precepts are a set of rules like the ten commandments.
nodes.response: They are more things to avoid to keep a positive mental state than rules to follow.

nodes.misconception: Buddhists find it easy to develop skilful actions.
nodes.response: All Buddhists have to work at developing these skills.

nodes.misconception: Moksha is a place or is heaven.
nodes.response: Moksha is where the atman (soul) is reunited with Brahman (the supreme being).

nodes.misconception: Dharma means the same thing across the dharmic religions.
nodes.response: The interpretation of dharma differs amongst Hindus, Buddhists and Sikhs.

nodes.misconception: Dharma is just about religious duties.
nodes.response: Dharma is about all humans do. Dharma is about making choices motivated by love and compassion.

nodes.misconception: Ahimsa only refers to non-violence towards humans.
nodes.response: Ahimsa refers to non-violence towards all living things, as all living things have value, worth and are interconnected.

nodes.misconception: Dharma is about following a fixed set of rules.
nodes.response: Dharma is about doing what is right and so rules may need to be applied flexibly.

nodes.misconception: Hindus only help other Hindus.
nodes.response: Hindus help all people as part of their dharma and sewa.

nodes.misconception: Hindus focus on devotion to deities rather than practical action.
nodes.response: Many Hindus are deeply concerned for the planet and are taking action to make a difference.

nodes.misconception: Hindus think that dharma is about caring only for people.
nodes.response: Dharma is about compassion for all living things, not just people.

nodes.misconception: Children may try to reflect in a diagonal line but not at a 45 degree angle, leading to inaccuracies when marking each vertex.
nodes.response: Encourage children to work horizontally and then vertically, rather than trying to reflect in a diagonal line. Explore how this can be done in either order, orienting the paper, and notice how the same point will still be marked on the grid.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with a diagonal of a shape being vertical or horizontal.
nodes.response: By reminding pupils of the definition, ask them to check if it fits and the shape could be rotated as well.

nodes.misconception: Students may think all carbon forms are alike, ignoring structure's impact on properties.
nodes.response: Emphasise structure-property relationships. Use models to show how diamond's and graphite's differing bonds affect their characteristics.

nodes.misconception: Communication after the ball is hit can be inconsistent in cricket. Having four players to coordinate means the need to communicate clearly about how many runs to make is even more important.
nodes.response: Allow pupils time to strategise about how they will communicate after the ball is hit. For example, they may nominate a captain to make all calls or decide that the batter who hit the ball makes the call.

nodes.misconception: To form the preterite tense I just take off the -er/-ir and add the correct ending (-ió - for she, he, it) to all the verbs.
nodes.response: Some verbs are irregular and don’t follow the pattern. e.g. hacer - hizo, tener - tuvo, ir - fue.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Scrooge's visit with the Ghost of Christmas Present is limited to Christmas Day.
nodes.response: Scrooge's time with the spirit goes beyond Christmas Day - to the Twelfth Day of Christmas, showing how time is manipulated in the novella.

nodes.misconception: A dictionary is a static data structure meaning you cannot add or remove items, only change the values that are available.
nodes.response: A dictionary is a dynamic data structure, which means you can add or remove items in the data structure during program execution.

nodes.misconception: All nouns ending '-n' must be in the dative case.
nodes.response: The definite article 'den' shows the dative plural form as well as the '-n' added to the end of the dative plural. However, a number of nouns form their plural by adding '-(e)n' and are not in the dative case.

nodes.misconception: If you know the usual meanings of prepositions, choosing which preposition to use with each verb is straightforward, as we translate the preposition directly from English.
nodes.response: Verb and preposition combinations need to be learnt. The prepositions often lose their usual meaning when combined with verbs, and we often use different prepositions after verbs in English and in German.

nodes.misconception: I can answer a role-play question with one or two words.
nodes.response: Role-play questions need to be answered in full sentences with at least one verb.

nodes.misconception: Cognates are pronounced the same as the English words.
nodes.response: Cognates may share similar spelling and meanings, but it is important to remember German pronunciation rules.

nodes.misconception: German says double digits the same way as English.
nodes.response: In German, we say units first and then tens.

nodes.misconception: All questions in German invert the subject and verb. Apart from that the word order is the same as English.
nodes.response: Subject and verb are inverted, but word order differs from English for a verb with a preposition - 'What are you talking about?'. In German, a preposition never ends a question. Use 'wo(r)' + preposition to start the question - 'Worüber redest du?'.

nodes.misconception: 'Lieber' means 'love'.
nodes.response: It is easy to confuse the words 'Liebe', 'liebe' and 'lieber', particularly in spoken German. Pay careful attention to pronunciation and listen out for [er]. 'Liebe' is a noun (love), 'liebe' is a verb (love) and 'lieber' is an adverb (more gladly).

nodes.misconception: All verbs use the auxiliary verb 'haben' to form the perfect tense.
nodes.response: A small number of verbs use the auxiliary verb 'sein' to form the perfect tense. These verbs usually refer to movement or a change of physical state.

nodes.misconception: 'On' and 'nous' both mean 'we' and can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: 'On' and 'nous' both mean 'we' but 'on' is used more to talk about people generally, 'nous' is always used to talk about yourself and another person/people. The verb endings are different, 'on' uses il/elle verb endings and the 'nous' ending is -ons.

nodes.misconception: When you add a question word at the end of a question, there is no need to change your intonation.
nodes.response: It is important to use your intonation by raising the pitch of your voice at the end of all questions in French.

nodes.misconception: Bonhoeffer was an absolute pacifist for his whole life.
nodes.response: Bonhoeffer was a pacifist, but had the opportunity to help with the attempt to assassinate Hitler, which he decided he should try to do, given the great evil and injustice Hitler was causing.

nodes.misconception: Squaring a binomial is the same as just squaring each term. This can then cause confusion with difference of two squares where expanding a pair of binomials does result in just two terms.
nodes.response: Using an area model and taking time to check the partial products each time, particularly with negative terms, should help students to check if they have expanded correctly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to name the features of a non-fiction text (contents, glossary, caption etc.)
nodes.response: This content will continue to be covered as the children move through school. The key learning here is understanding the difference between fiction and non-fiction. Continue to model the language and point out the differences for the children.

nodes.misconception: Non-infectious diseases such as heart disease can be passed from person to person.
nodes.response: Only infectious diseases caused by pathogens can spread from person to person.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a ‘balanced’ diet should include equal-sized proportions of the different food groups (rather than appropriate amounts of each food group).
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need to eat different amounts of foods, depending on how healthy or unhealthy they are for us. Explanation of the importance of eating different types of food.

nodes.misconception: All Christians believe that the Bible is a historical and factual account of history.
nodes.response: Some Christians take a literalist approach and believe that the Bible is a historical and factual account. However, some Christians regard parts of the Bible, including the creation accounts as metaphorical, this is known as a liberal approach.

nodes.misconception: Prayer only happens in a church.
nodes.response: Christians pray in churches but also in many other different places.

nodes.misconception: All people eat the same foods and have the same diet.
nodes.response: Explanation that different people have different diets for a variety of different reasons, such as allergies, intolerances or their own choice.

nodes.misconception: All Christians worship in the same way.
nodes.response: Worship differs across Christian denominations, with some denominations, such as the Catholic Church, practising liturgical worship, and others, such as the Religious Society of Friends and Pentecostal Churches, practising non-liturgical worship.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes children can revert back to cursive when comparing print and block capitals.
nodes.response: Remind the children that when writing in print, you lift your pencil after forming each letter. Emphasise this in your modelling to remind the children.

nodes.misconception: People with religious and non-religious worldviews have completely different ideas about how the world began.
nodes.response: People with religious and non-religious worldview share some ideas about how the world began.

nodes.misconception: Students may mix up rotation and circumduction.
nodes.response: When you rotate the shoulder joint you draw a dot with your hand (if the elbow is fully extended) whereas circumduction draws a circle.

nodes.misconception: All magnets look the same. The poles of all magnets are the ends.
nodes.response: Real examples and diagrams of different magnets and their poles will be given.

nodes.misconception: Maps are always accurate.
nodes.response: Maps are never completely accurate.

nodes.misconception: Muslims don’t compose or perform music for worship.
nodes.response: Some Muslims do compose or perform music to worship God (Allah).

nodes.misconception: Muslims only pray in the mosque for salat.
nodes.response: Muslims pray at home, in the mosque or any clean ground for salat.

nodes.misconception: That only men from England fought for Britain.
nodes.response: Men from all over the British Empire fought for Britain.

nodes.misconception: All Christians believe the same thing about abortion.
nodes.response: In reality, views vary between denominations, with the Catholic Church strongly opposing abortion, while the Church of England and Methodists allow it in some cases.

nodes.misconception: Animal experimentation always harms animals.
nodes.response: While animal experimentation can involve harm, modern practices aim to minimise suffering by using alternatives, reducing the number of animals used, and refining procedures to ensure humane treatment.

nodes.misconception: All members of a Christian denomination follow all its teachings.
nodes.response: Christians may use their conscience to decide which teachings to follow or not.

nodes.misconception: All Christians used to support corporal punishment
nodes.response: Early Christians often rejected violence; Quakers and Methodists led opposition in later periods.

nodes.misconception: All Christians completely oppose euthanasia.
nodes.response: While many Christian strongly oppose euthanasia, some take a more compassionate approach, considering quality of life and situation ethics. Some may support assisted dying in certain circumstances, though this remains a minority view.

nodes.misconception: Forgiveness comes naturally to all Christians because it is part of their faith.
nodes.response: Christianity teaches that forgiveness is important, but not that it is easy. Julie Nicholson’s story shows that even people of strong faith can struggle to forgive, especially after traumatic events. Forgiveness can be a long and difficult process.

nodes.misconception: Religious freedom means Christians never face challenges or restrictions today.
nodes.response: Religious freedom is protected by law, but Christians can still face censorship, legal cases, or public pressure.

nodes.misconception: All Christians are pacifists because Jesus taught peace and non-violence.
nodes.response: While some Christians, like Quakers, follow absolute pacifism, most Christian traditions accept that violence may be justified in certain circumstances, especially through Just War theory.

nodes.misconception: That liberal Christians do not think the Bible is important for their religion.
nodes.response: Liberal Christians view the Bible as important but will seek to understand it in the context and time that it was written, and are more accepting of modern ideas in relation to their religion than other approaches to Christianity may be.

nodes.misconception: All Christians are against sex before marriage.
nodes.response: Some believe that it is okay if it is between a committed couple, i.e., engaged to marry.

nodes.misconception: Most Christians support the death penalty because the Bible says “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth.”
nodes.response: Most Christians reject the death penalty because they agree with Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:38–39 “You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you, do not resist an evil person.”

nodes.misconception: All Christians believe that men and women should have different roles because the Bible says so.
nodes.response: Not all Christians agree. Some interpret Bible verses as cultural and support full gender equality, including leadership roles for women. Others, like the Catholic Church, believe men and women are equal in dignity, but have different roles.

nodes.misconception: Christianity teaches that wealth is bad
nodes.response: Wealth itself is not condemned, but greed and misuse of wealth are warned against (e.g., 1 Timothy 6:10).

nodes.misconception: Christians agree that no country should possess any weapons of mass destruction.
nodes.response: While Christians oppose the use of weapons of mass destruction because it contradicts teachings like the sanctity of life, some may accept their possession as a temporary deterrent if it helps prevent war and protect life.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not have an understanding of what moving at a particular speed means in the real world, and treat answers as ‘just numbers’.
nodes.response: Use real world examples of speeds through examples and questions asked (N.B. 10 m/s is approximately 20 miles per hour).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not have an understanding of what moving at a particular speed means in the real world, and treat answers as ‘just numbers’.
nodes.response: Use real world examples of speeds through examples and questions asked (N.B. 10 m/s is approximately 20 miles per hour).

nodes.misconception: All Christians use the same music styles.
nodes.response: Christians use music of many different styles in their worship.

nodes.misconception: Friction doesn’t have a direction; a force is needed to keep an object moving at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Provide examples, with images, to demonstrate the effects of friction on moving objects.

nodes.misconception: Friction always hinders motion therefore you always want to eliminate friction.
nodes.response: Multiple examples of positive uses of friction, including to help start motion by pushing off, are included.

nodes.misconception: All surfaces are only 2-dimensional. All surfaces are made by people (human-made).
nodes.response: Provide many examples, with images, of different types of surface including natural surfaces and 3-dimensional surfaces.

nodes.misconception: Children may not make the link between types of teeth and types of food we eat.
nodes.response: Show the children, through images and practical investigation, that humans all have the same variety of teeth to eat a variety of food. It might be useful to discuss how non-meat eating humans do still have canine and incisor teeth.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all equations are for straight lines so can be plotted from 2 points.
nodes.response: Explore different relationships, most relationships are not linear but we focus a lot on linear relationships and their unique structure.

nodes.misconception: All fat in the diet can cause ill health. A ‘balanced’ diet should include equal-sized proportions of the different food groups (rather than appropriate amounts of each food group).
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need to eat small amounts of fat and sugar, but that eating too much is unhealthy. Explanation of the importance of eating different types of food. The word “balanced” is not used in this lesson.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that all arable crops grown in the UK are required by humans for food.
nodes.response: Explain that 40% or 2/5 of the crops grown in the UK are used for animal feed.

nodes.misconception: The SSCs (sound-symbol correspondences) [ai] and [è/ê] make different sounds.
nodes.response: The SSCs (sound-symbol correspondences) [ai] and [è/ê] make the same sound in French: 'paire' and 'père'.

nodes.misconception: All soils are the same, they are just earth.
nodes.response: Through exploring different soil types  and their properties with the digital microscope, children will realise that soils differ depending on where and how they are formed.

nodes.misconception: All Christians celebrate Christmas in the same way.
nodes.response: Christmas is celebrated by most Christians in the UK. However, there are different traditions in different churches and groups.

nodes.misconception: Pupils always opt to perform the most simple movements. Pupils may not like performing in front of others.
nodes.response: Give pupils time to develop their movement ideas and be creative. Share creative ideas to improve the quality of movements. Encourage pupils to present in pairs to build up their confidence in performing to one another.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes with the calculations of surface area or volume are common. The concepts of surface area, volume and their ratio, with the effect that changing these have on diffusion, are difficult.
nodes.response: Plenty of practise on how to calculate surface area and volume, and compare these as a ratio, some simplified, is included. The experiment results are used to show the impact of changing surface area, volume and width on diffusion.

nodes.misconception: Particles want or intend to spread out; particles stop moving after equilibrium has been reached.
nodes.response: Animations show particles in continuous random motion.

nodes.misconception: Particles cannot diffuse through a seemingly solid material.
nodes.response: This practical lesson enables pupils to observe the diffusion of acid through permeable cubes of coloured jelly.

nodes.misconception: Particles only move through a selectively-permeable membrane in one direction.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the idea that particles move through a selectively-permeable membrane in both directions, but that net movement is down a concentration gradient.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that all, or no, substances can diffuse through the cell membrane. Thinking that cells choose to take in particular substances, or that cells breathe or suck in substances such as oxygen.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the idea that particles of some, but not all, substances are small enough to diffuse through holes in the selectively-permeable cell membrane.

nodes.misconception: Pupil confuse diffusion and Brownian motion.
nodes.response: Brownian motion is the random movement of particles due to collisions. Diffusion is due to concentration differences between 2 substances.

nodes.misconception: Food is absorbed without being digested; or "goodness" from food is what is absorbed.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the roles of mechanical and chemical digestion (by enzymes) of different food types into small molecules to be absorbed.

nodes.misconception: A poster that is created using software is digital even when printed out.
nodes.response: The source of the design is digital if it was created using software. However, once that digital design is printed onto a physical medium like paper, the resulting poster itself becomes a physical artefact.

nodes.misconception: Always use the imperfect tense to translate the English simple past, e.g., 'I chatted online.'.
nodes.response: The perfect tense is far more common in German and is used for both the English simple past and perfect tense in speaking. The imperfect is used mainly to narrate past events in writing. However, 'hatte', 'war' and 'es gab' are used in speaking too.

nodes.misconception: Digital devices are always better than non-digital tools.
nodes.response: Some tasks like reading a book might still be enjoyable or practical without digital devices.

nodes.misconception: Digital devices always need the internet to work.
nodes.response: Some digital devices work without the internet, such as watches and calculators.

nodes.misconception: A design portfolio should only include your best work and your best ideas.
nodes.response: A design portfolio should show the journey of the designer including all of the ideas that were not taken through or were not successful.

nodes.misconception: Emotions are only conveyed through words and physical gestures.
nodes.response: Facial expressions are a universal way to communicate emotions, even without words.

nodes.misconception: Symbols have to be detailed.
nodes.response: Symbols can be refined and made simple.

nodes.misconception: Editing an image always changes or damages the original file.
nodes.response: By using adjustment layers and layer masks, edits are non-destructive.

nodes.misconception: Photo editing is always obvious or “fake”.
nodes.response: In reality, edits can be extremely subtle and still have a significant impact on the final image.

nodes.misconception: Systems have to be made up of one part.
nodes.response: Systems are made up of many parts or components working together.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a bump shot needs the hands to come together to make a fist.
nodes.response: The correct technique is to place the back of one hand in the palm of the other hand with the arms extended and the elbows locked creating a platform with the forearms.

nodes.misconception: Assuming that to convert 1 metre squared to cm squared you multiply by 100 and not 10 000
nodes.response: Encourage any pupil who initially finds this challenging to ensure that the values are in the required unit for the answer before doing the calculation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the informal term 'speech marks'.
nodes.response: 'speech marks' is a term that signals the same thing as 'inverted commas' i.e. the dialogue in a sentence, but it is better to use the grammatical term 'inverted commas'.

nodes.misconception: Travelling sideways can only be performed by a side step.
nodes.response: There are many different ways to travel sideways, e.g. shuffling, stretching, wriggling, jumping.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they should always compromise to solve a dispute.
nodes.response: Emphasise that compromise is used when **both parties** have something they can give up or offer.

nodes.misconception: Research into existing products is a secondary research task.
nodes.response: Primary research through the disassembly of a product can be extremely beneficial to really understand a product, its materials and how it is manufactured.

nodes.misconception: A disassembly is the same as an evaluation.
nodes.response: A disassembly focuses on the different parts and workings of the product. The evaluation focuses on views of what people like and dislike.

nodes.misconception: Using a line graph or histogram to plot discontinuous data. All features show variation due to environmental and lifestyle factors.
nodes.response: The lesson explores why a bar chart is the correct choice for plotting discontinuous data, and the idea that discontinuous variation usually has only a genetic cause.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that organisms have, and always have had, their own names, rather than them being named by scientists and others.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain the naming process for living things used by taxonomists and other scientists.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that all carbon allotrope discoveries were recent and that these materials are primarily used in cutting-edge, futuristic applications.
nodes.response: Emphasise the timeline of discoveries (graphite > fullerenes > nanotubes > graphene), highlighting theoretical predictions preceding isolation. Discuss current uses (e.g. nanotubes in sporting equipment) alongside potential future breakthroughs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think archaeologists only find out about the past through excavation.
nodes.response: Archaeologists use a range of ways to find out about the past which include excavation, field walking, surveying and aerial photography.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will grip the discus by wrapping their fingers and thumb around the edges to prevent it from slipping out or dropping it.
nodes.response: The discus should sit on the palm of the hand with the edge of the discus sitting in the last joint crease of the fingers (if you turn the hand over to the top, it should fall out). The thumb should not grip the edge at all.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the tallest shape is always the largest.
nodes.response: Explore lots of different 3D shapes of different proportions. Allow children to handle and rotate the shapes. Use hollow shapes and explore filling them with water or sand to help children see that the largest shape is the one that can hold the most.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a shape must be larger because it is wider or longer than another shape, or that the smallest shape should always be the shortest or narrowest.
nodes.response: Encourage children to focus on the amount of space that a shape takes up. Explore cutting up shapes and manipulating them so that they have the same width or length to help children see which is the largest or smallest shape overall.

nodes.misconception: Some of the vocabulary and phrases in the text may be unfamiliar. This may present a barrier to comprehension, particularly during dense sections of description involving high-level vocabulary.
nodes.response: Make a bank of unfamiliar vocabulary from the text and provide definitions in context beforehand. E.g. looking at a primrose leaf and identifying a "furrow".

nodes.misconception: Some of the vocabulary and phrases in the text may be unfamiliar and even confusing. E.g. the use of the word "hollow" to describe Arrietty's "excitement".
nodes.response: Make a bank of unfamiliar vocabulary from the text and provide definitions. Explore interesting phrase choices. E.g. using the word "hollow" to describe Arrietty's "excitement" could imply that this is the only emotion she can feel.

nodes.misconception: That discussions are just 'chats' and aren't that important.
nodes.response: Think about all of the times you may need to use your verbal skills e.g. an interview or presentation. Being able to articulate yourself well verbally is an important skill to have.

nodes.misconception: All opinions phrases can be followed by 'dass' and word order 3 (subordination).
nodes.response: Whilst many opinion verbs, including 'meinen', 'glauben' and 'denken' are usually followed by 'dass' and word order 3, this is not always the case. 'Meiner Meinung nach' must be followed by word order 2 (inversion).

nodes.misconception: A person is either healthy or unhealthy.
nodes.response: Health is a range from good to ill health.

nodes.misconception: 'Damit' always means 'with it' or 'with them'.
nodes.response: 'Damit' has a double identity! It can be used as a conjunction meaning 'so that' as well as a da-compound meaning 'with it' or 'with them'.

nodes.misconception: Oberon finds the disorder between the Athenian nobles funny.
nodes.response: As soon as Oberon realises Puck's mistake, he swiftly tries to correct it.

nodes.misconception: The different 'kinds' of EM radiation are different phenomena to each other and to visible light. Pupils may also think all radiation is dangerous, none is natural and that light is not radiation.
nodes.response: Each 'kind' of EM radiation is the same phenomena as light (i.e. waves/ripples in electric and magnetic fields) just with different frequencies and wavelengths. Try to refer to different frequencies/frequency ranges rather than different 'kinds'.

nodes.misconception: The different 'kinds' of EM radiation are different phenomena to each other and to visible light. Pupils may also think all radiation is dangerous, none is natural and that light is not radiation.
nodes.response: Each 'kind' of EM radiation is the same phenomena as light (i.e. waves/ripples in electric and magnetic fields) just with different frequencies and wavelengths. Try to refer to different frequencies/frequency ranges rather than different 'kinds'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often have a tendency to believe that a velocity must have a positive value and have difficulty in associating a reverse in direction with a change in sign.
nodes.response: It is important to make sure pupils are secure in their knowledge of the vector–scalar distinction; use plenty of visual examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often have a tendency to believe that a velocity must have a positive value and have difficulty in associating a reverse in direction with a change in sign.
nodes.response: It is important to make sure pupils are secure in their knowledge of the vector–scalar distinction; use plenty of visual examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often have a tendency to believe that a velocity must have a positive value and have difficulty in associating a reverse in direction with a change in sign.
nodes.response: It is important to make sure pupils are secure in their knowledge of the vector–scalar distinction; use plenty of visual examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often have a tendency to believe that a velocity must have a positive value and have difficulty in associating a reverse in direction with a change in sign.
nodes.response: It is important to make sure pupils are secure in their knowledge of the vector–scalar distinction; use plenty of visual examples.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes pupils like to write methods in paragraph form, which can be difficult to follow.
nodes.response: Suggest pupils draw labelled diagrams of key steps, write a sentence to describe each diagram, then go back to number them in order.

nodes.misconception: Forces of attraction are broken when a substance dissolves.
nodes.response: Forces of attraction are *overcome*. They are still acting between the particles, but weaker than before so a different particle arrangement

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the volume of sounds are the same no matter how far away from them you are.
nodes.response: Pupils will carry out a fair test to find out for themselves how the volume of a sound decreases with distance from the sound source.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that sounds are inside the sound source waiting to come out. They may also think that the volume of sounds are the same no matter how far away from them you are.
nodes.response: Recap how sounds are made when an object vibrates. Pupils will plan an investigation to find out for themselves by measuring the volume of sounds as they move further away from the sound source.

nodes.misconception: Not looking at units when calculating the gradient of the line to find speed.
nodes.response: A recap on compound measures and units may be helpful here. The units of compound measures tell us how to calculate the measure. E.g. km/h is the distance in km/ time in hours. Pupils need to check the units on their graphs and convert if needed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think that heating a substance strongly and for extended periods will improve the quality of separation via distillation.
nodes.response: Stress that distillation is a skill which requires careful control of heating so only one substance is in the condenser at a time. Understanding the link between application of heat to the mixture, boiling point and reading a thermometer is essential

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that heating a substance strongly and for extended periods will improve distillation.
nodes.response: Stress that distillation is a skill which requires careful control of heating so only one substance is in the condenser at a time.

nodes.misconception: Heating a mixture strongly will cause distillation to occur more quickly.
nodes.response: Heating a mixture strongly could cause multiple components to enter a condenser (or delivery tube), resulting in a contaminated distillate. Careful, gentle heating of the mixture to ensure no bubbles near the condenser will reduce contamination.

nodes.misconception: Pupils to understand gas state; thinking solids, liquids and gases as 'types' of matter.
nodes.response: Refer to/use particle models to help clarify different states of matter and use these to describe why separation techniques work.

nodes.misconception: The only way to reduce environmental impact at the distribution stage is through using electric vehicles.
nodes.response: There are many ways such as designing flat pack, stackable, lightweight products, and location of manufacture.

nodes.misconception: All countries consume oil at the same rate.
nodes.response: Oil consumption varies based on industrialisation, population size, and economic factors.

nodes.misconception: The only way to reduce environmental impact at the distribution stage is through using electric vehicles.
nodes.response: There are many ways such as designing flat pack, stackable and lightweight products, packaging materials options and choosing where to locate manufacture.

nodes.misconception: An annulment is the same as a divorce
nodes.response: An annulment says the marriage was not valid, wheras a divorce ends a marriage.

nodes.misconception: Islam generally supports the use of violence in response to conflict.
nodes.response: Islam promotes peace-making first, and only allows limited force under strict conditions like self-defence or protecting the oppressed.

nodes.misconception: All Quakers have the same beliefs and practices.
nodes.response: Because Quakers place emphasis on personal relationships with God, beliefs and practices can differ for each individual Quaker.

nodes.misconception: All Christians celebrate the sacraments.
nodes.response: Many Christians do celebrate the sacraments, but not all Christians. For example, Quakers do not celebrate the sacraments.

nodes.misconception: Migration just brings people.
nodes.response: Migration brings other cultures, foods and fashion to the UK.

nodes.misconception: That all Sunni Muslims do not agree with visiting or praying at the shrines of important Muslims who have died.
nodes.response: This is a view held by some Sunni Muslims but there are others, for example Sufi Sunni Muslims who will visit and pray at the shrines of important Sufi Muslims who have died.

nodes.misconception: Muslims are all the same.
nodes.response: The Muslim community is highly diverse.

nodes.misconception: Some children may continue to share one by one when dividing.
nodes.response: Encourage children to skip count in the divisor and remind children that it is an efficient way of dividing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils not being able to regroup when dividing.
nodes.response: Use concrete resources to highlight regrouping of tens. Ask children 'What is the highest multiple you know?' to support with partitioning.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to record the remainder.
nodes.response: Remind children that if the ones are not divisible there will be a remainder and that this is expressed as 'r'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly arrange the dividend or divisor and quotient.
nodes.response: Clear modelling. Ask children 'What does this number represent?' - 'The dividend and it is placed inside the division frame.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils not understanding and/or recording the regrouped amount.
nodes.response: Continue to use language of unitisation. For example '7 tens ÷ 3 is 2 tens remainder 1 ten.' Ask what the regrouped amount represents.

nodes.misconception: Working through algorithmically without having an understanding of the regrouped amount.
nodes.response: Clear modelling with PVC. Ask children 'What does this number represent?'. Continue to use sentence stems.

nodes.misconception: Lack of understanding of place value may lead to the rise of incorrect partial quotients.
nodes.response: Encourage children to identify what each digit represents. If misconceptions persist - use place value counters to divide by skip counting.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to arrange digits within the division frame correctly and work procedurally.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling of arrangement of digits using the division frame. Continue to use stem sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly.
nodes.response: Encourage children to identify what each digit in the dividend represents. Ask, 'Is this digit a multiple of the divisor?'

nodes.misconception: The short division algorithm may not be correctly aligned.
nodes.response: Check that the decimal point aligns in the decimal fraction and the answer.

nodes.misconception: Children may scale the decimal fraction inaccurately or may forget to scale the answer accordingly to solve the original equation.
nodes.response: If a decimal fraction has only tenths, we multiply by 10 to form a whole number. If the decimal fraction has hundredths, we multiply by 100 to form a whole number. Remember to adjust the answer to solve the original equation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly.
nodes.response: Ask pupils what each digit represents. Continue to use skip counting when dividing each digit in the dividend.

nodes.misconception: Pupils not understanding why they may have to regroup or what the regrouped amount represents.
nodes.response: Ask pupils 'What does this digit represent?' draw attention to place value and use continue to use language of unitisation.

nodes.misconception: Numerators are divided and denominators are divided.
nodes.response: Emphasize the definition of division. "How many times does.... fit into it?"

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models, ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.

nodes.misconception: Using the unitising method with a remainder, the remainder is not written as a fraction of the unit.
nodes.response: Drawing bar models, ensure that the unit is subdivided so the remainder can be seen as a fraction of the unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to set out the long division algorithm correctly.
nodes.response: Use the modelling from the lesson to focus on this, especially when writing multiples of the divisor (e.g. 3 tens × 17 = 51 tens) and subtracting this from the dividend.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not make efficient use of multiplication facts when answering long division problems, especially 10 or 100 times the divisor.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make estimations using multiplication facts. Once the multiplication facts are completed, they could be used to ask quick-fire questions (e.g. what is 20 × 18? 50 × 18? 200 × 18?)

nodes.misconception: When the dividing numbers written in standard form changing the multiplication symbol between the number and power of ten to a division symbol.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write any division as a fraction.  This makes the maintenance of the multiplication symbol easier to see.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes converting from km into m or kg in g.
nodes.response: Pupils may need supporting converting units and multiplying by one thousand. Place value charts may be needed here.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway, sometimes using highlighters can help visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: Students try to divide an integer with an integer without simplifying.
nodes.response: Student are required to convert the divisor into an integer. Simplifying the denominator into a single integer digit is preferable.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Frankenstein is the name of the creature.
nodes.response: Frankenstein is the name of the scientist who created the hideous creature that students are often familiar with.

nodes.misconception: The pronoun "you" is the only example of direct address.
nodes.response: Direct address is any way in which a writer directly addresses their audience. This could be a title, name or term.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly summing the digits of an integer to identify a multiple of 3.
nodes.response: Use number bonds to sum large numbers of digits.

nodes.misconception: Often students only consider the last 2 digits of a number to check for divisibility for 8.
nodes.response: The last 2 digits check for divisibility for 4 not 8.

nodes.misconception: A number is a prime if it is not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 10.
nodes.response: A factor of a number can be greater than 10.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly summing the digits to identify a multiple of 3 or 9.
nodes.response: Use number bonds to sum large numbers of digits.

nodes.misconception: An annulment is the same as a divorce
nodes.response: An annulment says the marriage was not valid, wheras a divorce ends a marriage.

nodes.misconception: You can divorce for any reason.
nodes.response: Officially, you cannot divorce for any reason. An individual or couple will choose the most appropriate grounds for divorce based on their situation.

nodes.misconception: Diwali is celebrated in the same way everywhere in the world.
nodes.response: Diwali is celebrated by most Hindus. However, its celebration will vary according to geographical and cultural context.

nodes.misconception: 'Genes' and 'DNA' are exactly the same thing.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the idea that genes are sections of your DNA, and all the DNA together is the genome.

nodes.misconception: DNA is just 'genetic information' and not a substance; not all organisms contain DNA (e.g. plants).
nodes.response: The lesson demonstrates that DNA is a physical, chemical substance that can be extracted from cells, and shows that plants contain DNA.

nodes.misconception: All countries are members of international organisations.
nodes.response: Countries have many reasons for not joining international  organisations.

nodes.misconception: Any tools can be used for any campaign.
nodes.response: Some tools work better depending on the issue, level, who holds the power and what resources are available.

nodes.misconception: All people who live in Britain agree with the fundamental British values.
nodes.response: British values are shared beliefs about who we are as a group of people. It is a requirement that they are promoted by public sector organisations but they remain open to debate, not every citizen will agree with them in their current format.

nodes.misconception: We use opinion verbs without the definite article in Spanish as in English, e.g. I love Spanish.
nodes.response: In Spanish, opinion verbs always use the definite article before nouns, e.g. Amo el español.

nodes.misconception: The sounds [qui] and [ci] are pronounced the same in English and Spanish.
nodes.response: The sound [qui] is pronounced like a hard 'c' followed by [i] or like the word 'key' in English. The sound [ci] is pronounced like 'thi' in English.

nodes.misconception: When translating 'do you have' into Spanish, we need to translate every single word, including 'do'.
nodes.response: 'Do you have?' translate as '¿tienes?' and we do not translate 'do'.

nodes.misconception: Users of a machine learning application do not need to be aware of how accurate it is.
nodes.response: Model cards are good practice when developing machine learning applications. A model card is a short report on how a machine learning model works, how well the model performs and what people should know before using the model.

nodes.misconception: Documenting an artist’s journey is only about completed artworks.
nodes.response: Sketchbooks, notes, and drafts are just as important, showing the development of ideas, experimentation, and problem-solving along the way.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils could think that competitive games are only about scoring points and will focus on this role in a team.
nodes.response: Competitive games require attacking and defensive skills as well as team work, listening, communication, decision making, honesty, self-belief and more.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think they need to perform a dodge as soon as they see a defender.
nodes.response: Performing a dodge too early gives the defender time to react and move with you (shadow you).  Performing a dodge too late means you don't have space to use the best technique for your dodge.  The right timing will help you avoid the defender.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they can only be a good team member if they score lots of points.
nodes.response: Scoring a point means everyone in the team has done their job well, not just the individual who scored.  Only some team members need to have the role of scoring points; doing your job well will help the team members whose job it is to score points.

nodes.misconception: A dodge from a static position is a good place to showcase a dodge in isolation.
nodes.response: In game play, it is encouraged to be active and on the toes and thinking about a prelim movement before a change of direction or speed can be executed therefore encouraging this in early drills is advised.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that after one attacking or defending move, their job in the team is finished and they stand still and stop following the play.
nodes.response: Often in a game, you will need to do some attacking work and some defending work.  Concentrating and reacting to the actions of others will help you to decide if you need to attack or defend.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that performing one dodge will always be successful.
nodes.response: Pupils should remember that the defender will respond to the dodge.  Pupils might need to dodge again if the defender guesses which way they will dodge and block their run into space or another defender might move into the space they are running to.

nodes.misconception: The media always helps the public learn information.
nodes.response: Sometimes we are given misinformation, disinformation or malinformation. It is important to learn to spot this and realise that some of the media we are presented with is not always designed to help the public learn the true facts.

nodes.misconception: Democracy is not either strong or weak.
nodes.response: There are different features and areas of democracy, such as the type of democracy, electoral system, media and voting age. Each of these will have their own strengths and weaknesses that come together to form an overall judgement on democracy.

nodes.misconception: People think the survey and Domesday Book are one and the same thing.
nodes.response: In fact, the survey was ordered in 1085, and later compiled into what became known as Domesday Book.

nodes.misconception: Dominion is the opposite of stewardship.
nodes.response: Dominion is seen as authority or power, but, in common with stewardship, it is usually seen as including a duty to be responsible.

nodes.misconception: That Stevenson presents good and evil as complete opposites.
nodes.response: Remind students how easily Hyde and Jekyll blur into one.

nodes.misconception: All early engineers were men.
nodes.response: Many women have contributed to the development of engineering.

nodes.misconception: Reflexive pronouns appear after a conjugated verb.
nodes.response: The reflexive pronoun 'se' appears before a conjugated verb in any tense.

nodes.misconception: All participles in Spanish end in -ado or -ido.
nodes.response: Regular verbs do follow this pattern, but irregular ones do not. Some irregular verbs are: 'decir' - 'dicho', 'morir' - 'muerto', 'romper' - 'roto', 'volver' - 'vuelto', 'descubrir' - 'descubierto', 'cubrir' - 'cubierto'.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, 'mañana' always means 'morning'.
nodes.response: In Spanish 'mañana' has two meanings. It can mean 'morning' or 'tomorrow'.

nodes.misconception: The only way of saying 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugué'.
nodes.response: 'I played' could be translated as 'jugué' or 'jugaba'. The preterite verb 'jugué' implies a single, completed action in the past, whereas the imperfect verb 'jugaba' implies a habitual action in the past.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to see doubling where the numbers cannot be seen e.g. money contexts.
nodes.response: Children should be encouraged to represent the numbers using resources to support them in visualising the problem until they are confident to use mental strategies to solve.

nodes.misconception: Which side of the heart is the left when you look at the body and which side is oxygenated versus deoxygenated.
nodes.response: The left side of the heart is nearest your left armpit and carries oxygenated blood, the right side of the heart has deoxygenated blood (remember: LORD - left, oxygenated and right, deogygenated).

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to see that a double is two of the same thing.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring doubles that can be found in the children's immediate environment e.g. using their hands or playing a game of dominoes.

nodes.misconception: If pupils are not more fluent in their doubling facts within 5 they may struggle to efficiently double and halve larger numbers.
nodes.response: Provide examples of doubling facts within 5 using representations such as ten frames to support learners.

nodes.misconception: In doubles, players should stand on the left and right and just hit the ball on their side (like tennis or badminton).
nodes.response: In doubles in table tennis, players have to hit alternate shots which means once you have hit the ball, you need to move out of the way so your partner can hit the next shot. Just standing on sides will make it difficult to play alternate shots.

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't adapt their court position based on where their partner is and where the shuttle has been hit.
nodes.response: Work together to cover the court. If your partner is at the front of the court then it is important to step back to cover the back of the court. However, it is typically easier to assume side-by-side positioning and cover half the court each.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss the double letters in the middle of words that have a suffix.
nodes.response: Drawing attention to the patterns of how words are spelt when suffixes are added will help them to remember the double letter.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss the double letters in the middle of words that have a suffix.
nodes.response: Drawing attention to the patterns of how words are spelt when suffixes are added will help them to remember the double letter.

nodes.misconception: You do not need to plan a self-portrait concrete poem. You should just start by writing.
nodes.response: Remind children that planning some descriptive words or phrases can help to ensure their emotions or message are communicated effectively in their concrete poem.

nodes.misconception: Working out the tone, audience and purpose is an unnecessary step in planning. These things are always really obvious.
nodes.response: The foundations of convincing writing comes in the planning stage. This includes thinking carefully about tone, audience and purpose. Having a deep, rather than superficial, understanding of each will allow for a compelling piece of writing.

nodes.misconception: That a piece of writing is completely finished once you have written it.
nodes.response: The first time you complete a piece of writing is it in its draft form. You want to go back and continually revise it.

nodes.misconception: People don't use literary methods in nonfiction writing.
nodes.response: Whenever you write any thing - even a shopping list - you are employing methods. Every word is a choice, thus every choice can be evaluated. In nonfiction writing (even nonfiction writing by people who aren't writers) methods will be used for effect.

nodes.misconception: There is one source to a river.
nodes.response: There can be many different sources within a drainage basin system.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the eyes are drawn towards the top of the face.
nodes.response: The eyes are halfway between the top of the head and the chin.

nodes.misconception: It is not uncommon for pupils to mix up the x- and y-coordinates, meaning they end up plotting in the wrong position or giving the wrong coordinates.
nodes.response: A stem sentence has been included in the lesson which should be regularly referred to. Rhymes can also be used as an aide memoir but this should be in tandem with deep conceptual understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will have lots of familiarity with linear number lines but will be less familiar with circular ones. They may not understand that in terms of time, 12 is often followed by 1
nodes.response: Take frequent opportunities outside of the lesson to practise counting around the clock so that pupils get used to the sequence ... 11, 12, 1, 2 ...

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the insect needs to be in the centre of the page for a balanced composition.
nodes.response: Remind children that composition can be balanced even if the insect is placed off-centre. Balance is about how all elements (insect, plants, background) work together, not just where the main subject is.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are taught to choose a vertex then count horizontally and / or vertically when translating that vertex. Pupils may forget which vertex they started with and end up translating the wrong vertex.
nodes.response: You may wish to consider asking pupils to mark the starting vertex with a small circle as a reminder of which one they started with.

nodes.misconception: Pupils draw a straight line to begin to create their angle and then place the centre of the protractor in the middle of the straight line.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to place the middle spot of the protractor on one end of the straight line as this will make it easier to mark on the second line to create the vertex once the protractor has been removed.

nodes.misconception: All the lines in a building should go straight up and sideways.
nodes.response: Some lines go towards a vanishing point to show how things look smaller as they get further away. That’s how we create perspective.

nodes.misconception: There is a right and wrong way in which to rearrange lines and shapes when making abstract art.
nodes.response: There is no right or wrong - in abstract art shapes and lines can be rearranged according to the intentions of the artist.

nodes.misconception: The front view is always the most detailed side of the shape being drawn.
nodes.response: The front view is chosen based on the most informative and clear perspective, not necessarily the most detailed one.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not identify when a polygon has more than one pair of parallel or perpendicular sides especially when the polygon is not a rectangle.
nodes.response: Make use of right angle checkers to identify that some shapes have more than one right angle and take time to link this to perpendicular sides.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistakenly plot the y-coordinate (vertical distance) first, then the x-coordinate (horizontal distance), leading to incorrect point placement.
nodes.response: Reinforce that the x-coordinate comes first by using mnemonics such as "X before Y, along the ground before you fly." Practice plotting a few points together as a class to build this habit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that translating a shape changes its size, shape, or orientation, rather than just its position.
nodes.response: Clarify that translation only changes the position of the shape on the grid; the shape itself remains identical in size, shape, and orientation. Use visual examples to compare the shape before and after translation to reinforce this concept.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise that the same type of shape, such as a pentagon, can have different properties such as parallel or perpendicular lines.
nodes.response: Make use of geoboards if possible to create a pentagon and physically move one vertex. Focus on the fact that the shape still has 5 vertices and discuss what is similar and different.

nodes.misconception: Children overgeneralise about the appearance of polygons such as rectangles and pentagons and do not recognise them when they are less typical.
nodes.response: Ensure modelling and examples show a range of shapes. For example, show a range of rectangles and focus on the key properties of parallel and perpendicular sides to identify that they are all rectangles.

nodes.misconception: Straight lines rather than curved lines are used to draw a sphere.
nodes.response: Remind children that if straight lines are used, the sphere can look flat even though the artist has used tone. Curved lines help the moon to look spherical.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that leaves are uniform in shape, when in fact rainforest leaves vary greatly in shape and size.
nodes.response: Highlight the diversity of plant forms and individuality of shape in the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Artists always draw things exactly how they look in real life.
nodes.response: Artists sometimes draw things as they look in real life but can also draw things from their imagination.

nodes.misconception: You need to press down hard when using charcoal.
nodes.response: Pressing down too hard will break the charcoal. You need to be much more gentle.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to infer or justify an appropriate moral for the tale.
nodes.response: Model linking examples back to the story to ensure it is an appropriate inference. E.g. I think the moral of the story is that good deeds are returned because after Antelope did a good deed for Anansi, Anansi returned the favour.

nodes.misconception: Characters just need to look good, they don’t need to mean anything.
nodes.response: Great character design includes meaning with symbols and design choices conveying personality and mood.

nodes.misconception: To draw a graph, points should always be joined with line segments.
nodes.response: For the graph of $$y=x^3$$ show the line joining $$(0,0)$$ and $$(1,1)$$ and ask pupils to test some coordinate pairs from that line in the original equation. For example, $$(1/2,1/2)$$ does not satisfy the equation.

nodes.misconception: $$y = 2^x$$ evaluates to $$0$$ when $$x = 0$$
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the laws of indices that can be used to show that $$b^{0} = 1$$

nodes.misconception: Drawings always have to look exactly like the object the artist is observing.
nodes.response: Drawing exercises focus more on artists using their eyes to carefully observe lines and shapes, rather than trying to create a drawing that looks exactly like the object.

nodes.misconception: Using unconventional materials doesn’t have a deeper purpose in the drawing process.
nodes.response: Unconventional materials can lead to unique textures, effects, and creative outcomes, challenging traditional drawing methods.

nodes.misconception: All architectural designs are symmetrical.
nodes.response: Some buildings are also asymmetrical.

nodes.misconception: Charcoal is too messy to control, and mistakes can’t be fixed.
nodes.response: Charcoal is a flexible material. Smudging can be used to soften mistakes or use a rubber to refine shapes and add highlights.

nodes.misconception: $$1 / 0$$ evaluates to give $$0$$
nodes.response: Get pupils to consider what happens when $$x=1/2$$, $$x=1/3$$, $$x=1/4$$ etc. This will help them spot the role of the $$y$$ axis as asymptote for themselves.

nodes.misconception: Digital drawing doesn’t require the same skills as traditional drawing.
nodes.response: Core artistic skills like proportion, tone and composition still apply in digital artworks. Digital tools simply offer new ways to achieve them.

nodes.misconception: 3D drawings must look exactly like 2D sketches.
nodes.response: 3D drawing explores form and space - it’s about expressing line, contour and movement in three dimensions, not replicating flat sketches.

nodes.misconception: Any camera setting will capture light drawings.
nodes.response: Long exposure (slow shutter speed) is essential for creating light drawings, without it, the camera won’t capture light movement, only still images.

nodes.misconception: There is only value for $$y$$ for any given value of $$x$$
nodes.response: Pythagoras' theorem on a coordinate grid shows that there are two possible places where the $$y$$-coordinate could be for any given value of $x$$. This is also true for the $$x$$-coordinate for any given value of $$y$$

nodes.misconception: The plan and elevations should look exactly the same on squared paper as they do on a solid drawn on isometric paper.
nodes.response: The grid lines on the two types of paper are not the same which is why there is a visual difference. The measurements for each line however have not changed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have their calculator set to radians instead of degrees.
nodes.response: The first check for understanding is designed to catch this but it is worth checking that the correct unit of measurement is being used throughout the lesson.

nodes.misconception: The plan and elevations show every aspect of a solid.
nodes.response: The plan and elevations do not show the features inside a solid.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have their calculator set to radians instead of degrees.
nodes.response: The first check for understanding is designed to catch this but it is worth checking that the correct unit of measurement is being used throughout the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Colours are neutral and do not evoke emotion.
nodes.response: Colours can evoke a wide range of different emotions. For example, blue might suggest calmness while red might indicate anger.

nodes.misconception: 'Wenn' can be used in question words to ask 'When?'.
nodes.response: Use the question word 'Wann?' to ask 'When?' in German. Use 'wenn' to say 'when' in a present tense statement.

nodes.misconception: Like English, German uses 'it' and 'they' as subject pronouns to replace nouns.
nodes.response: In German, subject pronouns 'er', 'sie', 'es', 'sie' mean 'it' and 'they' and match the grammatical gender and number of the noun.

nodes.misconception: All Muslim women wear a hijab.
nodes.response: Some Muslim women wear a hijab whilst others do not. Many Muslim women feel wearing a hijab is an empowering element of their identity.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the curved side of their stick.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the flat side of their stick, rotating it when changing direction. Challenge pupils, but be lenient as they develop this difficult skill.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they can move with the ball more than 2 steps before starting to dribble.
nodes.response: This can be seen at the elite level but will break the travelling rule.

nodes.misconception: Pupils take strong touches of the ball and move with the ball too far away from themselves so lose control easily.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to take their time and keep the ball close to avoid losing control and possession.

nodes.misconception: Pupils kick the ball too far ahead of them, using their toes to kick it, rather than keeping control with lighter touches.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the further the ball is away from them, the easier it is for a defender to take it.

nodes.misconception: When bouncing a ball to dribble with it, pupils slap the ball down with their palms, focusing on power. Pupils dribble with their head down.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are pushing the ball down with control, using the flat part of their fingertips. Encourage pupils to keep their heads up whilst dribbling to ensure they can see space, don't bump into others and develops their peripheral view.

nodes.misconception: Pupils just want to shoot and score. They forget to look up and check to see if they should pass or dribble.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that we only shoot when we are in a suitable position and should take our time to make decisions first.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they can only dribble or pass and not effectively combine both, struggling to transition between the 2 actions.
nodes.response: Focus on the importance of both skills and how key decision making on when to use each action is vital.

nodes.misconception: Pupils throw the ball focusing on throwing it hard and high, instead of passing with accuracy.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that a pass requires control and accuracy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often try to bounce the ball too hard, resulting in dribbling it too high. Pupils believe they can only dribble with one hand.
nodes.response: Bending your knees and dribbling lower with control will make it harder for a defender to steal the ball. You can only dribble with one hand at a time, however switching between hands is an effective way to dribble with control.

nodes.misconception: When dribbling the ball eyes should always be down looking at the ball.
nodes.response: Whilst it's important to control the ball, always looking down means you can't see what's happening in the game. Keeping the head up improves decision-making, allowing players to see defenders, find passing options and spaces to dribble into.

nodes.misconception: Pupils turn without checking if there was actually space to turn into first. Pupils also turn when there is no need to.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to check for the space before they turn. Explain that we turn when we need to change direction to move away from a defender.

nodes.misconception: When dribbling in a game to score points, pupils forget to keep control and rush, causing them to kick the ball too far ahead.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of keeping the ball close and dribbling with control. Highlight how this will lead to scoring more points.

nodes.misconception: When dribbling using their hands, pupils use the tips of their fingers or their palms to push the ball towards the floor.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are using the flat part of their fingertips to push the ball towards the floor.

nodes.misconception: When using their fingertips to bounce the ball, pupils use the ends of their fingers.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand that using the fingertips refers to the flat part at the top of their fingers.

nodes.misconception: When dribbling with their feet in games, pupils sometimes think they can pick the ball up to protect it from defenders.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they cannot use their hands when dribbling with their feet and that they need to either use their body to protect the ball or move into open space.

nodes.misconception: Drones are boring because they are just a single note.
nodes.response: Drones can add depth and a focus point to a piece of music. They can sometimes even be soothing for the listener.  A piece of music can be built around a drone.

nodes.misconception: Pupils swing when hitting drop shots and net shots.
nodes.response: By reducing your backswing and almost eliminating your follow through, you will be able to perform more successful drop shots and net shots that trickle just over the net and put your opponent under more pressure.

nodes.misconception: All PEDs are automatically illegal and banned substances.
nodes.response: The use of some PEDs to enhance performance is perfectly acceptable. Many sportspeople use narcotic analgesics to get through an event or drink caffeine for its stimulating effect. WADA is responsible for determining which PEDs are allowed.

nodes.misconception: Whenever two-verb structures are used, the second verb - the infinitive or the past participle - always goes to the end of the clause or sentence.
