nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that longer sentences are always preferable to short ones.
nodes.response: Emphasise that text cohesion is best served by variety and that short sentences have a significant role in writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils need to understand that there has to be a closed loop of conducting material, from one end of the battery or power supply, through the device and back to the battery.
nodes.response: Pupils should test a faulty circuit in a systematic way,  e.g. starting at one point in the circuit and moving from component to component in order, going clockwise or anti-clockwise from that point.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they have 6 'downs/tags' like tag rugby or rugby league.
nodes.response: In flag football, teams only have 4 downs (or attempts) to advance the ball 10 yards or score. If they don't succeed within those 4 downs, the ball is turned over to the other team.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the attacking players can block the blitzer so that the quarterback remains able to pass the ball.
nodes.response: In flag football, blocking the blitzer is not allowed. Attackers must avoid physical contact and the quarterback must rely on quick throws and good timing to avoid being tagged by the blitzer.

nodes.misconception: Flexibility can only be challenged when we are holding a specific postion and staying still.
nodes.response: Flexibility of our muscles can be performed when still (static) and on the move (dynamic).

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to bend their knees on landing. Pupils bring their head to their knees when performing a tuck jump. Pupils forget to use their arms when jumping.
nodes.response: Pupils should repeatedly practise bending knees on landing. Pupils should raise their knees towards the chest in a tuck jump. Pupils should be reminded to swing their arms to give them momentum and to use their arms in the various jumps.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that you have to perform a font paddle arm action as quickly as you can.
nodes.response: A long and steady pull is more energy efficient and can increase propulsion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all light objects float and that all heavy objects sink.
nodes.response: Explore how mass and volume (determined by shape) affect whether objects float or sink - before discussing density.

nodes.misconception: Flooding only causes bad impacts.
nodes.response: In some parts of the world flooding can bring sediment to the soil which helps crops grow.

nodes.misconception: River flooding is only influenced by natural factors like the amount of rainfall.
nodes.response: Humans can make flooding more likely by building towns and cities and deforestation.

nodes.misconception: Plants do not reproduce sexually. Flowers are only produced to look attractive.
nodes.response: Show examples of the reproductive organs; discuss pollen and ova and relate them to gametes in humans.

nodes.misconception: When using operations with vectors, pupils do not use the priority of operations.
nodes.response: The priority of operations applies to vectors, even those expressed in component form. Use Desmos to demonstrate a resultant vector using multiplication and/or addition of vectors.

nodes.misconception: When using operations with vectors, pupils do not use the priority of operations.
nodes.response: The priority of operations applies to all calculations.

nodes.misconception: 'Aber' and 'sondern' mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use 'aber' to contradict a preceding statement that does not contain a negative. Use 'sondern' to mean 'but' or 'rather' following a negative statement.

nodes.misconception: Models are the final design.
nodes.response: Iterative design uses prototypes to model and test ideas, gather feedback and improve.

nodes.misconception: Every quotation in a main body paragraph should be analysed.
nodes.response: Some quotations should be analysed, but others you can simply embed into sentences.

nodes.misconception: Each point of light on an image comes from just one ray of light from a corresponding point on an object.
nodes.response: Show how multiple rays of light from each point of an object pass through a lens and are focused at a single point in the image. Show how covering half of a lens does not cause half of the image to disappear.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe when adapting a task that everyone needs the same level of challenge.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that everyone has different levels of skill, experience and confidence, therefore adapting a task should look to meet the needs of all the pupils engaging in it.

nodes.misconception: Hand positions should only change at the start of new phrases.
nodes.response: This depends entirely on what notes are used. Sometimes, like in Korobeiniki, it is more useful to change hand position during a phrase. When doing this, we should always practise making it seamless, so there is no obvious change in sound.

nodes.misconception: All major songs are happy. All minor songs are sad.
nodes.response: This is an oversimplification. All of the musical elements work together to create the character or mood of a piece of music. The context in which a piece is heard will also impact our emotional response to it.

nodes.misconception: Music can only be major or minor in tonality.
nodes.response: Music can be tonal - major, minor or other using modes. Music can also be atonal or go beyond tonality, not having a traditional sense of key or tonal note.

nodes.misconception: Children may describe movements around a grid using left, right, up and down rather than using the language of turn e.g. go forward, turn left.
nodes.response: Encourage children to act out their directions practically so they can feel themselves turning and see that they are making a turn and not taking sideways steps across the path or grid.

nodes.misconception: A hyperlink is always text.
nodes.response: A hyperlink can be text, images or other media.

nodes.misconception: Neglecting to follow the 3 conventions of bearings.  Particularly, going anticlockwise when given a bearing over 180 degrees.
nodes.response: Pupils can be asked to stand and turn 90 degrees.  Some will turn clockwise and some anticlockwise. This will create a discussion point about the direction being important.  Having the clockwise convention means a direction does not need to be given.

nodes.misconception: Every performance of a piece is the same.
nodes.response: We can use dynamics and tempo to tell the story of the words, different conductors and performers might do this differently.

nodes.misconception: Conductors are only needed to lead orchestras.
nodes.response: Conductors can direct any group of musicians - singers or instrumentalists. They can help each voice enter a round at the correct time.

nodes.misconception: Conductors are for orchestras and not for singing in class.
nodes.response: Following a conductor can help us to stay together and change our dynamics together. This adds focus to our singing as well as making the song more effective for an audience.

nodes.misconception: Pupils follow other teams assuming they’re going the correct way.
nodes.response: Highlight to pupils that orienteering is about independent navigation, and others can be wrong too.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not follow the instructions as they know how to make a sandwich themselves already.
nodes.response: Model the process with the printed instructions and slow the process down by going one step at a time, encouraging them to repeat the instruction. This could either be using 'I do, we do' as shown in the slides or in small groups.

nodes.misconception: Difficulties in understanding the science of climate change.
nodes.response: There are many resources about the causes and impacts of climate change available online.

nodes.misconception: Always use the partitive article after food and drink items, even with negative sentences.
nodes.response: The partitive article changes to 'de' to say what you don't eat and drink e.g. 'je ne mange pas de pizza'.

nodes.misconception: Articles can be missed out in French like in English.
nodes.response: Articles can't be omitted in French. Use the definite article with specific nouns/giving opinions and the partitive article with uncountable and non-specific nouns.

nodes.misconception: Food is only for eating and cannot be used as an art medium.
nodes.response: Food can be used as an art medium because it evokes the senses and carries deep cultural and emotional meanings.

nodes.misconception: Arrows mean "eats" in a food chain diagram. Each level is an individual organism.
nodes.response: This lesson explores the meaning of the arrows, and the idea that each level of a food chain diagram is a population of organisms.

nodes.misconception: Everyone in a religion celebrates a festival in the same way.
nodes.response: The way religious festivals are celebrated varies based on where people live, their culture and denominational differences. For example, Christmas is widely celebrated by non-Christians, focusing on family, giving and joy.

nodes.misconception: Sensory evaluation can only help us decide whether we like a food or not.
nodes.response: Sensory evaluation can help us decide whether we like foods, but also allows us to describe and compare foods.

nodes.misconception: There is a limited range of foods produced and made in the UK. This is why food from other countries are popular.
nodes.response: There is a huge range of food produced and made in the UK, including many traditional dishes. Food from other countries is often eaten to add variety to the diet.

nodes.misconception: Recipes from around the world can only be cooked using ingredients from those countries.
nodes.response: We can prepare and cook recipes from other countries using ingredients grown, reared or caught in the UK. Sometimes there are ingredients that are not grown or easily made in the UK, so foods from other countries are used.

nodes.misconception: Protein is the main source of energy in our diets.
nodes.response: Carbohydrates and fats are the main source of energy in our diets.

nodes.misconception: Traffic lights can be used to compare different types of foods for the healthiest option.
nodes.response: Traffic lights are designed to help people compare similar foods for the healthiest option, so they are comparing foods ‘like for like’.

nodes.misconception: 'Use by' and 'best before' date marks are the same. The food is still safe to eat after the date passes.
nodes.response: 'Use by' and 'best before' date marks are not the same. After the 'use by' date passes, the food is not safe to eat. After the ‘best before’ date passes, the food will probably be safe to eat, but may not look or taste as good.

nodes.misconception: People like and dislike the same foods.
nodes.response: There are no right or wrong foods to like to like or dislike. We all have different tastes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unaware of the provenance of their food and the possible environmental effect of eating foods from different countries.
nodes.response: Explanation of how some foods are grown in England and how eating local, seasonal food can minimise the impact on the environment.

nodes.misconception: 'Farm to fork' only applies to food produced on a farm and eaten with a fork.
nodes.response: 'Farm to fork' is a term used to describe the direct connection between food production (not just on farms) and its consumption (being eaten, not just with a fork).

nodes.misconception: Supply chains start at the manufacturing stage.
nodes.response: Supply chains start when raw materials have been taken from the earth.

nodes.misconception: Organic farmers do not use fertiliser on their crops.
nodes.response: Organic farming does involve the use of fertiliser but not the use of artificial chemical fertiliser (e.g. derived from fossil fuels). For example, farmyard manure is a good source of nutrients for crops on an organic farm but so too is seaweed.

nodes.misconception: It is not possible to be overweight and undernourished at the same time.
nodes.response: Undernourishment occurs when someone isn’t receiving enough calories or essential nutrients to grow and function well. So it is possible to over eat but not eat enough of the right foods to acquire sufficient nutrients.

nodes.misconception: All fat in the diet can cause ill health.
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need some fat in their diet but that they should not eat large amounts of fat regularly if they want to have a healthy diet.

nodes.misconception: 'Some' can be left out in French just like it can in English.
nodes.response: Always use an article before food nouns in French, if it is a whole item, use the indefinite article and if it's uncountable or part of an item, use the partitive article du, de la or de l'.

nodes.misconception: Honey is made from a plant.
nodes.response: Honey is made by bees in the hive. It is a food made by animals.

nodes.misconception: Confusing the reagents and the substances they test for, or the results of the tests.
nodes.response: Each test is dealt with separately and the positive and negative results are discussed sequentially.

nodes.misconception: Changes in population within a food web will only impact organisms within the same food chain.
nodes.response: Exemplify that disappearance of one population could affect populations in all parts of the food web (CfU questions address this also).

nodes.misconception: Pupils aren't aware of where different foods come from and how they are made.
nodes.response: Explain that some food is grown, some comes from animals and some is manufactured or processed in factories.

nodes.misconception: In a GCSE assessment the assessor will expect to see you be on the ball as an attacker and trying to beat defenders with tricks and feints.
nodes.response: An assessor is looking for the selection of the most appropriate skill for the situation to outwit an opponent which could be a passing option or creating space. It is more about the contribution to the team performance and strategic application.

nodes.misconception: A player has to pivot as part of footwork to create space after landing when the ball has been caught.
nodes.response: Although a pivot may be needed to create space and is permitted, it is better to turn in the air when reveiving the ball so landing is the right position for the next pass.

nodes.misconception: Getting out of position after hitting a shot.
nodes.response: Learning to lunge and recover quickly to the middle of the court requires explosive strength/power but avoids exposing space for your opposition to attack.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think they can freely move their pivot foot by dragging and sliding it. Pupils continue to move a few steps when holding the ball.
nodes.response: Reinforce the importance of keeping the pivot foot stationary and continue to practise the correct way to pivot. Remind pupils that stepping when holding the ball is a rule break and their team loses possession.

nodes.misconception: Learners may think a for loop will always repeat forever unless they manually stop it.
nodes.response: A for loop repeats a set number of times, based on the range or count value given. The loop ends automatically when the final value in the range has been reached.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that powerful actions should be performed quickly.
nodes.response: Powerful actions can be performed at any speed. However, rushing and moving too quickly can make it difficult to control the actions.

nodes.misconception: It is common for pupils to fail to consider the hanging mass as part of the accelerating mass.
nodes.response: Emphasise that all of the moving parts in the investigation are connected, are accelerated together, and need to be included in the measurement of the mass being accelerated.

nodes.misconception: It is common for pupils to fail to consider the hanging mass as part of the accelerating mass.
nodes.response: Emphasise that all of the moving parts in the investigation are connected, are accelerated together, and need to be included in the measurement of the mass being accelerated.

nodes.misconception: The words 'meilleur' and 'mieux' can be used interchangeably as they both translate the English word 'better'.
nodes.response: 'Meilleur' is an adjective and can only be used to describe nouns. 'Mieux' is an adverb and can only be used to describe verbs.

nodes.misconception: The velocity of an object must be in the same direction as the resultant force acting on the object.
nodes.response: Invite pupils to consider situations in which the resultant force is not in the same direction as the velocity, such as an object that has been thrown upwards and is slowing down as its height increases.

nodes.misconception: The velocity of an object must be in the same direction as the resultant force acting on the object.
nodes.response: Invite pupils to consider situations in which the resultant force is not in the same direction as the velocity, such as an object that has been thrown upwards and is slowing down as its height increases.

nodes.misconception: Hitting it hard and fast is the highest priority.
nodes.response: It is more effective to vary the pace, angle and positioning of where you hit the shuttle to create opportunities to win the point.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often stand with their paddle down by their side and are not in the ready position. Pupils often wait for the ball to reach them.
nodes.response: Keep repeating the ready positon throghout he lesson. Make sure pupils understand that the ball should only bounce once so they have to run to meet the ball.

nodes.misconception: Pupils hit their shots too hard and the ball travels out of court. Pupils do not return to the ready position after every shot. Pupils struggle to rally when the ball can only bounce once.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to follow through on their swing to develop more control over the shot. Remind pupils to return to the middle and be in the ready position after every shot. Allow pupils to continue to rally even when the ball bounces twice.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to swing hard at volleys.
nodes.response: When approaching the net to volley you already have momentum moving forwards into the ball which adds power so a more effective technique is to block and sometimes even cushion the pace out of the ball whilst angling it back over the net.

nodes.misconception: That 'Animal Farm' is a simple story about leadership and power.
nodes.response: Stylistically it is simple, but why does Orwell do this? What does he hope to achieve by making his novella accessible?

nodes.misconception: It is often believed that focusing on form means sacrificing function, and vice versa. The assumption is that a product can't be both beautiful and functional.
nodes.response: Good design brings together both form and function. The form of a product can enhance the function of a product by making it more enjoyable to use.

nodes.misconception: I can draw a 7 cm line with my ruler.
nodes.response: A line is a linear path that continues forever in both directions. We can draw line segments with a ruler, which have distinct endpoints.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can mix up describing how patterns grow or the relationships between objects in the pattern.
nodes.response: Pupils should verbalise their description, using the keyword 'term' , making it clear which way they are describing their pattern.

nodes.misconception: The horizontal side length of an isosceles triangle is always the base side.
nodes.response: The base side of an isosceles triangle can have any orientation. It is important to look at the hash marks, angle markers, or measurements.

nodes.misconception: The capital letter 'K' may look like a lowercase 'k' (without the loop).
nodes.response: Emphasise where the diagonal lines need to go to and model using the capital 'K' in words, such as 'Kevin' or 'Kick the ball!'.

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused about which of the tramlines to start and end b and p on.
nodes.response: Explicit naming of the start and end points and modelling of this.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes these letters get reversed.
nodes.response: Emphasise the starting position and direction for each letter.  You could use 'landmarks' in your classroom, such as "Start by the window."

nodes.misconception: Children can get confused about the direction to take when forming this letter.
nodes.response: Be very explicit about going anti-clockwise, use a clock to emphasise this to the children.

nodes.misconception: That capital letters are just bigger versions of the lower case letters.
nodes.response: Emphasise that some lower case and upper case are similar but some look completely different.

nodes.misconception: Direction of movement for the s and e can be challenging.
nodes.response: Use the clock in the classroom to remind children of the anti-clockwise direction. Put arrows on the children's page to support.

nodes.misconception: Thinking we can keep finding more fossil fuels to use, and that they are a renewable energy resource.
nodes.response: Teach that fossil fuels take millions of years to form and they are being used at a faster rate than they are produced.

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off the page for the letter k.
nodes.response: Emphasis should be placed on 'keep your pencil on the page' when modelling this letter.

nodes.misconception: The height of the vertical line is sometimes too short or too tall.
nodes.response: Emphasise starting the vertical line on the ascender line and finishing on the baseline.

nodes.misconception: Letter families are letters that appear close to each other within the alphabet.
nodes.response: Letters are within the same letter family if they are formed in a similar way.

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused with which direction to go when 'going over' for the m, n and r.
nodes.response: Explicit modelling and using a point in the classroom to direct the children. Check teacher tip.

nodes.misconception: Children may not use or know the letter names and rely on the phoneme the letter makes instead.
nodes.response: Use the teaching of the formation as an opportunity to revisit letter names vs. letter sounds (e.g. M vs. mmmm)

nodes.misconception: Often students will struggle with which direction to go to form the numerals 2, 3, 4 and 5.
nodes.response: Model clearly using physical things in the room to show which direction they will be drawing. 'To the left, towards the window' for example.

nodes.misconception: Children often put a large gap between the two digits when forming the number 10.
nodes.response: When modelling, emphasise that these two digits are 'friends' and like to be close together but not touching.

nodes.misconception: Children can get confused about the direction to take when forming the letters o, g and q.
nodes.response: Be very explicit about going anti-clockwise, use a clock to emphasise this to the children.

nodes.misconception: Drawing a large size j and dotting it to form the capital J.
nodes.response: Reminder that the capital J has a horizontal line across the ascender line.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils think that compaction and cementation are the same processes.
nodes.response: Highlight that compaction is due to pressure while cementation occurs when minerals act as a 'glue' holding sediments together.

nodes.misconception: Confusion on the direction for the 'curl up' on the y and j.
nodes.response: Be consistent with wording and modelling. Left direction is 'curl up' whereas 'flick' is when the direction is to the right.

nodes.misconception: There is a tendency for children to form the letter z backwards.
nodes.response: Model with directions in the room -  'straight across towards the door, diagonally back to the window, straight across to the door again'.

nodes.misconception: Children recognise how 'Y' is typed on the computer and try to write it like that.
nodes.response: Discuss and show children different fonts and compare to how letters should look when we are writing them by hand.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that prepositions are only used in writing.
nodes.response: Prepositions describe how things are arranged relative to other people or objects, so they can be used in all subject areas.

nodes.misconception: Contrast has to be opposites.
nodes.response: Opposites are an excellent example of a contrast since they are completely different. However, there are others, e.g. to contrast 'up' you could use 'forwards' since it is a distinctly different direction.

nodes.misconception: Spreadsheet software is so good now that you don't need to spend time formatting cells for the expected data as it will do it automatically.
nodes.response: Spreadsheet software can help, but you still need to format cells correctly to make sure the data will be displayed in the exact way you need it to be. Software doesn't always get this right.

nodes.misconception: The order of column and row in a cell reference are unimportant as columns are labelled with letters and rows are labelled as numbers.
nodes.response: Spreadsheet cell references are presented as the combination of the column letter followed by the row number, (eg. A1, B2). If the order is interchanged any other part of the spreadsheet that references them will not be able to locate them.

nodes.misconception: Conditional formatting needs to be applied each time a value in a cell changes.
nodes.response: Conditional formatting will automatically update if the value in a cell changes, as soon as a value meets the condition, the formatting will be appplied.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that just the tagger remains at the breakdown in T1 rugby.
nodes.response: After a tag/touch, 2 other defenders need to join the the tager to form a triangle at every breakdown.

nodes.misconception: The covalent bond is the shared pair of electrons; both electrons must come from different atoms. The central atom  is responsible for the formation of covalent bonds as they want a full outer shell.
nodes.response: All chemical bonds are an electrostatic force of attraction between positive and negative charges. The sharing of electrons is the process by which covalent bonds are formed. Avoid using anthropomorphic analogies to explain how covalent bonds form.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only using given measures or terms in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required to form an expression for the volume or surface area.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to clearly show how the are breaking down a compound shape, and label clearly any new or missing lengths they can determine.

nodes.misconception: Alternate angles are always equal to each other.
nodes.response: Alternate angles are equal when a transversal intersects parallel lines. If the transversal intersects a pair of lines that are not parallel then the alternate angles will not be equal.

nodes.misconception: Ions are not formed because atoms 'want' or 'need' a full outer electron shell. Pupils often find standard notation difficult and get confused about when to use superscript and subscript.
nodes.response: It is important that pupils understand that atoms do not have 'wants' or 'needs'. Emphasise that the driving force for the formation of atoms is an increase in stability when the outer electron shell is full.

nodes.misconception: Ions are not formed because atoms 'want' or 'need' a full outer electron shell. Pupils often find standard notation difficult and get confused about when to use superscript and subscript.
nodes.response: It is important that pupils understand that atoms do not have 'wants' or 'needs'. Emphasise that the driving force for the formation of atoms is an increase in stability when the outer electron shell is full.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will apply common plural rules to singular nouns that have irregular plural patterns.
nodes.response: Use spelling strategies such as 'big letters' or 'colour blocks' to help pick out the tricky elements of irregular plural spellings and embed them in the memory.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often incorrectly use an apostrophe when they hear an 's' at the end of the word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the rules for using apostrophes. Only use an apostrophe if you can name and recognise the rule - for omission or possession.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to spell the root word of plural nouns that are being focused on.
nodes.response: For pupils who need more support, provide the root word (singular noun) as a starting point for Practise Task B, so they can focus on securing the rules around plurals.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly identifying when simultaneous equations can be formed. This can lead to pupils using the same letter in two equations to represent different things.
nodes.response: Pupils should be writing down precisely what the variable represent in context. They can then compare whether they are using the same letter to represent the same thing in two different equations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils perform movements too fast or too slow which disrupts the flow of the kata.
nodes.response: Performing Chon-Ji at a consistent tempo and speed helps to develop cardiovascular and muscular endurance. It enhances mental focus and breath control. The different speeds simulate real combat situations which will vary in speed and acceleration.

nodes.misconception: The goal of samatha meditation is to achieve enlightenment or insight.
nodes.response: Samatha is primarily a concentration practice aimed at stilling the mind through focused attention, often using a single object like the breath or a visual object (kasina).

nodes.misconception: Vipassana meditation is primarily about relaxation or stress relief.
nodes.response: Vipassana meditation is aimed at cultivating insight into the nature of reality, specifically the impermanent, unsatisfactory, and non-self characteristics of all phenomena, known in Buddhism as the three marks of existence.

nodes.misconception: All Christians worship in the same way.
nodes.response: Worship differs across Christian denominations, with some denominations, such as the Catholic Church, practising liturgical worship, and others, such as the Religious Society of Friends and Pentecostal Churches, practising non-liturgical worship.

nodes.misconception: The fill handle can only be used to replicate formulas.
nodes.response: The fill handle can replicate formulas, text and numbers.

nodes.misconception: A good enquiry question is answered in the data collection stage.
nodes.response: A good enquiry question guides you through all stages of the enquiry to help you find an answer.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that fossil fuels have been made from fossils, such as the ones they may see in the classroom or museums.
nodes.response: Explain that fossil fuels are the remains of living things that have been changed over millions of years by heat and pressure.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often interpret the rock cycle as the cause of rock formation.
nodes.response: Stress the rock cycle is a representation of relationships between the rock types.  For rocks to change from one type to another requires specific conditions (i.e. igneous rock can change into metamorphic or melted into a different igenous rock).

nodes.misconception: Most students will be aware that bones can become fossilised but not realise that other remains such as wood or footprints can also become fossils too.
nodes.response: This lesson contains a broad range of examples of the types of remains that can become fossilised.

nodes.misconception: The Prophet Muhammad chose Ali to be his successor.
nodes.response: Shi'a Muslims believe that Allah chose Ali to be the successor to the Prophet Muhammad, and that the Prophet Muhammad announced this to the Muslim community before he died.

nodes.misconception: The six articles of faith are only believed by Sunni Muslims.
nodes.response: Most Muslims (both Sunni and Shia) hold beliefs about tawhid, prophecy, holy books, angels, the Day of Judgement and God's power, but they may not ascribe them as the 'six articles of faith'.

nodes.misconception: Northings come before eastings.
nodes.response: Eastings come first, then northings.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that any use of a co-ordinating conjunction creates a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that sentences like 'We ate cheese and ham.' cannot be a compound sentence because it does not contain two main clauses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse an exclamatory phrase with an exclamation sentence.
nodes.response: A phrase is a group of words with no verb. Any simple sentence must include a verb. Verbs in exclamation sentences are often being verbs.

nodes.misconception: Some students may think that fractional distillation produces new substances from crude oil.
nodes.response: It is important to emphasise that crude oil is a mixture, and the process of fractional distillation is to separate out the different hydrocarbons based on their boiling points.

nodes.misconception: Children may have some confusion around using a fictional tale to inform a non-fiction text.
nodes.response: Go through other examples, from fiction and real-life, that could be used as newsworthy events for newspaper articles.

nodes.misconception: Students tend to think of humans as being good and monsters as being evil.
nodes.response: In this novel, the line between good and evil is blurred. Shelley forces us to question who the real monster is in the novel.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget that the description of the Creature is written from Frankenstein's perspective.
nodes.response: Shelley describes the Creature so horribly through the eyes of Frankenstein to show his disgust with his creation.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Shelley was opposed to scientific advancement.
nodes.response: Shelley was not opposed to scientific advancement; she was opposed to unethical and limitless scientific practices.

nodes.misconception: Students do not appreciate the Creature's eloquence and the fact that he has educated himself.
nodes.response: The Creature is a persuasive and eloquent character who manages to convince Victor to begin making him a mate.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives don’t have capital letters in German, so to say ‘the green ones’ in German, no capital letter is needed.
nodes.response: Whilst adjectives don't have capital letters, adjectival nouns always have capital letters; ‘die Grünen’ - 'the green ones'.

nodes.misconception: Da-compounds can be used to refer back to any noun already mentioned.
nodes.response: Da-compounds can only be used with inanimate nouns. For people and animals, use object pronouns.

nodes.misconception: The verb ending -o means 'I' but only if you're a boy or man.
nodes.response: For regular verbs, the 'I' verb form always ends in 'o'. Verb endings match the person, but don't change for gender, so 'hablo' means 'I speak' for everyone.  It is adjectives that change ending -o to -a to describe a girl or woman.

nodes.misconception: It is easy to write Spanish from memory if I know what the words mean.
nodes.response: Knowing what words mean when you listen to or read them doesn't mean you can write them from memory.  To write from memory, you need to practise writing from memory, especially verbs, as these need to be right to communicate your message clearly.

nodes.misconception: When in English there are two nouns together to describe a particular type of something, e.g. 'train ticket', in Spanish we translate them in the same order.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the word order changes and the preposition 'de' is used between the two nouns, e.g. 'train ticket' is 'billete de tren'.

nodes.misconception: The word 'pie' is pronounced like the English word 'pie'.
nodes.response: In Spanish 'pie' is also a 1-syllable word but we hear each letter distinctly, and Spanish 'i' is pronounced 'i' as in the Spanish word 'idea'. To say it correctly, enunciate each letter but quickly so that the word sounds as one syllable, 'p-i-e'.

nodes.misconception: 'Qui' is always used as a question word.
nodes.response: 'Qui' is a question word meaning 'who' but is also used as a relative pronoun to introduce a relative clause, for example 'L'homme qui est grand est mon papa', meaning 'the man who is tall is my dad'.

nodes.misconception: 'Mettre' is a verb like 'entendre' and it follows the same pattern.
nodes.response: 'Mettre' has the same present tense endings as verbs like 'entendre' but the stem is different in the singular forms. Drop one of the 't's from the infinitive, leaving the remaining 't' as a silent final consonant.

nodes.misconception: All the words ending in '-ción' and '-ciones' must have an accent.
nodes.response: If a word ends in 'n' or 's' and has final syllable stress, it must have an accent, e.g. 'la opción'. However, if a word ending in 'n' or 's' has penultimate syllable stress, it does not need an accent, e.g. 'las opciones'.

nodes.misconception: Freedom of religious expression only protects religious people.
nodes.response: This freedom includes non-religious views and protects everyone’s right to think freely and speak respectfully.

nodes.misconception: Pankhurst and the suffragettes were peaceful protesters.
nodes.response: How does Pankhurst's speech convey some of the radical tactics or attitudes employed by the suffragettes? Pankhurst and her followers pushed boundaries and challenged societal norms to fight for women's rights.

nodes.misconception: The increased success of the direct action in the 1960s was the result of minimal opposition.
nodes.response: Direct action in the 1960s was increasingly successful because of the increased opposition that was captured by national and international news reporters.

nodes.misconception: When a sentence contains both a direct object and an indirect object, the indirect object always comes first.
nodes.response: When a sentence contains both a direct object noun and an indirect object noun, the indirect object always comes first. When a pronoun is used to replace either noun, the pronoun comes first.

nodes.misconception: All prepositions are followed by either the accusative or the dative.
nodes.response: The prepositions ‘hinter’, ‘neben’, ‘unter’, ‘über’, ‘vor’, ‘zwischen’ and ‘in’ are used with the accusative case when there is movement but the dative case when there is no movement.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with the 'sh' digraph so may spell words containing 'ch' incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between spellings containing the 'ch' spelling sounding like the /sh/ sound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 'g' and 'ck' at the end of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between words containing the 'gue' and 'que' spelling.

nodes.misconception: European countries only created colonies in Africa and the Americas.
nodes.response: European countries set up colonies all over the world, including in Asia.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be tempted to always use the total frequency from a tree as the denominator of any fraction.
nodes.response: The denominator of the fraction should be the total frequency of the group that is being selected from. This could be the total population or it could be a subgroup of the population.

nodes.misconception: Add -er to form all comparative adverbs.
nodes.response: Some comparative adverbs are irregular.

nodes.misconception: Questions words all have fixed spellings.
nodes.response: 'Wer', meaning 'who', changes spelling according to its case. This also used to be the case in English, but the 'whom' form is often not used nowadays.

nodes.misconception: All graphs can be used to present all types of data.
nodes.response: Examples given of different types of graph and sample data.

nodes.misconception: Friction is always unhelpful.
nodes.response: Examples given of positive uses of friction for braking and turning.

nodes.misconception: Friction is not a force.
nodes.response: Provide examples of friction slowing objects and preventing them from moving when they are pushed.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives already ending in -e follow the pattern of adjective agreement and change in the feminine form.
nodes.response: Adjectives already ending in -e do not change.

nodes.misconception: There is one word for 'is' in Spanish as there is in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, 'es' and 'está' are used to say 'is'. 'Es' is from the verb 'ser' and it is used for general traits and 'está' is from the verb 'estar' and it is used for temporary states and/or location.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is just one way of saying 'please' in French.
nodes.response: There are in fact two ways to say 'please' in French. Use 's'il te plait' with friends, family and people your own age and use 's'il vous plait' with adults outside of your family.

nodes.misconception: The verb ending for gustar-type verbs depends on who is affected, not on the subject.
nodes.response: The verb ending depends on the subject, i.e. what causes the feeling of liking, interest, importance or concern, etc., e.g. 'le encanta el juego' - 'the game delights him, her', 'le encantan los juegos' - 'the games delight him, her'.

nodes.misconception: Spanish always uses English word order when using indirect objects (subject + verb + object).
nodes.response: In Spanish, the indirect object can go before or after the verb. Both 'le doy un regalo a mi hermano' and 'a mi hermano le doy un regalo' are correct - the second just adds emphasis to who receives the gift.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the ship was called 'The Fighting Temeraire'.
nodes.response: 'The Fighting Temeraire' was the name of Turner's painting, the ship was called HMS Temeraire.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that they should breathe as little as often, or always breathe to the same side.
nodes.response: Breathing every 3 arms pulls maintains body position and oxygen supply to the working muscles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you need to dive from a straight forward position to land in a front landing position.
nodes.response: The hips should land in the same position as the take off for the front landing. This means the hips need to lift and move backwards slightly to initiate the forward movement.

nodes.misconception: Pupils swim front paddle with their head out of the water.
nodes.response: Get pupils to lean forwards to ensure their chin or face is in the water.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may create what they believe are fronted adverbial clauses, but they may omit the verb.
nodes.response: It is not wrong to omit a verb (this creates a phrase), but encourage pupils to circle or highlight the verb in a clause.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may create a clause instead of a phrase by using a verb in their fronted adverbial.
nodes.response: This is not wrong, but explain to children we are focusing on phrases and words today.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that the function of some words (e.g. before/after) depends on context.
nodes.response: Emphasise that sometimes these words are acting as subordinating conjunctions and sometimes they start phrases.

nodes.misconception: A seed is not living.
nodes.response: A seed is living, it contains an embryo and a food store and is a stage of development in the growth of offspring.

nodes.misconception: Confusing electrode reactions with those that occur in electrolysis. For example in a hydrogen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode but in electrolysis, hydrogen is produced at the cathode.
nodes.response: Discuss the electrode reactions in terms of electron loss or gain; rather that just relying on memory. This will provide pupils with the tools to work out the electrode reactions.

nodes.misconception: A team hit the kin-ball without properly nominating a team to defend.
nodes.response: Each hitting team must shout "Omnikin" followed by the colour of the bib worn by the nominated team before hitting the kin-ball.

nodes.misconception: When playing as part of a bigger team, pupils often bunch around the ball and do not hold their shape. They can also be more static off the ball thinking that teammates will be available for a pass.
nodes.response: Reduce the numbers on each team, assign clear roles or freeze the play regularly to demonstrate where players should be. Focus on movement off the ball as soon as players have passed.

nodes.misconception: Only the player taking the throw-off needs to be in their own half.
nodes.response: All players must be in their own half before the throw-off is taken, not just the thrower.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that blood sloshes around inside the body rather than travelling through different types of blood vessels. Pupils may also think that blood can be red or blue.
nodes.response: The learning cycle focusing on representing blood vessels in the human body helps pupils to understand that blood vessels are often drawn in different colours merely to help us distinguish between them and understand their different functions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that blood is made in the heart and the function of blood is to clean the heart.
nodes.response: This lesson provides plenty of opportunities for pupils to learn about the different functions of blood.

nodes.misconception: Children often think that the function of the heart is to make or clean blood. Also that the heart is 'love heart' shaped.
nodes.response: The model making in this lesson helps children to think about which objects and materials they can use to represent the heart and demonstrate how it pumps blood around the body.

nodes.misconception: When a function returns a value it can be used throughout the program that called it.
nodes.response: The return value needs to be stored if it is to be used later in the program that calls it.

nodes.misconception: When a function returns a value it can be used throughout the program that called it.
nodes.response: The return value needs to be stored if it is to be used later in the program that calls it. If it isn't stored, the value cannot be used again.

nodes.misconception: If the notes of a melody are changed, that just makes it a new melody.
nodes.response: Changing the notes of a melody does create a new melody, but if it is still recognisable as related to the original, we can consider it a developed version of the melody. If it is unrecognisable, then it is not a development but a totally new melody.

nodes.misconception: Tempo markings are a precise indication of speed.
nodes.response: Most tempo markings (like allegro) are a rough indication of the speed, but not an exact measurement. Composers usually leave it up to the performers to determine the exact speed. Often in modern music they will indicate a specific speed using BPM.

nodes.misconception: Unison and homophonic textures are the same thing and unison parts have to be played in the same octave.
nodes.response: In a unison texture, both the pitch and rhythm of the part must be the same. In a homophonic texture, only the rhythm needs to be the same - the parts can play different notes or chords. Parts played in octaves are also classed as a unison texture.

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to tell whether the 1st person plural of -ar verbs ('we') is in the present tense or the preterite tense because the verb endings are the same.
nodes.response: The verb ending of the 1st person plural of -ar verbs is the same in the present and the preterite tense. Therefore we rely on time markers to indicate which time frame it is, e.g. 'ayer jugamos al tenis' - 'yesterday we played tennis'.

nodes.misconception: Malaria is caused by mosquitos.
nodes.response: Mosquitos are the vector that transfer the protist to humans.

nodes.misconception: Related keys are those with the same home (tonic) note such as C major and C minor.
nodes.response: Related keys are those with the same notes, but a different home (tonic note). Major and minor scales have different tone and semitone patterns, so they need to start three semitones apart for the notes to be the same.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the formula for the number of days in a week is w=7d because a week has seven days.
nodes.response: Pupils should always write down exactly what the letter is representing. E.g. 'the number of days' and 'the number of weeks'. Then think about what calculation they are doing. 'To find the number of days I multiply the number of weeks by 7'. d=7w.

nodes.misconception: Pythagoras' theorem is just a relationship between the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
nodes.response: Whilst this is true, Pythagoras' theorem can more visually be represented as three squares whose sides are equal in length to the three sides of the triangle. The sum of the areas of the two smaller squares is equal to the area of the larger square.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the concept of 'obligation' in relation to modal verbs.
nodes.response: Talk about how sentences are showing that the speaker thinks they or someone else are 'obliged to' do something.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify prepositions within a sentence & distinguish them from determiners.
nodes.response: Prepositions always come before a noun or noun phrase to say when, where or why; they are distinct from determiners, which show specificity.

nodes.misconception: After exploring reduction, children may struggle to see partitioning as subtraction because a part is not taken away from the whole.
nodes.response: Make strong links between equations and different subtraction contexts by focusing on what the subtrahend represents in each case.

nodes.misconception: Musical fusion only refers to one type of blending of musical styles for example jazz and rock.
nodes.response: Fusion is a broad genre of music characterized by the creative integration of any two or more distinct styles.

nodes.misconception: Fusion music always requires specific, identifiable elements from each original style.
nodes.response: The fusion of styles can be so integrated that the original influences become indistinguishable.

nodes.misconception: Music from other parts of the world is 'traditional' and remains unchanged.
nodes.response: All music changes over time as different musicians shape it with their own creativity.

nodes.misconception: All CAD modelling is the same, whether working in Tinkercad or Fusion.
nodes.response: Different CAD applications work in three distinct ways, constructive solid geometry, solid modelling and parametric modelling.

nodes.misconception: Recommendations might not have been enacted or responded to but the enquiry was not a failure
nodes.response: Highlight the cost of enacting changes and the restrictions on budgets and resources.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that art has to last forever to be important or valuable.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that art can be ephemeral - meaning it lasts only a short time - and still be very important. Just like nature’s changes, temporary art helps us notice beauty, tell stories, and understand ideas about growth and resilience.

nodes.misconception: Progress will always be made at the same rate.
nodes.response: Sometimes different factors affect level of progress (sleep, hormones, nutrition) but also training results can plateau and changes to training are needed to continue to push the body to adapt.

nodes.misconception: All adverbs that tell us how and how often something happens come straight after the verb and we add -ment to all adjectives to make them adverbs.
nodes.response: There are exceptions to the adverb placement and adverb formation rules. For example 'parfois' usually comes at the start of a sentence. 'Dur' is an adjective which often doesn't change even when it is used as an adverb with certain verbs.

nodes.misconception: [en/an] and [on] sound the same in French.
nodes.response: Although the sounds are simililar and both nasal vowels, [en/an] is a nasal 'a' and [on] is a nasal 'o'. The mouth should be wide for [en/an] and almost closed for [on].

nodes.misconception: In French [qu] is pronounced the same as in English, in words like 'queen' and 'quiet'.
nodes.response: In French [qu] has the same sound as the hard 'c', this requires a lot of practice!

nodes.misconception: Always add 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
nodes.response: Some verbs, like 'werden' and modal verbs, do not require 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, we translate word-for-word from English to say 'I am going to', using 'soy' or 'estoy'.
nodes.response: Some structures do not allow for word-for-word translations between English and Spanish. To say 'I am going to' in Spanish, use the present tense of 'ir' + 'a' + 2nd infinitive verb.

nodes.misconception: A word for 'to' is always required in two-verb sentences in German.
nodes.response: 'Zu' is needed after verbs like 'hoffen' but after modal verbs and 'werden', 'zu' is not needed, e.g., 'Ich werde als Arzt arbeiten'.

nodes.misconception: Always add 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
nodes.response: Some verbs, like 'werden' and modal verbs, do not require 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.

nodes.misconception: When describing future plans, 'ir' + a is followed by a conjugated verb.
nodes.response: When describing future plans, 'ir' + a is followed by the infinitive form of a verb.

nodes.misconception: After ‘cuando’ I always need the subjunctive forms 'tenga', 'tengas', 'tenga' to mean ‘I have', 'you have', 'she, he, it has’.
nodes.response: After ‘cuando’ we use the subjunctive forms only when the action is not yet real, or is uncertain. When the action happens regularly, we use the indicative forms ‘tengo’, 'tienes', 'tiene’.

nodes.misconception: 'Cuando' is always followed by the subjunctive.
nodes.response: 'Cuando' + subjunctive is used for future actions, while 'cuando' + present is used for everyday present actions.

nodes.misconception: There are distinct words required in French to translate 'will' and 'would'.
nodes.response: The 1-verb future tense describes 'will + verb'. The conditional describes 'would + verb'. Students should be aware that both verb forms are 'simple' forms as all the meaning is contained within a single word.

nodes.misconception: Tackling harder always makes it more effective.
nodes.response: Controlled technique, not force, makes a tackle successful and reduces the chance of injury or penalties.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to hit the shuttlecock to the back of the court due to standing square on to the net. Pupils may avoid hitting backhand shots. Pupils may hit shuttlecock into the net.
nodes.response: Pupils must work on a side on position when hitting the shuttlecock to generate more power. Pupils should work on their backhand technique to develop confidence. Remove or reduce the height of the net if pupils are struggling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils give up if their team is not winning.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the more self-motvation, determination and  collaboration they show, the more likely they are to succeed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often underestimate many of the learnt skills and believe that shooting from anywhere on the court is effective.
nodes.response: Remind pupils the importance of passing and dribbling into space, teamwork and positioning.

nodes.misconception: When asking the pupils to hit the ball at pace, they may lose accuracy and control. You may have a wide range of abilities in your group which means that many of the games might not be competitive.
nodes.response: If pupils hit the ball too hard, remind them that accuracy and control is more important. Use the previous lessons to assess the ability of pupils so you can organise pairs who will have competitive games against one another.

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't discuss the benefits or potential problems of each tactic or power before making a selection that is right for their team at the time. One pupil takes over and rushes the decision making.
nodes.response: Explain that, for a tactic or power to have maximum impact and give their team a big advantage, they must discuss each option as a team.

nodes.misconception: Every point is equally important in tennis.
nodes.response: Break point and other points to the advantage side are far more important to avoid losing a game on your own serve or winning/losing a game respectively. In the 2019 Wimbledon final, Federer won 14 more points than Djokovic, but lost the match.

nodes.misconception: Pupils who are more experienced may ignore the contribution of less able pupils, or even belittle or berate them when they don't contribute well to the team.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use their knowledge to offer feedback which can help bring about an improvement, emphasising that in team games, an individual cannot and should not perform all roles or carry the team.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a short is associated with the height of a shot.
nodes.response: A short is when a shot misses the rebound frame completely. It results in a fault and change of possession with the defenders restarting play from behind the baseline.

nodes.misconception: When fielding in games, pupils believe that retrieving the ball and running it back to the bases is the most effective and quickest way to field.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to work as a team, by backing each other up and supporting each other. Ensure pupils understand that accurately throwing the ball to a teammate that is closer to the bases will be more effective and quicker than running with it.

nodes.misconception: A celebration can only be shown or given when they have been successful.
nodes.response: Children may feel a lack of inclusion and encouragement if acknowledgement of their efforts are only made when they have been successful.

nodes.misconception: When pupils are running around the bases and they have stopped on a base, they often lose concentration or do not understand when they need to run again, which can result in a run out.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that even though they have stopped, they still need to focus in order to make it round the bases without getting out. The batter can continue running again once the bowler has bowled the ball.

nodes.misconception: As a batting pair, pupils are often poor at communicating when to run, causing confusion and resulting in them being run out.
nodes.response: Teach pupils the importance of communication between the batters and ensure they understand the consequence of being run out.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think we only get a penalty stroke if we break a rule.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that a a penalty stroke is an extra stroke added to your score as a result of breaking a rule or hitting the ball into certain areas.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils don't consider the emotions of other people involved in a game which can lead to unsavoury comments after mistakes or poor play.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider the emotions of others and how they might be able to positively influence the emotions of others through words and actions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that batting is more important than effective fielding, when in fact, good fielding is equally vital to success in rounders.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the importance of good tactics in both batting and fielding. Pupils should realise that if they limit their opponents from scoring rounders, it will be easier to win the game.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think it is only defenders that screen attackers.
nodes.response: Attackers should also screen defenders to allow other attacking teammates to run into the space.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are often too slow to throw from backstop to 1st base when trying to run the batter out, resulting in the batter being able to continue running around the bases.
nodes.response: When backstop has the ball, they need to react quickly and focus on a flat, hard throw to 1st base to try and run the batter out.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils will think that success in bowling only comes if the ball hits the stumps.
nodes.response: In some situations, hitting the stumps is desirable, i.e., bowl a batter out / trap them lbw / win a bowl-out. However, all lengths have their uses and a good bowler can pitch the ball at a wide range of different lengths.

nodes.misconception: Fertilisation occurs in the uterus and can happen at any time.
nodes.response: Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tubes and this can only happen before the egg cell reaches the uterus.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rush these calculations and forget to take note of the units.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that units provide the comparison standard for values. Much practice ensuring the correct molar gas volume value is used in calculations is necessary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rush these calculations and forget to take note of the units.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that units provide the comparison standard for values.  Much practice ensuring the correct molar gas volume value is used in calculations is necessary.

nodes.misconception: The atmosphere is mostly oxygen.
nodes.response: Describe the atmosphere as ~78% unreactive nitrogen and ~20% oxygen. Explain that if the atmosphere were mostly oxygen, the planet would quickly be engulfed in fire.

nodes.misconception: The micro:bit understands movement like a human does.
nodes.response: The micro:bit records numbers (x, y, z acceleration) that are then interpretted using programmed instructions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all autistic people will be similar to Addie in the book or that all autistic people will experience the world in the same way.
nodes.response: Explain that autistic experiences are diverse and that Addie's experiences are not universal. The book is written by an autistic writer, who drew on her own experiences when writing the book. No autistic person 'represents' all autistic people.

nodes.misconception: When travelling around in the circle you should try to catch up with the duet ahead of you.
nodes.response: When travelling around in the circle you should aim to maintain the same distance from the duets in front and behind you.

nodes.misconception: Increasing the size of the driven gear, increases the output speed.
nodes.response: Decreasing the size of the driven gear (or increasing the size of driver gear), increases the speed of the driven gear.

nodes.misconception: Vor' and 'bevor' and 'nach' and 'nachdem' are interchangeable because they mean 'before' and 'after'.
nodes.response: 'Vor' and 'nach' are prepositions and are followed by a noun, 'bevor' and 'nachdem' are conjunctions which link clauses and trigger word order 3.

nodes.misconception: Gender inequality is the same around the world.
nodes.response: Gender inequality varies around the world.

nodes.misconception: That gender and sexuality are the same thing.
nodes.response: Gender is about your personal identity, how you see yourself, while sexuality is about who you are attracted to.

nodes.misconception: That Jesus said 'I do not permit a woman to have authority over a man'
nodes.response: This is attributed to St Paul in the letter to Timothy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it is acceptable to use the same letter for all expressions.
nodes.response: It may be acceptable for the letter to be the same but that depends on what the letter is representing. This is explored in the first learning cycle with chocolates.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may thing that letters represent an item e.g a week equals 7 days so w=7d
nodes.response: Get pupils to identify what value the letter represents e.g the number of days then say a number sentence that describes the relationship.

nodes.misconception: Designs need to be decided upon and followed.
nodes.response: Final designs can be adapted and changed, even during the making process. This is because it is always good to be reflective throughout the making process.

nodes.misconception: Children might find it difficult to grapple with morphology that supports forming a headline.
nodes.response: Provide examples of catchy headlines and model using words in different ways e.g. bliss, blissful, blissfully.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unclear as to the position of the addresses and the date in a letter.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the features of a letter follow strict layout rules. Have some examples of written letters for the children to engage with.

nodes.misconception: The position-to-term rule is the initial term add the common difference.
nodes.response: Once pupils have found the additive pattern get them to write each term as a value add the difference.

nodes.misconception: The difference in the given terms divided by the number of missing terms gives the common difference
nodes.response: Write the sequence out with gaps for the missing terms. Model how many additions (jumps) to get from one known term to the next.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use adjective choices that are not precise enough or appropriate for a certain moment.
nodes.response: Create a shared word bank for the characters at different moments that pupils can refer to.

nodes.misconception: Electricity comes from the plug sockets in our homes. When electrical appliances are used, the electricity goes into them but is not part of a complete circuit.
nodes.response: Pupils will be taught where and how electricity is generated and how it is transported to our homes.

nodes.misconception: Using sources of inspiration when designing is copying.
nodes.response: When using sources of inspiration, they are usually not solutions or similar products but instead any image or product that inspires a spark of creativity.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all adjectives are equally precise when describing a noun.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that adjectives need to be carefully chosen and selected because they describe the noun in the most precise way.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate ideas for role play.
nodes.response: You might choose to hot seat each character in turn as a whole class, choosing children who feel confident sharing ideas to play each role.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate ideas for Joseph's feelings and emotions at different points of the climax.
nodes.response: You may want to add in role-play tasks as a 'way in' to the different points, modelling your thoughts in role as Joseph before giving pupils the chance to do the same.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to decide where to insert parenthesis into a sentence.
nodes.response: The parenthesis will usually follow the noun or noun phrase it adds extra information about.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not take drama activities seriously or may give only surface-level responses.
nodes.response: Model the standard of response you expect and clarify expectations; remind pupils that we are empathising with real people and we should respect their experiences. Constantly showcase good examples from the class.

nodes.misconception: Children may be unfamiliar with the meaning of some of the vocabulary involved in exploring these author's lives. E.g. 'immerse', 'boarding school', 'hijab'.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities for children to highlight any words they do not know the meaning of within each cycle of the lesson and explain the meaning (providing visual aids where appropriate) to support children in understanding each author's life.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that bats are not nocturnal because they can be seen at zoos during the day.
nodes.response: Explain that zoos use carefully planned changes of lighting to help the bats think that it is night during the day.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that hedghogs can eat milk and bread, due to children's stories depicting this.
nodes.response: Explicitly teach the pupils that hedgehogs cannot eat milk or bread and instead eat insects and fruits. Watch videos online to support.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that the fire happened in the more recent past.
nodes.response: London was a very different city to what it is now and the buildings were entirely different, which played a key part in the fire spreading

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that hospitals have always been clean and organised as they are today.
nodes.response: Show pupils images of hospitals during the Crimean war and hospitals today and allow them to explore and make comparisons.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to adopt the formal tone required for this letter.
nodes.response: Ensure all pupils re-read Jean's letter in order to 'tune them in' to the formal tone. You may wish to generate more examples of similar letters for them to read.

nodes.misconception: Children find it hard to determine which suffix or word to use to form comparatives and superlatives
nodes.response: Encourage children to orally rehearse the comparative and superlative forms of adjectives to check that they sound correct.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that points should involve full and long explanations.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that points are only one sentence long and use the word 'because' to give one reason to justify an opinion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not remember the question mark at the end of a question.
nodes.response: When saying the questions aloud, encourage pupils to draw the question mark in the air, or say 'question mark' out loud to help them remember.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to determine which suffix or word to use to turn an adjective into its superlative form.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to practise saying the superlative form of an adjective out loud to check it sounds right. Model and demonstrate the rules for how to turn adjectives into their superlative form.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to create a formal tone without knowledge or exposure to formal vocabulary.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities for children to self-correct with the use of a thesaurus for more formal synonyms.

nodes.misconception: Children might not understand the nuance involved in forming alliteration.
nodes.response: Not all of the words in the phrase need to begin with the same letter/sound and the words don't always have to be 'next door neighbours'.

nodes.misconception: Using 'good vocabulary' automatically makes writing better.
nodes.response: There are no 'good' and 'bad words' in English. Rather, some are more precise and appropriate in certain contexts than others.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use adjective choices that describe the personality of the bee.
nodes.response: Adjective choices are formal and technical in an explanation text rather than descriptive.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use adjective choices that are descriptive and subjective.
nodes.response: Adjective choices are formal and technical in an explanation text rather than descriptive.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused by the structure of the diary entries proposed.
nodes.response: We will be writing a diary entry for Juliet written after the ball and then a short second entry in which she reflects on the marriage agreement.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe they can only use the words provided in the tasks.
nodes.response: You may wish to list the words provided on a whiteboard during the lesson, but then encourage children to apply their own ideas in the tasks or to use a thesaurus to explore deeper.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe they are expected to tell a detailed story using various sentence types at this stage.
nodes.response: The oral storytelling here is the basis on which the more detailed, varied writing will be built - pupils should try to make their storytelling 'interesting', but it doesn't need to use all the grammatical structures they know at this point.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may describe the setting solely based on what can be seen.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to use more than just one of their senses to create a more detailed description. Provide additional support, for example playing eerie sounds of the wind howling for them to hear or bringing in a gnarled piece of wood for them to feel.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find it hard to generate adjectives and description about a character they do not have a clear illustration of.
nodes.response: You could ask the children to draw their version of the main character, Tristan, at the start of this lesson. They will then find it easier to generate the descriptive vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging coming up with their own ideas for 'personification'.
nodes.response: You may wish to play a game using objects in the room and describing what they are doing using personification. E.g. the teacher's desk stood proudly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it harder to describe a character's personality, especially from an animation with nothing written down.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to analyse the character's actions in the animation carefully, thinking about what this tells us about their personality. Model some examples e.g. Emily leaves her parents and enters the arcade alone - this tells us she is brave.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may describe the setting solely based on what can be seen.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to use more than just one of their senses to create a more detailed description.  Provide additional support e.g. playing beach sounds, bringing in sand for children to feel.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to generate adjectives to describe the characters' personalities.
nodes.response: Watch the animation together, stopping at various points to discuss the actions of Anders and the green chameleons. Verbally generate adjectives together. Children can then work in small groups to create their lists.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use adjective choices that are not precise enough or appropriate for this narrative.
nodes.response: Create a shared word bank for the characters and setting that pupils can refer to.

nodes.misconception: Over-estimating the risks of genetic engineering and genetically modified (GM) organisms.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the need to weigh up possible benefits, risks and ethical questions when making decisions about genetic engineering.

nodes.misconception: Over-estimating the risks of genetic engineering and genetically modified (GM) organisms.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the need to weigh up possible benefits, risks and ethical questions when making decisions about genetic engineering.

nodes.misconception: Bacteria and plants do not have genetic material to be passed to offspring.
nodes.response: Examples of both bacteria and plants passing genetic material and features to offspring in reproduction, and the outcomes, i.e. growth.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that abortion is the only option following a positive genetic test result during pregnancy.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the various options and support that are available to parents who have a high probability of passing on alleles that can affect their child's health.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that an allele that increases the risk of a disease makes it certain to happen.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the idea the alleles can be risk factors for disease, and that in many cases other factors also affect the risk.

nodes.misconception: Mutations always have a negative effect on an organism.
nodes.response: Mutations can produce variation in a phenotype by producing alleles of a gene.

nodes.misconception: All DNA is genes that code for proteins; and that our characteristics are only affected by our genes
nodes.response: Most of the DNA is non-coding (non-genes), and controls when genes are expressed (i.e. when proteins are made). Changes (genetic variants) in non-coding DNA can affect characteristics (phenotype) as they control whether a gene is expressed or not.

nodes.misconception: 'Il y a' and 'il y avait' mean there is and there was in descriptions of singular things.
nodes.response: 'Il y a' and 'il y avait' mean there is or there are and there was and there were. They stay the same if you are talking about one thing or more than one.

nodes.misconception: I need to translate the word 'did' when I form a question in French.
nodes.response: To form a question in French, you can either raise your voice at the end of a statement to form an intonation question, or you can add 'est-ce que' at the beginning of a sentence. There is no French equivalent for 'did' in a question.

nodes.misconception: There are not many people who live in rural areas in England.
nodes.response: In 2020, 12.0 million people lived in rural areas – this is 21.3% of the England population (gov. website)

nodes.misconception: Republic of Ireland is a part of the United Kingdom.
nodes.response: Republic of Ireland is in the continent of Europe and only Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.

nodes.misconception: Difficulties in using digital mapping tools.
nodes.response: Provide additional teaching input in the use of digital maps.

nodes.misconception: There are only mountainous areas in Scotland.
nodes.response: There are different types of landscapes in Scotland include lakes, rivers and mountains. There are also lots of cities, towns and villages.

nodes.misconception: Mount Snowdon is the tallest mountain in the UK.
nodes.response: Ben Nevis is the tallest mountain in the UK which is in Scotland.

nodes.misconception: Some learners may be less confident with the use of aerial images, maps and data.
nodes.response: Spend additional time recapping and consolidating learners' geographical skills in using maps and other sources of information.

nodes.misconception: Geography is learning about the natural world.
nodes.response: Geography has many different aspects and includes learning about the natural world and learning about society.

nodes.misconception: Geography is something that happens in other parts of the world not in the place where we live.
nodes.response: Investigate the geography in local news stories as well as stories from elsewhere in the UK and other countries.

nodes.misconception: Geography is only something we learn at school.
nodes.response: Geography is all around us. We might learn it in school, at home and in many other places.

nodes.misconception: Geological timescales go back as far as human history.
nodes.response: Geological timescales are much greater than human history.

nodes.misconception: If we run out of oil, we can just make more.
nodes.response: Fossil fuels take millions of years to form – much longer than a human lifetime. We can’t just “make” more. Once we use them up, they’re gone. That’s why we need to balance using them with finding cleaner, renewable alternatives.
