nodes.misconception: It is important that the pupils listen to the music before beginning to choreograph their dances.
nodes.response: Engaging pupils in the active content of the lesson is likely to improve motivation and levels of engagement. By playing the music in the background they will become familiar with it and allow it to inform the work they create.

nodes.misconception: Dancers should be moving all the time.
nodes.response: Stillness is one of the five basic actions. Similar to punctuation in a sentence, it can help to bring meaning and context as well as highlight important moments. Stillness can include brief pauses as well as prolonged periods of inactivity.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway, sometimes using highlighters can help visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: German and English word order are the same.
nodes.response: English mostly uses subject-verb word order and time phrases appear most naturally at the end of phrases. German word order is much more variable. Any element (subject, object, time-manner-location adverb) can start a German sentence.

nodes.misconception: Germany has always existed as one country, or has existed in its current form for a long time.
nodes.response: Before 1871, 'Germany' did not exist as a single nation. It was a collection of over 30 independent, mostly German-speaking states, each with its own ruler.

nodes.misconception: The Kaiser could simply order naval expansion without resistance.
nodes.response: In reality, the Kaiser needed Reichstag approval for funding, so winning public support was a crucial step in pressuring parliament.

nodes.misconception: Mixing up the terms zygote, embryo and foetus. Thinking that the mother's blood mixes with the foetus' blood in the placenta.
nodes.response: The lesson explores how the zygote divides, grows and develops in stages including embryo and foetus until the baby is ready to be born. The foetal and mother's blood vessels are close to each other in the placenta but the blood doesn't mix.

nodes.misconception: Adjectival nouns behave like adjectives in every way.
nodes.response: Adjectival nouns, like adjectives, change endings according to gender, case and the article used with them. However, like nouns, they have a grammatical gender and a capital letter. Abstract adjectival nouns are neuter.

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When taking part in a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When taking part in a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfully answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfully answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, pupils should keep their answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, pupils should keep their answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: The present tense in German can only be used to refer to the present.
nodes.response: The present tense can also be used with appropriate adverbs of time to refer to the near future, e.g., 'Am Samstag spiele ich Tennis.'.

nodes.misconception: Indirect object nouns are always preceded by the words 'to' or 'for' in English, and this tells us we need to use the dative case for the indirect object in German.
nodes.response: Whilst the inclusion of 'to' or 'for' in English can be a helpful indicator that the dative case is needed in German, not all verbs require this in English, and many can use the same word order as German.

nodes.misconception: When writing in German, accuracy is the most important thing, so it's best to keep sentences short and clear.
nodes.response: When producing written work in German, try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity. This must, of course, be balanced with accuracy, which enables you to communicate your ideas clearly.

nodes.misconception: Confident players shooting from out of range and failing to pass when would have been a better option.
nodes.response: Getting in a strong position with a high probability of scoring if you shoot is essential. It is important to pass to a teammate in a better position rather than shoot when out of range.

nodes.misconception: If a pupil loses their balance, they may struggle to stand back up. Often, they instinctively put their hands on the pool floor, which can make it even harder to return to a standing position.
nodes.response: Pupils move their knees under their chest, lift their head and pull back with their hands. They can pratise adapted burpees to get used to this movement.

nodes.misconception: You can just type anything into an LLM and it will always give the best answer.
nodes.response: LLMs work best when you give them clear, specific and well-structured prompts. The quality of the input directly affects the quality of the output; this process of designing and refining inputs to get better results is called prompt engineering.

nodes.misconception: Most Jews murdered during the Holocaust were killed in gas chambers in concentration camps.
nodes.response: Gas chambers were set up in specially constructed extermination camps for Jews and killed millions, but roughly half of all Holocaust victims were killed by other means.

nodes.misconception: That the ionic bond is the transfer of electrons and not the electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions. The ball and stick model implies that there is a physical link between the ions.
nodes.response: Ensure that students have a good understanding of how ions are formed and that ionic bond forms when oppostive ions attract; before moving on to dot and cross diagrams for binary ionic substances.

nodes.misconception: The Jamaican characters all have a cynical view of Britain and the British empire.
nodes.response: The reality is more nuanced. Whilst characters like Elwood are openly critical, some characters (like Gilbert) are more positive, buying into wartime narratives of fighting for their 'mother country'.

nodes.misconception: Flooding only happens close to rivers.
nodes.response: Flooding can also happen away from rivers, especially after heavy rainfall. When the ground can't absorb the water fast enough, surface water builds up and causes floods — even in places far from rivers.

nodes.misconception: Countries with the highest GDP per capita always have the highest healthy life expectancy.
nodes.response: This isn't always the case as other factors also play a big role, like access to healthcare, lifestyle, diet, pollution levels, and inequality.

nodes.misconception: GIS web maps are only a tool for visualising geographical patterns in data; they can't help us explain geographical patterns.
nodes.response: GIS are a useful tool to visualise, interpret and analyse geographical data. This means they can be used to explain geographical patterns by comparing different layers.

nodes.misconception: The climate of Russia is always cold.
nodes.response: The climate of Russia varies across its territory and across the year.

nodes.misconception: GIS can only show one set of data.
nodes.response: GIS can show multiple layers of data as well as change over time.

nodes.misconception: Coastal erosion is likely to be the same in different places along a stretch of coastline.
nodes.response: Coastal erosion varies between different places. It is influenced by human factors, such as whether coastal defences have been installed, and physical factors, such as the rock type.

nodes.misconception: Cities are growing at the same rate everywhere around the world.
nodes.response: Cities are growing at different rates around the world. Often, cities in countries with a lower HDI are growing more rapidly than cities in countries with a higher HDI.

nodes.misconception: All rocks formed during the same geological period will be similar.
nodes.response: Although many rocks formed during the same geological period will be similar, volcanic processes may be creating rocks at the same time as sedimentary rocks are being created. These rocks will be very different and create contrasting landscapes.

nodes.misconception: China is about the same size as Greenland.
nodes.response: China is around four times the size of Greenland although it looks about the same size on some projections of the world map.

nodes.misconception: India is much smaller than Greenland.
nodes.response: India is similar in size to Greenland although looks much smaller on some projections of the world map.

nodes.misconception: Nigeria is a relatively small country.
nodes.response: Nigeria is a relatively large country. It is much bigger than France despite it looking a similar size on some map projections.

nodes.misconception: The DRC is a relatively small country.
nodes.response: The DRC is a very large country. It's position on the equator means that it often appears smaller than it really is on some world maps.

nodes.misconception: Rivers can't flow through areas with very low rainfall totals.
nodes.response: Rivers often flow through different climate zones, therefore their source may be in a mountainous area with high rainfall totals, but they may then flow through arid areas to the sea.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up directions, for example, moving left instead of right, or up instead of down. Pupils might start their movement from an incorrect position, leading to an inaccurate final location.
nodes.response: Use clear and consistent language when teaching directions. Reinforce understanding by having students physically point or move in the indicated direction.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to think of reasons for their opinions.
nodes.response: Give children the option of choosing from a list of reasons to help generate ideas.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to give short, simple instructions and may add in too many steps.
nodes.response: Model short, simple instructions before children are asked to complete Task B. Share some non-examples of long or complicated instructions. Remind children to always stop and wait after each instruction.

nodes.misconception: Feedback has got to be positive.
nodes.response: Feedback can be positive or negative and aims to help the designer to improve on their design.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse left and right turns when someone else, whose orientation is different from their own, is making a turn.
nodes.response: Encourage children to move themselves into the same orientation as the person whose turn they are trying to describe so that they can use their own left and right to help see which directions someone else is turning.

nodes.misconception: There is no need to summarise a short speech because the audience have just heard it.
nodes.response: Summarising an argument helps to reinforce the key parts and make the speech more convincing.

nodes.misconception: Glacial erosion is the only process that creates new landscapes.
nodes.response: Glacial erosion does create new landforms, but as glaciers transport and then deposit the eroded material, this also creates new landscapes.

nodes.misconception: Truncated spurs are created soley by glaciers.
nodes.response: Truncated spurs started as interlocking spurs which are a fluvial feature formed by rivers. Glaciers then modify this landform through erosion.

nodes.misconception: Glaciers are white.
nodes.response: Glaciers can appear dirty because they carry material.

nodes.misconception: Glaciers are made of salt water
nodes.response: Glaciers are made of fresh water from snow and rain

nodes.misconception: Pagans and other similar spiritualities define themselves against Christianity.
nodes.response: Pagan worldviews are highly diverse. However, they share a common reverance for the earth and a tolerance towards those of other worldviews.

nodes.misconception: All places of pilgrimage have remained the same.
nodes.response: Glastonbury was a famous early and medieval centre of pilgrimage in England and continues to be important today although it is different to the original centre and shrine.

nodes.misconception: Assigning a variable inside a function automatically makes it global.
nodes.response: A variable is local, unless it is specifically set as a global variable.

nodes.misconception: Assigning a variable inside a function automatically makes it global.
nodes.response: A variable is local, unless it is specifically set as a global variable.

nodes.misconception: The global atmospheric circulation systems controls the temperature of different climate zones.
nodes.response: Global circulation system redistributes heat received at the Equator, but latitude controls temperature of each climate zone. The amount of solar radiation received at each latitude is due to the curvature of the Earth.

nodes.misconception: All megacities are global cities because they are so big.
nodes.response: Not all megacities are global cities. While megacities have populations of over 10 million, global cities are defined by their international influence in areas such as finance, culture, politics, and transport.

nodes.misconception: Climate change only leads to hotter weather. Human activity has a negligible impact on climate change.
nodes.response: Explain the diverse effects of climate change, including extreme weather. Highlight the significant role of human activity in accelerating climate change.

nodes.misconception: Data is not important when presenting findings to support an argument.
nodes.response: Data makes your point stronger by showing real evidence.

nodes.misconception: That both volcanoes and earthquakes occur at all types of plate margin.
nodes.response: While earthquakes are produced by tectonic movements at all plate margins, volcanoes are not found at conservative plate margins.

nodes.misconception: All food is grown on farms.
nodes.response: Food we eat can be grown, reared or caught.

nodes.misconception: China has contributed most to CO₂ emissions.
nodes.response: North America and Europe have contributed the most to total CO₂ emissions, mainly because they industrialised first (in the 1800s).

nodes.misconception: Hot countries use less energy because it is warm all year so they do not need to heat their houses.
nodes.response: While people in hot countries may need to use less energy on heating, energy use depends most on how developed a country is - developed countries use more energy per person because they have more industries, transport and technology.

nodes.misconception: Water insecurity is due to lack of rain.
nodes.response: Water insecurity may be the result of physical water scarcity, though a water deficit may be due to high population density or use of large volumes of water for industry.

nodes.misconception: Globalisation is the process by which countries and people are becoming more developed.
nodes.response: Globalisation is the process by which countries and people are becoming more connected.

nodes.misconception: The Suez Canal is only important for the Middle East.
nodes.response: The Suez Canal is important globally as 30% of all global container traffic and 12% of all global trade passes through the canal.

nodes.misconception: The UK grows most of its own food.
nodes.response: We import about 50% of the food we eat.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the concept of migration.
nodes.response: Explain that some animals move from one region or habitat to another according to the seasons.

nodes.misconception: The first cities to become megacities are now the largest global cities.
nodes.response: Most of the world's largest cities are relatively young megacities that have only grown to a significant size since 2000.

nodes.misconception: Mixing up correlation and cause.
nodes.response: This lesson explores the correlation between data showing global warming and data showing increases in greenhouse gas emission, and that 99% of scientists believe the increased greenhouse effect is the causal link.

nodes.misconception: Globalisation is the world becoming more developed.
nodes.response: Globalisation is the world becoming more interconnected.

nodes.misconception: Western culture refers to only North America.
nodes.response: Western culture refers to North America, Europe and Australia.

nodes.misconception: Aid is separate from globalisation and has nothing to do with how Indonesia connects to the world.
nodes.response: When countries like Australia or organisations like the EU give aid to Indonesia, they are building connections through education and infrastructure. This support helps Indonesia grow economically, attract investment, and take part in global trade.

nodes.misconception: Globalisation is only beneficial to large companies.
nodes.response: Globalisation can improve the quality of life of people.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a goal or a target it the end product or outcome to be achieved.
nodes.response: A goal can be based on outcome, however it can also be a goal set about the performance or process of doing something. For example, building a 3-2-1 pyramid in the quickest time compared to building the 3-2-1 pyramid without dropping any objects.

nodes.misconception: It is common to see variants on the SMART acronym, for example, R = realistic, from other exam boards or sources. Some sources may extend the acronym to SMARTER.
nodes.response: Ensure it is understood that with the OCR exam board, SMART only ever refers to Specific, Measurable, Achieveable, Recorded and Timed.

nodes.misconception: It is common to see variants on the SMART acronym, for example R = recorded, from other exam boards or sources. Some sources may extend the acronym to SMARTER.
nodes.response: Ensure it is understood that with the Edexcel exam board, SMART only ever refers to Specific, Measurable, Achieveable, Realistic and Time-bound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you should only move slowly with the ball so you don't lose posession.
nodes.response: Moving fast with the ball can create more opportunities to beat defenders, create space and keep the attacking momentum strong.

nodes.misconception: The God of classical theism is distant and not involved with creation.
nodes.response: For most theists whose beliefs align with classical theism, such as Christians, God is personal and active within the world and is powerful, loving and all knowing by nature.

nodes.misconception: Each quality or characteristic of God is distinct and separate from the others.
nodes.response: God's qualities and characteristics complement each other. For example, many Christians believe that God exerts his omnipotence with love for humanity, which links to God as (omni)benevolent.

nodes.misconception: Everyone in Germany fully believed the Nazi propaganda.
nodes.response: While some people genuinely believed, many conformed due to fear, peer pressure, or habit. Propaganda created surface unity - not universal belief.

nodes.misconception: 'Jekyll and Hyde' is a stereotypically 'Gothic' novella.
nodes.response: Whilst certain elements of 'Jekyll and Hyde' do follow the conventions of the Gothic, others subvert it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils fail to fully commit to a tackle which allows players to break free and score.
nodes.response: Defenders must fully commit to tackle the ball carrier and keep hold until they are on the ground to avoid giving the opposition an overlap or charge through scoring opportunity.

nodes.misconception: Empires have to own land in order to control it.
nodes.response: Control can be gained through a variety of indirect means, such as through trade or tribute.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Golding sits on the 'nature' side of the nature/nurture debate.
nodes.response: Golding does not provide us with a concrete answer- he suggests that we all have the capacity (or the impulses) to behave sinfully, but it takes the right circumstances for brutality to emerge.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the island is presented as idyllic in the first chapter.
nodes.response: Whilst there are aspects of the description that present the island as idyllic, Golding's descriptions are characterised by a sense of threat in more ominous undertones. He achieves this through his use of dark and light and through his use of verbs.

nodes.misconception: Students think that symbols in a text have to be physical objects that represent ideas.
nodes.response: Symbolism is the use of images, words or nouns to represent abstract ideas or qualities - symbols do not have to be physical objects that can be picked up and held.

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [om] and [on] always sound the same.
nodes.response: When [om] or [on] appear at the end of a word or before a consonant, they have a nasal sound and are pronounced the same. However, before a vowel their sounds are oral, the 'm' and 'n' are pronounced more clearly, making these SSCs sound different.

nodes.misconception: Christians all believe in original sin.
nodes.response: While many traditional Christians teach that original sin means that humans inherit a sinful nature, others reject or downplay this idea. Instead, they believe humans are born essentially good or neutral, with the capacity to choose good or bad.

nodes.misconception: Only thinking about physical and not mental health; thinking health is a binary of "healthy or ill".
nodes.response: The lesson draws upon research on students' understanding of 'health' as a concept to specifically tackle the above misconceptions.

nodes.misconception: Christians from different churches always disagree and never work together.
nodes.response: Christians from different churches often agree with each other and work together.

nodes.misconception: Comments are added to code to help you understand your program.
nodes.response: Comments are used to make the code more readable to a programmer who seeks to understand it. The comments should be written in a style that would help them make sense of the program.

nodes.misconception: Gorbachev succeeded Brezhnev as leader of the Soviet Union in March 1985.
nodes.response: Brezhnev died in November 1982. Following his death, the Soviet Union was ruled by two leaders who were in poor health and ruled only briefly: Yuri Andropov (November 1982 - February 1984) and Konstantin Chernenko (February 1984 - March 1985).

nodes.misconception: Students often make the mistake of using a new word they have just learned inaccurately, in an attempt to show off their knowledge.
nodes.response: The point of learning new vocabulary is to give students options and choices so that they can select the most specific and useful word in their writing. Sometimes, the most specific word choice isn't the new vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Akbar's religious tolerance was absolute throughout his reign.
nodes.response: Akbar made some exceptions to his general policy of religious tolerance, such as when he declared a jihad against the Hindu Kingdom of Mewar.

nodes.misconception: Students may think all carbon allotropes have giant covalent structures due to strong covalent bonds.
nodes.response: Emphasise that fullerenes and nanotubes, unlike graphene and diamond, have discrete molecular structures.

nodes.misconception: Letters are only used for reading
nodes.response: Letters can be used to make interesting and beautiful designs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain as to whether an image has rotational symmetry.
nodes.response: Tracing paper may be useful here. Pupils can trace the image and then rotate the tracing paper to determine if an image has rotational symmetry.

nodes.misconception: All design drawings are drawn from one angle, usually a front view.
nodes.response: Isometric drawings show three angles at the same time.

nodes.misconception: Music is always notated on a score.
nodes.response: Some music is never notated, it is shared by singing and playing. Some notation uses graphic scores, or rhythm grids. Any way of sharing how the music is expected to be played is a form of notation.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to solve linear equations; by manipulation and isolating the variable(s).
nodes.response: When we plot more than one linear equation on a graph we can use the intersection to find the solution.

nodes.misconception: Assuming that any graph with a constant positive gradient represents variables that are in direct proportion.
nodes.response: Encourage the useful check of reading a pairs of values from the graph, doubling one of them and checking the graph to see if the other variable has doubled.  If it has it shows a directly proportional relationship if not it doesn't.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that given a graph is continuous, the sequence can contain all of the values represented by the line.
nodes.response: It is important that pupils know when it is appropriate to draw a line to graph sequences and whether values on the line have any meaning. Sequences are often given as a list of terms and without context we cannot assume the sequence is continuous.

nodes.misconception: Solutions for context-based problem can be listed as coordinate pairs with units e.g. 6 workers, 60 hours.
nodes.response: Solutions should always be fully interpreted in relation to the context e.g. It would take 6 workers 60 hours to paint the building.

nodes.misconception: Grassroots development was invented by western thinkers.
nodes.response: In reality, many communities around the world have practiced grassroots development for centuries, using their own knowledge and solutions before Western ideas became popular.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up the terms for weight and mass and use weight when they mean mass and vice versa.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a force lifts objects against the pull of gravity before introducing the term weight.

nodes.misconception: There is no gravity in space, even a short distance from the Earth.
nodes.response: Carefully whirl a rubber bung around your head on a length of string to show how force of a string keeps it orbiting in a circle, just as the force of gravity keeps the Moon orbiting the Earth and the planets orbiting the Sun.

nodes.misconception: 'Denn' triggers word order 3.
nodes.response: Not all conjunctions trigger word order 3. 'Denn' means 'because' and is followed by word order 1. 'Weil' also means 'because', but triggers word order 3.

nodes.misconception: The greenhouse effect is the same as global warming.
nodes.response: Discuss the natural greenhouse effect and how it enables life on Earth to flourish. Emphasise that global warming refers to an increasing temperature, rather than to a temperature that is warmer.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that global warming means that the weather is getting warmer everywhere.
nodes.response: Emphasise that not everywhere gets warmer all the time. Some places might experience colder weather, more storms, or other changes in climate.

nodes.misconception: All greenhouse gases are artificial and harmful. Increasing any greenhouse gas is bad.
nodes.response: Emphasise and explain the natural occurrence and necessity of greenhouse gases. Discuss the effect of human activity increasing amounts of greenhouse gases at a very fast rate.

nodes.misconception: The civil rights movement was always co-ordinated and led by older men and women.
nodes.response: In the 1960s, there was a shift in the civil rights movement as students began to take a leading role in the fight against racial injustice.

nodes.misconception: Only proper nouns have a capital letter.
nodes.response: In German, all nouns, regardless of where they are in a sentence, have a capital letter.

nodes.misconception: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender. If a word is feminine we think of it as a girl if it is masculine we think of it as a boy.
nodes.response: Grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender.

nodes.misconception: [a] is pronounced the same in Spanish and English.
nodes.response: Whilst the [a] sound varies in English, in different words and in different places, it is only pronounced as in 'alto' in Spanish.

nodes.misconception: Consonants at the end of words are pronounced in French.
nodes.response: Often, consonants are silent at the end of words in French. The exception to this rule are the letters c, r, f and l, which are pronounced.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'h' in hola is pronounced as it would be in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the letter 'h' is not pronounced in the word 'hola'.

nodes.misconception: To hit the ball in golf, you lift your head up to look at the target.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that in order to hit the ball successfully you need to keep your head down and focused on the ball.

nodes.misconception: Confusing the spelling of "noble" with "Nobel" and misunderstanding why noble gases are named so.
nodes.response: Clarify that "noble" refers to their stability and lack of reactivity due to a full outer electron shell, meaning they don't need to bond with other elements.

nodes.misconception: Group 2 metals are more reactive than Group 1 because reactivity increases across the groups.
nodes.response: Group 1 metals are more reactive with water; reactivity increases down a group (for Groups 1 and 2), not along a period.

nodes.misconception: All halogens are gases at room temperature because they're non-metals; all halogens form toxic compounds.
nodes.response: Not all halogens are gases at room temperature; bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid. Halogens can be toxic in their elemental form or in high concentrations, but they also form essential compounds, like table salt and disinfectants.

nodes.misconception: As pupils add more and more elements to their sequences, the quality of their performance decreases. There may be issues with group dynamics as pupils work in bigger group sizes.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of only moving on to add another element to the sequence once all members of the group are ready to move on. Pupils may have to delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a limited view of what an animal is: mammal with fur and four legs. This can affect the way they classify animals. Also, that its habitat is an observable characteristic.
nodes.response: Use a wide range of animals including invertebrates and vertebrates, and those that live on land and in the sea, to help them look at observable characteristics when grouping.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all micro-organisms are harmful and will cause us to become ill.
nodes.response: Explain that, while some micro-organisms can cause us harm, there are also many that are beneficial, such as those used in food production, water treatment or those living inside our digestive system.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all plants are green and have flowers.
nodes.response: Clarify with a range of examples that some plants have flowers and some don't. Discuss with the pupils if they think even flowering plants will always have a flower on them all year round.

nodes.misconception: Elements in the same period have similar properties.
nodes.response: Properties vary across a period; it is elements in the same group that share similar properties.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all food comes from shops. Pupils may think that all plants are edible.
nodes.response: Clear examples showing edible plants in their natural habitats. Warning that some plants can be harmful if ingested.

nodes.misconception: Farmers will not starve because they grow their own food.
nodes.response: Poor harvests can put a great deal of strain on the amount of food a farmer can grow, even food for subsistence.

nodes.misconception: Most of the food we eat is produced in the UK.
nodes.response: About 54% of the food on our plates is produced in the UK, the rest is imported from other countries.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that an animal’s offspring is always a smaller version of the parent.
nodes.response: Include examples of animals whose offspring do not resemble them e.g. caterpillar/butterfly, swan/cygnet, tadpoles/frogs etc.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a ‘fair test’ is one in which they all get an equal share in the roles or everyone gets to take a turn.
nodes.response: Explain that both a comparative and fair test are ones in which all variables are kept the same except for the one that is being investigated. This helps to ensure that our results show the effect of just the variable we are investigating.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think yeast is not a living thing because it doesn’t appear to have any of the characteristics of living things when we look at it dry straight from the packet.
nodes.response: Explain that yeast is a type of fungus so it is a living thing in the micro-organisms group. Throughout the lesson, reinforce the characteristics it has that makes it a living thing, such as its ability to grow and reproduce.

nodes.misconception: Our food comes from shops and supermarkets.
nodes.response: While food is purchased from shops and supermarkets, plants are grown, animals are reared and fish is caught for us to eat.

nodes.misconception: Multicellular organisms reproduce by cell division like unicellular organisms.
nodes.response: Multicellular organisms use cell division for reproduction. A non-example will be used to show reproduction is not part of reproduction in multicellular organisms.

nodes.misconception: All verbs with prefixes are separable.
nodes.response: Some prefixes are separable in some verbs but inseparable in others. For example, 'wieder' in 'wiedersehen' is separable, but not in 'wiederholen'. The stress always falls on the separable prefix.

nodes.misconception: There is no difference between 'ningún' and 'ninguno'.
nodes.response: 'Ningún' and 'ninguno' look very similar but they are used differently in Spanish. 'Ninguno' is a pronoun and it replaces a masculine singular noun. 'Ningún' is an indefinite adjective and it comes before a masculine singular noun.

nodes.misconception: Lady Macbeth's rejection of guilt in 2.2 means 5.1's characterisation is inconsistent.
nodes.response: The language in 2.2 foreshadows what is to come.

nodes.misconception: Highly-trained members of the military and government tend not to make mistakes.
nodes.response: Everyone is capable of making errors, sometimes big and far-reaching ones, especially if they are under a great deal of stress.

nodes.misconception: British victory in the Opium wars allowed it to conquer large areas of China and establish many new colonies.
nodes.response: Hong Kong was gained as a new British colony but Britain used its victory in the Opium Wars to force the Qing empire to change its behaviour, rather than to create new colonies.

nodes.misconception: Guru Nanak is considered a god by Sikhs.
nodes.response: Guru Nanak is not worshipped as a god but is respected as a spiritual guide and a guru.

nodes.misconception: Sikhs only do things for themselves.
nodes.response: Many Sikhs work hard to help other people and to live an honest and good life.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think the story is only about the physical objects (milk and flowers).
nodes.response: A clear explanation of the symbols is important, as the symbols represent the attitudes, behaviours and spiritual lessons of the story (such as purity, kindness or spiritual values).

nodes.misconception: Guru Nanak said that money is bad and that we shouldn’t have any.
nodes.response: Guru Nanak didn’t say that money is bad. He just taught that it’s more important to help others and be kind than to focus only on money.

nodes.misconception: I don't need to have a strategy when tackling a translation.
nodes.response: It is important to read Spanish sentences carefully before translating them into English. Identifying the tense in each sentence, for example, can really help to improve accuracy.

nodes.misconception: Hacking a computer system of someone you know as a joke is considered legal.
nodes.response: Even if there is no intention to commit a crime by accessing the computer system of someone you know, the fact that the access is unauthorised is considered a crime.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is no article when making physical descriptions, e.g. 'I have blond hair'.
nodes.response: In French, we use definite articles when making physical descriptions, e.g. 'J'ai les cheveux blonds'.

nodes.misconception: You use the article [a] or [an] with features as you do in English, e.g. a small nose.
nodes.response: In Spanish, we always use the definite article ‘the’ when describing someone's physical features.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that only men go on Hajj.
nodes.response: Men and Women may both go on Hajj. They might have different clothes to wear but will carry out the same actions.

nodes.misconception: When pilgrims stop to kiss or point to the 'Black Stone' as part of the Hajj ritual, they are worshipping that stone as an idol.
nodes.response: Muslims do not worship idols or anything other than Allah. The Black Stone is touched or kissed as that is what the Prophet Muhammad did upon his return to Makkah and the Ka'aba.

nodes.misconception: A Muslim can go on Hajj whenever they choose.
nodes.response: Hajj is expensive, so people may well save up. Saudi Arabia operates a quota for each country.

nodes.misconception: Getting the electrons confused; how many and which side of the half equations to write them on.
nodes.response: When writing a half equation, electrons should be added and not taken away and so should go on the side of the equation where they are added. All charges must cancel each other out and the atoms on each side of the equation balance.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly partitioning and halving odd multiples of 10
nodes.response: Ensure children use representations where they are able to see the partitioning of the number into an even multiple of 10 and 10 more. That way, they can clearly see they are still finding half of 30 for example.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to see that halving is the inverse of doubling.
nodes.response: Only progress to this lesson once children are fluent in doubling numbers zero to five. Present the same visual (e.g. 3 apples + 3 apples) and use this to discuss doubling and halving, revealing and covering one of the two equal parts each time.

nodes.misconception: Players are not allowed in the D apart from the goalkeeper.
nodes.response: If you land in the goal area (the D) after taking a shot, the goal will still count as long as the ball was released before you entered the area. However, if you enter the goal area during regular play, possession is awarded to the opposing team.

nodes.misconception: Screening is a defensive move only used to stop the team with the ball scoring.
nodes.response: Screening can be used by attackers to 'screen'  or block defenders to allow an attacking teammate more space to move or score.

nodes.misconception: Dribbling is always the best option to move with the ball.
nodes.response: While dribbling can be helpful to gain ground up the court, it can slow down the game, whereas passing can often be faster and more efficient at breaking through a defence.

nodes.misconception: If you are on the losing team, it automatically affects the score you get for your handball assessment.
nodes.response: For your GCSE PE moderation, you are measured against how well you can demonstrate certain skills, tactics and decision making, not the final score of your game.

nodes.misconception: Power is more important than accuracy.
nodes.response: Accuracy is crucial to keep the ball within possession of your team so you have more opportunities to score.

nodes.misconception: When attacking it is always best to just dribble/ step and pass the ball straight up the court.
nodes.response: Sometimes to create more space, a flat pass across the width of the pitch or a crossover move can be used to spread, reposition or confuse defenders which can be more successful at enabling a teammate to get through the gap that is created and score.

nodes.misconception: The best thing to do when a defender is about to tackle you is to (panic) pass the ball.
nodes.response: Panic passing before contact in rugby often leads to turnovers, as the pass is rushed, inaccurate, and easier for the opposition to intercept or disrupt, therefore the best decision can sometimes be to keep hold of the ball and take it into contact.

nodes.misconception: When children start to write quicker then they can begin to make more mistakes with the formation of their letters.
nodes.response: Remind the children of the importance of finding their balance between speed and accuracy. Model reviewing your writing so the children can become familiar with checking the legibility of their writing.

nodes.misconception: A menorah is just a decoration for a window.
nodes.response: A menorah has a deep significance for Jews.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think exercising and physical activity are only focused on winning and being the best.
nodes.response: Exercising alone or with others can provide opportunities to have fun and try new things. Getting better at something or feeling energised can feel just as good as winning a game.

nodes.misconception: A modulation is when the chords don't use the tonic.
nodes.response: A modulation is actually when the tonic changes. Sometimes music can sound like it will modulate, but then it stays in the same key. For a true modulation, it must feel like the tonic itself has changed.

nodes.misconception: Chromatic and atonal are the same thing.
nodes.response: Atonal music sounds chromatic, because there is no clear tonal centre. However, chromatic music isn't necessarily atonal - a piece can be in a key, but use chromatic notes from outside of it.

nodes.misconception: Harmony and tonality are the same thing.
nodes.response: Tonality is to the type of notes and chords that are used (e.g. major). Harmony is the way the notes and chords are used within that key. Think of tonality as a language (e.g. English) and harmony as the word choice and order in a sentence.

nodes.misconception: When singing in harmony, we need to ignore the other parts to concentrate on our own part.
nodes.response: When singing in harmony, we need to listen carefully to the other parts to ensure our part blends with the other voices.

nodes.misconception: All circuits have multiple pathways (like the underground map).
nodes.response: A series circuit is a continuous loop where all the components are connected one after another along the same path.

nodes.misconception: Harvest is an English custom.
nodes.response: It is celebrated by Christians in many different countries and in many different ways.

nodes.misconception: Harvest is only about collecting food.
nodes.response: It is about celebrating creation, giving thanks and sharing the benefits.

nodes.misconception: The decision to leave the EU has been either all good or all bad.
nodes.response: Whilst many politicians have strong views about the impact of Brexit, the truth is more nuanced. There have been advantages (such as creating our own immigration system) and negatives (like the loss of foreign direct investment).

nodes.misconception: Climate conferences are just an opportunity to talk, nothing gets done.
nodes.response: They are a chance to bring together world leaders to agree positive actions and work out problems. COP have secured important international agreements that have really helped to tackle climate change; the Paris Agreement is an example of this.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, to talk about 'having' a meal, food or drink in French, use the verb 'avoir': j'ai le petit-déjeuner (I am having breakfast).
nodes.response: To talk about 'having' a meal, food or drink in French, use the verb 'prendre', not 'avoir': je prends le petit-déjeuner.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not always appreciate that safety in the laboratory is a shared responsibility.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the hazards related to both common chemicals and regularly used equipment.

nodes.misconception: When using a Venn diagram students often mix up HCF & LCM.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check the reasonableness of their answer.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused between Britain and United Kingdom.
nodes.response: Reinforce that Britain is the landmass where the three countries of England, Wales and Scotland are located.

nodes.misconception: Product safety is only about consumer protection.
nodes.response: Industry safety also includes protecting workers.

nodes.misconception: Being active is only good for my physical health, such as healthy bones, muscles and heart.
nodes.response: While being active is good for your bones, muscles and heart, it can also make you feel fitter and happier, make new friends and try something new.

nodes.misconception: There is one form of malnutrition, intakes of energy and/or nutrients being below what is required.
nodes.response: There are two forms of malnutrition: undernutrition (intakes below what is required) and overnutrition (intakes above what is required).

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, I can use the verb 'ser' to talk about 'being' in any context.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the verb 'ser' means 'to be, being' for general traits. To refer to a location, mood or state, use 'estar'.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that being physically fit means someone is automatically healthy.
nodes.response: Explain that just because someone appears physically fit, it doesn't mean they have good emotional or social health.

nodes.misconception: As in English, there is one way of saying 'your' in Spanish.
nodes.response: Saying 'your' in Spanish depends on the number of people you are speaking to and the following noun. To mean ‘your’ for one person before a singular noun, use ‘tu’, and for more than one person, use 'vuestro' or 'vuestra'.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that protein can only be provided by foods that come from animal sources.
nodes.response: Explain to children that the protein we eat can often come from both plants and animals.

nodes.misconception: People in different communities follow different healthy eating advice.
nodes.response: Most people in the UK should follow the Eatwell Guide, and 8 tips for healthy eating, with the food and meals adapted for the needs of different groups.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the heart pumps air through the body, rather than blood, as part of a pneumatic-style system that powers the muscles.
nodes.response: Explain that the heart pumps blood around the body, beating faster when we exercise because it is transporting more oxygen within blood to keep the muscles working.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that thinness automatically equates to fitness, good health and having a healthy heart.
nodes.response: Explain that having a thin body does not necessarily mean that you also have good heart health. Whatever shape your body is, it is important to exercise and keep active in order to keep your heart healthy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that potatoes count as a vegetable.
nodes.response: In the Eatwell Guide, potatoes do not count as a vegetable. They are in the 'Potatoes, bread, pasta and rice' group.

nodes.misconception: When planning healthy meals, you do not have to include drinks.
nodes.response: Healthy meals should always include a drink. Water is a great choice.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that the lifestyle choices of a pregnant mother, including recreational use of drugs such as alcohol and nicotine, will not affect the foetus.
nodes.response: The lesson explores short-term and long-term effects that lifestyle choices of a pregnant mother, including recreational use of drugs such as alcohol and nicotine, can have on the developing foetus.

nodes.misconception: All snacks are unhealthy.
nodes.response: Not all snacks are unhealthy. We can use the Eatwell Guide to help us choose healthier snacks. We can choose snacks from each of the four biggest food groups.

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused by the difference between the words weather and climate.
nodes.response: By identifying types of weather in the early part of the lesson, you can then help pupils to understand climate by discussing how typical types of weather remain over a long period.

nodes.misconception: Sound waves are the same thing as the sound heard. Sound waves somehow 'have' sound.
nodes.response: Distinguish between the sound heard and the sound wave. The brain creates the sensation of hearing a sound when it receives nerve signals from the ear. The sound (heard) does not exist until created by the brain. Sound waves themselves have no sound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you need to be a good tennis player to participate in cardio tennis.
nodes.response: The focus is on the workout rather than the execution of shots. It is about having fun while exercising. You should prioritise keeping your heart rate elevated for the whole lesson rather than great shots or winning rallies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a very narrow definition of exercise, limiting it to activities such as running or weightlifting and not including more ‘fun’ types of exercise such as dancing or trampolining.
nodes.response: Explain that any physical activity where we intentionally use a lot of effort to move our bodies is exercise, backing this up with all the examples in the slide deck.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to understand what is taking place at the horizontal parts of the graph.
nodes.response: Be concise with your language and ask pupils to use the same language. 'have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction between particles', 'to slide past each other', 'to move past each other'.

nodes.misconception: Winds are cooling because they are moving air that is colder than the surrounding air.
nodes.response: Discuss with pupils how hotter objects heat the air around them, so the temperature difference between them and the air is smaller; and how wind blows away this warmer air. Provide opportunity for them to explain this in their own words.

nodes.misconception: Energy can appear and disappear.
nodes.response: Remind students about the conservation of energy.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that the midday Sun is higher in the sky because the Sun is further away then, or that the midday Sun has a greater heating effect because the Sun is closer or hotter then.
nodes.response: Use physical models (such as a globe, or a flat card in front of a light bulb with a thermometer attached) to show students how the changes observed over a day to Sun's position in the sky and the Sun's heating effect are caused by Earth's spin.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can often think that when the temperature is not increasing, i.e. at a change of state, that the experiment is 'not working'.
nodes.response: Question students whilst circulating the class about what they would expect to see and try to get them to imagine what is happening to the particles. Use the heating curve to explain why the temperature did not increase during state changes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse ideas about temperature and energy.
nodes.response: Use examples in different contexts to develop and consolidate ideas about differences between temperature and energy.

nodes.misconception: That Muslims believe hell (Jahannam) is a place where all sinners will remain in eternal pain and punishment.
nodes.response: The majority of Muslims believe that those who die without faith in God (Allah) will be punished eternally but sinners who fell short of good deeds will eventually enter paradise unless they committed the gravest of sins like shirk.

nodes.misconception: Past participles of -ieren verbs start with 'ge-' like most other past participles.
nodes.response: Unlike most other past participles, most German -'ieren' verbs act like some other weak German verbs, meaning that they do not have 'ge' at the beginning of their participles (for example, verbs beginning with 'be', 'er', and 'ver').

nodes.misconception: Adaptations just copy the story from the book. The writer doesn’t have to change much or make many decisions.
nodes.response: Adaptations need big changes to work on stage! Edmundson tested scenes in workshops, adjusted them in rehearsals, and watched audience reactions in previews to make sure the story was clear and powerful in performance.

nodes.misconception: The ending is happy because everything works out perfectly and offers hope for the future.
nodes.response: Edmundson says the ending is hopeful, but not perfect. There’s pain, loss, and compromise (Queenie gives up her baby), but real progress comes from facing reality with care and honesty.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that once a solution has been found to complete a challenge, this is the only option that should be used.
nodes.response: Many challenges and problems have various different solutions. One solution might suit the skills in your team and a different solution might suit another team.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'h' is pronounced like in English.
nodes.response: The letter 'h' is in fact often silent in French: j'habite.

nodes.misconception: Time phrases like 'an and 'année' are interchangeable in French.
nodes.response: Although they have the same meaning, 'an', 'jour', 'soir' and 'matin' are used to indicate specific units of time whereas, 'année', 'journée', 'soirée' and matinée' are used for description or duration.

nodes.misconception: To form the past participle of any verb in Spanish, remove the infinitive ending and add -ado.
nodes.response: To form the past participle of regular -ar verbs, remove the -ar and add -ado. However, to form the past participle of regular -er and -ir verbs, remove the -er/-ir and add -ido.

nodes.misconception: That France existed as a unified nation.
nodes.response: "Modern-day France" did not exist yet, instead the area we know as France, was actually a collection of separate lands/duchies .

nodes.misconception: The nobility in England identified as English.
nodes.response: This period marks a time when the nobility, who had their ancestral roots in France, had now come to see themselves as English.

nodes.misconception: Medieval and modern Church power is equivalent.
nodes.response: Explicitly outline the Church's organisational power: land ownership, clergy social status, and spiritual authority.

nodes.misconception: History is not relevant to today.
nodes.response: Henry II’s reforms to the English legal system established the foundation of English common law, still in use today.

nodes.misconception: Students may believed that the Yorkists and Lancastrians were from different families.
nodes.response: The Lancastrians and Yorkists were both part of the Plantagenet family.

nodes.misconception: Kings have the power to do whatever they want in their own countries.
nodes.response: For a great deal of English history, the power of the kings has been restricted by English laws and religious laws issued by the pope in Rome.

nodes.misconception: Features caused by the environment or lifestyle can be passed to offspring.
nodes.response: Examples of inherited features e.g. eye colour, those that are environment and lifestyle  e.g. scars, and those that are both e.g. height.

nodes.misconception: Offspring (esp. daughters) inherit all features from mum; parents can control inherited features.
nodes.response: Show examples of offspring inheriting features from both parents. Inherited features that are inherited in genetic material, not chosen.

nodes.misconception: It is common for students to believe that all types of variation can be passed on from parents to their offspring.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of variation that can and cannot be passed on from parents to their offspring, and links this to their causes.

nodes.misconception: You have to convert an 8 bit binary number in one go.
nodes.response: As a hexadecimal digit can be represented by 4 binary digits, it is useful to convert binary numbers in nibbles (4-bits at a time). This way each digit can be converted separately and then recombined for the final value.

nodes.misconception: Hexadecimal numbers are used to take up less memory on the computer.
nodes.response: Computers still only process and store binary data. Hexadecimal is used by humans to help them process long binary sequences more easily but the underlying number of bits is still the same.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to think of actions for certain lines of the rhyme.
nodes.response: Demonstrate lots of examples of actions or movements you could do and ask other pupils to perform their ideas to the group.

nodes.misconception: High-level languages are always better than low-level languages because they are easier to use.
nodes.response: High-level languages are generally easier to learn and use. However, low-level languages offer more direct control over the computer's hardware, which can be essential for certain tasks like writing operating systems or device drivers.

nodes.misconception: High and low refers to volume (loud and quiet).
nodes.response: High and low refers to pitch.

nodes.misconception: Pupils move their whole body at once in a bunny hop. Pupils point their toes the wrong way by flexing the ankle, causing the foot to point at a 90 degree angle to the leg. Pupils jump off wall bars.
nodes.response: Tell pupils to move their hands first, then their feet to their hands and repeat. Tell pupils to flex their ankles in the opposite direction and push their toes away from their leg, making the leg appear longer. Pupils only jump from flat surfaces.

nodes.misconception: High-fidelity prototypes are only about appearance and surface finish.
nodes.response: High-fidelity prototypes are about realism in both look and function. They should operate as closely as possible to the intended product - or convincingly simulate that functionality.

nodes.misconception: Pupils take an approach straight towards the bar which is not conducive to performing the Fosbury flop technique and maximising height jumped.
nodes.response: Pupils should take a curved run up which is J-shaped and will allow them to perform the technique required to gain the most height in their jump. The teacher can guide them to this through the activities.

nodes.misconception: Pupils jump too high and lose the quality of shapes. Pupils jump too far around in a half-turn jump and lose control of their landing. Pupils round backs on landing, causing hands to touch the floor.
nodes.response: Celebrate clear shapes over jumps that are too high. Spend time teaching what 'half-turn' means, reminding pupils to start facing one direction and end facing the opposite direction. Remind pupils to keep their backs straight so they land upright.

nodes.misconception: Pupils only use crawling actions to move over or under the apparatus. When reflecting on others' practice, pupils only say whether they liked or disliked their movements.
nodes.response: Give pupils other ideas to perform under apparatus, such as balance, swing, or slide, and other ideas to perform over apparatus, such as sliding or balancing on top or jumping over. Encourage pupils to be specific when reflecting on others' actions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that moving high only means traveling on tiptoes. Pupils focus on the task rather than good movements. Pupils do not hold their balances for long enough.
nodes.response: Celebrate the different ways pupils move high. Remind pupils to move silently with control, pointing fingers and toes. Encourage pupils to hold balances for at least 3 seconds.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the volume of sound and the pitch of sound is the same thing, or that high sounds are loud and low sounds are quiet.
nodes.response: It is important to expose children to a wide range of high and low pitched sounds. Continue to make the distinction between volume and pitch throughout the lesson.

nodes.misconception: That factors only apply to whole numbers and a factor needs to be a whole number.
nodes.response: Whilst this is true for numerical factors, the factors of 7ab are 1, 7, a, b, 7a, 7b and ab.

nodes.misconception: Common factors are put into the intersection of the Venn diagram twice instead of once.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check that the product of the factors in each set is the correct integer.

nodes.misconception: You always leave out the subject pronoun when using the imperative.
nodes.response: The 'du' and 'ihr' forms of the imperative omit the subject pronoun, but the 'Sie' form retains it.

nodes.misconception: That you need to be personally affected by something to make a speech about it.
nodes.response: Draw attention to Hillary Clinton as an advocate.

nodes.misconception: There is one Hindu creation story.
nodes.response: There are many Hindu creation stories. This is one example. The Hindu tradition is very broad and diverse.

nodes.misconception: Hip Hop culture focuses on 'disrespecting' your opponent and mocking them.
nodes.response: As in all competitive settings, the performers are trying to succeed and employ a variety of strategies to do so, but this also includes congratulating others on their successes and supporting those who are developing their skills.

nodes.misconception: Hip Hop is a dance style
nodes.response: Hip Hop is a generic term for a number of dance styles that are heavily influenced by street culture (DJing, graffiti, rapping). There are a large number of subdivisions which vary according to time and place of origin.

nodes.misconception: The verb ending -o refers to 'she', 'he' or 'it' in the preterite tense.
nodes.response: The verb ending -o refers to 'I' in the present tense. The verb ending -ó (with accent) refers to 'she', 'he' or 'it' in the preterite tense.

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.

nodes.misconception: To form the imperfect tense with all verbs, take the 'nous' form of the present tense, remove -ons and add the appropriate endings.
nodes.response: The verb 'être' is an exception to the rule. Use the stem -ét before adding the endings.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is always translated as 'used to' in English.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense is often translated as 'used to' in English but sometimes the simple past is used instead to convey repeated past actions.

nodes.misconception: Christianity is the oldest religion that originated in the Middle East.
nodes.response: Judaism is almost 2000 years older than Christianity.

nodes.misconception: Hitler was already an all-powerful dictator by 1934.
nodes.response: While Hitler had crushed political opposition, the military remained a powerful, independent force. The SA purge was crucial to win over the army, which still had the power to challenge him.

nodes.misconception: Many pupils stand too close or too far away from the ball which makes it hard for them to strike the ball effectively.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to stand roughly an arm's distance away from the ball in a well-balanced stance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't adjust their body position when preparing to stop the ball or return the hit. Instead, they stretch and try to hit the ball from an unbalanced position.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that positioning their body in line with the ball will make it easier to stop it going past them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils focus solely on their arm movements and neglect the use of their legs and hips to create power.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand how that bending their knees and rotating their hips can create more power for bigger hits.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think hitting your targets is the same as doing the maximum amount you can.
nodes.response: A target needs to be SMART. It needs to be specific to the group, one you can measure, the group agrees it and it is realistic to all the abilities and fitness levels in the group. It also needs an allocated time to achieve it.

nodes.misconception: In German, you always use 'müssen' to say what you have to do.
nodes.response: The verb 'sollen' is another way of expressing an obligation, something you have to do. It has several uses, including strong commands (e.g. 'you should ring the doctor straightaway'), which are similar to the 'have to, must' meaning of 'müssen'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not feel prepared enough for the debate.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have completed the previous lesson 'Preparing for a debate'. Speakers should all have written notes and have been assigned roles in their teams. They should have rehearsed their speeches and roles.

nodes.misconception: -er verbs have the same ending in the 1st person plural of the present and preterite tenses.
nodes.response: Unlike -ir verbs, -er verbs do not have the same ending in these tenses. The verb ending -emos is used in the present tense and -imos is used in the preterite tense.

nodes.misconception: 'Para' always means 'for'.
nodes.response: 'Para' often means 'for'. However, when followed by an infinitive, it means 'in order to'.

nodes.misconception: That the Torah and Gospels in the Jewish and Christian holy texts today are the same as those referenced in the Qur'an.
nodes.response: Muslims believe these have been changed over time from their original form and that the Qur'an corrects those changes.

nodes.misconception: Islam teaches or endorses the idea of Holy War as a religious duty.
nodes.response: The term Harb al-Muqadis does not appear in the Qur’an, Hadith or Shariah and is not part of classical Islamic teaching. Islam allows fighting only under strict moral conditions and not as a holy duty.

nodes.misconception: Christmas is the most important festival to Christians.
nodes.response: Easter is a more important festival to most Christians than Christmas.

nodes.misconception: It is necessary to use pronouns before verbs in Spanish to know who is performing an action.
nodes.response: It is not usually necessary to use pronouns before verbs in Spanish. You can tell who is performing an action by looking at the verb ending.

nodes.misconception: The line of a graph must go through all of the points.
nodes.response: Get pupils to invent plots to add to a graph showing a line of best fit that include small mistakes in the measurements.

nodes.misconception: Hooks and riffs are the same thing.
nodes.response: A riff is the more important feature in how the song fits together and tends to underpin some of the main sections in the music. It is also a more suitable musical starting point for a pop song composition.

nodes.misconception: Any melodic idea that repeats is a hook.
nodes.response: It's a bit more complex than that. In some cases, whether something is a hook or not could be a matter of opinion, not necessarily true or false. A hook must be short, memorable, and repeated.

nodes.misconception: Students might mistakenly believe hooliganism is limited to football.
nodes.response: Hooliganism can happen in other sports and activities but is it most widely known in football.

nodes.misconception: Pupils run instead of hopping or skipping. Pupils get upset if points are being lost in games (beanbags are taken by the Zookeepers).
nodes.response: Remind pupils that running is a rule break and celebrate pupils who are hopping/skipping not running.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are confusing the techniques for hopping and skipping and sometimes run instead.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that running is a rule break. Celebrate pupils who are hopping not running and demonstrate both techniques.

nodes.misconception: In horizontal resequencing, new musical sections should completely contrast with the preceeding section.
nodes.response: There should be contrast, but there also needs to be a feeling of continuity. Using some consistent features (like tempo, key, timbre) can help to create a feeling of some continuity, while still creating a large contrast.

nodes.misconception: The contraceptive pill can protect from STIs; that all contraception is 100% effective; there are no side effects to hormonal contraception.
nodes.response: Discuss barrier methods and their benefit in preventing STIs, oral contraceptive can be affected by user error or illness. Oral contraception has side effects but these are less in modern times.

nodes.misconception: That the menstrual cycle is not linked with reproduction; that hormones only control mood.
nodes.response: Diagrams to show the clear effect of hormones on changes in the menstrual cycle and discuss the importance of the process to fertilisation.

nodes.misconception: Hormones are only released in the brain and control the mood.
nodes.response: Hormones control many processes in the body and are secreted from many glands. Those involved in puberty and the menstrual cycle have physical effects that may also impact on mood.

nodes.misconception: Treatments in hospitals became significantly more effective as more medical staff were employed there.
nodes.response: Treatments in most hospitals continued to be based on the incorrect Theory of the Four Humours so unhelpful practices such as bloodletting remained common.

nodes.misconception: You don’t need any hardware for the cloud — everything just happens online.
nodes.response: The cloud still relies on physical hardware, like servers, storage devices and networking equipment.

nodes.misconception: Hot or cold colours can change the temperature.
nodes.response: Remind children that these colours do not really change the temperature, but they can make people feel warmer by looking at them, as they remind them of hot things like the sun or a fire.

nodes.misconception: No one is able to live in the Sahara desert.
nodes.response: 2.5 million people live in the Sahara desert.

nodes.misconception: When talking about what we like and hate, we change the ending of ‘amar’ or ‘odiar’ to say who loves or hates and add the gerund (-ing) of the verb that follows, as in English.
nodes.response: We change the ending of ‘amar’ or ‘odiar’ to say who loves or hates, but the verb that follows is in the infinitive.

nodes.misconception: When talking about what we like and hate, we change the ending of ‘amar’ or ‘odiar’ to say who loves or hates something and use the gerund (-ing form) of the following verb.
nodes.response: We change the ending of ‘amar’ or ‘odiar’ to say who loves or hates something, but the verb that follows is in the infinitive.

nodes.misconception: Migration only occurs because people are forced to leave their country due to negative reasons (e.g., war or persecution).
nodes.response: While people are often forced to migrate (due to push factors like war or persecution), others choose to migrate for reasons like better job opportunities, family reunification, or improved living conditions (pull factors).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals with soft, flexible bodies such as snakes or fish are invertebrates, or that any animal with a hard shell is a vertebrate.
nodes.response: Explain that the external appearance of an animal does not always give us enough information to classify it as a vertebrate or an invertebrate; the presence or absence of a backbone and internal skeleton is the only characteristic that matters.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants are green or that anything without a flower is not a plant.
nodes.response: Highlight the many examples of plants with different shapes, sizes and colours that are included in the lesson resources, reminding children that all of these are plants because they are living things that use the Sun’s light to make food.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all animals eat the same food, and also have food provided by humans.
nodes.response: Visuals to show lots of examples of different animals eating different food, and getting it in different ways.

nodes.misconception: Communities do not change and stay the same, regardless of the people in them.
nodes.response: Communities will always change due to many reasons including migration, politics, demography and the economy.

nodes.misconception: Low income countries (LICs) do not take action on climate change because they lack resources.
nodes.response: LICs do face challenges but are actively taking climate action with support from the UN and financial support from other sources. For example, Malawi is improving green energy, like solar power, to reduce emissions and adapt to climate impacts.

nodes.misconception: All democratic countries make decisions in the same way.
nodes.response: The decision-making process varies between democratic countries and depends on the type of system they follow.

nodes.misconception: All modern financial products are safe and designed to help people save money.
nodes.response: Apps and new financial products can be popular, so young people might not recognise the risks involved, such as overspending with Buy Now, Pay Later tools or misunderstanding investment risks.

nodes.misconception: Criminal law is only for very serious crimes, like murder or robbery.
nodes.response: Whilst criminal law deals with serious crimes like murder and robbery, it also covers a wide range of other offenses, such as theft and vandalism. Criminal law is used when someone's actions harm society, no matter how big or small the crime is.

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister alone makes all the laws.
nodes.response: Laws are created by Parliament, this involves members of both the House of Commons and the House of Lords debating and voting on what they should look like.

nodes.misconception: My rights are only protected if I go to court.
nodes.response: Rights do not only matter in legal cases, they are protected every day through laws, policies and the actions of public bodies like the police and the NHS.

nodes.misconception: That all civil cases must end up in court.
nodes.response: It is preferable for civil cases to be settled outside of court where possible as this is quicker, cheaper and less stressful for both parties.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to say 'they are' in Spanish.
nodes.response: There are two verbs meaning to be, being. To say 'they are' for location and temporary state, we use 'estan' from the verb 'estar'. To say 'we are' for general traits, we use 'son' from the verb 'ser'.

nodes.misconception: No young people are represented in Parliament.
nodes.response: The UK Youth Parliament has been running for 25 years and holds elections to join. These elections are open to all young people aged 11-18. They liaise with Parliament on various issues and campaign for change as a way to be represented nationally.

nodes.misconception: There is only one to say 'we are' in Spanish as in English.
nodes.response: There are two verbs meaning 'to be, being' in Spanish. To say 'we are' for location and temporary state, we use estamos from the verb estar and to say 'we are' for general traits, we use somos from the verb ser.

nodes.misconception: 'Raro' means 'rare'.
nodes.response: 'Raro' is a false friend and means 'strange'.

nodes.misconception: Spanish verbs always need pronouns, like in English, to convey the person doing the action.
nodes.response: Spanish verbs don't always need pronouns. The verb endings indicates the person doing the action.

nodes.misconception: It doesn’t matter whether I use 'ser' or 'estar' as they both mean 'to be,' so they’re interchangeable.
nodes.response: 'Ser' is used for permanent traits or characteristics, while 'estar' is used for temporary states, such as emotions or feelings.

nodes.misconception: As in English, the spelling of Spanish adjectives remains the same regardless of the noun they are describing.
nodes.response: The spelling of Spanish adjectives changes to match the nouns they describe in gender and number.

nodes.misconception: There is one verb for 'to be, being' as there is in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, there are two verbs for 'to be, being': 'estar' is used for location and temporary states and 'ser' is used for general traits.

nodes.misconception: Expressions such as 'I am cold' must use the verb 'être' (to be) when translated into French, as in English. The verb 'avoir' can only be translated as 'to have'.
nodes.response: Set expressions that use 'to be' in English, such as 'I am cold', use the verb 'avoir' in French, e.g. 'j'ai froid'. 'Avoir' means 'to have' but it can also be translated as 'to be' with set expressions.

nodes.misconception: Vowels have the same sounds in Spanish and English.
nodes.response: Vowels are pronounced differently in Spanish. In Spanish, vowels only have one sound and are pronounced in the same way no matter where they appear in a word.

nodes.misconception: There is one way to say 'you are' in Spanish, as in English.
nodes.response: There are two ways to say 'you are' in Spanish. 'Eres' is part of the verb 'ser' and used for general traits. 'Estás' is part of the verb 'estar' and used for location and temporary states.

nodes.misconception: Poetry about a personal event should be as emotional as possible.
nodes.response: Armitage suggests that poetry about personal events should convey emotion without being too obvious or too sentimental.

nodes.misconception: When drawing, artists only use their hands.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can use their whole body when creating marks.
