nodes.misconception: Baghdad was a city where everyone was expected to follow Islam.
nodes.response: People from all over the world visited Baghdad and practising other religions was tolerated.

nodes.misconception: As Christianity was popular in Roman times before its return, pupils may think this isn't a change.
nodes.response: Due to two forms of Christianity being practiced before the Synod of Whitby, there was a significant change to religion in Britain.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that everything was made from bronze during the Bronze Age.
nodes.response: Items such as jewellery were often made from gold.

nodes.misconception: Ordinary people have no real influence over the laws made in Parliament.
nodes.response: While politicians vote on laws, citizens play a powerful role in shaping them. By raising awareness, building public support, and working with their MPs, people outside of government have successfully influenced legal changes.

nodes.misconception: Young people cannot change anything in their communities, only adults can.
nodes.response: Young people, as well as adults, can make lasting change in their communities. Young people have many powerful tools, like social media, to campaign for change.

nodes.misconception: Only large businesses contribute to the local economy.
nodes.response: Small businesses also play a crucial role in job creation, local investment and community development. They generate employment, keep money circulating within the community and contribute significantly through taxation.

nodes.misconception: Community cohesion comes easily to all communities.
nodes.response: Community cohesion takes work and effort to maintain relationships and keep everyone together working towards the same goal.

nodes.misconception: You don’t need to worry about financial planning until you are older.
nodes.response: Financial planning starts as soon as you have any income, like pocket money or a part-time job. Learning to plan now helps build strong habits for the future.

nodes.misconception: That citizenship skills are only important for politicians, activists, or people with a lot of power.
nodes.response: Citizenship skills are important for everyone, because even small actions help strengthen communities and make a difference. These skills help ordinary people stand up for their rights, support others and create positive change in everyday life.

nodes.misconception: A campaign is always needed to challenge injustice.
nodes.response: Not all injustice needs a full campaign. Sometimes, speaking up, helping someone or reporting unfair treatment can challenge injustice effectively, for example, telling a teacher if someone is being bullied is a way of standing up to injustice.

nodes.misconception: Once my project ends, there's nothing more I can do to make a difference.
nodes.response: You can create systems, inspire others, or build partnerships so your impact continues even after you finish.

nodes.misconception: That success has to be huge.
nodes.response: Success can look different depending on the action and success can be subtle too.

nodes.misconception: Only Members of Parliament (MPs) can be part of select committees.
nodes.response: The public can contribute to select committees by submitting evidence or attending public consultations.

nodes.misconception: Investment always makes a local area better straight away.
nodes.response: Investment usually takes time to show its effects, and sometimes it can create challenges like rising rents or traffic before the benefits are fully seen.

nodes.misconception: Shopping locally or sustainably is always more expensive.
nodes.response: Many people may believe that making ethical or local shopping choices costs more, without realising the long term financial and environmental benefits, like durability, reduced waste or savings through reused and second-hand items.

nodes.misconception: Social media automatically leads to increased political participation because it reaches so many people.
nodes.response: Social media can engage many, but it doesn’t ensure political participation. Misinformation, digital divides, echo chambers, and apathy can hinder impact. Success depends on content quality, usage, and users’ critical thinking skills.

nodes.misconception: That it is negative or 'tempting fate' to consider what could go wrong.
nodes.response: Considering what could go wrong is a sensible part of planning for your goal, this helps to identify possible barriers and work to overcome them.

nodes.misconception: Only leaders, or those in power, can be active citizens.
nodes.response: Whilst leadership skills might help in some situations, many active citizens work behind the scenes, you don’t need to be a leader or in power to be an active citizen.

nodes.misconception: Voting is the only way to become involved in politics.
nodes.response: Voting isn't the only way to be involved in politics; you can raise awareness about important issues, join campaigns, speak out on social media or participate in protests and petitions.

nodes.misconception: You can only lobby MPs.
nodes.response: You can lobby MPs, local councillors and any politicans to try and influence change. Any decision-maker can be lobbied.

nodes.misconception: Careful consideration, through answering the key questions, is not needed to decide which research methods to use: research methods can be chosen at random.
nodes.response: Pupils must consider and answer the key questions to ensure they choose appropriate and suitable research methods for their chosen active citizenship project. Failure to do so will jeopdise the project's success.

nodes.misconception: Young people cannot make a difference because adults are the decision-makers.
nodes.response: Young people can make a difference. Article 12 of the UNCRC says children have the right to be heard in decisions that affect them. For example, Martha Payne was only nine years old when she helped change school meals by sharing her views.

nodes.misconception: Local democracy only happens during elections.
nodes.response: Local democracy is happening all the time. It occurs in council meetings, Youth Councils, local campaigns and anytime that people speak up about local issues. You do not need to wait for local elections to take part.

nodes.misconception: That what a pupil finds safe and appropriate to discuss will be for the same for everyone.
nodes.response: We all have different lived experience, which can impact whether we find topics distressing, a person's age can also have an impact.

nodes.misconception: Voting is the only way you can exercise your democratic rights.
nodes.response: There are several ways you can exercise your democratic rights, even if you cannot vote. You could: contact your local councilor or Member of Parliament (MP); express your opinion, join a protest or pressure group; or join a political party.

nodes.misconception: To make a difference within the school community an active citizen has to make a big change.
nodes.response: Even small actions at school can make a meaningful change.

nodes.misconception: Citizens aren't able to make a difference and hold leaders accountable.
nodes.response: Citizens hold leaders accountable through raising concerns, participating in inquiries and contacting MPs.

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the electorates.
nodes.response: The leader of each political party is voted in by members of that party. When the general election takes place, the party with the majority of seats forms the Government and the leader of that party becomes the Prime Minister.

nodes.misconception: Many young people believe they cannot influence decisions because they are not old enough to vote.
nodes.response: Emphasise that democratic participation is not limited to voting. Pupils can have power and influence through various actions such as campaigning, petitions, joining youth organisations and speaking to decision makers.

nodes.misconception: Hate crimes only count if someone actually hurts you physically.
nodes.response: Hate crimes include any criminal act where someone is targeted because of their disability, race, religion, sexual orientation or transgender identity. The law protects people from all kinds of harm motivated by prejudice.

nodes.misconception: All campaigns work the same way; if one method worked once, it will always work.
nodes.response: Never overlook the importance of choosing the right method for the right situation and evaluating its impact. Some campaigns will require a combination of methods.

nodes.misconception: Success is only measured by big changes.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to see that success is not just about large-scale change. Small improvements, like raising awareness, influencing opinions, or getting a response from decision-makers, also matter.

nodes.misconception: You only have to pay the minimum payment each month on a credit card to not pay any interest.
nodes.response: Unless your credit card is interest-free for an amount of time, if you pay the minimum payment each month, you will be charged interest. Some credit cards can charge up to 30% or more in interest, so it is best to pay it off in full each month.

nodes.misconception: An action plan is a static document, there is no need update it once it has been made.
nodes.response: Action plans are fluid and need to be reviewed regularly; they can become obsolete which can hinder the success as they are no longer relevant. Sometimes action plans need to be amended or adjusted to respond to challenges or barriers.

nodes.misconception: When a bank phones you they will ask you to tell them all of your personal details.
nodes.response: Your bank will only ever ask you to disclose some of your personal details, never all of them. If you are asked for all of your details, it is a scam.

nodes.misconception: Final editorial checks mean the news is always factual and true.
nodes.response: Even though clear procedures are in place, errors can still occur; these could be due to human error, rushing or embelishing a story to generate more sales.

nodes.misconception: As an individual, I am not responsible for taking action on global issues.
nodes.response: You can make a difference by being an active citizen and taking responsible action.

nodes.misconception: Low voter turnout means people are not interested in politics.
nodes.response: Voter apathy might play a part in low voter turnout but other reasons exist, such as feeling votes will not count.

nodes.misconception: Young people can't have a real influence on local decision making because they are not old enough to vote or be a councillor.
nodes.response: Young people can have a significant impact by speaking up, raising awareness, organising community actions and engaging with local leaders. They can be powerful voices for change, especially when working together and being persistent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think Christianity survived because of one reason.
nodes.response: Christianity survived because of a few reasons. It survived in the places the Anglo-Saxons did not settle. It also survived because monasteries were set up and missionaries spread the the religion to other places.

nodes.misconception: All Christians celebrate Christmas on the 25th of December.
nodes.response: Some Christians, such as many Eastern Orthodox Christians, celebrate Christmas on the 7th of January.

nodes.misconception: We know what Jesus looked like. The white Jesus seen in stained glass windows is an authentic representation of Jesus.
nodes.response: We do not know what Jesus looked like. Artists all over the world can paint or represent Jesus from within their own cultures.

nodes.misconception: All Christians view art in the same way.
nodes.response: There are differing Christian worldviews on the role of art. Some Christians use art as a form of devotion. Some, like many Orthodox Christians, venerate icons. Other Christians see art as distracting from a focus on God.

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of church. All churches have stained glass windows, towers and are made of stone.
nodes.response: Churches come in all shapes and sizes. Some look very traditional and some are modern.

nodes.misconception: All the data from a website travels together in one file and always takes the same route through the internet to reach your device.
nodes.response: Data is broken into packets, and each packet may take a different route. This makes transmission faster and more reliable, because the network can avoid delays or busy routes.

nodes.misconception: Magna Carta was a singular event which resulted in a powerless monarchy and human rights for all.
nodes.response: Magna Carta started a process of struggle. The medieval monarchy remained powerful, and it did not grant freedoms to everybody.

nodes.misconception: The Chartists achieved their aims and Parliament adopted their charter.
nodes.response: The charter was not adopted by Parliament and the next Reform Act wasn't passed until 1867, after the Chartists had disbanded.

nodes.misconception: Diversity only refers to ethnicity or race.
nodes.response: Diversity includes many aspects such as culture, religion, language, age, gender and socioeconomic background.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that success on changing a law is solely dependant on the citizen or citizens.
nodes.response: Whilst personal skills of the citizens involved is important, there are many other external factors that can impact success or failure, regardless of how persuasive the individuals trying to change the law are.

nodes.misconception: That special constables do not have the same police powers as regular police officers.
nodes.response: Special constables have police powers and wear the same uniform as regular police officers.

nodes.misconception: All citizens across the world are able to take action.
nodes.response: In some non-democratic countries taking action can be seen as civil disobedience and citizens can face punishment.

nodes.misconception: Only people in power can take effective action.
nodes.response: Every citizen can take effective action to make lasting change to their local, national or global community. You do not need to be in a position of power to take effective action.

nodes.misconception: Democracies are always more efficient and quicker at making decisions than dictatorships.
nodes.response: While democracies can be slower in making decisions due to debates, elections, and checks on power, this doesn't mean they are less effective overall. Decisions involving multiple viewpoints can lead to more thoughtful and balanced outcomes.

nodes.misconception: Democratic governments cannot have authoritarian features, and authoritarian regimes cannot have democratic elements.
nodes.response: Governments are not always purely democratic or authoritarian. Many exist on a spectrum and can have a mix of both democratic and authoritarian traits.

nodes.misconception: The only election in the UK is the general election.
nodes.response: There are many different elections including: general, local government, PCC, Mayoral and devolved parliament elections.

nodes.misconception: Elections are the same across the world.
nodes.response: Elections run differently and follow different systems in indvidual countries.

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the public during the general election.
nodes.response: The Prime Minister is not elected by the people; instead, they are the leader of the party that has the most seats in the House of Commons after the election.

nodes.misconception: Only people with very low incomes can apply for social housing.
nodes.response: While social housing is mainly aimed at people with lower incomes or in urgent need, you don’t have to be unemployed or on benefits to apply. Local councils assess need based on income, family size and housing situation, not just income alone.

nodes.misconception: Grassroots campaigns cannot make a big difference because they are local, small-scale, and led by people without influence or national recognition.
nodes.response: Grassroots campaigns often start small, but grow as more people join. Their local focus makes them powerful, and many have led to national policy changes or raised public awareness.

nodes.misconception: Pressure groups are usually violent.
nodes.response: Pressure groups can lobby MPs and protest for change but usually in a peaceful way. There is a wide range of different pressure groups in the UK using peaceful methods to perform effective action and bring lasting change.

nodes.misconception: There isn't a need for an action plan as long as pupils are passionate about the issue.
nodes.response: An action plan is vital as it ensures everyone knows what their responsibilities are.

nodes.misconception: Young people can't make a real difference in society or influence decision-makers.
nodes.response: Young people can create change by raising awareness, educating others, and working with leaders or organisations.

nodes.misconception: ‘Es’ and ‘estoy’ are part of the same verb.
nodes.response: ‘Es’ is from the verb ‘ser’, ‘estoy’ is from the verb ‘estar’.  In this lesson we bring together ser and estar so that pupils can contrast ‘es’ plus days of the week and ‘estoy’ to express their state or mood on that day.

nodes.misconception: That once the active citizenship project is complete, it's over.
nodes.response: By reporting about your project and sharing this with others, it can continue to amplify the issue and develop ongoing active citizenship skills.

nodes.misconception: Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.
nodes.response: Ireland is a separate country that gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1922, but Northern Ireland is part of the UK.

nodes.misconception: All candidates have the same level of resources and support during campaigns.
nodes.response: In reality, some candidates may struggle to reach voters due to limited funding or organisation, which can affect their visibility and chances of success.

nodes.misconception: NGOs and international agencies work separately and do not rely on each other.
nodes.response: NGOs often work closely with international organisations such as the UN to deliver aid, share information and promote human rights more effectively.

nodes.misconception: One type of government is better than the other.
nodes.response: It is not always that simple. Every country governs differently and the effectiveness of a government depends on many factors such as how well it protects people’s rights,  ensures fairness and responds to citizens' needs.

nodes.misconception: Issues do not need to be related to Citizenship concepts.
nodes.response: Active citizenship requires issues investigated and advocated for to have a clear link between a Citizenship concept and the issue.

nodes.misconception: The aging population are all financially secure because they receive pensions.
nodes.response: Not all people are financially secure. Some may struggle due to low pension incomes, rising living costs, or a lack of savings, which can make it harder to cover everyday expenses.

nodes.misconception: Everyone has the same retirement age.
nodes.response: Not everyone retires at the same age. Retirement age can vary greatly depending on personal finances, circumstances, health and family.

nodes.misconception: You need to pay to see a doctor in the UK.
nodes.response: The NHS is free in the UK; therefore you can see a doctor for no charge -  this protects our right to healthcare. Some people choose to have private healthcare in the UK, but this is a personal choice.

nodes.misconception: Use the same articles after 'il y a' and 'il n'y a pas'.
nodes.response: Use the indefinite article, depending on gender and number after 'il y a' but after 'il n' y a pas', always use de regardless of gender/number and d' for any nouns starting with a vowel.

nodes.misconception: 'Ma' is the possessive adjective for all feminine singular nouns.
nodes.response: Use 'mon/ton' before all nouns starting with a vowel/h.

nodes.misconception: Refugees are only protected by the laws of the country they arrive in.
nodes.response: Refugees are protected by international agreements and laws. The geneva convention is very important and outlines how we treat refugees. This is overseen and safeguarded by the UN agency for refugees.

nodes.misconception: Climate action is positive for all of the world.
nodes.response: Climate action aims to benefit the world, but political issues arise. Low income and emerging countries are asked to reduce industries, while the top five polluters are developed nations, creating an imbalance in responsibility for climate action.

nodes.misconception: Devolution means that areas become independent.
nodes.response: Devolution means powers are devolved but they are still part of the UK and Parliament still holds central power.

nodes.misconception: Devolved governments can make laws on any issue.
nodes.response: The powers of devolved governments are limited to specific policy areas defined by devolution agreements.

nodes.misconception: Non-democratic governments are lawless.
nodes.response: Non-democratic governments still have laws and rules but the citizens might not get a say in what these are and they are decided by those in power.

nodes.misconception: International law automatically replaces UK law.
nodes.response: International law does not override UK law automatically. Parliament decides how and when international law is applied in the UK.

nodes.misconception: The media can always hold the Government to account, no matter the country.
nodes.response: The media can only effectively challenge the Government in countries where press freedom exists. In these countries, journalists are free to investigate, report and criticise those in power without fear of government control or censorship.

nodes.misconception: Migration always causes problems in communities.
nodes.response: Migration can bring challenges, but it also brings many benefits like new skills, jobs and cultures. Communities often grow stronger by learning from each other and working together to solve problems.

nodes.misconception: All countries sentence in the same way as each other.
nodes.response: Although sentencing within a country follows sentencing guidelines, these can vary vastly between each other, e.g. the USA is able to pass the death penalty in some states.

nodes.misconception: Local taxation only funds national priorities like healthcare and defence.
nodes.response: Local taxation also supports local services, infrastructure and businesses. Council Tax and business rates are reinvested into local economies, funding initiatives such as skills training that benefits communities directly.

nodes.misconception: The UK Government must pay debt off completely, like a household paying off a loan.
nodes.response: Governments often carry debt indefinitely and focus on managing it rather than eliminating it. As long as the Government can afford interest payments and investors have confidence in its ability to repay, borrowing can continue.

nodes.misconception: The Budget just shows how money is allocated across the country.
nodes.response: The Budget maps all income and expenditure so it shows us what money goes where and how money is generated, not just allocated.

nodes.misconception: The only person in charge of finances in the UK is the Chancellor of the Exchequer.
nodes.response: There is a whole structure of people in charge of the UK economy within the Treasury, including the Prime Minister who is the First Lord of the Treasury.

nodes.misconception: All countries have fair and independent justice systems that protect everyone's rights equally.
nodes.response: Not all countries have justice systems that are fair or independent. In some countries, the Government may control the courts, leading to biased decisions and limited protection of human rights.

nodes.misconception: Justice is only about punishing criminals.
nodes.response: Justice is about punishing criminals but it is also about fairness, access to legal help and protecting the rights of all people, including victims and the accused.

nodes.misconception: Young people are treated the same as adults in the justice system.
nodes.response: Young people are treated differently in the justice system. Youth courts focus on rehabilitation with alternative sentences to prison, like community service or rehabilitation orders, to help young people learn from mistakes and avoid re-offending.

nodes.misconception: The local economy only depends on businesses and jobs.
nodes.response: While businesses and jobs are important, the local economy is also influenced by government policies, public services, infrastructure and consumer behaviour. Global events like recessions or technological changes can impact local economies.

nodes.misconception: There are no examples of the media holding those in power to account.
nodes.response: There are many examples of the media holding those in power to account, for example, if a politician makes promises about education and doesn't deliver, the media could publish an article about it to hold them to account.

nodes.misconception: There are limits to what the media can print about the Government.
nodes.response: As long as the media is following regulations, they have the freedom to print what they like, even if this is negative towards the Government.

nodes.misconception: The UK Prime Minister has the same level of power as other elected leaders.
nodes.response: The UK Prime Minister can be removed with a vote of no confidence. The US President has fixed terms and a stronger separation from the legislature.

nodes.misconception: The UK has a written constitution like the United States.
nodes.response: The UK Constitution is uncodified; it exists through laws, customs and conventions, but is not written down in one single document.

nodes.misconception: Only financial risks affect the economy.
nodes.response: The Government must work hard to manage a large range of risks in every area of life, such as health and education, so that the economy remains stable and balanced.

nodes.misconception: Democracy exists in all countries, just in different ways.
nodes.response: Democracy exists in many countries and the levels of it vary. However, in many countries, there is a large mix of democratic and non-democratic practices, and in others, there is no true democracy at all, with the government taking full control.

nodes.misconception: Young people are tried in the same courts as adults.
nodes.response: Young people are tried in a youth court, except for offences that are considered to be too serious.

nodes.misconception: Electrical insulators cannot conduct electricity at all.
nodes.response: Children will be taught that electrical insulators are materials that do not allow electricity to pass through them easily.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what 'feminism' or 'feminist' means.
nodes.response: Ensure that before beginning this lesson, you have developed pupils' understanding of what feminism is. You could use PSHE sessions to explore this in more depth.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that life returned to normal for everyone after the war was over.
nodes.response: Emphasise how the changes brought by the Second World War were permanent.

nodes.misconception: People who belong to a particular religion only help those from that same background.
nodes.response: Interfaith groups as well as religious and non-religious people can work together.

nodes.misconception: Discrimination in the past was not as harmful because people did not know any better.
nodes.response: Even though discrimination was accepted in the past, it still caused real harm. People lost rights, faced unfair treatment and suffered. Increased awareness led to campaigns and laws being made to protect people's rights.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may gain the impression that the Ancient Romans destroyed all aspects of Celtic worship.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that although the druids were wiped out, the worship of Celtic gods was tolerated as long as Ancient Roman ones were also respected.

nodes.misconception: Fossils are pieces of dead animals and plants and children often think that only dinosaurs make fossils.
nodes.response: By modelling and discussing fossil formation in various ways, children will understand how fossils are formed.

nodes.misconception: Gears only exist in bicycles and cars.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching of what gears are and where they are found.

nodes.misconception: Geologists only look at rocks and soils collected on Earth.
nodes.response: Geologists also work with data from space.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that provoking an emotional response in an audience is about making them sad.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know there is a wide range of emotional responses that audience members may have - and they may vary from person to person. These include anger, frustration, enthusiasm, determination, sadness, joy, hope and belief.

nodes.misconception: Migration to the UK is only about people coming from other countries to live here.
nodes.response: Migration includes both people coming to the UK (immigration) and those leaving (emigration). It’s shaped by global and local factors and impacts communities, industries and the economy in various ways.

nodes.misconception: Artists always depict water using the colour blue.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can use blue to represent water, but they can use lots of other colours as well.

nodes.misconception: All men had the right to vote before 1918.
nodes.response: Appoximately 40% of men could not vote before 1918.

nodes.misconception: Regeneration benefits everyone in the community.
nodes.response: Pupils may think regeneration always helps everyone, but if it is not planned in an inclusive manner  it can lead to gentrification, displacing long-standing residents and businesses.

nodes.misconception: That the relationship between trade unions and government has only ever been one of conflict.
nodes.response: Trade unions have also worked alongside government to create employment law.

nodes.misconception: The past never changes.
nodes.response: Our understanding of the past changes frequently, which causes us to look at events in different ways. As such, how we view the past is constantly changing.

nodes.misconception: People “should have known” what Hitler would do once in power.
nodes.response: In reality, many elites and citizens saw the Nazis as a lesser evil amid crisis — not as future dictators. The horror of what was to come wasn’t yet clear to them.

nodes.misconception: Climate change only affects the environment.
nodes.response: Climate change also impacts human rights, causing issues like food insecurity, displacement, and health risks, particularly for vulnerable communities.

nodes.misconception: Devolution means the regional governments are independent.
nodes.response: Devolution allows more powers, but the countries still remain part of the UK.

nodes.misconception: Local and national governments have the same powers.
nodes.response: The national government have broader powers and devolves some of this to local governments.

nodes.misconception: Local governments make laws.
nodes.response: Laws are made by central government, which must be followed by local councils. However, they can lobby the central government and influence policy through campaigns, consultations and public pressure.

nodes.misconception: Every local government runs in the same way.
nodes.response: Local governments do not all run in the same way. There are different type of councils including, county and district councils.

nodes.misconception: There are no alternatives to plastic.
nodes.response: There are lots of alternatives to plastic that are easier to break down or recycle and therefore have less of an environmental impact, for example, glass and metal.

nodes.misconception: [e] and [i] are pronounced the same in Spanish and English.
nodes.response: [e] is pronounced as in elefante and [i] is pronounced as in idea.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives ending in -e and -z change to -a when the person or animal described is female.
nodes.response: When an adjective ends in –e or -z , it can describe a female and male person or animal. It does not change.

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet have total control over the UK.
nodes.response: The Prime Minister leads the Government but must answer to Parliament. Members of Parliament (MPs) debate and approve laws and can challenge a Prime Minister. The Cabinet makes decisions but is accountable to Parliament and the law.

nodes.misconception: If a young person is accused of a crime, they are treated the same as an adult in court.
nodes.response: Young people have some special protections in the legal system, e.g., in youth courts, the focus is on rehabilitation and making sure young people are given the support they need to avoid reoffending. They also have extra rights when arrested.

nodes.misconception: Older people cannot use online banking at all.
nodes.response: With the right support and training, many older people have adapted very well to online banking. It is prejudiced to assume all older people struggle.

nodes.misconception: Globalisation does not benefit everybody.
nodes.response: Globalisation benefits everyone because with collaboration we can achieve more things together as a global community.

nodes.misconception: The Government can borrow unlimited money without consequences.
nodes.response: While the Government can borrow to fund services and support the economy, excessive borrowing leads to higher debt and interest payments, which can limit future spending and create financial risks.

nodes.misconception: Civil servants and public sector workers make political decisions.
nodes.response: Civil servants and other public sector workers are neutral professionals who work to implement government policies and decisions made by elected ministers, but they do not make political decisions themselves.

nodes.misconception: Population changes only happen through immigration.
nodes.response: Population changes include factors like birth rates, ageing and internal migration, as well as immigration.

nodes.misconception: All festivals are solemn.
nodes.response: In this festival, Jewish children act, shout, eat and dress up.

nodes.misconception: All levers work in the same way.
nodes.response: Teaching that the position of the pivot (fulcrum) and the effort compared to load can vary.

nodes.misconception: When children think of light, they do not necessarily think of it as travelling. Also that light is found only in bright areas and not in the space between.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for children to think of different ways to model and record travelling light so it is seen as a continuous straight line.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all prehistoric living things were on Earth at the same time, rather than understanding that life on Earth changed over millions of years.
nodes.response: Use the models and information in the lesson to explain that the different layers of rock beneath our feet were formed at different times, and there are fossils of different living things buried within each.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know about the differences in children's rights to education around the world.
nodes.response: Ensure that before beginning this lesson, you have developed pupils' understanding of how children's rights to education are different around the world. You could use PSHE sessions to explore this in more depth.

nodes.misconception: All plurals are formed in the same way.
nodes.response: Nouns have different rules for plurals depending on their gender and spelling.

nodes.misconception: When first learning about seconds, pupils come to realise they are very quick. They count seconds at the same speed in which they count other numbers - usually too quickly.
nodes.response: The classic way to slow down counting speed so that it more closely matches the pace of seconds is to use 'one Mississippi, two Mississippi' etc. For most pupils that is an obscure reference point - counting elephants is suggested as an alternative.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that repetition involves repeating just one word.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that repetition is often most impactful when repeating a phrase at the start of a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that their speech should be purely made up of rhetorical questions.
nodes.response: Highlight and explain how rhetorical questions can be interspersed with statements and information that reinforce the point and help to achieve the purpose too.

nodes.misconception: All mosques will look the same and have features such as a dome.
nodes.response: Mosques may be purpose-built or adapted. They may have some features such as domes or not. All mosques will have a place to pray and show the direction of Makkah.

nodes.misconception: Everyone pays the same rate of tax regardless of their salary.
nodes.response: The UK operates a progressive taxation system so people pay more if they earn more, according to the Government's band system.

nodes.misconception: We can develop a composition around any element of music.
nodes.response: Using the elements of music, particularly individually, is not always helpful for pupils to make a start on a composition. Finding a musical starting point such as a set of notes or rhythm allows pupils to then explore the elements through that idea.

nodes.misconception: There is a fixed and correct finger pattern for performing keyboard pieces.
nodes.response: With pieces that require a dexterous hand postition change, there are often several options. Encourage pupils to find a comfortable solution. Show examples of good keyboard technique that allows them to perform more difficult melodies with control.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know that we need to eat food to obtain essential nutrients to keep us healthy and alive.
nodes.response: Learning about different types of nutrients found in food, such as vitamins, proteins, carbohydrates and fats will help children to remember previous learning; that we get nutrition from what we eat.

nodes.misconception: 'On' is equivalent to 'one' in English and is therefore is very formal and rarely used.
nodes.response: 'On' is very commonly used in French and can mean 'everyone', 'people', 'you' and 'one'.

nodes.misconception: The possessive adjective 'son, sa, ses' matches the person who owns the noun that follows. So 'his' is 'son, 'her' is 'sa' and 'their' is 'ses'.
nodes.response: In French, the possessive pronoun matches the noun that follows it, not the person to whom the object belongs. This is why sometimes you cannot tell whether the owner is male or female because the words for 'his' and 'her' are the same in French.

nodes.misconception: I only use adjectives with comparative structures like 'plus ... que'.
nodes.response: Adjectives help us to compare two nouns with comparative structures such as 'plus ... que'. For example, 'Emily est plus petite que Lucy'. We can use adverbs in the same way to compare how people do things. For example, 'Emily va plus vite que Lucy'.

nodes.misconception: There is only one word for 'better' in French: 'meilleur'.
nodes.response: The adjective 'meilleur(e)' means 'better' in French and describes a noun, e.g.'il a un meilleur ordinateur' ('he has a better computer'). To describe an action as 'better' we use the adverb 'mieux', e.g. 'il chante mieux' ('he sings better').

nodes.misconception: The verb 'dar' always translates as 'to give, giving'.
nodes.response: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' but can also translate as 'to be' + adjective when describing how something makes people feel.

nodes.misconception: The verb 'tener' always means 'to have, having'.
nodes.response: The verb 'tener' translates into English as 'to be' when used as part of idioms, e.g. 'tengo suerte' translates as 'I am lucky'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Polynesia is a country.
nodes.response: Polynesia is not one single country. It is a large area of the Pacific Ocean containing lots of different islands.

nodes.misconception: All pulleys have the wheel attached to a ceiling.
nodes.response: Examples will be given of different types of simple pulleys.

nodes.misconception: Scientists do not communicate directly with the public.
nodes.response: Explanation of the different ways in which scientists can communicate with the public.

nodes.misconception: Scientific enquiry is only valid if variables can be controlled and changed.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will explain how some scientist cannot control variables and look for patterns in data and observations instead.

nodes.misconception: There is no order to the results given by a search engine, it is just whichever results have been found first.
nodes.response: Search engines order results following algorithms or rules to move some results nearer the top of the results list.

nodes.misconception: Search engines do not prioritise any results.
nodes.response: Search engines order results by ranking them using an algorithm.

nodes.misconception: Shadows only form in bright light; shadows and reflections are the same thing; a shadow shows the features of an object.
nodes.response: Children will explore shadow making and images/examples will be used to highlight the key features of shadows and reflections.

nodes.misconception: You should try to speak for other people in your writing.
nodes.response: We all have slightly different opinions and ideas, so you should try to communicate your ideas and emotions to other people through your writing.

nodes.misconception: A poem about those who have lost their lives will always be sad.
nodes.response: While laments for the dead contain sadness, they also often contain elements of hope and joy for the lives lived and the futures ahead.

nodes.misconception: A poem is completely separate from a narrative story.
nodes.response: Fundamentally, a poem is about the manipulation of language - so you can manipulate a narrative story into a poem.

nodes.misconception: A biography offers an authentic impression of that person.
nodes.response: We all might have different perspectives on the same person, so different biographies are likely to portray the same person in different ways.

nodes.misconception: Reading a poem aloud is the same as reading prose aloud.
nodes.response: When reading a poem, you need to consider the line breaks in a way that you don't have to with prose.

nodes.misconception: You should be objective when you are writing about world events.
nodes.response: Armitage suggests that poetry is about the individual and that we have a responsibility to reflect our personal responses to what's happening in the world.

nodes.misconception: Listening to a song or singing can affect our mood while we listen or sing but it doesn’t have a lasting effect.
nodes.response: Bonds created when singing in a group are strong, lasting and continue to strengthen over time. Upbeat, happy music causes our brains to release dopamine and serotonin which help evoke feelings of joy. Listening to calm music helps us feel relaxed.

nodes.misconception: Singing softly is easier and requires less effort.
nodes.response: Soft singing requires the same breath control as louder singing. The warm-ups and the breathing exercise help prepare for this.

nodes.misconception: English and Spanish sound-spelling links are the same.
nodes.response: Sound-symbol correspondence [i] is different in Spanish and English and reading aloud Spanish words with [i] leads to more secure knowledge.

nodes.misconception: Musical theatre is solely for light entertainment.
nodes.response: Songs in musical theatre can explore a range of emotions and experiences that an audience might relate to.

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that sound can be produced without using any materials.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for children to learn about objects vibrating in order to produce sounds.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that the role of the medieval monarch is comparable with today's monarchy.
nodes.response: A medieval king was judged by his ability on the battlefield. Success in battle was the best way for a king to become powerful.

nodes.misconception: As Nixon showed little interest in the civil rights movement after his election, the movement largely regressed in the 1970s.
nodes.response: The extent of progress in the civil rights movement was largely dependent on the area of life you consider. For example, there was little change politically but there was some progress economically.

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of synagogue.
nodes.response: Synagogues come in different shapes and sizes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that dystopian societies only involve dilapidated settings.
nodes.response: Explain that there are two sides in a dystopia: those with power and control who live in luxury and ordinary citizens in run down areas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Britain only changed for the worse because of the Vikings.
nodes.response: Britain changed in multiple positive ways because of Viking invasion and settlement through trade, changing place names, creating a new generation and even creating the England we know today.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a speech in a debate can be improvised on the spot and not follow a structure.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that following a structure will help to make their speech flow better and be easier for an audience to follow.

nodes.misconception: Upper body strength is the primary fitness component required for seated volleyball.
nodes.response: Core strength is fundamental to play seated volleyball effectively as it enables players to maintain their body position in the preparation and executon of skills throughout the game.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think that using long quotations offers the best evidence for your point.
nodes.response: Using short, embedded quotations is the most effective way of evidencing your ideas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rush to throw the ball without checking where their opponent is positioned. Pupils may forgt to return to the ready position in the middle of the court on the baseline.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to scan the court and look for spaces away from their opponent. Remind pupils to return to the middle of the court on the baseline after every shot and adopt the ready position.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that sound travels only to the person that hear it, directly from the sound source to their ear.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for children to draw diagrams of how they think sound travels, and then revisit the diagrams to make improvements or amendments with further learning.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that water is taken into the plant through the leaves or flowers, due to the way water can sometimes be seen pooling there after rain.
nodes.response: Use the slide deck and lesson activities to support pupils’ understanding that water is absorbed by the roots of a plant, then transported via the stem, and that the flowers and leaves are not able to take in water.

nodes.misconception: All online communication is the same.
nodes.response: Different tools are better for different purposes (e.g. chat for quick messages, video for a longer discussion).

nodes.misconception: Students may think that for something to be taught as history, all historians have to agree on it.
nodes.response: Historians do not always agree about the past and what sources tell us. It is important to remember this when being historians ourselves!

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not grasp that artefacts act like pieces to a puzzle that help us learn about how people lived in a specific time or place.
nodes.response: The more artefacts archaeologists uncover, the more opportunity there is to study them carefully to learn about how people lived in a specific time or place.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the Moon produces its own light, or that the Moon only comes out at night
nodes.response: Explore common reflectors of light, to enable pupils to observe how some objects, including the Moon, appear to shine as they reflect light

nodes.misconception: Light only reflects off mirrors and shiny objects, and doesn't reflect off dull surfaces.
nodes.response: All surfaces reflect (some) light. Use ideas of reflected light to explain how we see all the objects around us.

nodes.misconception: There is nothing that protects and supports children’s rights in the UK.
nodes.response: There are lots of organisations that protect and support children’s rights in the UK.

nodes.misconception: If digital democracy works in other countries, the UK can easily copy the same methods.
nodes.response: Success in other countries is dependent on specific factors like strong digital infrastructure, cybersecurity systems, and public trust in technology. For the UK to adopt similar methods, these factors must be carefully considered and adapted.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to comprehend the slow and painstaking nature of carrying out excavations.
nodes.response: Carter began excavating the Valley of the Kings many years before finding Tutankhamun's tomb; they were about to give up when they found it.

nodes.misconception: [ei] is pronounced like the English [e].
nodes.response: [ei] is pronounced as in the key word 'frei' and like the English 'eye'.

nodes.misconception: HTML is a programming language.
nodes.response: HTML is a markup language. It defines the structure and appearance of content on a web page, but does not not do any processing of data into information.

nodes.misconception: The Huffman tree is the compressed file.
nodes.response: The compressed file is a sequence of bits, and the tree is the representation of the coding system.

nodes.misconception: Huguenots were a separate Protestant denomination from other Protestants in Euope.
nodes.response: Huguenots were Calvinist Protestants, which was a very common form of Protestantism. The term 'Huguenot' merely means they were Protestants from France.

nodes.misconception: In a narrative dance you have to interpret every word into an action.
nodes.response: In a narrative dance performers aim to communicate the main parts of the story. They may add actions and join movements together to show the context and character or make it more interesting.

nodes.misconception: As individuals we are helpless in combatting climate change. Technology alone can solve climate issues.
nodes.response: Emphasise the impact of collective individual actions, especially in supporting national and international actions (including legislation) that cause appropriate change.

nodes.misconception: The names of the blood vessels and their functions and adaptations are often confused. Students often forget or misunderstand red blood cell adaptations too.
nodes.response: Both these areas are covered in detail, with clear step-by-step information given and tasks to check learning and reinforce understanding.

nodes.misconception: Learners may struggle to make sense of atlas maps which often show a lot of complex information.
nodes.response: Spend additional time exploring a digital atlas map as a class or group to reinforce learners’ understanding of different map conventions.

nodes.misconception: The capital city is always the country's largest city.
nodes.response: Use examples to explain that capital cities are chosen for various reasons.

nodes.misconception: Sound waves somehow “are” the sounds you hear.
nodes.response: The sensation of hearing sound (what you hear) is a different thing to what a sound wave is (longitudinal oscillations of particles).

nodes.misconception: Describing and identifying independent, dependent and control variables and following a method with care and accuracy are skills that take time to build and need frequent revisiting.
nodes.response: The variables in the practical and the method are outlined and discussed. Considerations on the ethicality of the experiment due to human subjects, and the presence of anomalous data, are also covered in detail.

nodes.misconception: Male reproductive systems are bigger and more complex than females, that they are totally separate systems.
nodes.response: Show female and male systems next to each other and how they work together as a unit to produce offspring.

nodes.misconception: Islam has a belief in original sin, that humans are born with the stain of a tendency to sin due to the actions of Adam and Eve.
nodes.response: Each person is blamed for their own sins, not for the sins of any other person, past or present.

nodes.misconception: That all Muslims believe all actions are predestined.
nodes.response: Whilst most Muslims believe that some events and actions are predestined, there is a diversity of opinion on this within Islam.

nodes.misconception: Rights are more important than responsibilities
nodes.response: Most people believe that true justice involves both: rights must be protected, but everyone has a duty to care for others.

nodes.misconception: That Jesus condemned same sex relationships.
nodes.response: Jesus is not recorded in the Bible speaking in favour or against same sex relationships.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans as we know them have always looked the same as they do now.
nodes.response: Use the images of skulls in the slide deck to clearly show how humans’ appearance has changed over many thousands of years.

nodes.misconception: Landmarks are only new, futuristic buildings.
nodes.response: Historical architecture and buildings linked to past cultures and places are also landmarks. These buildings represent places and evoke memories and feelings just as much as modern and futuristic buildings.

nodes.misconception: The word humanism means that humanists are only interested in other humans.
nodes.response: Humanism is a worldview that see humans as part of the natural world. Humanists are concerned with all life on earth.

nodes.misconception: Humanists are only found in Europe and North America.
nodes.response: There are humanists all over the world, across all continents.

nodes.misconception: Using empathy when making ethical decisions means that all humanists will reach the same conclusions.
nodes.response: Humanists may reach different moral decisions as they feel empathy differently.

nodes.misconception: It isn't possible to live a meaningful life without religion.
nodes.response: Humanism is a non religious worldview, in which people can live a meangful life without religion.

nodes.misconception: Ceremonies are only marked by people who believe in god.
nodes.response: Humanists do not belive in god, but have ceremonies to mark meaningful events in life.

nodes.misconception: Humanists don't believe in anything.
nodes.response: Humanists do have beliefs! They believe in people, kindness, fairness, and making good choices. But they believe without faith in a god.

nodes.misconception: Only religious people reflect and meditate.
nodes.response: Many people value time to reflect and meditate whether they are religious or not.

nodes.misconception: Humanists make decisions based on what suits them personally.
nodes.response: Humanists use empathy to make a decision that helps as many people as possible.

nodes.misconception: Humanists don’t think about about how the world began.
nodes.response: Humanists use ideas from science to ask and answer questions about how the world began.

nodes.misconception: Everyone has a faith ceremony.
nodes.response: Some people have a humanist naming ceremony.

nodes.misconception: Children may not realise that humans are animals.
nodes.response: Clear explanation that humans are a type of animal.

nodes.misconception: Mátyás Rákosi was the leader of Hungary at the start of the Hungarian Uprising.
nodes.response: Rákosi was forced to quit as leader in July 1956 when he lost the support of the USSR but widespread anger amongst ordinary Hungarians remained. Khrushchev installed Imre Nagy as leader on 26th October 1956 in an attempt to end protests.

nodes.misconception: Hurdles is daunting for many pupils who may fear hitting the hurdle, falling or getting hurt, which are justifiable concerns. This causes them to do things such as stutter their approach or even stop.
nodes.response: Be careful to provide hurdles which are achievable for all abilities and gradually allow pupils to build confidence and progress to higher hurdles when ready, rather than expect them to hurdle the full height.

nodes.misconception: Underestimating the amount of water the body needs throughout the day (not just during exercise) to maintain hydration.
nodes.response: The general recommendation is 2 litres of water per day, however when training, more should be consumed.

nodes.misconception: The main consequences of dehydration are headaches and dizziness.
nodes.response: Headaches and dizziness are likely effects of dehydration, however the GCSE specification expects students to be able to understand the physiological reasons behind these such as slow blood flow, increased heart rate and body temperature.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the prefix hydro- in the term hydrocarbons means they contain water; also that hydrocarbons and crude oil are synonymous.
nodes.response: Use diagrams to show hydrocarbon composition and compare crude oil to pure hydrocarbons, highlighting the difference visually.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start using hyphens for all prefixes.
nodes.response: Emphasise that not all prefixes require a hyphen - some prefixes frequently use them, but others rarely do.

nodes.misconception: Mr. Utterson is an example of a respectable, Victorian gentleman.
nodes.response: The reality is more complex. Utterson seems more concerned with protecting the reputation of Jekyll than pursuing any real justice.

nodes.misconception: The word 'serious' follows the same pattern as the word 'nervous', resulting in 'nervioso' and 'serioso'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the word 'serious' is 'serio'. It does not follow the same pattern as the word 'nervioso' that translates as 'nervous'.

nodes.misconception: I can only use 'estar' to talk about location.
nodes.response: The verb 'estar' can be used to talk about location as well as temporary states or moods.

nodes.misconception: Drawing has to be a replica of what is being looked at.
nodes.response: Drawing can be detailed and replicate an object, but it can also be many other things. Artists often play with techniques and process to try out different ways of exploring drawing and this can lead to experimental and exciting discoveries.

nodes.misconception: The sounds [r] and [rr] are pronounced the same.
nodes.response: The single [r] sound is pronounced as in the words 'pero', 'abrir', 'Francia'. The double [rr] sound is pronounced as in the words 'perro', 'correr', 'correo'.

nodes.misconception: Iago is simply a villain - unkind and evil.
nodes.response: Iago's character as a villain can be looked at through different lenses. One is Machiavellian.

nodes.misconception: Ian McCormack’s experience is unique and proves the truth of Christianity.
nodes.response: McCormack’s experience is similar to those in other religions, where people report encounters with divine beings or light, showing such experiences aren’t unique to Christianity.

nodes.misconception: There has only been one ice age.
nodes.response: There have been numerous periods of warming and cooling throughout Earth's history. This has meant there have been a number of ice ages throughout history.

nodes.misconception: Ice only affects landscapes during periods of melting.
nodes.response: Ice modifies landscapes through continuous processes of erosion, transportation, and deposition, not just during periods of melting.

nodes.misconception: Modal verbs must add ge- in the imperfect tense.
nodes.response: Modal verbs are normally used in the imperfect to describe past events. The imperfect is a different tense from the perfect and is formed differently.

nodes.misconception: The phrase 'zu Hause' means 'to home' because 'zu' means 'to'.
nodes.response: 'Zu Hause' means 'at home' and 'nach Hause' is used for 'going (to) home'.

nodes.misconception: Iconic images come from across all areas of art history.
nodes.response: Iconic images mainly come from Western art history which can mean that the diversity of our world is often not reflected.

nodes.misconception: Id ul-Adha celebrates the end of Ramadan and Id ul-Fitr comes at the end of the Hajj pilgrimage.
nodes.response: Id ul-Fitr is the festival of breaking the fast (at the end of Ramadan), and Id ul-Adha is the festival of sacrifice (at the end of the Hajj pilgrimage).

nodes.misconception: That Shi'a Muslims believe Ali was a 'prophet' following Muhammad.
nodes.response: Both Sunni and Shi'a Muslims believe Muhammad was the final 'seal of the prophets' but Shi'a Muslims believe Allah chose Ali to be Muhammad's successor, and that Muhammad announced this at Ghadeer Khumm.

nodes.misconception: The most aesthetically-pleasing idea is the best.
nodes.response: Strong design choices balance creativity with inclusivity, feasibility, and impact - aesthetics alone aren’t enough.

nodes.misconception: The first idea is always the best.
nodes.response: Creativity improves with divergent thinking and iteration - the first idea is rarely the final one.

nodes.misconception: 'inglés' can only be an adjective.
nodes.response: 'inglés' can be an adjective, as in 'la comida inglesa' (English food), or a noun, as in 'el inglés' (the English person (m)). The process of making a noun in this way from an adjective or verb is called nominalisation.

nodes.misconception: Drawing a graph with the axes incorrectly orientated (independent variable on y axis instead of x).
nodes.response: Outline and model graphs shown and discussed with links made between independent and dependent variables and the axes they appear on.

nodes.misconception: May think that a sphere has a circular face because when drawn, a sphere looks like a circle.
nodes.response: Physically handle and compare spheres, cylinders and cones. Explore why a sphere cannot stand but a cylinder and a cone can.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the part and the whole, or add the whole and one part to find the missing part.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of the stem sentence ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part, to reinforce what the numbers represent.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to understand that a group of objects can represent a whole.
nodes.response: Use the correct language to emphasise the 'whole group of ..........' and explore what happens when a part is missing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that large objects or things such as England cannot be a part of a whole due to its size.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to work with parts and wholes that they can handle and experience but where parts are large, such as their school or class environment.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the connection between the common divisions of 1,000, 100, 10 and 1 and they may not see the multiplication sign representing the word of when reading the equations.
nodes.response: Allow pupils time to explore the representations of the divisions of 1,000, 100, 10 and 1 alongside each other. Encourage the equations to be read using multiplied by and also of which is more commonly used with fractions of amounts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think there is only ever one right angle in an object or shape.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to explore objects and shapes that have more than one right angle and show that these are not always rectangular e.g. some trapeziums can have more than one right angle.

nodes.misconception: Not comparing the same or corresponding sides of related shapes.
nodes.response: Label the sides of shapes clearly and refer to them with consistent language of height and width.

nodes.misconception: That regular polygons include all familiar shapes even if they don't meet the definition.
nodes.response: Reinforce the definition and apply to the regular shapes which appear in this lesson.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the terminology of factor and product and therefore be inaccurate when describing equations.
nodes.response: Take time to clearly model use of terminology and ask questions such as: 'What does the 3 represent?' 'What does the 5 represent?' 'What does the 15 represent?' Continue to explicitly use key terms such as factor and products within explanation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand why equal groups can / cannot be made.
nodes.response: This is a challenging concept for Y2 children without visual representations. Take time to explore how even numbers can be grouped in equal groups of 2, whereas odd numbers cannot be and how multiples of 5 can be grouped into equal groups of five.

nodes.misconception: Fractions and decimals less than one are positioned to the left of zero or are negative in value.
nodes.response: Using a number line 0 to 1, label different fractions and decimals and show pupils that, though small in size, they are greater than zero.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not connect square numbers to their practical applications in problem-solving.
nodes.response: Highlight key words in the question to help children identify that they can use knowledge of square numbers to find the product.

nodes.misconception: Some children may find it harder to recognise the type of triangle when they are drawn in different positions and orientations.
nodes.response: Allow time for children to manipulate the triangles so that they can see them in different orientations and build their understanding of the properties of each type of triangle.

nodes.misconception: Envionmental impact can only be assessed after a product has been manufactured.
nodes.response: Environmental impact can be assessed at every and all stages of the iterative design process.

nodes.misconception: Children might find it hard to create their own puzzles in the final part of Task B as the dotted lines can be overwhelming.
nodes.response: Model the process heavily for those who need it, where possible using a visualiser and sharing finished examples. Make good use of the template. A bigger version can be found in the additional materials.

nodes.misconception: Children might think that the parts of the whole they create in Task B have to be able to fit together to make the same shape as the whole.
nodes.response: Reinforce the concept that the whole is about quantity and not necessarily about shape. Plasticine is a good way to demonstrate this.

nodes.misconception: Some children may not be fully aware that two shapes can have the same name but be differently shapes. For example, there are several different types of triangle.
nodes.response: Maintain a real focus on 'What's the same and what's different?'. Don't shy away from any questions or misconceptions about categories of shape, use them to further any learning.

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty identifying the number of parts when dealing with cardinality and quantity. For example, dividing a class up into equal groups.
nodes.response: Use a bar model to show a number of children being divided into equal parts. The bar model will then link to the paper strips in the slides.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only attribute one hundredth to an area model being broken into one hundred equal parts.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils see one hundredth in both linear and cardinal examples too.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the parts and the whole in an equation, especially when there is a missing number.
nodes.response: Bar models are helpful for representing and understanding the parts and the whole. Ensure that pupils understand that minuend and sum both represent a whole. Allow lots of opportunities for pupils to sketch bar models.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rely on the same strategies to solve all problems and may find it hard to remember when to add to find the missing part and when to subtract.
nodes.response: Emphasise the use of bar models, especially for pupils who are struggling. This will help them identify whether a part is missing or if the whole is missing, and whether they should add the parts or subtract a part from the whole to get the answer.

nodes.misconception: Children may be unable to see how they can use learnt strategies to solve worded problems.
nodes.response: Support children to visualise and represent each problem, first using physical resources that can be manipulated, e.g. socks to make pairs, before looking to represent the mathematics. This will help them to see what they need to calculate.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may count the number of equal parts that are shaded and write the numerator and then count the number that are not shaded and write the denominator.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils count all of the equal parts to find the denominator.  The denominator is the number of equal parts that make up whole. We encourage children to find, and then describe, the denominator before the numerator.

nodes.misconception: Children may count the marks rather than the equal parts between integers thereby determining the unit that we are working with incorrectly.
nodes.response: Show that we need to count the equal parts in between the given integers, not the marks. You could model this with the same line with increasing parts.

nodes.misconception: Children will often think that the total number within a set is always the denominator as shown in the plates and cupcakes example on the slides.
nodes.response: Put a set of 12 counters (or any countable objects) onto a mini-whiteboard. Children should practise dividing the set into equal groups, drawing rings around them. Repeat, 'The set has been divided into _  equal groups so the denominator is _'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to visualise when considering 3D parts and wholes and cannot identify a given fractional part of a 3D whole, particularly when presented on a screen as a picture.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to experience fractional parts of 3D shapes in real life situations e.g. base 10 blocks or using cuboids such as small cereal variety boxes or photocopying paper boxes. Physical manipulation can support visualisation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not recognise patterns of odd and even numbers across different times tables.
nodes.response: Recap what an odd and even number is. Remind children even numbers result from multiplying by even factors and odd numbers result from odd factors.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have trouble recognising right angles or lines of symmetry when shapes have been rotated.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to check every angle using a simple right-angle measurer, which can be hand made or even cut from the corner of a piece of paper. Ask them to physically manipulate the shapes so that they can identify properties more easily.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see other shapes and collections of lines as triangles when they are not (e.g. shapes with rounded corners, three lines that do not all meet).
nodes.response: Provide pupils with shapes, and explore shapes in the environment, classifying them as 'triangles' and 'not triangles'. Ask children, 'Does this shape have three straight sides? Does it have clearly defined, sharp vertices?'

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to identify appropriate sized bars that fit the problem as well as equate to the size of the whole.
nodes.response: Find parts that fit the structure of the problem first, then ask what the whole would be. Change the size of the whole and ask pupils which rod(s) would need to change. Encourage children to reason their decisions by comparing the size of the rods.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think one tenth consists of one shaded part and ten un-shaded parts.
nodes.response: Encourage children to use the stem sentence to identify the whole and how many parts make it up each time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to find the parts and the whole in column addition.
nodes.response: Emphasise the sum as being within the 'equals' sign in column addition. Take time to write equations, bar models and column addition and make connections between these.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle when horizontal calculations do not present the minuend at the beginning of the equation (e.g. 23 = 44 - 21).
nodes.response: Discuss with pupils the minuend as the whole. It is the number being subtracted from. In a column subtraction, we always write the minuend first but it does not always appear first in horizontal calculations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the missing part(s) must be a different colour rod to those parts already used within the example.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with various examples, in particular examples where there are two or more of the same part, drawing on the repeated addition/multiplicative structure not just the additive structure.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes parts can be deceptive and look equal but are in fact unequal. For example, the rhombus that has been split into parts with lines that are equally distributed.
nodes.response: Explore this further by presenting several examples like this if needed. You could ask the children to try and think of some examples where the parts look equal but are in fact unequal. Getting the children thinking of this will boost understanding.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to recall multiplication facts related to the 5 and 10 times tables.
nodes.response: Using times table charts where needed throughout this unit will support children in recalling facts and enable them to focus on seeing the relationships, e.g. between the 5 and 10 times table. These can be used until children become more fluent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use one to one correspondence to count all rather than counting on from a group of 10 to identify a teen number.
nodes.response: Provide concrete and pictorial examples where it is more difficult to count the ones in a group of 10 e.g. a bundle of straws or box of pencils. Encourage pupils to use the phrase 'one ten and ...' to focus attention on counting on from 10

nodes.misconception: Children may rely on counting from 0 rather than seeing the five and a bit structure of the numbers 6 to 10 and may therefore not partition efficiently.
nodes.response: Use fingers to expose the 5 and a bit structure. 'Grow' a number by putting up fingers one at a time while counting, 'show it' by putting up the fingers all at once, 'throw it' as you quickly throw the number of fingers forwards.

nodes.misconception: Children may work inefficiently, e.g. they may find the digit sum of 27 to find if it is a multiple of 6, instead of first reasoning that it cannot be because it is an odd number.
nodes.response: Encourage children to consider what they know about a number first (e.g. all even numbers have even multiples) before applying other parts of rules so that they work in the most efficient way. Display models of these to enable recall of them.

nodes.misconception: Children might want to use inequality symbols between representations showing different wholes.
nodes.response: Explain that inequalities can only be used when the whole is the same. Provide them with examples they may be familiar with such as offering half of a large and small apple and identifying that these are not the same because the wholes differ.

nodes.misconception: Some people think that crime fiction is a trivial genre.
nodes.response: Crime fiction explores the dark side of human psychology and reading crime fiction where the crime is solved can help reassure us that society is a safe place and criminals are punished.

nodes.misconception: Plot twists typically reveal something hidden about a character.
nodes.response: While plot twists may reveal something hidden about a character, plot twists can be used to subvert our expectations of life and resolution.

nodes.misconception: Anti-climaxes are always disappointing for the reader.
nodes.response: While unexpected, anti-climaxes are subjective and not necessarily always disappointing.

nodes.misconception: When artists look at the same landscape, their artwork will look similar.
nodes.response: Remind children that sometimes artists will make artwork that looks similar, but this is not always the case. Artists can interpret their inspiration using their own, individual style.

nodes.misconception: A speech should be approached like any other written text.
nodes.response: Speeches should be approached in a very different way to other types of written text as they are designed to be spoken aloud. Long sentences, for example, should avoided since they are difficult for audiences to follow when heard aloud.

nodes.misconception: Historical texts only portray stereotypical representations of women.
nodes.response: Even though societal expectations and stereotypes exist, this does not mean that all people conform to these standards - even in the past!

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the difference between 'homophone' and 'homonym'.
nodes.response: Give specific examples of homophones (e.g. hair and hare) and homonyms (e.g. bark) and discuss the differences.

nodes.misconception: Many of these words are high frequency or common exception words.
nodes.response: Be explicit about the difficulties in spelling these words and give time to practise spelling these common exception words.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that all writing should begin at the beginning and move through the middle to the end.
nodes.response: Encourage them to think about how stories, especially films, often start with an exciting scene.

nodes.misconception: That pathetic fallacy can only be used to give emotion to the weather.
nodes.response: Pathetic fallacy is where human emotions are given to any non-human object or thing.

nodes.misconception: Mental health and wellbeing challenges are too personal or 'invisible' to be designed for.
nodes.response: Designers don’t solve mental health itself, but create supportive products, services, or environments that ease challenges.

nodes.misconception: We won't be able to hear what instruments are playing when they're playing at the same time.
nodes.response: We can identify the instruments playing by their unique timbre and tune our ears to recognise each sound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the concept of different shapes (and sizes, for number of objects) a little confusing.
nodes.response: Show pupils images where parts are different shapes (area fractions - parts of a whole shape) but can easily be seen to be the same size.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the formal tone of a biography challenging.
nodes.response: You may wish to provide additional time for children to read a range of biographical writing to 'tune in' to the text type.
