nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a diary is written entirely in the past tense.
nodes.response: Examples of present and future tense are referred to and modelled in the examples given. Emphasise repeatedly to pupils that a range of tenses will be used in a diary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be confident with the idea of paragraphs being composed of several linked sentences.
nodes.response: As you read, draw out the idea that all the sentences in each section are related to each other and deepen the reader's understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that non-chronological reports can be informal.
nodes.response: Identify key linguistic features, such as subject-specific vocabulary and fronted adverbials, which contribute to a formal tone. You could keep a lot of these on a classroom display or English-themed table.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse rhetorical questions and standard questions.
nodes.response: Most questions demand an answer; in a rhetorical question, the question itself contains the implied, expected answer.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that essays are an opportunity for writers to share their own opinions.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to the word 'arguments' rather than 'opinions' or 'viewpoints'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that essays are an opportunity for writers to share their own opinions.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to the word 'arguments' rather than 'opinions' or 'viewpoints'.

nodes.misconception: Explanation texts  can be written in any order.
nodes.response: Explanation texts are written in chronological order; they explain a process in the order in which it happens.

nodes.misconception: All instruments can play different notes.
nodes.response: Some instruments are unpitched. This means they do not create different high and low sounds when played.

nodes.misconception: All three poems convey a negative view of romantic relationships.
nodes.response: All three poems begin by conveying a negative view of romantic relationships. This continues throughout 'Neutral Tones' and 'When We Two Parted' however 'Winter Swans' undergoes a shift to a hopeful tone by the end as the couple are unified.

nodes.misconception: In 'Mother, any distance', the 'child' figure yearns for independence while the parent isn't ready to let them go.
nodes.response: It is possible to interpret the poem in this way but it is also possible to infer that the speaker feels nervous about the prospect of their independence, worrying whether they will succeed or "fall".

nodes.misconception: Shelley's poem presents a purely positive view of love.
nodes.response: Interspersed among his speaker's overblown philosophical descriptions focused around the beauty of natural symmetry, it's possible to read an element of frustration that the speaker's feelings of desire are unrequited.

nodes.misconception: All three poems reflect on memories of a loved one who is now dead.
nodes.response: Causley's use of an uncanny setting implies that the two parents are now in the afterlife, guiding the speaker's "[c]rossing", however Duffy and Waterhouse use language linked to death/loss ("ghost", "pulse") but do not imply the relative has died.

nodes.misconception: Singing is only useful for singers.
nodes.response: When identifying intervals, singing is incredibly useful, even for those who aren't confident singers. Hearing the intervals back through singing or humming allows us to compare them to the reference melodies. Without this, it is much harder.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that imagery appeals to just one of the senses.
nodes.response: Through interpretation, imagery in the poem may fall under more than one sense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up linguistic features with persuasive techniques.
nodes.response: Linguistic features and persuasive techniques are addressed in isolation through the two distinct learning cycles. Build in more time for checking pupils' understanding if their knowledge is still not secure at the end of each.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all questions need a full explanation to answer.
nodes.response: By working through the examples on the slide deck and completing the tasks, pupils will see that some questions can be answered with a simple yes or no. This is an important skill when using and creating identification keys for classification.

nodes.misconception: Songs with a minor tonality are always sad.
nodes.response: Tonality is one of the elements that gives a melody its character. While minor tonalites often feel dark, it is the combination of how all the elements of music are used that will make a song sound sad.

nodes.misconception: Only advanced musicians can work out a set of notes by listening to them.
nodes.response: Anyone can work out notes by ear, if they practise the correct strategies. Identifying the melodic shape, representing it with a line, then carefully converting it into notes is an effective first step in melodic dictation.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to describe what has happened to an object to create its image.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 explores how different transformations can produce the same image. This is a good way of demonstrating that there is more than one possible description.

nodes.misconception: Children may overgeneralise that parallel lines can only come in pairs or must be horizontal or vertical in orientation.
nodes.response: These misconceptions are addressed in the lesson. You may wish to use these to create additional examples and non-examples to compare and share.

nodes.misconception: The gradients of two perpendicular lines are a number and its reciprocal.
nodes.response: In order for two lines to be perpendicular, the two gradients cannot have the same sign. Therefore it is a number and its negative reciprocal.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that differences need to be large when comparing texts.
nodes.response: Encourage them to look for subtle differences.

nodes.misconception: Fossil fuels (coal, gas and natural oil) are infinite.
nodes.response: Fossil fuels are finite - if used at the current rate, they will run out and are not sustainable.

nodes.misconception: Longer note values (like minims) are impossible to verbalise, because the words sound the same as a crotchet.
nodes.response: Longer note values are tricky to verbalise. A minim uses one syllable, just like a crotchet. The key is to make sure you count how many beats they last for - that will help you tell the difference between crotchets, minims and longer notes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not fully simplify due to not identifying the highest square factor.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to check the resulting radicand for any further square factors.

nodes.misconception: All artists take inspiration from one source.
nodes.response: Artists might take inspiration from a wide range of sources including surroundings, objects, personal experiences, memories, artist's work or historical and contemporary movements.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe any words after a verb are an object.
nodes.response: An object must be a noun, noun phrase or pronoun that the verb is done to directly.

nodes.misconception: Explanation texts can be written in any order.
nodes.response: Explanation texts are written in chronological order; they explain a process in the order in which it happens.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find identifying linguistic features of the text type challenging.
nodes.response: Explicit explanations are given for key linguistic features and modelled in the example biography.

nodes.misconception: Children may just think that writing a diary is just another task they have to do, rather than a personal and creative outlet.
nodes.response: Teach the children the benefits of keeping a diary. Link this to their mental health and how this will help them to maintain positive mental health.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to identify journalistic tone.
nodes.response: Journalistic tone is explicitly identified and modelled in explanation and check slides throughout the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that non-chronological reports can be informal.
nodes.response: Identify key linguistic features, such as subject-specific vocabulary and fronted adverbials, which contribute to formal tone.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the terms peritext and paratext interchangeably.
nodes.response: It can be helpful to think of the peritext as everything on the ‘outside’ of the book, the paratext as extra information 'inside' the book.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know the difference between the different types of fronted adverbial.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that an ‘and’ formal fronted adverbial builds on a point, a ‘but’ formal fronted adverbial introduces a contrasting idea to the previous sentence and a fronted adverbial of cause tells the reader the cause and effect of something.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify opinions and reasons in a persuasive letter.
nodes.response: Look for sentences where the writer expresses their emotions and a reason for why they are feeling that way.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a recount needs to include every single detail rather than just the most important moments.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to be selective about the most important parts when recounting. This could be taught by playing a game looking at a school day and choosing the most important parts (lunch, playtime, home time) compared to the least important.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will find this lesson difficult if they do not have a secure understanding of what a syllable is.
nodes.response: Ahead of the lesson, ask pupils to show you how many syllables there are in three different words (using their hands to 'clap the syllables') so you can assess if there are any pupils who need support prior to the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that an essay is always a two-sided discussion leading to the writer's own conclusion.
nodes.response: In this unit, we will write a one-sided essay which makes the argument posed in the title; we will avoid presenting this as the writer's own opinion.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the difference between layout features and linguistic features.
nodes.response: This lesson focuses primarily on layout features to support children in understanding how to organise and structure information in an information text. Explain that the linguistic features refer to the type of language used and explore examples.

nodes.misconception: The narrator in a story always remains the same.
nodes.response: There can be more than one narrator in a story. A change in narrator can demonstrate a shift in time or offer a different perspective.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes parts can be deceptive and look equal but are in fact unequal. For example, a rhombus that has been split into parts with lines that are equally distributed.
nodes.response: Explore this further by presenting several examples like this if needed. You could ask the children to try and think of some examples where the parts look equal but are in fact unequal.

nodes.misconception: When describing an instrument’s timbre, we can say it is high or low, loud or quiet, fast or slow.
nodes.response: Timbre describes the unique sound of an instrument, not its pitch, dynamics or tempo.

nodes.misconception: Learning the gender of nouns is not important.
nodes.response: It is important to learn the gender of nouns so that you can use them accurately in sentences.

nodes.misconception: All tests for ions are interchangeable and can be used in any order without affecting the outcome.
nodes.response: Clarify that each test is specific and must be conducted in a particular order to avoid interference. For example, testing for sulfates before halides can prevent false positives caused by overlapping precipitates, ensuring accurate identification.

nodes.misconception: All tests for ions are interchangeable and can be used in any order without affecting the outcome.
nodes.response: Clarify that each test is specific and must be conducted in a particular order to avoid interference. For example, testing for sulfates before halides can prevent false positives caused by overlapping precipitates, ensuring accurate identification.

nodes.misconception: All tests for ions are interchangeable and can be used in any order without affecting the outcome.
nodes.response: Clarify that each test is specific and must be conducted in a particular order to avoid interference. For example, testing for sulfates before halides can prevent false positives caused by overlapping precipitates, ensuring accurate identification.

nodes.misconception: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
nodes.response: For the value to be in the sequence, the value for $$n$$ must be a positive integer. If it is not, then the value is not in the sequence as the term number must be a positive integer.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may conflate cyclic quadrilaterals with cases of "the angle at the centre of a circle is twice the angle at the circumference" theorem, when the angle at the centre is a reflex angle.
nodes.response: While the two diagrams may look similar at a glance, pay extra attention to whether all four points of the quadrilateral are on the circumference or if one of the points is in the centre.

nodes.misconception: Students may be more accustomed to writing informative articles. In Learning Cycle 2, they may want to explain how love has changed over time rather than give their opinion on it.
nodes.response: Students can create a more engaging article, which is more vibrant with a clear sense of voice, by including their opinion on a topic.

nodes.misconception: Nouns in German only change for the plural, like in English.
nodes.response: Adjectival nouns, weak masculine nouns and dative plural nouns all change their spelling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise the meaning associated with body language.
nodes.response: Pupils could model some key aspects (such as eye contact, open/closed postures) beforehand to better understand underlying emotions that the characters in the text exhibit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find thinking and speaking in role as the father or Beatrice challenging.
nodes.response: Drama activities, such as 'thought tapping' or 'hot seating' may be useful to provide pupils with examples of thoughts and speech.

nodes.misconception: All artists make art with the intention of sharing with an audience.
nodes.response: Some art is made as an act of pure self-expression. Even deeply personal works are shaped by history, identity, and society, meaning they can take on wider meanings even if the artist did not intend them to.

nodes.misconception: Idiomatic rhythms are rhythms that are only used in a specific style.
nodes.response: Idiomatic rhythms are rhythms that are typically associated with that style, but can also be heard in different styles. For example, while the skank rhythm is very idiomatic in reggae, there are many other styles that also repeat off-beat quavers.

nodes.misconception: Some think all lavas/magmas are the same and the type of igneous rock formed depends on cooling rate.
nodes.response: Stress that the type of igneous rock formed depends upon the mineral composition of the lava/magma *and* the rate of cooling.  Use examples to reinforce this.

nodes.misconception: The subject of a sentence can only be a noun or pronoun.
nodes.response: A verb can be used as the subject of a sentence. In French, it must be in its infinitive form. When translated to English, use the -ing form of the verb.

nodes.misconception: 'Plusieurs' and 'chaque' have singular and plural forms.
nodes.response: 'Plusieurs' is always written with an 's' and introduces a plural noun e.g. plusieurs problèmes. 'Chaque' is always written in the singular and introduces a singular noun e.g. chaque problème.

nodes.misconception: There is only one word for "it" in French.
nodes.response: Nouns are either masculine or feminine. "It", when replacing a noun, also has a masculine and feminine form. Use 'le' for masculine nouns and 'la' for femnine nouns. 'Le' and 'la' shorten to 'l'' when the next word starts with a vowel sound.

nodes.misconception: There are specific laws that are designed for online crimes.
nodes.response: In the UK, we don’t currently have one law that decides what is and is not illegal online. Instead something is illegal if it is illegal offline or is included as an offence in one of many pieces of legislation that govern the internet in the UK.

nodes.misconception: All past participles follow the regular -er verb pattern: change the -er to -é: 'j'ai commencé' ('I started').
nodes.response: Some past participles are irregular and do not follow the regular -er verb pattern: 'j'ai fait' ('I did').

nodes.misconception: Artists need to observe from reality to make art.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that art can be an observation, but it can also be taking an idea we have in our heads and making it into an artwork.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that every detail in the text needs to be literally depicted in the illustration.
nodes.response: Effective illustration often involves capturing the feeling or atmosphere of the writing rather than just visualising specific objects.

nodes.misconception: Reflexive pronouns are only used to talk about actions done to oneself.
nodes.response: Reflexive pronouns are also used with verbs to indicate a reciprocal (shared) action between two or more subjects. Verbs can only be reciprocal with plural subjects, i.e. 'nous', 'vous' and 'ils/elles'.

nodes.misconception: All verbs using reflexive pronouns are reflexive.
nodes.response: Reciprocal verbs use the reflexive pronouns 'se', 'nous' and 'vous'. They are used to express actions that two or more people perform with, or for, each other, e.g. 'nous nous écrivons souvent' - 'we often write to each other'.

nodes.misconception: The perfect tense can only be translated as what happened in French.
nodes.response: The perfect tense refers to the past in two ways: what happened and what has happened. Context tells us the intended meaning. 'Hier, je suis allé en ville' - yesterday I went to town. 'Je suis déjà allé à Paris' - I have already been to Paris.

nodes.misconception: An adjective agrees with the person who is talking, not the person being described. For example, if a boy says to a girl 'you are happy', 'happy' will be in the masculine form.
nodes.response: An adjective agrees with the person who is being described, not the person who is talking. For example, if a boy says to a girl 'you are happy', 'happy' will be in the feminine form.

nodes.misconception: The French [r] makes the exact same sound as the English 'r'.
nodes.response: The SSC [r] is pronounced very differently in French, compared to English. E.g. 'horrible'.

nodes.misconception: [n] and [ñ] make the same sound.
nodes.response: The sounds [n] and [ñ] are pronounced differently. [ñ] is pronounced as in 'español'.

nodes.misconception: Expressions such as 'I am cold' must use the verb 'être' (to be) when translated into French, as in English. The verb 'avoir' can only be translated as 'to have'.
nodes.response: Certain expressions that use 'to be' in English, such as 'I am cold', actually use the verb 'avoir' in French: J'ai froid. 'Avoir' means 'to have' but it can also be translated as 'to be' with set expressions.

nodes.misconception: If someone cannot view an image on a web page it can be ignored as text on the page will be sufficient.
nodes.response: Images are used in web pages to provide the reader with extra context. By not describing them in some way the reader might not understand the information in the same way than if it was viewed.

nodes.misconception: Stereotypes are always negative and untrue.
nodes.response: Stereotypes usually contain an element of truth in them, and can also be positive.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that art is only about copying what you see, not what you feel or imagine.
nodes.response: Art can involve expressive mark-making, imaginative thinking and communicating mood or ideas.

nodes.misconception: Set designers work only in theatre and film.
nodes.response: Set design is used in many different contexts, including theatre, film, fashion, art and music.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate interesting vocabulary to explain the expressions and movements.
nodes.response: The purpose of Learning Cycle 1 is to provide the children with vocabulary. Narrate how the children are feeling in their freeze-frames and get them to repeat. For example, you may say 'You look panicked.' and the children repeat 'We are panicked.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate vocabulary to explain the expressions and movements.
nodes.response: The purpose of learning cycle 1 is to provide the children with vocabulary. Narrate how the children are feeling in their freeze-frames and get them to repeat. For example, you may say 'You look horrified.' and the children repeat 'We are horrified'.

nodes.misconception: We should not eat fat.
nodes.response: Fat makes up an important part of our diet. We use it as a store of energy and to make cell membranes.

nodes.misconception: Malnutrition is all about being too thin.
nodes.response: Clear statement included to dispel this myth.

nodes.misconception: Mixing up immediate, short-term and long-term effects of exercise.
nodes.response: Immediate effects are what happens as soon as we start exercising to cope with it, whereas short-term effects are those that happen over the next 36 hours. Long-term refers to the adaptations that happen in response to training.

nodes.misconception: Antibodies remain in the blood for years, which makes a person immune to a disease.
nodes.response: Antibodies don't stay in the body longer term, the memory cells do and they provide long lasting immunity against a pathogen.

nodes.misconception: Christians believe life on earth is unimportant because the afterlife is what truly matters.
nodes.response: While Christians believe in an afterlife, they still see life on earth as valuable. It is God-given and is an opportunity to do good (Matthew 25:40). Their actions in this life have eternal consequences.

nodes.misconception: Melting icebergs and sea ice cause sea levels to rise.
nodes.response: A detailed explanation of the anomalous properties of ice is not appropirate for most pupils at this stage. Instead, draw attention to water taking up exactly the same space as the part of a floating iceberg that is underwater.

nodes.misconception: England has almost never been conquered.
nodes.response: England was conquered repeatedly before and during the medieval period, and was even arguably conquered as late as 1688.

nodes.misconception: All migration in this period was voluntary and driven by individual choices.
nodes.response: Not all migrations were voluntary at this time. For instance, indentured labour schemes often coerced individuals into migration under harsh conditions. Additionally, Jewish migration was frequently driven by persecution.

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that European settlement completely destroyed indigenous communities.
nodes.response: Native Americans were devastated overall by European colonisation but indigenous communities persisted and were never completely overwhelmed.

nodes.misconception: Europeans conquered the Americas easily because they had better weapons and technology.
nodes.response: European diseases killed and weakened many Native Americans, undermining indigenous resistance to European conquest.

nodes.misconception: A war that ended 50 years ago does not affect anybody any more.
nodes.response: Much of the Vietnamese landscape and people are still impacted or recovering from the effects of the war even today.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse greenfield and greenbelt.
nodes.response: Greenfield refers to land which has never been built. Greenbelt is protected land around major cities in England and is a policy designed to prevent urban sprawl.

nodes.misconception: Impact statements only consider the design specifications.
nodes.response: Impact statements consider the outcome and the impact the product has had on the user.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that species can choose or plan to evolve new adaptations to help them to survive climate change.
nodes.response: Part 2 of the lesson explores the idea that evolution occurs at random and may be too slow to save many species from climate change.

nodes.misconception: Climate change simply means hotter, drier summers in the UK.
nodes.response: Warmer temperatures in summer and fewer cold spells in winter are due to climate change. There is also some evidence that the UK is also experiencing more heavy rain events.

nodes.misconception: Tsunamis and landslides are primary impacts of earthquakes because they can cause massive damage to people and property.
nodes.response: Tsunamis and landslides are secondary impacts of earthquakes because they happen as an indirect result of an earthquake. For e.g, ground shaking destabilises slopes, making a landslide more likely, especially if there is then also heavy rain.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that a small increase in greenhouse gases and a small rise in Earth's temperature will not have much impact on organisms on Earth beyond land ice melting.
nodes.response: The lesson discusses how small changes in weather patterns can have a significant impact on organisms as their habitats change and no longer provide them with food, shelter and a place to reproduce.

nodes.misconception: Only manufacturing industries harm the environment.
nodes.response: All sectors of industry have the potential to harm the environment, though manufacturing continues to be highly wasteful.

nodes.misconception: Immigrants, asylum seekers and refugees are all the same thing.
nodes.response: The three terms are often confused and misused. All asylum seekers are immigrants but not all immigrants are asylum seekers. Some people seeking asylum may be granted refugee status while others may not.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that as the focus of the lesson is about migration, that inflows and outflows are responsible for all population change.
nodes.response: Migration is important to understand when addressing population change but changes to birth and death rates must also be considered alongside for complete understanding.

nodes.misconception: Migration is a problem for the UK as we are already 'full'.
nodes.response: Without migrants, the UK's population would be shrinking and many important jobs would not be done. Migrants contribute to the UK's culture.

nodes.misconception: Greenhouse gases are only emitted in the life of a vehicle when it is moving.
nodes.response: Discuss greenhouse gas emissions caused by the extraction of resources, production of materials, manufacturing of parts and the vehicle itself, as well as the recycling and disposal of the vehicle at the end of its life.

nodes.misconception: Impacts of volcanic eruptions are always more severe in developing and emerging countries than in developed countries.
nodes.response: A lot depends on the eruption type and factors such as population density. Economic impacts are often highest in developed countries because of the higher value of the property impacted by the eruption.

nodes.misconception: The rise of Germany and the USA and the growth of nationalist movements in the late 19th century contributed to imperial decline.
nodes.response: The British Empire responded to this rise in anxiety by showcasing their supremacy at Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee.

nodes.misconception: The trend of British imperial decline was caused by foreign policy and external threats.
nodes.response: There is a link between foreign and domestic policy, both of which contributed to imperial decline.

nodes.misconception: Boolean logic is only used in logic circuits and logic gates.
nodes.response: The three fundamental Boolean operators are AND, OR and NOT. These are used in programs to perform selection and control program flow. In Python, these are written in words as: and, or, not.

nodes.misconception: All video can be improved using editing tools.
nodes.response: Some video can’t be improved using the editing tools or the process will take too long, in this case it might be better to reshoot the video altogether.

nodes.misconception: the difference between exports and imports.
nodes.response: Exports are selling good and services to another country and imports are bringing good and services into a country from another one.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not recognise the heart as a muscle because we cannot consciously move it in the same way we can other muscles in the body.
nodes.response: The body has voluntary and involuntary muscles. The heart is an involuntary muscle that doesn't require conscious thought to make it contract and send blood around the body. Exercising regularly can improve the strength and endurance of our heart.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that for an effective stretch, you should push or reach until it is painful.
nodes.response: Stretching should never be painful. You might feel tension which can be described as resistance, a pull or tightening and this indicates that the muscle should not be stretched any further. Tension might ease with some deep breathing.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that humans only need strong muscles if they want to excel in sports such as weight lifting and climbing.
nodes.response: Strong muscles are essential for humans to complete everyday tasks including breathing, blinking, sitting, lifting, chewing etc. Strong muscles also help our joints to work effectively which helps to avoid injury and pain.

nodes.misconception: Always use 'können' to translate 'can' into German.
nodes.response: 'Can' is often used with two different meanings in English - ability or permission. Use 'können' to express ability (e.g., 'Kannst du schwimmen?') and 'dürfen' to express permission (e.g., 'Darfst du schwimmen?').

nodes.misconception: The infinitive follows the conjugated verb, as in the English 'I can play'.
nodes.response: In German, the infinitive is placed at the end of a sentence when used with a modal verb, as in 'Ich kann spielen.'.

nodes.misconception: Building infrastructure projects will create long term employment opportunities.
nodes.response: In most cases the jobs created by building infrastructure projects are likely to be short term and highly specialist. This means they are unlikely to last the length of the build time.

nodes.misconception: The government fully implemented Edwin Chadwick's recommendations.
nodes.response: Chadwick's recommendations were included in the 1848 Public Health Act but were not compulsory, so many local authorities ignored them.

nodes.misconception: I put the "change score by" block in my code, but the score isn't changing when I expect it to.
nodes.response: The location of your "change score by" block dramatically affects when and how often the score changes.

nodes.misconception: More data is always better as it means the model can be better informed to make a prediction.
nodes.response: Poorly labelled or inconsistent data can make a model's predictions inaccurate. It is better to use a smaller amount of higher quality data to make more accurate predictions.

nodes.misconception: A macro can only be used to clear data in a spreadsheet.
nodes.response: A macro is used to record and repeat tasks that can be automated in a spreadsheet. They are not just used to clear or reset data.

nodes.misconception: That proofreading is a waste of time.
nodes.response: Proofreading helps you to spot errors that might hinder the readers' understanding of your work.

nodes.misconception: I've finished my game — there's nothing else to do.
nodes.response: A part of being a good programmer is knowing how to evaluate and improve your projects. Think about how your game could be even better.

nodes.misconception: May believe that if you have small, weak muscles you can’t make them bigger and stronger.
nodes.response: Show the children that through using certain exercises most people can make their muscles stronger.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to improve something.
nodes.response: Improvements can be in any shape or form. If we think about our school grounds it could be to paint some areas, add extra climbing frames/ slides or plant more flowers etc. Everyone's ideas about improvements are different and unique.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a tangent to a curve at a given point cannot intersect the curve at another point.
nodes.response: Define the tangent at a point as the line which has the same gradient as the curve at that point. If the graph is cubic then it is possible for the tangent at a point to intersect the graph again. There are examples in the lesson that show this.

nodes.misconception: Students think that once they have put their pen down and stopped writing, that they have finished.
nodes.response: Students should think of their first attempt as simply a first draft. The second redraft is their chance to fine tune their argument.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that Lee's account is true of all North Koreans.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the fact the book is a memoir. It is personal and about what she recalls and what she felt. The context helps us appreciate her own experience.

nodes.misconception: Students think that using lots of the pronoun 'you' is an effective use of direct address. They tend to do this a lot in rhetorical questions.
nodes.response: Using 'you' too many times can create an accusatory tone that can actually make the reader defensive. Sometimes, it can be better to approach direct address more subtly, by speaking to an imagined reader or addressing the readers collectively.

nodes.misconception: All music is worked out beforehand and can’t be made up on the spot.
nodes.response: Improvisation is the spontaneous creation of musical melodies and rhythms during a live performance.  These musical ideas are made up on the spot and not written down so it is very hard to exactly recreate them a second time.

nodes.misconception: A live performance will always be exactly the same.
nodes.response: Live performances, especially of an improvisation will alter very slightly between each concert.

nodes.misconception: Improvising is music created solely on the spot.
nodes.response: Musicians might not know exactly what they are going to do, but they are building on and working from a bank of known ideas and motifs that they can draw upon, use and adapt.

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is music completely made up on the spot.
nodes.response: Improvised music is not completely made up on the spot. Preparation and the practising of musical ideas is important.  It is more a form of spontaneous reconstruction of musical ideas built upon knowledge and practice.

nodes.misconception: There are 'rights' or 'wrongs' in improvisation.
nodes.response: While there are rules that help us improvise effectively, a big part of learning to improvise is experimenting and seeing what works and what doesn't. Be willing to make 'mistakes' and don't fixate on doing it perfectly first time.

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is complicated and scary!
nodes.response: Improvisation can be as simple as changing one note. Try to play what you might already be able to hear in your head. Are you planning your improvisations well?

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is complicated and hard to do.
nodes.response: Using fewer notes and focusing on creating short improvisations can be very effective and help us to introduce the idea of conveying emotion through our music.

nodes.misconception: Beatboxing artists use only rhythmic patterns in their music.
nodes.response: Beatboxing is not always just about drum machine mimicry. Artists like Jason Singh, combine other sounds in his recordings.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that improvising a scene means taking a long time rehearsing it before a performance - like a normal play.
nodes.response: A cast of actors do not usually rehearse an improvised scene. They might spend only 30-60 seconds organising themselves on the stage and telling each other a very brief idea about how they are going to act.

nodes.misconception: The grammatical gender of feminine nouns changes to masculine in the dative case.
nodes.response: Feminine nouns are always feminine, no matter what case their article may change to.

nodes.misconception: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
nodes.response: The unit is said before the ten in German, e.g., 'neunundvierzig' = '9 and 40' = 49. It is helpful to write from right to left when taking down numbers so that you produce them in the correct order.

nodes.misconception: In German, ‘Uhr’ means ‘hour’.
nodes.response: ‘Die Uhr’ looks and sounds a bit like ‘hour’ but it means ‘clock’ and ‘um … Uhr’ means ‘at … o’clock’. 'Die Stunde' means ‘hour’.

nodes.misconception: All past participles have the pattern 'ge-' + stem + '-t', e.g., 'gemacht'.
nodes.response: While most weak verbs form past participles like this, most strong verbs have the pattern ge- + stem + -en, e.g., 'gelesen', some with vowel changes, e.g., 'gesungen'. Verbs beginning with be-, er- or ver- don’t add ge-, e.g., 'erlebt', 'verbracht'.

nodes.misconception: [er] in French sounds the same as in English; as in the word 'colder', for example.
nodes.response: [é] and [er] have the same sound in French.

nodes.misconception: [é] and [er] make the same sound as [e].
nodes.response: [é] and [er] make the same sound, which is different from [e].

nodes.misconception: When there are two verbs together, e.g. 'I must go', we need to conjugate both.
nodes.response: English confuses us here. We say 'I must go' rather than 'I must to go' as English uses an infinitive but without 'to'. In Spanish, after modal verbs 'deber', 'poder' and 'querer' the 2nd verb must always be an infinitive; 'I must go' is 'Debo ir'.

nodes.misconception: All present tense forms of the model verb 'poder' have the same vowel change in the stem, o-> ue.
nodes.response: The 1st, 2nd, 3rd persons singular ('puedo', 'puedes', 'puede') and 3rd person plural ('pueden') forms all have a stem change from 'o' to 'ue' but 1st person plural 'we' form is 'podemos'; it keeps the same vowel as the infinitive 'poder'.

nodes.misconception: Spanish infinitives, like English, have two words: 'to + verb' like the infinitive 'to eat'.
nodes.response: In English, infinites are often written as 'to + verb' whereas in Spanish infinitives often end in -ar.

nodes.misconception: Spanish verbs always need pronouns, like in English, to convey the person doing the action.
nodes.response: Spanish verbs don't always need pronouns. The verb endings indicates the person doing the action.

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [eau], [au] and [o] are spelt differently therefore they make different sounds.
nodes.response: The SSCs [eau], [au] and [o] are spelt differently however they make the exact same sound.

nodes.misconception: You have to swap words around to make yes/no questions in Spanish.
nodes.response: 'You are' does not swap around to 'Are you ...?' in Spanish because 'you are' is one word, 'estás'. Spanish yes/no questions can be made simply by raising the tone of voice at the end of any statement.

nodes.misconception: Changing intonation doesn't affect meaning.
nodes.response: If you raise your voice at the end, you can turn a statement into a question.

nodes.misconception: Many English superlatives use 'most', so you need to use 'meist' in German.
nodes.response: German superlatives use 'am -sten'. 'Most interesting' ist 'am interessantesten', and 'most difficult' is 'am schwierigsten'. No additional German word is required for 'most'.

nodes.misconception: It is important to say as much as possible when carrying out any speaking task.
nodes.response: When completing a role-play exam task, it is important to use at least one verb for each prompt. However, this is not the time to show off extended and developed sentences; it's more important to get the message across accurately and succinctly.

nodes.misconception: Adverbs have the same word order in French as they do in English in two-verb sentences.
nodes.response: Adverbs that tell us 'how' and 'how often' come before the infinitive e.g. 'Elle peut souvent visiter les musées'. 'Tu ne peux pas encore visiter Alger.'

nodes.misconception: MPs don’t vote digitally at all, it is all done on paper or by hand.
nodes.response: It is true that MPs vote in person, but since 2020 they have used electronic systems in the division lobbies to record their votes by scanning a pass.

nodes.misconception: Because 'muchos' and 'muchas' are plural, you don't need to pluralise the noun that follows them.
nodes.response: The agreement of 'muchos' and 'muchas' must be in both gender and number so the nouns must be pluralised too, e.g. 'muchas playas', 'muchos pueblos'.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to translate the Spanish present tense into English.
nodes.response: There are two ways of translating the Spanish present tense into English: the present simple (habit - 'I go') or the present continuous (ongoing action - 'I am going'). The context or time adverbs can help to tell us which one to choose in English.

nodes.misconception: Spanish always uses subject pronouns with verbs, like English.
nodes.response: Spanish rarely uses subject pronouns; they are used for contrast or emphasis only. The ending of the verb in Spanish tells you who the subject is.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way of saying 'they' in French.
nodes.response: There are in fact two ways of saying 'they' in French, depending on whether it is referring to a feminine (elles) or a masculine (ils) noun.

nodes.misconception: All adjectives are postnominal in French; they come after the noun.
nodes.response: Most adjectives in French come after the noun but there are a group of prenominal adjectives. We use BRAGS to remember that adjectives of Beauty, Rank, Age, Goodness and Size come before the noun like adjectives in English.

nodes.misconception: We need to use pronouns when talking about she, he, it or we.
nodes.response: We usually don't need pronouns because the verb ending indicates whether it is 'she, he, it' or 'we' doing the action.

nodes.misconception: 'In' is always translated as 'en' in Spanish.
nodes.response: When 'in' is followed by the time of day, it translates as 'por' in Spanish.

nodes.misconception: I can use 'an' and 'auf' interchangeably to mean 'on' or 'onto'.
nodes.response: We use 'an' to mean 'on' or 'onto' when the position is vertical, e.g., 'on the wall' - 'an der Wand'. We use 'auf' to mean 'on' or 'onto' when the position is horizontal, e.g., 'on the table' - 'auf dem Tisch'.

nodes.misconception: 'Nicht' goes before the verb like 'not' in English.
nodes.response: In German, 'nicht' usually goes before the element it negates — unless it's negating the whole sentence, in which case it tends to go at the end, e.g., 'Ich kaufe das Auto nicht' - 'I'm not buying the car'.

nodes.misconception: Context should be included in one sentence at the end of each analytical paragraph.
nodes.response: You can include contextual ideas where relevant - this could be at the start, middle or multiple times in a paragraph. Contextual ideas will often help you develop your analysis of a particular quotation or character.

nodes.misconception: Inclusive design only applies to disability or accessibility-related products.
nodes.response: Inclusive design applies to everyone. It’s about designing for human diversity - age, ability, background, culture, and mental wellbeing - across all industries.

nodes.misconception: The problem of evil only causes people to doubt God's existence.
nodes.response: The problem of evil also causes some people to doubt God's nature, rather than God's existence. The inconsistent triad challenges the belief that God is omnibenevolent and omnipotent.

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3. This error continues when increasing amounts e.g increase 40 by 3% has a multiplier of 1.3
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to covert a percentage into a decimal we divide by 100. This applies with increase too e.g 120% has a multiplier of 1.2

nodes.misconception: All of these poems present relationships which are dysfunctional in some way.
nodes.response: Although 'Porphyria's Lover' and 'The Farmer's Bride' appear to show abusive, controlling relationships, the relationship in 'Singh Song!' is presented as a much more conventionally loving one.

nodes.misconception: Pupils only focus on winning and become disappointed if they don't win.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to be motivated to try and win, but to understand that performing to the best of their ability and enjoying themselves is what they need to aim for.

nodes.misconception: Indoor caving is just about squeezing through tight spaces as quickly as possible.
nodes.response: Caving isn't just about speed. It involves planning, moving carefully, using spatial awareness and thinking ahead to create and navigate a route that is both enjoyable and challenging.

nodes.misconception: Students often assume that the production of sulfuric acid in the Contact Process is a one-step process (similar to the Haber process).
nodes.response: Clarify that the Contact Process involves multiple stages, each requiring specific conditions. Emphasise the importance of these conditions in maximising yield and minimising energy consumption.

nodes.misconception: Students find it difficult to understand why continuous removal of ammonia is required to increase yield.
nodes.response: Highlight that the Haber Process is a dynamic equilibrium. If ammonia is not continuously removed, the equilibrium will shift back towards the reactants, reducing the yield.

nodes.misconception: The SPD had genuine power after becoming the largest party in the Reichstag.
nodes.response: The Reichstag could debate and vote on budgets, but the Kaiser chose the chancellor, controlled the military and could close the Reichstag at will. Foreign and military policy stayed entirely in his hands, so real political power never shifted.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can make sweeping statements about people that live in places.
nodes.response: It is important that data is used as an average and not the characteristics of every individual. The word stereotype is useful to use in this instance.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly interpreting the inequality diagram.
nodes.response: A filled in circle means the value is valid. An empty circle means the inequality is strict.

nodes.misconception: Most people who have to flee their home due to war will travel a long distance away from their country.
nodes.response: Although some refugees will travel a long distance, most people who have to leave quickly for their own safety will travel to a neighbouring country.

nodes.misconception: Incorrect use of the error interval i.e $$a ≤ x ≤ b$$ or writing the error interval as $$a ≤ x > b$$
nodes.response: As a check, encourage students to round the upper limit interval by the degree of accuracy to see if it evaluates to the rounded number.  Also,  draw a number line to show the meaning of  $$a ≤ x > b$$ and allow students to see the error.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think an inference is just a guess.
nodes.response: Inferences are built on evidence, but they also make use of empathy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make generalisations based on the gender of the parents.
nodes.response: Explain that it can be harmful to make assumptions based on gendered stereotypes. Family structures are different and unique. Explain that both mothers and fathers can perform a variety of actions.

nodes.misconception: Posture doesn't matter in Hip hop dance.
nodes.response: Posture immediately communicates clues about a dance style, whether it is forceful and energetic like Hip Hop or light and graceful like Ballet. It enables the audience to know what to expect.

nodes.misconception: Like other question words in French, 'quel' does not change based on the gender of the noun.
nodes.response: Unlike other question words in French, 'quel' does change based on the gender of the noun, it becomes 'quelle' in the feminine form.

nodes.misconception: IT is only used by teachers in schools.
nodes.response: IT is used by everyone in schools, including students (e.g. on tablets or computers) and other staff (e.g. librarians using scanners).

nodes.misconception: IT can only be found indoors.
nodes.response: IT is found in many outdoor settings too, like traffic lights and security cameras. IT is used not just by humans sitting at desks.

nodes.misconception: The term 'cooking' only means to add heat to food, such as baking, boiling and grilling.
nodes.response: The term 'cooking' includes: (1) the preparation of food, e.g. peel, slice and and mix; (2) heating food, e.g. baking, boiling and grilling. It is a term used to describe the entire process.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that environmental variation, such as scars, piercings or muscle size and tone, can be passed on to offspring in the same way that inherited characteristics can.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the lesson to make clear the difference between characteristics that we are born with and those that are acquired, and how only those we are born with can be passed on to offspring.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about collaboration is that everyone has to agree on every detail or work in the same style for it to succeed.
nodes.response: In reality, differing approaches and opinions can make the final artwork more dynamic and original.

nodes.misconception: The USSR did not believe that the USA would be bothered by nuclear missiles in Cuba.
nodes.response: The Soviets were aware that missile deployments to Cuba could trigger a crisis but believed they could help resolve the balance of power and deter any American attacks on Cuba.

nodes.misconception: As long as a product is planned, it does not matter which type of planning document is used.
nodes.response: It is important to use the correct planning document to ensure the planning stage is useful for the creating stage.

nodes.misconception: Every risk can be planned for.
nodes.response: There may be some risks that cannot be planned for, so we must be able to dynamically risk assess on an ongoing basis (e.g. the piece of equipment you were planning to use breaks and becomes unfit for purpose).

nodes.misconception: Pupils think interval training is completed to increase speed and power only.
nodes.response: The rest intervals are really good to enhance stamina and cardiovascular endurance. The intense workout does develop power especially in the lower body muscles which supports injury prevention when running.

nodes.misconception: Injury prevention means injuries will not occur.
nodes.response: Nothing can guarantee that injuries will not happen, however the measures discussed in this lesson will significantly reduce the risk of injury. With the best prevention measures in place, accidents may still happen.

nodes.misconception: Innovation has to be revolutionary and entirely original.
nodes.response: Innovation can be revolutinary like the 'cats eye' or evolutionary where ideas change gradually and evolve over time.

nodes.misconception: Three design ideas are enough to avoid design fixation.
nodes.response: There are many ways to generate design ideas that avoid design fixation and produce a range of successful ideas that pupils can develop on their iterative journey.

nodes.misconception: Sensors on a micro:bit work automatically.
nodes.response: Micro:bits need a program to control the sensors.

nodes.misconception: Input and output of a program happen automatically, without the need for coding. The computer uses it in the correct part of your program.
nodes.response: Computers process instructions in code that requires input and output. The programmer needs to specify exactly where and how it should be handled.

nodes.misconception: Systems only use one input.
nodes.response: Systems often have multiple inputs. These can be switches and sensors.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the insect is dead inside the pupa, or that the pupa is not a living thing.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that the insect is alive and changing inside the pupa, even if the pupa itself doesn't move.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all parts of the plate will print.
nodes.response: Show and remind pupils that only the raised parts of the plate will print, and the carved parts will stay blank.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Chine collé is just gluing paper onto a print after it is finished.
nodes.response: Explain that the thin paper is applied before printing, so it bonds as part of the printmaking process.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that monoprinting means making multiple copies of the same image.
nodes.response: Through discussion and observation, remind pupils that each print is slightly different because of the way ink is applied and removed.

nodes.misconception: There is not enough food in the world, and that bees are the only pollinators.
nodes.response: Emphasise that food distribution and nutrition is an issue in food security; also that there are many types of pollinator.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all small creatures, or ‘minibeasts’, are insects.
nodes.response: Explain that an animal is only an insect if it has the characteristics of insects. Use lots of examples and non-examples to make this clear.

nodes.misconception: An insertion sort is slower than other sorting algorithms.
nodes.response: While other algorithms offer better time complexity for large, unsorted arrays, insertion sort can still be faster in practice for smaller and partially sorted lists.

nodes.misconception: "Inside" and "outside" in design always refers to physical spaces, like buildings or rooms.
nodes.response: In photography, "inside" and "outside" can mean more than places - they can show how someone feels on the inside, how people hide emotions, or the contrast between personal and public life.

nodes.misconception: Earthquakes and volcanoes happen on tectonic plates.
nodes.response: Tectonic plates cover the whole world, this would mean they happen everywhere. The majority of earthquakes and volcanoes occur at plate boundaries (where two plates meet), though there are some which happen away from boundaries.

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to classify rocks by colour, shape or size - not useful for distinguishing rock types.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on the texture of a rock (the grains and how they are arranged) to classify them and consider uses of those rocks.

nodes.misconception: Sikhs are not allowed to use music in their worship.
nodes.response: Music is an important element of Sikh worship at home and in the gurdwara.

nodes.misconception: 'Il faut' works like modal verbs, it changes for different subject pronouns.
nodes.response: 'Il faut' is only used in the 3rd person singular and it is impersonal, it is used to talk about what it is necessary for people in general to do or what they must do.

nodes.misconception: Flame colours are unique, even in mixtures.
nodes.response: Explain that strong colours, like sodium's yellow, can mask others. Use spectrometry to identify masked elements.

nodes.misconception: Flame colours are unique, even in mixtures.
nodes.response: Explain that strong colours, like sodium's yellow, can mask others. Use spectrometry to identify masked elements.

nodes.misconception: Flame colours are unique, even in mixtures.
nodes.response: Explain that strong colours, like sodium's yellow, can mask others. Use spectrometry to identify masked elements.

nodes.misconception: Synthesiser vs synthesised sound
nodes.response: You can use a synthesiser if you have one or show a youtube clip of one in action. Use keyboard and different sounds to explain synthesised

nodes.misconception: Insulation is used only to keep houses and other buildings warm.
nodes.response: Pupils will learn that insulation is designed to slow down heat exchange between buildings and the outside, keeping buildings warm in cold seasons or climates, or cool in warm seasons or climates.

nodes.misconception: Not linking the idea that glucose concentration is important for cellular respiration, even during times of rest.
nodes.response: There are a selection of slides in LC2 that specifically link glucose and respiration and discuss the idea of respiration occurring during rest.

nodes.misconception: Not linking the idea that glucose concentration is important for cellular respiration, even during times of rest.
nodes.response: There are a selection of slides in LC1 that specifically link glucose and respiration and discuss the idea of respiration occurring during rest.

nodes.misconception: Only one method of integrating the components in a control system is used.
nodes.response: Different methods of integrating components can be combined, depending on the device's function and features.

nodes.misconception: Crocodile clips have to be used to connect the components together.
nodes.response: Whilst crocodile clips can be used effectively, electrical wire from educational stockists can be used as a cheaper alternitive.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will swing the bat across their body like a baseball bat which increases the chance of missing the ball, edging it or getting out.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand that because of the way the ball is bowled in cricket, playing with a straight bat is often the most effective way to strike and not risk your wicket.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'r' is always pronounced the same in Spanish.
nodes.response: In Spanish, 'r' is pronounced differently depending on its position within a word. 'r' in the middle or at the end of a word is pronounced as in 'pero', whereas 'r' at the beginning of a word and 'rr' are pronounced as in 'perro'.

nodes.misconception: The Enlightenment was a complete rejection of Christianity.
nodes.response: While it challenged traditional religious views, most people remained Christian, and many Enlightenment thinkers still believed in God, such as those who supported deism.

nodes.misconception: Rivers only change due to natural processes.
nodes.response: While natural processes like erosion and sedimentation affect rivers, human activities such as deforestation and dam construction also significantly alter river landscapes.

nodes.misconception: It is common to think that organisms, especially humans, can survive without other organisms.
nodes.response: This lesson highlights and explores the key concept that all living organisms are dependent upon other organisms for their survival.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may solve angle problems by using methods which are less efficient than others.
nodes.response: While less efficient methods are fine, encourage pupils to review their work each time they solve a problem to consider alternative methods.

nodes.misconception: When splitting a polygon into triangles, pupils may draw line segments that cross inside the shape.
nodes.response: By choosing a single common vertex for all the triangles, the line segments will not cross inside the shape.

nodes.misconception: Rounding incorrectly for the stated context.
nodes.response: Pupils should consider the situation and ask - if rounding down, will there be enough? If rounding up, does this cover all cases? Thinking about the situation and trying different values to see what works can also help.

nodes.misconception: Only wealthy HICs give aid to other countries.
nodes.response: Newly-emerging economies such as Indonesia, China and India also give aid to other countries, especially within their regions.

nodes.misconception: The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia created the risk of war between the superpowers.
nodes.response: The USA opposed the invasion but was unwilling to become involved in a military conflict involving the USSR and so limited its oppositions to criticism rather than taking steps to protect Czechoslovakia.

nodes.misconception: Everyone knew what was agreed by countries which had made alliances before the start of the war.
nodes.response: Explain that important parts of the alliance agreements were not made public so other countries did not know about them.

nodes.misconception: The internet knows website names, not numbers.
nodes.response: Computers use IP addresses (numbers, and DNS helps match names to those numbers).

nodes.misconception: The World Wide Web is a single entity stored in one place.
nodes.response: The World Wide Web is a vast collection of interconnected websites and documents hosted on servers all over the world. Your web browser accesses these different locations to display the information you see.

nodes.misconception: Indirect object pronouns are the same as emphatic pronouns.
nodes.response: Indirect object pronouns refer to a person or thing indirectly affected by the verb and go before 'interesar'-type verbs, while emphatic pronouns are used for emphasis after prepositions.

nodes.misconception: The internet of things (IoT) is only about smart homes and appliances.
nodes.response: IoT are everyday devices that are connected to the internet and can communicate with each other. They might not collect data for the same purpose but they can collect information about how people use the devices.

nodes.misconception: Interpolation and extrapolation always produce accurate predictions.
nodes.response: Extrapolation may not be valid as this is outside the observed set of data values (e.g. a linear trend might not continue indefinitely). Interpolation may not be valid due to the limitations of the data set.

nodes.misconception: In the ‘then’ part of the story, the change in amount may be hard to identify.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the change, talking about it as a increase in amount.

nodes.misconception: The change in amount during the 'then' part of the story may be hard to identify.
nodes.response: Draw attention to explicitly to the change, talking about it as a decrease.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that line graphs are only used for continuous data, where the points between those that are plotted have meaning.
nodes.response: Show children examples of graphs where there is no meaning between divisions on the x-axis (e.g. heights of children). Here, the points cannot be joined to make a line graph.

nodes.misconception: Pupils focus on the tempo of the music, matching the beat and tempo, instead of considering the full effect of the music in creating an emotional response. (e.g., pupils run to fast music.)
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it is important to be still and listen to the music before moving. Pupils should also be reminded to consider their facial expression, ensuing this matches their movement responses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to recognise that numbers exist to the left of zero.
nodes.response: Expose pupils to images in familiar contexts showing negative numbers. Take lots of opportunities to count bridging zero.

nodes.misconception: Orthographic views are are separate drawings and do not connect.
nodes.response: Explain that each view (top, front, and side) represents a different perspective of the same object.

nodes.misconception: Negative temperatures relate to positive e.g.  −5℃ is warmer than −3℃ because 5℃ is warmer than 3℃.
nodes.response: Emphasise directional relationship e.g. numbers decrease as they move to the right. Practical examples can help e.g. freezer temperature.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make errors interpreting information from pie charts, especially with making links between angles, fractions, percentages and working out an answer to a question.
nodes.response: Display 'benchmarks' in the classroom, showing a pie chart with labelled sectors (e.g. showing that 10% is equal to one tenth or 36° of the chart; 25% is equal to one quarter or 90°).

nodes.misconception: Pupils can often confuse the x and y axis and therefore not read the correct x axis information.
nodes.response: On a bar or line graphs pupils should get into the habit of physically going along the bottom to read the information along the x axis.

nodes.misconception: All Christians believe that the Bible is a historical and factual account of history.
nodes.response: Some Christians take a literalist approach and believe that the Bible is a historical and factual account. However, some Christians regard parts of the Bible, including the creation accounts, as metaphorical. This is known as a liberal approach.

nodes.misconception: Using the highest value on the y-axis rather than the total frequency when calculating the values to read off for the lower quartile, median and upper quartile.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that the total frequency must be used.  A graph where the y-axis goes up to 100 and the total frequency is 40 can be used to highlight this.  Then repeat with the same data, but with a graph where the y-axis goes up to 200.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the gradient of the line to model simple interest is always the interest rate.
nodes.response: This works when investing £100 but not with other start values. The gradient is the amount of interest added each time which depends on the amount invested and the interest rate. There are examples to show this in the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Interpolation is always more accurate than extrapolation.
nodes.response: If a graph is plotting data collected at set points then there is no way to know what is happening between the points. The trend between the points could be a curve, a line or could fluctuate. Interpolation could therefore be inaccurate.

nodes.misconception: It should be obvious how to explore a theme and reponses will be similar.
nodes.response: Every person brings their own experiences to a theme so which aspect and how you explore it will depend on you, your background and your unique artistic voice.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can struggle to interpret information that contains several samples on one chromatogram.
nodes.response: Stress a systematic approach to interpreting chromatograms (i.e. use rulers). Live model this (using a visualiser helps enormously).

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that a distance or time value read from a distance-time graph is the speed.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the definition of speed, pointing out that it requires two pieces of information to find - both the distance and time.

nodes.misconception: All Christians believe that the Bible is a historical and factual account of history.
nodes.response: Some Christians take a literalist approach and believe that the Bible is a historical and factual account. However, some Christians regard parts of the Bible, including the creation accounts, as metaphorical. This is known as a liberal approach.

nodes.misconception: An anomaly in a data set means that an error was made in the way the data was collected.
nodes.response: Anomalies could be found in data sets for many reasons, including human error during data collection. It is more likely however that a variable that was not investigated is having an influence on that particular value, causing it to seem 'wrong'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often cannot apply the main I–V graphs to similar components.
nodes.response: Describe how the p.d. and current in components behaves to draw out similarities that can be used to describe unfamiliar components.

nodes.misconception: All Christians volunteer to do the same things.
nodes.response: Christians feel called to volunteer to help in different ways.

nodes.misconception: Two sectors on two different pie charts that have the same angle represent the same frequency.
nodes.response: 90° of a pie chart of 4 data points represents less frequency (frequency of 1) than 90° of a pie chart of 200 data points (frequency of 50).

nodes.misconception: A feasibility report outlines the key requirements of a system.
nodes.response: A feasibility report is a document used in project management that assesses whether a project can be completed successfully.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that all there is always a connection between variables in scatter graphs.
nodes.response: Emphasise examples showing no/weak connections, but explain that the tasks use data containing stronger connections for purpose of practice.

nodes.misconception: All Muslims will come to the same conclusion about a moral or social issue.
nodes.response: Different scholars will interpret sources differently meaning there is a diversity of opinion about issues such as the Eid moon sighting, and wearing of trousers and beards.

nodes.misconception: All Christians give up wealth and follow the teaching of Jesus literally.
nodes.response: Different Christians will interpret the teachings in different ways. Some may become monks or nuns and own no money. Others will campaign or support charity to follow these teachings.

nodes.misconception: The census tells us how many people follow a religion in England and Wales.
nodes.response: The census can only tell us what people ticked in the census. This may not be the reality.

nodes.misconception: Forgiveness is easy and instant.
nodes.response: Forgiveness can be hard and complex.

nodes.misconception: Christians today would not challenge people in power or laws they feel are unjust.
nodes.response: Some Christians do campaign against unjust laws and have done so throughout history.

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that the graph displayed always shows the number of solutions.
nodes.response: It is important to compare the range of values that the graph is displaying against what is being defined in the question.

nodes.misconception: Christians do not challenge society around them.
nodes.response: Christians might challenge the laws and customs of their society.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may place too much confidence in the accuracy of predictions based on extrapolating time series graphs into the future.
nodes.response: While extrapolating a time series graph provide an indication of what future results may be, predictions are not guaranteed. Context should also be considered in these cases (e.g. whether there is a natural limit to how high a variable may reach).

nodes.misconception: Not referring to the context of the question when comparing the data.
nodes.response: Highlight that just saying the median or the interquartile is bigger is of little use unless you know what the data was about.

nodes.misconception: In the future tense and other 2-verb structures, the 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence.
nodes.response: The 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence in WO1 and 2. In WO3, where the main verb goes to the end of the sentence, the 2nd (infinitive) verb is in 2nd-last place - 'Ich weiß, dass du nächste Woche nach Berlin fahren wirst.'.

nodes.misconception: German has two ways to formulate present tense questions - just like in English; e.g., 'Do you do play guitar?'; 'Are you playing guitar?'.
nodes.response: German just has one present tense; this means that the question 'Spielst du Gitarre?' means 'Do you play guitar?' and 'Are you playing guitar?'. The context and/or the temporal adverb (on Tuesdays, today) help us to use the correct translation.

nodes.misconception: If you use inversion or 'est-ce que' as a questioning device, you don't need to change your intonation.
nodes.response: Even if you are changing the word order to use inversion, or adding 'est-ce que', you still need to make your voice go up at the end of a sentence to show that you are asking a question.

nodes.misconception: Using closed questions in an interview will provide enough effective information to support further developments.
nodes.response: Using open-ended questions in an interview will allow for more detailed and flexible reponses, providing oppotunites for effective outcomes to support further developments.

nodes.misconception: You need to use the plural form of 'todo' or 'mucho' with 'gente'.
nodes.response: 'Gente' is a singular noun, so you use the 3rd person singular form of 'todo' and 'mucho' with 'gente'. Remember, these words also agree with the gender of the noun: 'toda', 'mucha'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may switch hands if the ball is hit towards their backhand side rather than using two hands on the racket to hit the ball. Pupils may place their dominant hand at the top of the racket handle.
nodes.response: Pupils should keep their dominant hand at the bottom of the racket handle for control and place their non dominant hand at the top to play a backhand shot with both hands on the grip. Explain that the hand at the bottom provides the control.

nodes.misconception: When reading the face map, pupils misidentify the equipment, especially when differentiating between quoits and cones.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the key when looking at their map, rather than just looking at the objects on the face. This will help them to identify what each object represents.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that more space always makes an activity better or more challenging.
nodes.response: In reality, too much space can make games too easy or boring because pupils don’t have to use skills like dodging, teamwork or quick thinking to avoid others.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to generate adjectives.
nodes.response: The adjectives in this lesson have been deliberately chosen. Repeat the adjectives together and emphasise them when reading.

nodes.misconception: That Ariel is a female character.
nodes.response: There is no gender assigned to Ariel.

nodes.misconception: We only warm up for a performance.
nodes.response: No, it is important to warm up whenever we are making music.  Warming up will help us to focus, it will stretch and relax our vocal muscles ready for using them and will help us to listen and work as a group of musicians.

nodes.misconception: That weather and climate are the same thing.
nodes.response: Weather changes from day to day, from place to place and from one season to another. Weather refers to the conditions at any particular place or time. Climate describes the average pattern of those weather conditions over a much longer period of time

nodes.misconception: Coal, gas and oil are the only natural resources.
nodes.response: There are many other natural resources, including water, food and precious stones.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rely upon an organism’s habitat to classify it, rather than its physical features; this can lead to misunderstandings and misclassification.
nodes.response: As you model groupings, be clear to use observable features of the objects you are grouping - focus on what you can observe as a characteristic of being human.

nodes.misconception: To create polyrhythms, all rhythms must be complicated.
nodes.response: The layered rhythms don't need to be complex, they just need to give a contrasting feel of the beat or metre. It's the layering that makes things more complicated.

nodes.misconception: All prayer looks the same.
nodes.response: There are many different ways of praying.

nodes.misconception: Since there is no common difference, further terms in the sequence cannot be generated.
nodes.response: Pupils have seen sequences where the first difference is not common and seen examples of other rules. In this lesson, the concept of a second difference is introduced and this can be used to generate the next first difference.

nodes.misconception: Rivers start at the sea and flow across the land.
nodes.response: Rivers start at their source in the mountains and flow to their mouth at the sea.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that renewable resources are 'safe'.
nodes.response: Explain that even water - a renewable natural resource - could become too polluted to use or if trees are cut down quicker than they can be replanted then that supply of wood will be exhausted.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the terms 'Commonwealth' and 'British Empire' interchangeably.
nodes.response: Provide opportunity for pupils to conduct research into the Commonwealth and the British Empire to support their understanding of the context of the text.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may encounter new or unfamiliar vocabulary in the additional material resources.
nodes.response: Pre-teaching specific terms with definitions or visuals will support less confident readers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect direct translations for Spanish text.
nodes.response: Explain that untranslated Spanish is the author and illustrators intention. Meaning can be inferred by exploring the surrounding panels for clues and context.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not fully understand the context in which the song was written.
nodes.response: It would be useful to complete/recap the unit 'Coming to England: reading' prior to starting this unit, to further contextualise the experience from a biographical perspective.

nodes.misconception: The quote on page 3 refers to violence, war and persecution. Pupils may be unsure about some/all of these terms.
nodes.response: Depending on the context of the class, appropriate definitions can be provided to better contextualise the introduction to the text.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that life for all Victorians was positive.
nodes.response: Depending on social class, life was very different. There was a big divide between rich and poor, with many people living in poverty.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to note down qualities for each of the Duleep Singhs.
nodes.response: Mind maps could be displayed for each family member with information added as pupils read.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused with the northern and southern polar regions.
nodes.response: Reiterate that Antarctica is the southern polar region, the Arctic, the northern.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may describe Nate’s mother in a negative light.
nodes.response: Discuss the portrayal of Nate’s mother as you continue reading.

nodes.misconception: The Eatwell Guide tells you exactly what foods to eat each day.
nodes.response: The Eatwell Guide shows that we should eat a wide variety of food from each food group.

nodes.misconception: Children may think the Lake District has the highest mountains and longest/deepest lakes in the UK.
nodes.response: Point out that although Scafell Pike is the tallest mountain in England, it is not as tall as Ben Nevis (tallest in the UK). Similarly, although Windermere is over 10 miles long it is not longer than many Scottish lochs.

nodes.misconception: Earth orbits the Sun and does not rotate on its axis at the same time.
