nodes.response: Earth rotates on its axis, one full rotation is 24 hours. While it rotates on its axis it orbits the Sun. This takes 365 1/4 days, or one year.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have encountered many wordless or silent texts.
nodes.response: Have a range of wordless or silent texts accessible in the class or school library.

nodes.misconception: The weather for that day is constant.
nodes.response: Weather is constantly changing. It can change between hours or even minutes.

nodes.misconception: Variables are only for numbers.
nodes.response: Variables aren't just for numbers, they can also hold letters.

nodes.misconception: Know later, when zero is added to another number, some children believe the answer is zero.
nodes.response: Secure the idea that zero shows that there is no amount in many ways. Give children zero [noun] to hold.

nodes.misconception: Computers are only used to make imaginary models that can’t be created in real life.
nodes.response: Architects who design real buildings use 3D modelling software to ensure their designs are accurate.

nodes.misconception: AI applications can think.
nodes.response: AI systems follow programmed rules or improve performance based on data, but they do not think or have emotions like humans.

nodes.misconception: Animation is a single picture.
nodes.response: Animation is a way of making pictures or objects look as if they are moving by showing a sequence of them quickly one after another.

nodes.misconception: The user interface is only about how the app looks.
nodes.response: The user interface includes both how the app looks and how users interact with it. A good user interface is both visually clear and functionally simple.

nodes.misconception: Children can think that there is only one way to respond to a poem and you can have the right or wrong understanding of it.
nodes.response: Avoid posing questions which may lead children to the idea that there is a right or wrong answer when discussing the poem.  Try to encourage open responses to the poem, celebrating each unique response from individuals.

nodes.misconception: CSS rules must always include < > like HTML tags.
nodes.response: CSS uses just the tag name, without brackets.

nodes.misconception: Design thinking is only for artists or people who are good at drawing.
nodes.response: Design thinking is for everyone - it's more about problem-solving than creating beautiful artworks. Sketches help communicate ideas, and they don’t have to be visually striking to be effective.

nodes.misconception: All narratives are fiction stories.
nodes.response: Some narratives tell the story of real life events, making them a non-fiction text. A biography is an example of this.

nodes.misconception: Enlargement only refers to an increase in size.
nodes.response: The transformation 'enlargement' refers to a change of size that can be either a stretch or a shrink.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the arrows in the food chain mean "eats".
nodes.response: Explain that the arrows in a food chain mean "is food for". Provide pupils with lots of opportunities to use this language.

nodes.misconception: Heavy objects fall faster than light objects.
nodes.response: The activity of dropping two plastic bottles (one filled and one half-filled with water) will help children see what happens.

nodes.misconception: Many children will not securely use the correct pencil grip.
nodes.response: Ensure to spend sufficient time checking children's pencil grip and intervening where they need extra support.

nodes.misconception: ASEAN is only focused on trade and does not deal with other important issues like politics or security.
nodes.response: ASEAN focuses not only on trade but also on political stability, security, and regional cooperation to maintain peace in Southeast Asia.

nodes.misconception: Only computers are considered IT.
nodes.response: IT includes items made to work with computers, such as printers and barcodes, not just standalone computers like laptops or tablets.

nodes.misconception: As logic gates are limited to two input, logic statements should also be limited in the same way.
nodes.response: Logic gates can be combined to created complex circuits that represent any number of logic statements combined.

nodes.misconception: As logic gates are limited to two input, logic statements should also be limited in the same way.
nodes.response: Logic gates can be combined to created complex circuits that represent any number of logic statements combined.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that metaphors have to be real.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that metaphors are used when you make a comparison and say something is something else when it actually isn't.

nodes.misconception: We would react the same way towards the characters and events as would the Jacobean audience.
nodes.response: Explain that societal beliefs were different in the 1600s so a Jacobean audience would likely react differently to the events and characters

nodes.misconception: Pupils sprint and then slow up and then sprint again and slow again, especially at the start of the run.
nodes.response: Explain that having a steady rhythm may not get pupils to the front initially, but their overall time will be quicker than if they sprint and stop continuously.

nodes.misconception: Physical computing is just about programming robots.
nodes.response: Physical computing is much broader than just robotics. It includes any system where a computer interacts with the physical world through sensors and actuators, for example wearable devices, environmental sensors and smart home devices.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to give a reason for their opinion.
nodes.response: Model lots of examples using 'because' to expand upon their choice. Call on confident pupils to share their reasons for their opinions and give lots of praise for using 'because' in a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Project management will not alter the outcome of a project or make it a success.
nodes.response: Project management will not guarantee success of a project, but effective project management will increase the likelihood of a project being successful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to travel too fast without having control of the ball on the racket. Pupils may want to hit the ball over the net instead of playing 'Floor tennis'.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to move slowly to develop their hand eye coordination when using a racket before increasing their speed. Explain to pupils that floor tennis will help to develop better control when using the racket before they move on to hitting.

nodes.misconception: Just because the sense has changed, it doesn't mean a reflection has occurred.
nodes.response: If an image has a different sense to its object, there has definitely been a reflection - the line of reflection may be at an obscure angle.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that a reversible reaction will always go to completion in one direction before reversing.
nodes.response: Explain that in a reversible reaction, if the conditions allow it, both the forward and backward reaction can occur at the same time.

nodes.misconception: May have confusion around classification of rock – thinking rocks in the ground and materials such as concrete, tarmac and bricks are a type of rock.
nodes.response: Help children to understand the material ‘rock’ is a natural material and not an object, and that materials like brick, tarmac and concrete are human-made and therefore not the same as natural rock material.

nodes.misconception: After an object has been rotated, the orientation stays the same if the image looks the same.
nodes.response: This is only true if the object is rotated through 360°. Otherwise, the orientation is different as each vertex is in a different position.

nodes.misconception: Many children will not securely use the correct pencil grip.
nodes.response: Ensure to spend sufficient time checking children's pencil grip and intervening where they need extra support.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all writers start writing and are successful from a young age.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that Coelho wrote poems for a long time before he became successful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to identify the differences between the original Cinderella and the one in the poem.
nodes.response: Recap the traditional Cinderella story and how Cinderella is made to do all the chores. Highlight that she needed a prince to save her whereas in the poem she takes control of her own future.

nodes.misconception: Phones produce high quality photos, so photography with cameras is redundant
nodes.response: Phone cameras are powerful, but professional cameras give more control, lens options, and depth of field, which matters for creative and technical work.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know that a fiction text can be based on real themes, events and issues.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that although the story 'Leaf' is a made up story, it is based on the real-life issue of climate change.

nodes.misconception: The poem contains some examples of antiquated / archaic language.
nodes.response: A definition sheet could be provided to support pupils in understanding what happens in each verse.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify features of traditional tales independently.
nodes.response: Use tales that are relevant to your curriculum, including tales they already know well. If pupils know stories well, they will find it easier to make links and will find it easier to spot other similar features.

nodes.misconception: Students may confuse the term transformation for translation.
nodes.response: Translation is one type of transformation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the text has autobiographical features due to its tone and form.
nodes.response: 'Walter Tull's Scrapbook' is a biography. It is a non-fiction text with factual evidence. It is presented as a fictionalised scrapbook.

nodes.misconception: A cross rhythm is when two players play in different time signatures.
nodes.response: A cross rhythm only sounds like there are different time signatures at the same time, but in reality they both use the same time signature (but sound otherwise).

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to think of a time when they were greedy with something.
nodes.response: Make sure children are clear about the definition of greedy and share different examples of things you can feel greedy for. Give children opportunities for lots of discussion before Task B.

nodes.misconception: I don't need to bother with a conclusion.
nodes.response: Who will be reading your response? Imagine them reading your final sentence, how do you want them to feel?

nodes.misconception: The general statement about the text in the introduction can be any fact you know about it.
nodes.response: The general statement, the first sentence of your introduction, should still connect to the essay question.

nodes.misconception: Introductions and conclusions aren't important.
nodes.response: An effective introduction means you can impress your reader from the outset and clearly layout your overarching argument for your essay.

nodes.misconception: When including 'the impact of the text today' in your conclusion, you just need to explain why the book is still studied today.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to 'step outside the text' and think about why themes, characters or moral messages might resonate with readers today.

nodes.misconception: Introductions and conclusion aren't important.
nodes.response: An effective introduction and conclusion means that a written response is more likely to be well considered and cohesive throughout.

nodes.misconception: French adjectives never change form.
nodes.response: French adjectives do change; this is called adjective agreement. One change is to match the gender of the person described.

nodes.misconception: Introductions are the same as thesis statements.
nodes.response: An introduction includes a thesis statement. However, an introduction should include a more general statement about the text, as well as a more general statement about the given character or theme as well as the thesis.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives remain the same when describing a boy or a girl.
nodes.response: Adjectives can change spelling based on the gender of the noun they describe. Adjectives often add an -e in the feminine form, when describing a girl or a woman.

nodes.misconception: Everyone in the group has to have the same ideas.
nodes.response: It's okay to have different ideas as good teams listen, share, and find ways to combine or choose ideas together.

nodes.misconception: That the Industrial Revolution was only about the use of steam power.
nodes.response: Many key changes in the Industrial Revolution related to developments beyond the use of steam power, such as the exploitation of water power.

nodes.misconception: The graph representing a inversely proportional relationship is of the form x + y = a and will eventually meet the axes.
nodes.response: The dimensions of the rectangle are ideal for highlighting this, particularly the latter part as a you cannot have a rectangle with a length of 0 cm.

nodes.misconception: A closed question requires 'do/does' or 'am/are/is' at the start in French, like in English.
nodes.response: Closed questions in French do not start with 'do/does' or 'am/are/is', they simply invert the subject and the verb: tu es anglaise, es-tu anglaise ?

nodes.misconception: The more arousal you have, the better you perform.
nodes.response: The inverted-U theory recognises that after an optimal level of arousal, performance will deteriorate with any further heightening of arousal levels.

nodes.misconception: All buildings look the same because they follow similar rules.
nodes.response: While buildings need to be safe and follow certain rules, architects use creativity to make them unique.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to recognise right angles presented in unusual orientations.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to continue to check angles with a right angle measurer. Teach them to recognise where vertices are clearly not right angles and differentiate these from ones that could be right angles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are not able to identify right angles and therefore struggle to identify pairs of perpendicular sides.
nodes.response: Provide children with a right angle checker. Take time to model its use, focusing on aligning one edge of the checker with a side of the angle they want to check.

nodes.misconception: Only strong emotions can be seen as facial expressions.
nodes.response: Facial expressions can sometimes be subtle or mixed, making them challenging to identify accurately.

nodes.misconception: Children may apply the names of 2D shapes to 3D shapes (such as square and cube).
nodes.response: Have examples of the confused 2D and 3D shapes (such as square and cube) for the children to handle and explore. Discuss what is the same and what is different about them.

nodes.misconception: Children may not recognise a line of symmetry when it is neither horizontal nor vertical.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities for exploring lines of symmetry practically by folding cut outs of lots of different shapes. Encourage children to view and describe these in different orientations to help them see that a line of symmetry can be in any direction.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a rectangular flag has diagonal lines of symmetry.
nodes.response: Allow children to cut out and fold the flags to help them see that a rectangle does not have any diagonal lines of symmetry.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to recognise when an angle is greater than a right angle.
nodes.response: You can model this by trying to move the obtuse angle (though pupils don't need to know the term yet) within a right angle checker. They should be able to see that it is too large to fit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may provide 'answers' to the journalist's questions rather than a full quotation that stands alone.
nodes.response: You may wish to model writing one of the quotations to show pupils that it needs to stand on its own without the questions as prompts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume any combination of words they create forms a compound word.
nodes.response: Look at some non-examples such as 'starwhere' and 'somefish' to teach them that not every combination makes a compound word.

nodes.misconception: Students often 'think' they understand a context without having fully explored it.
nodes.response: Students need to be encouraged to fully explore a context so to understand it fully before moving onto designing. This is great practice for the NEA.

nodes.misconception: Homophones sound the same, so they may rely on previous spelling rules and so, spell them the same.
nodes.response: Spend time showing each word in a sentence, use images to support understanding and make sure each homophone is practised using a strategy.

nodes.misconception: Patterns in art are always symmetrical and repetitive.
nodes.response: While many patterns do follow symmetrical or repetitive structures, patterns in art can also be organic, irregular, and asymmetrical.

nodes.misconception: When sorting 'ee' spellings, children can assume all the identified graphemes are making the 'ee' sound.
nodes.response: Stretch the 'red herring' words with an identified grapheme that makes a different sound e.g. qu-i-e-t.  The same spelling can represent a range of sounds.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it very difficult to identify when 'fer' is stressed or unstressed.
nodes.response: Model saying the words with 'fer' aloud and stressing the appropriate syllable.  Ask pupils to copy you.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with only being able to rotate anticlockwise on Desmos.
nodes.response: Turning clockwise x degrees is equivalent to turning anticlockwise (360 - x) degrees.

nodes.misconception: There may be occasions when pupils cannot find the tool they are looking for.
nodes.response: Ask them to click 'more' in the toolbar, scroll down and then click 'more' again.

nodes.misconception: Urban design is solely about constructing buildings.​
nodes.response: Urban design encompasses the planning of entire city environments, including streets, public spaces, transportation systems and the relationships between different urban elements.​

nodes.misconception: The voltage of a cell is proportional to the size of the cell. Voltage is a tangible substance rather than a measure of electrical “push”.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and CfUs will clarify that voltage is a measure of the size of the push provided by a cell or other source of electricity and that cell size is not proportional to voltage.

nodes.misconception: The voltage of a cell is proportional to the size of the cell. Voltage is a tangible substance rather than a measure of electrical “push”.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and CfUs will clarify that voltage is a measure of the size of the push provided by a cell or other source of electricity, and that cell size is not proportional to voltage.

nodes.misconception: Religions and worldviews will look the same in our local area compared to England and Wales.
nodes.response: Data may look similar or different. There may be local variations, meaning that your local data may be very similar or completely different to national data.

nodes.misconception: Iona is only visited by pilgrims to see its historical sites.
nodes.response: People make a pilgrimage to Iona for many reasons, but many come to see the modern community that has been reestablished.

nodes.misconception: Christianity spread in a similar way across Europe.
nodes.response: Celtic people developed distinctive practices and artefacts such as Celtic crosses.

nodes.misconception: The ionic bond is the transfer of electrons and not the electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions. Dot and cross diagrams show the empirical formula of the lattice and not an ionic molecule.
nodes.response: Ensure students have a good understanding of how ions are formed, the arrangement of ions in a giant lattice structure and empricial formula before moving on to disucss using dot and cross diagrams to model ionic bonding.

nodes.misconception: All ionic compounds dissociate completely in aqueous solutions.
nodes.response: Not all ionic compounds dissociate completely in water; some may not dissolve at all. It's important to know the solubility rules to correctly predict the behaviour of compounds in solution.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse oxidation and reduction when involving electrons. They often mistake a positive charge on an ion as meaning electrons have been added and vice versa for negative ions.
nodes.response: It is very important to teach from first principles what causes the charges and then work up to half equations where the pupils can see the electrons in the equations, finally combining these to form ionic equations.

nodes.misconception: Ionic equations only include ions involved in the reaction, not all ions in the reaction mixture.
nodes.response: Stress the difference between reacting ions and spectator ions.

nodes.misconception: Gamma rays are always higher energy (or power), or more dangerous, than other frequencies of EM radiation.
nodes.response: EM waves transfer their energy in 'chunks' or 'packets'. The energy transferred by one 'packet' of radiation (and so its ionising ability) does depend on frequency. But the power of a beam of radiation depends on the intensity of the radiation too.

nodes.misconception: Alpha and beta particles and gamma radiation are radioactive.
nodes.response: Differentiate between radioactive particles that can emit radiation and the radiation itself. Radiation consists of fast moving particles or radiation that can cause ionisation because their electric fields interact with those of outer electrons.

nodes.misconception: In dance, you count all music in 8's.
nodes.response: In dance, counting corresponds to the musical time signature which varies enormously. Many are 4/4 timing and can be counted in patterns of 4's or 8's, others may be in contrasting patterns such as 3/4 or 6/8, so would need to be counted accordingly.

nodes.misconception: All those in Northern Ireland were Protestant and all those elsewhere in Ireland were Catholic.
nodes.response: Ireland was predominantly Catholic but there was a population in the north who were predominantly Protestant, who remained part of the UK as Northern Ireland after partition.

nodes.misconception: The missionaries found it easy to convert people to Christianity.
nodes.response: The missionaries like St Columba and St Columbanus experienced resistance from kings and bishops which sometimes led to major problems and even battle.

nodes.misconception: That by connected we mean geographically or physically rather thank via communication and trade.
nodes.response: Discuss the meaning of the word connected. Explore maps of the areas concerned. Explain that Britain and Europe were connected by communication and trade.

nodes.misconception: 'Briskly' means fast, so you can run.
nodes.response: 'Briskly' means quick and energetic. This does not include running.

nodes.misconception: Children are always protected during wars and conflicts because there are laws and organisations to help them.
nodes.response: Even though laws and organisations aim to protect children, conflict can still put them in danger. Many lose homes, schools or family, and may not get the help they need. Protection efforts are vital, but they can't always reach every child in time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that infleuncers can only ever positively influence.
nodes.response: Although influencers can have positive impacts, when posting about politics there can also be negative impacts if they are posting incorrect information or simplifying issues.

nodes.misconception: A country just uses direct democracy.
nodes.response: Direct democracy can be used on its own or with other forms of democracy, such as representative democracy.

nodes.misconception: 'Ça va ?' means 'How are you?' - it can only be a question.
nodes.response: ‘Ça va ?’ with raised intonation at the end of the sentence is a question and means ‘is it going OK?' or ‘how’s it going’?. ‘Ça va’ without intonation is a statement and means ‘it’s going OK’.

nodes.misconception: All democracies have a free press.
nodes.response: Democracies generally support press freedom; some still have restrictions and controls.

nodes.misconception: Most young people are involved in crime because the media shows so many negative stories about them.
nodes.response: While the media often focuses on negative stories, the majority of young people are not involved in crime. Recent statistics show that many stop and searches and arrests don’t lead to charges, and the number of young people in custody is low.

nodes.misconception: The Speaker is able to influence decisions in the House of Commons.
nodes.response: The Speaker is politically neutral and there to chair debates and keep order in the House of Commons.

nodes.misconception: The UK no longer has any influence in the world.
nodes.response: Although the UK's influence has declined in some areas, it still holds significant global influence. Through its membership in organisations like NATO, the UN and the Commonwealth, the UK continues to shape global events.

nodes.misconception: Respect and tolerance happen naturally without effort or laws.
nodes.response: Mutual respect requires active effort, education and legal frameworks like the Equality Act 2010 to support fairness and prevent discrimination.

nodes.misconception: Inflation is always a negative thing because it raises prices of goods and services.
nodes.response: A small amount of inflation is actually necessary to keep the economy stable and encourage spending.

nodes.misconception: Jews, Muslims and Christians are all descended from Abraham in the same way.
nodes.response: Jews and Christians trace their ancestry through Isaac to Abraham. Muslims trace their ancestry through Ismail to Abraham.

nodes.misconception: Muslims support violence or terrorism because of the concept of jihad.
nodes.response: Muslims reject terrorism, and jihad mainly refers to personal struggle to live a good life. Islam teaches peace, justice and the protection of innocent life.

nodes.misconception: All Muslims support the idea of lesser jihad and believe in using violence to defend Islam.
nodes.response: While some Muslims accept the conditions for lesser jihad, others reject physical fighting today and focus on peaceful, spiritual struggle instead. Islam teaches that war must be a last resort and only under strict moral limits.

nodes.misconception: Islamic views on punishment are primarily focused on retribution.
nodes.response: In Islam, justice is the central aim of punishment, and retribution is only one way of achieving it. The Qur’an allows for qisas (equal retaliation), but it also encourages forgiveness, mercy and the opportunity for repentance and reform.

nodes.misconception: The death penalty is widely used in Islam.
nodes.response: While Islamic law does permit the death penalty for certain very serious offences, its application is extremely limited and rare due to strict conditions and a strong emphasis on mercy and forgiveness.

nodes.misconception: All Muslim countries follow Islamic law exactly as it is in the Qur’an.
nodes.response: In reality, some Muslim-majority countries mix Islamic principles with national laws, and not all follow the Qur’an’s teachings fully, especially on justice and human rights.

nodes.misconception: Muslims mainly live in the Middle East.
nodes.response: Islam is the second most popular religion in the world, with Muslim-majority countries spread as far as Morocco in the west to Indonesia in the east.

nodes.misconception: That the Torah and Gospels in the Jewish and Christian holy texts today are the same as those referenced in the Qur'an.
nodes.response: Muslims believe these have been changed over time from their original form and that the Qur'an corrects those changes.

nodes.misconception: Students often confuse the subatomic particle responsible for making an atom an isotope, and how isotopes are responsible for the relative atomic masses to 1 d.p.
nodes.response: Practice determining the number of neutrons in multiple isotopes.

nodes.misconception: Students often confuse the subatomic particle responsible for making an atom an isotope, and how isotopes are responsible for the relative atomic masses to 1 d.p.
nodes.response: Practice determining the number of neutrons in multiple isotopes.

nodes.misconception: Israeli music is very similar to other Middle Eastern music because Israel is in the Middle East.
nodes.response: Israeli folk music has a very different history to other music from the region, as it was influenced by Jewish migrants from other parts of the world. Jewish folk music uses many European instruments and has similarities with European folk music.

nodes.misconception: 'Viel' and 'viele' and 'wenig' and 'wenige' are interchangeable.
nodes.response: Use 'viel' and 'wenig' with uncountable nouns (i.e., you cannot put a number in front of it) and use 'viele' and 'wenige' with countable nouns (i.e., you can put a number in front of it).

nodes.misconception: Modelling using CAD is the final step in the development of designs.
nodes.response: CAD is part of the iterative process. CAD should be used as a way to develop your idea by viewing it virtually and analysing the idea. Sketching over your CAD drawings can help to develop the idea before going back to make those improvements in CAD.

nodes.misconception: Iterations of models are purely based on the thoughts of the designer.
nodes.response: Iterations can be based off a range of analysis and evaluations such as evaluating against the users needs and wants as well as direct feedback from the user.

nodes.misconception: Strings are mutable meaning that any character within the string can be changed.
nodes.response: Strings are immutable. The elements of a string cannot be changed. If changes to the string are required, the whole string must be rewritten.

nodes.misconception: Refinement is just “making it look nicer.”
nodes.response: Refinement is purposeful change based on evidence; it improves inclusivity, usability, and overall function, not just appearance.

nodes.misconception: A while loop is the most appropriate loop to use when you know exactly how many iterations will need to be performed.
nodes.response: While loops should be used when the number of iterations can change. Even though while loops can be used in this way, for loops are a more appropriate choice as they will track the number of iterations as part of their operation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often already know what they want to design and feel that their first prototype is the final solution that doesn't need further development.
nodes.response: The iterative journey transforms an idea into a successful product. Pupils should carefully explore, experiment, test, and develop ideas while keeping design requirements central to the process.

nodes.misconception: Days of the week start with a capital letter in French, as in English.
nodes.response: Days of the week start with a lowercase letter in French, unless at the start of a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Like English, Spanish uses two different words to make verbs negative — just as English uses 'do not/don't' and 'does not/doesn't.'
nodes.response: In Spanish, simply use 'no' before the verb for all subjects (I, you, he, she, etc.) to make a negative, e.g. 'no hago' - I don't do, 'no hace' - she, he, it doesn't do.

nodes.misconception: The sound-spelling correspondences  [r] and [rr] look similar so are pronounced the same way.
nodes.response: [r] and [rr] are pronounced differently. The [r] is  a soft sound like a quick tap of your tongue and the [rr] is a rolling sound - your tongue vibrates or rolls, like when you make the sound of a telephone ring - brrrrring, brrrrring!

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the island turned Jack into the cruel and bloodthirsty leader he is by the end of the novel.
nodes.response: From the very beginning, Jack was characterised as unpleasant and egomaniacal. He treats the choir terribly in the first chapter. Jack arguably always had the traits of a dictatorial leader. The island has exacerbated these traits, not created them.

nodes.misconception: Some might assume that jade is always green in colour.
nodes.response: Jade is a natural stone and so the colour varies greatly. It can appear as many colours including black, brown, yellow, white, green and blue. Different colours have been more desirable at different points in Chinese history.

nodes.misconception: When changing a positive to a negative statement, words like 'un', 'une', 'du', 'de la' and 'des' stay the same, e.g. 'je mange du gateau' - 'je ne mange pas du gâteau'.
nodes.response: When making a sentence negative, 'un', 'une', 'du', 'de la' and 'des' change to 'de', e.g. 'je mange du gâteau' - 'je ne mange pas de gâteau'.

nodes.misconception: You must only use verbs in the same tense as the task question in your answer.
nodes.response: Students should practise combining different tenses of verbs when giving their answers (ensuring they give a relevant response to the task) in order to demonstrate a wider knowledge of language and to give a richer response.

nodes.misconception: The expression 'j'ai mal' only means 'I have a pain'.
nodes.response: The French expression 'avoir mal' covers a number of symptoms which might be variously translated into English as an ache, a pain and sore or hurting body parts. Students should think about what sounds most natural when translating into English.

nodes.misconception: The indefinite and partitive articles are used with the structure 'ne ... ni ... ni', e.g. 'Tu n'as ni des pommes ni du fromage'.
nodes.response: When using 'ne ... ni ... ni', the nouns do not require an indefinite or partitive article, e.g. 'Tu n'as ni pommes ni fromage'.

nodes.misconception: Only children of the monarch are next in line for the throne, not siblings.
nodes.response: As Charles II did not have any legitimate children, his heir was his brother, James II.

nodes.misconception: When talking about being hungry, thirsty, right, wrong or afraid, use 'être' as the verb.
nodes.response: In French, ideas like being hungry and thirsty are expressed using 'avoir' plus a noun. In French, 'j'ai faim' is correct. It translates literally as 'I have hunger'. Ideas like being thirsty and afraid are expressed the same way.

nodes.misconception: JavaScript changes the original HTML file.
nodes.response: JavaScript only changes what the user sees in the browser. It does not change the actual HTML file saved on your computer or server.

nodes.misconception: A common mistake pupils make is using a 'bowling' style of throw in which the throwing arm remains straight throughout the action.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to think about pulling the javelin through, with the elbow leading first.

nodes.misconception: A common mistake pupils make is using a 'bowling' style of throw in which the throwing arm remains straight throughout the action.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to think about pulling the javelin through, with the elbow leading first.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only used to describe how things were or used to be in the past.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense is also used to say what was happening when another thing occurred where it is used in combination with the perfect tense e.g. il regardait la télé quand son portable a sonné.

nodes.misconception: The 'vous' form of address is only used for plural situations.
nodes.response: In formal situations, it is essential to address somebody as 'vous' in order to be polite and to show respect. Careful consideration of the context of a conversation is very important.

nodes.misconception: All scientific developments during the Industrial Revolution were positive in terms of their impact on society.
nodes.response: While the Industrial Revolution was considered to be the 'golden age' of scientific development and innovation, much of the pioneering research was conducted under unethical conditions.

nodes.misconception: Immoral behaviour was something only the lower classes engaged in.
nodes.response: Immoral behaviour was something that crossed class boundaries but it manifested differently; for the lower classes, vice was survival-based with many turning to crime to survive whereas the wealthy engaged in debauchery and illicit affairs.

nodes.misconception: Most Victorians were religious people which meant that they behaved in a way that was morally good.
nodes.response: While most Victorians were religious and followed stict moral codes, they did so only in public. Behind clsosed doors, immoral and debaucherous behaviour was common.

nodes.misconception: There were lots of treatments available to Victorians to help them recover from psychological conditions.
nodes.response: While there were lots treatments available, many showed serious misunderstandings about human psychology. They were ineffecive, some were inhumane and many left patients with long-term psychological damage.

nodes.misconception: The Industrial Revolution was a wholly positive change for society because machines created jobs and allowed for foriegn travel.
nodes.response: While there were many advantages to the Industrial Revolution, there were also many disadvantages such as pollution, worsening of working conditions and a widening of the class divide.

nodes.misconception: There isn't much point analysing setting to learn about theh characters or themes of text; it just provides the scenery for the action to take place in.
nodes.response: Often writers use setting to subtly foreshadow events or symbolise important paralells to characters. Analysing settings is a useful way to learn more about characters and key themes.

nodes.misconception: Just mentioning Stevenson's choices surrounding form and structure is valuable analysis.
nodes.response: All comments regarding Stevenson's use of form and structure should be tied back to Stevenson's purpose.

nodes.misconception: When analysing, all pupils need is a clear viewpoint.
nodes.response: A clear viewpoint is important, but adding nuance will improve the quality of pupil responses.

nodes.misconception: Only Roman Catholic Christians visit Jerusalem.
nodes.response: Christians from different traditions visit many places on pilgrimage. Jerusalem is the most sacred place as it is where Jesus was crucified and was raised from the dead.

nodes.misconception: Jerusalem is only a place of pilgrimage for Jews.
nodes.response: Jews, Christians and Muslims go on pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

nodes.misconception: Jesus was born a Christian.
nodes.response: Jesus was Jewish. He lived in a Jewish society and responded to the issues of wealth and poverty he saw around him.

nodes.misconception: Jesus replaced the Ten Commandments as they were outdated.
nodes.response: Jesus summarised the Commandments with his call to love others.

nodes.misconception: Jesus always followed Jewish laws.
nodes.response: Jesus challenged some of the laws in Jewish society.

nodes.misconception: Jesus only had meaningful conversations with his disciples.
nodes.response: Jesus had a very deep conversation with the Samaritan woman.

nodes.misconception: The story of Zacchaeus is a parable.
nodes.response: The story of Zacchaeus is a narrative about Jesus and someone he met.

nodes.misconception: Jesus is entirely distinct and separate from God.
nodes.response: For most Christians, Jesus is God in human form. Jesus is both fully human and fully divine.

nodes.misconception: Jesus is entirely distinct and separate from God.
nodes.response: For most Christians, Jesus is God in human form. Jesus is both fully human and fully divine.

nodes.misconception: Jesus did not suffer during his crucifixion.
nodes.response: The Gospels recall Jesus crying out loudly during his crucifixion, which many Christians interpret as a sign of Jesus' pain.

nodes.misconception: Jesus is entirely distinct and separate from God.
nodes.response: For most Christians, Jesus is God in human form. Jesus is both fully human and fully divine.

nodes.misconception: Jesus ascended to heaven immediately after his resurrection.
nodes.response: Jesus ascended to heaven 40 days after his resurrection, according to the New Testament.

nodes.misconception: Jesus is not important within Islam.
nodes.response: Jesus is highly regarded within Islam as one of the greatest prophets.

nodes.misconception: The Gospels present exactly the same stories about Jesus, just in slightly different ways.
nodes.response: Whilst there are many similarities across the Gospel books, there are also many differences. Some of the Gospels contain stories that others do not. For example, Jesus' birth is only recorded in Matthew and Luke, not in all four of the Gospels.

nodes.misconception: Christian teaching on forgiveness is simply to forgive people the first time.
nodes.response: The teaching of Jesus on forgiveness was challenging at the time and challenging for Christians today.

nodes.misconception: All Christians believe in the incarnation.
nodes.response: There are a small number of Christians who do not believe that Jesus was God. For example, many of Jehovah's Witnesses do not believe in the incarnation.

nodes.misconception: The Old Testament is not relevant to Jesus' teachings.
nodes.response: Jesus developed many teachings from the Old Testament.

nodes.misconception: The covenant was only made between Abraham and God.
nodes.response: The covenant was forever and continued through his descendants, including Jesus.

nodes.misconception: Shared Jewish heritage meant that all European Jews lived similar lives.
nodes.response: Jews made individuals choices and were affected by factors such as wealth which led to the Jewish population living many different types of lives.

nodes.misconception: Jewish persecution and antisemitism only happened in Europe during the 1930s and 1940s.
nodes.response: Jewish persecution and antisemitism had been happening for thousands of years, with Britain expelling all Jews in 1290, without letting them return for hundreds of years.

nodes.misconception: Resistance always involves the use of violence.
nodes.response: Jews adopted many nonviolent forms of resistance. Actions like smuggling resisted Nazi attempts to starve Jews and continuing education secretly resisted Nazi attempts to destroy Jewish culture.

nodes.misconception: The story of Job shows that God causes suffering.
nodes.response: For many Christians, the story of Job shows that Satan (the devil) is one cause of suffering, but that God may allow suffering to test humans, or for a greater purpose which may be a mystery to humans.

nodes.misconception: Add an -e to all adjectives to make them agree with feminine nouns.
nodes.response: The majority of adjectives need an -e adding in the feminine form but there are other patterns and exceptions to the rules. A common pattern is that adjectives ending -x change to -se in the feminine form.

nodes.misconception: Add an -e to all person nouns to make them feminine.
nodes.response: The most common way to make a person noun feminine is to add an -e to the masculine version. If nouns already end in -e, person nouns usually stay the same but the article changes. Jobs ending in 'eur' usually change to 'rice' in the feminine form.

nodes.misconception: Learners may have limited knowledge about the jobs that people do.
nodes.response: Spend more time at the start of the lesson discussing the different jobs that people do in the UK.

nodes.misconception: Everyone who works in a school gets paid.
nodes.response: There are many volunteers who work in schools to help them run smoothly. These people don't get paid, they give up their time for free.

nodes.misconception: 'Ils ont' and 'ils sont' sound the same.
nodes.response: Although these two verbs sound similar, there is a distinction between the 'z' sound created by s-liaison in 'ils ont' and the 's' sound at the beginning of 'sont' after the silent 's' on 'ils'.

nodes.misconception: There is no need to use intonation when using inversion and 'est-ce que'.
nodes.response: Even when we form questions with inversion or 'est-ce que', it is still important to use intonation to signal that it is a question.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that John's sisters would be in line to the throne before him.
nodes.response: Explain that this is the case today in the UK - Princess Charlotte became the first female royal to benefit from The Succession to the Crown Act in 2013. The Act stated that girls born into the Royal Family will not be overtaken by younger brothers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find it confusing that John Cabot sounds like a very English name yet he was Italian.
nodes.response: John Cabot is the English version of the name he was born as, Giovanni Caboto. He lived in England for so long he was known by John Cabot.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not correctly identify right angles within a shape to join them.
nodes.response: Make sure that pupils have opportunities to identify right angles within a range of shapes prior to the lesson. If possible, encourage them to mark the right angles to help them. They should only be joining these right angles around a point.

nodes.misconception: The items in the background can move.
nodes.response: The background is a static image and the parts it shows are part of the same picture and therefore cannot move. Only sprites can move as they are separate objects.

nodes.misconception: The whole puppet needs to be stitched.
nodes.response: There are other joining technqiues that can be used to join the felt together. The running stitch is one which is advised for this unit, however, staples or fabric glue / PVA can be used as an alternative.

nodes.misconception: A common mistake is not understanding that different joining methods need to be used for different materials and reasons.
nodes.response: Some joining techniques such as PVA can be more messy and cause colours in materials to run, for example. Through adding PVA to the object being attached, this usually causes a neater, better presented outcome.

nodes.misconception: All joining methods work the same for every material.
nodes.response: Different materials need different joining methods based on their properties.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to link related ideas together.
nodes.response: Give some non-examples to show what it sounds like when two ideas are unrelated e.g. Dad baked bread and she missed her sister.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they have written a compound sentence just because they have included 'and'.
nodes.response: Look at sentences on a balancing scale with 'and' in the middle. Highlight that both ideas either side of 'and' must make complete sense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that 'but' can be used in any sentence and may not recognise where it is suitable.
nodes.response: Show compound sentence examples that use the same first idea and let pupils hear the different joining words in action with the second idea.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise when 'or' is joining two main clauses and when it is joining two words.
nodes.response: Show, explain and say aloud many examples of 'or' joining two main clauses in compound sentence examples.

nodes.misconception: Students may mix up rotation and circumduction.
nodes.response: When you rotate the shoulder joint, you draw a dot with your hand (if the elbow is fully extended) whereas circumduction draws a circle.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the only way to learn something by heart is to keep reading it.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that they can also check their progress with cloze procedure exercises.

nodes.misconception: Main and subordinate clauses are merely grammatical terms not worthy of analysis.
nodes.response: A writer's decision to use subordinate and main clauses is a creative choice. Their use can achieve different things (e.g. tension, pace).

nodes.misconception: Although some German words have more than one meaning, most of them have a main meaning and it's not important to know the other meanings.
nodes.response: Some very frequent words have several different meanings, all of them commonly used. It is important to know the meanings and to use context to select the right meaning. For example, 'vor' can mean 'in front of', 'before' and 'ago'.

nodes.misconception: The time-manner-place rule means that all sentences must have time before manner before place.
nodes.response: German sentences can start with any adverb to emphasise that element. The TMP order is then retained for any other adverbs in that sentence. For example, 'Mit dem Zug (M) fahren wir morgen (T) nach Liechtenstein (P).'.

nodes.misconception: A performance should be to the whole class.
nodes.response: Performing can be to another person, duet or group. This can feel less daunting and is a good way to get feedback.

nodes.misconception: French indirect object pronouns are all the same as direct object pronouns.
nodes.response: While some object pronouns are the same when used both indirectly and directly (e.g. me, te), there are some differences that students need to learn. It is a good idea to provide plenty of practice in this area to help students gain confidence.

nodes.misconception: Most Muslims believe in the immortality of the soul but not the body.
nodes.response: The majority of Muslims believe in a physical resurrection.

nodes.misconception: Children might think that judging a debate needs to be done by adults.
nodes.response: Children can most definitely judge a debate themselves once they know what they're looking for.

nodes.misconception: The body is only balanced when it is still. Pupils find it difficult to balance still.
nodes.response: The body is always balancing whether it is still or moving (static and dynamic balances), but focusing on stillness allows pupils to show control in a static balance and feel stable. Try focusing on a fixed spot ahead of you to help keep still.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the top of their heads in a forward roll and forget to make their back curved. Pupils bend their backs too much when landing a jump, causing their hands to touch the floor.
nodes.response: Pupils should tuck their heads in, put their chin on their chests and use the back of their head by keeping their back rounded in a forward roll. Remind pupils to keep their backs straight so they can land upright ('land and stand').

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to jump high enough to turn due to a weak push off. Pupils are wobbly and unbalanced when turning. Pupils turn too much or too little.
nodes.response: Emphasise bending the knees and pushing through the balls of the feet. Pupils should practise engaging their core muscles to help them turn with control. Make sure pupils focus on rotating from the shoulders and hips not just the arms.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to understand that this combination of three elements creates one jump that can be measured from the start of the hop, to the end of the jump.
nodes.response: When we combine elements into a hop, step, jump combination we can benefit from the power and momentum that builds up. By increasing the distance travelled in each element, we increase the overall distance covered in the jump combination.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that their ability to jump far is fixed and cannot be changed or improved.
nodes.response: Everyone is capable of improving their performance. Practice, developing a good technique and showing self-belief can all help us to improve.

nodes.misconception: In the triple jump, pupils collapse the middle 'step phase' rather than getting equal height and distance from every phase.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the importance of all phases of the jump, especially the step phase and that they understand all phases of the triple jump should contribute to an equal proportion of distance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that jumping competitions only focus on individual ability.
nodes.response: When we are competing as part of a team, our performance is a combined effort and everyone in the team can contribute in lots of different ways.

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't land in a controlled way. Pupils do not use the correct technique for jumping. Pupils are distracted and jump looking at others.
nodes.response: Demonstrate an effective jump with a controlled landing. Demonstrate the correct technique. Reiterate the importance of jumping with heads focused forwards.

nodes.misconception: When building up to the jump, the pupil steps forward slightly, jumping off 1 foot.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that jumping off 1 foot or stepping forwards before jumping is a foul. They must jump and land using both feet.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the triple jump consists of a step, step and jump, rather than a hop, step and jump.
nodes.response: Allow pupils time to practise hopping and stepping and highlight the difference between the two. Pupils must understand that a hop requires them to land on the same foot they took off on, and a step is from one foot to the other.

nodes.misconception: When perfroming the long jump, many pupils take a long step into the pit which means they land with one foot in front of the other which reduces the distance they achieve.
nodes.response: Pupils should be taught to land with feet parallel by bringing the take-off foot through and in front of them so that no distance is lost and they achieve a maximal score.

nodes.misconception: When learning the scissors technique, pupils often use an incorrect take-off foot, choosing to jump from the foot closest to the bar instead of the foot furthest away.
nodes.response: Allow pupils to practise jumping off their right foot, then their left, before performing the full action to establish which they prefer to take off with.  Be observant during full performances and be ready to suggest a pupil changes approach side.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the techniques for leaping and jumping. Pupils focus on not being tagged and forget to jump or leap properly.
nodes.response: Demonstrate both techniques. Explain the importance of using the correct technique and demonstrate.  Bring in a rule that if pupils run instead of using their jumping skills, they have 'tagged' themselves and must stop and perform 5 star jumps.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that jumping is all about strength and do not consider the importance of coordination and technique.
nodes.response: The power needed for jumping high comes from the combined actions of a range of different body parts. The coordination of all these body parts creates a great technique for jumping high.

nodes.misconception: Pupils run instead of skipping to avoid being caught. Pupils don't follow the rules and take more than one piece of equipment at a time.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that running is a rule break and celebrate pupils who are hopping/skipping not running. Explain that this is a rule break and build in a consequence for this happening.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to communicate when working in bigger groups. Poor timing in unison and canon may result in a lack of flow throughout the sequence.
nodes.response: Pupils should communicate and listen to each other's ideas. Pupils should develop ways to help them improve their timing, ensuring there are no long pauses when performing in unison and canon so their sequence still flows throughout.

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't land in a controlled way. Pupils don't focus forwards or use their arms when they jump.
nodes.response: Demonstrate an effective jump with a controlled landing. Explain and demonstrate jumping by swinging the arms up then down and while focusing forwards.

nodes.misconception: When an adjective follows 'ein', always add 'en'.
nodes.response: Adjective endings reflect the case and gender of the word they refer to. Dative case adjectives end in -en. In nominative and accusative, use -e for feminine and -es for neuter. Masculine -er  and -en match (d)er (nominative) and (d)en (accusative).

nodes.misconception: To say 'it' in German, always use 'es'.
nodes.response: As a pronoun, 'es' only replaces a neuter noun. 'Das Buch? Ich lese es gern.' ('A book? I like reading it.'). Use 'ihn' or 'sie' for masculine and feminine nouns. 'Der neue Film? Ich finde ihn (it) toll.'. 'Berlin? Ich besuche sie (it) gern.'.

nodes.misconception: Alll German words of foreign origin form their plural by adding 's'.
nodes.response: Inanimate nouns add 's': 'Interviews', 'Songs'. Person nouns ending in -er (e.g., 'Reporter') do not change in the masculine plural. Weak masculine nouns (e.g., 'Journalist') add -en in the plural. Feminine plurals add -nen (e.g., 'Journalistinnen').

nodes.misconception: We always use accusative reflexive pronouns ('mich', 'dich', etc.) with reflexive verbs.
nodes.response: If there is already an accusative object in the sentence, we use dative reflexive pronouns ('mir', 'dir', etc.) instead, e.g., 'Ich wasche mir die Hände'.

nodes.misconception: Trial by combat and trial by ordeal were punishments for crimes.
nodes.response: Trial by combat and trial by ordeal were ways of finding out who God judged as being innocent and guilty, though the ordeal was certainly punishing for both parties.

nodes.misconception: Opinions do not need to be justified in a debate.
nodes.response: Opinions need to be justified to convince the audience.

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to tell if 174 368 is in the sequence -8,-3,2,7, ...
nodes.response: Generalising the rule for forming a given sequence can help us see if a value is in the sequence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to chant "Kabaddi Kabaddi" when they are a raider.
nodes.response: Remember chanting "Kabaddi, Kabaddi" is how the raider shows they haven't taken a breath during the raid and if they forget, the raid doesn't count.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that as a defender they need to rush individually to stop the opposition.
nodes.response: Rushing alone often leaves space for the raider to escape. Defenders are more effective when they move together, stay connected and communicate to trap the raider as a team.

nodes.misconception: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
nodes.response: The unit is said before the ten in German, e.g., 'neunundvierzig' = '9 and 40' = 49. It is helpful to write from right to left when taking down numbers so that you produce them in the correct order.

nodes.misconception: Karma and rebirth is the belief in a 'self' or 'soul' that is reborn. Many people assume that karma dictates the fate of a permanent, unchanging soul that carries over from one life to the next.
nodes.response: There is no eternal, unchanging self or soul. Instead, Buddhism teaches the concept of anatta, meaning 'no-self'. What is reborn is not a permanent soul, but a continuing process or stream of consciousness influenced by past actions (karma).

nodes.misconception: Only Khalsa Sikhs wear the Kara.
nodes.response: While the Kara is one of the 5 Ks worn by Khalsa Sikhs, many Sikhs wear it even if they haven’t taken Amrit, as a sign of their faith and a reminder of God.

nodes.misconception: The Hajj pilgrimage to Makkah is the only pilgrimage for Muslims.
nodes.response: Karbala is a place of pilgrimage for Shi'a Muslims. Jerusalem is also a place of pilgrimage for Muslims.

nodes.misconception: Students assume all communists and socialists shared the same ideas.
nodes.response: Marx's ideas were interpreted differently by different groups of socialists. In Russia, this led to the split of the Social Democratic Party.

nodes.misconception: Hindus believe in heaven.
nodes.response: Hindus believe in reincarnation as part of samsara. The ultimate goal for Hindus is moksha, or being released from the cycle of samsara.

nodes.misconception: Verbs are only followed by the dative case if we translate the verb with 'to' or 'for' in English.
nodes.response: There are several impersonal verbs in German which require the dative case, e.g., 'gelingen' (to succeed).

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense of the modal verb 'mögen' is formed like other modal verbs.
nodes.response: The stem of 'mögen' in the imperfect tense is 'moch-'.  It is normally followed by a noun rather than a second verb in the infinitive.

nodes.misconception: Traditional dance styles are how all the people in that country dance.
nodes.response: Traditional dance styles are still danced by some people in their communities on certain occasions. They will also dance other styles too and these will change depending on whether they are in a theatre, temple or at a social event.

nodes.misconception: Beat and rhythm are interchangeable terminology.
nodes.response: The beat is the consistent audible sound of the underlying pulse. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences which can be a combination of sounds of any duration.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the best thing to do when a defender is about to tackle you is to (panic) pass the ball.
nodes.response: Panic passing before contact in rugby often leads to turnovers, as the pass is rushed, inaccurate, and easier for the opposition to intercept or disrupt, therefore the best decision can sometimes be to keep hold of the ball and take it into contact.

nodes.misconception: Only Sikhs who have taken Amrit wear head coverings.
nodes.response: Many Sikhs, regardless of whether they have taken Amrit or not, may choose to wear a head covering like a turban or scarf to show respect for their faith and culture.

nodes.misconception: In Indonesia, agriculture remains the dominant sector in the economy.
nodes.response: Agriculture was once Indonesia’s economic backbone, but its role has declined since the 1990s. Today, industry and services dominate GDP, with manufacturing, finance, tourism, and digital sectors growing.

nodes.misconception: $$y=x^3$$ has one root so all cubic graphs have one root.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils see a wide variety of cubic graphs; ones with one root, two roots and three roots and link every one back to its equation and that the highest exponent of the variable is $$3$$ so they are all cubic graphs.

nodes.misconception: Parabolas are 'upwards' or 'downwards'.
nodes.response: Encourage use of language such as "The turning point of this parabola is a maximum/minimum value" and "As the absolute values of $$x$$ increase, the $$y$$ values decrease/increase".

nodes.misconception: All reciprocal graphs appear only in two quadrants and have both axes as asymptotes.
nodes.response: Show pupils the graphs of the $$y={1\over{x}}$$, then $$y={1\over{x}}+1$$, then $$y={1\over{x+1}}$$ and get them to compare which forms have which axes as asymptotes.

nodes.misconception: $$y=b^x$$ will reach zero; the curve will touch the $$x$$ axis eventually.
nodes.response: Get pupils to input large absolute $$x$$ values to appreciate that no matter how small the $$y$$ value it is still a fraction greater than zero.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that some jobs are gendered - e.g. tractor drivers or lifeboat crew are men.
nodes.response: Model jobs being done by a variety of people showing diversity where appropriate, in terms of gender, age, ethnicity and ability.

nodes.misconception: William always planned to replace Anglo-Saxons in key government positions with loyal Normans.
nodes.response: At first, William intended to boost his claim to be the legitimate heir of Edward by keeping earls Edwin, Morcar and Waltheof in place in his government of England - alongside new earls such as Earl Odo of Kent or Earl William of Hereford.

nodes.misconception: Every frame of an animation needs to be created by the animator.
nodes.response: Most modern animations are created using tweening. Tweening creates the frames between keyframes and stitches them together. This reduces the time taken to create animations and can improve quality.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that Islam doesn't have much to say about environmental ethics
nodes.response: Islamic teachings provide a strong and ancient vision for sustainable living.

nodes.misconception: The arms race only made the superpowers more hostile towards one another.
nodes.response: The high costs and growing power of nuclear weapons developments meant both the USSR and USA were interested in finding ways to improve relations between them.

nodes.misconception: Kicks may lack the necessary power or accuracy, or they might often miss their target. High catches can be intimidating and pupils may mistime their jump.
nodes.response: Focus on good technique before increasing distance or adding movements to kicks. When performing a high catch, track the ball early and use the jumping technique to meet the ball when it is at its highest point.

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold the pads at the wrong height or angle or keep their arms too stiff or too relaxed.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to communicate if the pads are at the wrong height or angle to give each other corrective feedback. Teach pad holders to “meet” the strike with slight forward pressure and a bend in the arms.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often start exercises with too much intensity and quickly recognise that they cannot continue when performing conditioning exercises.
nodes.response: When trying to improve muscular endurance and condition, steady and continuous activity over a longer period of time gives the best results. Start at a pace that is comfortable to begin with and can be maintained as muscles start to fatigue.

nodes.misconception: A kick is only good if it is kicked far.
nodes.response: Kicking a ball successfully involves accuracy and tactical placement to find space, kicking into touch or to allow one of your team to catch and maintain possession.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that they need to kick the ball as hard as possible to make a good pass, leading to a loss of control.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of accuracy over power and that pupils need to be able to kick the ball where they want it to go first.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that it is always best to pass when in a difficult situation.
nodes.response: Retaining possession through accurate kicks can at times make more yards than passing and being tagged.

nodes.misconception: Pupils stay upright while kneeling in the tripod position, meaning the ball is too high for hitting.
nodes.response: It is easier to hit the kin-ball when it is lower down, so be sure to bend forward in the kneeling position.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the Church is the same as a church building.
nodes.response: The Church is the name of the organisation that includes all the people who lead the Christian religion. Buildings are also called churches.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that kings and queens after King John forgot about Magna Carta.
nodes.response: Kings and queens after King John still followed Magna Carta and it remained as a very important document of rights for the people. Today, there are still four of the original 63 clauses in use in England.

nodes.misconception: King John only ruled England.
nodes.response: King John inherited the Angevin Empire which stretched across England and France.

nodes.misconception: The work of Martin Luther King ended with the Voting Right Acts in 1965.
nodes.response: With continued violence, rioting and protests, King continued to fight for change in the North. However, he faced greater opposition than he did in the South.

nodes.misconception: Definite and indefiniete articles are used the same way in German as in English.
nodes.response: Differences occur with some country names, some abstract nouns and professions: e.g., 'die Schweiz' (Switzerland), 'die Freiheit' (freedom). It's 'Er ist Arzt' (He is a doctor), but an article is needed before the adjective - 'Er ist ein guter Arzt'.

nodes.misconception: Time, manner, place adverbs must always be used in the order TMP.
nodes.response: When using WO1, the order TMP applies. However, each of the elements can be used at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis. In that case, use WO2 and put the remaining elements in the order time before manner before place.

nodes.misconception: Pupils need to look at the interior angles in the shape. They may think that an interior angle of 270° is a right angle.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we need to measure the interior angles of a shape. Show them examples of this (e.g. an arrowhead) to illustrate.

nodes.misconception: Many polygons appear regular as all of the sides are the same length. However, it is possible (as the lesson shows) to have polygons which are the same length sides but different interior angles.
nodes.response: Pupils should have previous experience of right angles. Use a right angle 'measurer' to prove that some of the angles in a shape are greater than a right angle and some smaller; as the angles are not all equal, it is not a regular polygon.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that squares are rectangles.
nodes.response: Emphasise to pupils that all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares. Rectangles are quadrilaterals with 4 right angles, but squares have 4 sides of equal length.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the importance of the order of the numerals in equations, so may not understand that the amount added or subtracted is of key importance when undoing a change made.
nodes.response: Present errors to discuss and correct. Encourage children to use practical equipment to demonstrate how they know they are right or to show why an error made cannot be correct.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that there is only one way to add the perimeter of a shape - typically clockwise, starting from the top. This is untrue and will limit the efficiency of the arithmetic.
nodes.response: The lesson presents the idea of the side lengths being given in counters. The counters can then be re-ordered, for example so that a number bond to ten can be utilised. Using counters or sticky notes or similar may support pupils.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may count a side twice, or miss a side, if they do not remember where their starting point was on the shape when counting the perimeter.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to mark a starting point, or use dots to mark the units they have counted.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the whole 360 degrees must be composed of different sized angles.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are exposed to examples where two or more of the angles summing to 360 degrees are the same.

nodes.misconception: The largest angle that can be created is a 360 degree angle or one full turn.
nodes.response: Explore examples in everyday life where rotations are greater than one full turn. Discuss how multiples of 180 degrees or 360 degrees are often used to describe movements in sports and other contexts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the angles on a straight line only applied to lines that are horizontal.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are exposed to straight lines in a range of orientations, encouraging them to draw on the 180 degree angle and how this can apply to both sides of the straight line.

nodes.misconception: When finding the perimeter of a shape, pupils may count one side twice, or not count one of the sides.
nodes.response: Examples and non-examples of perimeter are given but encourage pupils to mark a 'start point' when they find the perimeter of a shape, so that they know where to end.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that, even when one of the long side and short side lengths is missing in a rectangle, they still have enough information as these are the same as the given lengths.
nodes.response: Counters are encouraged in this unit. It may be that some pupils still need the missing side lengths written on counters, but as with all scaffolding, this should only be temporary. Ask them - do you need this counter? Do you already know the number?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see a rectangle with the perimeter given and only one of the side lengths and think that there is insufficient information as there are three missing side lengths.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that because it is a rectangle, the side length opposite the given side length is in fact known. A counter can be added on and then removed again to show that they actually know two of the missing side lengths, not just one.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget how many days are in each month. They do not particularly follow a pattern or sequence. For example, pupils might be tempted to say that August has 30 days because it follows July.
nodes.response: You could 'interrupt the forgetting' by providing frequent opportunities for pupils to recall these facts outside the Maths lesson, using flashcards for each month with the month on the front and the number of days on the back.

nodes.misconception: Children may understand a day as the amount of time in which they are awake.
nodes.response: The lesson counts and names each of the 24 hours, using morning, evening and night. Take time to discuss what the children will typically be doing during these hours, including when they will usually be asleep.

nodes.misconception: When producing written work in German, I should stick to short simple sentences.
nodes.response: When producing written work in German, you should try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget that after 2 goals are scored they swap positions.
nodes.response: After 2 goals are scored in Korfball, the attackers then swap and become the defenders and the defenders swap and become attackers (on both teams).

nodes.misconception: Dharma is just about religious duties.
nodes.response: Dharma is about all human life. Dharma is about making choices motivated by love and compassion.

nodes.misconception: The rhythm is the definitive version of the Kuku rhythm.
nodes.response: There are different versions of this piece from both Guinea and the Ivory Coast. There are also local versions within each of these. This version is a guide and can be adapted to suit your local context.

nodes.misconception: The solo section has to be made up in the moment.
nodes.response: The solo section can use ideas that are already planned. This is a good starting point for adding solos to build confidence and then build up to doing improvised ideas.

nodes.misconception: The German [w] is pronounced like the English 'w'; the German [v] is pronounced like the English 'v'.
nodes.response: The German [w] is pronounced like the English 'v'; the German [v] is pronounced like the English 'f'.

nodes.misconception: The Kumbh Mela is simply about sadhus and crowds at the Ganges.
nodes.response: The Kumbh Mela is a spiritual pilgrimage linked to the sacred rivers and sacred time. Hindus may bathe in the river, speak to and learn from the wisdom of sadhus and sadhvus. They may also offer acts of service to other pilgrims.

nodes.misconception: An accent does not change the pronunciation of a letter, [e], [é] and [è] sound the same.
nodes.response: An accent can change the pronunciation of a letter. [e], [é] and [è] make different sounds in French.

nodes.misconception: There are two present tenses in French, simple present and present continuous, like English.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in French, which is used to communicate both English present tenses. For example, 'je joue au foot' can be translated as both I play football and I am playing football.

nodes.misconception: Cognates are pronounced the same way in French as they are in English.
nodes.response: Cognates are often pronounced very differently in French.  Students should not overlook the importance of practising pronunciation of cognates in order to better respond to listening stimuli as well as to develop a more authentic pronunciation.

nodes.misconception: It isn't important to answer both bullet points in the longer writing task equally.
nodes.response: Students should plan carefully to address both bullet points in an equal manner, giving detailed answers and using a rich selection of language. Using the BORDER acronym helps students to fully answer the task.

nodes.misconception: There is always a word for 'do' or 'did' in Spanish.
nodes.response: There is no word for 'do' or 'did' in Spanish questions.

nodes.misconception: 'Tener' + noun always translates in English as 'to have' + noun.
nodes.response: The idiomatic expression 'tener' + noun is translated in English as 'to be' + adjective.

nodes.misconception: When writing, talking about what someone does, has done using a text written in the first person for information, only the subject pronoun needs to be changed in each sentence.
nodes.response: When writing, talking in the third person using a text in the first person for information, change the subject pronoun, verb, object pronouns and possessive adjectives (words like 'my', 'your', 'his', 'her').

nodes.misconception: 'Era' only means 'she, he, it was' or 'she, he, it used to be'.
nodes.response: 'Era' also means 'I was' or 'I used to be'. Look for the pronouns 'yo', 'él' and 'ella' to understand the meaning of 'era' in context.

nodes.misconception: 'Eso' and 'esto' can appear before a noun.
nodes.response: 'Eso' and 'esto' cannot appear before a noun because they are pronouns. Instead it is necessary to use 'este' and 'esta' (to mean 'this') and 'ese' and 'esa' (to mean 'that').

nodes.misconception: 'Ese' and 'esa' are the only words for 'that' before a noun in Spanish.
nodes.response: 'Aquel' and 'aquella' also mean 'that' and refer to something far away in space or time.

nodes.misconception: Use 'ne ... pas' to mean 'no, not one, not any'.
nodes.response: The structure 'ne ... pas' is used to negative a verb. To say that there was 'no, not one, not any' of a noun, use the structure 'ne ... aucun/e' e.g. il n'y a aucun fruit ici.

nodes.misconception: Reading or listening texts are only useful for developing general comprehension skills.
nodes.response: Careful use of reading and listening texts to enrich topic-specific vocabulary is beneficial for students.

nodes.misconception: The word for 'people' in Spanish - 'la gente' - uses the 3rd person plural form of the verb  - 'they' - like in English.
nodes.response: 'La gente' is a singular noun and therefore uses the 3rd person singular form of the verb - 'she, he, it'.

nodes.misconception: The affirmative imperative is the same as 2nd person singular  form of the verb.
nodes.response: When talking to somebody familiar to you, using tú, the affirmative imperative is the same as the 3rd person singular form of the verb.
