nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunities to calculate energy usage with appliances that have different power ratings and are used for different lengths of time.

nodes.misconception: Making loop passes are effective in attacking situations.
nodes.response: Such passes are easy to intercept as they are easy to track and often don't go very far.

nodes.misconception: We only warm up before a singing performance.
nodes.response: Warming up protects and strengthens our voice, prepares our mind and develops our musical skills. It is beneficial and advisable to warm up for every music lesson and every singing practice.

nodes.misconception: The capital city is always the country's largest city.
nodes.response: Use different examples of cities in Europe to explain that capital cities are chosen for various reasons.

nodes.misconception: It is common to try and play songs too quickly when learning them on an instrument.
nodes.response: It's always better to start slowly and at a steady tempo, then gradually build up speed when feeling confident.

nodes.misconception: Songs with a major tonality are always happy.
nodes.response: Tonality is one of the elements that gives a melody it's character. While major tonalites often feel bright, it is the combination of how all the elements of music are used that will make a song sound happy.

nodes.misconception: We can use as much clay from the Earth as we want!
nodes.response: Remind pupils that we share natural resources and use them carefully, so there is enough for everyone.

nodes.misconception: That all artwork is permanent.
nodes.response: Remind children that some artwork can be made to be permanent, but other artwork can be made to only last a short time.

nodes.misconception: Nature and cities can’t go together.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that many cities already mix nature into their design - with green roofs, gardens, trees, and wildlife spaces. Cities can be sustainable and nature-friendly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that the characters are the only important part of the animation and that scenery doesn't matter. They also may believe that scenery is only for decorative purposes.
nodes.response: Addressing these misconceptions through discussion and reference to examples can help students understand the importance of scenery in clay animation and how it enhances storytelling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may press too lightly and as a result their marks will not be clear.
nodes.response: Give plenty of oportunity to create drafts of their monoprint, improving the line quality each time.

nodes.misconception: The pupils may think that one layer of papier-mâché is enough.
nodes.response: We need multiple layers to make it strong. Artists build layer by layer to shape and secure their sculpture.

nodes.misconception: Pneumatic systems will fit neatly into a product.
nodes.response: Systems and products will need to be adapted to ensure correct position and fit.

nodes.misconception: It is easier to sketch an outline without first using shapes.
nodes.response: Remind children that if we use shapes to plan our drawing, it becomes much easier to achive the correct position and proportions with our outline.

nodes.misconception: You need to press down hard to engrave a design.
nodes.response: Children should be encouraged not to press too hard when engraving their design to avoid making holes in the matrix.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a repeat pattern means just stamping the same image randomly.
nodes.response: Demonstrate how patterns can follow a structured repetition, showing examples of tiling techniques.

nodes.misconception: Silhouettes must be made of black card or paper.
nodes.response: Remind children that silhouettes are often made of black paper or card as this shows up well against a light background, but it is up to the artist which solid colour they will use to make their silhouette.

nodes.misconception: Some children might think cross-hatching is just drawing straight lines to create shading.
nodes.response: Show pupils different examples of cross-hatching and allow time to practise other shading techniques.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that tone is only about making things darker and that shading should be done with harsh, straight lines.
nodes.response: Tone includes both light and dark areas, and the goal is to show the full range of tones, from light highlights to deep shadows. Using the side of the pencil for softer shading, helps to avoid harsh lines.

nodes.misconception: Windmills just need a wide base to stand by themselves.
nodes.response: When the wind catches them, they move or fall - windmills need ballast to secure them.

nodes.misconception: Artistic choices never change during the creative process.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists often make creative adjustments as they work, changing their ideas, materials, or processes based on how the artwork is developing.

nodes.misconception: Stitching onto paper is exactly the same as stitching onto fabric.
nodes.response: Remind children that stitching on paper requires a few things to be mindful of, including preparing holes in your paper and not pulling your thread too tightly.

nodes.misconception: A paper-cut printing process cannot be used to create multiple prints from the same templates.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists might choose this process as they can make multiple prints from the same templates.

nodes.misconception: A common mistake is inaccurate measuring which means the box frame will not be square.
nodes.response: It is important to measure accurately to make sure the box frame is square.

nodes.misconception: If the model looks good, it doesn’t matter if it does not stand properly.
nodes.response: A successful architectural model is both visually creative and structurally sound. Aim to build with purpose to create stability.

nodes.misconception: The position of axle holes and axles doesn't need to be accurately measured.
nodes.response: Axle holes and axles need to be positioned accurately on order for the wheels and pulleys to rotate correctly and produce the correct movement. Accurate measuring is essential.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find remembering the types and properties of quadrilaterals challenging.
nodes.response: Take time to repeat and revisit the key properties within the lesson and beyond. Consider providing a scaffold for some pupils so they can create quadrilaterals without having to recall the specific properties each time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to recognise that the properties of composed shapes may be different from the shapes they are composed of.
nodes.response: Drawing around compound shapes can really support children thinking about this as a 'new' shape with new properties.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may overgeneralise about the way a triangle should look e.g. not recognising a scalene triangle as a triangle.
nodes.response: Throughout the lesson, model different triangles in different orientations. Ensure pupils see boundary examples such as scalene triangles with one very small acute angle, or long and thin isosceles triangles.

nodes.misconception: German has one general verb meaning 'to put, putting'.
nodes.response: German has 3 placement verbs meaning 'to put'; 'stellen' - to make something stand (vertically), 'setzen' - to make something sit, and 'legen' - to make something lay down (horizontally). Equivalent position verbs are 'stehen', 'sitzen', 'liegen'.

nodes.misconception: A computer always types in capital letters.
nodes.response: The default for a keyboard is lower case letters. You need to use the caps lock/shift to type in capital letters.

nodes.misconception: Marbling prints can only be made in one way.
nodes.response: Marbling can be made in lots of different ways, such as ink or chalk  floating on water. Marbling can also be made with shaving foam.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that column subtraction is  always the most efficient strategy where regrouping is needed.
nodes.response: Emphasise calculations where adjustment is the most efficient strategy (e.g. 456 - 199). Regrouping is needed in both the tens and hundreds, but is is not the most efficient strategy.

nodes.misconception: Texture can only be shown with drawing or painting
nodes.response: Remind pupils that artists might choose to use clay to represent textures as it can show a wide range of different surfaces.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they will need to always use leaves when creating a frottage. Pupils may think frottage involves drawing objects such as leaves.
nodes.response: Frottage involves rubbing over textures, not drawing them. It captures the texture of surfaces rather than depicting them with lines. While leaves are commonly used, frottage can be done with various textured objects like coins or wood.

nodes.misconception: The word German is always 'allemand' with a lower case 'a' in French.
nodes.response: With a capital letter, Allemand is a noun meaning a person from Germany. With a lower case letter it is an adjective describing someone or something that comes from Germany and also a noun meaning the German language.

nodes.misconception: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
nodes.response: The unit is said before the ten in German, e.g., 'neunundvierzig' = '9 and 40' = 49. This can be very confusing for English speakers. It is helpful to write from right to left when taking down numbers so that you produce them in the correct order.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not recognise the new shape and only identify the smaller shapes it is composed of.
nodes.response: Using plastic shapes to compose a new shape and drawing around the shape can support pupils to see the properties of the new shape. Drawing around removes the joined sides inside the new polygon.

nodes.misconception: Air is empty because we can't see it.
nodes.response: Air takes up space and can make things move or change shape, such as when we inflate a balloon or a bike tyre.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that stop motion animation is the same as a video recording. They may think that you need expensive equipment to create stop motion animations.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that stop motion animation is created by taking individual still images. A video recording captures continuous motion. It can be created using simple and readily available devices.

nodes.misconception: Feedback is useful because people can tell you what you have done wrong and correct it for you.
nodes.response: Feedback is useful because people might raise your confidence by complimenting your hard work and they might be able to highlight improvements that you had not thought about.

nodes.misconception: Grouping an object turns all of the objects blue-coloured forever.
nodes.response: Objects can be ungrouped, which will return the objects to their original colours.

nodes.misconception: Testing needs to be completed at the end of the making task.
nodes.response: Through testing throughout the making process, any issues and changes can be addressed. This will make the product more successful.

nodes.misconception: Baking tins do not need to be greased and/or lined.
nodes.response: It is important to grease (with oil) or line (with greaseproof paper) a baking tin, as this acts as a barrier and prevents the food from sticking.

nodes.misconception: Collaborative art is just a group project with a leader.
nodes.response: Collaborative art is a collective process of co-creation where ideas and efforts are deeply intertwined.

nodes.misconception: A recipe cannot be changed, as it will not work.
nodes.response: Recipes can be changed, for example swapping chicken for chickpeas, or adding extra spices. The new recipe should be tested to make sure it works and tastes good.

nodes.misconception: Couscous is a grain.
nodes.response: Couscous is not a grain. However, couscous is made from semolina, which is coarsely ground durum wheat which is sprinkled with water and rolled to form small granules. It more closely resembles pasta.

nodes.misconception: When you put a placeholder inside a shape, make sure both of them are flat on the workspace with no gap.
nodes.response: If you don't raise the placeholder off the workplane so there is a hole at the bottom of the shape, the shape will be completely hollow and can't work as a container.

nodes.misconception: Branching databases can only be used to identify objects.
nodes.response: In the real world, branching databases can be used for many reasons such as finding faults and diagnosing illnesses.

nodes.misconception: There is always a correct solution to a geographical issue.
nodes.response: There is not a 'correct' answer to a geographical issue. Geographers try and balance economic, social and environmental concerns and use evidence to justify their opinion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a sandwich always uses sliced white bread.
nodes.response: Sandwiches can use a range of breads from around the world and are eaten often in many countries.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the amount of emissions per mile, pupils may forget to convert the information given from grams to kilograms.
nodes.response: Always check whether the units for any values given in the information match the units that are required for the formula.

nodes.misconception: When making pâté, they must always be cooked.
nodes.response: Not all pâtés must be cooked first, some are non-cook. This pâté uses canned mackerel (which is already cooked), soft cheese and vegetables. Vegan and vegetarian pâtés can also be made.

nodes.misconception: You don't need to sequence images or photographs you took on your route.
nodes.response: Sequencing photographs (keeping them in the correct order) helps us to remember a route correctly and helps us find the correct end point (destination).

nodes.misconception: Food lessons are just cooking.
nodes.response: Food lessons include cooking, which is important, but also applying healthy eating, where food comes from, safety (preventing accidents) and hygiene (making sure food is safe to eat), science, and consumer and food culture. Food is who we are.

nodes.misconception: All fruit and vegetables should be peeled before use.
nodes.response: Not all fruit and vegetables need to be peeled, such as apples and potatoes. The peel, or skin, can be tasty and be good for us. However, they should be washed to remove any dirt, insects and bacteria.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not understand that observing excess metal oxide in the reaction mixture means that the acid has fully reacted.
nodes.response: Emphasise how to observe the end of the reaction and what these observations mean, i.e. excess metal oxide in the reaction mixture or using pH paper to indicate the solution is neutral. Both are evidence of the acid having fully reacted.

nodes.misconception: UK seasonal fruit and vegetables tend to be more expensive.
nodes.response: UK seasonal fruit and vegetables tend to be less expensive, as there are lots of them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think of a circuit diagram as a map of a circuit when, in fact, it is a stylised representation that is drawn in a particular way to increase its clarity.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the diagram shows the sequence of the components in the circuit, not the position. A component can be moved to a different place but still be in the same sequence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that 'bad' weather is evidence against any drastic change in the climate.
nodes.response: Temperatures are rising, which leads to more extreme weather generally - not just to more dry and hot weather.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to summarise the main points of their essay into their speech.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add to their notes as they orally rehearse their speech, jotting down additional thoughts that come to them as they practise.

nodes.misconception: Testing your program once is enough.
nodes.response: Programs should be tested many times to find all bugs.

nodes.misconception: Food hygiene is only about being clean when preparing, cooking and storing food.
nodes.response: Food hygiene is necessary in order to prepare and cook food which is safe to eat. It involves the 4Cs: cleaning (including personal hygiene), cooking, chilling and preventing cross-contamination.

nodes.misconception: The base of a pizza is always covered in a sauce made from tomatoes.
nodes.response: While a sauce made from tomatoes is traditional, the base can also be covered in pesto, a cheese sauce, or just garlic and oil.

nodes.misconception: If a food is placed in the fridge, there is no need for it to be covered or placed in a container, as the fridge is a cold and safe storage area.
nodes.response: All food placed in the fridge must be covered or placed in a container to prevent cross contamination with other foods, preventing food poisoning. It also helps to stop the food drying out.

nodes.misconception: When baking, the baking trays (or foil trays) do not need to be greased or lined.
nodes.response: Baking trays (or foil trays) should be greased with a little oil, or lined with greaseproof paper, to create a barrier between the cake and the tray. The barrier helps to prevent the cake from sticking.

nodes.misconception: Potatoes can form part of our 5 A DAY.
nodes.response: Potatoes do not count towards our 5 A DAY. They are a starchy carbohydrate in the Eatwell Guide.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think ammonia is safe to handle without precautions because it's a common household chemical.
nodes.response: Emphasise ammonia's toxicity and the importance of using PPE and proper ventilation.

nodes.misconception: A salad must contain lettuce, cucumber and tomato.
nodes.response: Salads can contain a wide range of different ingredients. We can take inspiration from around the world and choose different ingredients.

nodes.misconception: The conductor is the only person responsible for keeping the pulse and pitch is only high and low.
nodes.response: The conductor can set the tempo but all performers are responsible for keeping the pulse in a performance. Pitch as high and low is slightly limiting. Help pupils make connections to other related words that they might know.

nodes.misconception: Points of information always have to be accepted by the speaker.
nodes.response: If points of information challenges are always accepted, a speech will be completely derailed, they should only accept one or two.

nodes.misconception: The flapjack recipe contains apple and sultanas, so must be part of our 5 A DAY.
nodes.response: No, the flapjack does not count towards our 5 A DAY. There is not enough fruit, and they are high in sugars and fat (from butter). If we eat these types of foods, we should have them occasionally and in small amounts.

nodes.misconception: Following the Eatwell Guide is only about eating more healthily.
nodes.response: While following the Eatwell Guide will help people eat more healthily, it also has a 32% lower environmental footprint, compared to the current national diet, so can help us eat more sustainably too.

nodes.misconception: When using the hob, boiling and simmering cooking methods are the same.
nodes.response: Boiling is at the boiling point, bubbling rapidly. Simmering is below the boiling point, bubbling gently.

nodes.misconception: Leftovers will still be safe to eat after 3 - 4 days, as they still look good.
nodes.response: Leftovers should be used within 48 hours from when it was made (24 hours for rice dishes). Longer periods of time increase the risk of food poisoning bacteria multiplying.

nodes.misconception: Everyone needs the same amount, or portion, of food.
nodes.response: Everyone needs slightly different amounts of food, depending on their age and activity levels.

nodes.misconception: Recipes cannot be modified.
nodes.response: Recipes can be modified, for different occasions and the needs of people. Ingredients can be changed and other ingredients added.

nodes.misconception: Cheese is only made with milk from dairy cows.
nodes.response: Cheese is made with milk from many animals, including goats, sheep, buffalo, reindeer and alpaca, as well as dairy cows.

nodes.misconception: Beans can count as many portions towards 5 A DAY, depending on the number of portions eaten.
nodes.response: Beans count as a maximum of one portion of 5 A DAY, no matter how much is eaten.

nodes.misconception: Any flour can be used to make a bread-like dough.
nodes.response: Although most flours will produce a dough, a strong flour is recommended as it is high in protein (gluten), which is needed to help trap the air and form the bread structure when baked.

nodes.misconception: Children may conclude that they can't make any mistakes with pens.
nodes.response: Emphasise to the children that pencils are used if there are going to be a lot of mistakes or changes like a sketch or a calculation. Explain that it's OK to make some mistakes with a pen and that these will need to be crossed out neatly.

nodes.misconception: A balanced digital life means using IT every day.
nodes.response: Balanced means making responsible choices in the way you use IT. It should not be seen as something that must be used every day.

nodes.misconception: An urban area should implement all of the strategies to make itself greener.
nodes.response: Not all strategies are viable for every urban area and some will be more effective than others depending on the location.

nodes.misconception: Believing that sustainability is only about the environment.
nodes.response: It relates to the social, economic and environmental impact of a city. This lesson focuses mainly on environmental issues but a city would not be judged to be sustainable if its citizens did not have their basic economic or social needs met.

nodes.misconception: Children may have questions or misconceptions around how the 'red-headed female heroine' is portrayed within stories.
nodes.response: It is important to explain that in life we do not judge somebody's qualities or traits based on their appearance. However, authors do sometimes use appearance to communicate certain messages.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see connections between Joseph and Adonis in the second task.
nodes.response: You may wish to discuss the idea of a metaphorical 'cage' midway through pupils' discussions, discussing ways in which Joseph is 'caged' by his difficulties.

nodes.misconception: That comparative essays should only focus on the differences between poems.
nodes.response: The most successful comparative essays focus on both the similarities and the differences between the poems.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to draw similarities between Walter's home life and life at war.
nodes.response: Modelling a few additional examples will support pupils e.g. he excelled in football and at war.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may label characters like Emily and Miss Murphy as simply 'bad', instead of trying to see their motivations.
nodes.response: Emphasise that giving reasons for someone's actions is not the same as excusing them; most things we do have a reason - that reason might just be a bad one!

nodes.misconception: Conjectures have to be correct so it's really hard to make a conjecture as you don't want to be wrong.
nodes.response: Conjectures are thought to be true but they may not be. This is why we test and see ways to prove whether a conjecture is true or not. It is perfectly acceptable for a conjecture to be proved wrong.

nodes.misconception: Effective comparative analysis leads by comparing the poets' use of literary methods.
nodes.response: The most effective comparative analysis writing should lead by comparing key ideas of attitudes in both poems.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the clothing mentioned in the slides are the only styles worn in Australia and Morocco.
nodes.response: Both countries have other forms of dress/attire - seen in the two scenes (hardware store, market). You could ask pupils to conduct more research into both cultures.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to agree on the placement of the statements in Task A.
nodes.response: Consider printing the statements and the Venn diagram, to allow pupils to move them as they discuss and work in small groups or pairs.

nodes.misconception: Any Cornish pasties made and sold in the UK can use the name ‘Cornish pasty’, as it is based on a recipe.
nodes.response: Only pasties made in Cornwall to a specific recipe can be called a ‘Cornish pasty’; it is legally protected in the UK by Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status.

nodes.misconception: Curry powder is a spice from a plant.
nodes.response: Curry powder is a mixture of different spices blended together, not a single spice.

nodes.misconception: Drawings can only be adjusted by eye view.
nodes.response: Using zoom, you can have a much more detailed view and make smaller adjustments.

nodes.misconception: We don't need to analyse the writer's attitude in non-fiction because it's all factual information.
nodes.response: Analysing the writer's attitude in non-fiction is important because it helps us to understand why the writer has presented information in a certain way and how they want us to interpret the information.

nodes.misconception: Mould on fruit, yogurt or bread can be cut off, so the remaining food can be eaten.
nodes.response: If food has mould, the food should not be eaten, especially with soft foods like bread, yogurt or fruit. It is unsafe to eat and can cause illness.

nodes.misconception: No matter the size of the scones, they are baked for the same length of time.
nodes.response: The heat from the oven will take longer to penetrate and cook the scones the bigger they are. Therefore smaller scones will cook more quickly than bigger scones.

nodes.misconception: Knowing the differences between mitosis and meiosis. In particular when they are used, the number of cell divisions and if variation is present.
nodes.response: The final learning cycle of the lesson serves to compare the features of mitosis and meiosis, this includes CFU questions and a practice task.

nodes.misconception: Sasusages contain meat, usually pork.
nodes.response: Many sausages contain meat, but there are many recipes that are vegetarian or vegan. Glamorgan sausages are vegetarian (as they contain cheese and egg).

nodes.misconception: A roux sauce can have all the liquid (milk) added at the same time, and whisked occasionally.
nodes.response: A roux sauce must have the liquid (milk) added gradually, and the sauce should be whisked continually to prevent lumps.

nodes.misconception: An object can be in both the 'yes' and the 'no' group, or neither group.
nodes.response: An object can only be in either the 'yes' or the 'no' group, not both or neither.

nodes.misconception: Coeliac disease is caused by a reaction to gluten in wheat flour only.
nodes.response: Coeliac disease is caused by a reaction to gluten (a protein), which is found in flours from wheat, barley and rye.

nodes.misconception: Students think that attitudes are often strong and one dimensional.
nodes.response: Encourage them to think about how it is possible for a book or a film to be both frightening and enjoyable.

nodes.misconception: People with an allergy cannot eat bread.
nodes.response: Some people have an allergy to flour made from wheat, which many breads are made from. There are other flours that can be used, so they can eat bread.

nodes.misconception: The dishes we cook, eat and serve, along with our food experiences, have stayed the same over time.
nodes.response: The dishes we cook, eat and serve, along with our food experiences, continue to evolve (change over time) due to a variety of factors, such as history, culture, social media and health.

nodes.misconception: Rice should be stirred when cooked, so ensure it is covered in liquid.
nodes.response: It is best not to stir most rice dishes. Stirring breaks the rice and releases starch, making the rice feel mushy and ‘over cooked’. Risotto is stirred though, as the starch helps the dish have a creamy texture.

nodes.misconception: Vegetables and fruit do not need to be washed before use as they look clean or have been taken from a packet.
nodes.response: Vegetables and fruit should be washed thoroughly before use. This removes dirt (soil/grit), insects and bacteria which could cause food poisoning.

nodes.misconception: For extra flavour in a recipe, only salt and pepper can be used.
nodes.response: There are lots of ingredients that could be used, such as spices, herbs, and other aromatic ingredients e.g. lemon grass, harissa.

nodes.misconception: The 'all-in-one' method produces poor results, as the ingredients are not creamed together and/or whisked.
nodes.response: The 'all-in-one method' is a quicker cake making method, producing good results. Using self-raising flour and mixing throughly ensure the cakes rise well.

nodes.misconception: You do not need to wash your hands after touching a raw egg.
nodes.response: You should always wash your hands after touching a raw egg. This helps to prevent the spread of bacteria. Some bacteria can cause food poisoning.

nodes.misconception: A sponge and cake are the same.
nodes.response: Often the term ‘sponge’ and ‘cake’ are used interchangeably. However, sponges are traditionally made from eggs, flour and sugar (no butter), e.g. Swiss roll, and cakes are made from eggs, flour, sugar and butter, e.g. lemon drizzle cake.

nodes.misconception: Sequence, retrograde and inversion are they only way to develop ideas and they have to be used perfectly.
nodes.response: Sequences, retrograde and inversion provide a concrete way for pupils to show development in their melodic ideas, but providing there is some similarity or recognisable quality in repeated ideas, any subtle changes within melodic ideas can work.

nodes.misconception: Augmentation and diminution are not the same as augmented and diminished.
nodes.response: Augmentation and diminution are devices that affect the rhythm of music. Augmented and diminished are types of chords and refer to the harmony of music.

nodes.misconception: When making two recipes at the same time, you should cook them separately in order. This takes longer, but the recipes are made well.
nodes.response: When making two dishes at the same time, read both recipes first to decide which order to complete the steps in each recipe - this is known as dovetailing. Dovetailing results in a better use of time, where tasks fit together easily.

nodes.misconception: All plants and animals 'eat' food.
nodes.response: Explanation of how plants can make their own food and that animals cannot.

nodes.misconception: Limited understanding of what a supply chain is.
nodes.response: Refer back to the example of commercial bread production in Lesson 1. Investigate the supply chain of other common food products.

nodes.misconception: Components of a parallel circuit must match the exact layout of a circuit diagram.
nodes.response: Focus on pupils starting at one end of the battery and building each loop up in turn, focusing on putting the connections in the correct order.

nodes.misconception: Bread dough does not need to be kneaded.
nodes.response: Bread dough should be kneaded for 10 minutes, as it helps it to become smooth and elastic. Kneading helps the dough to rise.

nodes.misconception: Hands only need to be washed and dried before and after cooking.
nodes.response: Hands should also be washed and dried well after touching the bin, blowing your nose, and cleaning.

nodes.misconception: Traditional fried falafel is healthy, as it is made from chickpeas.
nodes.response: While the chickpeas are a healthy choice, falafel is usually deep-fried, so less healthy. Alternative cooking methods could be used which use less oil, such as grilling, baking, or air-frying.

nodes.misconception: Designs need to be decided upon and followed.
nodes.response: Final designs can be adapted and changed, even during the making process. This is because it is always good to be reflective throughout the making process.

nodes.misconception: Children often use an apostrophe s, when they hear an 's' at the end of the word.
nodes.response: Remind children of the rules for using apostrophes.  Only use an apostrophe if you can name and recognise the rule - for omission or possession.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to spell the root word of plural nouns in focus.
nodes.response: For children who need more support, provide the root word (singluar noun) as a starting point for Practise Task B, so they can focus on securing the rules around plurals.

nodes.misconception: A speaker does not need to follow a set structure when making a speech in a debate.
nodes.response: There are many benefits to following a structure when making a speech in a debate.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be used to analysing picturebook texts in finer detail.
nodes.response: Adults could model text marking - asking questions and interrogating certain pages. Thoughts could be verbalised to model possible processes that you would encourage the pupils to use.

nodes.misconception: It is better to know everything about a character or text before reading.
nodes.response: Making predictions can help us with our comprehension of complex texts and independent thinking.

nodes.misconception: You can bake cookies of different sizes on the same tray, making a bigger one for yourself.
nodes.response: The cookies need to be the same size, for even cooking. If smaller, they will burn, if bigger, they will be undercooked.

nodes.misconception: The dried fruit in rock cakes counts towards our 5 A DAY.
nodes.response: The dried fruit does not count towards our 5 A DAY, as it is in small amounts. Rock cakes are sweet foods, containing sugar and fat. We need to eat less of these types of foods.

nodes.misconception: Scotch eggs originate from Scotland.
nodes.response: While its name may sound Scottish, the Scotch egg has origins in 1738 London (a snack for travellers), India (nargisi kofta), and Yorkshire (a fish version).

nodes.misconception: Thinking that everyone else's emotional state is as it appear to be.
nodes.response: People can’t support you if they don’t know you need it. When someone wears an emotional mask, it’s hard to know the real person.

nodes.misconception: Shadows contain details of the object, such as facial features of a human’s shadow. Also that a shadow can be a different shape to the object, and formed in between the light source and the object.
nodes.response: Explanation of how shadows are formed.

nodes.misconception: All sushi includes raw fish.
nodes.response: Although raw fish is a common ingredient, not all sushi includes fish. Other ingredients are used, such as vegetables, fruit, egg, and cooked fish and meat.

nodes.misconception: Spring rolls are always fried.
nodes.response: Spring rolls can be oven baked or steamed. There are many different varieties.

nodes.misconception: Recipes cannot be modified for different budgets, as the stated ingredients must always be used.
nodes.response: Recipes can be modified for different budgets, using a number of strategies, such as comparing costs, buying own-brand items, and using seasonal fruit and vegetables.

nodes.misconception: The Eatwell Guide recommends a plant-rich, non-meat diet.
nodes.response: The Eatwell Guide recommends that we should have a plant-rich diet and reduce the amount of red and processed meat, if we eat too much.

nodes.misconception: All fish is the same.
nodes.response: There are lots of different types of fish in the world. They look, smell and taste different. Tuna is one type of fish.

nodes.misconception: You do not need to get ready to cook every time you prepare and cook food.
nodes.response: We should always get ready to cook, so that we are hygienic (clean).

nodes.misconception: When cooking it is fine not to weigh and measure accurately, approximate measurements are fine.
nodes.response: It is important to weigh and measure ingredients accuarely, so that the recipe works well.

nodes.misconception: Shortcrust pastry works best when cold butter (or baking fat) and water are used. If warm, the fat is harder to rub into the flour, and the pasty is hard to roll-out and use.
nodes.response: Make sure the butter or baking fat is cold, and that pupils use cold water, this helps to ensure that the pastry works better.  When rubbing-in the fat to the flour, use fingertips only, as less heat is passed from the hands to the fat.

nodes.misconception: Sushi, raw fish, is the only common food eaten in Japan.
nodes.response: Japan has huge range of foods and dishes, of which sushi is one important aspect. There is a range of cooked dishes, including yakisoba (noodles), teriyaki (grilled with a glaze), yakiniku (grilled meat), and tempura (battered fried foods).

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that interlocking requires us to connect together using our hands and arms.
nodes.response: Interlocking involves two or more things fitting together or overlapping, which could be done using a range of different body parts.

nodes.misconception: You can only get malware on a computer if you download a file.
nodes.response: Malware can infect a computer in other ways, like visiting unsafe websites, clicking bad links, or through software flaws, not just by downloading files.

nodes.misconception: Malware only affects computers, not phones or tablets.
nodes.response: Malware can infect any idevice that is connected to the internet, including smartphones, tablets and smart TVs. Mobile malware is increasingly common and can steal data, track location or lock users out of their devices — just like on computers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans are not animals, but something different.
nodes.response: When mammals are discussed in the lesson, remind pupils that humans are animals and mammals because of their shared characteristics.

nodes.misconception: All adaptation strategies are expensive and complex.
nodes.response: Some adaptation strategies are cost-effective and simple, such as rainwater harvesting and crop rotation.

nodes.misconception: Individuals cannot make significant contributions to mitigation.
nodes.response: Although national and international mitigation strategies are essential to achieve meaingful mitigation of climate change, individual actions, such as reducing energy use, collectively contribute to mitigation efforts.

nodes.misconception: Exclusive focus on winning limits satisfaction and enjoyment.
nodes.response: Games like Kubb should be as much about the enjoyable social experience and finding ways to support each other as well as demonstrating honesty and fair play as winning the match.

nodes.misconception: You need to include 'pas' when using a negative subject pronoun.
nodes.response: The whole negative meaning is contained in the negative subject pronoun (rien or personne) with 'ne' before the following verb. An additional negative element is not necessary e.g. Personne ne mange sainement - nobody eats healthily.

nodes.misconception: Removing mangroves on the coast will not affect people inland or out at sea.
nodes.response: Mangroves provide many services, including flood protection for settlements inland and nurseries for young fish (who may be caught for food when they have grown and left the protection of the mangroves).

nodes.misconception: Shapes in Tinkercad can only be created from scratch.
nodes.response: The shape library has a range of prepared objects that can be added to a workplane.

nodes.misconception: Generative AI always has a negative affect on society.
nodes.response: Generative AI isn't always negative; it depends on its use. Generative AI tools can help artists, educators and scientists create innovative designs, engaging learning materials and advanced simulations.

nodes.misconception: Drawing always has to be neat, precise, and done with traditional materials like pencil.
nodes.response: Artists can experiment with non-traditional materials and looser techniques like splashes, drips and sprays to develop freedom and unexpected results.

nodes.misconception: Each object has to be worked on one at a time.
nodes.response: Objects can be grouped together to duplicate or edit at the same time.

nodes.misconception: Distorting a photograph with manipulation techniques only damages it.
nodes.response: In art, photos are not just static records of the past; they are versatile tools that can be reinterpreted and manipulated to express new ideas and perspectives.

nodes.misconception: It is impossible for large numbers of people to cross the Sahara Desert.
nodes.response: Although extremely dangerous, the Sahara Desert has been crossed many times by large groups of people. Large amounts of provisions are needed though, which is why it is not a common occurrance.

nodes.misconception: Every character is a foil to another because all characters are different.
nodes.response: Whilst characters, like humans, are unique, not every character serves as a foil. Strangely, character foils often have similarities in terms of who they are, and what has happened to them, but their reactions to these things are different.

nodes.misconception: Quality is only considered when the product has been completed.
nodes.response: Quality is considered at all stages of manufacture.

nodes.misconception: Fairtrade is just the label on bananas.
nodes.response: Fairtrade is a system that ensures farmers and workers receive fair prices, decent working conditions and support for sustainable community development through trade.

nodes.misconception: The only environmental decision at the manufacture and materials processing stage is the choice between renewable/non renewable sources of energy.
nodes.response: Environmental decisions include sources of energy, use of recycled materials, sustainable land management such as deforestation, pollution including water pollution and transportation. During manufacture, ethical impacts should also be considered.

nodes.misconception: Students become so busy manufacturing their design solution that they often forget to evidence their manufacture.
nodes.response: It's easy to overlook the effort behind a product from the final photo. Documenting the manufacturing process highlights the skills, techniques, safety, and quality checks students use, proving their work, not the technician's.

nodes.misconception: Manufacturing process selection is solely based on cost.
nodes.response: Factors like product complexity, material properties, production volume, and lead time also play crucial roles.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils will assume that they know how to manufacture their design without the need for a manufacturing specification.
nodes.response: Designs are rarely understood by verbal explanation, they need visual representations with specific details of materials, dimensions, finishes and suitable processes. Communication methods will vary depending on your design.

nodes.misconception: Manufacturing specifications only include dimensions and materials.
nodes.response: Manufacturing specifications also include finishes, safety requirements, assembly instructions and what tasks need completing. These details ensure that a product is made correctly, safely, and consistently.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a value has to be added to each term in an expression.
nodes.response: When adding a term to an expression we can write it as a single addition and then collect like terms if necessary. Show with numbers first

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to align north on the compass with north on the map before navigating
nodes.response: Hold the compass next to the arrow representing magnetic north on the map and rotate your body until the arrow on the map and the arrow on the compass line up with north, then keep the map facing that way even when you change direction.

nodes.misconception: Trees are a renewable resource and can just be cut down then replanted without any negative impact.
nodes.response: It can take hundreds of years for some woodland to become established with the same benefits. It is important to protect the global forests that we currently have.

nodes.misconception: All non-coniferous woodland is ancient.
nodes.response: Using historical maps we can see if deciduous woodland has been recently planted - like the National Forest in the Midlands.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that older parts of a place have not changed since they have been built.
nodes.response: Use the photographs and evidence from fieldwork to challenge these misconceptions.

nodes.misconception: Maps in art are literal,
nodes.response: Artists might use mapping through literal geography, map-like work or more abstract or subjective representations of movement, memory, and relationships.

nodes.misconception: All symbols on the map key are universal.
nodes.response: Some map keys use different symbols for different places. It's important to check the key to make sure you know each symbol means on that particular map as it might mean something different to what you are used to.

nodes.misconception: Places on the route can be visited in a random order.
nodes.response: A route has a start point and end point and the stops in between help us find the last place of our route. If we visit places in a different order we may get lost.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the local area is either one particular place or has a particular size.
nodes.response: Share examples of where we go, and think about this in the context of everyday lives in urban and rural areas, using different examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that cliffs and headlands are the same thing or that all cliffs are headlands.
nodes.response: A headland is surrounded on three sides by water. Headlands can consist of cliffs, but cliffs can be found on coastlines that are not headlands. So it is true to say that not all cliffs are headlands, therefore cliffs and headlands are not the same.

nodes.misconception: Africa is country.
nodes.response: The continent of Africa contains 54 countries.

nodes.misconception: Coniferous forests are all recently planted.
nodes.response: There are some remaining ancient Caledonian pinewood forests in Scotland which are coniferous.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that maps show only real places, exactly as they are in real life.
nodes.response: Artists create expressive maps from their memory and imagination that may not look like real life.

nodes.misconception: We can add just one word to make a sentence negative in French, like the English word 'not'.
nodes.response: In French, we have to add two words to make a sentence negative, these are sandwiched around the verb: 'ne' and 'pas' (je ne chante pas).

nodes.misconception: In a written dictation in German, the only thing that matters is the correct sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs).
nodes.response: SSCs are important, but the text needs to make sense grammatically. Check for correct spelling of known words, verb forms and tenses, and singular or plural nouns. Encourage students to check the details and to read back the texts in their head.

nodes.misconception: Every mark or shape needs to be identical and placed in a perfectly regular sequence to make a pattern.
nodes.response: Remind children that patterns do not always have to be exactly the same each time, but they still follow a rule or idea.

nodes.misconception: When observing a stimulus, it is best to respond using pencil.
nodes.response: Different stimuli, call for different methods like, loose washes, impasto, detailed line work, collage, etc. Matching technique to stimuli ensures the artwork communicates its idea effectively.

nodes.misconception: All paintings are made with paint brushes.
nodes.response: Using different types of tools helps abstract artists create lots of different types of expressive marks and textures in their work.

nodes.misconception: Art materials must be bought rather than made.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can buy their ink from a shop, but they can also make their own from natural materials.

nodes.misconception: Artists start a painting or drawing on a plain piece of paper
nodes.response: Often artists create surfaces and backgrounds to work on, it makes the piece have less gaps and is interesting to work over.

nodes.misconception: Any marking tool will work on any material.
nodes.response: Using the wrong tool (e.g a pencil on metal) can result in unclear or inaccurate marks. Different materials require specific marking tools, such as pencils for paper and boards and marking knives for wood.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not start counting from the origin (0,0) but from another point on the grid, leading to incorrect placement of the point.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of always starting from the origin when plotting or describing coordinates. Have students physically point to or touch the origin before plotting any point.

nodes.misconception: Each defender can only mark 1 attacker.
nodes.response: Netball positions are paired, however the competitive situation will determine if players swap, if they double mark and which stage of defence they need at that point.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think defence is a solo effort and only needed when marking the player with the ball.
nodes.response: Individual defensive skills are crucial, however defending as a cohesive unit leads to the attacking team being denied space and vision to move the ball.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils commit to zone defence but others get distracted into chasing the ball, therefore moving out of position.
nodes.response: It is essential that all team members follow the same defensive strategy of player-to-player or zonal marking to avoid leaving big gaps.

nodes.misconception: All the most important people in the Jesus movement were male.
nodes.response: There are many stories in the Gospels which show that Jesus gave women power and challenged how they were treated in society.

nodes.misconception: A single person cannot shape history by themselves.
nodes.response: The Great Man Theory in History - the idea that a single person is responsible for important events - is somewhat outdated, but occasionally, as is the case with Martin Luther, an argument can be made that individuals can radically shape events.

nodes.misconception: That Martin Luther King was an important figure in the Protestant Reformation.
nodes.response: Martin Luther King lived in the 20th century, but was named after Martin Luther who lived in the 16th century when the Protestant Reformation happened.

nodes.misconception: Martin Luther King Jr had always been part of the civil rights movement.
nodes.response: King entered the spotlight following the Montgomery Bus Boycott and became a successful, popular leader as he was not associated with any large organisations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that during the time that Mary Anning lived women did not work in science.
nodes.response: Explaining to the pupils that Mary Anning was a trail blazer and, although it was difficult for her to work in the field of science, she continued to prove new theories and develop knowledge of fossils.

nodes.misconception: Philosophy is just abstract thinking and doesn’t apply to everyday life.
nodes.response: Some people think philosophy is just for debates or theories, but Mary Midgley shows it’s actually a practical tool for thinking clearly about real issues like animal welfare.

nodes.misconception: That the Immaculate Conception is when Mary conceived Jesus miraculously through the Holy Spirit.
nodes.response: The Immaculate Conception is the Roman Catholic belief that Mary was born without sin. When the Angel Gabriel greets her for the first time she is called ‘Mary, full of Grace’, which would mean she was without sin even before Jesus is born.

nodes.misconception: Macduff acts as a foil to Macbeth solely because he is noble and courageous.
nodes.response: Ask pupils if Macbeth had dealt with his grief/devastation like Macduff would there have been different outcomes?

nodes.misconception: A single thick layer of modroc will create a strong sculpture.
nodes.response: Modroc works best when thin layers are built up gradually. This allows the material to dry properly and allows the sculpture to become stronger.

nodes.misconception: All masks are used for disguise.
nodes.response: Masks can also be used for cultural ceremonies, art and storytelling.

nodes.misconception: My sculpture has to look like a real person to say something important.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that sculptures can be bold, simplified or abstract and still carry strong messages. Artists like Sokari Douglas Camp use pose, pattern and costume to express complex ideas about history, power and pride.

nodes.misconception: Children may not read scales accurately, particularly when the type of scale changes from a horizontal line to a circular scale.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities to explore different types of scales. Find where the same mass would be on different scales and talk about what is the same and what is different about each scale.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: Students may believe that mass movement only occurs in mountainous areas or during extreme weather events.
nodes.response: Mass movement can happen anywhere there are slopes, even in places with mild weather conditions. While extreme weather can trigger events, even light rainfall can cause mass movement if the slope is steep or the material is already weathered.

nodes.misconception: In 3D or sculptural work, mass is just about how much it weighs and its physical presence.
nodes.response: Mass can be symbolic due to the materials used. Materials can carry more or less visual weight.

nodes.misconception: All peaks in a mass spectrum represent intact (and neutral) molecules or atoms.
nodes.response: Clarify that in mass spectrometry, all detected peaks represent ionised species, not neutral molecules or atoms. The peaks can correspond to either the molecular ion (M⁺) or smaller ionised fragments, as well as different isotopes of an element.

nodes.misconception: It might be believed that certain sports only require one type of practice structure.
nodes.response: Practice structures vary depending on the skills being practiced and the level of ability. Two different skills from within the same sport might benefit from different practice structures.

nodes.misconception: Annotations can replace the need for a clear and accurate sketch.
nodes.response: Annotation provides further explanation or clarification on what is not visible in the sketch.

nodes.misconception: I can effectively practise my presentation in my head.
nodes.response: Although it is good to think about your presentation, you will need to practise delivering it out loud. This will give you a much better idea of timing and pace.

nodes.misconception: There may be issues with group dynamics as pupils have to negotiate which movements they will use when working in bigger groups. Not all pupils in the group may be able to perform the movements.
nodes.response: Pupils may have to delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups. Pupils may have to consider adapting their sequences when working with bigger groups.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to distinguish between a matching and mirroring movement. Pupils struggle to execute their movements simultaneously.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to work with peers to check whether a movement is matching or mirroring. Pupils should work on communication to improve their synchronisation.

nodes.misconception: Forming a capital letter is just doing the lower case letter formation bigger.
nodes.response: Highlight every time the lower case and capital letter is different so it is clear the formation is different not just the size.

nodes.misconception: All film music has to be precise to the second to fit the action perfectly.
nodes.response: Some film scenes do have to be exact where the music mirrors precisely what is happening on screen, but much film music is about creating the correct atmosphere and feel and this can be just as important when composing programmatic music.

nodes.misconception: When pupils perform their sequence on apparatus, they lose control, extension and flow.
nodes.response: Make sure that pupils carefully consider how they can adapt their sequences to work on apparatus so they don't lose quality. Pupils can also focus on communication to help improve the quality of their sequence on apparatus.

nodes.misconception: One pupil always leads the other. Only one pupil can perform the movement with quality.
nodes.response: Use strategies such as counting or music to help pupils move at the same time. Encourage pupils to ensure that both of them can perform the skills, and if they can't, they should work on improving or changing the movement.

nodes.misconception: Textiles are not made from fossil fuels.
nodes.response: Synthetic fibres are usually made from fossil fuels such a polyester and ripstop nylon.

nodes.misconception: The cheapest material is always the best choice.
nodes.response: Material selection involves balancing multiple factors, such as strength, durability, weight, sustainability, and ease of manufacturing; in addition to cost.

nodes.misconception: The atmosphere is made up of mainly oxygen and carbon dioxide.
nodes.response: Explain that Earth's atmosphere is delicately balanced. There is enough oxygen to maintain life, and enough carbon dioxide to help insulate the planet, maintaining the temperature that allows life to exist.

nodes.misconception: The water cycle only includes the processes of evaporation from the Earth's surface to the atmosphere and condensation returning water to the Earth.
nodes.response: There is exemplification of how the water cycle involves percolation of water into the ground and how plants use this water. Some of this is released by transpiration.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that soft means smooth. Younger pupils may find it hard to describe a material based only on its properties (and not its function).
nodes.response: Opportunities to rehearse expressing ideas and describing properties. Teacher to model and correct as necessary, making clear the difference between the function of an object and the properties of its material(s).

nodes.misconception: There is only one suitable material for each product.
nodes.response: There are many different materials which can be suitable once a choice has been made; it is important to explain and justify this.

nodes.misconception: Recycling is good for the environment.
nodes.response: Recycling ensures that materials are useful for longer before being discarded, but the processing is an envionmental cost.

nodes.misconception: The word material can be challenging, it has a different meaning in everyday life. Understanding that an alloy is a mixture and not a compound is hard because the elements are difficult to separate.
nodes.response: Provide lots of different examples of materials and use the word correctly within the scientific contexts. An alloy is the exception to the rule and is separated by thermal or chemical processes.

nodes.misconception: Choosing materials is always based on aesthetics.
nodes.response: Many factors determine the material choice, such as the purpose and environment of the product. For example, MDF is absorbent and not suitable for damp or humid places, unless finished with a waterproof layer.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Examples of different objects made from different materials to promote discussion of the properties of materials.

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Reminders of the difference between the object, what it is used for, and the material it is made from. Use of real-life objects for children to explore to aid this understanding.

nodes.misconception: Wood, plastic and fabric are the correct terminology
nodes.response: Timbers and boards, polymers and textiles are the correct terms

nodes.misconception: Mathematical operations cannot be performed on items held in a list; the items must first be stored in a new variable.
nodes.response: Mathematical operations can be performed directly on list items by using an index value to reference the value used.

nodes.misconception: Women were forbidden from ruling in their own right in England during the medieval period.
nodes.response: The first time the concept of a woman ruling in her own right in England occurred it took everyone by surprise. No one had considered that a woman might rule alone, so there was no law preventing it from happening.

nodes.misconception: Once a king dies or is taken prisoner, that is the end of the war.
nodes.response: Although a king is very important, there are many examples throughout history of a king's followers continuing to fight on successfully after their leader has been killed or captured.

nodes.misconception: Women in England were not allowed to fight in wars.
nodes.response: We have many examples of women leading the defence of castles throughout English history, and occasionally leading the attack on enemy territory as well.  It was uncommon, but not unheard of.

nodes.misconception: It has always been illegal for children to get married.
nodes.response: Throughout history, royal children were regularly betrothed at a young age in order to secure alliances between nations. Marriage followed later when the children had grown up, although they regularly still married younger than we do today.

nodes.misconception: Barons must obey the their monarch's orders.
nodes.response: Although this is true in theory, in reality the barons and their monarch worked as a partnership: the monarch relied upon the barons and if they weren't doing a good enough job, they could expect to lose the support of their barons.

nodes.misconception: Asking yes/no questions in the past is much more complicated than the present tense, as the rules are different. You need to translate 'did'.
nodes.response: The English 'did' isn't needed. Swap subject and verb for a yes/no question. 'Er sprach' (imperfect) becomes 'Sprach er?'. In the perfect tense, the past participle stays at the end of the sentence: 'Er hat gesprochen' - 'Hat er gesprochen?'.

nodes.misconception: All Christians renew vows on Maundy Thursday.
nodes.response: Deacons, priests and bishops from the Church of England church renew their ordination vows on Maundy Thursday.

nodes.misconception: Angelou copied Dunbar. Copying is not allowed.
nodes.response: Many writers learn from, and are inspired by, others. Angelou's poem is very different to Dunbar's - her personal style and voice come through - but the central metaphor 'speaks' from one poem to another, developing a relationship between them.

nodes.misconception: You shouldn't talk about poems as a group. This will make your comments too general.
nodes.response: You can make clear comments about a poet's work as a whole, as long as these comments are supported by specific examples from specific poems.

nodes.misconception: When you skip, you always travel forwards.
nodes.response: Skipping often involves travelling forwards, but it can also be performed on the spot or even travelling backwards.

nodes.misconception: Final consonants that are pronounced in English are also pronounced in French.
nodes.response: The letters d, s, t and x are usually silent at the end of words in French.

nodes.misconception: Covenants are only found in the Old Testament or Torah.
nodes.response: Many covenants are found in the Old Testament or Torah, but the new covenant is contained within the New Testament.

nodes.misconception: The means of salvation are grace, Jesus, biblical law and the Holy Spirit, which are distinct and separate from each other.
nodes.response: These concepts are intertwined. Grace can come through Jesus, the law of the Bible and the Holy Spirit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might count a part square - such as a triangle - as one square unit.
nodes.response: The slides show two parts moving together to make a whole square. Cutting out and physically moving the parts is an effective strategy.

nodes.misconception: Some children may find it difficult to align the cubes with the ends of the objects, particularly when the object cannot be placed close to the cubes because it is curved or an irregular shape.
nodes.response: Use objects such as pencils and pens that can be placed close to the cubes, or support children with aligning the start of the object with the cubes by placing them both against a wall or a straight object such as a book.

nodes.misconception: The length or height of an object is the numerical value at the end of the ruler (if not at zero).
nodes.response: If an object is not measured from zero, its length is the difference between the numerical value at the start and end of the object.

nodes.misconception: Children may align the end of their object with the end of the ruler, rather than zero.
nodes.response: Use a sticker or coloured pen to highlight the zero on the ruler so that children's attention is drawn to the zero when they are measuring length using a ruler.

nodes.misconception: Children may not use cubes accurately, for example leaving gaps between the objects. They may also miscount the cubes.
nodes.response: Encourage children to build a straight line of cubes with no gaps first, then place the object they want to measure along the line of cubes. Encourage them to touch each cube as they count.

nodes.misconception: Children may not use objects to measure accurately, for example following the shape of the object they are measuring rather than placing objects in a straight line. They may miscount the objects.
nodes.response: Encourage children to build a straight line of objects with no gaps first, then place the object they want to measure along the line. Encourage them to touch each object as they count.

nodes.misconception: Children may not use objects to measure accurately, for example leaving gaps between the objects. They may also miscount the objects.
nodes.response: Encourage children to build a straight line of objects with no gaps first, then place the object they want to measure along the line. Encourage them to touch each object as they count.

nodes.misconception: Composition of 1,000 is Year 4 content so children may make mistakes when giving masses in kg and g.
nodes.response: Use of stem sentences to help: 1,000 is composed of __ equal parts of __.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils count fractions of a square, such as a right-angles triangle, as a whole square unit.
nodes.response: Cut out the shape to show that two ‘parts’ of a square sometimes go together to make a complete square unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that an area of one square metre has to be in the shape of a square.
nodes.response: Take two large pieces of paper, each one square metre, and fold them in half in different ways. Bring them together to form a square metre.

nodes.misconception: Misreading of scales by counting marks rather than equal parts in between the marked intervals.
nodes.response: Remember to look at the number of equal parts in between the marked intervals then use your knowledge of the composition of 100.

nodes.misconception: Pupils incorrectly place the protractor on the angle and therefore cannot measure the angle. Pupils use the incorrect scale to read the angle.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of using the middle spot on the protractor to line this up with the vertex of the angle as well as placing one of the lines on a zero line, ensuring the remaining line crosses the scale of the protractor.

nodes.misconception: Children further learn about the composition of 1,000 in Y4, so may make mistakes in reading scales.
nodes.response: Rehearse 1,000 is composed of two equal parts of 500 ml, four equal parts of 250 ml, five equal parts of 200 ml, 10 equal parts of 100 ml.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare their progress to other pupils and feel disappointed if others have made a faster rate of progress.
nodes.response: Progress is personal and depends on many things - starting fitness, goals, technique and even how well rested you are on test day. Even small amounts of progress should be celebrated.

nodes.misconception: Mega is larger than giga.
nodes.response: The order of prefixes from smallest to largest is kilo, mega, giga, tera.

nodes.misconception: Bits and bytes are the same thing. They all refer to binary numbers.
nodes.response: A bit is the smallest unit of data. A byte is a group of 8 bits and is used to summarise larger sequences of bits in a more convenient way.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.

nodes.misconception: GDP per capita is the most effective way to measure development.
nodes.response: Although useful, GDP per capita is not as effective as composite indicators such as HDI, which include a measure of health and education

nodes.misconception: Children may not be familiar with tally charts as a method of recording.
nodes.response: Practise reading and writing tallies prior to the lesson would support their understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often analyse circuits sequentially, starting from the battery, which makes predicting what current does at a junction impossible.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to analyse each complete loop of a parallel circuit as whole loops. The currents through each loop then add to give the current through the battery (rather than current from the battery miraculously ‘knowing’ how to split at a junction).

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the mass or weight of an object with density.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a range of objects of varying sizes that they are going to measure the density of. Before measuring density, ask the pupils to rank the objects in order of density with explanations. Compare results to the list after measurements.

nodes.misconception: That everyone in a country with a high GNI is well off, with a good quality of life.
nodes.response: A country’s income is not equally divided by everyone who lives there. This is why GNI per head should be used along side other measures in order to understand differences in quality of life.

nodes.misconception: Earthquakes are their strongest at their epicentre.
nodes.response: Earthquakes are felt their strongest at their epicentre as that is where humans first feel them. Earthquakes are actually their strongest at their focus point, but humans do not feel them until seismic waves have travelled through the Earth's crust.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often hold a consumption model of electric current, believing it is used up in a circuit. They misuse the terms voltage, current and electricity, and may choose a voltmeter to measure current.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to investigate the size of the current through a range of different conductors (and insulators) using an ammeter in a simple circuit. This will help them become familiar with the ammeter and its correct use.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are often unable to match their experience of different forces with forces in newtons.
nodes.response: Pupils are provided with opportunity to both measure and describe a range of forces.

nodes.misconception: It is important for the same person to take all the measurements.
nodes.response: Emphasise that if the method is a good one then everyone carrying it out carefully should get similar results that show the same pattern (the results are repeatable and reproducible).

nodes.misconception: It is important for the same person to take all the measurements.
nodes.response: Emphasise that if the method is a good one then everyone carrying it out carefully should get similar results that show the same pattern (the results are repeatable and reproducible).

nodes.misconception: When the trolley is released, it speeds up quickly at the start and then rolls at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Show a video of an accelerating trolley in slow motion identifying the distance travelled in successive equal intervals of time.

nodes.misconception: When the trolley is released it speeds up quickly at the start and then rolls at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Show a video of an accelerating trolley in slow motion, identifying the distance travelled in successive equal intervals of time.

nodes.misconception: The length or height of an object is the numerical value at the end of the ruler (if not at zero).
nodes.response: If an object is not measured from zero, its length is the difference between the numerical value at the start and end of the object.

nodes.misconception: Only shiny surfaces reflect light. Light does not always travel in straight lines when it bounces off a mirror.
nodes.response: The lesson gives the children a chance to explore reflection of light in mirrors to see for themselves that it does reflect in a straight line.

nodes.misconception: To measure the angle where light hits a surface, measure in between the beam of light and the surface.
nodes.response: The lesson gives children an opportunity to explore a new concept: the normal line. They should become familiar with measuring between the beam of light and the normal line drawn at a right angle to the surface.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the time periods discussed in this lesson.
nodes.response: You could make a washing line timeline in the classroom with dates familiar to the children as markers then add the maps to the timeline.

nodes.misconception: A systematic error can be spotted by taking repeat readings.
nodes.response: Discuss why the heating of the beaker when measuring specific heat capacity of water will always increase energy measured by the same proportion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils commonly confuse instantaneous and average speeds.
nodes.response: Be very careful when using the word speed, always use 'average' or 'instantaneous' explicitly, linking average speed to a time period.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the constant force on the trolley will cause it to move at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that the trolly speeds up as it rolls, by finding speed near the start and near the end of the ramp.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often estimate the temperature of an object based on its materials, rather than the temperature of the surroundings.
nodes.response: Measure the temperature of several things that are all at room temperature such as water, sand and the air, in order to show that they are all the same.

nodes.misconception: The gradient of an I–V graph is equal to 1/R because I = V ÷ R.
nodes.response: Explain how the equation for a straight line graph y = mx + c does not apply in this case because the graph is not a straight line.

nodes.misconception: The terms current, voltage, resistance, energy and power, together with the properties of each, are often mixed up.
nodes.response: As each term is introduced during this lesson, spend a few moments checking pupils’ understanding.

nodes.misconception: Many pupils believe that in order to determine a population size within a habitat, all organisms within a habitat have to be counted.
