nodes.response: Populations can be estimated using sampling techniques. As long as a sample size is large enough, it will provide a reliable estimate of the population size. Pupils should understand that counting all individuals in a habitat is very difficult to do.

nodes.misconception: If measurements are repeatable (or precise) then they will also be accurate.
nodes.response: Repeatable (or precise) measurements may involve a systematic error making them inaccurate.

nodes.misconception: Calculating a mean of repeat readings reduces (random) errors in measurements.
nodes.response: Calculating a mean reduces the effect that random errors have on a final result. The random errors in the original readings are unaffected.

nodes.misconception: Children may read the scale incorrectly - confusion between equal parts and marks on the scale.
nodes.response: The scale is a number line. Remember to look at the number of equal parts between the marked numbers not the marks themselves.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that volume of sound cannot be measured, as they may not have encountered equipment or the units of measurement for doing so.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities to measure the volume of a range of everyday sounds so that pupils become familiar with decibel levels.

nodes.misconception: Using a thermometer to take a reading is an accurate representation of the temperature.
nodes.response: Temperature can change depending on the time of day. When taking the temperature and comparing it over time, it needs to be taken at the same time everyday to make it a fair test.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are likely to use the words current, voltage, power, and energy interchangeably. They often have a consumption model of current and believe that voltage flows through a circuit.
nodes.response: It is essential that pupils distinguish between the current flowing through the circuit (which is conserved), the energy stored in the cell or battery and transferred elsewhere, and the voltage across the cell, battery or component.

nodes.misconception: In the equation for the speed of a wave, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and/or wavelength.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the speed of a wave depends only on the wave medium and not on frequency or wavelength.

nodes.misconception: In the equation for the speed of a wave, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and/or wavelength.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the speed of a wave depends only on the wave medium and not on frequency or wavelength.

nodes.misconception: Frequency or wavelength of waves on a string will affect the wave speed.
nodes.response: The speed of waves on a string only depends on the properties of the wave medium (the string) e.g. tension, density

nodes.misconception: Tidal volume is the amount of air breathed in and out per breath and the lungs completely empty of air when we expire.
nodes.response: Tidal volume is the volume of air breathed in or out per breadth and it increases during exercise to enable more air and hence exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide to occur. A residual volume of air always remains in the lungs to keep them inflated.

nodes.misconception: To help the split pin to turn, create a bigger hole.
nodes.response: If the hole is too big, this will allow the split pin to wobble and cause the mechanism to not work accurately. Use a standard pencil and turn the split pin when it is in place and this will help it the lever to move smoothly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle in the first learning cycle with where each object should be placed.
nodes.response: The closer to the observation point an object is, the larger it appears to be. So if we want an object to appear larger than something else, we need to place it closer to the camera.

nodes.misconception: Substituting the wrong values into the formulas.
nodes.response: The formulas are written in words so ensure pupils check that what they are substituting is the correct value by rereading the description for each value.

nodes.misconception: All medieval approaches to treatment and prevention were ineffective.
nodes.response: Some effective methods, such as the use of mint in herbal remedies, existed but the scientific reason for their health benefits was not understood.

nodes.misconception: There was limited access to medical care in medieval Britain.
nodes.response: Although few people were able to afford physicians, most people were able to turn to other sources of care such as that offered by hospitals, wise people or members of their own family.

nodes.misconception: Religion was the only medieval explanation for the causes of disease and illness.
nodes.response: Religion was a widespread and commonly used explanation for disease but many other theories were also used including miasma, astrology and the Theory of the Four Humours.

nodes.misconception: There was no change in medieval surgery.
nodes.response: New developments did occur, such as the use of opium as an anaesthetic and wine to use against infection, but the impact of these was limited.

nodes.misconception: Medium-fidelity prototypes are just “tidier” versions of low-fidelity ones.
nodes.response: Medium-fidelity is not about neatness - it’s about using stronger materials and semi-functional builds to test ergonomics and usability.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is never used in spoken German.
nodes.response: The irregular verbs 'haben' and 'sein', modal verbs and 'es gab' are all common in spoken German. Other verbs in the imperfect mainly appear in written texts.

nodes.misconception: That we will all have the same answer to a question about how a writer presents a particular character or theme.
nodes.response: The way we respond to how a writer presents a particular character or theme will be very individual since our responses depend on our own experiences or memories.

nodes.misconception: That meeting someone unknown in a strange place will always be scary.
nodes.response: Instead of feeling scared, you might also feel excited or intrigued and you can use language to have this effect on the reader.

nodes.misconception: All relevant information comes only from the dialogue in plays.
nodes.response: What is the role of stage directions? Explore how they are crafted to further characterisation. What extra information do they give us?

nodes.misconception: We use 'wann' to say what we did, do or will do 'when'.
nodes.response: 'Wann' is a question word and means 'when' in questions and indirect questions. Use 'als' for 'when' when referring to specific past events or points in time and 'wenn' for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.

nodes.misconception: 'Um' always means 'at' and is used with clock times.
nodes.response: Whilst 'um' is used commonly with clock times to mean 'at', it can also mean 'around' when referring to places, e.g., 'around the corner', or 'about, approximately' with numbers, e.g., 'about 10km'. It also follows some verbs, e.g., 'es geht um'.

nodes.misconception: 'Bei' always means 'at (the)' or 'with (the)'.
nodes.response: 'Bei' can mean 'at (the)' or 'with (the)' when followed by a noun, but it can also be used to mean 'whilst' or 'in the process of' before a nominalised infinitive.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
nodes.response: German has several rules for forming plurals. The best way to correctly form plurals is to learn the rules, use an example for each rule as a guide, and frequently practise them. As in English, some nouns are used without plurals.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
nodes.response: German has several rules for forming plurals. The best way to correctly form plurals is to learn the rules, use an example for each rule as a guide, and frequently practise them. As in English, some nouns are used without plurals.

nodes.misconception: All German past participles start with 'ge-'.
nodes.response: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.

nodes.misconception: All German past participlies start with 'ge-'
nodes.response: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives don't change their endings, like in English.
nodes.response: German possessive adjectives change their endings based on case and gender.

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives don't need endings.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives take the same endings as 'ein'.

nodes.misconception: Only the tense of the verb can tell us whether a sentence is referring to present, past or future events.
nodes.response: Adverbs of time are also very important in helping us to identify time frames, particularly when the present tense is used for future meaning.

nodes.misconception: Always use the comparative form of an adjective as the starting point for forming the superlative.
nodes.response: Superlatives can change in the same way as comparatives, such as adding an umlaut, (alt, älter, der/die/das älteste). Where the comparative removes ‘e’, use the original adjective to form the superlative (teuer, teurer, der/die/das teuerste).

nodes.misconception: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in all present tense forms.
nodes.response: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in the first person singular of the present tense only.

nodes.misconception: 'z' is pronounced the same way in both English and German.
nodes.response: German [z] sounds like the English 'ts'. German [s-] is pronounced like the English 'z'. Use example words to remind you of the difference, e.g., 'Zug' (train) and 'Suche' (search).

nodes.misconception: You can only succeed in listening comprehension if you know all the vocabulary.
nodes.response: Whilst vocabulary knowledge is the most important element for success, other strategies can help, for example, close pre-reading of the questions, predicting vocabulary, avoiding distractors and checking answers carefully.

nodes.misconception: Using new ideas in every bar is the best way to compose a melody
nodes.response: Finding a balance of repetition and variety is usually more successful as it helps the melody become memorable.

nodes.misconception: An ostinato is a rhythm pattern only.
nodes.response: An ostinato can be melodic as well as rhythmic. In pop music they’re often called a ‘riff’ and in electronic music, a ‘loop’. A repeated pattern can add to the texture of a piece of music and help drive it forward.

nodes.misconception: A raga is just a scale.
nodes.response: A raga is a bit more complex than being just a scale. It has specific times of day, moods and emotions associated with it, as well as rules about how it should be played.

nodes.misconception: Fusion only refers to the blending of two contemporary styles of music.
nodes.response: Fusion is the blending of any two or more styles of music.

nodes.misconception: The bouzouki sounds the same as a guitar.
nodes.response: The bouzouki has very specific techniques that give it its characteristic sound. These include use of tremolo, slides and thirds. Although these can be used on the guitar, they are not as common as on the bouzouki.

nodes.misconception: Children may not have heard of glaciers and may think that the only year-round ice is at the poles. Melting ice caps and glaciers do not affect sea level.
nodes.response: Teaching slides introduce ice caps and glaciers and note that they are found all over the world. The effect of melting ice caps and glaciers on sea level is explained and children have a chance to model it.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils can't understand that substances can change from one state to another state.
nodes.response: Ensure that the language used is solid state, liquid state and gas state, not solid, liquid and gas.

nodes.misconception: Particle spacing can be overemphasised at the expense of particle movement.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that although particles can move over each other, the forces of attraction mean that the particles are touching.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials such as ice melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures which range from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures, ranging from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials such as ice melt; that materials cannot melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures which range from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.

nodes.misconception: You can't explore the dramatic function of off stage characters.
nodes.response: Off stage characters can help develop a world beyond the stage itself, grounding the play in its own reality.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may struggle to believe the impact your mindset can have on performance.
nodes.response: Your mindset can be the difference between giving up and persisting, through the use of mindfulness, visualisation and positive self talk anything is possible.

nodes.misconception: Mental preparation is just for elite athletes.
nodes.response: Students should understand that everyone can benefit from mental preparation techniques and that performers in many fields of work practice them. They too could benefit in their own pursuits.

nodes.misconception: Mental preparation is just for elite athletes.
nodes.response: Students should understand that everyone can benefit from mental preparation techniques and that performers in many fields of work practice them. They too could benefit in their own pursuits.

nodes.misconception: Add an 'e' to all adjectives in French, in the feminine form.
nodes.response: Some adjectives in the feminine form are irregular. They do not follow the normal pattern of adding an 'e' to the masculine form. E.g. beau (m) and belle (f).

nodes.misconception: Like in English, we use 's to show possession in French.
nodes.response: In French, unlike English, there is no possessive apostrophe. Use the preposition 'de' (of) to show possession: Pierre's brother - le frère de Pierre.

nodes.misconception: African women’s experiences and theology can be adequately represented by either white women or African men.
nodes.response: African women have unique experiences and should share their own stories. Others can support them, but real representation comes from their own voices, not others speaking for them.

nodes.misconception: Merge sort is the most efficient sorting algorithm for all cases.
nodes.response: For smaller data sets, simpler algorithms such as insertion sort or bubble sort can be faster due to the overhead in merge sort of having to break apart the data to be sorted.

nodes.misconception: Roots are not a tissue of the plant, or contain living cells, also that wood is not made of living cells.
nodes.response: Show the cells of roots and how they divide to allow the length and width of the root to grow; also the rings on trees that indicate new cell division in the trunk of a tree.

nodes.misconception: When saying what you will do in French, a separate word is needed for 'will'.
nodes.response: The simple future in French is a simple tense because it is made of one word. The idea of 'will' is created through the correct verb stem and ending. Most -er verbs use the infinitive as stem for the simple future.

nodes.misconception: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
nodes.response: There are key irregular verb stems to learn for the future tense. Confident use of these verbs will add greatly to overall accuracy and help students to express themselves confidently in the future tense.

nodes.misconception: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
nodes.response: There are key irregular verb stems to learn for the future tense. Confident use of these verbs will add greatly to overall accuracy and help students to express themselves confidently in the future tense.

nodes.misconception: Superlative sentences have the same word order in English and French.
nodes.response: Take care when writing or translating superlative sentences as the French word order differs quite significantly from English, e.g., 'the most interesting lesson' > 'the lesson the most interesting'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think floods are only destructive.
nodes.response: Explain that floodwaters can be very dangerous and cause much damage, but they also bring water and nutrients to the land for growing crops.

nodes.misconception: It is best to focus first on the unfamiliar words in a longer text.
nodes.response: This should be done in last place, when context has been read.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, we use the verb 'I am' ('je suis') with age.
nodes.response: In French, we use the verb 'I have' ('j'ai') with age, e.g. 'j'ai huit ans' - 'I am (have) eight (years)'.

nodes.misconception: Verbs like 'ecrire' are formed the same way as verbs like 'lire'.
nodes.response: Although verbs like 'écrire' do have the same endings in the singular persons (je, tu and il/elle), they are different in the plural form, so it is better to think of them as different types of -re verb.

nodes.misconception: All Jews reject Jesus as the Messiah.
nodes.response: There is a very small number of Jews, known as Messianic Jews, who regard Jesus as the Messiah.

nodes.misconception: Metadata is only used when a user needs to know when a file was made or changed.
nodes.response: Metadata can be used in a variety of ways. For example, software can be designed to make use of metadata for effective cataloguing and providing extra information about the properites of a file being used.

nodes.misconception: The metallic structure model is a replication of reality. Therefore, metals contain seawater. The concept of electric current is challenging. Some may think that electrons jump from atom to atom.
nodes.response: Discuss why scientists use models with the pupils, explaining that a model is only as good as what it can explain, so it develops over time. Remind pupils how an electric circuit works before discussing why metals are good conductors.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to carry out a complex 3-stage practical.
nodes.response: Demonstrate the practical or do a 'follow with me' step-by-step method. If you are short on time you could just carry out the first part of the practical to produce the copper sulfate solution then stop.

nodes.misconception: Recycling metals reduces their quality.
nodes.response: Most metals, including aluminium and steel, can be repeatedly recycled without negatively impacting their properties.

nodes.misconception: All metals have similar properties.
nodes.response: When metals are grouped into ferrous, non-ferrous, and alloy metals, their properties are different.

nodes.misconception: There are exceptions for both metals and non-metals, which have different properties.
nodes.response: Use examples such as mercury and graphite in your teaching.

nodes.misconception: A metal is an individual atom. The property of a metal atom is the same as the bulk material. Pupils get confused between the attractive forces in the metal atoms and the metallic bond.
nodes.response: Reinforce the idea that atoms are tiny and not visible to the naked eye. The material we know as metal is many millions of atoms joined together. Revisit the structure of the atoms before introducing the idea of metallic bonding and giant structure.

nodes.misconception: Pressure and heating caused by burying alone is enough to cause metamorphism or rock to melt.
nodes.response: Highlight that the temperatures / pressures needed for metamorphism or rocks to melt are typically found at plate boundaries / hot spots.

nodes.misconception: Retrograde is a term only used in dance.
nodes.response: Retrograde is a term used in many artforms, it is particularly prevalent in music and films.

nodes.misconception: Projection means that you have to look up.
nodes.response: Projection is effectively communicating a dance idea. This often involves looking outwards towards an audience but would not be appropriate if communicating a concept such a secrecy, nervousness or reluctance.

nodes.misconception: That everyone in power sees education as a way to better society.
nodes.response: How does it feel when you don't understand something? Confusing? Scary? Disorientating? How could the pigs use this to their advantage?

nodes.misconception: Conversation answers should be kept as short and simple as possible.
nodes.response: It is important to develop conversation answers to showcase a range of vocabulary and grammar. This can be achieved by using adverbs to add more detail and by incorporating a range of grammatical persons.

nodes.misconception: Micro:bits can work on their own by being connected in a circuit
nodes.response: Micro:bits have to have a program downloaded before being connected into a circuit

nodes.misconception: External components must be used with microcontrollers to create control systems.
nodes.response: Microcontrollers have on board inputs and ouputs and connection points for additional external components.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that micro-organisms are very tiny animals or that they are not living things. Pupils may think that all micro-organisms are harmful germs.
nodes.response: Explain that micro-organisms are living things as they carry out the same processes as other living things, but they aren't animals because they have a simpler structure than animals. Explain that some helpful micro-organisms live inside our bodies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that mould is a type of plant because of its colour or the way it grows.
nodes.response: Explain that plants make their own food using photosynthesis and mould does not, so it cannot be a plant. Instead, it gets its nutrients from the organic matter that it is growing on. Also, unlike plants, mould does not need light to survive or grow.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not consider mould to be a living thing because it does not move in the ways we are familiar with animals moving.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that all living things grow, reproduce and move, and that mould can do all of these things. It is a type of fungus. Which is a living thing that is part of the micro-organisms group.

nodes.misconception: To test simple circuits, you need to create a physical representation of the circuits.
nodes.response: Like many CAD applications, Tinkercad can simulate circuit operation within the circuit workspace.

nodes.misconception: An adequate intake of micronutrients is possible by always eating the same types of foods.
nodes.response: To ensure an adequate intake of micronutrients, it is important to have a varied diet. This is because different foods provide different types and amounts of vitamins and minerals.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all moulds and fungi are harmful and no useful products can be extracted from them.
nodes.response: Explain that, while many moulds and fungi can be harmful to humans and other animals, many have uses in medicine such as penicillin, once they have been properly processed by scientists.

nodes.misconception: Scientific drawings made using a microscope are difficult to do and often sketched like an artwork. The requirements are clear and precise and require practise to get right.
nodes.response: The expectations for scientific drawings are clearly stated and shown visually. Opportunities to practise drawing different structures are included throughout the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils expend far too much energy by sprint starting instead of finding their race pace, leading them to tire in the second half of the race.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on finding their race pace, not getting over excited at the start line, beginning too fast or being influenced by others who do. Ideally, the second half of the race is completed quicker than the first (called a negative split).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may perform middle distances by jogging the majority to conserve energy and putting a sprint in at the end. This often leads to pupils wishing they had put more effort into the initial stages.
nodes.response: A well performed 800m requires a fine line between holding back some energy for the finish but also performing at around 80-90% maximum effort for around the first 600m.

nodes.misconception: 'Mieux' and 'plus mal/moins bien' can be used interchangeably with 'le mieux' and 'le plus mal' or ''le moins bien'.
nodes.response: 'Le mieux' and 'le plus mal'/'le moins bien' are superlative adverbs to describe actions as '(the) best' or '(the) worst'. 'Mieux' and 'moins bien'/'plus mal'  describe actions as 'better' or 'less well'/'worse' and are comparative adverbs.

nodes.misconception: There are long rivers on every continent.
nodes.response: There are no permanent rivers in Antarctica

nodes.misconception: The sound-symbol correspondence [ie] is always pronounced as in 'Liebe'.
nodes.response: When [ie] is the final but unstressed syllable in a word, pronounce [i] and [e] as separate vowel sounds, e.g., 'Familie'.

nodes.misconception: All migrants are refugees
nodes.response: Not all migrants are refugees; some move for economic or educational reasons. Explain the differences between refugees and other migrants.

nodes.misconception: -er and -ir verbs have the same verb ending in the 1st person plural, present tense.
nodes.response: -er and -ir verbs have different endings in the 1st person plural, present tense. For -er verbs, it is -emos and for -ir verbs, it is -imos.

nodes.misconception: 'Huir' works in exactly the same way as all regular -ir verbs, e.g. 'escribir'.
nodes.response: The verb 'huir' has a spelling change (i → y) in the present tense in the 1st person singular, 2nd person singular, 3rd person singular, and 3rd person plural forms: huyo, huyes, huye, huyen. This makes the vowel pronunciation easier - huyo not huio.

nodes.misconception: At the end of a word, [e] sounds the same as short [e].
nodes.response: Final [e] sounds like 'uh', as in 'danke', 'Klasse'. Short [e] sounds more like 'eh' as in 'denken'.

nodes.misconception: Modal verbs require a 'zu' before the infinitive.
nodes.response: Two-verb structures without a modal verb require 'zu' before the infinitive, e.g., 'Ich habe Lust, schwimmen zu gehen.'.

nodes.misconception: All migration in the Middle East is forced due to conflict.
nodes.response: While war and displacement are significant in parts of the Middle East, the region is also a major destination for voluntary economic migration, especially to the Gulf States like the UAE, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia.

nodes.misconception: Migration only has negative impacts.
nodes.response: Migration also brings benefits such as skills and expertise for the jobs market, economic benefits and a more diverse society.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that 10 mm are larger than 1 cm.
nodes.response: There are 10 mm in 1 cm.  1 cm is made up of 10 mm.  10 mm and 1 cm are equivalent in length.

nodes.misconception: A belief that our identity is fixed and permanent.
nodes.response: Who we are and how that is expressed can be changed, and is likely to shift throughout our life. We can communicate who we are through our expression, how we dress, how we speak and by taking part in activities that are important to us.

nodes.misconception: Minimising waste means reducing the size of a product.
nodes.response: Using materials efficiently can be achieved by reducing size, but also by working accurately. This can be done by using stencils / templates, tesselation and nesting.

nodes.misconception: A scale always starts on the note do.
nodes.response: We are used to using the Solfège note names in the order - do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. This is only correct for major scales. A minor scale starts on the note la.

nodes.misconception: Pupils move in the wrong direction so they are parallel instead of mirroring. When pupils perform their sequence on apparatus, they lose control, extension and flow.
nodes.response: Practise mirrored movements to create muscle memory. Pupils should adapt their sequences to work on apparatus so they don't lose quality. Pupils can also focus on communication to help improve the quality of their sequence on apparatus.

nodes.misconception: One pupil always leads so that their timing is out. Variations in angles of movement make the mirroring look uneven. Pupils move in the wrong direction so they are parallel instead of mirroring
nodes.response: Pupils should practise counting or using music to help them improve their timing. Pupils need to practise so they have identical body positions and use feedback to help improve this. Practise mirrored movements over and over to create muscle memory.

nodes.misconception: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
nodes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

nodes.misconception: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
nodes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction to successfully complete listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Strategies like prediction can be useful, but the most important way to successfully answer listening comprehension questions is by having a broad vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction to successfully complete listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Strategies like prediction can be useful, but the most important way to successfully answer listening comprehension questions is by having a broad vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives in Spanish only ever appear after the noun.
nodes.response: Most adjectives in Spanish appear after the noun. However, some are used before it. These are called prenominal adjectives.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that drawing a graph with a broken axis is incorrect.
nodes.response: It is fine to do this (and is sometimes necessary) but it is important to acknowledge this when trying to draw conclusions from the graph.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may work out missing angles without writing out their justifications.
nodes.response: Each time a number which is not on the original diagram is used or found, an explanation should be given for where it has come from.

nodes.misconception: Evangelism always involves preaching in public.
nodes.response: Evangelism can involve preaching and public speaking, but it can also be carried out through subtle actions and living out the teachings of Jesus in everyday life.

nodes.misconception: Artists only use paintbrushes to apply paint.
nodes.response: Artists can use a paintbrush to apply paint, but they can also use other tools, such as leaves, sticks and pinecones.

nodes.misconception: Primary colors are made by mixing other colours together.
nodes.response: Remind children that primary colours cannot be created by mixing other colours. Secondary colours are made by mixing two primary colours together. For example, blue and yellow make green.

nodes.misconception: Paint can only be mixed in a paint palette.
nodes.response: Paint can be mixed in a paint palette, but it can also be mixed on paper to create a blend.

nodes.misconception: When samples of water are added at different temperatures, some pupils add or subtract the temperatures, applying a mathematical process without appearing to think about what is happening.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to predict changes to the resulting temperature using water at a range of starting temperatures and then demonstrate each one, measuring the temperature of the resultant mixture each time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse similarly sounding key terms; solute, solvent, solution, soluble, insoluble.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing ways to remember the differences, e.g. solvent has more letters = have more of it in the solution.

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to misidentify similar looking apparatus.
nodes.response: Focus on the uses of each apparatus, highlight its distinguishing features to help pupils correctly identify apparatus.

nodes.misconception: Pupils either put too much or not enough detail into their drawings = muddled representations
nodes.response: Use the 'less is more' approach, and remind pupils to include labels - **clarity is key**. Allows for less detail and avoids any confusion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the concept of 'obligation' tricky to grasp.
nodes.response: Explain that obligations are things we think we should do or that should happen or that others think we should do or should happen.

nodes.misconception: Simulating in Tinkercad is exactly like physical testing.
nodes.response: Tinkercad is excellent for digitally testing ideas, but you should always expect to make adjustments when you build the physical models.

nodes.misconception: User needs and wants are the same thing.
nodes.response: Needs are the essential features required for the product to function, while wants are additional features that aren't necessary but would enhance the product if included.

nodes.misconception: Analysis means zooming in to individual words and explaining what they mean.
nodes.response: Exploring quotations is more than just looking at individual words and offering paraphrase or synonym. Your exploration of the quotation should develop your ideas about the question, and look at dramatic methods (more than just individual words).

nodes.misconception: Looking at other essays is cheating or copying.
nodes.response: Working with model responses helps develop your critical skills in order to evaluate your own work. Using and adapting others' ideas is a great thing to do!

nodes.misconception: You don't need to plan topic sentences in full.
nodes.response: Write topic sentences in full when planning. They give the essay structure and make sure you develop and support your thesis.

nodes.misconception: Robots will take all human jobs in the future.
nodes.response: Robots can sometimes replace people in certain jobs, especially when the work is dangerous, boring, or very hard for humans to do. People will still be needed to design, build and program robots.

nodes.misconception: The line on a distance time graph can go in any direction.
nodes.response: The line may be horizontal, time changing without a change in distance, but it can not be vertical. That would be a change in distance without a change in time. Additionally, our line cannot go backwards; time is always moving forwards.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that photosynthesis is just one simple reaction, as depicted by the word equation and balanced symbol equation.
nodes.response: This explores the idea that the word equation and balanced symbol equation are useful but very simple models of photosynthesis, and also explores a slightly more detailed two-stage model of the process.

nodes.misconception: The dominant allele is stronger than the recessive allele preventing its expression or that the recessive allele is an absence of the dominant allele, also that all genetic disorders are recessive.
nodes.response: Linking the allele to change in protein structure, showing that proteins are produced in the case of dominant and recessive alleles. Examples of dominant and recessive disorders provided.

nodes.misconception: A gamete has two alleles, Punnett square has too many alleles for gametes. Also that only four offspring are produced and therefore each will definitely have the genotype and phenotype shown.
nodes.response: Model the alleles within gametes so it is clear. Refer to half the gametes having each version, moving away from the idea of divisions of 4.

nodes.misconception: Lifestyle factors have only been considered important for a person's health in the modern period.
nodes.response: Lifestyle factors like diet have been considered important for many centuries, but before the 20th century this was often based on inaccurate ideas like the Theory of Four Humours.

nodes.misconception: Alternative medicines were mostly abandoned during the course of the 20th century.
nodes.response: Alternative medicines, including practices like homeopathy and the use of herbal medicines, have remained popular, even in 21st century Britain.

nodes.misconception: Vaccinations have been made compulsory to ensure uptake in modern Britain.
nodes.response: Vaccinations have been voluntary for people to receive in modern Britain but many have been provided free of charge and their benefits promoted to encourage people.

nodes.misconception: The use of technology in modern medicine means doctors aren't very involved in making diagnoses.
nodes.response: Technology can help patients to monitor some health conditions themselves but many technologies that help diagnosis require a doctor to operate them or to interpret the information they provide.

nodes.misconception: Modern materials only provide advantages to designers and users.
nodes.response: Modern materials are often difficult and expensive to produce and are also difficult to recycle.

nodes.misconception: Modern materials only provide advantages to designers and users.
nodes.response: Modern materials are often difficult and expensive to produce and are also difficult to recycle.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the atomic number and mass number with regard to the number of electrons in an atom. They also can confuse the number of electrons which can be held by each shell.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the lower number (atomic number/proton number) represents the number of electrons (reference to the mass being larger can help). Practise as many electron arrangements as possible.

nodes.misconception: The dorian mode is the same as a minor scale.
nodes.response: There is a slight difference, with one different note. All of the modes are closely linked to major and minor scales, but have slightly different notes that help to create different moods.

nodes.misconception: Industries only modify products to make them cheaper.
nodes.response: Industries also improve products for better performance, sustainability, customer satisfaction, safety and compliance with regulations.

nodes.misconception: Designs are drawn on paper and then manufactured.
nodes.response: Computer Aided Design helps designers accurately draw their ideas before manufacturing them.

nodes.misconception: The shape inspector is only used to change the length or width of a shape.
nodes.response: You can use the shape inspector to customise different properties of a shape, including recolouring shapes.

nodes.misconception: Using a 'repeat 1000' block is just the same as using a 'forever' block to make a character keep doing something in a game.
nodes.response: Even though a repeat 1000 runs many times, a forever loop runs without an end point, which is better for actions that need to continue through the entire game.

nodes.misconception: Performing group routines often means some members of the group may struggle with the choreography and therefore feel self-conscious and demotivated.
nodes.response: Stress to each group the importance of adapting choreography to suit the needs of everyone in the group. For example, some pupils could perform backward rolls whilst others perform a more basic roll. Or everyone may change the skill they perform.

nodes.misconception: Children may use a range of observational methods to assess hardness, e.g. “heaviness” of the object, and if it breaks on impact (test for brittleness), neither of which are a test for hardness.
nodes.response: Be aware of using the correct vocabulary around testing for hardness. Explain that hardness is the ability to withstand pressure.

nodes.misconception: Assuming that substances like sodium chloride (NaCl) are diatomic.
nodes.response: It is very important to emphasise that only non-metals exist as monatomic or molecules.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to link a mole to number of particles.
nodes.response: Use real world examples of converting volumes / masses into number of particles so pupils become more comfortable converting between moles, number of particles particles and masses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to link a mole to number of particles.
nodes.response: Use real world examples of converting volumes / masses into number of particles so pupils become more comfortable converting between moles, number of particles particles and masses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a lever gives you ‘something for nothing’ when used as a force multiplier.
nodes.response: Ask a pupil to lift an object by a particular height (say 10 cm) without a pivot, then with a pivot and a plank as a lever to compare the effort and distance moved in each case.

nodes.misconception: 'Il', 'elle', 'ils' and 'elles' only refer to people and not things. 'Il' therefore only means 'he' and 'elle' only means 'she'.
nodes.response: It is useful to keep in mind that 'il, elle' and 'ils, elles' can refer to things as well as people.  In this case, 'il, elle' means 'it' rather than 'he, she'.

nodes.misconception: Silent final consonants are always silent.
nodes.response: The liaison rule means that Silent Final Consonants are pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel sound (including silent h).

nodes.misconception: The noun 'un être', meaning 'a being', changes to 'une être' when referring to a girl or woman. 'Un être humain' changes to 'une être humaine' in the feminine.
nodes.response: The noun 'être' is masculine, even when referring to a girl or a woman. The phrase 'un être humain', 'a human being', refers to both genders.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that being healthy can be achieved through physical fitness, not taking into account anything else.
nodes.response: Explain that a range of different factors contribute to a healthy lifestyle, including eating a balanced diet, getting a good amount of sleep and taking part in activities that help our mental well being.

nodes.misconception: Monoclonal antibodies can act as a 'magic bullet' to deliver medication to certain cells.
nodes.response: The human body is complex and therapies using monoclonal antibodies have had some serious side effects. New treatments should always be treated with caution.

nodes.misconception: Collages are always three-dimensional.
nodes.response: Remind children that collages can be three-dimensional, but can also be made on a flat surface.

nodes.misconception: It always rains during the monsoon season.
nodes.response: Explain that the rainfall intensity and frequency during the monsoon season can vary from year to year. Although it can rain every or most days, this is often a short period of intense rainfall followed by a period of dry conditions.

nodes.misconception: Monsters in myths and films are always portrayed as evil.
nodes.response: Monsters in myths and films are not always portrayed as evil. Creating monsters can involve using different features that portray a friendly or approachable character.

nodes.misconception: Months of the year start with capital letters in French, as in English.
nodes.response: Months of the year start with lowercase letters in French, unless at the start of a sentence.

nodes.misconception: [ai] and [é] sound the same in French.
nodes.response: In some regional accents  [ai] and [é] can sound similar.  Officially there is a difference in pronunciation and meaning as the ending of the imperfect tense is supposed to be pronounced [ai], whereas a common ending of the past participle is [é].

nodes.misconception: You can use a time phrase to show whether you mean a completed action in the past or a regular past event/activity.
nodes.response: In French, the verb alone already shows whether you mean a completed action in the past (use the formation rule for the perfect tense) or a regular past event/activity (use the formation rule for the imperfect tense). Time phrases can also be added.

nodes.misconception: A subject pronoun or noun is always required when using a verb in French.
nodes.response: When using the imperative, neither subject pronoun nor noun is required. Match the spelling of the verb to the person or people who are being instructed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they personally can't do anything to prevent animals becoming endangered/extinct.
nodes.response: Use the resources to explain the things pupils can do to help, and encourage them to think specifically about which are possible for them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that old discovered objects, like bits of pottery, coins and jewellery are fossils.  They also may believe that the fossil is always the actual plant or animal itself.
nodes.response: Being clear that only things that have been alive may become fossils, and not all living things are fossilised.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that human development milestones happen at the same time for everyone.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that humans are all different and so grow and develop at different rates. This is why we need surveys to find out more information, as one rule cannot be applied to all humans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants can decide or choose to grow in whatever way they think is best.
nodes.response: Explain that plant adaptations are inherited characteristics and the plant does not have any choice or understanding of its adaptations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know how humans use different senses to stay safe.
nodes.response: Examples of different scenarios where humans use different senses to check for danger and to stay safe.

nodes.misconception: A lot of people think we only touch with our hands rather than our skin. Also, that we only ever use one sense at a time.
nodes.response: Examples including touching with other parts of the body such as feet, or touching an arm against a cold metal table leg and feeling the difference in temperature.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all the food we eat is used by the body.
nodes.response: When pupils model the lower part of the digestive system they will see some of the food is absorbed as nutrients and other parts form waste which leaves the body.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Sun is a planet.
nodes.response: Explain that the Sun is a star because, like other stars, it is a huge ball of glowing gas which has planets travelling around it.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes with partial products are even more common where algebraic terms in the binomials have coefficients greater than 1. It is common to find pupils writing that the product of 2x and 3x is 5x
nodes.response: Reminding pupils that because multiplication is commutative the product of 2x and 3x can be thought of as 2 × 3 × x × x

nodes.misconception: You can use the same verbalisation in compound time as simple time signatures.
nodes.response: This will create problems, because there are 3 quavers in each beat in compound time. The counting method in compound time avoids confusion by ensuring there are three quavers in each beat.

nodes.misconception: All bubbles produced contain air and that it is a reversible change.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that the bubbles produced when acids react with bicarbonate of soda contain carbon dioxide and that this change is irreversible as a new material is produced.

nodes.misconception: Changes in state and dissolving and mixing are not reversible processes.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will show which processes can be used to reverse state changes and dissolving.  This will be explored and embedded during the practice tasks.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think these words can be used interchangeably. A 'mesmerising reputation' for example.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the word pairs when they write their sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think the words 'gargantuan' and 'bulky' can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use the word pairs to help pupils see and hear the words in nuanced contexts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might use the word 'rustling' incorrectly.
nodes.response: A 'rustling' object implies a level of movement. If leaves weren't moving, we wouldn't describe them as 'rustling' but we would if the breeze was blowing them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think the words can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use the word pairs to help pupils see and hear the words in nuanced contexts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that all three words can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use the word pairs to help pupils see each word and its nuances.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think 'heavy-handed' can only be used in the physical sense.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that the word 'heavy-handed' can be used if someone is insensitive. For example, a heavy-handed remark.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find it difficult to understand how a 'stare' or a 'silence' could be described as 'frosty'.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that 'frosty' can also be used to describe something as 'unwelcoming'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that the two prefixes 'pre' and 'un' have the same effect on a root word.
nodes.response: Spend time teaching that each prefix has a different purpose and changes the root word in a different way.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might use 'splattered' as a verb instead of an adjective. For example, 'The raindrops splattered onto her forehead' instead of 'She wiped the splattered drops of rain off her forehead'.
nodes.response: Allow pupils to also use the word as a verb; just make sure they understand that this is a different word class. Look at sentences where it is used as a verb and an adjective and ask pupils to identify the word class.

nodes.misconception: Vacant can be used to describe eyes, but it can also be used in many other contexts.
nodes.response: Ensure children can use the word 'vacant' in all its different contexts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might get confused with the adjective 'suffocating' and the verb 'suffocate'.
nodes.response: You could include a sentence where you have used a verb from the infinitive 'to suffocate' and discuss what word class this is and why.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think only pain related to burning can be described as 'searing'.
nodes.response: Use examples of sentences where 'searing pain' is caused by something other than heat.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think the words can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use the word pairs to help pupils see and hear the words in nuanced contexts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think the words can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use the word pairs to help pupils see and hear the words in nuanced contexts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find the word classes difficult for these words. For example, they might think 'fragrance' is an adjective, confusing it with the word 'fragrant', or that 'reek' is an adjective.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to look at the word pairs to help to understand that most of these words are nouns. This is because the word pairs are adjectives.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might use the word 'lashing' as a verb E.g. 'The rain was lashing against the window'.
nodes.response: If pupils use the word as a verb, that is fine. Just make sure to explain to them that they have used the word as a verb because it is an action and not describing a noun.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to use the word ‘howl’ in a sentence.
nodes.response: Explain that as this word is a verb, we can change the tense to make it fit with our sentence. ‘Howled’ or ‘howling’ are alternatives.

nodes.misconception: May consider the size of objects when comparing rather than the numerosity of the group.
nodes.response: Ensure any groups compared throughout the day are very obviously different before comparing more small things with fewer large things.

nodes.misconception: There are just two words for 'the': a masculine and feminine version.
nodes.response: There are four different ways to say 'the' in French: 'le', 'las', 'les' and 'l'' (masculine singular, feminine singular, plural and preceding a vowel/h).

nodes.misconception: Pronouns need to be used to indicate the person doing the action.
nodes.response: Pronouns are often unnecessary in Spanish as verb endings indicate the person doing the action.

nodes.misconception: Moscow represents life in Russia.
nodes.response: Moscow is not representative of all of Russia; life in other regions can be very different. Moscow is the richest and most developed part of the country and other regions vary in terms of culture, economy, and infrastructure.

nodes.misconception: Moses and Musa are two different people.
nodes.response: Musa is the term Muslims use for Moses, translated from the Arabic.

nodes.misconception: This is an ancient story and has no meaning for today.
nodes.response: This story continues to be remembered and celebrated by Jews today.

nodes.misconception: Friday is the only day Muslims go to Mosque.
nodes.response: Muslims pray five times a day and may do this at home or at the mosque.

nodes.misconception: The pronouns 'il' and 'elle' can only mean 'he' and 'she' in French.
nodes.response: The pronouns 'il' and 'elle' mean 'he' and 'she', they can also be translated as 'it' as all noun have a gender in French.

nodes.misconception: There is one form of the possessive adjective 'my' in French, as in English.
nodes.response: There are two forms of the possessive adjective 'my' in French: 'mon' (masculine) and 'ma' (feminine).

nodes.misconception: Motifs and symbols are the same.
nodes.response: A motif is a recurring image whereas a symbol is one thing that represents something else.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often apply equations incorrectly or do not spot obvious errors when using them due to not thinking about the science.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often apply equations incorrectly or do not spot obvious errors when using them due to not thinking about the science.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often apply equations incorrectly or do not spot obvious errors when using them due to not thinking about the science.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often apply equations incorrectly or do not spot obvious errors when using them due to not thinking about the science.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to come up with suitable motions.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in small groups for this task. As a class, come up with some ideas of what you might change or discuss related to the different aspects and have these visible for children when coming up with their motions.

nodes.misconception: Intrinsic motivation is always the best type of motivation.
nodes.response: Extrinsic motivation has its time and place, particularly with short term goals or with very young people. Intrinsic is much better when long term commitment and persistence is required.

nodes.misconception: Simply changing the instrument makes a leitmotif change mood.
nodes.response: While it does have an impact, changing other elements can make this even greater. Harmony, rhythm, dynamics, articulation and tempo are particularly useful for motivic transformation.

nodes.misconception: All motors operate in the same way.
nodes.response: DC motors use open-loop systems, and servo motors use a closed-loop system.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that castles only had a military function.
nodes.response: However, castles also had a psychological impact on the people of England. They served as a permanent reminder to the English of a foreign occupier in their land. They were also centres of administration.

nodes.misconception: There are no mountain ranges in Antarctica.
nodes.response: There are mountain ranges on every continent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that it is warmer at the summit of a mountain because you are 'closer to the sun'.
nodes.response: There is low pressure at altitude which means that air is thinner at the summit of a mountain. The thin air causes the cold temperatures.

nodes.misconception: The audience are always directly facing the stage/performers.
nodes.response: Whilst most theatres use an 'end on' arrangement, this isn't always the case. Fashion shows traditionally use a 'thrust' stage, lecture-demonstrations might use 'in the round' and performances such as Mummers' plays, may use 'promenade'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may miscount the squares when moving the shape, leading to inaccurate placement.
nodes.response: Encourage students to carefully count squares from the current position of each vertex and ensure consistency in their counting across the entire shape. Practice counting out loud as a class or in pairs. Relate it to counting on using a number line.

nodes.misconception: Detailed and complex 3D models are always created from scratch and therefore take a long time to create.
nodes.response: 3D models usually start off by using, adding and modifying simple 3D shapes. Further detail and complexities are then added to increase the realism of the model.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that sport and physical activity is all about competing and winning.
nodes.response: Moving and exercising is an important part of daily life, not just for organised competition. Exercising can be done for fun and is important to help our bodies and minds to stay healthy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the chest pass is only used for shorter distances.
nodes.response: The chest pass is a very versatile technique that can be used for short and longer distances. It works well as a technique to pass when aiming for the space a teammate is moving into.

nodes.misconception: The only way to gain MA is by increasing the input force.
nodes.response: MA can be increased by increasing the distance from the fulcrum and the effort. For example, increasing the arm length on the handle of a flat head screwdriver when opening a can of paint.

nodes.misconception: Pupils make a big touch so they don't have close control of the ball. Pupils slow down after turning with the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to keep the ball close to the body so they have control at all times. Pupils should explode after the turn pushing off with their standing leg.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often dribble with their head down, focusing too much on the ball and not on teammates, spaces to move into or defenders within the space.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to develop the habit of looking up regularly to scan the area.

nodes.misconception: Migrants all experience the same hardships and migrated for similar reasons.
nodes.response: Migrants' experiences differed greatly from group to group and from person to person. Motivations amongst migrants also differed, even within particular migrant groups.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that muscles can push bones (when in fact they can only pull).
nodes.response: The lesson makes clear that muscles can only pull bones, and work in antagonistic pairs to pull bones in opposite directions.

nodes.misconception: Students may mix up rotation and circumduction.
nodes.response: When you rotate the shoulder joint you draw a dot with your hand (if the elbow is fully extended) whereas circumduction draws a circle.

nodes.misconception: Sprites will move when you press a key or click the mouse, even if they don’t have any code.
nodes.response: Sprites always need code to control their movement. Computers do not guess what is required as they need some direction to carry out actions.

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.

nodes.misconception: You can't prepare in advance for a discussion.
nodes.response: Developing an effective strategy and learning some phrases, will enable you to take part in discussions successfully and confidently. These can help you feel more prepared in discussion scenarios.

nodes.misconception: Magnetic field effects are often mistaken for electric field effects.
nodes.response: Be explicit in teaching that electric charges and charged objects are not magnetic.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes with the definitions of diffusion, osmosis and active transport are common, as are their application to biological scenarios.
nodes.response: The definitions are clearly stated and contextualised using key human biological processes and examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse dribbling with simply kicking the ball away, believing that any contact with the ball is dribbling.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of soft, controlled touches with the inside of their feet.

nodes.misconception: Some people have the view that they are local people and new arrivals are not welcome.
nodes.response: In reality, everyone in the UK is descended from new arrivals into the UK from outside. Few people are linked to a place for a long period.

nodes.misconception: Any quotation that supports your argument can be used.
nodes.response: Select a quotation from learning cycle 1, such as "it wasn't like a man" and ask how much pupils could say about the quotation.

nodes.misconception: Hyde is solely presented as a dangerous character from the start to the end of the novella.
nodes.response: Through the character of Hyde, and others' interactions with him, we can explore Stevenson's wider cautionary message.

nodes.misconception: That the dream is only caused by Utterson being in a state of distress.
nodes.response: Unpick the details of the dream to show the parallels with the plot.

nodes.misconception: Mughal authority collapsed in the 17th century.
nodes.response: Mughal rule faced challenges, but the emperors still had enough military power and political control to maintain their authority during the 17th century.

nodes.misconception: Violence was not important during the reign of some monarchs such as Akbar the Great.
nodes.response: Violence was consistently part of the reigns of Mughal emperors. Akbar ordered the massacre of 30 000 people living in Mewar after they resisted the Mughal army in 1568.

nodes.misconception: That Prophet Muhammad wrote the words of the Qur'an down once it was revealed to him.
nodes.response: The Prophet Muhammad recited, or said aloud, the words of the Qur'an but this was written down by those who had memorised the revelations.

nodes.misconception: The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was the founder of Islam.
nodes.response: The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was messenger sent to deliver the message of Islam.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that Muhammad communicated directly with Allah.
nodes.response: Muslims believe that Muhammad was given the revelation of the Qur'an via an angel.

nodes.misconception: There are only two types of cell: plant and animal.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the cells of unicellular organisms and some of their adaptations.

nodes.misconception: Pretending to be an object is drama, not dance.
nodes.response: Pretending to be an object is often categorised as 'physical theatre'. This is where dance and drama overlap and it draws upon skills from both disciplines. A similar connection is made when dancers represent characters or scenes from a story.

nodes.misconception: Proofs have to be solely algebraic and do not involve diagrams.
nodes.response: Proofs involve showing that a conjecture holds for multiple cases (general case). A diagram can represent multiple cases.

nodes.misconception: All screens run at the same time.
nodes.response: Only one screen is active at a time; users navigate between them when needed.

nodes.misconception: One object can only cast one shadow.
nodes.response: Children will investigate how the number of light sources affects the number of shadows cast by an object.

nodes.misconception: The number of spaces to translate a shape can be worked out by counting the squares on the grid.
nodes.response: If there are axes, then it is important to check the scales. The length of one square does not always represent one unit.

nodes.misconception: A negative exponent implies that the entire value is negative.
nodes.response: Refer back to the table showing the structure of how the negative exponents occur and highlight that none of the decimal values are negative.

nodes.misconception: Pupils lack fluency in pairs for 10 and so struggle to connect this to 2-digit numbers.
nodes.response: Promote fluency through games and chants and consider providing a scaffold of pairs for 10 which will help pupils develop automaticity

nodes.misconception: When working with counters students may count them and not appreciate they represent negatives.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of 2 different coloured counters as there is a need to represent positive and negative integers differently.

nodes.misconception: Using the phrase '2 negatives make a positive'.
nodes.response: Ensuring pupils understand the structure of the maths and not 'tricks' is so important. Encourage the use of correct language at all times

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not simplify after multiplying surds.
nodes.response: Surds should always be written in their simplest form for the final answer.

nodes.misconception: A reflection of a vector in the x or y axis is not the reverse of a vector.  This is often seen with equilateral triangles and vectors.
nodes.response: When multiplying the vectors by -1 this gives the opposite direction of the vector only.  The magnitude remains the same.  Investigate with pupils by drawing column vectors and multiply by -1 and compare.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly drawing or interpreting the scales on axes.
nodes.response: Use the approach where pupils count the number of intervals of the scale and divide the difference between the intervals. For example, if there are 5 intervals and the difference is between 20 and 30, they divide 10 by 2, so each interval is 2

nodes.misconception: Rather than learning to rearrange multiplicative relationships pupils can just learn the rearrangements or use a trick.
nodes.response: There are many situations in school and out where this skill is valuable and understanding how to manipulate these relationships will help pupils to understand the mathematics rather than just learn a set of procedures or lots of formulae.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the π symbol represents a variable, similar to letters such as r and d.
nodes.response: Reiterate the difference between variables and constants. Explain that while the radius may differ between circles, π is always the same.

nodes.misconception: Only seeing multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies for ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts. Ratios allow the multiplicative relationship to be seen.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly drawing a scaled axis is common.
nodes.response: Use the approach where pupils count the number of intervals of the scale and divide the difference bewteen the intervals. For example, if there are 5 intervals and the difference is between 20 and 30, they divide 10 by 2, so each interval is 2

nodes.misconception: Using additive strategies instead of multiplicative.
nodes.response: Emphasise that proportional relationships maintain a constant multiplier so we are looking for a multiplicative relationship.

nodes.misconception: The short multiplication algorithm may not be correctly aligned.
nodes.response: Check that the decimal point aligns in the decimal fraction and the product. Scaffolding with place value columns may support further.

nodes.misconception: Children may scale the decimal fraction inaccurately or may forget to scale the product accordingly to solve the original equation.
nodes.response: If a decimal fraction has only tenths, we multiply by 10 to form a whole number. If the decimal fraction has hundredths, we multiply by 100 to form a whole number.  Remember to adjust the product to answer the original equation.

nodes.misconception: When using the expanded method, pupils may not align the digits correctly with the same place value.
nodes.response: Use clear teacher modelling and continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents and link back to the place value chart.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Model accurately what happens when we regroup from 10s to 100s. Why did this happen? How do we record this?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents. Demonstrate the regrouping using base ten blocks to help.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly if they do not understand the place value of digits in a factor.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences / array to identify when they may need to regroup.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences / array to identify when they may need to regroup.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not record partitioned factors as tens and ones leading to incorrect calculation.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences to support their thinking. Use the language of ___ tens to support place value.

nodes.misconception: When using the short method, pupils may not align the digits correctly with the same place value.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents, linking back to the place value chart.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Reiterate that if the product of the single digit and the tens number is greater than 100 then you regroup ten tens into one hundred.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Ask children about the additional ten or tens as a small digit to be added in with the tens. What does this show? What is the value?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may partition numbers incorrectly and arrange grid model incorrectly.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling, ask pupils 'what does this digit represent?'

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly regrouping or forgetting to record a regrouped amount.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling. 'What does this digit represent?' 'Where do we place the regrouped amount?'

nodes.misconception: Misalignment of digits when setting out short multiplication.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling, ask pupils 'what does this digit represent?' Return to expanded layout briefly, before re-doing the problem.

nodes.misconception: Children may misalign digits when arranging into the short multiplication layout.
nodes.response: Children should use unitising language to help them understand and apply this to formal written methods.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may look to calculate each expression straight away.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are encouraged to estimate expressions, showing how this can be more efficient particularly when looking to compare expressions. The product is not always needed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to represent the problem as an expression or equation as they misinterpret what the whole is.
nodes.response: Draw attention to what the whole is in each example. You might like to build up each image with a whole at a time, describing the fraction of the whole that is shaded/represented.

nodes.misconception: Pupils resort to a procedure with little understanding for how we convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make connections between improper fractions and mixed numbers using both area models and number lines. Focus on reasoning by manipulating parts to complete wholes and where the wholes and parts are represented on the number line.

nodes.misconception: Pupils multiply both the numerator and denominator by the whole number.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are given time to explore how equations are represented using multiple representations and avoiding 'finding the answer' initially. Encourage children to reason how each equation is linked to the representations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to identify how much the rod has been scaled by as they cannot visualise the fractional size of the new whole.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to visualise how much the whole has shrunk by. Avoid pupils using the rods to immediately  find out what size of the new whole, encourage pupils to visualise and estimate prior to checking with the rods.

nodes.misconception: Children may get confused with the vocabulary when we say, for example, zero point one two rather than zero point twelve. They may also confuse how we write, for example, 32 hundredths.
nodes.response: We say zero point one two to show that there is one tenth and two hundredths. 32 hundredths is composed of 30 hundredths - this is the same as 3 tenths and we have 2 more hundredths so 32 hundredths is written 0.32

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly write the amount of tenths e.g. 49 tenths may be written as 0.49
nodes.response: There are ten tenths in one whole. So e.g. 49 tenths is composed of 4 ones and 9 more tenths. We write this as 4.9

nodes.misconception: 3(y+2) expands to 3y+2.
nodes.response: 3 lots of 12 isn't 3x10+2 so 3 lots of (y+2) isn't 3y+2. Get students to draw this out. To visualise it.

nodes.misconception: How to deal with exponents. y^2 times by y makes 3y. Or at least has a coefficient that is not 1.
nodes.response: Unsimplifying first. Not sure? Break it down. What is it? a^2 is a x a. So a^2 x a must be a x a x a.

nodes.misconception: Children may 'add' a zero when multiplying or vice versa when dividing. Children may place a zero at the end of the decimal fraction when multiplying, or vice versa when dividing.
nodes.response: When we 'add' zero, the value of the number does not change. When we multiply or divide by a power of 10, we need to move all the digits the appropriate spaces to the left/right even if this means bridging one and moving into the decimal places.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse use of the Base 10 equipment. They may also confuse the equivalence between dividing by 10/100/1,000 and multiplying by 0.1/0.01/0.001.
nodes.response: The large cube now represents one whole. The smaller blocks represent decimal fraction numbers. Use stem sentences to support common mistakes: when a number is divided by ___, it is the same as multiplying by ___

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think 5(y+1)-2(y+3) = 5y+5-2y+6
nodes.response: Correct use of the distributive law with either algebra tiles or an area model will demonstrate why this is wrong.

nodes.misconception: When multiplying terms with coefficients, pupils also add the coefficients as well as the exponents.
nodes.response: Pupils should be encouraged to rewrite their expression using the associative and commutative laws, with the number parts grouped and powers grouped. This hopefully avoids this error as they can see it is the product of the numbers.

nodes.misconception: When pupils multiply decimals, they use the column method and align the decimal points.
nodes.response: If the column method is used, encourage integer multiplication and use of powers of 10 to adjust the answer to the original calculation.

nodes.misconception: Confusion about the difference between global cities and megacities.
nodes.response: Global cities are well-connected cities that are recognised as being of global importance. Megacities are cities with more than 10 million inhabitants. Not all global cities are megacities.

nodes.misconception: Students may misinterpret Murakami's semantic field and assume the text is a horror, mystery or thriller story.
nodes.response: If you really break down Murakami's use of semantic field, his word choice is more centered around dynamism of a living organism.

nodes.misconception: Hindus worship images and murtis.
nodes.response: Hindus use murtis and images to focus their worship or to align with the energy of a murti.
