nodes.misconception: Pupils can incorrectly write a number in standard form or use a number in incorrect standard form whereby the number A does not satisfy 1 ≤ A < 10 or pupils use division of positive powers of 10.
nodes.response: Standard form represents a multiplicative relationship, so there should always be a multiplication. Embedding the understanding that negative exponents refer to 1/10^n is important. Using the place value chart with fractional and exponent form helps.

nodes.misconception: May identify which number is greater than or less than another but then sequence incorrectly.
nodes.response: Encourage children to visualise each number on a number line so they can see their order. Print a number line for constant use in class.

nodes.misconception: Changing all fractions and decimals to a common format without considering obvious comparisons.
nodes.response: This could be an opportunity to talk about familiar conversions including halves, quarters and fifths.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may look at all the digits at once when ordering numbers and this may lead to mistakes.
nodes.response: When ordering 3-digit numbers, encourage pupils to compare the 100s digits first and then the 10s digits (and the 1s) afterwards.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse ordinal and cardinal numbers.
nodes.response: Place an emphasis on these numbers in speech throughout the day. Continue to highlight the links between them.

nodes.misconception: May initially struggle with first and second as they do not contain the number names one and two.
nodes.response: Link these names to their shortened written forms (1st and 2nd) so children can see their relationship to one and two.

nodes.misconception: To create smooth organic surfaces and models, individual geometry such as vertices, edges and faces must be edited individually.
nodes.response: Free-form, organically shaped models can be created by using modelling tools such as proportional editing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that a knock out tournament is always the best type of tournament to do in sport/ PE.
nodes.response: With 4 or less teams (or if you have a lot of time) a round-robin tournament is better so that all teams are able to play each other.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that adding more players and making the task bigger, makes it better and more enjoyable.
nodes.response: Too many players can mean some stand around and don’t get get chance to join in properly. Ensure the number of players, attackers and defenders is suitable for the task.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often reveal things early-on in descriptions by saying things like 'it was a painting' and then proceeding to describe it.
nodes.response: It can be much more effective to describe your narrator's view before revealing what the view actually is. This way, the reader is kept in a state of anticipation, as they try to work out what the view is.

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold the map the wrong way round, not matching it to their direction of travel, making it harder to locate points accurately.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils orient the map so it matches the direction they're facing. They must turn the map until the features on the map line up with what they can see around them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush off without planning a logical route, leading to wasted time or missed checkpoints.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils allow time to plan their route with their partner and that they understand the value in doing this.

nodes.misconception: Confusion transferring the route from the map to real life.
nodes.response: By orientating the map and holding it facing the same way relative to key features/north, you can quickly navigate around and avoid confusion every time you change direction.

nodes.misconception: 'Jihad' always refers to an external battle or war.
nodes.response: 'Jihad' can refer to both an external battle or war and the internal struggle to be a better Muslim.

nodes.misconception: That Orwell offers a solution to the problems he highlights.
nodes.response: Focus on the cyclical structure and lack of resolution. How does this reflect Orwell's purpose? Is he just being critical and cynical?

nodes.misconception: The distance between two crests of an oscilloscope graph is equal to one wavelength.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need to read scales of graphs first and that the horizontal scale of an oscilloscope graph is time.

nodes.misconception: A tragedy is simply a sad play.
nodes.response: Tragedies have specific conventions, such as a tragic hero and their hamartia, a tragic fall and elements of fate or the supernatural.

nodes.misconception: Shakespeare wrote only according to Aristotle's notion of tragedy.
nodes.response: Shakespeare had his own beliefs about tragedy and combined them with Aristotle's ideas.

nodes.misconception: Othello's jealousy is the only thing that causes him to be considered a tragic hero.
nodes.response: Othello also has hubris, stubbornness and anagnorisis that can add to his status as tragic hero.

nodes.misconception: Egypt and Mesopotamia are the only places to have had early civilisations.
nodes.response: Look at a map of the world and point out the locations of the Indus Valley and Shang civilisations.

nodes.misconception: Imitation and a countermelody are the same thing.
nodes.response: They are related, but not the same. Imitation has to include copying part of the melody, normally immediately. A countermelody usually tries to contrast with the main melody so that it can be heard clearly separately.

nodes.misconception: Umlauts do not make a difference to the pronunciation of a letter.
nodes.response: German vowels (with or without umlauts) can be short or long. Vowels are short when followed by more than one consonant. Vowels are long when there is a double vowel, followed by 'h', or a single consonant.

nodes.misconception: Polyrhythm and cross rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: They are related, but not the same. A polyrhythm doesn't necessarily have to create different senses of pulse - it can just have different rhythms playing together. A cross rhythm has to create different senses of pulse at the same time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the 'ei' spelling only represents the 'ee' phoneme.
nodes.response: Show a range of words with 'ei' representing different sounds.  You can stretch and sound button to show the direct phoneme - grapheme correspondence.

nodes.misconception: Some children may think a letter string can only represent one sound.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the key phonics principles: a sound can be represented by more than one letter,  one sound can be represented by more than one spelling and one spelling can represent more than one sound.  It is why the English language is so hard!

nodes.misconception: Sentences such as 'when I was little, I would do the shopping with my mother' can be translated by using both the imperfect tense and the conditional mood.
nodes.response: In French, when writing or translating sentences about what used to happen, all verbs should be in the imperfect tense. 'Used to' and 'would' (meaning habitually) are translated by the imperfect.

nodes.misconception: A separate word for 'will' and 'would' needs to be translated into French when using future or conditional verbs.
nodes.response: The 1-verb future and conditional verb forms express 'will' and 'would' in their spellings. No separate word is required.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that all change involves places becoming urbanised or developed.
nodes.response: Show children examples of areas that have been re-greened.

nodes.misconception: Cultural appropriation is just appreciation and admiration of other cultures.
nodes.response: Cultural appropriation can be the unacknowledged or inappropriate adoption or use of elements of a minority culture by members of the dominant culture, often in a way that is disrespectful, stereotypical, or exploitative.

nodes.misconception: Climate change is going to cause the planet to get hotter and drier.
nodes.response: The planet is getting hotter. Some places are going to get hotter whereas some places are going to get wetter.

nodes.misconception: That birth rates and death rates are the total number of people who have been born or died.
nodes.response: Birth and death rates are per 1 000 people per year.

nodes.misconception: All houses look the same from above.
nodes.response: You can identify that some houses have flat roofs while others have pitched roofs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to give extended reasons for their opinions and then lose their full sentence structure.
nodes.response: Provide clear speaking frames and model sentence stems for the children to encourage them to speak in full, clear sentences. They only need to give one reason for each opinion.

nodes.misconception: Cities and towns are words used to describe a settlement of the same size interchangeably.
nodes.response: Towns are used to describe settlements with a population of thousands whereas cities are usually used to describe settlements of over 100 000 or millions.

nodes.misconception: All settlements grew in the industrial revolution because factories were built to provide jobs.
nodes.response: There are a variety of reasons settlements grow including developing as a tourist location or market town.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse National Parks with other protected sites.
nodes.response: Protected areas fall into two categories: internationally designated (Biosphere Reserves and World Heritage sites) and nationally designated (National Parks, Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty and National Scenic Areas). Identifying these may help.

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go after the noun in French: un chien noir.
nodes.response: Some adjectives go before the noun in French. These are prenominal adjectives that refer to beauty, age, good/bad or size (BAGS): un petit chien.

nodes.misconception: You don't have to be in a field to be doing fieldwork.
nodes.response: Fieldwork means going outside to gather information. Going outside and exploring our school grounds is fieldwork.

nodes.misconception: Ground photos can only be taken close to the ground.
nodes.response: They can also be taken at eye level (if you are lying on the floor, sitting down or standing up). They all count as ground level photos.

nodes.misconception: All schools look the same.
nodes.response: Many schools have the same key features and complete similar activities but don't all look the same.

nodes.misconception: Stars and the planets in our solar system are intermingled, with stars between the planets.
nodes.response: Make it clear with diagrams, scaled examples and/or videos (freely available online) that 'zoom out' from Earth, that the second nearest star to Earth is 10 000 times further away from the Sun than Neptune, the most distant planet.

nodes.misconception: China and the USSR fought alongside North Korea from the beginning of the Korean War.
nodes.response: China and the USSR supported the North Korean invasion but did not participate. China only joined the war at a later stage.

nodes.misconception: A condition will keep being checked on its own.
nodes.response: Conditions need to be inside forever loops if you want them to be repeatedly checked.

nodes.misconception: A program’s outcome can only be achieved in one way.
nodes.response: Using different combinations or sequences of commands can achieve the same outcome even though the finished solution might not have been the best way to produce the outcome .

nodes.misconception: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender. If a word is feminine we think of it as a girl if it is masculine we think of it as a boy.
nodes.response: Grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender. Spelling clues help to identify Spanish grammatical gender: nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, nouns ending in -a are usually feminine.

nodes.misconception: There is one word for 'the' in Spanish, like in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the definite article must match the gender of the noun. 'El' is the word for 'the' for masculine nouns (e.g., 'el uniforme') and 'la' is the word for 'the' for feminine nouns (e.g., 'la tarta').

nodes.misconception: An outlier always has values that are outside the range of the dataset (i.e. at the start or end of a dataset).
nodes.response: For bivariate data, a data point may be distinct from the rest of the data because the value of one of its variable is extremely less/greater than other points that have a similar value in its other variable.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often throw the ball from where they have caught it, and then stay in that position. Pupils throw the ball towards their opponent instead of into space.
nodes.response: Pupils should be reminded to always return to the middle of the court after throwing the ball. Pupils should always be looking to throw ito space away from their opponent.

nodes.misconception: An attacker should move as as soon as their teammate catches the ball.
nodes.response: A feint is an effective way to create space as we wait for the ball handler to present the ball ready to make the pass, rather than moving too early and the defender being able to catch up with you.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that when they are not batting, they don't need to pay attention to what is happening on the field.
nodes.response: Being a good team member requires us to encourage our teammates and be aware of what is happening in the game, even when our turn to bat has not finished or even started yet.

nodes.misconception: Pupils get confused about which side to serve from and who serves next.
nodes.response: A server keeps serving after winning a point and they alternate sides each point —from the right if their score is even and left if it is odd. If the opposition wins a rally, they earn a point and the service with the other partner serving next.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the best way to win is to hit ithe ball harder.
nodes.response: Sometimes just keeping the ball in and waiting for your opposition to make a mistake is the best way to win points, but it is also helpful to disrupt the rhythm by varying pace/spin, breaking the angle or using disguise to wrong foot your opposition.

nodes.misconception: The most common error made when beginning to learn how to bowl in cricket is that pupils throw the ball with the elbow bending in the action which is not allowed.
nodes.response: Pupils need to understand that the action requires a straight arm and this should be emphasised throughout the lesson. It is perhaps a unique throwing action which takes time to adjust to.

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold onto the object too tightly and for too long, releasing it too late.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of holding the object with a relaxed grip and releasing it high for greater distance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that the throw should primarily come from the arm, rather than using their whole body.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that for greater accuracy and distance, they should also use their legs, feet, hands, hips and body.

nodes.misconception: When subtracting or dividing, the largest value is found by subtracting or dividing the largest rounded number by the largest rounded divisor or additive inverse.
nodes.response: Drawing a number line to show the subtraction of the smallest number will help students see how to achieve an overestimate or underestimate. When using division, reiterating the division of number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

nodes.misconception: The Welsh lords were chanting 'Owain Glyndwr, Prince of Wales' because he was the Prince.
nodes.response: Ensure children know that the Welsh lords were chanting because they wanted Owain to become the Prince of Wales and their leader.

nodes.misconception: If you find something on the web, you can use it as your own.
nodes.response: Most online content is owned by someone and you need permission to use it as your own.

nodes.misconception: Ozone layer and climate change are linked/the same thing.
nodes.response: Ozone layer depletion was caused by human activity, but not through use of burning fossil fuels/greenhouse gas emissions. Both are atmospheric issues, but not the same issue.

nodes.misconception: Pacifism just means being against war.
nodes.response: Pacifism is broader than just opposing war. It’s a belief that all violence is wrong, which can affect how someone responds to conflict, punishment, protest and even self-defence.

nodes.misconception: I can only use the words I have learnt in lessons when speaking and writing in French.
nodes.response: Reference resources like bilingual dictionaries give you the freedom to look up new words that are important to you, and include them in your work. You can build up a treasure trove of vocabulary this way.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might use the same brush size for the entire painting.
nodes.response: Demonstrate how larger brushes are best for covering big areas like the background, while smaller brushes are ideal for details like leaves, veins, or animal features. Provide examples of how different brush sizes create varied textures and effects.

nodes.misconception: All maps have to look like the ones on phones or paper.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that some artists make maps with patterns, colours and memories.

nodes.misconception: All opinions should be the same.
nodes.response: Remind children that other people might disagree with you or have a different opinion. This is what helps to make art exciting.

nodes.misconception: A portrait has to look real or neat to show who someone is.
nodes.response: Portraits can show feeling, memory, or mood without looking realistic. Artists use colour, texture and shape to tell a story about the person.

nodes.misconception: The largest features of a facial expression convey the most emotion.
nodes.response: Applying details and small adjustments to a facial expression such as tone, texture and highlights can make them more dynamic, expressive and realistic.

nodes.misconception: Faces are symmetrical and all proportions should fit to set guidelines.
nodes.response: Most faces are asymmetrical with different proportions. Guidelines for drawing faces give only a rough estimation of where features might be placed, and will differ for each person, as we are all unique.

nodes.misconception: That each part of a triptych is separate and unconnected.
nodes.response: Remind children that in a triptych, each panel shares ideas with the others to create one single artwork.

nodes.misconception: The screen is like a piece of paper, so you should be able to touch it to draw.
nodes.response: Digital devices work in different ways. Some devices use a finger but other devices can be used with a mouse, a trackpad or in other ways.

nodes.misconception: That portrait means the picture is always a person's face, and landscape means it can only be a big outdoor scene.
nodes.response: Remind children that portrait just means the paper is taller than it is wide, and landscape means it’s wider than tall. You can use both for many different kinds of pictures, not just faces or outdoor scenes.

nodes.misconception: When throwing at a target, pupils will often think only of hitting the target and not the consequences of missing it - which often leads to losing more runs through overthrowing it.
nodes.response: Pupils understand the need to back up their teammate as they throw, and the need for the thrower to check that someone is backing up before throwing.

nodes.misconception: 'Il est' always means 'he is'.
nodes.response: 'Il est' can be used as an impersonal verb where 'il' means 'it' and is not referring to a specific thing but talking about 'it' in general. e.g. 'Il est difficile de croire' means 'It is difficult to believe'.

nodes.misconception: 'Il' always means 'he' in English.
nodes.response: In impersonal phrases, ‘il’ never means ‘he’. It often means ‘it’, but does not refer to a specific person or thing. It is often used in weather phrases, saying what time it is and what you must (not) do.

nodes.misconception: Paper and boards are often seen as weak materials.
nodes.response: Many types of paper and boards are designed to be robust and durable, such as corrugated cardboard used for packaging.

nodes.misconception: Injuries can be prevented by using methods such as PAR-Q
nodes.response: Nothing can guarantee that injuries will not happen, however the measures discussed in this lesson will significantly reduce the risk of injury. Accidents will always happen.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not appreciate all the steps required to prove what type of shape is shown.
nodes.response: A warm-up for the lesson could be to review properties of shapes. Consider describing a shape, one property at a time. How much information is needed before pupils can be certain they know which shape is being described?

nodes.misconception: Push-pull and parallel linkages are made of more than one lever.
nodes.response: Levers can be joined together to form a linkage. A parallel and push-pull linkage is made up of multiple levers.

nodes.misconception: Lines are parallel if they have the same gradient.
nodes.response: Lines are parallel if they have the same gradient and different y-intercepts. Two lines are parallel if they are straight lines that are always the same non-zero distance apart.

nodes.misconception: Parallel vectors can only be in the same direction.
nodes.response: Two vectors are parallel if one can be written as a scalar multiple of the other. This scalar multiple can be negative therefore the direction can be opposite, but the gradients remain equivalent.

nodes.misconception: Parallel vectors must be in the same direction.
nodes.response: Two vectors are parallel if one can be written as a scalar multiple of the other. This scalar multiple can be negative therefore the direction can be opposite, but the gradients remain equivalent.

nodes.misconception: The final ‘-s’ in ‘sus’ refers to more than one person.
nodes.response: The final ‘s’ refers to a plural noun.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe dashes and commas are used interchangeably in fiction writing.
nodes.response: We favour using dashes when we are showing a dramatic effect and commas when simply adding detail.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include within brackets information that is essential to the sentence's coherence.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to cover the parenthesis in a sentence and see if what's left makes complete sense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify where to add parenthesis in a sentence.
nodes.response: It is easiest to add parenthesis after nouns or verbs - encourage children to identify these if needed.

nodes.misconception: Indefinite adjectives always agree in number and gender.
nodes.response: 'Tout le' agrees in number and gender but 'même', 'autre' and 'quelque' agree in number only. 'Chaque' and 'plusieurs' do not change.

nodes.misconception: When translating from French to English or vice versa, you simply translate word-for-word.
nodes.response: Word order is often different in French and English. In many cases, we can't translate word-for-word and you may need to paraphrase.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often take-off with the wrong foot when performing the thief vault or they take-off too close to the obstacle.
nodes.response: Work on take-off in isolation, focusing on taking-off with the outside foot and ensuring there is enough space between them and the obstacle to ensure continued flow through the vault.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may choose obstacles that don't link well and therefore don't allow for smooth transitions.
nodes.response: Provide lots of route planning support and examples/advice throughout the lesson.

nodes.misconception: 'Cuál' and 'cuáles' may appear directly before a noun.
nodes.response: 'Cuál' and 'cuáles' may not appear directly before a noun. As they are pronouns, they either stand alone or appear before a verb.

nodes.misconception: Takadi and Ta-dimi are the same thing.
nodes.response: Takadi is quick-quick-slow. Ta-dimi is slow-quick-quick.

nodes.misconception: We only need to warm up before a performance.
nodes.response: It is important to warm up before we sing, whether that is when we rehearse, in a lesson, or before a performance. Warming up develops our vocal skills and protects our voice from injury.

nodes.misconception: The idea that there is air between the particles in a gas.
nodes.response: Emphasis on explaining that air contains particles and has nothing between them.

nodes.misconception: Children may think two-digit numbers can only be partitioned into tens and ones.
nodes.response: Use practical equipment to manipulate tens and ones on part-part-whole models to help children to understand the many ways that a number can be partitioned.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle when partitioning hundreds and tens (e.g. partitioning 340 into 220 and 120).
nodes.response: Give pupils opportunities to manipulate base ten blocks, rearranging them and partitioning both the hundreds and the tens.

nodes.misconception: Children may forget to start with the whole group when writing subtraction equations.
nodes.response: Maintain a strong focus throughout on what the numbers in equations represent. Explore mistakes that are made to clarify understanding.

nodes.misconception: When describing the partitioning of a number, children may mix the parts and the whole.
nodes.response: Reinforce the stem sentence, ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part highlighting, the whole and each part using gestures.

nodes.misconception: Counters are being used for unitisation in this lesson but sometimes pupils can struggle to understand that counters can be worth different amounts without a proportional change in size.
nodes.response: Count up and down in different amounts using the counters so that children understand they represent a unit that can have different values in different examples.

nodes.misconception: When using patterns to identify combinations, pupils may struggle to be systematic and not identify all options systematically.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring the value of recording combinations within a simple table. Encourage checking, e.g. the amount of counters totals six. Look for patterns and support children in spotting these.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are not yet fluent in number pairs and partitions of numbers 6 to 10 and so rely on counting to find missing parts.
nodes.response: Develop subitising skills so that pupils are able to recognise small partitions instantly. Encourage choral repetition of stem sentences emphasising wholes and parts.

nodes.misconception: When using patterns to identify combinations, pupils may struggle to be systematic and not identify all options systematically.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring the value of recording combinations within a simple table. Encourage checking, e.g. the amount of counters totals eight. Look for patterns and support children in spotting these.

nodes.misconception: When using patterns to identify combinations, it will be easy to make errors in recording.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring the value of recording combinations within a simple table. Encourage checking, e.g. the amount of counters totals 5.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the importance of the order of the tens and ones digits in indicating the value of each part of a two-digit number.
nodes.response: Use place value charts, place value arrows and Gattegno charts to reinforce the value of each digit.

nodes.misconception: Children may reverse the digits in a two-digit number, not understanding the value of each digit, or partition, for example, 54 into 5 and 4
nodes.response: Return to the use of practical equipment and ask children to prove they are right using it. They could also explain their ideas to a friend to encourage them to spot their own errors.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the link between partitioning 100 into 2, 4, 5 and 10 equal parts and partitioning 1,000 into those equal parts.
nodes.response: You may wish to revisit partitioning 100 into equal parts, using representations familiar to pupils, to help them to understand that their knowledge of partitioning 100 can be applied to partitioning 1,000

nodes.misconception: Pupils may miscalculate measures questions involving unit conversions if they are not secure with the key conversions of 1 m = 1,000 mm, 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 kg = 1,000 g and 1 l = 1,000 ml.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing the etymology of the words so pupils are not necessarily relying on memory and can figure out the equivalences if they cannot recall them. 'Milli' means 'thousandth' and 'kilo' means 'thousand': both relate to a thousand parts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't perform the animal actions for a count of 6. Pupils think they have to find the cards for the animal action scavenger hunt in numerical order.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that keeping the rules demonstrates fair play and ensures everyone enjoys the game. Pupils can find and perform the animal action cards in any order.

nodes.misconception: Pupils shout too loudly, thinking this will improve communication. Pupils place floor markers too close together, resulting in slow movement across the river.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of good sentences spoken at a normal talking volume. Highlight pupils who place floor markers an arm's length from each other and move across the river more efficiently.

nodes.misconception: Pupils push or hit their partner too hard when they are the chaser. Pupils bump into each other playing tag.
nodes.response: Teach pupils how to tag and remind them to tap gently. Remind pupils to slow down or dodge to avoid collisions.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might dominate the partnership.
nodes.response: Cooperation and communication are key factors in any partnership: they must share roles and listen to one another's ideas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can only stand when making letter shapes.
nodes.response: Pupils can lie, sit, or stand to make letter shapes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils throw equipment too high or throw overarm, and then blame their partner for being unable to catch it.
nodes.response: Encourage underarm throwing with a gentle force to help ensure all partners can catch and succeed.

nodes.misconception: Singing two songs together or the same song at different times will clash and not sound harmonious.
nodes.response: Partner songs and rounds have melodies that fit together harmoniously, and the parts are sung following the same steady beat.

nodes.misconception: Singing two songs together will clash and not sound harmonious.
nodes.response: Partner songs are made of notes that sound good together. The songs are partnered up because they fit harmoniously and can be sung following the same steady beat.

nodes.misconception: Parts lists are only needed for materials or components which need to be bought in.
nodes.response: A parts lists supports the thinking needed in preparation of manufacture for all components of a design. They help identify quantities and can highlight mistakes. A well-structured parts list speeds up production and ensures cost efficiency.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants make seeds automatically as a part of their life cycle, rather than needing pollination to take place.
nodes.response: Explain that flowers can only make seeds once pollination and fertilisation has happened.

nodes.misconception: All separable verbs in German have their word-for-word English equivalent, e.g., 'stattfinden' - 'to take place', 'mitbringen' - to bring with, along'.
nodes.response: Many two-part separable verbs in German have single word English translations, e.g., 'einkaufen' - 'to shop', 'anfangen' - 'to start'. It is especially important with these verbs not to forget the separable prefix in German.

nodes.misconception: German has one general verb meaning 'to put, putting'.
nodes.response: German has three placement verbs that translate into English as 'to put, putting'. 'Stellen' - to make something stand (vertically), 'setzen' - to make something sit, 'legen' - to make something lay down (horizontally).

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that for GCSE assessment, passing is only required in isolation to demonstrate the correct techniques.
nodes.response: Passing needs to be seen in progressive and conditioned practices to showcase the technique when faced with opposition and decision making.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they only have 3 seconds to pass the ball like in netball.
nodes.response: In Korfball pupils have 4 seconds to pass the ball.

nodes.misconception: Pupils stand still once they are in a space and just wait for the ball to come to them.
nodes.response: Explain that we must keep moving to find spaces to ensure our team always has several passing options. If we stand still, the defenders could intercept the ball.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think they need to take multiple touches before passing the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make quick decisions using one or two touch passes, and encourage pupils to scan before receiving the ball so they know where to pass to next.

nodes.misconception: Pupils make a pass and stand still, waiting for the next ball. This is a common issue, especially in futsal, where quick transitions and movement are key.
nodes.response: After passing, always move to create an option. A great habit is to perform a give-and-go, where you pass the ball and immediately make a run to receive it back. This keeps the game fluid.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that by dodging they will always create space and outwit the defender. Pupils dodge to find a space then stand still waiting for a pass.
nodes.response: Pupils need to remember that the defenders role is to respond to the dodge, therefore they may need to dodge again and look for new space. Persevering with this technique will help pupils successfully outwit their opponent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they can pass the ball forward. Pupils get confused with the meaning of passing the ball backwards and think that means passing over their head, rather then in relation to their attack.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the rule that passes must go laterally or backwards, so the player receiving must not go ahead of the player in possession of the ball.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will try and make a pass to score from too far away. Pupils run into the endzone boxes to receive a pass too early and are just standing still in the box.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to be closer to the scoring zones before trying to make a pass to score. Explain that if we just stand in the box, we aren't helping our team with a passing option.

nodes.misconception: Pupils panic when receiving the ball and throw it away quickly, especially if there is a defender close to them.
nodes.response: Explain that this may result in losing possession and that players have 4 seconds before they have to pass. Encourage pupils to use this time to choose the most suitable pass.

nodes.misconception: Pupils panic when there is a defender and kick/strike/throw the ball away quickly to prevent the defender getting too close to them.
nodes.response: Explain that if we panic, we will probably lose possession in a game. Encourage pupils to take their time. Bring in walking defenders instead to slow the game down.

nodes.misconception: Pupils just stand still when receiving the ball, not understanding the importance of positioning.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to understand the importance of moving towards the ball and getting set when receiving it.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils struggle with over or under throwing the ball, throwing either too hard or too soft. In game situations, pupils often all gravitate towards the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to continue to use the correct technique and focus on following through towards their target. This will eliminate the need to throw harder or softer as the technique will support accuracy. Ensure pupils are using the whole space.

nodes.misconception: Spin passes are always better to use.
nodes.response: Short or soft pop passes can be more effective for quick, controlled distribution, especially in close quarters or wet conditions where accuracy and catchability matter more than speed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils make simple ball handling mistakes due to rushing.
nodes.response: You lose possession if the ball is dropped, so whilst you need to make a pass within 3 seconds, it is essential not to make rushed decisions for passing and focus on catching the ball carefully with both hands before making your next move.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often rush their shots and look to try and score as soon as they get the ball, without considering their location in relation to the post or target.
nodes.response: Pupils must remember that they have approximately 4 seconds to prepare and then shoot. Remind pupils that using the correct shooting technique will increase their chances of success.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that spin passes are always better to use.
nodes.response: Short or soft pop passes can be more effective for quick, controlled distribution, especially in close quarters or wet conditions where accuracy and catchability matter more than speed.

nodes.misconception: I don't need to practice passing because I can already catch well and have good technique.
nodes.response: Passing isn’t just about mechanics, it’s also about teamwork. Practicing with different teammates helps improve subtle communication, like eye contact and timing, and allows you to understand how others prefer to receive the ball.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that once they have moved into a space, they can stay still and wait for the ball to come to them.
nodes.response: Pupils must be reminded to keep moving, creating angles for passes to the sides of their opposition. If they stand still, it makes it really easy for the defender to mark them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that the harder they throw the ball, the better the pass will be.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of accuracy and remind the pupils that a softer, better-placed pass will be more effective and easier for teammates to receive.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can panic when receiving the ball in a game situation and rush to throw it away. Pupils all run towards the ball carrier rather than finding space.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of finding space and looking around to understand what to do when receiving the ball. Make sure they understand they have time to react and think before sending the ball on to their teammates.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that GCSE assessment for passing is just looking at the techniques in isolation.
nodes.response: Passing needs to be seen in progressive and conditioned practices to showcase the technique when faced with opposition and decision making.

nodes.misconception: To talk about the future in German you have to use the future tense with 'werden'.
nodes.response: In German, you can use the present tense and a future time phrase to talk about the future: 'ich spiele nächste Woche Tennis' - 'I'm playing/going to play tennis next week'. 'Planen' and 'vorhaben' in the present tense also express future intentions.

nodes.misconception: Historical factors no longer impact on global inequality around the world.
nodes.response: There is an enduring impact of history on global inequality. Historical factors have shaped wealth, opportunities, and power today.

nodes.misconception: It does not matter whether I use the preterite or the imperfect as both refer to the past.
nodes.response: To talk about something completed in the past, we use the preterite tense. However, to talk about something that happened repeatedly in the past, with the meaning 'used to', we use the imperfect tense.

nodes.misconception: Climate change and global warming are the same thing.
nodes.response: Global warming is the increase in Earth's average temperature over a long period of time, whereas  climate change is a large-scale and long-term change in the planet’s climate, including weather patterns and average temperatures.

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter if the action was completed or repeated - I can use any past tense verb.
nodes.response: In Spanish, we choose between the preterite and imperfect based on how the action happened in the past. Use the preterite to communicate an action that happened once and the imperfect for actions that were repeated over a period of time.

nodes.misconception: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' only.
nodes.response: 'Dar' usually translates as 'to give' but it is also used to describe how something makes people feel. e.g. da rabia - it makes me angry.

nodes.misconception: When asking questions like 'Did you travel by plane?' in Spanish, I need to start by translating the word 'did'.
nodes.response: To ask a 'did'-style question in Spanish, you can form an intonation question by simply raising your voice at the end of a past-tense sentence. It is not necessary to translate the word 'did'.

nodes.misconception: To say what I did in the past, remove the infinitive ending and add -é.
nodes.response: To say what I did in the past for a regular -ar verb, remove the infinitive ending and add -é. To say what I did in the past for a regular -er or -ir verb, remove the infinitive ending and add -í.

nodes.misconception: All words ending in -ia must have an accent.
nodes.response: Words ending in a vowel usually stress the penultimate syllable. Words ending in -ía have stress on the final syllable, so they need an accent e.g., energía. Words ending in -ia stress the penultimate syllable, so no accent is needed e.g. ciencia.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure about the past tense form of some verbs, particularly irregular verbs.
nodes.response: Use a range of past tense irregular verbs in modelled sentences. Give pupils a sentence scaffold including past tense verbs for Task B.

nodes.misconception: 'Fue' means 'I went'.
nodes.response: 'Fui' means 'I went' and 'fue' means 'she, he, it went'. The two have similar spelling so are easily confused.

nodes.misconception: Patterns need to be regular and ordered.
nodes.response: Pattern can be irregular or regular.

nodes.misconception: Repetition is only about numbers and how they are repeated.
nodes.response: Repetition means any repeated action, not just counting (e.g., brushing both sides of your teeth).

nodes.misconception: Patterns in medieval paintings were just decoration.
nodes.response: Patterns actually had symbolic and spiritual meanings, helping people understand religious ideas when most couldn’t read.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all repeating patterns are natural patterns, even if they are man-made.
nodes.response: To help clarify, you could emphasise that natural patterns are found in nature. Nature walks can be a hands-on way to help students discover natural patterns.

nodes.misconception: All the parts of a mobile phone come from one country.
nodes.response: The raw materials which go into making phones come from all around the world.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that as soon as someone is arrested, they go to prison.
nodes.response: This doesn't happen and is not what happened to Paul Stephenson. He was kept in a holding cell in the police station until midnight.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the only people not allowed to work for the Bristol bus companies in 1963 were black people.
nodes.response: The bus companies did not allow anyone who was not white to work for them.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that people only came to Britain from the Caribbean.
nodes.response: People from all over the world came to Britain, including from places like India and Poland.

nodes.misconception: That evacuation was a negative experience for all children.
nodes.response: Lots of children had healthier diets, more freedom and enjoyed their lives in the countryside.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that only Paul Stephenson's actions directly led to the 1965 law.
nodes.response: Paul's actions had an impact as did many other people's in the 1960s.

nodes.misconception: Allies are open and honest with each other, as friends should be.
nodes.response: Countries break alliances frequently and regularly act against the interests of long-time allies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that it is okay to turn over on to your front when finishing a backstroke race.
nodes.response: When swimming backstroke you should use the flags to count your strokes so that you finish a race on your back.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty making edits to their work in a practical way - where to write extra words etc.
nodes.response: Writing double-spaced is a good way of allowing room for editing - or you may want to have pupils re-draft the opening completely, depending on your school's approach.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty in making edits to their work in a practical way - where to write extra words etc.
nodes.response: Writing double-spaced is a good way of allowing room for editing - or you may want to have pupils re-draft the report completely, depending on your own school approach.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty in making edits to their work in a practical way - where to write extra words etc.
nodes.response: Writing double-spaced is a good way of allowing room for editing - or you may want to have pupils re-draft the report completely, depending on your school's approach.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means correcting spelling and handwriting only.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving language choices, sentence structure and enhancing the overall quality and effectiveness of the writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think the more edits they make the better.
nodes.response: Praise pupils not on the amount they have edited, but on how well they are working as a team to find things that need correcting or improving.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which elements of their writing to edit.
nodes.response: Learning cycles explicitly model how to edit different aspects of writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means correcting spelling and handwriting only.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving language choices, sentence structure and enhancing the overall quality and effectiveness of the writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty making edits to their work in a practical way - where to write extra words etc.
nodes.response: Writing double-spaced is a good way of allowing room for editing - or you may want to have pupils re-draft the opening completely, depending on your school's approach.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means correcting spelling and handwriting only.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving language choices, sentence structure and enhancing the overall quality and effectiveness of the writing.

nodes.misconception: When conjugating verbs in Spanish, you always need to start by taking off the infinitive ending.
nodes.response: Some verb tenses, such as the inflectional future, are formed by adding the relevant ending to the infinitive. As such, the infinitive ending is not taken off.

nodes.misconception: When producing written work in Spanish, I should stick to short simple sentences.
nodes.response: When producing written work in Spanish, you should try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity.

nodes.misconception: The inflectional future communicates what is 'going to' happen.
nodes.response: The inflectional future communicates what 'will' happen. 'Voy a + infinitive' communicates what is 'going to' happen.

nodes.misconception: Shocks of earthquakes only happen once.
nodes.response: Large earthquakes will often have an initial shock and then be followed by a series of aftershocks as the tectonic plates settle.

nodes.misconception: 'Su' is the only possessive adjective for 'his' and 'hers' in Spanish.
nodes.response: 'Su' is his', 'hers' or 'its' before a singular noun. 'Sus' is 'his' 'hers', or 'its' before a plural noun.

nodes.misconception: When a weak vowel is next to a strong vowel, we pronounce them separately.
nodes.response: When a weak vowel is next to a strong vowel, like for example [i] next to [a], [e] or [o], it merges with them to make a single syllable.

nodes.misconception: When investigating a context you should only consider the users preferences.
nodes.response: There are many different groups of people from different places that should be considered when investigating a context. These different groups of people like stakeholders all have different preferences which the designer should consider.

nodes.misconception: The word for 'who' in German is 'wer'.
nodes.response: We use 'wer' to ask or report a question: 'Wer ist das?', 'Ich weiß nicht, wer das ist.' But in sentences like 'that is someone, who ...' we use a relative pronoun - 'der', 'die', 'das' - which matches the gender of noun it refers to.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think all or most Indigenous peoples in the Amazon rainforest live traditional lifestyles.
nodes.response: Many indigenous people in the Amazon rainforest live a modern lifestyle and have a range of jobs.

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter which Spanish translation of the verb 'to be' we use, as they both mean 'to be, being'.
nodes.response: The verb 'ser' is used to talk about permanent traits, and the verb 'estar' is used to talk about temporary states/moods and location.

nodes.misconception: The 'h' is sometimes pronounced in Spanish.
nodes.response: The 'h' is never pronounced in Spanish, regardless of its position in the word (hola, zanahoria).

nodes.misconception: Children may rush through the drawing without observing carefully, believing that drawing quickly means drawing well.
nodes.response: Children could be reminded to take their time and look closely at the subject.

nodes.misconception: We translate 'de' into English with 'of'.
nodes.response: Sometimes we don't actually need to translate the 'de' in a French sentence into English. For example, there is no possessive apostrophe in French so to express 'Sophie's sister' we have to say 'the sister of Sophie' - 'la sœur de Sophie'.

nodes.misconception: All Indigenous people have a traditional lifestyle.
nodes.response: Indigenous people may have a traditional lifestyle, e.g. reindeer herders, or may have taken on less traditional lifestyles and/or migrated.

nodes.misconception: Only people that live in/near the rainforest use it.
nodes.response: Many products grown/extracted from the rainforest are exported and used by people all over the world.

nodes.misconception: The singular imperative form for 2nd person 'tú' is the same as the present tense ending: -as or -es.
nodes.response: The singular imperative form for 2nd person 'tú' is the same as the 3rd person present tense - the ending is -a for -ar verbs, and -e for -er and -ir verbs.

nodes.misconception: All past participles in Spanish end in -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er/-ir verbs).
nodes.response: Although most Spanish past participles do follow these regular patterns, some verbs have irregular past participles which just need to be learnt, e.g. 'escrito' ('written'), 'visto' ('seen'), 'hecho' ('done'), 'dicho' ('said').

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe they can just win by hitting the ball with power.
nodes.response: Winning in table tennis isn’t just about power as control, spin, placement and consistency are just as important. A well-placed shot forces your opponent into difficult returns and increases your accuracy in rallies.

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%

nodes.misconception: Students often confuse percentage yield with atom economy, thinking both measure the same efficiency aspect.
nodes.response: Clarify that percentage yield measures actual vs. theoretical product amount, while atom economy measures reactants' mass converted to desired product.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse percentage yield with atom economy, thinking both measure the same efficiency aspect.
nodes.response: Clarify that percentage yield measures actual vs. theoretical product amount, while atom economy measures reactants' mass converted to desired product.

nodes.misconception: Students do not take the time to plan properly before writing.
nodes.response: Not taking the time to plan a response properly makes your argument less concise and less coherent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might presume that the past participle is always the same as the simple past tense.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to hear what sounds correct, for example, 'it has flown off', 'it has flew off'. This should be 'it has flown off'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused between progressive and perfect tenses.
nodes.response: Focus on the auxiliary verbs and main verb forms - 'to be' vs 'to have' and -ing forms vs past tense forms.

nodes.misconception: When singing in parts it's better to sing loudly so that you are not distracted by the other parts.
nodes.response: If everyone sings more gently, they can hear themselves, and others, properly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rush to complete their sequence and therefore do not perform to their potential. Pupils may give very brief, low quality feedback to their peers.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to reflect on feedback and keep striving to produce the best sequence by continually making changes to improve their performance. When pupils feedback to each other, encourage them to use key terminology and give quality feedback.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not contribute to reflections as a group as they may lack confidence to speak up in front of others. Pupils may lose flow in their sequence when they add balances.
nodes.response: Encourage every pupil to contribute in group reflection tasks and consider ways in which everyone can give feedback. Pupils should think carefully about how they will get into and out of their balances to maintain flow throughout the sequence.

nodes.misconception: All performance enhancing drugs are illegal/banned/negative.
nodes.response: The use of some PEDs to enhance performance is perfectly acceptable. Many sportspeople use narcotic analgesics to get through an event or drink caffeine for its stimulating effect. WADA is responsible for determining which PEDs are allowed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to give a reason for their opinion.
nodes.response: Model lots of examples using 'because' to expand upon their choice. Call on confident pupils to share their reasons for their opinions and give lots of praise for using 'because' in a sentence.

nodes.misconception: That we can't do anything to help control our nerves.
nodes.response: While we can't stop the feeling of nervousness entirely, we can trick our body into relaxing more by smiling and using deep breathing.

nodes.misconception: There may be pupils who do not know a nursery rhyme by heart.
nodes.response: Use the Y1 'Nursery rhyme' unit prior to this lesson to familiarise children with a range of nursery rhymes. Spend time in class singing and reciting nursery rhymes together. Children may wish to choose their favourite nursery rhyme to perform.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel they can simply read out their written journalistic report.
nodes.response: A radio broadcast will likely be shorter, more succinct and more informal than a written journalistic report. We also have the chance to include interviews directly with the people involved.

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing isn't important. We can just do it if we have time.
nodes.response: Rehearsing helps us to practise and prepare, so our performance can be successful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel they can simply read out their soliloquies.
nodes.response: Explicitly model the difference between reading and performing. You could also find some clips of actors performing in a Shakespeare play and discuss why their performance was strong and how that helped us to understand how the character is feeling.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may struggle with the choreography, leading to frustration and disengagement.
nodes.response: Differentiate within the choreography so that pupils have choices over the skills they perform. If you would like all pupils to perform the same skill, make sure this skill is accessible for all pupils.

nodes.misconception: Syncopation always makes music sound more energetic and driving.
nodes.response: Syncopation can make a piece feel laid back by relaxing the timing to give a 'behind the beat' effect.  Syncopated rhythms often leave gaps between sounds, which can make the groove feel more spacious and less rushed.

nodes.misconception: Improvising doesn't require any thought.
nodes.response: Before we improvise, we think about what notes or rhythms we might play and how we will structure our playing, but the final product is played in the moment.

nodes.misconception: Once we can play the notes correctly, there's nothing we need to do to improve a performance.
nodes.response: Listening and watching the overall performance and getting feedback from others can help us to identify how to refine the performance such as adding dynamics, playing sensitively within the ensemble and playing precisely in time.

nodes.misconception: When working in bigger groups, there may be issues with group dynamics as pupils have to negotiate which movements they will use. Not all pupils in the group may be able to perform the movements.
nodes.response: Pupils could delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups. Pupils may have to consider adapting their  routines to help other members of their group.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that they need to feel hyped up or overly energised to perform well.
nodes.response: Overexcitement can lead to mistakes, such as, starting too fast or losing focus. Controlled breathing and mental rehearsal help you stay calm, focused and perform more efficiently.

nodes.misconception: When pupils are teaching, they do not use the additional materials and therefore provide incorrect teaching points or unsuitable adaptations for their group.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are using the additional materials to support their understanding of each skill and make sure they know how to provide adaptations so that everyone in the group can achieve success when performing the skill.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person can be 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill.   By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them.  You could show videos of real poets performing their own poetry.

nodes.misconception: The longer (taller) bars on a pitched percussion instrument make a higher pitch.
nodes.response: On a pitched percussion instrument, the bars with a longer length make a lower pitch and the bars with a shorter length make a higher pitch.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to mark up their own poems.
nodes.response: Model marking up the poem as a class, highlighting the different areas you might annotate. Pupils could mark up the poem in pairs or small groups.

nodes.misconception: Once we can play the rhythms and melodies correctly, there is nothing else we need to do to prepare for a performance.
nodes.response: We can think about a range of ways to make the music more expressive, for example, adding dynamics to make our music have more impact for an audience.

nodes.misconception: Performing poetry is just about reading it aloud.
nodes.response: Watching people perform poetry is very popular. The most engaging performers carefully consider how they will say the poem, and how they will engage with their audiences.

nodes.misconception: Performing poetry is just about reading it aloud.
nodes.response: Watching people perform poetry is very popular. The most engaging performers carefully consider how they will say the poem, and how they will engage with their audiences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that performing animal themed meditative balances requires acting like animals and making animal noises. This also means that pupils forget to control their breathing as they balance.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that if we make noises and actually act like animals, we are creating actions and using characterisation, not balancing to ensure calm, focus and relaxtion. We must remain silent and focus on long, slow breaths in and out.

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush their deep breathing, which reduces the impact of the technique.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it’s important not to rush deep breathing, otherwise they won’t be able to focus their minds and the technique won’t work.

nodes.misconception: Pupils over complicate the balances they are holding and fail to hold them still. This also means they will not be able to focus as they try to hold the balance.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to create a stable base, enabling their body to focus throughout and successfully use the balances as a tool to relax.

nodes.misconception: As long as the content of a poem is good, the performance will automatically be good.
nodes.response: Performance requires practise in a unique set of skills which are worth practising as a good performance can enhance the poem content.

nodes.misconception: Performance of poetry must be done only one way.
nodes.response: Whilst poetry performance should adhere to the poem's original structure and rhythm, it is an art form that invites personal interpretation.

nodes.misconception: If we've rehearsed our songs, we don't need to warm up for a performance.
nodes.response: Warming up for a performance encourages everyone to feel engaged, connected and alert as well as supporting a good quality of vocal sound.

nodes.misconception: If we know our songs well, we do not need to rehearse before a performance.
nodes.response: A rehearsal can really help to settle the nerves, helping us know what will happen and how things will feel different during the performance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to initiate the turn with their head and don't spot their landing, which leads to disorientation and a lack of control.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on looking where they want to land. You should start the spin with your eyes and your head.

nodes.misconception: The accompaniment part is semibreves throughout.
nodes.response: Two bars of the accompaniment is in minims. Encourage pupils to practise this bar specifically on its own when putting both hands/parts together.

nodes.misconception: To add shape to a melody, the emphasis will always be on the first note of the phrase.
nodes.response: This is not always the case. Quite often, when the first note of the phrase lands on the downbeat this is naturally where the emphasis falls, however, this is more about where the main beats are rather than where the phrase starts.

nodes.misconception: Both hands change position at the same time
nodes.response: Highlight to pupils that the left hand remains in the C position even though the right hand moves to the F position and back again.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find learning the entire poem off by heart challenging.
nodes.response: The lesson focuses on learning the first two verses by heart. If pupils are successful, they could try committing the entire poem to memory.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that free verse poems have no structure to them.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils read and re-read the poem many times. Each time they do so, they will hear more of the natural rhythms, beats and flow within it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that performing a poem is the same as reading a poem aloud.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that performing a poem involves carefully considering how to use volume and gestures to bring the poem to life for an audience.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may overuse gestures and movement when performing poetry.
nodes.response: Gestures and movement used in the performance should add rather than detract from the focus, which is the poem.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person can be 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill. By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them.

nodes.misconception: When pupils take a big breath, they raise their shoulders.
nodes.response: A singing breath is from the diaphragm; the upper body and shoulders should remain relaxed.

nodes.misconception: Creating a performance is the same as singing together in our normal music lessons/there is no difference between singing together and creating a performance.
nodes.response: When we perform we are sharing our work with an audience.  We need to use our performing skills such as standing like a singer and capturing a song's character using our voices to communicate the meaning of the song to the audience.

nodes.misconception: Students might try to read the poem rather than recite.
nodes.response: Encourage students to learn as much of the poem as possible.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that performing poetry is something that does not require rehearsal and careful consideration beforehand.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that to have the greatest impact on the audience, you should look through your poem and consider how you will perform it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person can be 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill. By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them. You could show videos of real poets performing their own poetry.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to select the correct process of perimeter or area.
nodes.response: Pupils should consider whether a space is to be covered in which case it is most likely area.

nodes.misconception: Shapes with the same area also have the same perimeter.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that component parts being rearranged has no effect on its area, but may affect its perimeter.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can always double the length and width to calculate the perimeter.
nodes.response: This only works for composite rectilinear shapes if the lengths do not overlap.

nodes.misconception: I can use a ruler to measure the midpoint of a line segment, and a protractor to find 90°.
nodes.response: Constructions, such as perpendicular bisectors, are methods of creating & modifying shapes & angles in ways that don't require measurements.

nodes.misconception: Perpendicular lines have to be drawn as a horizontal and vertical pair.
nodes.response: Some pupils may struggle to see that two lines are perpendicular when they are not drawn horizontally and vertically. Drawing this on paper and then rotating the paper will help them see that it is the angle between the lines that matters.

nodes.misconception: You can't accurately draw the perpendicular to a point on a line segment close to its endpoint.
nodes.response: The perpendicular to a line segment through any point can be found; some line segments just require extending in length first.

nodes.misconception: Because Christianity is the world's largest religion, Christians do not face persecution.
nodes.response: Christians have been persecuted throughout history and this continues today in some countries where Christianity is a minority religion.

nodes.misconception: The God helmet experiment has been reliably replicated and proves that religious experiences are just caused by brain stimulation.
nodes.response: In reality, the experiment has not been consistently replicated, and the results have been debated.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unfamiliar with train timetables and how to interpret them.
nodes.response: Each column of times can be given a header of Train 1, Train 2 etc. This will make it clearer that the times in a column refer to when that train will reach a station.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may spread their images separately across the page without using layering.
nodes.response: Layering is used in collage to create further meaning and depth to the artwork.

nodes.misconception: PANs are limited to Bluetooth or Wi-Fi connections.
nodes.response: PANs can use a variety of technologies, including wired connections like USB and FireWire, and wireless connections like Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and more.

nodes.misconception: Once a photo or drawing is finished, it can’t be changed or developed further.
nodes.response: A finished photo or drawing is just a starting point—artists often rework, edit, layer, or translate their images into new forms using different media to explore deeper meaning or fresh creative directions.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about technical aspects in art is that technical skill only means making artworks look realistic.
nodes.response: Technical skill also includes mastery of materials, control of techniques and the ability to use those skills effectively in any style, whether abstract, expressive, or conceptual.

nodes.misconception: I need new resources for my response.
nodes.response: You need suitable resources, ideally first-hand. They don't need to be new they can be sourced from bits of your project so far.

nodes.misconception: More detail always makes an artwork better.
nodes.response: Too much detail—especially if it’s unfocused—can make an artwork feel cluttered, overwhelming, or take attention away from the focal point.

nodes.misconception: If you don’t use traditional art materials, your work won’t be taken seriously or get a high grade.
nodes.response: Art & Design encourages experimentation with a wide range of materials — not just pencil, paint and clay. Using unusual or personal materials can strengthen marks if they are purposeful, linked to ideas and part of a thoughtful process.

nodes.misconception: Composition is more relevant to 2D work.
nodes.response: Composition is relevant to all areas of art practice as it's about deciding on the best arrangement for your work. It will be dictated by your intentions for the piece. In 3D, we consider the composition from all angles or in the round.

nodes.misconception: You should take forward all of the suggestions from your critique to improve your response.
nodes.response: You should listen to and consider all suggestions carefully, but you are expected to respond in a personal and meaningful way, so trust in your own artistic voice. You should take the suggestions forward if they align with your vision and style.

nodes.misconception: Art only connects people if everyone understands it the same way.
nodes.response: Art connects people because it sparks emotions and ideas, even if everyone sees it differently. It’s the shared experience, not exact understanding, that brings people together.

nodes.misconception: This lesson gives the impression that there are only two types of people and people should be defined as one or the other personality.
nodes.response: Although the AQA specification has clear definitions of how introverts and extroverts typically behave, which will be required knowledge in the exam, students should understand that people's personality is more nuanced and goes beyond these.

nodes.misconception: Inequality just refers to the uneven distribution of wealth.
nodes.response: Inequality is about more than wealth. It is the uneven distribution of resources, opportunities, and living conditions. It includes different categories such as economic, political, social, environmental and digital.

nodes.misconception: All Sikhs take Amrit.
nodes.response: Not all Sikhs take Amrit. Only those who choose to commit to the Khalsa, following its principles, take Amrit during a special ceremony.

nodes.misconception: Semicolons can be used to join any two clauses of any length.
nodes.response: The clauses joined by a semicolon must be both be independent clauses (which means they make sense of their own) and should be linked in terms of their subject matter.

nodes.misconception: Philosophers only think about moral issues related to humans.
nodes.response: Some philosophers also consider animals and what level of conciousness or sentience they may have.

nodes.misconception: All indicators provide precise pH values and give the same information as pH meters.
nodes.response: Indicators do not provide exact pH values; they only indicate whether a solution is acidic, neutral, or alkaline by changing colour. A pH meter, on the other hand, measures the exact pH value of a solution and is more accurate.

nodes.misconception: The difference between concentrated and dilute vs strong and weak when referring to acids and alkalis (not covered in this lesson).
nodes.response: For acids and alkalis concentration is the amount of hydrogen dissolved in a certain volume of solution. The higher the concentration, the lower the pH. Strong and weak refer to the ability of an acid to release hydrogen (not covered in lesson).

nodes.misconception: We are sourcing more energy from renewables than fossil fuels.
nodes.response: Over 80% of global energy still comes from coal, oil, and gas.

nodes.misconception: Rushing to complete the task and therforemfailing to listen to, or consider, all group members.
nodes.response: Together Everyone Achieves More, it is essential to work as a TEAM and ensure everyone is valued.

nodes.misconception: Matching a similar and incorrect photo as a result of rushing.
nodes.response: During photo orienteering, it is important to take your time and look at details carefully.

nodes.misconception: Urban landscapes cannot contain any natural features.
nodes.response: Remind children that both natural and urban landscapes can have a mix of natural and human-made features, but natural landscapes focus more on nature, and urban landscapes focus more on buildings and roads.

nodes.misconception: Landmarks are always human-made.
nodes.response: Remind children that some landmarks are made by humans but others are natural formations, such as cliffs, trees or waterfalls.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about this lesson is that photography is just about capturing what you see, when in fact it involves making creative choices.
nodes.response: Photography is about deciding how to show the subject to communicate an idea or feeling. Understanding that really opens up creative possibilities.

nodes.misconception: The Second World War was happening in the 1950's.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that the Second World War ended half way through the 1940's. In the 1950's people and cities were recovering from the effects of the war. New houses, technology and transport was available.

nodes.misconception: That photographs are the only way to find out about the 1960s and 1970s.
nodes.response: Explain that photographs are one source that historians can use. They also look at written evidence such as newspaper articles and diaries. They can talk to people who were alive in the 1960s and 1970s and look at artefacts.

nodes.misconception: Research is separate from making work.
nodes.response: Research feeds directly into experimentation and outcomes.

nodes.misconception: It is a common misconception to think that light (or energy) is a substance and a chemical reactant in photosynthesis that is converted into glucose.
nodes.response: The role of light in transferring energy to chlorophyll for photosynthesis is explored.

nodes.misconception: Failing to realise that the plateau on a rate graph can occur because another factor (not named on the axes) has become limiting.
nodes.response: The lesson explores rate graphs in which multiple limiting factors are affecting the rate of photosynthesis.

nodes.misconception: Light is a chemical reactant in photosynthesis and it is turned into food.
nodes.response: Challenge the misconception that light is a chemical reactant in photosynthesis.

nodes.misconception: Drum fills must be more complex than the fundamental groove.
nodes.response: Show how absence of sound can be as powerful as added sound by giving an example of the groove briefly stopping.

nodes.misconception: Learners may have difficulties in identifying different features in satellite images and aerial photographs.
nodes.response: Use Google Earth to first locate and zoom in on features near your school that are already familiar to learners.

nodes.misconception: Physical properties and working properties are the same thing.
nodes.response: Physical properties describe inherent features (like density, colour, or conductivity), whereas working properties describe how a material behaves under stress (like flexibility, toughness, or hardness).

nodes.misconception: All network devices connect to each other wirelessly.
nodes.response: Not all network devices use wireless connections. Many devices, like switches, routers and servers, are connected using wires to create a stable and fast network.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that being physically fit means that someone is healthy.
nodes.response: It is possible to be physically fit but unhealthy. It is essential to consider social and emotional benefits/aspects of health as well as strength, cardiovascular endurance etc.

nodes.misconception: Students think the only benefits to exercise are physical benefits.
nodes.response: Explain the importance of social and emotional benefits too, particularly for participants such as elderly people.

nodes.misconception: Learners may struggle to make sense of atlas maps which often show a lot of complex information.
nodes.response: Spend additional time exploring a digital atlas map as a class or group to reinforce learners’ understanding of different map conventions.

nodes.misconception: Economic development can be fully explained by physical geography.
nodes.response: Physical geography is one factor in influencing a country’s development. Other factors such as history and politics often have a greater influence.

nodes.misconception: The landscape in North and South America is mainly the same.
nodes.response: Use lesson to emphasise the diversity of landscapes in these continents.

nodes.misconception: That Russia is entirely a harsh, cold, mountainous, barren landscape.
nodes.response: Some parts of Russia do experience a harsh environment, but Russia is the largest country in the world by area, and so it has a diverse range of environments within it from mountains and volcanoes to vast plains and mighty rivers.
