nodes.misconception: That the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighbouring country, the Republic of Congo, are the same country. Students can inadvertently shorten DRC to 'Congo' in verbal or written work.
nodes.response: The DRC and the Republic of Congo are two separate countries in central Africa. The Congo River forms part of the border between the countries; their capital cities Kinshasa and Brazzaville are located on oppposite banks of the river from each other.

nodes.misconception: The Middle East is all desert.
nodes.response: Students will learn that the Middle East contains diverse landscapes including mountains, valleys, and fertile land.

nodes.misconception: Adding physical materials to components in Fusion is for aesthetic purposes only.
nodes.response: Adding physical materials to components alters their appearance and properties.

nodes.misconception: Students think that being physically fit means they are automatically healthy.
nodes.response: Explain the importance of social and emotional benefits too, particularly for participants such as elderly people.

nodes.misconception: Physical and working properties are the same.
nodes.response: Physical properties are the characteristics of a material, such as appearance and features.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all rocks are hard. Also that if a rock is heavy it is therefore hard.
nodes.response: Share a wide range of rocks the children can handle to explore the property of hardness so they realise some rocks are much softer than others.

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused with the word permanent and permeable.
nodes.response: Be clear on your definition of permeable, perhaps use some actions to help them remember. Clear up at the start that although permeable sounds rather like permanent it is completely different and explain the difference using examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils equate 'weathering' as the breakdown of rock caused only by the 'weather'. They also tend to use 'weathering' and 'erosion' interchangeably.
nodes.response: Provide many opportunities for pupils to identify weathering from erosion or classify examples of weathering or erosion.

nodes.misconception: Changing the aperture or shutter speed only affects how bright the photo is.
nodes.response: While both aperture and shutter speed do affect exposure (how light or dark a photo is), they also have creative effects on how the photo looks, such as blur.

nodes.misconception: Depth of field is only controled by moving the camera nearer or further away from the subject.
nodes.response: Depth of field is mainly controlled by adjusting the aperture (f-stop).

nodes.misconception: Lighting is just a technical tool in photography.
nodes.response: Lighting has the power to transform a photograph, shaping its mood, tone, and clarity.

nodes.misconception: Photographers can't control the way movement is depicted in their photographs.
nodes.response: Photographers can freeze action sharply or blur it creatively, depending on the photographer’s intent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often fail to recognise Ralph's role in the ostracism of Piggy.
nodes.response: Ralph is the first person to ostracise Piggy, by banning him from accompanying the boys on their expedition. He also calls Piggy by the name he begged Ralph not to use - Piggy. Once Jack senses Piggy's vulnerability within the group, he exploits it.

nodes.misconception: Pilates is easy and only develops flexibility.
nodes.response: Pilates builds core strength, stability and muscular endurance, and can be challenging for all types of athletes. It’s not just stretching, it’s a full-body workout that improves posture, balance and overall strength.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that resistance bands make exercises easier
nodes.response: Resistance bands actually add extra tension, making movements more challenging. They engage muscles throughout the entire movement, improving strength, control and stability more effectively than bodyweight exercises alone.

nodes.misconception: Pilgrimage destinations are always places linked to Jesus.
nodes.response: Christian pilgrimage destinations can be places linked to Jesus, such as Jerusalem, but they can also be places that are significant for other reasons, such as Iona, which was an important early Christian site in Western Europe.

nodes.misconception: Only Christians visit Iona.
nodes.response: Many people visit Iona, including Christians, people who belong to other religions and people with no religion at all. Iona has historical significance as well as religious significance.

nodes.misconception: Only Roman Catholic Christians go to Lourdes.
nodes.response: Many Roman Catholic Christians do go to Lourdes, but all people, regardless of religion or denomination, are welcome to visit Lourdes.

nodes.misconception: Only people who are religious go on pilgrimage.
nodes.response: Anyone can go on a pilgrimage, whether they are religious or not. However, most pilgrims are religious.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may field fly balls by putting their arm up in the air then running to where they think it'll land.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to beat the ball to the landing spot by running fast - something which can't be done with one arm in the air - then position themselves to catch.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes when using number lines to represent fractions, especially with bar representations that do not begin at zero.
nodes.response: Link teaching to measurement. When measuring the length of a object, the measurement needs to begin at zero.

nodes.misconception: Students can incorrectly insert a digit in the wrong place value column.
nodes.response: Printing or white board drawings of a place value chart will support student understanding of the different column headings and place value.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get mixed up between metric and imperial units.
nodes.response: You may wish to refer to Lesson 6 of this unit, which explains the metric system’s use of prefixes, and compare this with imperial measures.

nodes.misconception: It is easier to create a document by adding all the detail first and changing the layout later.
nodes.response: It's more efficient to plan the layout first before adding all the details. Organising the structure early helps avoid major formatting changes later, making the document easier to edit and read.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume that maps always have to be accurate like road maps or atlases.
nodes.response: Artists can creative in the way they express their ideas or experiences.

nodes.misconception: 'Was' and 'had' have different forms in German for 'ich' and 'er, sie'.
nodes.response: In German, 'war' means 'was', 'hatte' means 'had'. Both forms remain unchanged for 'ich' and 'er, sie', like in English.

nodes.misconception: Spanish adjectives always follow the noun.
nodes.response: This is the general case, but it is not a rule. There are many cases where the adjective precedes the noun, like for certain collocations ('una gran amistad') or when more flair is sought.

nodes.misconception: The definite article 'the' translates as 'el' in Spanish and it can be used with singular nouns, both masculine and feminine.
nodes.response: There are two words for 'the' with singular nouns. The masculine singular definite article 'el' and the feminine singular definite article is 'la'.

nodes.misconception: 'à' + 'le' = 'à le'.
nodes.response: When 'à' is followed by 'le' it becomes 'au'.

nodes.misconception: To say 'to (the) ...' in French before a masculine noun, use 'à le'.
nodes.response: There is no such thing as 'à le' in French; it becomes 'au'.

nodes.misconception: The comparative form of 'gern' is 'besser'.
nodes.response: The comparative form of 'gern' is 'lieber'. 'Besser' is the comparative form of 'gut'.

nodes.misconception: 'Gefallen' means ‘to like’ and works like a normal verb where I am the subject that does the action of ‘liking’.
nodes.response: 'Gefallen' means ‘to please’, so works differently. You are not doing the ‘liking’, the thing you like is ‘pleasing’ you. E.g., 'das Kleid gefällt mir' - literally, 'the dress pleases me'. More naturally translated - 'I like the dress'.

nodes.misconception: Notes are always placed on the lines of a stave
nodes.response: Notes can be placed on, above, or below the lines on a stave

nodes.misconception: The word low is sometimes associated with quiet.
nodes.response: The word low refers to low pitch.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that storyboards need to be perfect and spend more time on the details of the drawing as opposed to thinking about the sequence of events of their animation.
nodes.response: Remind children that storyboards are rough sketches that help plan the sequence of the animation.

nodes.misconception: Action plans cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Action plans can be changed and adapted throughout the project.

nodes.misconception: Objects in art are just for decoration.
nodes.response: Objects often have meanings. For example, a crown might mean power. When planning, think carefully about what each object could represent in your story artwork.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that walking is boring and too easy.
nodes.response: Walking can be at different speeds, does not have to be boring and is a good opportunity to be present in the moment, which enhances positive mental health.

nodes.misconception: It is only necessary to use 'du' when saying 'you' in German.
nodes.response: In German, there are four words for you: 'du' for friends or family; 'Sie' in formal situations e.g., talking to teachers or strangers; 'ihr' when speaking to several friends or family members; 'man' to talk about people in general.

nodes.misconception: Once a product is completed it does not need to be improved if I am happy with it as the creator.
nodes.response: Listening to other opinions and referring to the success criteria of the client brief is essential to help develop a product that meets the client brief completely.

nodes.misconception: Tally charts can only be completed on paper.
nodes.response: Data loggers can record tally charts electronically.

nodes.misconception: Cutting and shaping are not the same.
nodes.response: Cutting can be a form of shaping.

nodes.misconception: All of the detail of the puppet needs to be added to the template.
nodes.response: The template is the basic outline of the puppet. The extra detail, such as ears, can be added later.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use specific facts from their research in the introduction.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to 'general information' with clear modelling of what this looks like as exemplified in learning cycles one and two.

nodes.misconception: Assemblage sculptures are carved or moulded.
nodes.response: Remind children that an assemblage sculpture is not usually carved or moulded, but parts are assembled using glue, tape, wire or thread.

nodes.misconception: Orthographic projections are completed after manufacture.
nodes.response: Orthographic projections are known as a working drawing. These are sent from a designer to a manufacturer before manufacturing to enable them to manufacture the product or component.

nodes.misconception: 'Solange' and 'sobald' have to be used with 'als' to translate the 'as' in 'as long/soon as'.
nodes.response: The single word 'solange' is the translation for three English words - 'as long as' - and the same for 'sobald' - 'as soon as'.

nodes.misconception: Any of the three planes can be paired with the three axes.
nodes.response: Planes and axes are always paired as; sagittal plane with the transverse axis, frontal plane with the sagittal axis and transverse plane with the longitudinal axis.

nodes.misconception: Any of the three planes can be paired with the three axes.
nodes.response: Planes and axes are always paired as: sagittal plane with the transverse axis, frontal plane with the frontal axis and transverse plane with the longitdinal axis.

nodes.misconception: Any of the three planes can be paired with the three axes.
nodes.response: Planes and axes are always paired as: sagittal plane with the frontal axis, frontal plane with the sagittal axis and transverse plane with the vertical axis.

nodes.misconception: The saggital plane is linked with the saggital axis.
nodes.response: They share the same name; however, the sagittal plane is linked with the frontal axis. The saggital axis is linked with the frontal plane.

nodes.misconception: The transverse plane is linked with the transverse axis.
nodes.response: They share the same name, however the transverse plane is linked with the longitudinal axis. The transverse axis is linked with the sagittal plane. The frontal plane and axis however have the same name and are linked.

nodes.misconception: When developing a conversation about future travel plans, it is important to consistently use the future time frame in answers.
nodes.response: Whilst it is important to be able to refer to the future confidently, it is also helpful to add in different time frames to give more detail as well as opinions.

nodes.misconception: Verbs of emotion like 'gustar', 'encantar', 'dar', 'molestar', etc. are always followed by the infinitive.
nodes.response: Use a verb of emotion + infinitive to react to your own actions. Use a verb of emotion + 'que' + subjunctive to react to someone else’s. Both forms often talk about emotions, but the change of subject triggers the use of subjunctive.

nodes.misconception: The transverse plane is linked with the transverse axis.
nodes.response: They share the same name, however the transverse plane is linked with the longitudinal axis. The transverse axis is linked with the sagittal plane.

nodes.misconception: 'El' and 'lo' are interchangeable, as 'la' (article) and 'la' (DOP) and 'las' (article) and 'las' (DOP) look exactly the same.
nodes.response: Remember that direct object pronouns (lo, la, los and las) come before a verb. 'El' is the masculine singular form of the definite article 'the'.

nodes.misconception: When completing a photo description in Spanish, I should stick to short, simple sentences.
nodes.response: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to plan extended sentences to talk for a prolonged period of time.

nodes.misconception: All the shapes of a model can be seen from one perspective.
nodes.response: Some shapes may be not able to be seen from one perspective, they may be hiding behind other shapes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to describe Darwin's theory of evolution in simple terms.
nodes.response: You may wish to allow time to model this section to pupils, showing them that a simple explanation can cover the main points briefly.

nodes.misconception: Any question can be used to create a branching database successfully.
nodes.response: A good question should split the data evenly to make sure the number of questions required to reach what is being looked for is minimised.

nodes.misconception: Students often think of methods exclusively as 'similes/metaphors' etc.
nodes.response: The writer's method is anything they do consciously. This could be choosing one, single word over another.

nodes.misconception: That you should only look for differences between poems in a comparative response.
nodes.response: A comparative response involves analysing and exploring the similarities and differences in how two poems present an idea or concept.

nodes.misconception: Sherlock Holmes mystery stories are almost identical.
nodes.response: Whilst all Sherlock Holmes mystery stories are part of the detective fiction genre, the stories can differ a lot.

nodes.misconception: Young children are still developing understanding of the concept of quantifying time and as such they can significantly overestimate how much they can do and see in just one day.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to think about travel time between points of interest when they are planning their route, as well as how long they will spend in each place. Use the length of a school day and how it is punctuated with lessons and breaks for comparison.

nodes.misconception: Students think that the more items within a scene they can describe, the better the description.
nodes.response: Ask them to consider how they can create atmosphere by limiting their focus to 3-4 focal points in the setting and using figurative language

nodes.misconception: Action is a key part of a description.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the purpose of a description is to focus on certain aspects of a scene in order to set the tone and genre.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log precise and ambitious vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from.

nodes.misconception: Fairy tales are written solely for children.
nodes.response: Fairy tales are primarily stories about transformation and therefore this form appeals to many writers, especially those who are interested in social issues.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel that they need to record the direct speech in full to ensure it is 'accurate'.
nodes.response: Although real journalists would want to keep the quotations exactly the same, it is fine for us to write notes in a plan.

nodes.misconception: Integrating factual information into the main paragraphs can be challenging.
nodes.response: We can't tell the whole story in the introduction; the story of what happened is gradually revealed as the perspectives are given.

nodes.misconception: Learners may be confused about the difference between physical and human geographical features.
nodes.response: Physical geography features are part of the natural world whereas human features have been created or changed by humans.

nodes.misconception: Users don't ever see the underlying file structure of a website, so it's organisation is unimportant.
nodes.response: Organisation of resources can make the creation and maintainence of websites an easier task. The quicker a developer of website can find the component parts, the less time will be wasted when changes need to be made.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may 'start from scratch' with their notes in this lesson.
nodes.response: Pupils have already generated ideas for descriptive and emotive details ready to use in this lesson and they should feed these details and ideas into their plans today.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be aware that a non-finite subordinate clause can be used before and after a main clause.
nodes.response: Ensure that you say and model a variety of non-finite complex sentences where the non-finite clause is positioned both at the start of the sentence and at the end of the sentence.

nodes.misconception: Direct speech should mimic real-life conversation exactly.
nodes.response: Direct speech should serve specific purposes, such as advancing the plot, developing characters or providing necessary information.

nodes.misconception: Each section of the five part narrative structure equals one paragraph in your writing.
nodes.response: The five part narrative structure is a helpful way to help plan plot and character. However, some sections might be longer than others. Some might require multiple paragraphs, others just one.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to avoid repetition for describing each encounter.
nodes.response: Model a range of ways for saying the same thing. For example 'bumped into', 'came across', 'encountered', 'stumbled across', etc. Create a class bank of phrases and ideas they can use in their plan.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to write in the character of the red crayon.
nodes.response: Ensure that you have additional resources like word banks for pupils to refer to that reference 'I', 'me', 'my', 'we', 'our' and 'us' words.

nodes.misconception: Audio tracks need to play separately from one another so that the sound is clear.
nodes.response: Layering tracks can create new and interesting audio where the sound works well together to create something new and interesting.

nodes.misconception: Planning is not necessary to write an effective response.
nodes.response: Not only is planning an efficient way to consider different questions and arguments, it also leads to more cohesive, well sequenced responses.

nodes.misconception: That there is one correct way of organising your thoughts for a plan.
nodes.response: Creating a plan is designed to help you see what your argument is - there is no definitive way of how you should organise your thoughts.

nodes.misconception: The most direct route to a play area might not be the safest.
nodes.response: Just because a route might be the shortest, it does not mean it's the best route to take if there are no safe areas or pavements to walk along or safe crossing points. The best route must consider the time taken, most direct way and be safest.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log key vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log key vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log key vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log key vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to ensure their 'show and tell' language is appropriate for each paragraph. For example, paragraph one is meant to convey concern but not complete fear yet.
nodes.response: Model different examples of 'show and tell'. Ask children to identify whether they convey concern or fear. E.g. for concern, we might say 'chest tightened slightly at the strange sight'. For fear, we might say, 'heart pounded rapidly in her chest'.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to develop appropriate 'show and tell' language for a range of emotions.
nodes.response: Identify the emotions of characters during this section first and ask children to imagine how they might convey that feeling. E.g. Homily is feeling stubborn and firm. 'Show and tell' for this might be: She gave Pod a stern and silent look.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Teach children how to write notes which are short and capture key vocabulary and important information. Encourage use of bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recall, define and use different figurative language structures.
nodes.response: Use Joseph Coelho's 'MORERAPS' poem to provide additional examples of effective figurative language.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify appropriate adjectives and verbs and develop their own pieces of personification.
nodes.response: Brainstorm as a class and create a shared bank of human adjectives and verbs that would be appropriate for personifying elements of the scene. Children can then use this bank to support them in forming their own pieces of personification.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify different sentence and clause types.
nodes.response: Ensure there is explicit teaching of simple, compound and adverbial complex sentences that is additional to this lesson, for example in discrete grammar lessons.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel tempted to write in complete sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Model and encourage note-taking; this gives pupils more flexibility when they come to write and it allows them to jot down more ideas - some of which they can reject later.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log precise and ambitious vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note form.

nodes.misconception: Concluding sentences are the same as conclusions.
nodes.response: Concluding sentences conclude a single paragraph. Conclusions come at the end of a full essay.

nodes.misconception: An argument is a disagreement and something which is confrontational.
nodes.response: In an article, an argument is a reason or set of reasons given in support of an idea, action or theory that you give the reader in order to convince them that your idea is correct.

nodes.misconception: Progressive overload only applies when weight training.
nodes.response: Gradually increasing frequency, intensity and time or altering the type of exercise through the manipulation of different training methods can develop all fitness components. Clear examples must be shared across activities other than weight training.

nodes.misconception: A script is just used for what people will say on a video.
nodes.response: A script can be used to plan what people will say or what audio will be used. A script has enough detail to understand the range of audio that will be used.

nodes.misconception: Writing down any number in a piece of non-fiction writing is enough to show you know how to use statistics.
nodes.response: Statistics need to be credible. When creating your own statistics, you need to think carefully about how to make them sound believable by giving details like their source, date and data sample size.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that they only need to plan one single paragraph outline.
nodes.response: Students will need to plan one paragraph outline per section of their response.

nodes.misconception: You should always write about the poem you know best.
nodes.response: You should write about the two poems that form the best complementary pairing for the question.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that characters are not methods. They tend to think of methods as just 'similes' or 'metaphors'.
nodes.response: Any choice that the writer makes consciously is a method. This includes their use of characterisation. Anything the character says or does is a method.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that they can only compare two poems from the same thematic cluster within the anthology.
nodes.response: Students can compare any pair of poems as long as the poems have some similarities.

nodes.misconception: Planning isn't a useful step in the writing process and it takes too long.
nodes.response: How might planning help to organise our thoughts into a coherent response? How can planning improve the efficiency of the writing process?

nodes.misconception: Planning takes too long.
nodes.response: A detailed plan will speed up the writing process and ensure a cohesive and well structured argument.

nodes.misconception: Students often think they have to be balanced when they deliver persuasive presentations.
nodes.response: Be clear about taking a stand and picking a side. A presentation which is clear in its stance has much more impact.

nodes.misconception: An emotive piece of narrative can sometimes overuse melodrama, exaggerating characters' feelings and actions too much.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils' representations of characters’ emotions and reactions are believable and consistent with their personalities.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might mistakenly believe that generational conflict only refers to disagreements between parents and children, overlooking the broader societal influences that shape the conflict.
nodes.response: Generational conflict in 'Leave Taking' isn't just about family disagreements; it is also influenced by the different social, cultural, and historical experiences that shape each generation’s view of identity and belonging.

nodes.misconception: Concluding sentences are the same as conclusions.
nodes.response: Concluding sentences conclude a single paragraph. Conclusions come at the end of a full essay.

nodes.misconception: That an argument only means a heated, angry exchange.
nodes.response: An argument about a text means presenting your idea and your points to prove that your idea is correct.

nodes.misconception: Planning an essay just means listing points I want to cover and then writing a draft straight away.
nodes.response: Whilst this can work, clearly understanding your argument, structuring your ideas, and deciding what evidence or quotations to use before you start writing can be much more efficient and effective.

nodes.misconception: That people generally believe in free will and always have.
nodes.response: In Elizabethan England, people typically believed that fate controlled their lives - they believed they did not have free will.

nodes.misconception: That thesis statements and topic sentences are the same.
nodes.response: Differentiate; the thesis statement is a comment on the text as a whole, and a topic sentence has a focus on a specific part of the text.

nodes.misconception: Ideas for one essay question can't be used in any other essay on the same text.
nodes.response: By the end of exploring and writing about a text, you will realise that there are certain ideas and references which you can rely on over and over.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter which two poems you choose to compare as all of them can be compared with each other.
nodes.response: In theory, you can compare any two poems from the anthology however it's important to remember that some have more connections than others. You should aim to select two poems with a range of connections to avoid tenuous links.

nodes.misconception: Students think that it doesn't matter which quotations they select for use.
nodes.response: It can be difficult to bring any new interpretations to commonly-used quotations, so try to pick some lesser-used ones.

nodes.misconception: While comparing poems, you should only look for similarities between them.
nodes.response: To create an effective comparison, you want to find nuanced differences within overall similarities.

nodes.misconception: Students often don't think to include rhetorical devices within their topic sentences.
nodes.response: Just because the topic sentences introduces the main idea for the paragraph, that does not mean the topic sentence can't be really creative and engaging. It's crucial that it is engaging to motivate the reader to learn more about the topic.

nodes.misconception: A final piece must be large scale and completely finished.
nodes.response: A final piece or outcome is just the end point in your journey so far, it should resolve your ideas but it can do this in many ways and in different scales.

nodes.misconception: Slam poetry always has to be serious and about personal or social issues.
nodes.response: While slam poetry often tackles serious personal and social issues, it can also be playful, humorous or lighthearted. Slam poetry is about expressing yourself in an engaging and authentic way. You can write about anything that matters to you.

nodes.misconception: Planning a collage or assemblage takes away creativity.
nodes.response: Planning provides structure but doesn’t mean the design is fixed. Many artists start with an idea but adapt it through experimentation. A plan helps build confidence, but the best results often come from unexpected discoveries along the way.

nodes.misconception: That you should use generic sensory language to create an effective description.
nodes.response: You need to use sensory language tailored to the atmosphere that you want to create in order for it to be effective.

nodes.misconception: Websites don't need to be engaging if they only provide information.
nodes.response: What is the purpose of a website? If you want people to read the information, how are you going to engage your reader?

nodes.misconception: You don't need to, or shouldn't, use rhetorical devices in your topic or concluding sentences.
nodes.response: Just because the topic sentences introduce the main idea for the paragraph, that does not mean the topic sentence can't be really creative and engaging. It's crucial that it is engaging to motivate the reader to learn more about the topic.

nodes.misconception: Many students often think that planning isn't a useful step in the writing process and that it takes too long.
nodes.response: How might planning help to organise our thoughts into a coherent response? How can planning improve the efficiency of the writing process?

nodes.misconception: You can only use figurative language in fictional writing.
nodes.response: Non-fiction writers, just like fiction writers, are trying to create interesting, original and compelling ideas that their readers will remember, enjoy and learn from.

nodes.misconception: You should always use the most impressive sounding words in your description.
nodes.response: While you should reach for ambitious words, you want to ensure that all the words you use are creating a consistent atmosphere.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly include information that is not relevant to section one.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 explicitly outlines which aspects of prior research are appropriate for this section.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write the full section as one paragraph.
nodes.response: Parts of the plan are explicitly allocated into paragraphs one and two. This is also modelled in the second learning cycle.

nodes.misconception: Pupils could get carried away with using Shakespearean style language and use it too frequently, taking away from them showing their understanding of the character of Macbeth.
nodes.response: Use your shared writing section to exemplify only using a few words or phrases to give it a 'Shakespearean feel'. Remind pupils that we still want to include different sentence types to achieve text flow.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might spend too long drawing in Task A, which is not the point of the task.
nodes.response: You could set a one-minute timer for pupils to draw. You could also model sketching a dagger yourself so that they see that it does not need to be perfect.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly introduce new information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: Specific reference to keeping information in the conclusion general and teacher guidance on appropriate information to include is given in learning cycle one.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a conclusion simply summarises what has already been said, in the same way as the summary section of the PEPS structure.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the conclusion can continue to have a persuasive impact by using linguistic techniques such as presumption and veiled threats.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to add additional, new and specific information into the conclusion.
nodes.response: Information in the conclusion must be kept general and it must summarise the rest of the letter.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include information that is too specific for the conclusion.
nodes.response: Explicit reference to 'general information' must be made and visual prompts across planning slides will help remind pupils.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include information that is too specific for the conclusion.
nodes.response: Explicit reference to 'general information' must be made and visual prompts across planning slides will help remind pupils.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that a modal verb 'helps' another verb.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the fact that a modal verb comes before a main verb to modify it, e.g. 'will show', 'might help', 'should do' or 'would lead'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect complex ideas with appropriate linguistic features.
nodes.response: Model and encourage oral rehearsal and use shared writing to model the process of selecting between various possible linguistic features you could use.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly include information that is not relevant to section one.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 explicitly outlines which aspects of prior research are appropriate for this section.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include the part where Macbeth sees the dagger, which is what they will write in the closing in the subsequent lesson.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils understand that they are writing about the visualisation of the dagger in the next section of the soliloquy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use facts that are too specific in the introduction.
nodes.response: General facts and information should be explicitly shared. Visuals that represent **general** versus **specific** information should be referred to throughout the planning process. Visuals help pupils 'see' which information belongs where.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use specific facts from their research in the introduction.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to 'general information' with clear modelling of what this looks like as exemplified in learning cycles one and two.

nodes.misconception: The last sentence of the modelled paragraph is a command and an exclamation. Children may form the misconception that a command is always an exclamation or visa versa.
nodes.response: Explore examples of imperative verbs used to form a command and show examples of commands without an exclamation. Explore examples of exclamations that are not a command.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that only statistics are forms of evidence.
nodes.response: Explanations and facts, as well as expert views and references to official reports, can be used as forms of evidence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may show incorrect speech punctuation skills.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle is focused on punctuating speech first and second sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to adopt the formal tone required for an essay.
nodes.response: You may wish to provide a bank of 'essay phrases' like 'contributes to', 'has strengthened' and 'is driven by' to support some pupils.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to describe a range of aspects of Tim's appearance and feelings.
nodes.response: Explicit modelling of adjectives, including compound adjectives, and show-not-tell will help pupils with their descriptions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write the full section as one paragraph.
nodes.response: Parts of the plan are explicitly allocated into paragraphs one and two. This is also modelled in the second learning cycle.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may refer to Tubman's activism and later life experiences in this section.
nodes.response: Explicit re-exposure to the information learned about Tubman's early life occurs in Learning Cycle 1 to keep pupils focused on this aspect of her life.

nodes.misconception: Students think that if they write a horror story that is full of blood and gore, that this makes it Gothic.
nodes.response: Gothic literature is about unsettling and mystifying the reader - not traumatising them with gory descriptions and extreme violence. There can be more fear in what is not revealed, than what is revealed.

nodes.misconception: Students believe that the topic sentence has to be a straight-forward statement of opinion.
nodes.response: The topic sentence, like any other part of their writing, can be written creatively, forcing the reader to infer the writer's opinion.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils think that planning isn't a helpful or worthwhile exercise.
nodes.response: Planning allows us to carefully consider our ideas before writing and allows us to work out what ideas work best for the task we've been given. Planning often results in a final stronger piece of work so is very worthwhile!

nodes.misconception: Language devices - like extended analogies - are more appropriate for analysis in stories and narrative fiction.
nodes.response: Using language devices such as extended analogies can be a very effective way of communicating ideas in non-fiction writing.

nodes.misconception: Students may believe that open letters have to be written to those in powerful positions.
nodes.response: There are open letters on a wide range of topics and niches. All that an open letter requires is a strong feeling about something.

nodes.misconception: Students may not understand the subtle difference between imagery and figurative language.
nodes.response: Whilst imagery can include figurative language and vice versa, imagery does not always have to be figurative.

nodes.misconception: That there is a set formula to follow when it comes to choosing what to focus on in an image.
nodes.response: When looking at an image for descriptive writing, you should think about what catches your eye and then focus on those elements.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the idea of jumping between past and present tense.
nodes.response: Explain that this is a common way of writing a diary: the person writing begins by saying how they feel right now before going back to explain the events that led up to them feeling this way.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will use only their manufacturing specification when making.
nodes.response: Many pupils will struggle with time managment when manufacturing. Pupils need to plan out their time so that they can keep on track to meet their deadline whilst thinking about the operational elements.

nodes.misconception: All narratives have to follow the traditional story arc and have a chronological order for them to make sense.
nodes.response: Short stories often have to manipulate the traditional story structure to be engaging from the very beginning.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate some of their own ideas for precise and ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Model use of a thesaurus to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'tired', children might use 'exhausted', 'fatigued' or 'worn out'.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate some of their own ideas for precise and ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Model use of a thesaurus to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'fell', children might use 'crumpled', 'collapsed' or 'sunk'.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate some of their own ideas for precise and ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Model use of a thesaurus to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'hot', children might use 'scorching', 'blistering' or 'burning'.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate synonyms for 'said'.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to use character perspective to understand how Lila and Razvani felt when they were speaking. Provide opportunity for partner talk and develop a shared bank of synonyms for 'said'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not use a range of sentence structures and openers in their plans for writing.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils know the full range of sentence structures (simple, compound and a variety of complex). Full coverage can be found in the 'Year 5 Grammar: Five sentence types' unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up physical and mental health benefits, leading to an unclear argument in the main body paragraph.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle task involves pupils categorising key arguments across the two main body paragraphs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recall, define and use different figurative language structures.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of additional examples of effective figurative language. A display board or working wall of the different types of figurative language with examples that match the text type will be helpful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unclear in their understanding of different complex sentence types.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know that an adverbial clause is one **type** of subordinate clause. There are also relative clauses and non-finite clauses that pupils should be taught.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of how to use different types of complex sentences.
nodes.response: Learning cycle one models different complex sentence types that can be used in the main body of pupils' letters.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might spend too much time on their sketch, not leaving them with enough time for their annotations.
nodes.response: Model drawing a sketch yourself. You could also give pupils a timer of two minutes to complete their sketch in. For pupils who are struggling, you might provide a printed sketch of the witches to support them.

nodes.misconception: Only governments help make decisions on where flood protection is used.
nodes.response: Many stakeholders are invloved in making decisions on flood defences.

nodes.misconception: Students may struggle with the concept of note-taking and write in full sentences.
nodes.response: Model examples of note-taking by asking students to share their special item and demonstrating how to translate this into notes on a flipchart or whiteboard.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to list adaptations in their plan without explaining how they benefit survival.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to functions of adaptations throughout the planning stage and set aside space on plans to refer to each function.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to develop their own ideas for 'show and tell' to convey Scrooge's emotions.
nodes.response: Ask the children to recall a time when they have felt the emotions Scrooge does (e.g. nervousness or fear) and ask them what kind of physical sensations they experience during these moments. Examples to offer might be 'clammy hands' or 'tight chest'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel they have to cover every event from this part of the book in this piece of writing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to zoom in on just two moments, drawing out all the details from these; this will allow them to really focus on the quality of writing rather than the plot details.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only log key vocabulary and it should be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have key vocabulary and be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that they can **only** include the narrative elements in their writing.
nodes.response: There are other things we can write about - for instance, thoughts the characters have - but the narrative elements are a helpful structure we can use to generate ideas. There is no need to limit pupils to just these categories.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to generate ambitious verbs, adverbs, nouns and adjectives all at once.
nodes.response: Depending on the abilities in the class, you may wish to focus on just one of these aspects in the plan e.g. only adjectives and nouns. Alternatively, children could work in pairs or small groups to generate their plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they need to write full sentences on their plan.
nodes.response: Plans are written to support pupils with future writing. Plans include ambitious vocabulary in note form.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they need to write full sentences on their plan.
nodes.response: Plans are written to support pupils with future writing. Plans include ambitious vocabulary in note form.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only log key vocabulary and it should be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate a range of precise and ambitious vocabulary in order to avoid repetition in the build up.
nodes.response: Model the use of a thesaurus for uplevelling vocabulary. E.g. Instead of 'ran', when describing the movements of Hogarth and his father, show other examples like 'raced', 'sped', 'sprinted', 'hurried', 'darted'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to develop 'show-not-tell' ideas.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to act out different parts of the build up and to show the character's emotions through body language and facial expressions, while others describe what they are doing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel tempted to rush through the plan with too little detail in each paragraph.
nodes.response: This is the purpose of encouraging pupils to engage with the narrative elements - model and encourage reflecting on each event through these four lenses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can write a narrative by briefly explaining each key moment.
nodes.response: It is important we choose a range of adjectives, verbs and adverbs to include in our plan that create a full, descriptive narrative. The reader needs to be able to 'see' the pictures we paint with our words.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand some of the vocabulary modelled (e.g. indifference) and they may struggle to generate their own vocabulary ideas to convey an ominous atmosphere.
nodes.response: Model the use of a thesaurus to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'lonely', children might use 'isolated' or 'deserted'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to segment Addie's speech into three sections.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about past drama tasks where they looked at Addie's feelings before, during and after her speech.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can write a narrative by briefly explaining each key moment.
nodes.response: It is important we choose a range of adjectives, verbs and adverbs to include in our plan that create a full, descriptive narrative. The reader needs to be able to 'see' the pictures we paint with our words.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have key vocabulary and it should be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to remember all the action in the climax.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to break down the climax into smaller sections and then focus on what happened in that section. Provide children will printed images from the animation, to support them with planning their climax.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to generate varied speech ideas for Hogarth and ambitious vocabulary for the reporting clause that conveys the appropriate tone.
nodes.response: Get children to hot seat as Hogarth and imagine what they would say to the Iron Man in order to persuade him and win his trust. Ask children to consider how they said it in order to generate ideas for the reporting clause. Create a shared bank.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may begin to retell key events or add too much detailed information about the day when planning the closing.
nodes.response: Make continued explicit reference to keeping information general; a visual aid of 'general' may help to support pupils remember this distinction.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use inaccurate verb forms when switching between the present and future tense.
nodes.response: Prompts are included on the planning document and slides to remind pupils to write in the correct tense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils want to add additional information about tigers' diets or adaptations to the conclusion.
nodes.response: Information in the conclusion must be kept general and must summarise the rest of the report.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe a diary entry can only use the past tense.
nodes.response: The diarist will also explain what they are doing and feeling in the present moment.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use 'who' when writing relative clauses about tigers.
nodes.response: Explicitly teach that the relative pronoun 'which' is used when writing about anything other than a person.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to distinguish between the narrative elements.
nodes.response: The elements often overlap - we use action to show emotion, for instance. Encourage a relaxed approach to this; the main aim is to ensure that we have covered a wide range of content in our plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to come up with ambitious vocabulary for each part of their plan.
nodes.response: Come up with precise and ambitious vocabulary as a class first and create a word bank for display. Pupils could work in pairs or small groups to complete their plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that it is not important to following a structure when writing their argument.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that by following a structure, such as PEPS, their argument will be more professional and flow better.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the notes.
nodes.response: Re-read the corresponding section from the text to highlight which part we are using for our diary entry. Model making notes and identifying which events, thoughts and feelings are most important.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include details in their plan from other times in Florence's life.
nodes.response: Ensure the children are clear that this entry is about just one day, the day she arrived at the hospital in Crimea. Use the three sections in the planning form to reiterate the key moments - arriving, seeing soldiers on the floor, the hospital food.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the notes.
nodes.response: Re-read the corresponding pages from the text to highlight which part we are using for our diary entry. Model making notes and identifying which events, thoughts and feelings are the most important.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rush through the planning process and miss opportunities to describe and extend key moments.
nodes.response: The planning worksheet breaks down each section into smaller parts, prompting pupils to focus on key details.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include quotes from bystanders or other interested parties at the event.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils know that there will be a specific section devoted to quotes from bystanders in another part of the journalistic report.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to write concise notes that also contain appropriate detail and description.
nodes.response: Developing precise adjectives for their writing is important but the main focus should be on recording precise and accurate information. You may wish to provide them with a structured planning frame.

nodes.misconception: Pupils want to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: Use a 'general' and 'specific' visual during the lesson and the tasks to support pupils' understanding of the difference between the two.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an introduction involves explaining their points in detail.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that an introduction only needs to be three sentences long and it provides a general overview of the letter, rather than specific facts and details.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to include information in the introduction that is too specific.
nodes.response: 'General information' is explicitly referred to throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate some of their own ideas for precise and ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Model use of a thesaurus and brainstorm ideas as a class to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'walked', children might use 'trudged', 'dragged' or 'stomped'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may accidentally include too much detail of the recount in the opening.
nodes.response: Whilst some recount is important, reinforce to pupils that they must write from the personal viewpoint of the character, using feelings and thoughts to convey their character.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to write with too much detail in the opening.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to 'general information' and remind pupils to keep information in the opening general.

nodes.misconception: Notes in a plan can be written in any order.
nodes.response: The key moments in the opening are written in chronological order. Notes in the plan should be concise and follow this chronological order.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have key vocabulary and be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all words are ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there can be multiple options when selecting vocabulary and they need to carefully choose the most precise words in their writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all words are ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there can be many options when selecting vocabulary and they need to carefully choose the most precise words for each part of their writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they need to write full sentences on their plan.
nodes.response: Plans are written to support pupils with future writing. Plans include ambitious vocabulary in note form.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only log key vocabulary and it should be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they need to write full sentences on their plan.
nodes.response: Plans are written to support pupils with future writing. Plans include ambitious vocabulary in note form.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse similes with metaphors.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that similes use 'like' and 'as' and metaphors are not comparing but saying something actually is something else.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to know what makes certain vocabulary ambitious.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there can be many options when selecting vocabulary and they need to carefully choose the most precise words for each part of their writing. This is best explained by what effect they want to create for the reader.

nodes.misconception: You can write the opening of a story without knowing the ending.
nodes.response: An effective opening builds up the atmosphere in order to lead the reader to the ending; therefore, you have to know what the ending is in order to create a cohesive atmosphere in the opening.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Children may think they need to include the name of the witness in the reported clause.
nodes.response: Model to the pupils if the sentence preceding the reported speech introduces the witness, the reporting clause can use a pronoun instead.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the notes.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities for identifying appropriate note examples and identifying which keywords are most important.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can write a narrative by briefly explaining each key moment.
nodes.response: It is important we choose a range of adjectives, verbs and adverbs to include in our plan that creates a full, descriptive narrative. The reader needs to be able to 'see' the pictures we paint with our words.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have key vocabulary and be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify or generate appropriate exaggerated synonyms.
nodes.response: Model the use of a thesaurus to identify appropriate exaggerated synonyms and create a shared bank of appropriate vocabulary for the children to use when writing their notes.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have key vocabulary and be written in note-form using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that their second point can be similar or a continuation of their first point.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the two points used as arguments in their persuasive lettter should be different and appeal to the reader in different ways.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the plan.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities for identifying appropriate note examples and identifying which events, thoughts and feelings are most important. Model taking notes and just capturing the most important information.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Teach children how to write notes which are short and capture key vocabulary and important information. Encourage children to include adverbs and joining words that they want to use, but written out of full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the notes.
nodes.response: Re-read the final pages from the text to discuss how she is feeling at the end of the story. Model making notes and identifying which thoughts and feelings are the most important.

nodes.misconception: Pupils' non-finite complex sentences won't make sense if both clauses have different subjects.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to the subject that performs the verb in each non-finite clause being the same subject in the main clause.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Teach children how to write notes which are short and capture key vocabulary and important information. Encourage use of bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to incorporate linguistic features that highlight chronology in their plan.
nodes.response: Highlight the use of 'after education' and 'eventually' in the model notes on slide 17 as examples of language that support in communicating the chronology of the author's career. Ask the children to brainstorm other examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to use the most accurate, precise vocabulary when describing the historical and social context at the time.
nodes.response: Information about Tubman's activism and subject-specific vocabulary are reviewed and explicitly re-taught.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find correctly punctuating speech first and speech second sentences challenging.
nodes.response: Use visual speech scaffolds to support pupils with correctly punctuating speech first and speech second sentences.

nodes.misconception: Solar panels do not work in the shade.
nodes.response: Solar panels do work in the shade and on cloudy days but they are less efficient in these conditions.

nodes.misconception: During the writing process, pupils may find it hard to come up with adjectives to describe the nouns they are using.
nodes.response: Teach the pupils that first we select a noun that will need to be described, then we select the most suitable adjectives to describe them. Encourage pupils to plan their expanded noun phrases first, so they can easily put these into their recount.

nodes.misconception: Children may write in full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Model to the children how to use bullet points for notes and give them lots of examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include every detail when writing their plan.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a plan will help them when writing by guiding them on what content to include in each sentence. Model a written plan.

nodes.misconception: Children may write in full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Model to the children how to use bullet points for notes and give them lots of examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include every detail when writing their plan.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a plan will help them when writing by guiding them on what content to include in each sentence. Model a written plan.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they do not need to plan the ordering fronted adverbials they'll use because they are self-explanatory, with 'First' at the beginning and 'Finally' at the end.
nodes.response: Teach them that there are lots of different ordering fronted adverbials and some of them can be interchanged, such as 'Next' and 'Then'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write in full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Model writing in note form and support children to do this themselves. Teach them that when we write we use our notes and turn them into full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to generate enough ambitious vocaulary for their plan.
nodes.response: Model each part of the climax and work as a class to generate vocabulary before they write their own plan. Pupils could complete plans in pairs or small groups.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write in full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Highlight that a plan is written in note form and model this explicitly to the children. Explain that you will turn your plan into full sentences when you write.

nodes.misconception: A potential tree planting site needs to meet all of the survey requirements.
nodes.response: The most suitable location will be the site which has the most points. It would be ideal to score full points on the survey but trees could still be planted if some requirements weren't met.

nodes.misconception: Planning is not necessary before writing.
nodes.response: Planning is important in helping us structure our work and keep a clear focus.

nodes.misconception: If there are two verbs in a German sentence, the infinitive stays with the subject of the action.
nodes.response: If there are two verbs in a German sentence, the infinitive goes to the end of the sentence. This is different word order to English and is called the ‘two-verb rule’.

nodes.misconception: You can only begin an inversion sentence  (word order two) with a time phrase, nothing else.
nodes.response: The emphasis is on whatever comes first in the sentence when using inversion (word order 2). It is acceptable to put the object of the sentence before the verb. For example, 'Den Kaffee trinken wir heute'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that, while animals need to be well adapted to survive, plants do not and they simply grow where and how they can.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the slide deck to exemplify the various ways plants are adapted to survive in different environments, just like animals are.

nodes.misconception: Animals and plants in the taiga struggle to survive due to extreme cold and lack specific adaptations.
nodes.response: Taiga species have key adaptations. Conifers have needle-shaped leaves with waxy coatings to reduce water loss. Animals like lynxes grow thick fur, and some hibernate or migrate to survive harsh winters. These adaptations ensure survival.

nodes.misconception: The challenges faced by plants and animals in the canopy layer are the same as challenges on the forest floor.
nodes.response: Plants and animals face different challenges in the different habitats of the tropical rainforest. For example, plants on the forest floor have to have adaptations for low light levels.

nodes.misconception: A camel's hump stores water.
nodes.response: A camel's hump does not hold water at all – it actually stores fat. The camel uses it as nourishment when food is scarce. If a camel uses the fat inside the hump, the hump will become limp and droop, but with food and rest the hump will normalise.

nodes.misconception: Plants are not living; plant cells all have the same shape and structures (as depicted in textbooks)
nodes.response: This lesson consolidates understanding that plant cells are living, and that different plant cells can have different shapes and structures.

nodes.misconception: A palisade cell is not a specialised cell as it is used as the plant cell model. All plant cells contain chloroplasts.
nodes.response: Presentation outlines that the palisade cell is a specialised cell. Question in the check for understanding that is designed to show chloroplasts are not in root hair cells.

nodes.misconception: Plants have no defence against pests or pathogens.
nodes.response: Plants have physical, chemical and mechanical defences against pathogens.

nodes.misconception: Plants have no defence against pests or pathogens.
nodes.response: Plants have physical, chemical and mechanical defences against pathogens.

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.

nodes.misconception: Habitats can only be divided into 'hot' and 'cold' habitats. Plants are not living things.
nodes.response: Examples of different habitats where plants live and how these meet their needs, including different conditions such as underwater, desert, grasslands and savannah.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that we observe using only our eyes
nodes.response: Show how we can use other senses to observe, we might listen, smell or touch when we observe

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse pollination and seed dispersal, as both involve something from the flower being moved from one place to another.
nodes.response: Explain that each of these processes happen at different times and have different purposes. Pollination happens before seeds have formed and leads to fertilisation, whereas seed dispersal spreads the fully formed seeds away from the parent plant.

nodes.misconception: Plants take in food from their surroundings.
nodes.response: This lesson explores why the things taken in by plants are not food, and the idea that plants make the food they need to survive.

nodes.misconception: There is a misunderstanding about the origin of food, and lack of awareness of where food comes from.
nodes.response: All food we eat comes from plants and animals. Food from plants includes fruit and vegetables. Food from animals includes milk, eggs, fish and meat.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that observations from enquiries should only be in written or numerical form.
nodes.response: Explain that there are many ways to represent the information we gathered during enquiries, including with diagrams, writing or even video recordings.

nodes.misconception: Plant-rich means that we should not eat meat or dairy foods for healthier and more sustainable diets.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to cut out meat or dairy from our diet completely for healthier and more sustainable diets. Follow the Eatwell Guide: have plenty of fruit and veg; diversify sources of protein; and limit foods high in fat, salt and sugars.

nodes.misconception: Some students do not realise the significance of the shape of the root hair cell and do not explain this in terms of increasing its surface area.
nodes.response: The idea of surface area as the significant adaptation of root hair cells is clearly introduced, checked, and reinforced with specific tasks that explicitly enquire about this adaptation.

nodes.misconception: All habitats are microhabitats. All minibeasts are insects.
nodes.response: Clear explanation and definition of what a microhabitat is and how it differs from other habitats, e.g. ocean, forest, Arctic, desert etc. Examples of a variety of minibeasts including insects and non-insects.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that biodiversity is the number of organisms that live in a place, rather than the number of different species that live in a place.
nodes.response: There is extensive coverage in the lesson around biodiversity being the range of species that are found in an area.

nodes.misconception: Plants have flowers and are grown in pots.
nodes.response: Examples of plants in different environments and different sorts of plants.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants grow from seeds.
nodes.response: Show everyday examples of plants that grow from bulbs, as well as plant bulbs to observe them grow.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the only way for plants to reproduce is by creating seeds.
nodes.response: Explain that, as well as making seeds, plants can also reproduce asexually in a range of ways, including form cuttings taken from a plant by humans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think plants appear from the ground or that big plants like trees do not grow from seeds.
nodes.response: Ensure first-hand experience of handling and planting a range of seeds, and observing them grow.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a plant without light will grow less, rather than grow taller initially.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for first-hand observation of plants growing without light over an extended period of time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants can support themselves and stay upright without roots as the stem provides support.
nodes.response: The task carried out in Learning Cycle 1 will demonstrate to pupils that plants need roots anchoring them in the soil in order to stay upright.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the warmer the plant, the better it grows and the healthier it is.
nodes.response: Show that different plants need different amounts of warmth, and to expose a plant to high or low temperatures could cause it damage

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants need lots of water everyday
nodes.response: Remind pupils that different plants need different amounts of water, and a plant with too much, or not enough, water could become unhealthy

nodes.misconception: Plastic will eventually biodegrade, even if it takes hundreds of years.
nodes.response: Plastic is not biodegradable, it just breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces and eventually turns into microplastics (tiny plastic pieces, smaller than 5 mm).

nodes.misconception: The oceanic plate subducts at a destructive plate margin and melts to form magma.
nodes.response: The water in the oceanic plate lowers the melting point, helping mantle rocks above to melt and form magma, not the subducting plate itself.

nodes.misconception: Tectonic plates float like rafts on liquid magma.
nodes.response: The mantle is semi-solid rather than a sort of liquid sea of magma.

nodes.misconception: Students might think Plato believed we are born knowing everything.
nodes.response: Plato believed learning was a form of remembering knowledge hidden in us.

nodes.misconception: fundamental movement skills (FMS) are only needed at primary school.
nodes.response: FMS underpin good movement in any activity and in wider life, so it is essential that we continue to practise and hone these basic movements.

nodes.misconception: Ta-di and Ta-mi are the same because they both have two notes in one beat.
nodes.response: With the Ta-di rhythm both notes divide the beat equally in half. With Ta-mi, the notes are not distributed equally - the first is longer (¾ of a beat) and the second is shorter (¼ of a beat).

nodes.misconception: Folk dances and folk songs are different names for exactly the same thing.
nodes.response: Not necessarily. Many folk songs are for storytelling or other purposes, not dancing. Some folk songs are designed for dancing, which often have different features, including an upbeat tempo, strong pulse and rhythmic drive.

nodes.misconception: We play the same tune as what we're singing.
nodes.response: A melodic ostinato can add more interest to the overall sound and, with practice, we can play a different tune to the one we're singing.

nodes.misconception: Mistaking F (or another note) for C and not understanding the impact this has on the finger prompts.
nodes.response: Reinforce 'C to the left of the two black keys', why F is a common mistake and the finger prompts only work if the C position is correct.

nodes.misconception: Adjacent white notes on the keyboard are all a tone apart.
nodes.response: Most of the adjacent white notes are a tone apart but because of the pattern of the black notes on the keyboard some of the adjacent white notes are also semitones. It's important for pupils to count the notes to work out an interval.

nodes.misconception: The best way to learn to play a piece is to start at the beginning.
nodes.response: We can be clever when learning pieces, looking for patterns and easy parts to fit together first whilst internalising the sounds of trickier parts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the number prompts but not find the correct C position on the keyboard.
nodes.response: Reinforce the position of the note C on the keyboard and ensure the pupils are sitting to play comfortably in the C position.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think when they go offside or do footwork they have to stand out of play as this is a penalty pass.
