nodes.response: Both of these infringements do not include another player so a free pass is awarded. If a player obstructs or contacts an oppositing player a penalty pass is then awarded.

nodes.misconception: An ostinato is not a very exciting accompaniment.
nodes.response: An ostinato can make a singing performance more interesting and memorable. Ostinatos are used to great effect in many pieces of music in different styles and genres.

nodes.misconception: Rhythm and pulse in music are the same thing (particularly as there are a lot of crotchets used).
nodes.response: Pupils could clap/tap the beat with the audio examples to reinforce how it is different to the rhythm of the melody..

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that winning is the most important thing.
nodes.response: Learning to value a fair competition and choosing to lose in preference to cheating to win or only playing opponents you know you can beat, is a much more rewarding outlook.

nodes.misconception: Warming up is only needed for outdoor lessons and in the cold weather.
nodes.response: Warming up is a gentle and gradual way of getting the body and mind ready for exercise. Our bodies might not be ready for sudden, energetic movements even in warm weather or when we are indoors.

nodes.misconception: Pulse, beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Beat is the playing of the steady pulse. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils wait until a defender is too close before trying to make a pass and consequently lose possession often.
nodes.response: By getting control of the ball quickly, looking up to find teammates in space and passing before a defender gets too close you can keep possession better.

nodes.misconception: Pupils attack territory down the middle of the court or pitch and it becomes crowded.
nodes.response: By using accurate passing and movement of the ball out wide, you draw defenders out and create more space to invade. Similarly, by moving the ball back and then forward again, you can create more space.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use both sides of the stick like they see in ice-hockey.
nodes.response: In field hockey you are only allowed to use the flat side of the stick. If the ball touches the other side or your foot it is a foul.

nodes.misconception: Music has four beats in a bar and we always finish at the last beat in the bar.
nodes.response: Rhythm cycles in Hindustani classical music can have anything from 3 beats to 128 beats.  The rhythm is cyclical and ends on the first beat of the rhythm cycle.

nodes.misconception: A scale uses all the notes in step with no leaps.
nodes.response: A scale is a series of notes arranged in an ascending or descending order.  Each scale has a unique pattern of intervals (the distance between notes) that defines its character and the intervals are not always the same.

nodes.misconception: Overdoing the emphasis on the first note of the bar and the music becoming stilted.
nodes.response: Play the pupils a non-example where the first beat is so strong it becomes unmusical and follow this with a good example.

nodes.misconception: Pulse and beat are the same thing.
nodes.response: Pulse is the regular, steady heartbeat of the music. We feel the pulse. The beat is when we can hear the pulse out loud, like the ticking of a clock.

nodes.misconception: In an ensemble performance, one part, usually the melody, is the most important part.
nodes.response: In an ensemble performance each part is crucial.  Each part adds something different to the final performance such as harmony, melody or rhythmic foundation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that success is only achieved by winning and being the best.
nodes.response: Success can be achieved in lots of different ways. You can be successful by improving your own performance (regardless of anyone else's performance), setting yourself a challenge and reaching a new target or working in cooperation with others.

nodes.misconception: Collage landscapes should always look realistic.
nodes.response: Collage allows us to create landscapes that don’t have to follow real world rules. Surreal landscapes encourage imagination and creativity beyond what we see in everyday life.

nodes.misconception: Colour is just used to make a space look good.
nodes.response: Colour in a room can have a big impact on the way a space feels and how we feel in that space.

nodes.misconception: All types of monoprinting follow the exact same process.
nodes.response: There are a number of methods for monoprinting that have different steps and outcomes.

nodes.misconception: When we compose music we always notate it using a stave.
nodes.response: Using stick notation with the notes written underneath is a quick way to notate simple melodies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may join up their coordinates but not extend their line.
nodes.response: Lines are used to represent all coordinates that follow a rule. Unless given restrictions, lines should be infinitely long.

nodes.misconception: The murder of Banquo and Fleance (attempted) is the same as the murders that have preceded it.
nodes.response: Macbeth doesn't tell Lady Macbeth his plan, he hires murderers rather than doing it himself, and Fleance is a child.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that coordinates that make a square/ rectangle follow a linear pattern.
nodes.response: In order for coordinates to follow a rule written as an equation, there needs to be a relationship between the values within a coordinate.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to spot patterns between consecutive coordinates. E.g. the y value goes up in ones.
nodes.response: Get pupils to think about the relationship between x and y within a coordinate. Include non-integer values and coordinates not in order.

nodes.misconception: The magnetic field is only at the poles of a magnet.
nodes.response: Provide opportunity for pupils to plot magnetic field lines around pairs of bar magnets and to experiment with a second magnet as described in the teacher tip.

nodes.misconception: That coordinates only exist, and can only be plotted, on the lines of graph paper.
nodes.response: Between any two vertices there are infinitely more points. Ask pupils to consider what numbers are between 1 and 2.

nodes.misconception: Pneumatic systems always cause something to expland or inflate.
nodes.response: Pneumatic systems can cause directed movement of an object without inflation.

nodes.misconception: The sounds for [b] and [v] are different, as in English.
nodes.response: This is one of the rare cases in Spanish where one sound can have two spellings.

nodes.misconception: Adding an -e to an adjective is the sole way to change an adjective from the masculine to the feminine form.
nodes.response: There are different ways to change a masculine adjective to a feminine adjective; adding an -e to the end being the most common. When an adjective ends in -eux in the masculine form, however, it changes to -euse in the feminine form.

nodes.misconception: All nouns in Spanish are always used with an article, a word for 'a', 'some' or 'the'.
nodes.response: Some nouns are uncountable and have no plural. Use these without an article, as in English. For example, 'quiere dinero' means 'she, he wants money'.

nodes.misconception: Add '-s' to form the plural of all nouns in German.
nodes.response: There is a set of rules that help you know how to form plural nouns in German. Not all nouns form their plural in the same way, so the rules need to be learned.

nodes.misconception: As long as we know the meaning of a noun, we don't need to worry about its grammatical gender.
nodes.response: Knowing the grammatical gender of a noun is very important, because the gender affects the form of other parts of a sentence, such as the article or preposition. This in turn affects the clarity and comprehensibility of the message.

nodes.misconception: The definite and indefinite articles don't change. Thet stay the same like 'the', 'a' or 'an' for whatever noun they precede, like they do in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, nouns have gender. Definite and indefinite articles change according to the gender: 'el' and 'un' for masculine nouns; 'la' and 'una' for feminine nouns.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse a metaphor with a simile.
nodes.response: Explain that both metaphors and similes are ways of using language to compare.  Metaphors compare by saying something 'is' somthing else, whilst similes use the word 'as' or 'like'.  There are no similes in this poem.

nodes.misconception: Students may be unfamiliar with the term 'region'.
nodes.response: Help students recognise and learn about their own region.

nodes.misconception: Muslims do not use poetry to understand ideas of God.
nodes.response: Poetry is an art form that Muslims use as a way of expressing their beliefs.

nodes.misconception: Poetry is always descriptive and doesn't tell stories.
nodes.response: Ballads are poems that tell stories with a sequence of events. They include scene-setting, action, change moments and a conclusion. Ballads are also lyrical - they use poetic language, imagery, rhythm, rhyme - and dramatic - often with direct speech.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a partner balance is a counter balance. One pupil pulls harder or doesn’t pull enough, leading to a collapse of the position. Pupils do not have a secure grip with one another.
nodes.response: Show the difference between a partner balance and a counter balance. Encourage pupils to communicate with their partners pulling gently at first, then increase force gradually to find the balance point. Grip using wrists as an alternative to hands.

nodes.misconception: Radicals encouraged the use of violence to solve the problems that industrial workers faced.
nodes.response: Radicals like Cobbett and Hunt emphaisised the importance of peaceful protests and the need to persuade government to extend voting rights.

nodes.misconception: Pollen are seeds, or that seeds are not made by sexual reproduction.
nodes.response: Clearly show the difference between pollen as a gamete and the seeds as the offspring that grows into a new plant.

nodes.misconception: The interdependence of organisms within ecosystems arise from more than just feeding relationships.
nodes.response: This lesson demonstrates that feeding relationships are important and that producers often rely on consumers for reproduction.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that bees and other pollinators pollinate flowers to help them out, rather than it being a by-product of them getting food from the flower.
nodes.response: Explain that pollinators visit flowers to get something for themselves (nectar and/or pollen), not to intentionally pollinate flowers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals are pollinating flowers to intentionally help them.
nodes.response: Explain that pollinators are visiting flowers to find food for themselves, rather than to help the plant; they do not pollinate flowers on purpose.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that the polymer identification codes mean that all these polymers can be recycled as the symbols look similar to the recycling symbol.
nodes.response: Only some polymers can be recycled. These normally have the code 1 or 2.

nodes.misconception: All polymers are non biodegradable and can last for hundreds of year.
nodes.response: Polymers come in many forms including biodegradable and bio-based polymers that will break down more easily in the environment.

nodes.misconception: Not including the bonds either side of the repeating unit.
nodes.response: The slide deck states the need for open bonds to show how repeating units are bonded to each other.

nodes.misconception: Polymers can all be recycled and are therefore environmentally ok.
nodes.response: Polymers are usually made from non renewable resources and even if recycled, are not sustainable.

nodes.misconception: All of the parts are necessary to make the project work.
nodes.response: Ideally pupils will record in all of the parts of the batucada, but the project will still work successfully with the core ensemble of surdo, caixa and repinique.

nodes.misconception: We only need to rehearse if we find our part difficult.
nodes.response: Rehearsing can warm you up for a performance and make sure you feel alert and ready to perform. It also makes sure you know when and how to play and not just what to play.

nodes.misconception: Researching means copying images exactly into your final artwork.
nodes.response: Research is about gathering inspiration and developing ideas, not copying. Artists reinterpret and combine sources in creative and personal ways.

nodes.misconception: All Pop Art looks the same - it’s just bold colours and celebrities.
nodes.response: Each Pop artist had a unique message and approach. Some explored consumerism, others made emotional or political statements.

nodes.misconception: A final outcome must look identical to the original plan.
nodes.response: Artists adapt ideas during making. Their plan is a starting point - not a rule. Changing materials or layout during creation is part of the artistic process.

nodes.misconception: Chord inversions are inserted randomly by composers.
nodes.response: Chord inversions are used to add interest by bringing subtle amounts of tension to a chord and to create smoother transitions from one chord to another. They are not chosen randomly and are used sparingly to create a particular effect.

nodes.misconception: The Roman Catholic Church is only focused on Catholics and personal morality.
nodes.response: This encyclical is addressed to the whole world as Pope Francis saw that all the world was a common home for everyone.

nodes.misconception: Records of speeches from previous time periods are accurate representations of what these people actually said.
nodes.response: Accurate recording of speeches was not a priority for many historians or record keepers up until fairly recently. It was seen as acceptable to put words into the mouths of past people based on what happened after or to reflect present sensibilities.

nodes.misconception: Historians all agree about what happened in the past.
nodes.response: Historians are constantly arguing and changing their minds about events in the past as new evidence comes to light.

nodes.misconception: That all contemporary sources can be accepted based solely on the value of their content.
nodes.response: Historians must consider how the provenance of a source may have affected the way it discusses and portrays a historical issue.

nodes.misconception: Global resources are running out because the global population is rising.
nodes.response: Population growth is just one of many factors contributing to increased demand for resources.

nodes.misconception: All countries have ageing populations.
nodes.response: Not all countries have ageing populations. It is more common in higher income nations with longer life expectancies.

nodes.misconception: Overpopulation and underpopulation are only about the number of people in a country.
nodes.response: It’s not just about numbers—it’s about how well a country’s resources match the needs of its population.

nodes.misconception: Population density is the same everywhere in China.
nodes.response: Population density varies across China; urban areas such as Shanghai are densely populated, but rural areas, such as the mountainous regions covering much of western China, are sparsely populated.

nodes.misconception: Population density is the same everywhere.
nodes.response: This misconception arises because students may not realise that geographical factors vary widely. Address this by comparing different regions.

nodes.misconception: Cities only grow because of migration.
nodes.response: While migration is a key factor, natural increase (more births than deaths) is often just as important - especially in cities with young populations.

nodes.misconception: Population pyramids only show us the total population size.
nodes.response: A population pyramid provides information about the structure of the population; the age and gender profile of the location represented. This can help governments with future planning.

nodes.misconception: Population pyramids only show us the total population size.
nodes.response: A population pyramid provides information about the structure of the population; the age and gender profile of the location represented. This can help governments with future planning.

nodes.misconception: Everyone in the Middle East lives in the desert.
nodes.response: Although deserts cover a vast amount of land, people tend to cluster around water sources like rivers and coasts. That’s why cities like Cairo (near the Nile) are densely populated.

nodes.misconception: All population pyramids are pyramid-shaped.
nodes.response: Population pyramids can have different shapes depending on demographic factors. Some may be more rectangular or even inverted, reflecting various population structures.

nodes.misconception: Portraits are just about what someone looks like on the surface with no deeper meaning.
nodes.response: While capturing someone’s physical appearance can be part of a portrait, photographers often go much deeper. Portraits can reveal who someone is, exploring culture, identity, relationships, life experiences and even social or political themes.

nodes.misconception: 'Tiene' and 'hay' are interchangeable.
nodes.response: Both 'hay' and 'tiene' can be used to describe details. However, sentences with 'hay' usually start with or contain 'en'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make errors using the halfway steps between numbers (e.g. wrongly label 374 as 379).
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to find and label the halfway steps (e.g. the 5 or the 50s numbers).

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to position five-digit multiples of 1,000 on a 0-1,000,000 number line.
nodes.response: It is important to check if pupils are secure in placing numbers on a 0-1,000 number line. This is a fundamental prerequisite to be able to achieve with this learning, so spending time securing this prior learning may be necessary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to position five-digit multiples of 1,000 on a 0-100,000 number line.
nodes.response: It is important to check if pupils are secure in placing two-digit numbers on a 0-100 number line. This is a fundamental prerequisite to be able to achieve with this learning, so spending time securing this prior learning may be necessary.

nodes.misconception: Defending in netball is mainly a role when your opponent has the ball.
nodes.response: Defending occurs in all positions and each player needs to track their opponent to try to deny them the opportunity to receive a pass.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often find passing over distance much harder and try to kick the ball too hard. Often pupils are too close together so no one is in a wide position to aim for.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to slowly increase the distance at which they pass so they maintain control and accuracy. Pupils should be encouraged to adopt wide positions when attacking, stretching defenders to create space.

nodes.misconception: There is a lack of movement off the ball or teammates position themselves too close to the ball carrier therefore making it easier for the defenders to gain possession.
nodes.response: Pupils should always be moving off the ball to drag defenders out of positions. Pupils should also spread out and position themselves at different angles and distances from the ball carrier.

nodes.misconception: Believing that technology always improves performance without considering potential drawbacks.
nodes.response: Technology has both positive and negative impacts on different people in sport including performers, sponsors, spectators and officials.

nodes.misconception: Pupils count squares to calculate gradient instead of looking at scales.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to pick points on the graph to use to find the gradient and write down the coordinates rather than count squares.

nodes.misconception: Pupils focus only on winning instead of adapting their tactics to the game scenario.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have time to plan their tactics in each scenario and highlight effective team work.

nodes.misconception: 'Esta' means both 'this' and 'she, he, it is'.
nodes.response: ‘Esta’ is a demonstrative adjective, it means ‘this’ and goes before a noun. ‘Está’ is a verb, means ‘she, he, it is’ and describes an state or location. As there is an accent, we must stress the last syllable.

nodes.misconception: There is only one word for 'your' in Spanish and that is 'tu'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, if the possessive adjective 'your' comes before a singular or uncountable noun, we say 'tu', but if it comes before a plural noun we say 'tus'.

nodes.misconception: There is no preparation needed before I read Spanish aloud.
nodes.response: Trickier sounds can trip us up when we read aloud in Spanish. Identifying any tricky sounds, then mentally rehearsing before we read aloud can help us read more accurately and fluently.

nodes.misconception: Decolonisation happened in a peaceful and orderly way in all of Britain's African colonies.
nodes.response: Decolonisation in many of Britain's African colonies was mostly peaceful; however, there were exceptions. For example, in Kenya there was significant violence as the British authorities used brutal measures to suppress the Mau Mau Uprising (1952-60).

nodes.misconception: All migrants from Kenya and Uganda during the mid-20th century were of Asian descent.
nodes.response: Not all migrants from Kenya and Uganda during the mid-20th century were of Asian descent; however, large numbers of them were due to the discrimination they faced in newly-independent Kenya and Uganda.

nodes.misconception: The Falkland Islands have always been uncontested British territory.
nodes.response: There is a complex and prolonged sovereignty dispute with Argentina over the Falkland Islands and there were once historical claims by Spain.

nodes.misconception: The Empire Windrush brought all Caribbean migrants to Britain.
nodes.response: The Empire Windrush brought the first group of Caribbean migrants to Britain.

nodes.misconception: A logo is a brand.
nodes.response: A logo is not a brand but a key part of a brand's or organisation's identity. A logo is a graphic that represents the visual identity of a brand or organisation.

nodes.misconception: Plans cannot change as a project progresses.
nodes.response: Initial planning helps focus the purpose, content and layout of a product. However, due to feedback or changing needs, plans may need to be changed as a project progresses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to think that all water is the same. Pupils tend to forget that non-visible substances are also found in water.
nodes.response: Stress that pure water only contains H₂O molecules.  Other types of water may include varying amounts of dissolved salts, other solids or micro-organisms. Stress that microbes must be killed for water to be potable, but are too difficult to remove.

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to think that all water is the same. Pupils tend to forget that non-visible substances are also found in water.
nodes.response: Stress that pure water only contains H₂O molecules. Other waters may include varying amounts of dissolved salts, other solids or micro-organisms. Stress that microbes must be killed for water to be potable, but are too difficult to remove.

nodes.misconception: A battery pushes a constant current around a circuit.
nodes.response: Provide opportunity for pupils to measure p.d. across a power supply when the resistance of a circuit it is connected to is altered.

nodes.misconception: All agent nouns are formed by adding either -eur or -ateur to the stem of the verb.
nodes.response: Most agent nouns follow this rule but there are exceptions, for example éduquer - to educate, becomes éducateur - educator. A stem change is needed here.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up the terms power and force, which are often used interchangeably in everyday speech.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the terms need to be used appropriately, for example in lifting two different sized weights (different forces) whilst increasing their energy at the same rate (same power).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up the terms power and force, which are often used interchangeably in everyday speech.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the terms need to be used appropriately, for example in lifting two different sized weights (different forces) whilst increasing their energy at the same rate (same power).

nodes.misconception: Thinking that flexibility is only useful for gymnasts or dancers.
nodes.response: Discuss wider examples such as hurdlers, footballers and swimmers that will also benefit from high levels of flexibility.

nodes.misconception: The folktales have no connection to the frame story.
nodes.response: The folktales are being told by Shahrazad. The fact that she is trying to save her life by telling the stories is important. But more than this, you can also make connections between the ideas, plot and characters in the folktales to the frame story.

nodes.misconception: When different bases are used student multiply the bases.  e.g. 2 x 5^2 = 10^2
nodes.response: Calculate and compare the 2, 2 x 5^2 = 50 & 10^2 = 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils often use the terms power and energy interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use concrete examples to show pupils that a greater power transfers energy more quickly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up the terms power and force, which are often used interchangeably in everyday speech.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the terms need to be used appropriately, for example in lifting two different sized weights (different forces) whilst increasing their energy at the same rate (same power).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up the terms power and force, which are often used interchangeably in everyday speech.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the terms need to be used appropriately, for example in lifting two different sized weights (different forces) whilst increasing their energy at the same rate (same power).

nodes.misconception: Power stations generate most of the electricity that we use in the UK.
nodes.response: Highlight how over half of UK electricity is now generated using renewable energy resources and that power stations contribute about a third of the electricity. Also highlight the continuing need for power stations due to varying weather and demand.

nodes.misconception: Paragraphs can only focus on one character at a time.
nodes.response: Comparing characters can be a useful way to deepen your understanding and analysis.

nodes.misconception: Students forget to scroll right to exit the exponent function.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check what they have on their screen matches the calculation exactly.

nodes.misconception: Children may not appreciate the size of one million or that it is composed of 1,000 thousands. Children may find grasping the concept of 'power of 10' tricky.
nodes.response: Use the place value chart and place value counters to represent the composition of one million. Use the stem sentences: 'One million is composed of 1,000 thousands' and 'Each column is ten times the value to that on its right'.

nodes.misconception: Compression is only useful for saving storage space.
nodes.response: While saving storage is one benefit, compression is also critical for faster transmission of files over the internet, reducing bandwidth usage on networks, and enabling smooth real-time communication.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are unsure about situations when the body works aerobically and when it works anaerobically.
nodes.response: Aerobic exercise requires oxygen from the air we breathe to totally break down glucose to release energy for exercise. This is the most efficient mechanism but requires exercise to be at a low/ moderate intensity whereas high intensity is anaerobic.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the red cabbage will change to the same colours as universal indicator solution.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that there are many different indicators used to show different pH.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes children can think days of the week are only capitalised if at the beginning of a sentence
nodes.response: Model and show examples of the days of the week in the middle of a sentence with a capital letter.

nodes.misconception: That the letters h, b, d and k are x-height letters.
nodes.response: Modelling through the lesson that although parts of the letter are x-height, they are not x-height letters because they have ascenders.

nodes.misconception: That g, y, p and q are x-height letters.
nodes.response: Model through the lesson that although part of the letter is x-height, they are not x-height letters as they have descenders.

nodes.misconception: Some children may ask why b, d, g, p, q and y are not x-height letters.
nodes.response: Use pictures of these letters to emphasise to the children that they have ascenders or descenders.

nodes.misconception: If your data is not sorted then you cannot use a binary search.
nodes.response: Data does need to be sorted to use a binary search, though use of a sorting algorithm first would allow binary search to be used. However, consideration must be given as to the benefit of this approach for searching.

nodes.misconception: You read French in the same way as you read English.
nodes.response: French is pronounced, and therefore read, differently than English. This can be seen with the five vowel sounds which are pronounced and read differently in French and English.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume that every word with a short vowel sound should have a double consonant.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that this is not always the case and give them examples of words such as 'hot' not 'hott' and 'shut' not 'shutt'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to double the consonant after a short vowel, such as fun - funny.
nodes.response: Make links to other suffixes used, such as -ed or -ing, when the consonant is also doubled.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the spellings of homophones: eight and ate, weight and wait.
nodes.response: When you review the spellings of these words, ensure to identify that they are homophones and suggest ways to remember which is which.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think words are compound words if they can spot one word within another word.
nodes.response: Show examples e.g. 'yesterday'. Whilst it has the word 'day' in it, if you were to separate this, the word 'yester' would not make sense.

nodes.misconception: Remind pupils to use the root word to help them spell the new word created by adding the suffix.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have a good understanding of the vocabulary. If they do not know the root word, they will find it harder to spell. Use images.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the difference between 'homophone' and 'homonym'.
nodes.response: Give specific examples of homophones (e.g. hair and hare) and homonyms (e.g. bark) and discuss the differences.

nodes.misconception: Many homophones are common exception words and pupils often confuse homophones within sentences.
nodes.response: Give pupils the chance to choose the spellings they find most difficult and give them the strategies to help them practise.

nodes.misconception: All words with a suffix will have a recognisable root word.
nodes.response: Show that not all words with suffixes or common word endings will necessarily have a root word that we can recognise.

nodes.misconception: Not all words have a word hidden in a word.
nodes.response: Show that this is a useful strategy to use when you can spot a word in a word, but it isn't always suitable.

nodes.misconception: Pupils misspell the words with prefixes because they cannot spell the root word.
nodes.response: Draw attention to tricky elements of the root words as necessary, e.g. the 'ea' in healthy - unhealthy.

nodes.misconception: When practising spellings, children can practise wrong by copying out incorrectly.
nodes.response: Ensure to place emphasis on carefully looking and checking the spellings when practising.  This can be done individually or in pairs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that you can add -er or -est to any adjective and use it to make comparisons.
nodes.response: Make pupils aware that we cannot always add the suffix -er or -est to compare. For example, good - better - best or bad - worse - worst.

nodes.misconception: Children may spell words with the suffix -ful using a double 'l'.
nodes.response: Explicilty make the distinction between the word 'full' and the suffix -ful, which only has one 'l'.  Practise spelling both in a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might use 's after words ending in 'ch', 'sh', 'ss' or 'x'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that apostrophes are used for contraction or possession and to make these nouns plural we need to add the correct suffix.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may add -es or -ies to all words ending in the letter 'y'.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that words ending in a vowel, then a 'y', follow a different rule. Remind them we just add -s to make them plural.

nodes.misconception: Calligraphy is just decorative handwriting.
nodes.response: Calligraphy is an art form with specific techniques, not just decorative handwriting.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the -es suffix is always pronounced as 'is'.
nodes.response: Model saying words like 'dominoes' (domino-is) and 'wishes' (wishs) incorrectly. Talk about making meaning when we read and spell.

nodes.misconception: When practising in an ensemble we need to practise at our own speed so we can play our part accurately.
nodes.response: When practising as an ensemble, we all need to play at the same tempo, we should start off slowly and speed up as we feel more confident.

nodes.misconception: When we practise, we just need to repeat the music a few times.
nodes.response: Thinking about what we want to improve and choosing the best stragtegy to help us is the best way to practise.

nodes.misconception: Playing a piece of music numerous times will improve the performance.
nodes.response: Playing sections of a piece multiple times will only improve a performance if a small part is focused on and improvements are considered and rehearsed effectively.

nodes.misconception: As the words get longer, children can rush, causing the letter spacing to become uneven and the writing illegible.
nodes.response: Remind and model to the children that the flow and movement of the pencil is the same at the end of the word as it is at the beginning.

nodes.misconception: A particular piece of Folk music is always played in eactly the same way.
nodes.response: Folk music is passed down via an oral tradition and is often interpreted differently. Melodies, harmonies and instrumentation may change over time and when played in different places.

nodes.misconception: Some children might forget to add the capital letter for the direct speech within a speech second sentence or might try to join the capital letter to the other letters.
nodes.response: Model the habit of looking and thinking about your sentence before you write it. Where will my punctuation be? Where will my capital letters be? This way children will have the time to think about it before they start writing.

nodes.misconception: As children start to write longer paragraphs in cursive handwriting their hands can get sore which can lead to them making mistakes.
nodes.response: Model to the children that it is good practice to take a break when writing to stretch your hand if it is becoming sore.

nodes.misconception: Children can get confused when writing the headline and start to join the capital letters to the lower case letters.
nodes.response: Model to the children that you think about the headline before writing it. Which words will have capital letters? When forming the capital letter, exaggerate the action of lifting your pencil after the formation to remind the children.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes children will forget to add the lead in for the first letter in the letter string or the first letter after the capital letter.
nodes.response: Use the 'Ready, line, go' technique to remind children to start on the baseline.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes when writing quotations, the children may forget to start with a capital letter as they are concentrating on using the inverted commas.
nodes.response: Model clearly by saying your thought process out loud to remind the children that a capital letter is needed. For example, 'quotation mark, capital letter, lift my pencil...'.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes when writing quotations, the children may forget to start with a capital letter as they are concentrating on using the inverted commas.
nodes.response: Model clearly by saying your thought process out loud to remind the children that a capital letter is needed. For example, 'quotation mark, capital letter, lift my pencil...'.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes children can forget the capital letter after the inverted commas.
nodes.response: As you model, repeat the same words to remind the children that the capital letter comes after the inverted commas. For example, 'Let's start, inverted commas, capital letter, pencil off, lead in...'.

nodes.misconception: That as long as they are using language devices in their speeches, this is enough.
nodes.response: There is great variety in quality in the execution of language devices. The best devices are creative, original and well-matched to purpose.

nodes.misconception: Everyone will respond to an image in the same way.
nodes.response: How you respond to an image, and what you choose to zoom in on, will be different for each person since we're all unique with different memories and experiences.

nodes.misconception: Fusion music is less authentic or valuable than traditional genres.
nodes.response: Fusion music is in itself innovative and musically complex and is recognised as a genre in its own right.

nodes.misconception: More figurative language in descriptive writing is always better.
nodes.response: Overuse of personification, similes or other figurative devices can overwhelm the reader or dilute the impact of the description.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that punctuation rules in direct speech are optional or may apply them inconsistently.
nodes.response: Explain that the reader must know where the direct speech begins and ends to understand what is being said. Display examples of speech with and without punctuation to emphasise this.

nodes.misconception: Children may form the print version of the letter and then add the 'lead in' separately.
nodes.response: Model and emphasise saying 'Ready, line, go' to remind them that the letter starts with the lead in on the baseline for pre-cursive letters.

nodes.misconception: For these letters, children may finish on the baseline and forget the curved stroke as the lead out
nodes.response: Emphasise to the children through modelling that there has to be a 'tail' for the letter to join to the next letter.

nodes.misconception: The two loops on the pre-cursive letter f can be challenging for children at first.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and opportunities to trace the grey examples will support correct formation.

nodes.misconception: Children may form the print version of the letter and then add the 'lead in' seperately.
nodes.response: Model and emphasise saying 'Ready, line, go' to remind them that the letter starts with the lead in on the baseline for pre-cursive letters.

nodes.misconception: The lead out on the pre-cursive letter r can be challenging and children can sometimes dip too far.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and opportunities to trace the grey examples will support correct formation.

nodes.misconception: The lead out on the pre-cursive letter g and q can be challenging for children at first.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and opportunities to trace the grey examples will support correct formation.

nodes.misconception: Children can struggle with the shape and size of the loop at the end of the descender.
nodes.response: More tracing practice will support children to get a feel for the size and shape of the loop.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume all pre-cursive letters have a lead out.
nodes.response: When modelling the break letters, ensure to emphasise 'break' to remind the children not to add a lead out.

nodes.misconception: The change in the size of a population will only affect another population if they are predator-prey
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils are given opportunities to see how changes in population size impact all other organisms in the food chain.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that all animals in a food chain are predators, or that all carnivores are predators.
nodes.response: Some animals can be carnivores but not predators. These animals are scavengers because they eat meat from animals they have found or that have been killed by other animals.

nodes.misconception: You can't believe in both predestination and free will.
nodes.response: Christians can believe in both because: 1) God knows the free choices we will make, which enables him to predestine us; 2) We have been created with a nature which predetermines us to heaven or hell, we can still act freely within this nature.

nodes.misconception: That Sunni Muslims believe we have no free will due to predestination, or that Shi'a Muslims believe there is no predestination due to free will.
nodes.response: Most Muslims take a middle ground between them when considering the relationship between free will and predestination in Islam.

nodes.misconception: That Sunni Muslims believe we have no free will due to predestination, or that Shi'a Muslims believe there is no predestination due to free will.
nodes.response: Most Muslims take a middle ground between them when considering the relationship between free will and predestination in Islam.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse physical and chemical changes and think that all particles look and act like those shown in the particle model.
nodes.response: Give the pupils an array of different examples of physical and chemical reactions and get the pupils to consider if new substances have been produced. Show the pupils, using molymods, how different molecules can be.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse physical and chemical changes. Also, pupils do not appreciate that substances can exist in any state of matter depending on temperature.
nodes.response: Use the phrasing 'substances in a solid state' rather than solids to avoid pupils thinking that the substance only exits in one specific state.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that multiplication always makes things larger. Children may scale incorrectly.
nodes.response: When a number is multiplied by a value less than 1, the product is smaller than the original number - multiplication doesn't always make things larger. Compare numbers: if one factor is made ___ times the size, the product will be ___ times the size.

nodes.misconception: If the weather report has the rain icon, it means it will rain.
nodes.response: The rain symbol is to denote what type of rain it is likely to be should it rain. The percentage chance of rain then informs us about how likely it is to rain.

nodes.misconception: Only generative AI systems require training data to complete tasks.
nodes.response: All AI systems rely on training data to perform tasks by using patterns identified in the data.

nodes.misconception: 'Me gusta' is always the correct way to say 'I like'.
nodes.response: 'Me gusta' is 'I like' for a singular or uncountable noun, but plural nouns require 'me gustan'.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, like in English, the object always goes after the verb.
nodes.response: In Spanish, unlike in English, the object can go before or after the verb.

nodes.misconception: The verb 'aimer' means 'to like', and 'adorer' means 'to love'.
nodes.response: The verb 'aimer' means both 'to like' and 'to love'. 'Adorer' does also mean 'to love', but can be translated as 'to adore'. When saying 'I love you' in French, we say 'je t'aime'.

nodes.misconception: There are two ways of referring to the present tense in French, as in English, e.g. 'I watch' and 'I am watching'.
nodes.response: There is only one way to refer to the present tense in French: 'je regarde'. This can be translated as both 'I watch' and 'I am watching'.

nodes.misconception: Children may want to take their pencil off after forming the prefix as they see it as separate to the root word.
nodes.response: Encourage children by modelling and emphasising that the pencil only comes off the page once the letter string is complete. Getting them to identify the last letter before starting can help to remind them of this.

nodes.misconception: All Christians think same-sex sexuality is wrong.
nodes.response: Not all Christians believe same-sex sexuality is wrong, some denominations welcome same-sex couples. Even where same-sex acts are considered sinful, individuals with same-sex sexuality are not seen as sinful and should be treated with compassion.

nodes.misconception: That a modern reader and Victorian reader perceive the text and characters in the same way.
nodes.response: Use Victorian context to explain the difference between our attitudes.

nodes.misconception: Producing a line drawing with sketched broken lines, shading, no labelling and no magnification.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 2 in this lesson explores how to produce a scientific line drawing to record observations from light microscopy.

nodes.misconception: Early warning systems can predict when an earthquake will happen.
nodes.response: Early warning systems cannot predict when an earthquake will happen, but can notify scientists of an imminent earthquake. This then gives families and individuals valuable seconds to prepare.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all points are equally effective in a debate.
nodes.response: Whilst it is good to generate lots of points when preparing for a debate, they will vary in how effective they are.

nodes.misconception: Beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: The beat is the showing or playing of the steady pulse.  They rhythm is the pattern of sounds which we play in time to the beat.

nodes.misconception: Pitch is the same as melodic shape.
nodes.response: Pitch refers to how high or low an individual note is. Melodic shape refers to the up and down contour pattern created by a series of pitches.

nodes.misconception: Pesach is only for Jewish people in the past.
nodes.response: Pesach is still celebrated today by Jewish families all over the world.

nodes.misconception: Buttresses, bracing, anchors, wider bases and reinforced sides need to be on every single mock-up model for it to be freestanding.
nodes.response: Not all structures need a buttress, bracing, anchors, wider bases or reinforcing, it depends on the materials that are being used, the size, height and what the object is going to do.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to know if adjectives are positive or negative.
nodes.response: Display lists of positive and negative adjectives on the wall and generate example sentences together.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that speakers in a debate are reading their speech word for word.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that speakers in a debate should just be using notes to guide their speech, not reading it word for word. Model how to do this effectively while maintaining eye contact with the audience.

nodes.misconception: The response from the timed period is marked as a stand alone outcome.
nodes.response: The marks are awarded holistically and take in the whole creative process. This period is a great way to resolve your ideas and spend time focusing on realising your intentions. It shouldn't be incredibly stressful or worry you!

nodes.misconception: Pupils can be unsure which values to add and which to subtract when collecting like terms.
nodes.response: Rewrite the equation with like terms grouped together before combining like terms.

nodes.misconception: Mind mapping is the only way to plan a piece of writing.
nodes.response: Mind mapping is a good place to start, but isn't always useful for considering structure. Using single paragraph outlines is an effective way to ensure a cohesive stricture and a clearly developed line of argument.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to choose appropriate synonyms for the precise context in LC2.
nodes.response: Allow children to work in pairs or small groups to generate ideas. Mind map some more synonyms together as a class before they complete the task.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any small object can be a good subject for poetry.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the subject of a poem should be something that inspires poetry and will be interesting to write about. Provide children with a range of ideas for them to decide whether they are inspiring or not.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to include the full details from their research notes in their oral rehearsal.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the purpose of the first task is to practise giving a summary of the whole argument, not to give all the evidence that supports it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of some of the definitions and synonyms of words associated with the heat.
nodes.response: It would be beneficial to have completed the Y4 Mrs Wordsmith vocabulary unit on 'Weather: wind and hot words' ahead of this lesson, to support children with generating vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of some of the definitions and synonyms of words associated with rain.
nodes.response: Dictionaries, thesauruses and rhyming dictionaries would support pupils when completing Task B.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that words stay as prepositions irrespective of what follows them.
nodes.response: Some words are prepositions when followed by a noun phrase, but they can be conjunctions or adverbs in other circumstances.

nodes.misconception: As long as a model is shown, it doesn't need to be explained.
nodes.response: It’s important to explain your ideas clearly - your model shows the design, but your words help others understand why and how you made it.

nodes.misconception: When your final design has already been decided, it is a waste of time reflecting back on the design journey.
nodes.response: Even though the final design may be decided, reflection is not about changing the outcome, it's about understanding how you got there, what you learned, and how you can improve in the future.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to change the verb into the correct form to fit the rest of the sentence.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities to practise saying and reading present and past tense sentences.

nodes.misconception: All data can be presented as a graph or chart.
nodes.response: The way in which data is presented will depend on whether the data is quantitative or qualitative.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think some phrases are sentences because they can look longer than full simple sentences.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that simple sentences must contain a verb in order to make sense. Note that phrases are often adjectives and nouns.

nodes.misconception: Evaluating a design uses only the user feedback.
nodes.response: Evaluations should be reflective and allow the designer to consider their thoughts as well as the user's.

nodes.misconception: Questions using intonation or 'est-ce que' have different meanings: Tu aimes l'histoire ? vs. Est-ce que tu aimes l'histoire ?
nodes.response: 'Tu aimes l’histoire ?' and 'Est-ce que tu aimes l’histoire ?' mean the same thing, they are two different ways of asking the same question (using intonation or 'est-ce que').

nodes.misconception: Presentation is just for decoration.
nodes.response: Presentation is part of communication, not decoration.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the rules for presenting always remain the same.
nodes.response: Look at examples of presenting for different purposes and highlight the nuanced differences. Watch CBBC Newsround as a good model.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their narrative writing.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that there is one right way to deliver a presentation of a persuasive advert.
nodes.response: Discuss how the target audience impacts the delivery. E.g. difference in delivering to investors (Dragon's Den style) or potential consumers

nodes.misconception: Technical jargon impresses the audience and makes the presentation better.
nodes.response: Presentations should be clear and accessible, using simple language and examples that everyone can understand.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about portfolios is that you need to include everything you've made.
nodes.response: It's much better to select work that clearly shows your ideas, development, artistic journey and skills.

nodes.misconception: The way you show your work doesn't really matter so long as it's tidy.
nodes.response: A creative, careful presentation will support the idea, message or mood and help make your work impactful.

nodes.misconception: Graphically presented data is always easier to understand than data in tables.
nodes.response: Graphical charts help to spot patterns in the data they are based on but they are not intended to be able to read actual values. Tables should be used to provide the exact values.

nodes.misconception: Not all data may fit the pattern they have identified.
nodes.response: These are called anomalies and can sometimes be explained away but individual anomalies would not disprove a pattern exists.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they are either a 'good communicator' or a 'bad communicator'.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils have a growth mindset when it comes to developing presentation and communication skills. All the presentation skills showcased in this lesson can be practised, including those that pupils feel confident in!

nodes.misconception: There is only one strategy to making a moving windmill.
nodes.response: There are multiple ways to make the windmill turn. It can be made using different materials - such as wood, card, straws, split pins and pins

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a predator can always be identified by its size and ferocity in comparison to its prey.
nodes.response: This lesson gives examples of some predators that are smaller in size than their prey.

nodes.misconception: Geographers present data to make it look more attractive.
nodes.response: Geographers present data so that it becomes more meaningful. It allows geographers to see patterns and relationships in the data that will help them answer their enquiry question.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to speak sufficiently loudly or clearly when presenting.
nodes.response: Model the volume, stance and eye contact you expect. You may want to have children present to smaller groups if possible.

nodes.misconception: If someone asks you for your personal information, you should share it.
nodes.response: You should not share your personal information with other people. If you are not sure, check with a trusted adult.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that they should present a balanced view in opinion-based writing.
nodes.response: It is much more convincing and persuasive to only present one side of the argument.

nodes.misconception: Maps are only used to help us find out where places are.
nodes.response: Maps are a brilliant tool that geographers can use to record and present information as well as use for navigation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their learning.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise there are many ways to present information as well as writing.
nodes.response: By sharing many ways that information is communicated throughout the lesson, pupils will have a variety of ways that they can choose to present what they have learned about the digestive system.

nodes.misconception: When wicket keeping, pupils have a tendency to stand right up to the wickets, no matter how fast the bowler is. This means they can't react quick enough to faster balls.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand that they can adjust the distance between wicket keeper and stumps, depending on the speed of the bowler, so they are catching the ball around thigh height. There is no standard wicket keeper position.

nodes.misconception: Pressure is greater at the bottom of a wider container than at the bottom of a narrower one.
nodes.response: Discuss how the force of water in the wider container is acting over a bigger area and refer to pressure = force ÷ area.

nodes.misconception: The pressure at a particular depth depends on the shape of the container the liquid is in.
nodes.response: Demonstrate different shaped containers with the same depth of water in each and an identical shaped hole 1 cm above the base of each. Identical sized jets of water should shoot out of each hole as the pressure at each hole is (initially) the same.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that sustainability is only about protecting the landscape and environment of the Lake District.
nodes.response: Remind children that sustainability also includes economic sustainability.

nodes.misconception: Pressure and force are terms that are often used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Explore examples with pupils in which similar sized forces are used to create different pressures that the pupils can experience first hand.

nodes.misconception: As long as you use all security measures, a computer system connected to a network can be totally safe from cyber attack.
nodes.response: No computer system on a network can be completely safe, even with all security measures. Cybercriminals can find new ways to attack, so security only reduces the risk and doesn't completely eliminate it.

nodes.misconception: Primary effects always cause the most damage.
nodes.response: Sometimes it is the secondary effects of a hazard that cause the most destruction, for example mudslides following a volcanic eruption.

nodes.misconception: Add 'ième' to make all ordinal numbers.
nodes.response: Add 'ième' to make the majority of ordinal numbers but 'first' (premier/première) is an exception and cardinal numbers ending -e, drop the final -e before adding 'ième'. There are a few other spelling exceptions like 'neuvième' and 'cinquième'.

nodes.misconception: Asymmetrical designs don't balance.
nodes.response: Asymmetrical designs can use visual weight to create a type of balance even if the work is different on both sides.

nodes.misconception: Depth can only be created in a realistic scene or in a realistic way.
nodes.response: Depth can be entirely imaginary or realistic. Artists can manipulate elements to create the illusion of shapes, colours and lines standing out or recessing in an image.

nodes.misconception: An object has the same mass whether in real life or in a 2D representation.
nodes.response: Whilst an object in real life may have a certain physical mass, if it is depicted in an image its visual weight might not represent this physical mass accurately. Especially compared to other items. This is due to the use of visual elements.

nodes.misconception: In two point perspective, some lines don't need to recede to the vanishing point
nodes.response: All lines recede to one of the vanishing points. Otherwise your drawing won't be realistic

nodes.misconception: Proportions are set rules and always apply
nodes.response: Proportions are relative to the unique form you are observing. They relate to the different sizes of the different parts but may be different for each person, place or object

nodes.misconception: Rhythm is just another way of saying pattern
nodes.response: Rhythm is a visual beat that utilises pattern and repetition across an artwork to direct your eye across the work.

nodes.misconception: Scale means size.
nodes.response: Scale is specifically about relative size.

nodes.misconception: To create unity, all elements in a piece must look exactly the same or be repeated in a uniform manner.
nodes.response: Variety can still contribute to a cohesive composition, as does repeating elements in a non-uniform way.

nodes.misconception: For artwork to employ variety, it needs to be overwhelming or not unified.
nodes.response: Artwork that employs variety can do so in a unified way to still create work that is cohesive.

nodes.misconception: Lines create an edge but they don't create volume.
nodes.response: Contour lines and directional hatching lines can be used to describe the volume of a 3D object in a 2D drawing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse key terminology, as many words are similar, and confuse electrolysis with physical methods of separation.
nodes.response: Emphasise the keywords and provide plenty of opportunity for them to be used in the correct context. Compare electrolysis to physical methods of separation, such as filtration, and explain that chemical reactions occur at the electrodes.

nodes.misconception: Overload is negative and should not be encouraged during training.
nodes.response: Overload is encouraged as a positive aspect of training as progression is being managed correctly to bring about adaptations to fitness. It is not to be confused with 'overuse' which can cause injuries.

nodes.misconception: Overload is negative and should not be encouraged during training.
nodes.response: Overload is encouarged as a positive aspect of traning as progression is being managed correctly to bring about adaptations to fitness. It is not to be confused with 'overuse' which can cause injuries.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think pressing down hard makes the print clearer.
nodes.response: Applying even pressure will result in a clearer print.

nodes.misconception: You need special or expensive things to make fabric patterns.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that you can use natural objects, paper and wax to make patterns on fabric. You can use simple, safe materials to tell powerful stories through cloth.

nodes.misconception: Patterns can only be made with shapes and lines.
nodes.response: Remind children that shapes and lines can be used to make patterns, but motifs can be used to create more complex patterns.

nodes.misconception: Symbols are just pictures - they don’t really mean anything.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that symbols are pictures with power. People use them to show who they are, what they believe in, or what they want to change. On banners, every shape and colour can tell a story.

nodes.misconception: The use of negatives are confused with subtractions.
nodes.response: Writing the negative numbers in brackets and using the additive inverse will help minimise errors.

nodes.misconception: Priority of operations does not apply to fractions
nodes.response: Priority of operations applies to all numbers. They can check with a scientific calculator as the priority of operations is programmed in.

nodes.misconception: Students do not see the implicit brackets. Eg. Sqrt(49 + 36) is not sqrt(49) + sqrt(36)
nodes.response: Look for extended lines or operations which indicate an implicit brackets.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may give the probability as a fraction with the wrong denominator.
nodes.response: Check that pupils understand the difference between the probability of event A given B, P(A|B), and the probability of event A and B occurring.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure whether a variable represents a probability, frequency or a particular outcome.
nodes.response: Variables can be used to represent either of these pieces of information. It can be helpful to start a problem by writing down what any variables represent (e.g. "Let x = the total number of marbles).

nodes.misconception: Many students think the mantle is liquid or semi-liquid. Some think it contains soil or water.
nodes.response: The mantle is almost all solid rock. Less than 1% of it is liquid e.g. at spreading plate boundaries, subduction zones and hot-spots.

nodes.misconception: The task is impossible.
nodes.response: Each stage of the challenge is possible. A reset in order to start again may be a good strategy if you get confused.

nodes.misconception: Letting the most vocal pupils make all the decisions as they have the answers.
nodes.response: The loudest people don't always have the best ideas. If you are a dominant character it is especially important to invest time in learning how and when to be quiet, to listen or to invite others to contribute.

nodes.misconception: Children may misinterpret a word problem especially where they are insecure on the key words such as 'difference' or 'how much more'.
nodes.response: Teacher should model own thoughts when problem solving and encourage children to represent the word problems in a bar model. Construct bar models alongside a retelling of the problem so children can see where the mathematics is found.

nodes.misconception: Programming constructs cannot be combined in the same code block.
nodes.response: The programming constructs of sequence, selection and iteration can be combined within the same code block to make more complex programs.

nodes.misconception: When finding the perimeter of a rectilinear compound shape, pupils might sum the perimeters of each rectangle.
nodes.response: Part of the perimeter for each rectangle is inside the compound shape. Therefore, not all of the perimeter of each rectangle contributes towards the perimeter of the compound shape in this problem.

nodes.misconception: Thinking the multiplier for a 2% increase is either 0.02 or 1.2
nodes.response: A 2% increase is 100% + 2% of the original amount. 102% is equivalent to 1.02 as a decimal.

nodes.misconception: "One shape has an area that is 21% larger than another shape. I can't find the area scale factor between the shapes, since I don't know the actual area of either shape."
nodes.response: It is possible to find scale factors, even if only a percentage that describes their areas is given. One shape will have an area of 100%, so the other shape will have an area 21% larger, at 121%. The scale factor is 1.21 because 100% × 1.21 = 121%.

nodes.misconception: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
nodes.response: Pupils should finish every problem by substituting their solutions back into the original problem. This will help them check their answers but also make them think about whether their solutions are valid in context.

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question.
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.

nodes.misconception: Lines cannot be added to the given diagram.
nodes.response: Often adding additional or found information to a given diagram can help progress towards a solution. Pupils should not be afraid to extend given line segments nor add notation if appropriate.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly inputting a mixed number into the scientific calculator.
nodes.response: A mixed number has it's own separate button. Incorrectly inputting in the mixed number will return brackets on the calculator screen.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not measure the angle from North and simply measure the angle between two line segments.
nodes.response: Reiterate bearings are always measured from North, in a clockwise direction and stated as 3 figures. Encourage pupils to draw North on the correct position before attempting the question.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise or confuse which circle theorems to apply in a multi-step problem.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add more to a diagram in order to deduce more information about the problem. Drawing an additional line segment, such chord or radius may a useful first step.

nodes.misconception: Claims can be made based on the data displayed in a chart.
nodes.response: A claim is only valid for the particular selection of data shown. This can mean that any conclusions are very limited.

nodes.misconception: For the problems with squares inscribed inside circles, pupils may think that the length of the square is equal to the diameter of the circle.
nodes.response: This would be the case if the circle was inscribed inside a square. But when the square is inscribed inside a circle, the diagonal length of the square is equal to the diameter of the circle.

nodes.misconception: E.g 4.5 hours is 4 hours and 50 minutes
nodes.response: Encouraging pupils to use ratio tables to represent proportional relationships using minutes allows them to appreciate the multiplier of 60 when converting hours to minutes, or minutes to seconds.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may represent probabilities in the wrong position on the probability scale by miscounting the number of intervals required.
nodes.response: Before using any probability scale, it can be helpful to make a note of the sizes for each major and minor interval.

nodes.misconception: You always need to draw circles that are the same size to construct any polygon.
nodes.response: Some polygons, such as kites, require you to construct two circles of different size, as long as they still intersect at two points.

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.

nodes.misconception: Directly proportional graphs all start from (0,0) and are above the y axis.
nodes.response: Directly proportional means there is a multiplier between y and x. This graph is always y=kx and is linear passing through (0,0). A proportionality graphs show the multiplicative relationship between y and x^n and can be linear and non linear.

nodes.misconception: Using the wrong limits when dividing or subtracting in order to find the upper limit of a calculation or lower limit of a calculation.
nodes.response: Drawing a number line to show with subtraction will help students see how to achieve an upper or lower limits of an error interval calculation. When using division, reiterating the division of number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

nodes.misconception: A variable and an unknown are the same thing.
nodes.response: A variable's value is not fixed. It can take any value within a given range. This means algebraic statements using variables can form proofs

nodes.misconception: When subtracting expression pupils forget to subtract both terms from the second espression.
nodes.response: Watch out for mistakes with negatives here. Pupils should find it much easier to re-write subtractions as additions of additive inverses and that way they only need to add.

nodes.misconception: Real life measurements aren't always integers. Use of integers can give more a practical application
nodes.response: e.g. find the largest with 200 blocks, the cbrt(200) is not an integer so we use 5 x 5 x 5  =125

nodes.misconception: Assuming  that there are 100 minutes in an hour and converting 3.25 hours to 3 hours 25 minutes.
nodes.response: Start with half an hour, pupils should be happy that half an hour is 30 mins, show it written as a decimal to highlight it's not 3.3 hours

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with showing why the false proofs are false.
nodes.response: Checking what each variable represents will help pupils see why each of the 'proofs' do not work.

nodes.misconception: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%
nodes.response: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 30%

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse whether they need to calculate the volume or surface area of a 3D shape, if not told specifically to do so in a problem.
nodes.response: Use the context to decide which calculation is needed. If the question refers to packaging or painting the shape, a surface area calculation is needed.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to describe what has happened to an object to create its image.
nodes.response: There may be multiple transformations or combinations of transformations that map the object to the image.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the link between transformations and manipulating algebraic expressions.
nodes.response: Be explicit in highlighting that the graph of $$y=x^2+10x+22$$ is the graph of $$y=(x+5)^2-3$$ which is the graph of $$y=x^2$$ transformed by the translation, "$$5$$ units left, $$3$$ units down".

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that data is only presented using the types of graphs that they learn in school.
nodes.response: Data can presented visually in anyway that helps people to understand it. Explore other types of graphs and infographics used in the media.

nodes.misconception: A distance time graph will always be constructed with straight lines.
nodes.response: A straight line represents a consistent rate of a change, a consistent speed. In reality we need to model acceleration and deceleration which will involve curved lines.

nodes.misconception: There is one answer to everything in maths.
nodes.response: We often see arithmetic and equations with one answer but, maths can be used to compare and justify multiple answers to a single problem.

nodes.misconception: Students are unsure where to start on problem solving questions.
nodes.response: Starting with one sentence at a time and isolating what the strategy is first before doing any calculation is important.

nodes.misconception: An iterative formula can always be used to find the solutions to an equation.
nodes.response: This lesson addresses limitations of iteration. Some formulas will cause an error becasue we are unable to evaluate the square root of a negative or divide by 0. Other formulas may not converge. Different values of $$x_0$$ produce different results.

nodes.misconception: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
nodes.response: The skill of solving a pair of simultaneous equations can be applied to a wide variety of problems and provides us with answers in a wide variety of contexts.

nodes.misconception: That algebra, in particular solving equations, is abstract and not related to the world around us.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to solve $$4(x+3)=20$$. Then show a square with length $$x+3$$, tell them the perimeter is $$20$$ and ask them to find $$x$$.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not appreciate all the steps required to prove what type of shape is shown.
nodes.response: A warm-up for the lesson could be to review properties of shapes. Consider describing a shape, one property at a time. How much information is needed before pupils can be certain they know which shape is being described?

nodes.misconception: We are only interested in points that are in the region satisfied by all inequalities.
nodes.response: With practical contexts, such as project management, it is useful to know when one constraint is not being met as it can suggest where additional resources (if available) should be allocated.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not consider that, in some contexts (e.g. a corded lawnmower), the shape of the locus will include sectors of different radii, if a shape/object is creating a barrier.
nodes.response: Have pupils consider the impact of going around the corner of a shape.

nodes.misconception: A graph drawn on axes with no scale shown means nothing is known about the graph.
nodes.response: Understanding the shape of a parabola, cubic curve, and reciprocal graph and then applying key features like positive/negative coefficients and $$y$$-intercepts enables pupils to infer much about the equation without needing actual coordinate values.

nodes.misconception: If you combine two sequences of the same type the resulting sequence will still be that type.
nodes.response: Adding corresponding terms of two sequences will be good preparation for future units but it also a way to explore what sequences can be generated by combining other sequences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they have to use the sine or cosine rule.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider all the trigonometric knowledge they have and choose the most appropriate piece for the problem they are dealing with.

nodes.misconception: Reporting two averages when asked to make two comparisons between sets of data.
nodes.response: Mean, media and mode essentially measure the same thing: central tendency. So use one of the comparisons to comment on the spread of data.

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to find the percentage change.
