nodes.response: Emphasise the word change. Encourage pupils to write down the 2 percentages with their relevant values.  Go back to the question and calculate the actual change they should notice that this is neither of the 2 values but the difference between them.

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to determine whether a question is asking about the perimeter or the area.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to draw a diagram to represent the situation as this can make it clearer as to whether perimeter or area is required.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to decide whether the question is needing length, area or volume.
nodes.response: Support could be given by providing the units for the answer or pupils may be encouraged to think of contexts for each before hand.

nodes.misconception: You have to convert to the same unit to decide if a measure is the same as another.
nodes.response: For metric units it is possible to compare the digits. Any conversion within metric has the same digits in the same order.

nodes.misconception: Curves cannot be drawn on isometric paper.
nodes.response: It is perfectly possible to draw a curve on isometric paper.

nodes.misconception: Adding the length of the side onto the wrong value within a coordinate.
nodes.response: Use sketches/ erasable axis/ Desmos to plot points and see if they are reasonable. Encourage writing/drawing on diagrams as working out.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not know how to start an angle problem if they focus too much on the final solution.
nodes.response: You can start an angle problem by working out any angle on the diagram. The more angles you work out, the easier the final solution becomes.

nodes.misconception: Outcome tables and outcome trees only work for outcomes that are all equally likely.
nodes.response: Outcome tables can be separated into more rows and columns, and outcome trees split into more branches, to show outcomes that are more or less likely than other ones. This does mean these diagrams do get massive very quickly!

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.

nodes.misconception: When matching, or sketching, distance-time and speed-time graphs pupils may think these have a similar shape.
nodes.response: Questioning helps. Ask pupils to explain what is happening on a variety of graphs. For example, "A diagonal line with positive gradient on a speed-time graph. What is happening?" "A horizontal line on distance-time graph. What is happening?"

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be confident in knowing whether to apply Pythagoras' theorem or a trigonometric ratio.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to label the diagram with all the information they have and then consider what they can deduce.

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.

nodes.misconception: Biased samples are always bad.
nodes.response: A biased sample is sometimes useful if the sample is proportional to the population and/or it focuses on a section of the population relevant to the investigation.

nodes.misconception: A plausible conclusion or claim must be true when it is presented with data.
nodes.response: Graphs can be misinterpreted, which can lead to invalid conclusions.

nodes.misconception: The answer to the 'handshake' problem is 15, or 15x15
nodes.response: Group pupils into 3s and ask them to record how many handshakes are made. Then group as 4s and repeat. What do they notice?

nodes.misconception: Every question that has a right-angled triangle must use Pythagoras' theorem to be solved.
nodes.response: It is easy to get into a habit of using Pythagoras' theorem when learning the topic, but it is likely you have seen several maths problems in the past with right-angled triangles, which ask to find areas and angles, without using Pythagoras' theorem.

nodes.misconception: A ratio of 1 : 400 for a scale model of a car to a real car will have units of cm and metres, because a scale model is measured in cm and a real car is measured in metres.
nodes.response: Unless the scale explicitly includes different units of measure for each part, you must always use the same unit for each part of a ratio. So, 1 : 400 should be seen as 1 cm : 400 cm, not 400 metres, which is far too long for a car!

nodes.misconception: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
nodes.response: The skill of solving a pair of simultaneous equations can be applied to a wide variety of problems and provides us with answers in a wide variety of contexts.

nodes.misconception: Incorrect use of the calculator when finding the mean of numbers.  Omitting the brackets when summing the values.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to calculate the sum of the values and record this before dividing by the number of values.  This also encourages a record of a method.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can incorrectly write a number in standard form or use a number in incorrect standard form whereby the number A does not satisfy 1 ≤ A < 10 or pupils use division of positive powers of 10.
nodes.response: Standard form represents a multiplicative relationship, so there should always be a multiplication. Embedding the understanding that negative exponents refer to 1/10^n is important. Using the place value chart with fractional and exponent form helps.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain how to solve problems with surds.
nodes.response: Many problems can be solved through reasoning what you know, such as fully simplifying a surd.

nodes.misconception: Using the laws of indices, when dividing by a number with a negative exponent pupils can incorrectly subtract the negative exponent.
nodes.response: When the bases of all the numbers are the same, forming an equation with the exponents can reduce errors.

nodes.misconception: When increasing a probability by 50%, pupils may choose to add 50% onto the existing probability rather than multiplying by 1.5.
nodes.response: Make links to any previous work pupils may have done on increasing by a percentage and emphasise that a percentage increase is being applied to the probability.

nodes.misconception: When completing an inverse translation, students may believe they need to flip the vector.
nodes.response: Ask students to say in words how you would return to the starting point, to highlight the direction needed and then link to the vector.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify a right-angled triangle in the problem.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch the question out and add any known right angles or perpendicular lines, as this may lead to a right-angled triangle.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway, sometimes using highlighters can help visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: Letting the more vocal students take the lead improves team outcomes.
nodes.response: Outcomes are better if the voices of the whole group are listened to and considered.

nodes.misconception: The computer understands procedure names and knows what to do based on the chosen name.
nodes.response: The name is for humans, the computer only follows the instructions inside the procedure.

nodes.misconception: Functions and procedures are just different names for the same thing.
nodes.response: A function is a type of subprogram that returns a value whereas a procedure is a type of subprogram that does not return a value.

nodes.misconception: Functions and procedures are just different names for the same thing.
nodes.response: A function is a type of subroutine that returns a value whereas a procedure is a type of subroutine that does not return a value.

nodes.misconception: Volcanoes occur at all plate margins.
nodes.response: While volcanoes are a feature of both destructive and constructive plate margins, there are no volcanic eruptions at conservative margins because no magma is produced.

nodes.misconception: Volcanoes only occur on land.
nodes.response: In fact, volcanoes occur underwater as well as on land, especially at constructive plate margins and hot spots.

nodes.misconception: That volcanoes occur directly above where the oceanic plate starts to subduct.
nodes.response: In fact, the melting of the oceanic plate occurs deep in the mantle, so magma rises to the surface some distance away from the plate margin.

nodes.misconception: Weathering and erosion are the same process.
nodes.response: Weathering breaks down rocks in place without movement, while erosion involves the removal and transport of that material by wind, water, ice, or gravity.

nodes.misconception: Students frequently mix up the different types of processes, their names and definitions.
nodes.response: Flag up words for processes that sound similar or have similar spellings as you encounter them. Signpost the differences in their meanings, and encourage students to highlight them in a way that is most useful for them, for example by colour coding.

nodes.misconception: Food processing does not happen at home to prepare and cook food, only at a factory.
nodes.response: Food processing steps are used in the home to prepare and cook food, such as peeling, slicing, grating, mixing and baking.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a plant is at the start of the food chain because it is the smallest organism or because it cannot eat an animal.
nodes.response: This lesson makes reference to the fact that the plant is the producer in a food chain because it makes, or produces, its own food.

nodes.misconception: It is a common misconception that consumers (including humans) could survive without producers.
nodes.response: The dependence of consumers on photosynthesis in producers in explored in depth.

nodes.misconception: Food can only be produced on a farm or in a field.
nodes.response: Food can be produced (grown) at home, such as fruit, vegetables and herbs. Some food can be foraged.

nodes.misconception: Product analysis leads to copying of designs.
nodes.response: Product analysis identifies successful features and those which can be improved, this can lead to inspiration for new or improved ideas.

nodes.misconception: Product analysis is only about identifying flaws or problems in a product.
nodes.response: In reality, product analysis is used to improve design, meet user needs, and stay competitive.

nodes.misconception: Designing is only creative when innovative ideas are produced.
nodes.response: Designing is creative at every stage, not just when coming up with brand-new ideas. Creativity is also shown in solving problems, improving existing products, and making designs more user-friendly, sustainable, or affordable.

nodes.misconception: Considering a product's energy use is the only way to design a sustainable product.
nodes.response: There are many other ways to design a product to be sustainable when in use, including designing products to grow with users, be adjusted, modular, reused etc.

nodes.misconception: Considering a product's energy use is the only way to design a sustainable product.
nodes.response: There are many other ways to design a product to be sustainable when in use, including designing products to grow with users, be adjusted, modularity, reused etc.

nodes.misconception: All specifications must use the same subheadings.
nodes.response: Specifications must be specific to the context, design opportunity and design brief.

nodes.misconception: A mould and a former are the same thing.
nodes.response: A mould contains the material and shapes it as it sets or solidifies. A former is a shape around which a material is bent or stretched.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, all masculine adjectives end in -o.
nodes.response: Many masculine adjectives end in -o, but this is not always the case. For example, many masculine adjectives of nationality end in -és e.g. 'inglés' and 'francés'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that, in a profile portrait, both eyes and ears are visible.
nodes.response: In a true profile portrait, only one eye and one ear are typically visible, as the subject is viewed from the side.

nodes.misconception: The size of the sprite doesn't matter when programming movement.
nodes.response: Sprite size is important, especially in a maze, as if the sprite is too big it will touch the walls.

nodes.misconception: Control systems are programmed with text-based languages.
nodes.response: Control systems can be programmed using different languages including text, blocks or flow charts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the 'and' statements in the logic part of the lesson.
nodes.response: For the statement to be true, the whole statement must be true. This refers to both clauses that are joined by the word 'and'. If even one of the clauses is not true, then the entire statement can be declared not true (even if one clause is true).

nodes.misconception: The computer can understand what I meant even if I make a small mistake.
nodes.response: Computers follow exact instructions, so even a tiny error (like typing f 100 instead of fd 100) will cause problems. Programmers need to carefully check the programs they make.

nodes.misconception: Point in direction turns the sprite the amount of degrees from which it is already facing.
nodes.response: The point in direction block includes numbers which represent the turn in degrees from the upward reference point.  90 degrees makes the sprite face right, 180 degrees faces down, -90 faces left and 0 makes the sprite face the top.

nodes.misconception: Selecting a sprite automatically assigns it to the background that you want it on.
nodes.response: You need to manually place sprites and ensure their code corresponds to the intended background.

nodes.misconception: A project brief always includes success criteria.
nodes.response: Sometimes a project brief may not include success criteria, but a brief description of what the program needs to do. You may need to generate success criteria from the project brief.

nodes.misconception: Once a program has been developed, it is finished and there is no need to evaluate or reflect on what you have done.
nodes.response: Evaluation is about judging how well the program meets the original success criteria or requirements. It can help you to revisit and make improvements to a program, as well as reflect on lessons learnt for your next project.

nodes.misconception: I don’t need to follow the project brief to draw a flowchart.
nodes.response: The project brief gives you the purpose and requirements of the program. A flowchart must reflect those to show how the program will work step by step.

nodes.misconception: I finished the code and it runs, so I don’t need to test it.
nodes.response: Just because a program runs doesn’t mean it works correctly in all situations. Testing helps find hidden errors, especially with unusual or unexpected inputs that you might not think of.

nodes.misconception: Pseudocode is the same as a programming language and must follow a particular syntax.
nodes.response: Pseudocode is independent of a specific programming language and does not need to follow any particular rules. All that is required is that a programmer can read the pseudocode and understand how to implement it.

nodes.misconception: If a program has a logic error it will not work and will give error messages.
nodes.response: Logic errors are errors that cause a program to work incorrectly or unexpectedly. With a logic error, the program can be run without failing, but it does not return the expected result. The user might not realise that there is an error.

nodes.misconception: You must have the physical Sense HAT device to practice coding with the Sense HAT.
nodes.response: You do not have to have the physical Sense HAT to try this out. The Sense HAT emulator provides a digital representation of the device.

nodes.misconception: A list is static, so once it is created it cannot be edited or amended.
nodes.response: A list is a dynamic data structure that can change in size. The append() function can be used to add elements to a list.

nodes.misconception: I can just start coding and figure it out as I go. Planning is a waste of time and boring.
nodes.response: Planning is like building a strong foundation. A good plan helps you write better code faster.

nodes.misconception: Testing is just about making sure the program runs.
nodes.response: It's not just about running the program. We test to make sure the program does exactly what it's supposed to do, in all situations. This means checking if it handles correct input and incorrect input correctly.

nodes.misconception: A project brief is a set way to solve a problem.
nodes.response: A project brief outlines the requirements of a system, but there may be many ways to solve the problem.

nodes.misconception: A system should only be tested with normal data that will be expected.
nodes.response: A system should be tested with a range of test data, including erroneous data that is not meant to be accepted.

nodes.misconception: A project brief is a set way to solve a problem.
nodes.response: A project brief outlines the requirements of a system, but there may be many ways to solve the problem. The brief explains what needs to be solved, not how.

nodes.misconception: A system should only be tested with normal data that will be expected. If it works with normal data it will work all the time.
nodes.response: A system should be tested with a range of test data, including erroneous data that is not meant to be accepted. Programs should make sure that there is no way to stop the software from working if invalid inputs are entered.

nodes.misconception: A program will run automatically whenever we require it.
nodes.response: A program will not run automatically. It needs a specific command or action to start (like clicking the green flag or double clicking on an icon).

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that a code block applies to all the sprites in a project.
nodes.response: Multiple sprites can be controlled using separate commands and they each need their own code blocks to control them.

nodes.misconception: Commands can be used wherever they are found in the program you are using.
nodes.response: Commands must be dragged into the programming area so that they can be carried out otherwise the program will not know which object they need to be applied to.

nodes.misconception: When the Supreme Court ordered all schools to desegregate, they were quick to follow this instruction because it came from the Supreme Court.
nodes.response: Although the Supreme Court was the highest court in the USA, many schools were slow to desegregate and some refused to desegregate until they were eventually forced.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that using a being or having verb means they've written a sentence in each tense.
nodes.response: Being verbs as auxiliary verbs are for progressive tenses; having verbs as auxiliary verbs are for perfect tenses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any time a word ends with -ing, it is a verb in the progressive tense.
nodes.response: Sometimes, words ending -ing are acting as adjectives. We must look at the word before the word ending in -ing to check if it's a verb.

nodes.misconception: All PEDs are automatically illegal and banned substances.
nodes.response: Not all are instantly illegal or banned. For example, some stimulants are legal such as caffeine which is used by many as a stimulant. Beta blockers are available on prescription and so have certain restrictions.

nodes.misconception: Pseudocode can be executed by a computer.
nodes.response: Pseudocode cannot be executed by a computer. Pseudocode must be translated into a real programming language such as Python, Java or C# for it to be executed by a computer.

nodes.misconception: The lifecycle is a plan you follow from start to finish in sequence.
nodes.response: Once you get to the testing and evaluation stage, you may move back to the execution stage until you are happy with the product.

nodes.misconception: Idioms are the same in different languages.
nodes.response: Idioms can be specific to a language, culture or group of people. They are often impossible to translate directly. Their use adds variety and authenticity to students' work but it is necessary to discuss the idiom carefully when it is taught.

nodes.misconception: Films made for entertainment are an accurate representation of a social dance style.
nodes.response: Whilst many choreographers may have researched a social dance and employed the key features, it is unlikely that it is a detailed and accurate representation, and should be considered to be 'in the style of' rather than an authentic account.

nodes.misconception: Dance actions should always be performed as big as possible so they are clear and stand out to an audience.
nodes.response: Whilst this is often the case for performance dances, social dances are often much smaller and more relaxed in their execution since they are often performed in a limited amount of space and purely for pleasure, rather than an audience.

nodes.misconception: Dance styles are set and never change.
nodes.response: Dance styles continually evolve. When studying dances from history or other places, we are able to pinpoint key attributes that were relevant at a point in time, they may remain or they may be adapted.

nodes.misconception: Success criteria are only for the teacher to use when marking work. They don't help me.
nodes.response: They're not just for marking. Think of them like a checklist or a guide to help you create your best work. They tell you exactly what you need to do to succeed.

nodes.misconception: Adverts are the only way to promote a product.
nodes.response: Products can be promoted through presentations, exhibitions, videos, posters and competitions.

nodes.misconception: Personal exercise programmes are only used by people that play sport.
nodes.response: Perosnal exercise programmes can be used by everyone to increase physical activity levels.

nodes.misconception: Promoting a show is just about putting up a poster or posting once online.
nodes.response: Effective promotion requires planning, multiple methods, and consistent communication.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that covalent bonds are broken when any covalent structure undergoes a change of state; not just those in giant covalent structures.
nodes.response: Use physical models to show the difference between a simple covalent structure and a giant covalent structure. Explain that it is the weak intermolecular forces that are overcome when a simple covalent molecule changes state.

nodes.misconception: Students often confuse the difference between chemical and physical properties.
nodes.response: A chemical property describes how an element will react with other substances. Physical properties describes the appearance and behaviour.

nodes.misconception: There are several misconceptions associated with properties such as when something dissolves it disappears, electrical conductivity is a flow of electrons rather than charge.
nodes.response: When discussing electrical conductivity, emphasise the idea of electrical conductivity being a flow charge with ions behaving as charge carriers. The electron transfer that occurs during ion formation is nothing to do with conductivity.

nodes.misconception: Spelling of noble re- Nobel and the concept of why they were given this name, i.e. due to having a full outer shell of electrons which means they do not need to bond with other elements.
nodes.response: Explain that the name noble was due to the fact that they are so unreactive and did not need to bond with other elements due to already having a full outer shell of electrons making them so stable.

nodes.misconception: Spelling of noble re- Nobel and the concept of why they were given this name, i.e. due to having a full outer shell of electrons which means they do not need to bond with other elements.
nodes.response: Explain that the name noble was due to the fact that they are so unreactive and did not need to bond with other elements due to already having a full outer shell of electrons making them so stable.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse the trend in reactivity down the group.
nodes.response: The practical reacting the metals with water helps to memorably demonstrate the trend, however it is important to ensure that pupils can explain why this happens.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse the trend in reactivity down the group.
nodes.response: The practical reacting the metals with water helps to memorably demonstrate the trend, however it is important to ensure that pupils can explain why this happens.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget that the halogens are diatomic molecules.
nodes.response: Explanation of the bonding to form molecules helps to explain why they exist as diatomic molecules.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget that the halogens are diatomic molecules.
nodes.response: Explanation of the bonding to form molecules helps to explain why they exist as diatomic molecules.

nodes.misconception: All materials of a given type, such as wood, metal and plastic have the same properties.
nodes.response: Children will consider examples of different objects made from different types of wood, metal and plastic to promote discussion of the properties of materials.

nodes.misconception: All paper and card comes from trees.
nodes.response: Some paper and card can be from recyclable materials

nodes.misconception: I can tell a 3D shape is a prism because the 2D faces on both ends are congruent.
nodes.response: The cross-sectional face must be the same throughout, not just at the two ends of the shape. Also, the two end faces must be parallel.

nodes.misconception: A material can only exist as a solid, liquid or gas, rather than having different forms at different temperatures.  Gases have no mass or volume.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that most materials can exist in different states and that gases have a mass and volume.  Investigations help children explore the properties of materials in different states.

nodes.misconception: The Prophet Muhammad was only concerned with spiritual matters.
nodes.response: The Prophet Muhammad taught about caring for the world and other people. These teachings and examples are followed by millions of Muslims today.

nodes.misconception: The Prophet Muhammad taught his companions not to respect other beliefs.
nodes.response: The Prophet Muhammad taught to respect other beliefs such as Judaism and Christianity.

nodes.misconception: Everyone welcomed Prophet Muhammad's message.
nodes.response: Prophet Muhammad faced opposition and persecution as not everyone welcomed his message.

nodes.misconception: Prophets are people who can tell the future.
nodes.response: Prophets are regarded as inspired leaders who communicate the will of God. Very few prophets are believed to foretell the future.

nodes.misconception: That Muslims believe Muhammad was the first prophet of Islam.
nodes.response: Muslims belive that Adam was the first prophet of Islam and Muhammad was the final prophet.

nodes.misconception: The constant of proportionality shows the gradient for inversely proportional graphs.
nodes.response: The constant of proportionality shows the gradient for directly proportional graphs only. The constant for a reciprocal graph in the form k/x^n, shows the distance of the reciprocal from the origin.

nodes.misconception: All prototypes must be life size.
nodes.response: It is not always possible to manufacture life size prototypes. The space to manufacture and store may be limited plus the materials may be expensive. A smaller scale product saves space and materials but still allows for a product to be manufactured.

nodes.misconception: Those living in Britain during World War One faced no threat or privation other than their loved ones being far away.
nodes.response: World War One was what is known as 'total war' meaning that those in Britain felt its impact in their day to day life.

nodes.misconception: PNF can sometimes be confused as a partner simply helping to deepen the stretch by pushing a bit further.
nodes.response: The method of contracting the muscle activates the nervous system which helps improve flexibility more effectively than static stretching alone.

nodes.misconception: That it's obvious how a character should be interpreted by the audience.
nodes.response: The staging of a performance from body language to costuming can make a huge difference in how different audiences interpret a character.

nodes.misconception: That characters are only meant to be read as themselves.
nodes.response: Often in literature, the characters are the writer's way of commenting on something happening in the world.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that women in Shakespeare's time always obeyed the male figures in their life.
nodes.response: There are many examples of women being disobedient and not following the rules of the male figures in their life.

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that animals in decline are only found in faraway places like rain forests. They might not realise that the UK has its own species in decline, such as the red squirrel.
nodes.response: Through the use of the slides and doing further secondary research about their own local environment, children will become aware that there are animals in the UK that are in decline too.

nodes.misconception: Antarctica is owned by a group of countries.
nodes.response: Antarctica is one of the global commons, meaning it belongs to all of humanity, not individual nations.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that human actions can have an impact on animals and plants but that these actions do not affect food chains.
nodes.response: Explanation of different ways in which humans can protect plants and animals in their habitats.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all minibeasts are insects. Children may think that all minibeasts like the same conditions (e.g. damp and dark).
nodes.response: Provide examples of different microhabitats with differing conditions, e.g. light, dark, wet etc.

nodes.misconception: You cannot protect yourself against the content you see online.
nodes.response: There are number of steps you can take to reduce the likelihood of seeing unwanted content online, these include using safe search tools, only streaming content legally and on a secure connection and using privacy-preserving search engines.

nodes.misconception: Using security measures will stop every cyber attack.
nodes.response: Security measures reduce the risk of cyber attacks but cannot stop all of them. New threats and advanced techniques can sometimes bypass even the best defenses.

nodes.misconception: It is safe to look at the Sun on a cloudy day or when wearing sunglasses. Only lighter skin tones require protection from UV light.
nodes.response: Reminders that pupils should never look at the Sun. All skin tones require protection from UV light.

nodes.misconception: It is safe to look at the Sun on a cloudy day or when wearing sunglasses.
nodes.response: Clear explanation that pupils should never look at the Sun, even if wearing sunglasses or if the weather is cloudy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that nobody is taking action to protect the Amazon rainforest.
nodes.response: Many people around the world are taking action to protect the Amazon rainforest.

nodes.misconception: Laws are put in place by Parliament to stop crimes from happening.
nodes.response: Laws don't completely stop crime, but act as a deterrent by outlining the consequences of committing crimes.

nodes.misconception: Students often think they need to be balanced in their writing and discuss both sides of a debate.
nodes.response: Teach the difference between opinion writing and argument writing.

nodes.misconception: An idea that protecting the land is always the right decision.
nodes.response: Sometimes protecting one stretch of coastline can have negative consequences for the coastline nearby. It may become sediment starved or impacted by higher energy waves.

nodes.misconception: Stopping deforestation just means preventing the felling of trees.
nodes.response: There are many approaches to preventing and even reversing deforestation not just one, for example national parks, selective logging, small-scale agroforestry and ecotourism.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that coastal defences stop erosion entirely.
nodes.response: Coastal defences aim to protect the coastline from erosion, and can greatly reduce erosion but they can't stop it completely. Defences don't last forever, so eventually the power of the sea will regain strength in areas previously protected.

nodes.misconception: DNA is the endpoint of a characteristic rather than the fact that it codes for proteins that give a protein; also that all characteristics are visible.
nodes.response: Clear examples, analogies and models to show the code in genes, leads to the order of an amino acids in a protein; examples of structural and functional proteins.

nodes.misconception: Computers only need protocols when sending emails or accessing websites.
nodes.response: Protocols are essential for all sorts of activities, not just email or browsing websites. Protocols are also needed for streaming movies, playing online games, making video calls, etc. Anything being sent across a network needs to follow a protocol.

nodes.misconception: Devices automatically know how to communicate to any other device, regardless of brand or type, without needing specific rules.
nodes.response: Devices rely on shared protocols to communicate and exchange data effectively, like a common language or set of rules. This ensures all devices follow the same process.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that everyone has access to safe drinking water, and that water just 'appears' clean from a tap.
nodes.response: This lesson explains how approximately 1.6 billion people in the world today do not have access to water that is safe to drink. Also, that water is usually filtered and treated to make it safe to drink.

nodes.misconception: A demonstration is a proof.
nodes.response: A demonstration shows that it works for that one specific case. A proof allows us to know all cases that are true.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfully answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfully answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary

nodes.misconception: The only way to extend my sentences to add complexity is to add a subordinate clause with 'weil'.
nodes.response: There are many ways to add complexity, including using subordinate clauses with a wide range of conjunctions, as well as adding relative clauses or infinitive constructions.

nodes.misconception: The only way to extend my sentences to add complexity is to add a subordinate clause with 'weil'.
nodes.response: There are many ways to add complexity, including using subordinate clauses with a wide range of conjunctions, as well as adding relative clauses or infinitive constructions.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers following the picture task should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers following the picture task should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: When translating into English from German, I only need to understand the gist of the sentences.
nodes.response: When translating, it's important to ensure that you have accounted for the meaning of every German word, even though you might not translate word-for-word into English.

nodes.misconception: When translating into English from German, I only need to understand the gist of the sentences.
nodes.response: When translating, it's important to ensure that you have accounted for the meaning of every German word, even though you might not translate word-for-word into English.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: Like in a picture description and conversation, I should develop my role-play answers as much as possible.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should be a short phrase or sentence. Pupils should not add too much unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: Like in a picture description and conversation, I should develop my role-play answers as much as possible.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should be a short phrase or sentence. Pupils should not add too much unnecessary detail.

nodes.misconception: When a sentence contains both a direct object and an indirect object, the indirect object always comes first.
nodes.response: When a sentence contains both a direct object noun and an indirect object noun, the indirect object always comes first. When a pronoun is used to replace either noun, the pronoun comes first.

nodes.misconception: Puberty happens overnight.
nodes.response: A clear slide with a guide to timings of puberty stating that it takes place over several years.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their diary entry.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their writing.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their writing.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have negative attitudes towards publishing their work.
nodes.response: Publishing becomes highly motivating when there is a real audience for the work - for instance, you could copy the reports and illustrations and gather them into a presentation book that can be taken home by each child in turn.

nodes.misconception: Captions shouldn't just reiterate what's obvious in the visual.
nodes.response: Captions should complement diagrams by explaining the visual, highlighting key points and giving any additional facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their non-chronological report.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.

nodes.misconception: Children may identify rhyming words that are not subject appropriate for the slogan.
nodes.response: Model examples and non-examples in context. E.g. 'hall' would not be a relevant rhyming word for 'ball'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their writing.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that illustrations are always drawn in pencil.
nodes.response: Include access to a wide range of materials which pupils can use to create an illustration for their poem. This might include colouring pencils, charcoal, watercolour, oil pastel, clay etc.

nodes.misconception: Illustrations should merely echo or repeat what the words convey.
nodes.response: Illustrations can be an extension of the poem, adding layers of meaning or emotion beyond what words convey.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their writing.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.

nodes.misconception: You should only ever consider one Shakespearean play at a time. Comparing plays and characters is irrelevant and confusing.
nodes.response: Comparing characters can be an excellent way to deepen your understanding of Shakespeare as a writer, and to understand the significance of how a particular character has been created.

nodes.misconception: It is not significant that Puck performs the epilogue. It could have been any of the characters.
nodes.response: There are many different ideas to explore in terms of why Puck performs this epilogue. It could speak to his centrality to the plot, his infamous reputation amongst the play's first Elizabethan audiences, and the way we should interpret key themes.

nodes.misconception: It isn't important that Puck's mistake is genuine.
nodes.response: Without understanding what happens, and why, in Act 2, Scene 2, we won't have an accurate understanding of Shakespeare's characterisation of Puck which deepens and develops throughout the play.

nodes.misconception: Puck tries to create more chaos after realising his mistake.
nodes.response: Puck is consistently shown to follow Oberon's orders in relation to the Athenian nobles, and to try and do so correctly. However, he does find it very funny, even though he didn't deliberately create the situation.

nodes.misconception: Puck is a disrespectful character.
nodes.response: Puck's disrespect is targeted at particular characters. He is shown as respectful to Oberon, for example, and other high status characters.

nodes.misconception: Puja in Buddhism is the worshipping of a god or gods, in the same way as in some other religions.
nodes.response: The Buddha is not a god, but a teacher who reached enlightenment. Puja is a way to show respect, devotion and strengthen commitment to the Buddhist path of enlightenment.

nodes.misconception: Hindus all have the same murti in their puja.
nodes.response: Hindus use different murti to ask for different aspects in their lives.

nodes.misconception: The size of a pulley does not effect the speed of rotation.
nodes.response: Smaller pulleys rotate faster than larger pulleys on the same system.

nodes.misconception: When using adjustment (e.g. 456 − 199), pupils may forget to subtract or add 1 to both parts.
nodes.response: The emphasis of same difference can encourage children to ensure they have subtracted or added to both parts of the calculation. Clearly display the visuals in this lesson to support with this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can struggle to decide on the scales needed for an axis on a graph.
nodes.response: Suggest a suitable scale that will fit on the graph paper they will use or use a computer to draw graphs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils mistake common (everyday) usage of pure (i.e. 'pure orange juice) as being a pure substance
nodes.response: 'Everyday' usage refers to one *source* whereas scientific usage refers to particle composition. Take particular care when discussing water.

nodes.misconception: Pupils keep their head away from the water.
nodes.response: Pupils should be made aware that if the face is in the water it is much easier for the legs to float.

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of switch.
nodes.response: Switches break the electrical flow of a circuit but they can be activated in different ways - they can be pushed, slid, twisted or pulled.

nodes.misconception: Forces only act on moving objects.
nodes.response: Examples of forces being used to move stationary objects will be included.

nodes.misconception: When introducing defenders, pupils often neglect technique and moving with close control.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to use gentle, small touches when moving with their ball.

nodes.misconception: When moving into space and away from defenders, pupils panic and rush which causes them to lose control of their ball.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of always moving with control, even if it means moving a little slower at first.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that hitting the ball hard is the best way to move and control it.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to keep close contol of their ball by using soft touches to keep it close.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to hit the ball hard to slice effectively.
nodes.response: Pushing and slicing require a light touch and controlled movements, not power.

nodes.misconception: Magnetic poles may exist singly, not just in pairs.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching and examples will be used to address misconceptions.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that the biomass increases as you move to the next trophic level, presumably  because pupils incorrectly assume that biomass refers to individuals rather than populations.
nodes.response: The lesson gets pupils to estimate the biomass of populations at each trophic level to demonstrate that biomass decreases at each trophic level.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the size of organisms has to increase at each trophic level within a food chain diagram.
nodes.response: The lesson addresses the misconception through exemplification. There is coverage of inverted pyramid of number to show that some producers are larger organisms that are eaten by smaller organisms.

nodes.misconception: I need to be given a triangle in order to use Pythagoras' theorem.
nodes.response: You do not need to be given a triangle. It is an important skill to be able to sketch and label a triangle for yourself from given information, or go straight into an algebraic stage of calculation if aware that lengths given are perpendicular.

nodes.misconception: Once an item is added to a list it is fixed in to the structure of the list and it cannot be altered.
nodes.response: Items can be removed, inserted and amended in a list using list methods. These methods change the structure of the list. Values of items can also be updated.

nodes.misconception: Since there is no common difference, it is impossible to find the n^th term.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle shows how we can build quadratic sequences from n^2 and a linear sequence.

nodes.misconception: All Christians worship in the same way.
nodes.response: There are many different Christian churches and denominations and all of these have different styles of worship.

nodes.misconception: Quakers are all Christians and believe in God.
nodes.response: Quakers come from many backgrounds. Quakers speak of the light within all and that all humans are equal.

nodes.misconception: Quality control and quality assurance is the same thing.
nodes.response: Quality control focuses on identifying defects in finished products, while quality assurance is about preventing defects through planned processes and systems during production.

nodes.misconception: Quality control are checks that are done on products once made to ensure they are a high enough quality to be sold or used.
nodes.response: Quality control checks are done throughout the process to ensure quality is a constant.

nodes.misconception: Quality control is only about looking at the product at the very end of production.
nodes.response: Quality Control can happen throughout production (in-process checks, sampling, functional tests), not just at the end.

nodes.misconception: Quality control checks are performed on products after they are made to ensure they meet the required quality standards for sale or use.
nodes.response: Quality control checks are performed throughout the process to ensure quality remains constant.

nodes.misconception: Quality of life is about reducing suffering.
nodes.response: Quality of life means different things to different people. Whilst it can be about reducing suffering, it is influenced by individual values, preference and circumstances.

nodes.misconception: QA and QC are the same thing.
nodes.response: QA (Quality Assurance) focuses on preventing defects by improving the production process, while QC (Quality Control) focuses on identifying and fixing defects in the finished product.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only translated by 'was doing' in English e.g. I was listening to the radio.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense has more than one translation in English according to its use in French. Students need to be aware of the different meanings that might be conveyed when they encounter the imperfect tense e.g. I listened, I used to listen.

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused as to how to write mixed numbers.
nodes.response: As a school, establish how mixed numbers will be recorded so that you have consistency.

nodes.misconception: 'She, he is doing' translates as 'es haciendo' in Spanish.
nodes.response: She, he is doing is 'está haciendo'. To form the present continuous, use 'estar' and a verb in the present participle (-ando, -iendo).

nodes.misconception: The subjunctive is a matter of the speaker's attitude so when I am the speaker I can always choose whether to use the subjunctive or not.
nodes.response: Certain situations and structures always require the subjunctive: 'cuando' + subjunctive + future tense for events that have not yet happened; 'es' + adjective + que for subjective points of view; verbs of wishing that someone else does something.

nodes.misconception: 'Estaba' only means 'I was' in the imperfect.
nodes.response: 'Estaba' means 'I was' but also 'she, he, it was' in the imperfect.

nodes.misconception: The ending -aient is pronounced differently to -ais and -ait.
nodes.response: Although the third person plural ending of the imperfect tense contains a lot of letters, it is pronounced the same way as -ais and -ait. Students will need a lot of practice saying the -aient ending out loud to become confident with this verb form.

nodes.misconception: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.
nodes.response: Verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' can’t always be translated word-for-word - they don’t work the same way as English verbs. You need to choose the most idiomatic or natural-sounding translation based on the context.

nodes.misconception: One-word answers are sufficient in the role play.
nodes.response: It's important to say a few words or a short phrase/sentence in response to each prompt/bullet rather than one-word answers.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, you can always repeat language used in the question to form your answer.
nodes.response: If 2nd person language is used in a Spanish question, this must be converted into 1st person language for the answer.

nodes.misconception: In the inflectional future with all verbs, the endings are added to the infinitive and they are the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
nodes.response: A small number of verbs are irregular in the inflectional future and have irregular future stems.

nodes.misconception: 'Connaitre' and 'savoir' both mean 'know' so they can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: 'Connaitre' and 'savoir' both mean 'know', but 'connaitre' is used for being familiar with people/places/things, whereas 'savoir' usually means 'to know how to' or used on its own/with 'que'.

nodes.misconception: When talking about the weather, I can translate directly from English (e.g. 'it's cold').
nodes.response: It's important to remember that Spanish uses the verb 'hacer' when talking about the weather. For example, 'it's cold' translates as 'hace frío'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that Elizabeth was only queen of England.
nodes.response: Reinforce that she was queen of four nations - the United Kingdom.

nodes.misconception: [qu] is pronounced the same way in French as in English.
nodes.response: In French, [qu] is always a hard sound and must be carefully practised in order to ensure clear communication with French speakers.

nodes.misconception: 'Chaque' and 'plusieurs' change form and can be written as 'chaques' and 'plusieur'.
nodes.response: The indefinite adjectives 'chaque' and 'plusieurs' are invariable and only have the one form. As they are highly useful, encourage students to use them frequently in their work.

nodes.misconception: 'Nous' always means 'we'.
nodes.response: 'Nous' means 'we' when used as a subject pronoun, but it means 'us' when used as a direct object pronoun and '(to) us' when used as an indirect object pronoun.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that a conversation only involves speaking aloud.
nodes.response: In dance, we can show a conversation by using our actions to represent the words being spoken. We can communicate the idea of dialogue without saying a word.

nodes.misconception: Questionnaires are only used to present data in graphs when investigating a context.
nodes.response: Questionnaires inform designing and provide evidence to justify design decisions.

nodes.misconception: Nationalities use capital letters as in English: I am French.
nodes.response: In French, nationalities do not use capital letters: je suis français.

nodes.misconception: The accents é and è are pronounced the same in French and can be written interchangably.
nodes.response: It is essential to write an accent accurately as the accents é and è are pronounced differently. É is pronounced as in the word 'écrire' and è is pronounced as in the word 'trés'.

nodes.misconception: When forming a question the verb form changes in Spanish like it does in English (auxiliary 'did' + verb).
nodes.response: The verb stays the same in Spanish and only the intonation (spoken) or punctuation (written) marks the sentence as a question. There is no need to translate a form of 'do', 'did' etc.

nodes.misconception: Two vowels together are always read as one vowel.
nodes.response: In Spanish, when two strong vowels [a], [e] or [i] appear next to each other they are pronounced separately. This is why we call them 'strong' vowels.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think you use exclamation marks at the end of every command.
nodes.response: Clearly show pupils when and why an exclamation mark is needed with some commands but not others.

nodes.misconception: All French verbs use 'avoir' as the auxiliary to form the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Verbs expressing changes of state, location or condition often use 'être' to form the perfect tense.

nodes.misconception: 'Qui' always means the question 'who?'.
nodes.response: When used in an interrogative sense, 'qui ?' means 'who?'. As a relative pronoun, 'qui' introduces more information about the subject in the main clause and can be translated as 'who', 'which' or 'that'.

nodes.misconception: The second element of the negative structure goes after the past participle when forming past tense phrases.
nodes.response: The second element of the negative structure is always placed after the auxiliary verb and before the past participle. This requires practice as students are likely to misapply the negative structure learned with present tense.

nodes.misconception: All -re verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense, just like regular -er verbs.
nodes.response: -re verbs can be divided into four groups, following the patterns of entendre, prendre, traduire and écrire.  Encourage learners to be able to categorise -re verbs and to draw comparisons between the groups.

nodes.misconception: Students might think a blik is a belief or opinion that can be easily changed with evidence.
nodes.response: A blik is a fundamental worldview that is unchanged by evidence or facts.

nodes.misconception: Being anti-racist just means not being racist.
nodes.response: Anti-racism means more than just avoiding racist behaviour. It involves actively challenging racism, speaking out against unfair treatment and working to create a more equal society. It’s about action, not just belief.

nodes.misconception: There is no point talking about the minor characters in a play - they are not important.
nodes.response: Each character, no matter how seemingly insignificant, is crafted by the writer and placed in the text for a specific purpose. It is your job to consider what their purpose is.

nodes.misconception: Students might believe that fascism was only a factor in Nazi Germany, and be unaware of the existence of  fascist groups in Britain.
nodes.response: Fascism spread across Europe in the 1930s, including to Britain, although Britain's strong democratic tradition meant it did not take hold as it did in other countries at the time.

nodes.misconception: Children may only extend in one direction, rather than in all directions beyond a central point.
nodes.response: Count the spaces to fill around the outside, and then count each pattern block as it is placed around the outside.

nodes.misconception: Most pupils have difficulty in truly understanding randomness.
nodes.response: Use analogies to explain randomness.

nodes.misconception: Identifying language devices is the most important skill when analysing author's language choices.
nodes.response: When looking at the question, ask pupils whether 'Guthrie uses a simile' would be an appropriate response to the question. If not, why not?

nodes.misconception: Western portraits are the artworks where artists represent stauts effectively.
nodes.response: Many artefacts and artworks around the world and throughout history do this.

nodes.misconception: All Muslims mark Ramadan in the same way.
nodes.response: Muslims all around the world mark Ramadan in different ways.

nodes.misconception: You have to write the full code for random number generation yourself.
nodes.response: Python's standard library includes the random module, which already has functions like randint() to generate random numbers. You just need to import it.

nodes.misconception: Moving your arms faster makes you swim faster.
nodes.response: When learning front crawl and backstroke pupils must have opportunity to catch the water and feel the water so that they are able to pull as much water as possible.

nodes.misconception: Breaststroke is always swam with the head up.
nodes.response: Breaststroke can be swam with the head up in a survival situation or with the head submerging and lifting during each arm cycle.

nodes.misconception: Rare earth materials are rare.
nodes.response: Despite their name, they’re not actually rare in quantity, they’re just rarely found in concentrated, economically viable deposits.

nodes.misconception: When calculating gradient from coordinates, pupils get positive and negative gradients mixed up.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch the coordinates first and then always look at a positive increase in x.

nodes.misconception: To find one part,  some students simply divide the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio.
nodes.response: Strengthen understanding of which amount represents which part of the ratio.  Matching problems to bar models helps.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the simplest form means a simplified surd as a denominator.
nodes.response: A fraction is not fully simplified if the denominator contains a surd term and must be rationalised as is convention.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see why using the difference of two squares is important.
nodes.response: The grid method for multiplication can be used to explore why two of the terms cancel each other.

nodes.misconception: P is a point such that AP : PB is in the ratio of 1 : 3 means that point P is a third of the distance of AB from A.
nodes.response: There are 4 equal parts in total, meaning that point P is a quarter of the distance of AB from A.

nodes.misconception: Rewriting and improving responses is a waste of time
nodes.response: How does the process of revising and rewriting develop vocabulary use? How does rewriting support the writing of future responses?

nodes.misconception: Rewriting and improving responses is a waste of time.
nodes.response: How does the process of revising and rewriting develop vocabulary use? How does rewriting support the writing of future responses?

nodes.misconception: That reaching heaven by faith alone means that works and deeds do not matter in that understanding of Christianity.
nodes.response: Good works and deeds are still important even though they do not help a person reach heaven. In this understanding of Christianity, these actions and deeds come about because of faith and show the faith is genuine.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse energy with temperature and therefore expect the products to be higher than the reactants for exothermic reactions i.e. due to temperature increase, and lower for endothermic.
nodes.response: It is useful to discuss the energy transfers occurring during the reaction e.g. exothermic reactions involve the reactant's chemical energy store converting to a smaller chemical energy store in the products and a thermal energy store.

nodes.misconception: Halogen solutions are coloured and sometimes it can be difficult to determine colour changes during displacement reactions.
nodes.response: Displacement of iodine gives the darkest colour change (turns brown), while bromine will provide one which is lighter (turns orange).

nodes.misconception: 'C'est' only translates to 'it is/that is'.
nodes.response: When talking about objects, 'c'est' translates to 'it is/that is' but when applied to people it can also mean 'he/she is'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not write negative numbers beginning with the negative symbol e.g. writing 3- and not -3.
nodes.response: Take time to model the writing of a negative number. "I know it is negative so I begin with the negative symbol."

nodes.misconception: Children who struggle reading/writing teen numbers may struggle to read or write larger numbers. Children may group in threes from the left, rather than the right.
nodes.response: Use a place value chart to support the reading of the numbers. Remember to identify the hundreds, tens and ones first, then group in threes to the right of those.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget the use of zero as a place holder when there are for example, 0 ten thousands in a number, e.g. 503,000
nodes.response: Encourage children to transfer the represented number into a place value chart prior to reading the number. However, it is important for pupils to be able to read numbers without a place value chart so ensure time is taken to reduce the scaffold too.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to articulate larger numbers, confusing when to give the place value unit within the number.
nodes.response: Provide a sentence stem like this: _ _ _ thousand and _ _ _ , encouraging the children to notice the groupings of thousands and ones.

nodes.misconception: Pupils record numbers like 29 thousandths incorrectly as 0.0029
nodes.response: Continue to link representations of thousandths to the place value chart and use language of ten thousandths being equal to one hundredth.

nodes.misconception: Children may align the end of their object with the end of the ruler, rather than zero.
nodes.response: Use a sticker or coloured pen to highlight the zero on the ruler so that children's attention is drawn to the zero when they are measuring length using a ruler.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to create axis for their graphs that have equal intervals.
nodes.response: You could spend some time with pupils simply practising drawing each axis. Ensure pupils do not draw a line and then try to divide into equal intervals. Instead encourage marking the intervals as the line is drawn.

nodes.misconception: Part of the lesson requires pupils to decide whether times are before midday, at midday or after midday. Pupils can find categorising 12:00 and 00:00 tricky.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching points are made based around this in the slide deck. However, it is worth really focusing on these points as they come up and, when assessing the pupils during the Practice tasks, paying particular attention to those times.

nodes.misconception: Children may write fraction notation with the numerator and denominator the wrong way round.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentence shown in this lesson each time you write a fraction, and give children opportunities to explain what each numeral in the fraction represents.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify which words should be included in bullet-point notes.
nodes.response: Model non-examples, e.g., 'downhill' and ask which keyword might be missing. 'Flows downhill' summarises appropriately.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when reading aloud their persuasive letter.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when reading aloud their letter.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective reading aloud should be explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.

nodes.misconception: Children sometimes find it difficult to learn and distinguish between raised voice and projection.
nodes.response: Model the differences and look at techniques for projection (e.g. breathing and speaking from our core).

nodes.misconception: That Old English was created exclusively by the Anglo-Saxons.
nodes.response: The Anglo-Saxons' Germanic languages contributed to Old English but languages already spoken in Britain – and Latin – also played a part.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the Creature did something to terrify/hurt Victor.
nodes.response: Victor takes an instant dislike to the Creature because of its ugliness. Victor shuns the Creature immediately, purely because of its looks.

nodes.misconception: Students might not recognise this as a Gothic setting, as it is not overtly frightening or eerie.
nodes.response: Brontë's use of contrasting colours, isolation and cold make this a Gothic setting. Gothic descriptions do not have to be terrifying at all times.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might recognise common features or character types from other fairy tales leading them to think that the characters must conform to a stereotype.
nodes.response: 'Blackberry Blue' uses a range of fairy tales for inspiration. Use the text to discuss how characters do not always conform to stereotypes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they are either 'good' or 'bad' at acting.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know that **performance techniques** can be learnt, practised and developed and that 'real' actors work hard on their craft.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it is **always** easier to perform a play with a small number of characters.
nodes.response: The difficulty of a play is not just down to the number of characters in it. Often, the most difficult plays are the ones with the most troubling or complicated themes - central messages that the playwright wants the audience to think deeply about.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plays are put on quickly without much preparation or work.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand how much work from a dedicated team of actors, directors and stage crew goes into putting on a play. You could tell pupils that professional theatre companies take, on average, between 8-16 weeks to put on a play.

nodes.misconception: If we make a mistake during a performance, we should start again.
nodes.response: While sometimes we might need to re-start, practising finding our place and carrying on playing is a great skill for a performer to develop.

nodes.misconception: If we make a mistake when performing we should always stop and start again.
nodes.response: While you might sometimes need to start again, it's good practice to try and find your place and carry on if you make a mistake when performing.

nodes.misconception: A rhythmic ostinato is the same as the rhythm of the words.
nodes.response: We can make an ostinato using the rhythms of the words but often the ostinato has a different rhythm.  It can be tricky to play an ostinato and sing a different rhythm!

nodes.misconception: We can play a melody quickly when we are learning it.
nodes.response: It's always better to start slow, then speed up when confidence is built.

nodes.misconception: Music is always notated on a musical stave.
nodes.response: There are many different ways to notate music. Stick notation, for example, is a quick way to notate simple rhythms and melodies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify different poetic techniques or examples of figurative language.
nodes.response: Pupils could text mark a physical copy of the poem with their thoughts and ideas. Highlighters could be used to mark rhetorical questions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to discuss how perspective can have an effect on their understanding of the poem and its themes.
nodes.response: It may be useful to remind pupils of the different perspectives that writing can take and the effect they can have on a reader or listener.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a poem cannot be written from the perspective of an object that isn't alive.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that personification is a fun and imaginative poetic technique to know and use.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that creating vivid imagery for the reader is not an essential part of poetry.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a writer will want the reader to be able to visualise the different parts of the poem and this is achieved through creating vivid imagery.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse metaphors with similes.
nodes.response: Emphasise that metaphors compare things by saying one thing actually is another, while a simile uses the words 'like' or 'as'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to read the poem aloud and with expression.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have an understanding of what the poem means and some of the key vocabulary that they may not know. Model reading the poem aloud with expression for the children to get ideas and talk through the different ways to use your voice.

nodes.misconception: There is only one correct interpretation of a poem.
nodes.response: Emphasise to pupils that each reader brings their unique perspective, experiences and emotions to the poem. There is no 'right or wrong'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to engage in the story if they don't like cats.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing Lulu's interest in cats, inviting the children to join in by sharing their own passions. This serves as a captivating hook, fostering a connection between stories and the children's personal interests.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find some of the language in the poem difficult to understand.
nodes.response: Pre-teach some of the language in the poem before reading e.g. "adolescent", "gamelan", "dengue" and "dialects".

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to see the differences between metaphors and similes.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that metaphors say something is something else and similes compare two things using 'like' or 'as'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find identifying individual aspects of the personal response challenging.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils who may need greater scaffolding to discuss similar quotes or moments to the examples given.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that this poem is inaccessible because the language is difficult to understand.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that poems can be easier to understand once we work out the meaning of each line and explore the vocabulary used.  This is modelled in LC1.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find some of the language new or unfamiliar to them.
nodes.response: An extended definition list could be created to support pupils in understanding. Explain that it is normal to not understand all the language in a poem, especially when we first read it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that words can only rhyme if they are spelled the same.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that sometimes words have different spellings at the end, but can still be rhyming words as they make the same sound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to work together as a pair to perform the poem.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that performing 'Please Mrs Butler' as a pair will help to create the scene and express how the characters are feeling. Model with another adult how to work together to perform and react to what the other one is saying.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify why a poem may be laid out in a certain way.
nodes.response: Present the poems on a class board or visualiser so that the children can clearly see how the poems have been presented on the page. Ask pupils what they notice and text mark the pages together.

nodes.misconception: When completing Task A, pupils may struggle to generate ideas.
nodes.response: Adults could provide a word bank and work with pupils to create a mind map of ideas. Examples can be included from 'Tempest Avenue' to further support.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know the birds described prior to reading the poems.
nodes.response: Pupils could research the three species before reading. Alternatively, the poem could act as a stimulus to prompt further reading.

nodes.misconception: Many readers might interpret the poem literally.
nodes.response: The listeners are non-human objects, described as phantoms by Walter de la Mare.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the poet is limited to putting real items into the box.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that with poetry the possibilities are endless and a good poet is creative.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to make a prediction if they know the story already.
nodes.response: Celebrate any stories the pupils know already. Play a game to imagine that the memory has gone from their heads and just get them to use the front cover as clues imagining they are detectives.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that poems are always about imaginative things and based in fantasy worlds.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that poems can also be about everyday experiences and familiar scenarios.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect alliteration to be when words are placed next to one another.
nodes.response: Alliteration also includes words that are placed close together. Pupils could text mark a copy of the poem to identify cases where the poetic device is used in the poem.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spot similarities between two traditional tales in LC3.
nodes.response: Throughout LC3, share statements as examples, such as "The story is about three pigs. There were three goats in The Three Billy Goats Gruff" in order to support the pupils to retrieve information from the story they have just read.

nodes.misconception: Children may already know the story, so therefore will be unable to make a prediction.
nodes.response: Celebrate if children have heard a version before. Play a game to imagine that memory has gone from their heads and just get them to use the front cover as clues imagining they are detectives.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find some examples of imagery and language challenging to understand.
nodes.response: It may be useful to provide a visual sheet accompanying the poem, exploring some of the more complex terms (anvil, furnace).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to find examples of personification and explain the impact of using this.
nodes.response: You could show the whole poem on the slides and work as a class to find different examples. Then children can work in pairs to find more examples at their tables.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to emphasise the different people in the conversation when reading aloud.
nodes.response: You may wish to act out the poem using two people so the pupils can see it performed as a conversation. Model changing your voice and using gestures to show the pupils how this has an effect.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that every poem has to include rhyme.
nodes.response: Rhyme does not have to be included in each poem. Should pupils wish to include rhyme, a list of rhyming words can be generated with the whole class, in line with the positive imagery.

nodes.misconception: Children may think rhyming words have to have the same spelling of the repeated sounds.
nodes.response: Explain that rhyme is repeated sounds, not spelling.  Highlight the rhyming sections of the rhyming words within the poems.  Look at the different spellings.  Generate further rhyming words and identify the same or different spelling patterns.

nodes.misconception: Children can think that there is only one way to respond to a poem and you can have the right or wrong understanding of it.
nodes.response: Avoid posing questions which may lead children to the idea that there is a right or wrong answer when discussing the poem. Try to encourage open responses to the poem, celebrating each unique response from individuals.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to remember features found in non-fiction texts.
nodes.response: Display/print out common non-fiction text features, alongside layout features, to support pupils when comparing and contrasting.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find thinking of connections between 'Greenling' and the rewilding non-fiction text challenging.
nodes.response: Model making connections aloud, focusing on character, setting and plot. Some pupils may benefit from printed double-page spreads of certain illustrations to support.

nodes.misconception: Depending on the abilities of the pupils, Task B may be too challenging.
