nodes.response: Have an adult read the poem out loud to the children and the children echo read while also adding some of the actions and voices.

nodes.misconception: That Mayhew describes everything in the prison in a negative light.
nodes.response: Focus on the descriptions of the prisoners. Why does Mayhew present them in this way? What is he trying to say about prisoners?

nodes.misconception: It is not possible to interrogate a CSV file in Python without importing a specialised library.
nodes.response: A CSV file behaves in the same way as a txt file in Python. Data is read from the file as strings and methods can be used to remove extra characters like commas, spliting the values either side in to separate items.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often interpret distance-time graphs (intuitively) as pictures.
nodes.response: Guide pupils step by step through interpreting d-t graphs and link each line with a motion (repeatedly).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be familiar with fireworks and how they look and sound.
nodes.response: Find a video of a fireworks display to show the children. Ensure the video is a good example of the different sounds and sights that are synonymous with firework displays.

nodes.misconception: Since linear equations (typically) have one solution, all equations have one solution.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to compare the graphical solution to a linear equation with the graphical solution to a quadratic equation. This will enable them to see that it is possible for a quadratic equation to have more than one solution.

nodes.misconception: Music is always notated on a score.
nodes.response: Some music is never notated, it is shared by singing and playing. Some notation uses graphic scores, or rhythm grids. Any way of sharing how the music is expected to be played is a form of notation.

nodes.misconception: 'Il' and 'elle' mean he and she and can only refer to people.
nodes.response: Every noun has a gender in French. Therefore 'il' and 'elle' can mean 'it', and 'ils' and 'elles' mean 'they' (people and things).

nodes.misconception: All verbs can be followed by a direct object.
nodes.response: Not all verbs can be followed by a direct object; J'habite dans une maison; 'une maison' is connected to the verb by the preposition 'dans'. The verb 'j'habite' (I live) stands alone and does not have a direct object; we cannot say: I live a house.

nodes.misconception: Anyone who breathed in gas died immediately.
nodes.response: Gas attacks killed about three percent of people immediately, but there were long term physical and psychological effects for those who experienced gas attacks.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to attribute a feeling or emotion to a metaphor.
nodes.response: Some pupils could have visuals of the imagery contained in the poem, to support when attributing the change in emotional state of the speaker from verse 1 to verse 3.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not be able to think of a text that they have an emotional connection with.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of texts that they have shared in class during the year or previous years. Model an example using a shared text.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise all of the rhyming words.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that some words may not rhyme based on the accent of the person reading them. Likewise, other words may rhyme when read in Dickinson's native American accent.

nodes.misconception: Pulse, beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Pulse is the underlying feeling of uniformed beats - it is the heartbeat of the music. When organised into metres, we then feel it as beats e.g. counting 1,2,3 1,2,3. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations.

nodes.misconception: Responses are always the same in call and response songs.
nodes.response: The response can be different every time. The call can also be different. Call and response can be any kind of back and forth musical conversation.

nodes.misconception: That you don't need to analyse non-fiction texts - just absorb the information.
nodes.response: Analysing non-fiction texts is essential because it helps us understand who is offering us this information and why are they offering it to us.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all words with similar sounds rhyme.
nodes.response: Explain that words need to have the same sound at the end to rhyme. Look at words that rhyme and words that do not rhyme, but have the same sound in the middle.

nodes.misconception: We always count to four in music.
nodes.response: Music can be organised into any number of beats. The first beat is always the strongest.

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that a text has a sole purpose e.g. only to persuade or only to argue.
nodes.response: Draw their attention to the tone of Mark Twain's speech - he's quite humorous.

nodes.misconception: A text file can be stored anywhere to be used in a program using just the file name.
nodes.response: A text file must be stored in the same location as a program to be used to be accessed by file name alone. If it is stored elsewhere, the full path of the file will also need to be included.

nodes.misconception: McCarthy's son is definitely guilty.
nodes.response: It is suspected that McCarthy's son is responsible for the murder of McCarthy, however Holmes still has a lot of investigating to do.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to remain connected to the different strands of the story. E.g. Lila has made it to the Grotto safely, but Chulak and Hamlet's journey is still crucial.
nodes.response: Ask children to consider why a huge element of suspense remains even though Lila has made it to the Grotto. Answer: She may have overcome the challenge of getting there but if Chulak doesn't get the magical water to her then she is still in danger.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to read words that are unfamiliar or not always decodable with phonics strategies e.g. 'jealous'.
nodes.response: Firstly, ensure that your school's chosen SSP has covered the GPCs covered in the book. Before independent reading, pull out words that you think the pupils may struggle with or are common exception words to practise strategies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think reading with expression is purely about volume.
nodes.response: Model reading words, phrases or sentences with and without expression and varying volume, pitch and speed. Then model your thought process about why you read it that way.

nodes.misconception: Children may have questions or misconceptions around the 'illusion' element of the special ingredient and how Lila was still successful in completing her quest.
nodes.response: Do not delve too deeply into the 'illusion' element as it is not key for the writing of the climax. We can summarise that the true quest was to show no fear in facing fire in order to pursue her dreams which Lila demonstrated.

nodes.misconception: The notes on the stave can be written like dots on the line or inbetween the lines.
nodes.response: It is important that the size of the notes matches the size of the stave. This makes the notation easier to read.

nodes.misconception: When writing out music notation, the exact position of the notes doesn't really matter.
nodes.response: The part that matters the most is the note head - the circle at the bottom of the stick. Where that sits (on a line or space) tells us what pitch to play, so accuracy in where it is placed is important.

nodes.misconception: Mr. Woodifield intentionally tries to upset the boss.
nodes.response: Mr. Woodifield seems unaware that he has upset the boss, and his cruelty in mentioning his son's grave in Belgium is thoughtless rather than deliberately cruel.

nodes.misconception: Children may include unnecessary details when summarising the story.
nodes.response: Model non-examples when summarising the story. For example, model a sentence where an unnecessary detail has been included and ask the children to spot which piece of information could be taken out.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may consider Chaos to be a Greek god.
nodes.response: Chaos is considered a primordial being. It represents the formless, shapeless state from which everything else emerged.

nodes.misconception: It's best to give the reader all of the backstory at the start of a novel so that they understand the context of the events.
nodes.response: By feeding information to the audience slowly, it arguably builds discomfort in the reader and creates an unsettling environment.

nodes.misconception: Children may not know or understand that owls are nocturnal and therefore not find it unusual or funny for an owl to be scared of the dark.
nodes.response: Allow the children to research owls ahead of the lesson, using non-fiction texts and the internet.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to read words that are unfamiliar or not decodable with phonics strategies, e.g. 'special'.
nodes.response: Pre-teach important vocabulary from the text and explore their definitions.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a climax and a turning point are exactly the same thing.
nodes.response: As you continue to read the text, discuss the climax with pupils as the highest point of tension and discuss differences.

nodes.misconception: Conan Doyle creates a scary atmosphere all the way through 'The Speckled Band'.
nodes.response: If you look carefully, Conan Doyle carefully alters the atmosphere in order to build tension in the reader.

nodes.misconception: Students might not recognise that there is a possibility that the sound of the old man's heart beating, may be the sound of the narrator's own heart beating.
nodes.response: Some may interpret the sound of the old man's heart beating as the sound of the narrator's own heart beating, with anticipation and excitement at the prospect of the imminent murder.

nodes.misconception: Tension is only about scary or dangerous situations.
nodes.response: While scary or dangerous situations can create tension, tension can also arise from emotional conflicts, difficult decisions, or unresolved mysteries. It's about keeping readers eager to know what will happen next.

nodes.misconception: As long as I have used "like" or "as", I have created an effective simile.
nodes.response: Consider this simile: 'Her voice was like a salad.' The comparison is unclear and doesn't enhance understanding.

nodes.misconception: The front cover is just for 'show' and a way to identify a book.
nodes.response: The images and font on a front cover can give you lots of clues about themes and genre.

nodes.misconception: A theme is any idea or plot point in a text.
nodes.response: Themes are the most important ideas in a text. There may be multiple. The most important themes are the ones that are returned to over and over again, and explored in a number of different ways.

nodes.misconception: Settings are only there to provide a backdrop for the story.
nodes.response: Setting plays a crucial role in shaping the mood and atmosphere of a novel. It can also help us gain a deeper understanding of the characters and themes.

nodes.misconception: The Norns are whimsical and conventionally beautiful.
nodes.response: Look at the descriptions of the Norns. Their beauty lies in their power and wisdom.  They are "gnarled" and "wrinkled", which adds an air of authority to their presence. They are also described as "fierce".

nodes.misconception: Letters are only used in novels to drive the plot forward.
nodes.response: Letters can also give a reader an insight into a character's thoughts and feelings, as well as background information. They can also be used as an effective way to create dramatic irony.

nodes.misconception: The climax comes at the end of a story.
nodes.response: The climax is actually the high point of tension and action in a story, not necessarily at the end. It usually occurs towards the end but is followed by the resolution where the remaining conflicts are settled.

nodes.misconception: Villains are easily identifiable and will be always be introduced from the outset of a text.
nodes.response: Consider the draugr's subtle and encroaching presence. Burge uses this slow reveal to create tension.

nodes.misconception: That discussions are just 'chats' and aren't that important.
nodes.response: Think about all of the times you may need to use your verbal skills e.g. an interview or presentation. Being able to articulate yourself well verbally is an important skill to have.

nodes.misconception: Including the theme of fate means that characters have no choice or control over their actions and are simply puppets of destiny.
nodes.response: While fate in 'The Twisted Tree' suggests that certain events and abilities are predestined, characters still have the power to make choices that shape their journey.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to read words that are unfamiliar or not always decodable with phonics strategies e.g. 'carriage'.
nodes.response: Firstly, ensure that your school's chosen SSP has covered the GPCs covered in the book. Before independent reading, pull out words that you think the pupils may struggle with to pre-teach them this vocabulary and practise strategies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think reading with expression is purely about volume.
nodes.response: Model reading words, phrases or sentences with and without expression and varying volume, pitch and speed. Then model your thought process about why you read it that way.

nodes.misconception: The Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) was fully operational when it was announced by Reagan in 1983.
nodes.response: Although they were technologically more advanced than the USSR, the USA did not have the necessary technology to launch SDI in 1983. Reagan hoped the USSR would attempt to compete and this would cause their struggling economy to collapse.

nodes.misconception: Reflecting on your work only happens when you have finished making it.
nodes.response: Remind children that reflecting on the success of your work and areas that could be improved can happen both during and after the making of your work.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are often quick to focus their feedback on something which went wrong or needs improvement, without considering the impact of identifying what is also being performed well.
nodes.response: Pupils can use methods such as the 'feedback sandwich' which encourages them to think about identifying positive aspects of performance as well as areas for improvement.

nodes.misconception: Rendering and sketching are the same process.
nodes.response: Sketching is like creating the blueprint or the structure of the 3D model. Rendering happens afterward and focuses on adding realistic appearances to the sketch, like making glass look transparent or wood look grainy.

nodes.misconception: To subtract from both the variable and numerical terms when subtracting from both sides.
nodes.response: To subtract $$2$$ from $$5x+3$$ leaves $$5x+1$$, not $$3x+1$$. Use visual representations like balance scales and bar models to show this.

nodes.misconception: The numbers used as side lengths in this lesson are generally relatively low, and based around times tables. As a result, pupils might be tempted to guess / estimate the missing side lengths.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the shapes are not to scale and encourage them to use subtraction skills instead - what is the difference between this known side length and this known side length?

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to make a fraction in a simpler form by finding separate factors for the numerator and denominator to simplify.
nodes.response: Share examples for why this cannot be true with images to highlight the difference in the size of the fractions. Draw attention to the fact that it is both the numerator and denominator that needs to be scaled by a common factor.

nodes.misconception: Area and perimeter are easily confused. In this lesson, both concepts are explored, often at the same time.
nodes.response: Use your knowledge of the pupils' attainment (including using the Starter Quiz) to see which pupils are confusing the terms. All pupils will benefit from access to a working wall which gives a clear reminder of which is which.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that composing larger polygons of smaller triangles that are not formed as a result of drawing a line from one vertex to another will help them to identify the sum of the angles.
nodes.response: Highlight how the formation of triangles within a polygon must be from vertex to vertex and demonstrate how the angles of each triangle where they meet sum to the internal angle of the polygon.

nodes.misconception: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
nodes.response: For the value to be in the sequence, the value for $$n$$ must be a positive integer. If it is not, then the value is not in the sequence as the term number must be a positive integer.

nodes.misconception: Fitness testing brings about improvements in components of fitness.
nodes.response: Training methods bring about improvement in fitness. Fitness testing is merely about identifying the strengths and weaknesses of a fitness component so the right training method can be allocated and used.

nodes.misconception: Hate crime is only about violence.
nodes.response: Hate crime can also include speech, vandalism or online abuse driven by prejudice.

nodes.misconception: Help and punishment are opposites.
nodes.response: Many religious and secular views argue that support and accountability can go together. A person may still be responsible for their actions, but helping them through treatment or rehabilitation can reduce reoffending and lead to real change.

nodes.misconception: Christianity teaches that poverty or upbringing excuses crime.
nodes.response: Christian teachings often show understanding of causes, but still uphold moral responsibility and stress the need for repentance and justice.

nodes.misconception: All Christians believe in retaliation because the Bible says ‘an eye for an eye’.
nodes.response: Many Christians interpret this as an instruction to keep punishments fair and stop them going too far. Instead of justifying retaliation, it was about justice being equal to the harm done.

nodes.misconception: Sending the fyrd defences home in September is evidence of Harold's poor decision making.
nodes.response: In fact, Anglo-Saxon leaders had always struggled with the 60-day limit for the fyrd. Harold had actually kept the fyrd out for twice as long as usual: evidence of his impressive influence as a leader.

nodes.misconception: Sending the fyrd defences home in September is evidence of Harold's poor decision making.
nodes.response: In fact, Anglo-Saxon leaders had always struggled with the 60-day limit for the fyrd. Harold had actually kept the fyrd out for twice as long as usual: evidence of his impressive influence as a leader.

nodes.misconception: One individual, Martin Luther King, was responsible for the success of the civil rights movement from 1960 to 1965.
nodes.response: While Martin Luther King played a huge role of the success seen in these years, the success was also the result of several civil rights leaders and the work of their organisations as well an increasing support from the president.

nodes.misconception: Knowing and understanding that one-fifth as a fraction is equivalent to 0.2 as a decimal and that counting in steps of 0.2 is the same as counting in fifths.
nodes.response: Make sure that pupils have the opportunity to rehearse the fact that one-fifth is equivalent to 0.2 more frequently during the lesson and at other times when looking at fractions and decimals.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to see that a double is two of the same thing.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring doubles that can be found in the children's immediate environment e.g. using their hands or playing a game of dominoes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils call their score first and get confused which side they should serve from.
nodes.response: You should always call the serving player's/team's score first. If their score is even, then they serve from the right, whereas if their score is odd, they serve from the left.

nodes.misconception: Children may resort to counting strategies to find the difference e.g. counting back to subtract. Children may incorrectly identify the even/odd number 'before' or 'after' the one given.
nodes.response: Provide practice for children to identify numbers before/after or odd/even numbers before/after a given one. Initially, allow children to use a number line. Remove this scaffold once feeling more confident.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what 'lifestyle' means.
nodes.response: Explain that 'lifestyle' encompasses all the ways that humans choose to live, from what they choose to include in their diet to how much exercise and sleep they get.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may dominate the discussion with less confident pupils unwilling to take their turn at leading. Pupils might take too long explaining and not leave enough time to practise.
nodes.response: Select the numbers carefully so that pupil 1 and 2 are more confident and can model teaching first, giving less confident pupils time to get used to this process. Stress the importance of practise time and keep explanations concise.

nodes.misconception: The French for the Internet is 'l'Internet'.
nodes.response: In common usage, the Internet is translated as 'internet' in French. It does not require a capital letter as it counts as a common noun. It is one of very few common nouns that doesn't require a determiner in common usage.

nodes.misconception: The perfect tense is used only in speaking and the simple past only in writing.
nodes.response: The perfect tense can be used in informal writing and to describe a past event which has relevance to the present. The simple past is normally for writing, but 'war', 'hatte', 'gab' and modal verbs ('musste', 'wollte') are commonly used in speech.

nodes.misconception: The question word 'wer' is used whenever we want to say 'who'.
nodes.response: 'Wer' means 'who' in the nominative case only. It changes to 'wen' in accusative and 'wem' in the dative case. In English, 'wen' and 'wem' also mean 'whom', although this word is used less frequently.

nodes.misconception: There are no musical sounds in Islamic ritual.
nodes.response: Recitation of the Qur’an and the call to prayer have cadence, melody and rhythm.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may paint the fox and background in similar colours, making the sculpture blend in.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the fox should stand out - encourage warm, bright colours for the fox against darker shades in the background.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that larger coins or a greater number of coins represents a larger value.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens to draw attention to the value of the 10 p coin. When comparing 1 p and 10 p coins, ensure children swap coins for equivalent amounts to draw attention to the value of the coins as opposed to their size or quantity.

nodes.misconception: Children may not automatically link what they know about additive relationships to money contexts.
nodes.response: Explicitly link known facts and stem sentences to money contexts where appropriate.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that larger coins or a greater number of coins represent a larger value.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens to draw attention to the value of the 2 p coin. When comparing 1 p and 2 p coins, ensure children swap coins for equivalent amounts to draw attention to the value of the coins as opposed to their size or quantity.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that larger coins or a greater number of coins represents a larger value.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens to draw attention to the value of the 5 p coin. When comparing 1 p and 5 p coins, ensure children swap coins for equivalent amounts to draw attention to the value of the coins as opposed to their size or quantity.

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that a line drawn through the middle of something means that the whole has been divided in half.
nodes.response: Children will benefit from practical experiences where they can explore finding half of shapes and objects in different ways. Encourage them to compare the size of the parts and make sure they are equal.

nodes.misconception: Children can find it difficult to see if the four parts are equal, particularly when they are presented in different orientations rather than horizontal and vertical lines.
nodes.response: Allow children to handle practical objects and cut-outs of shapes that have been divided into quarters so they can rotate them and see them in different orientations.

nodes.misconception: Children can find it difficult to see if the three parts are equal, particularly when they are presented in different orientations rather than horizontal and vertical lines.
nodes.response: Allow children to handle practical objects and cut-outs of shapes that have been divided into thirds so they can rotate them and see them in different orientations.

nodes.misconception: Some children might not count the sides or vertices accurately because they lose track of where they started counting.
nodes.response: Ask children how they can make sure they only count each side or vertex once. Model marking each side or vertex as you count it.

nodes.misconception: Children may count coins in the order they are already arranged, or begin with smaller value coins first, leading to inefficient counting methods.
nodes.response: Consider the most efficient ways to count, grouping coins of the same value together, starting with greatest value coins or adding groups of coins in ways that enable them to use the addition strategies with which they are already familiar.

nodes.misconception: Children might begin to confuse 2D and 3D. For example, describe a cube as a square.
nodes.response: Use geometric construction materials to explore the 2D shapes within 3D shapes. Look for familiar 3D shapes in the environment and discuss.

nodes.misconception: Children may initially think that two quarters is larger than one-half because the numerals in the fraction are larger.
nodes.response: Try to avoid introducing the fractions in numeral form until children are familiar with recognising two-quarters in different representations such as shapes and small sets. Support understanding with stem sentences as modelled in this lesson.

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused by the pound sign being written before the digit rather than after. They may also include the pence sign as well as the pound sign when recording using the decimal point.
nodes.response: Make deliberate errors for children to identify. Discuss the reason for correct notation. For example, explain that the pence sign is not needed in the decimal notation because we know the digits after the 'dot' (decimal point) indicate the pence.

nodes.misconception: After becoming very familiar with arithmetic sequences pupils can find the difference between the first two terms and just assume the sequence is arithmetic.
nodes.response: Explore a large number of geometric and arithmetic sequences and see if pupils can articulate how they check if a sequence is geometric. They might say the terms of the sequence grow more quickly (for some geometric sequences).

nodes.misconception: High and low refer to volume (loud/quiet).
nodes.response: High and low in music refers to pitch. Not to be confused with high and low volume (like on a T.V.).

nodes.misconception: After becoming very familiar with arithmetic sequences pupils can find the difference between the first two terms and just assume the sequence is arithmetic.
nodes.response: Explore a large number of geometric and arithmetic sequences and see if pupils can articulate how they check if a sequence is geometric. They might say the terms of the sequence grow more quickly (for some geometric sequences).

nodes.misconception: Spellings such as 'practice', 'advice' and 'device' can be more difficult for children.
nodes.response: Explore words ending in -ice and words ending in -ise. Listen to the difference in pronunciation of these words and discuss the difference in word class too e.g. practice, advice, device = nouns, practise, advise, devise = verbs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that all words with the letter strings 'ough' and 'au' are pronounced the same way.
nodes.response: Show pupils that these letter strings can sound different depending on the word they are in. Explore different words and talk about which sounds are the most and least common.

nodes.misconception: Changing image colouring will make everyone think and feel the same way about the image.
nodes.response: Lots of people might have similar feelings but not everyone will necessarily have the same thoughts and feelings.

nodes.misconception: Apartheid was a system that existed in an unelected country.
nodes.response: Apartheid was the system under the South African Government.

nodes.misconception: Desmond Tutu was only active during the apartheid era.
nodes.response: Desmond Tutu played a role after apartheid and was a lifelong campaigner for justice and reconciliation.

nodes.misconception: Jesus' death on the cross ended the need for reconciliation.
nodes.response: Reconciliation is still important for many Christians; many Christians believe that the duty to promote reconciliation extends to Christians today.

nodes.misconception: Exploring different perspectives just means drawing the object from different angles.
nodes.response: To explore perspectives, you also need to change how you look at the object—by positioning yourself differently, changing your distance, or experimenting with different materials and techniques. It's about seeing the object in new ways.

nodes.misconception: Children may require some support to generate their own yes/no questions.
nodes.response: You could play the yes/no game to get children thinking about how to elicit answers of just two words.

nodes.misconception: Any digital device can play audio.
nodes.response: In order for a digital device to play audio it needs to have an appropriate output device. These are sometimes in-built in the device but for some devices they may need to be attached separately.

nodes.misconception: There is no way to store multiple records in one data structure in Python.
nodes.response: If you want to use multiple records in a database, then you can add multiple dictionaries to a list.

nodes.misconception: Insoluble and soluble solids are separated from liquids using the same methods: dissolved solids, like salt and sugar, can be removed from solution by filtering.
nodes.response: Methods specific to the separation of insoluble solids are taught and applied in this lesson. Task A will help pupils understand that filtering does not separate dissolved solids, like salt and sugar, from a solution.

nodes.misconception: People are either healthy or unhealthy.
nodes.response: Health is a range from good to ill. Fitness is one indicator of general health.

nodes.misconception: Synthesisers are most effective for melodic lines.
nodes.response: Different types of synthesiser suit different musical roles. While synth leads are very effective for melodic lines, synth pads are well-suited to playing accompaniments, particularly sustained notes and chords.

nodes.misconception: All drum grooves have exactly the same rhythms in the kick, snare and hi-hat.
nodes.response: Many typical drum grooves do have the same features or features very close to this, however encourage pupils to identify where there are subtle differences and how the kick, snare and hi-hat patterns can be varied within these features.

nodes.misconception: Only highly skilled and naturally gifted musicians can work out music by ear.
nodes.response: Anyone can work out music by ear. It just takes practice and is made easier through use of effective strategies, including working out rhythm and pitch separately, and identifying individual pitches through trial and error.

nodes.misconception: Because alcohol is legal it isn't as harmful as other drugs.
nodes.response: Alcohol is related to many lifestyle diseases. The WHO estimated 5 % of all deaths are related to alcohol.

nodes.misconception: Legal drugs cannot lead to addiction.
nodes.response: Nearly all drugs used for recreation, legal or illegal, can lead to addiction.

nodes.misconception: When adapting a question to a different form of 'you', just change the pronoun, e.g., from 'du' to 'Sie'.
nodes.response: When adapting a question from 'du' to a different form of you ('ihr' or 'Sie'), it's important to also change the verb form. With strong verbs, this can also involve a stem vowel change e.g., 'isst du?' becomes 'essen Sie?'.

nodes.misconception: Winning is the only metric of success and losing is always bad.
nodes.response: You can make improvements to your own/your team's performance in many different ways, regardless of the outcome of a competition.

nodes.misconception: Redesigning a product for the circular economy only means making it recyclable.
nodes.response: Redesign in the circular economy involves designing products to last longer, be repaired, reused, or upgraded to reduce waste throughout the product’s entire life cycle.

nodes.misconception: Redesigning a product for the circular economy only means making it recyclable.
nodes.response: Redesign in the circular economy involves designing products to last longer, be repaired, reused, or upgraded to reduce waste throughout the product’s entire life cycle.

nodes.misconception: Redesigning and evolving existing products is not really designing and does not show any creativity or innovation.
nodes.response: Redesigning existing products is a part of design work and often requires significant creativity, insight, and innovation. Some of the most impactful design breakthroughs came not from inventing something new, but from improving what already exists.

nodes.misconception: To show the spectator ions in an ionic equation.
nodes.response: Spectator ions are ions that remain the same throughout a reaction. They are not included in the ionic equation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that air pollution can be seen, and that there are no pollutants in the air if it looks ‘clean’.
nodes.response: Explain that many things that can pollute the air cannot be seen by the naked eye and air pollution can exist even when we can’t see it around us.

nodes.misconception: Energy efficiency and energy conservation mean the same thing.
nodes.response: In fact, energy efficiency is about using technology to do the same task but with less use of energy, while energy conservation is about changing people's behaviour so they use less energy.

nodes.misconception: It is pointless to take action on climate change if some other countries are not.
nodes.response: Discuss how international agreements can enable many countries take action together. And that developing green technologies ahead of other countries may help UK industry in the future.

nodes.misconception: Driving at a high speed does not have much effect on the amount of energy a car uses for a whole journey.
nodes.response: Discuss the idea that the faster a car travels, the greater the drag force pushing back on the car. A good analogy is walking slowly or quickly through water in a swimming pool - it's much harder to walk quickly because of the increased drag.

nodes.misconception: Individuals can't make an impact on reducing energy usage.
nodes.response: We all have a part to play in reducing energy usage.

nodes.misconception: Food waste happens mostly outside the home.
nodes.response: Food waste happens mostly inside the home - around 60%.

nodes.misconception: The type of graph chosen to represent data can just be personal choice.
nodes.response: Specific kinds of graph should be chosen to represent specific kinds of data.

nodes.misconception: Friction is only between solids that are rubbing together.
nodes.response: Highlight the different amounts of friction between the solids that are separated by different liquids.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think their carbon footprint relates only to air pollution that can be seen, such as smoke or soot.
nodes.response: Explain that greenhouse gases cannot be seen, smelled or tasted; just because we cannot see them, it doesn’t mean they are not in the air around us.

nodes.misconception: Because we know the location of plate margins, scientists can predict when earthquakes will happen.
nodes.response: While scientists can identify areas that are at high risk of earthquakes, exact predictions for when and where an earthquake will occur (or what magnitude it will be) are not possible.

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms cannot be accurately predicted.
nodes.response: While it is challenging, advances in technology and meteorology have improved the accuracy of tropical storm predictions.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives come before the noun in Spanish as they do in English. They do not need to change.
nodes.response: In Spanish, adjectives generally come after the noun. They agree with the number and gender of the noun.

nodes.misconception: Pupils could think the maquette is the final version of their sculpture, rather than a starting point for refining and improving their design.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a maquette is a guide for their sculpture, not a final blueprint. Emphasise that it's okay to make changes as they work to improve stability and functionality.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that adding more detail will always make a print better.
nodes.response: While detail can be important in some art, too many tiny or delicate details can get lost or not transfer properly when printing. It’s actually more effective to use bold, simple shapes and lines to create a clear and striking print.

nodes.misconception: It is important to focus on the creation of complex methods like metaphor or anaphora. Verbs don't matter.
nodes.response: Every sentence should contain a verb. As such, choosing them requires careful thought, and can dramatically impact the tone and pace of your writing.

nodes.misconception: Word choice is more important than rhythm.
nodes.response: Word choice and powerful literary methods (for example metaphor) are hard things to craft and deserve time and attention. But so too does your sentence construction. Consider if you heard one of your favourite songs but there was no rhythm to it.

nodes.misconception: That you always have to plan before a piece of creative writing.
nodes.response: While a plan is very useful, and should be used in most cases, sometimes free writing can be a way of unleashing creativity that can then be revised.

nodes.misconception: Once an essay is completed it's not worth thinking about again.
nodes.response: How does rewriting support the writing of future responses? Consider the strategies, tips and phrases explored. Revisiting our own essays can make feedback become really personalised and allow you to work and focus on your own targets.

nodes.misconception: A function and a procedure are the same.
nodes.response: A function is different from a procedure because it returns a value or values to the main program.

nodes.misconception: A function and a procedure are the same.
nodes.response: A function is different from a procedure because it returns a value or values to the main program.

nodes.misconception: A poem with a good rhythm always rhymes.
nodes.response: Rhythm is about the flow, beat and sound of a poem. Rhyme can sometimes develop rhythm, but it is not necessary.

nodes.misconception: A heart only symbolises love.
nodes.response: Whilst love is the most common interpretation of a heart symbol, it can also represent unity, gratitude, hope, care, comfort, friendship, romance, resisting oppression and acceptance.

nodes.misconception: Experimentation just means making new things each time.
nodes.response: When you experiment you are thinking and doing. Always think about what works and what new ideas are generated.

nodes.misconception: That we can develop a personal response by asking the same questions of every non-fiction text.
nodes.response: While some questions are universal, a non-fiction text such as a personal essay may require us to ask questions about what the writer want us to understand about their lives in order for us to respond to it.

nodes.misconception: Children may translate or copy a shape rather than 'flipping it' over the line of symmetry.
nodes.response: Use mirrors to support children's understanding of how a shape flips when it is reflected. Explore this idea with a wide variety of shapes.

nodes.misconception: Children may miscount the number of squares from the mirror line when plotting each vertex to reflect the shape.
nodes.response: Encourage children to work systematically by only marking one vertex at a time to reduce the chance of errors. Also encourage use of mirrors to check.

nodes.misconception: One of the most common mistakes pupils make when reflecting is to flip the shape. Essentially, they translate the shape rather than reflecting it.
nodes.response: Attention is given at the start of the lesson to examples and non-examples of reflections, including the above misconception. Use real mirrors and ask pupils to reflect objects in them, noticing the direction in which the reflection is facing.

nodes.misconception: Mirrors must somehow turn images around or ‘flip’ them to make reflections laterally inverted.
nodes.response: Explicitly teach that a mirror merely (and passively) reflects what is directly in front of each part of it. Pupils can observe the reflection of text on clear plastic: the image is the same as what is seen looking through the back of the text.

nodes.misconception: All materials reflect the same amount of light.
nodes.response: Explanation that we can measure the differing amounts of light reflected by different materials.

nodes.misconception: Only mirrors and very shiny materials reflect light.
nodes.response: Explanation that lots of different materials reflect different amounts of light.

nodes.misconception: Light shines out of our eyes; a light ray is a long thin piece of light; light is made of light rays added together; light can only be reflected off shiny surfaces.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching about sources of light, what a light ray is; plenty of demonstrations and practice of drawing diagrams.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often describe an absorbing surface as trapping a sound and do not correctly describe how the vibrations of air particles are reduced by making particles in a surface vibrate more.
nodes.response: Provide opportunity for pupils to describe how vibrations of air particles are reduced when sound waves make particles in a surface vibrate more.

nodes.misconception: Colour is the sum of the colour of the object and the colour of light falling on it.
nodes.response: Use coloured lights to show that red coloured objects reflect red light, but not blue or green.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils think that a ray of light can reflect off at an angle different to that at which it hits a plane mirror and perhaps in several directions.
nodes.response: Give pupils practical experience of measuring the angles at which light reflects off a plane mirror to confirm the correct rules; share results to confirm; and discuss potential sources of error that may lead to small discrepancies.

nodes.misconception: Diagonal reflections that incorrectly look like rotations or translations of the object.
nodes.response: False reflections that look like this are due to students not counting diagonals of grid squares, perpendicular to the mirror line.

nodes.misconception: There is no point in doing an evaluation once a project is finished as you are not going to go back and make any more changes.
nodes.response: Evaluations help learning by understanding your creative process and finding ways to improve. This often informs projects that you do in the future.

nodes.misconception: Once the performance is done, our learning is done too.
nodes.response: Watching a performance back and/or getting feedback from an audience/ director/teacher is hugely valuable in cementing our learning. We can see and hear how we used our voices and bodies to tell a story and how we applied the techniques we learnt.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know how to divide up the extract for Reader's Theatre.
nodes.response: Explain that all members of the group should share in the process of reading aloud. Smaller sections could be highlighted for less confident readers (for example, Fishlegs).

nodes.misconception: Geographers should try to hide the things that do not go to plan in their fieldwork.
nodes.response: An important part of being a geographer is to be reflective and to take opportunities to improve on your practice.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a speech is either good or bad.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a speech can have strong elements, but still have areas for improvement.

nodes.misconception: Everyone believes in God.
nodes.response: Some people believe in God, and some people don’t. Everyone has their own way of thinking.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that there are multiple answers to open-ended or personal reflection questions.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to refer to the text as they discuss the questions. Also encourage them to think about the text in relation to their own lives, finding any parts that are relatable to themselves.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that light rays are actual physical things that are the constituents of light.
nodes.response: It needs to be made explicit through teaching that light rays are imaginary lines that show the direction in which light is travelling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that light rays are actual physical things that are the constituents of light.
nodes.response: It needs to be made explicit through teaching that light rays are imaginary lines that show the direction in which light is travelling.

nodes.misconception: Ideas about the nature of light and reflections are often taken for granted at this stage and simple misconceptions often persist, e.g. that all reflections appear to be on the surface of mirrors.
nodes.response: Give pupils practical experience of systematically investigating reflections, e.g. measuring the apparent location of a mirror image. Explicitly assess for misconceptions about the location and visibility of mirror images of an object.

nodes.misconception: The same tools and methods are used for both small-scale and industrial manufacturing.
nodes.response: The scale of production heavily influences tool choice, speed, accuracy, and repeatability.

nodes.misconception: Reforming is the same as deforming.
nodes.response: Reforming changes the state AND the shape; solid, liquid and back to solid. Deforming only changes the shape; the materials always remain a solid.

nodes.misconception: A ray of light curves as it passes through glass, perspex or water.
nodes.response: Use a perspex block with the bottom painted white to demonstrate the path of a ray of light through it. Avoid putting too much emphasis on the term 'bending' light, instead try to primarily refer to light changing direction at a boundary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rote-learn what specific examples of refraction look like, rather than developing a more general understanding of the direction waves turn based on changes in wave speed.
nodes.response: Teach pupils the general theory of refraction and apply it to a variety of different examples where wave speed changes (e.g. sound waves refract in the opposite direction to light at an air-glass boundary due to the different wave speeds).

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rote-learn what specific examples of refraction look like, rather than developing a more general understanding of the direction waves turn based on changes in wave speed.
nodes.response: Teach pupils the general theory of refraction and apply it to a variety of different examples where wave speed changes (e.g. sound waves refract in the opposite direction to light at an air-glass boundary due to the different wave speeds).

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rote-learn what specific examples of refraction look like, rather than developing a more general understanding of the direction waves turn based on changes in wave speed.
nodes.response: Teach pupils the general theory of refraction and apply it to a variety of different examples where wave speed changes (e.g. sound waves refract in the opposite direction to light at an air-glass boundary due to the different wave speeds).

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rote-learn what specific examples of refraction look like, rather than developing a more general understanding of the direction waves turn based on changes in wave speed.
nodes.response: Teach pupils the general theory of refraction and apply it to a variety of different examples where wave speed changes (e.g. sound waves refract in the opposite direction to light at an air-glass boundary due to the different wave speeds).

nodes.misconception: 'Me' and 'te' are always the direct object pronouns 'me' and 'you'.
nodes.response: 'Me' and 'te' are used as direct object pronouns but also the reflexive pronouns meaning 'myself' and yourself'.

nodes.misconception: Urban regeneration only means building new houses.
nodes.response: Regeneration is not just about new housing—it also improves transport, creates jobs, and provides community services.

nodes.misconception: The UK is the same as Great Britain
nodes.response: The UK is short for the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland is not in Great Britain.

nodes.misconception: When performing in parts children often try to block out listening to the other parts and focus only on their own.
nodes.response: Children will gain in confidence when they listen to all the parts and will improve their performance.

nodes.misconception: Some parts in an ensemble piece are more important than others.
nodes.response: Through learning all the parts you will come to see the importance and difficulty and unique qualities of each. Often the hardest part is just holding the beat!

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing simply means playing a piece again and again.
nodes.response: To rehearse effectively, we need to work on sepcific areas for improvement to help us to play and sing together and create a balanced sound.

nodes.misconception: When playing layers of ostinati we have to ignore the other parts in order to focus on playing our own layer accurately.
nodes.response: When performing layers of ostinati, it is important that each group is aware of how their part fits into the whole. Layers should work together, ensuring they are keeping a steady pulse and that the start of their musical sentences align.

nodes.misconception: I only need to worry about my own part in an ensemble.
nodes.response: It is important to be able to play your own part confidently in an ensemble but it is also important to understand how your part fits in with the rest of the ensemble.

nodes.misconception: A musical piece or performance is unchangeable.
nodes.response: There can be many interpretations of a piece of music, even if certain directions are suggested by the composer. As the composers of your own minimalist piece, anything is changeable and each performance may also be different.

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing is just singing the songs through.
nodes.response: Rehearsing helps us to work out what needs further practice.  It helps us know when to start and stop singing, to feel the steady beat and is a regular reminder to follow the conductor. Feeling more confident will enable a more accurate performance.

nodes.misconception: We can play at our own tempo without listening to the other groups.
nodes.response: The songs we are layering are all played at different tempi. Feeling the steady pulse and following a conductor, as well as listening to the playing of all groups will help the class to play to the same steady pulse.

nodes.misconception: The strongest materials make the best bridges.
nodes.response: Rather than using the strongest materials, sometimes it's better use materials the bend a little.  This is important in case it is windy or the ground shakes.

nodes.misconception: If I don't have a dictionary in an exam, I won't be able to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words.
nodes.response: If you cannot use a dictionary, look at the surrounding words. Is the word part of a compound noun? Is it a cognate? Using the words and grammar you know, generate a working translation and try to fill the gap. Consider the topic of the text, too.

nodes.misconception: Spanish words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s always show final syllable stress.
nodes.response: Spanish words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s show final syllable stress unless otherwise indicated by an accent.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to find the whole when they are told the size of the half and may try to find half of the half.
nodes.response: Use a bar model representation to help children see the structure of double and half. Use gesture, colour and/or circling when discussing what each part of the bar model represents.

nodes.misconception: All inequalities are graphed with solid lines.
nodes.response: When graphed, strict inequalities are indicated with a dashed line. This is important as it visually tells us that values on the line will not satisfy the inequality.

nodes.misconception: The = operator is used for comparison.
nodes.response: When using Python for programming the == operator is used for comparison and the = operator is used for assignment. Other languages may not always use these operators for these tasks.

nodes.misconception: If you use 'me' in Spanish you need 'myself' in English.
nodes.response: When the action of a verb is directed towards the self, Spanish always uses a reflexive pronoun. English does not always do this; for example, 'me levanto a las siete' - 'I get up at seven'.

nodes.misconception: 'Me' and 'te' mean 'my' and 'your' in Spanish.
nodes.response: 'Me' and 'te' are reflexive pronouns in Spanish and mean 'myself' and 'yourself' respectively. 'Mi' and 'tu' are the possessive adjectives 'my' and 'your' in Spanish.

nodes.misconception: Mirroring and copying are the same
nodes.response: Mirroring is a type of copying, it specifically requires the movement to be translated to the opposite side of the body to produce the effect of a reflection. Copying can be a direct replication of the action.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the atomic number rather than mass when calculating the relative formula mass. Also, the number of atoms can be missed for the percentage of an element in a compound.
nodes.response: Emphasise that  atomic mass is the larger number for each element on the periodic table and encourage pupils to use the key present to help them identify the mass.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think yin yoga is boring.
nodes.response: Yin Yoga provides a chance to deeply connect with your body and mind. It can be a deeply meditative practice, allowing for self-reflection and stress relief. For many, it’s an opportunity to slow down in an otherwise fast-paced life.

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush different relaxation techniques and actions with their bodies when performing sequences.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that mimicking different emotions requires concentration and controlled movements, which are often performed slowly in order calm our bodies.

nodes.misconception: When pupils are receiving the baton, they turn their body to face the incoming runner to give them a better view and try to grab the baton from them.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that although this technique may seem easier, it will cause their team to lose speed. Pupils should face forwards, with their hand out behind them and communicate to ensure the exchange is successful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to stand still and wait for the baton to be passed to them before they start running.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils start jogging as their teammate approaches them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often perform relay changeovers with the receiver standing still until they receive the baton, then accelerating into their sprint.
nodes.response: Changeovers should be performed at high speed. The receiver begins to accelerate at just the right moment to high speed but not too far ahead of the incoming runner. This will be different for each pupil  (~3.5m is a good point to work from).

nodes.misconception: If you read something on the internet, it must be true.
nodes.response: Anyone can publish any content on the internet, which means not everything can be trusted. When looking at content other people have made, you should always consider what you can believe about what has been published.

nodes.misconception: Students may attempt to create a piece that resembles a two-dimensional image as a result of not layering the materials.
nodes.response: Students should be reminded to layer materials to create a three-dimensional piece.

nodes.misconception: Religious art only includes paintings or sculptures.
nodes.response: Religious art isn’t just paintings or sculptures, it includes architecture, textiles, calligraphy and even temporary creations like Rangoli and sand mandalas, all used to express and connect with the spiritual.

nodes.misconception: Pacifists and peace-makers are the same, both reject all forms of violence.
nodes.response: Pacifists believe all violence is wrong, while some peace-makers may accept limited use of force if it helps protect others or restore peace.

nodes.misconception: The Crusades were only about religion.
nodes.response: Religion was a big reason for the Crusades, but they were also about gaining land, power, and wealth. Wars often have multiple overlapping causes, not just one simple reason.

nodes.misconception: Like non-person or object nouns, identity nouns exist in only one form and gender.
nodes.response: Unlike non-person or object nouns, identity nouns can have both masculine and feminine forms: le chrétien - la chrétienne. This is the same as other French person nouns you may know, e.g. le directeur/la directrice.

nodes.misconception: Like nationality adjectives, nationality nouns use lowercase letters in French: il est anglais - c'est un anglais.
nodes.response: Unlike nationality adjectives, nationality nouns use capital letters in French: il est anglais - c'est un Anglais.

nodes.misconception: The play is definitely a religious allegory, and all interpretations align with this view.
nodes.response: While the religious allegory is a valid interpretation, it’s important to consider it as one lens. Focussing on one interpretation may limit a deeper analysis of the text’s complexity.

nodes.misconception: All Christian weddings are the same.
nodes.response: Christian weddings will vary depending on denomination, cultural/family traditions, etc.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that as soon as Christianity returned to Britain, pagan traditions disappeared completely.
nodes.response: Paganism did not completely vanish. Though the majority of Anglo-Saxons were Christians, pagan beliefs and traditions were still present.

nodes.misconception: Victims of war are only civilians or refugees.
nodes.response: Victims can also include traumatised soldiers, prisoners, and even civilians from aggressor nations, showing the complexity of suffering in war.

nodes.misconception: The Big Bang theory and Genesis 1-2 cannot be reconciled.
nodes.response: Many Christians see the Big Bang as part of God’s creation.

nodes.misconception: All Christians interpret the Genesis creation story literally.
nodes.response: Many Christians see Genesis as metaphorical or compatible with scientific explanations, such as theistic evolution.

nodes.misconception: Aurangzeb was completely intolerant towards and alienated all non-Muslims.
nodes.response: Aurangzeb continued to support non-Muslim places of worship and to promote non-Muslim officials in the empire, leading to increased numbers of Hindus and Sikhs serving the Mughal Empire by the end of his reign.

nodes.misconception: An annulment is the same as a divorce.
nodes.response: An annulment says the marriage was not valid, wheras a divorce ends a marriage.

nodes.misconception: It is only WWI soldiers who are remembered with memorials.
nodes.response: All those who lost their lives in WWI are remembered through memorials (medical staff, civilians, animals etc).

nodes.misconception: Supporting an employee's mental or physical wellbeing only costs an organisation.
nodes.response: Supporting an employee's mental or physical wellbeing can actually benefit an organisation through reduced time off and increased productivity.

nodes.misconception: Saltwater is safe to drink.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will explain that drinking saltwater can make us ill and will explain the process of desalination.

nodes.misconception: Renaissance and Enlightenment thinkers gave up the belief in God.
nodes.response: Renaissance and Enlightenment thinkers questioned religious authority but didn't necessarily stop believing in God, focusing instead on reason and human potential.

nodes.misconception: Criticisms of bloodletting meant it was practiced less.
nodes.response: Bloodletting and other humoural treatments remained popular and were even used to try and treat King Charles II in 1685.

nodes.misconception: Corrections to Galen's work were accepted virtually immediately.
nodes.response: Many medical professionals were reluctant to challenge Galen's works and so new ideas, like those of Vesalius, were not accepted immediately.

nodes.misconception: The Renaissance led to widespread acceptance of scientific ideas in medicine.
nodes.response: Opposition to change from physicians and the limits of new discoveries meant that many ideas about the causes of disease remained unchanged.

nodes.misconception: The most detailed renders should always be produced.
nodes.response: Render engines and settings should be chosen with consideration to the requirements of the project. This may include considering factors such as time constraints and hardware limitations.

nodes.misconception: When rendering the light source, location might not be correctly identified.
nodes.response: Start with real objects and a light source to help students visualise where the shadow and highlight would be. Get students to label where the light source is.

nodes.misconception: Renewable energy sources are 'free'.
nodes.response: There are significant costs involved in setting up and maintaining renewable sources of energy.

nodes.misconception: Repair, maintenance and recycling is the sole responsibility of the user.
nodes.response: Design decisions made at the design/redesign stage can determine the ease and ability of a product to be repaired, maintained and recycled.

nodes.misconception: Repair, maintenance and recycling is the sole responibility of the user.
nodes.response: Design decisions made at the design/redesign stage can determine the ease and ability of a product to be repaired, maintained and recycled.

nodes.misconception: Artwork is often seen as a passive object that hangs on a wall.
nodes.response: Art can also be used to activate social change and is a process that can helps spark conversation and raise awareness. The act of creating and sharing the work is powerful in itself.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that using exclamatory sentences is appropriate in a newspaper article about Mormor's death to express strong emotions.
nodes.response: Explain that while exclamatory sentences express sudden or strong emotions, they are not appropriate for a factual newspaper article. Instead, emphasise using emotive language and other devices that convey the community's feelings respectfully.

nodes.misconception: Pupils should not be encouraged to think about 'adding a zero' to the 2-digit numbers.
nodes.response: Make careful use of the stem sentences and representations to make sure that pupils are clear that e.g. 12 tens is equal to 120.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to represent numbers where tens or ones are missing (e.g. 307 or 680).
nodes.response: Use place value grids to represent numbers, showing that there are 'no tens' or 'no ones'. Use alongside base ten block representations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misread numbers when using number lines (e.g. read 105 as 95).
nodes.response: Encourage children to say the 10s number before and after (e.g. the number is in between 100 and 110).

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that subtraction is commutative and therefore equations can be written in any order.
nodes.response: Model with physical resources such as marbles in a bag that 4 - 6 results in a negative change but 6 - 4 results in a positive change.

nodes.misconception: When representing two-digit numbers practically, children may start each number anew, instead of using what they know about number patterns to adapt existing representations.
nodes.response: Use the questions 'What's the same?' and 'What's different?' to draw attention to the patterns in number sequences and how these can be used. Link the abstract to the pictorial and concrete by drawing attention to what each digit represents.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that a square number is simply any number or a number multiplied by 2
nodes.response: Remind children that a square number is the product of a number multiplied by itself (e.g., 4 × 4 = 16). Take time to use square arrays to demonstrate this.

nodes.misconception: Without correct representation, children may struggle to know what to calculate.
nodes.response: If needed, provide support at this stage so that the structure of the mathematics is clear to children.

nodes.misconception: Children may fail to appreciate the importance of the equals sign in an equation, e.g. making errors such as 16 = 4 + 20, or confuse the value of the digits, making errors such as 43 = 4 + 30
nodes.response: Use the language of parts and whole to activate/link to prior learning. Encourage drawing of own part-part-whole models. Encourage children to spot errors and explain why they are are incorrect and to articulate their thinking around correct answers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to draw a bar model to represent an equation without a context.
nodes.response: Refer back to the language of parts and wholes to help pupils identify which numbers in the equation represent the parts and which number represent the whole. You may like to reduce the numbers to number within 10 to emphasise the structure at first.

nodes.misconception: Pupil may multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the integer therefore finding an equivalent fraction.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to represent the maths using unitised counters as this will support them to recognise the multiplicand and the multiplier.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the removal of the multiplication symbol can result in the number becoming a two-digit number rather than two, single digits being multiplied together.
nodes.response: Using the language of 'lots of' may support pupils to see that an algebraic equation with coefficients represents multiplication. For example: 40 can be read as 'four lots of 0'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 5s
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: counters can support children to practise skip counting in 5s

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the 7 times table is just counting by sevens without recognising it as multiplication.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the 7 times table is not just counting by sevens but a series of products of 7 and whole numbers (e.g., 7 × 1, 7 × 2, etc.).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 10s
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: 10 frames, number lines and 100 squares and can support children to practise skip counting in groups of 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.

nodes.misconception: When writing equations to represent part-part-whole models, children may have difficulty recording the number of groups (as this numeral is not written in the model) and revert to repeated addition.
nodes.response: Encourage children to articulate their thinking as they record, e.g. there are ___ groups of ___ and a remainder of ___

nodes.misconception: Children may not see the link between sharing and grouping as sharing has traditionally been done by sharing out objects one by one. This becomes far less efficient when working with larger numbers.
nodes.response: To develop understanding of 'dividing between', ensure that physical objects are shared out in groups each time (forming an array beneath a bar model), rather than one by one.

nodes.misconception: Children are not able to explain the multiplication expression.
nodes.response: Children are encouraged to identify exactly how the equation relates to the image. For example 3 groups of 2 shoes: 3 x 2 - with the questions ‘What does the 3 represent?’ ‘What does the 2 represent?’ ‘What does the 6 represent?’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand how to represent the repeated addition expression and a multiplication expression.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to identify exactly how the equation relates to the image: with the questions ‘What does the 3 represent?’ ‘What does the 2 represent?’ ‘What does the 6 represent?’

nodes.misconception: Pupils might confuse the number of groups with the value of the groups and therefore write incorrect expressions.
nodes.response: Once familiar with building the relevant additive expression, the multiplicative expression is introduced alongside e.g. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 is the same as 5 x 3  Take time to connect these ideas using `groups of language' and physical representations.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that each group of ten is worth more than the last when we count up in tens.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that we count all as we go along to find how many things are in a group, the last number we say tells us how many there are.

nodes.misconception: Children may get the tens and teens numbers confused and may muddle up the digits when writing the numerals.
nodes.response: Show numbers on a place value chart and talk about what each number represents. Take time to over pronounce teen and multiples of 10 words focusing on the sound of -teen and -ty and encouraging learners to practise with silly voices.

nodes.misconception: Children may get the tens and teens numbers confused and may muddle up the digits when writing the numerals.
nodes.response: Show numbers on a place value chart and talk about what each number represents. Emphasise the relative value of the digits, focusing on the groups of 10 and how this is shown. Support pupils to generalise e.g. teen numbers always have one ten.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the number of groups and group size.
nodes.response: Continue to use the number stems and arrays to highlight the relationship between the factors and products.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 10s and recognise this as groups of 10
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: 10 frame and 10 p coins can support children to practise skip counting in 10s. Then move onto counting in 10s on a number line.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 2 and want to count in steps of 1
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: counters can support children to practise skip counting in 2s

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 5s
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: 10 frame and 5 p coins can support children to practise skip counting in 5s. Then move onto counting in 5s on a number line.

nodes.misconception: Children may look at the numbers but not be able to visualise the context, for example, they may try to undo 6 + 4 = 10 with 10 - 6 = 4
nodes.response: Use practical equipment to illustrate the importance of the number added and subtracted being the same. Link equations to contexts ensuring that children are secure with what each part of an equation represents when linked to a story context.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to recognise five fingers on a hand or subitise numbers up to five in familiar arrangements such as dice patterns.
nodes.response: Play games to practise subitising and recognising five e.g. dominoes or dice games and finger games such as bunny ears. Allow regular opportunities for pupils to familiarise themselves with common patterns of numbers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils opt for a trial and improvement approach, without working systematically either.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to identify the structure of the problem and represent the maths in a way that makes sense for them. You can then take their representations of the maths and refine them so they are more efficient.

nodes.misconception: It is very common for children to generalise the linguistic pattern of adding the suffix of 'th' to create fraction names even though there are special cases mentioned in the slides.
nodes.response: Make good use of your learning wall here and display the names prominently paired with their fractional notation. Inject some fun by making a game of it: say incorrect fraction names during your own explanations and get the children to correct you.

nodes.misconception: The sample rate and bit depth of samples adjusts based on the sound that is being digitsed.
nodes.response: The digitsation of sound needs to be consistent so that the binary sequence represented can be processed as expected.

nodes.misconception: Binary is only used to represent numerical data.
nodes.response: Binary digits can be used to form sequences that can be used to represent any data. As long as it is identified what each sequence represents, binary digits can become any form of data or instructions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils mistake that the same mass of different substances = the same number of particles.
nodes.response: This activity reinforces the mathematical relationship between relative formula mass of a substance, the number of particles present and the mass measured in the lab.

nodes.misconception: Pupils mistake that the same mass of different substances = the same number of particles.
nodes.response: This activity reinforces the mathematical relationship between relative formula mass of a substance, the number of particles present and the mass measured in the lab.

nodes.misconception: Pupils count all the triangles in a row to determine length rather than only counting the ones which have an edge on the line.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider what they are using to measure when they draw each line on isometric paper.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think a=1 b=2 ... or that a letter represents an object
nodes.response: Letters represent a numerical value either unknown or variable. Avoid always using the first letter of the words used in a scenario.

nodes.misconception: Both lines of a double number line must start at zero and these zeros must be aligned.
nodes.response: When drawing double number lines, ensure to align the zeros and the known equivalents. Showing how a graph is formed from a DNL can help.

nodes.misconception: A flowchart should always be created before writing a computer program.
nodes.response: For simple programs, a flowchart may not be needed and could add to development time. Sometimes the program code itself might be clear enough without a flowchart.

nodes.misconception: Pseudocode can be directly run or executed by a computer.
nodes.response: Pseudocode is a human-readable representation of an algorithm's logic but doesn't follow the syntax or rules of any particular programming language. It should only be used as a planning tool.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that letters always represent a set value that can be 'found'.
nodes.response: Highlight the distinction between unknowns and variables. Allow pupils to explore expressions intrinsically before substituting in values.

nodes.misconception: Bitmap images that are large on screen are always poor quality.
nodes.response: The quality of a bitmap image depends on its resolution, not just its size on the screen. A high-resolution bitmap can appear sharp and detailed, while a low-resolution bitmap may look pixelated when enlarged.

nodes.misconception: A leitmotif and a film theme are the same thing.
nodes.response: Not quite. Many films have themes that represent the overall mood, and can be heard throughout the film. The difference with a leitmotif is that it explicitly represents one thing - a character, place or an idea.

nodes.misconception: The representation length does not include any spaces.
nodes.response: The representation length is the total number of symbols in the sequence including spaces.

nodes.misconception: Inaccurate representation of the number rhymes.
nodes.response: Once again, ensure all children have access to any countable objects needed and ensure the visuals on the slides are not replied upon. Take time to revisit early counting principles, modelling how these can be used to help represent a given visual.
