nodes.response: Give supportive clues, e.g., "Which young Swedish girl has done a lot to tackle climate change?".

nodes.misconception: 'El' is used for all dates.
nodes.response: 'El' is used to mean 'on the' for specific dates. It is not used for today's date.

nodes.misconception: I use 'notre' to mean 'our' in French just with masculine nouns.
nodes.response: The possessive adjective 'notre' is used before masculine and feminine singular nouns to mean 'our' in French. We use 'nos' when the 'possessed' noun is plural.

nodes.misconception: All cells are exactly like the standard animal and plant cell models shown in textbooks.
nodes.response: The lesson explores different shapes, sizes, and structures, of specialised cells that are adapted for specific functions.

nodes.misconception: Only animals are multicellular; that specialised cells are individual; all DNA in a cell is the same so will produce the same proteins.
nodes.response: Examples of multicellular plants, with specialised cells, tissues and organs provided; show images of cells as tissues rather than just individual. All cells have the same DNA, but it is whether the genes are turned on that makes them specialise.

nodes.misconception: In a rugby scrum you have to push (like in union).
nodes.response: Because the scrum half can throw the ball in at angle that is advantageous to their team, there is not much point pushing. It's better to save energy to get back to defend but if the other side are being lazy, it might be beneficial to push.

nodes.misconception: Using machinery to manufacture requires little skill when compared to using hand tools.
nodes.response: Using machinery to manufacture products takes skill and effort to achieve a high quaility finish, much like using hand tools.

nodes.misconception: Hand tools are outdated and less accurate than power tools.
nodes.response: Hand tools offer high precision when used correctly, especially for detailed work.

nodes.misconception: The temperature of ice is always 0ºC and the temperature of water in the liquid state cannot be 0°C.
nodes.response: Make explicit observations that water can be in either or both of the solid and liquid states at 0°C.

nodes.misconception: The temperature of ice is always 0ºC and the temperature of water in the liquid state cannot be 0°C.
nodes.response: Make explicit observations that water can be in either or both of the solid and liquid states at 0°C.

nodes.misconception: The temperature of ice is always 0ºC and the temperature of water in the liquid state cannot be 0°C.
nodes.response: Make explicit observations that water can be in either or both of the solid and liquid states at 0°C.

nodes.misconception: Believing that spectators always have a negative effect on performance and safety and the impact of spectators is only relevant in professional sport.
nodes.response: Spectators have positive contributions to sport like creating an atmosphere and providing home-field advantage which can not only affect professional sport, but also amateur and youth sport too.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that both the reporting clause and the direct speech begin with a capital letter.
nodes.response: Emphasise that when the speech comes first, the reporting clause has no capital.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what 'speech first' means.
nodes.response: Explain that if the direct speech opens or comes first in the sentence with the reporting clause afterwards or second, this can be referred to as a speech first sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may omit the commas from a speech interrupted sentence or include an extra capital letter.
nodes.response: Use the graphic included in the slides as a visual prompt for pupils when writing speech interrupted.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may omit the comma after the reporting clause, or they may use a comma to end the sentence.
nodes.response: Reinforce the point that commas are never used to close a sentence, even in speech second sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to choose a position in which to interrupt a speech sentence.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think of the complete sentence they want to say and interrupt it at a comma.

nodes.misconception: Anaphora and refrain are the same. They are both types of repetition.
nodes.response: While both anaphora and a refrain are both types of repetition, they function differently. Anaphora occurs when the beginning of a sentence is repeated, whereas a refrain when a key idea is repeated throughout a text, like a chorus in a song.

nodes.misconception: High pitched sounds (higher frequency sound waves) travel faster than low pitched sounds (lower frequency sound waves).
nodes.response: Take measurements for the speed of sound using a high-pitched blast of a whistle as well as the lower pitched sound of hitting pieces of wood together to show they are the same (within error).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a horizontal line on a speed-time means the object is stationary.
nodes.response: The $$y$$-axis is plotting speed so a horizontal line means the speed has not changed in that time. But this can be at any speed. Pupils need to double check axes to know what sort of graph they are using.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unaware of the variety of training methods available to use for improving fitness and performance.
nodes.response: Continue to give pupils experiences which demonstrate different methods of training and ways to structure sessions, such as interval and plyometric training.

nodes.misconception: To pretend to be an object such as a car, we have to use mime.
nodes.response: Miming is one way of describing an object, theme or story to an audience without using words. You will need to use your imagination to think of other ways that the audience will also understand.

nodes.misconception: Homophones sound the same so pupils may rely on previous spelling rules and so, spell them the same.
nodes.response: Spend time showing each word in a sentence, use images to support understanding and make sure each homophone is practised using a strategy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils keep the 'e' when adding -y to words ending in 'e', writing 'slimey' or 'stoney'.
nodes.response: Focus on the rule, remove the 'e' and add -y, and make links to other suffixes that use the same pattern.

nodes.misconception: Children might confuse pairs of words against compound words. e.g. bus stop.
nodes.response: Give examples of both and model mistakes. e.g. write butterfly as butter fly and discuss.

nodes.misconception: It can be difficult to know when words should be hyphenated and when they should not.
nodes.response: Notice patterns such as vowel sounds and encourage the use of dictionaries to check words pupils are unsure of.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may select the wrong spelling for the wrong sentence.
nodes.response: Spend time talking about the meaning of the words as you come across them. Show pupils how to use the context of the sentence to help you decipher the meaning and if relevant, discuss its etymology.

nodes.misconception: Homophones sound the same so pupils may rely on previous spelling rules and so, spell them the same.
nodes.response: Spend time showing each word in a sentence, use images to support understanding and make sure each homophone is practised using a strategy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may select the wrong spelling for the wrong sentence.
nodes.response: Spend time talking about the meaning of the words as you come across them. Show pupils how to use the context of the sentence to help you decipher the meaning and if relevant, discuss its etymology.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may overgeneralise applying regular -ed rules to irregular verbs such as 'buy' -'buyed'.
nodes.response: Expose pupils to irregular past tense verbs in reading activities, encourage them to use mnemonics and hunt for words in sentences together.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss the double letters in the middle of words that have a suffix.
nodes.response: Drawing attention to the patterns of how words are spelt when suffixes are added will help them to remember the double letter.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may pronounce homonyms incorrectly in sentences.
nodes.response: Show pupils that we can use the context of the sentence to help us uncover the meaning of the homonym and therefore its pronunciation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to distinguish between decodable and common exception words.
nodes.response: Be explicit about the difficulties in spelling these words and give time to practise spelling these common exception words. Supplement the slides with any visuals linked to your school's SSP to support building on any learning from Rec and Y1.

nodes.misconception: Children may not know the spelling due to not always being able to rely on rules.
nodes.response: Remind children of the range of spelling strategies they could use to remember the spellings, such as naughty letters or big letters.

nodes.misconception: When starting a strategy, pupils may have copied the spelling down incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model the process of looking at it, considering what's difficult about the spelling and thinking about it. Then, model copying it for the first time, carefully checking each letter and verbalising what you notice.

nodes.misconception: Children might confuse pairs of words with compound words. e.g. bus stop.
nodes.response: Give examples of both and model mistakes e.g. write butterfly as 'butter fly' or bus stop as 'busstop' and discuss.

nodes.misconception: Many of these words are high frequency and common exception words.
nodes.response: Be explicit about the difficulties in spelling these words and give time to practise spelling these common exception words. Supplement the slides with any visuals linked to your school's SSP to support building on learning from Rec and Y1.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will mistakenly use -ce endings for verbs instead of -se endings or vice versa.
nodes.response: Look at a selection of words that fit this spelling pattern and help them to recognise that -ce typically indicates a noun, whilst -se indicates a verb.

nodes.misconception: Children can confuse the homophones 'stationary' and 'stationery'.
nodes.response: Use the mnemonic 'the stationer sells stationery' to help remember.

nodes.misconception: Children may use the wrong vowel letter when spelling words with unstressed vowels.
nodes.response: Stretching the word and saying it slowly, how it is spelt, can help pupils to remember the correct spelling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start using these spellings in place of the most common spellings.
nodes.response: Emphasise that 'ay', 'ai' and 'a-e' are the most common spellings and tell pupils to try those out first.

nodes.misconception: Children may forget the most common spellings and use the most recently learnt spellings.
nodes.response: Always emphasise prior learning. Show examples of words including incorrect and correct spellings to discuss (e.g. train and trean).

nodes.misconception: 'ea' can be pronounced in a number of different ways (/ee/, /ay/, /e/)
nodes.response: Explicitly teach the most common spellings of the 'ea' spelling for the 'e' sound. Give time to practising both reading and writing them.

nodes.misconception: Children can confuse 'th' with 'f' and 'v' in some words because they pronounce it that way.
nodes.response: Focus on pronunciation of the sounds before spelling, and show the tongue moving forward for words with 'th' in them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spell the root word.
nodes.response: As we are adding new learning, it's key to refer back to prior learning (in prior Y2 units as well as Rec and Y1). Refer back to learning in line with your school's SSP to support cognitive load, so pupils can focus on the suffix.

nodes.misconception: The ending -ture can be easily mixed up with (t)cher.
nodes.response: Help pupils to spot words with a root ending in 'ch' or 'tch' with the suffix -er.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that all curriculum words are common exception words.
nodes.response: Discuss that the list is made up of words with the rules they have learnt or should have come across. Discuss the rules some words use compared to words that may be exceptions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can mix up the representations of 'l' and forget the representations which are most likely.
nodes.response: Frame any new learning on -al in the context of prior knowledge around representations of 'l', highlighting the most common representations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be familiar with the 'ck' digraph so may spell words containing 'ch' making the /k/ sound incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words and draw links between spellings containing the 'ch' spelling sounding like the /k/ sound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be familiar with the 'ff' and 'gh' digraph so may spell words contain 'ph' making the /f/ sound incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words and draw links between spellings containing the 'ph' spelling sounding like the /f/ sound and where it's most likely to go in the word.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 's' at the beginning and 'ss' in the middle of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between words containing the 'sc' spelling and looking at examples where it appears at the beginning and in the middle of a word.

nodes.misconception: It can be hard to identify the sounds a word makes when looking at the spelling.
nodes.response: Encourage children to listen to the word without looking at the spelling.  Stretch the word and identify each sound in turn.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a word can only contain a hard c or a soft c.
nodes.response: Look at some words that contain a soft c and a hard c, such as bicycle or access.  Use sound buttoning to help identify the phoneme grapheme correspondences.

nodes.misconception: Children may use an apostrophe for plurals ending in 's'.
nodes.response: Explicitly look at non-examples where the apostrophe isn't used. Help the children to  identify when and why the apostrophe isn't used.

nodes.misconception: Children may form the apostrophe incorrectly - back to front or locate it at the wrong height.
nodes.response: Spend time practising how and where to write the apostrophe, so that it is the correct height and orientation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 'g' and 'ck' at the end of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: The ‘gue’ and ‘que’ sounds nearly always appear at the end of words e.g. vague and antique. The ‘g’ and the ‘k’ sound with the more common spellings, can appear anywhere within a word e.g. eagle, kid and back.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 's' at the beginning and 'ss' in the middle of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between words containing the 'sc' spelling and looking at examples where it appears at the beginning and in the middle of a word.

nodes.misconception: Children see words as unconnected and so don't see the link between 'write' and 'wrote'.
nodes.response: Explicitly show how the spelling of connected words is linked, such as 'know' and 'knowledge' and 'write and 'wrote'.

nodes.misconception: Children mix up the -ible and -able spellings.
nodes.response: Use the rules shown in the lesson: Is there is a recognisable root word without the ending? Is this a modern word? Is there a related word ending in -ation? These will all help to identify the -able spelling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often don't notice that they have written a phrase showing belonging.
nodes.response: Give chances to edit looking explicitly for where an apostrophe for possession is missing. Spot apostrophes in sentences when reading.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to double the consonant when adding the suffix -er.
nodes.response: Show non-examples when the consonant has not been doubled after a short vowel sound (hot-hoter). Explain how this alters our pronunciation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the 'ei' spelling only represents the 'ee' phoneme.
nodes.response: Show a range of words with 'ei' representing different sounds. You can stretch and sound button to show the direct phoneme - grapheme correspondence.

nodes.misconception: Some children may think a letter string can only represent one sound.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the key phonics principles: a sound can be represented by more than one letter, one sound can be represented by more than one spelling and one spelling can represent more than one sound. It is why the English language is so hard!

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume all words ending in -ible do not have a root word.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that some words ending in '-ible', like 'sensible', are derived from recognisable English root words. However, there are also '-ible' words whose roots are not complete English words but may originate from Latin, like 'vis' to 'visible'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that for every word with a prefix the meaning of the prefix will be very literal.
nodes.response: Show a range of words with the focus prefixes in.  Whilst with some words the meaning of the prefix may be clear, with others it is not.  Explain this is linked to the complex way that language develops over time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all words with prefixes must have a recgonisable root word.
nodes.response: Look at some words with the focus prefixes that do not have a recognisable root word.  Discuss how the meaning of the prefix can still support children with understanding the meaning of the word, e.g. translate or transmit.

nodes.misconception: Children may not remember double letters at the start of some words with prefixes, such as illogical or dissatisfied.
nodes.response: Help the children to see that if they recognise the prefix and the base word, they can work out the spelling of the new word, as prefixes do not change the spelling of the root word.

nodes.misconception: Every word with a prefix will have a root word that is recognisable, such as 'stroy' in 'destroy'.
nodes.response: Some words have roots that we will not recognise or no longer use.  Recognising the prefix can still help to spell and understand the word.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think every word with a prefix will have a recognisable root word.
nodes.response: Show that some roots we don't recognise may have Latin roots that we don't know.  We can call this a 'stem' or a 'root'.  Recognising the prefix can still help with spelling and understanding.

nodes.misconception: Children can often misspell words with prefixes as they spell them how they sound.
nodes.response: Help children to recongise when a word has a prefix and use that to support this with spelling, e.g. the prefix mis- has one 's'.

nodes.misconception: Children may think all words with the letters strings have prefixes.
nodes.response: Discuss words using the letter sequence but not as a prefix, e.g. disturb, imp and uncle.  Reinforce the definition of 'root word' and 'prefix'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse 'silent letters' and 'digraphs'.
nodes.response: 'kn' is a digraph making the /n/ sound but, in general, silent letters are individual letters in a word that are not pronounced, whereas digraphs are pairs of letters that represent a single sound.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think letters are silent in some digraphs for example, the 'h' in 'ch'.
nodes.response: Discuss difference between silent letters and digraphs. In 'chaos' the letter 'h' is silent but the other letters make a sound. Whereas, in the word 'clench' the 'h' is part of the 'ch' digraph where the two letters together make one sound.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the vowel sound preceding the 'l' will always determine the spelling.
nodes.response: Showing examples of incorrect use of 'el' and 'le' alongside the correct use can be very useful for children to spot the correct spelling.

nodes.misconception: Children mix up the -ible and -able spellings.
nodes.response: Use the rules shown in the lesson: Is there is a recognisable root word without the ending? Is this a modern word?  Is there a related word ending in -ation? These will all help to identify the -able spelling.

nodes.misconception: Pupils mix up the double letters in 'disappear'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that 'disappear' is made of the prefix dis- and appear.  That way, you know there will only be a single 's'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may easily confuse the vowels in -ant and -ent spellings.
nodes.response: Say the word clearly how it is spelt in order to emphasise the vowel spellings.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that all verbs ending in 'y' follow the rule remove the 'y' and add -ied.
nodes.response: Look at examples that add -ed and remove the 'y' and add -ied.  Focus on the sound the 'y' is making and see if it is part of a digraph.

nodes.misconception: Children can spell past tense verbs how they sound, ending them with 't', 'd' or 'id'.
nodes.response: Explicitly discuss the examples of words where the ending sounds different and remind pupils that the spelling is still -ed.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think all words ending in -ent are the same word class.
nodes.response: Whilst the suffixes -ent and -ence can change word class, not all words ending in -ent are the same word class.  Give examples in a sentence to demonstrate, using the words contentment, (to) frequent, and silent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume all words ending in -ible do not have a root word.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that some words such as sensible do have a recognisable root word in English (sense).  However, other -ible words do have roots (stems) but not whole 'words' from English, they may be Latin roots, such as 'vis'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think 'y' is removed and replaced with an 'i', like with the suffix -ed.
nodes.response: Show that we end up with two 'i's in a row if this happens: fly becoming fliing, so we keep the 'y'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often assume words ending in the suffix -ing indicate the present tense.
nodes.response: Refer to the Year 3 grammar lesson on 'being' verbs and give plenty of examples to show the verbs in both past tense and present tense.

nodes.misconception: Children write words like 'basically' how they sound: 'basicly'.
nodes.response: Show the root words ending in 'ic' and how -ally is added.  Say the words how they are spelt to help remember.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know or understand the meaning of many words encountered in the lesson.
nodes.response: Put all unfamiliar vocabulary into simple sentences to expose children to the meaning. Make links to root words where possible.

nodes.misconception: You can hear the 'ee' in all words ending in -ious and -eous.
nodes.response: You cannot hear the 'ee' in words ending -geous, like 'courageous' (the 'e' is making the 'soft g' sound).

nodes.misconception: You can hear the 'ee' in all words ending in -ious and -eous.
nodes.response: You cannot hear the 'ee' in words ending -geous, like 'courageous' (the 'e' is making the 'soft g' sound) or words with 'xi' or 'ti'.

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty identifying the word class of focus words in the lesson.
nodes.response: Help the children to put the words into simple sentences in order to help identify the word class.  Is it a naming word for a person, place, thing or idea?  Is it describing a noun? etc.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may easily confuse the vowels in -ant and -ent spellings.
nodes.response: Say the word clearly how it is spelt in order to emphasise the vowel spellings.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss out the 'e' or 'a' in words ending in  -ery or -ary, as they are not always clearly pronounced.
nodes.response: Identify the endings -ary and -ery in focus words.  Say the words how they are spelt to help emphasise the vowel spellings.

nodes.misconception: Children may think the root word will help determine the spelling, but this does not always help.
nodes.response: Review links to root words when helpful, but encourage use of the rule about vowels and consonants to determine the spelling.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to think of related words to create word maps independently.
nodes.response: Use a dictionary to support generating words and to check spelling.  This will help pupils to find words with different suffixes as the start of the spelling will be the same.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think all words ending in -ent are the same word class.
nodes.response: Whilst the suffixes -ent and -ence can change word class, not all words ending in -ent are the same word class. Give examples in a sentence to demonstrate, using the words contentment, (to) frequent, and silent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to double the consonant when adding the suffixes -er or -est.
nodes.response: Show non-examples when the consonant has not been doubled after a short vowel sound (hot-hotest). Explain how this alters our pronunciation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the -est suffix is spelt 'ist' or 'st' because that is what you can hear.
nodes.response: Review pupils' misconceptions after practice tasks. Even though the word can sound different, -est is always spelt in the same way.

nodes.misconception: All root words can take both suffixes -ful and -less.
nodes.response: Show a variety of words with suffixes -ful and -less.  Choose ones familiar to the pupils and put into sentences to demonstrate the meaning.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not know the related root word or see how they are connected.
nodes.response: Put the /shun/ word and the associated root word into a simple sentence to help secure their meaning. This will help pupils see the connections in meaning and spelling between the words.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to know which /shun/ spelling to use.
nodes.response: If needed, refer back to the Year 4 content where the /shun/ spellings are introduced initially. Emphasise that -tion is the 'best bet' and most common spelling and use that as the focus for the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the -est suffix is spelt 'ist' or 'st' because that is what you can hear.
nodes.response: Review pupils' misconceptions after practice tasks. Even though the word can sound different, -est is always spelt in the same way.

nodes.misconception: Believing that sponsorship only involves financial support.
nodes.response: Sponsorship can include financial support but also include equipment, clothing or facility provisions.

nodes.misconception: To conjugate 2nd person plural -ar verbs, use the verb ending -ais.
nodes.response: To conjugate 2nd person plural -ar verbs, use the verb ending -áis. The accent on the 'a' is important as it tells us to stress the final syllable.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, I can use the same form of the verb to adress 'you' for one person and 'you' for several people.
nodes.response: In Spanish, there are different verb endings to refer to 'you' (singular) and 'you' (plural). For -ar verbs these are -as and -áis.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that circuit training is solely to improve components of fitness but not for developing skilled sports performance.
nodes.response: While circuit training is great for improving components of fitness, it can also be designed to develop sport-specific skills. For example, in basketball, a circuit can include dribbling, shooting and passing stations, alongside fitness exercises.

nodes.misconception: RICE is the treatment required for all injuries.
nodes.response: RICE in only suitable for soft tissue injuries such as strains and sprains. For other types of injuries , other types of medical care should be sought.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that improvement comes from choosing the maximum options for training straight away.
nodes.response: In order to protect the body and give it time to adjust/grow, coaches will gradually increase the intensity of a training programme. This helps to prevent injury to the athlete.

nodes.misconception: To say 'I do sport' in French, I use 'je fais sport'.
nodes.response: When using the verb 'faire' with sports we use the preposition 'de' afterwards, e.g. 'I do sport' is 'je fais du sport'.

nodes.misconception: My friend (girl) is 'ma amie' in French.
nodes.response: Even though 'amie' is feminine in this example, we use 'mon amie' because the word 'amie' starts with a vowel and this makes the pronunciation smoother.

nodes.misconception: To express 'I play tennis' I say 'je joue le tennis'.
nodes.response: To express 'I play' with any singular sport, you use 'à + le, la' after the verb e.g. 'je joue au tennis', 'je joue à la pétanque'.

nodes.misconception: Students may incorrectly assume that sportsmanship and gamemanship are the same thing.
nodes.response: Sportsmanship is positively conforming to the rules and etiquette of the sport, whereas gamesmanship is more negative because a performer may bend the rules to gain advantage.

nodes.misconception: Students may incorrectly assume that sportsmanship and gamemanship are the same thing.
nodes.response: Sportsmanship is positively conforming to the rules and etiquette of the sport, whereas gamesmanship is more negative because a performer may bend the rules to gain advantage.

nodes.misconception: In German sentences, the word order changes every time you use a conjunction.
nodes.response: Word order does not change after common co-ordinating conjunctions. 'Und', 'aber', 'oder', 'denn' just join two standard sentences together. 'Subordinating' conjuctions send the verb to the end of the sentence. Practise with 'weil', 'wenn', 'dass'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that each time data is changed in a spreadsheet the formulas will also need to be changed.
nodes.response: Using cell references within a formula means that the formula will recalculate when the values in those reference cells change.

nodes.misconception: Spreadsheet forumlas need to use values that are typed directly into the formula.
nodes.response: A formula in a spreadsheet should use cell references where possible. Whilst a forumla can use a typed value, cell references saves having to retype values and also benefits from updating the results of the calculation if data changes.

nodes.misconception: Spreadsheet formatting is only used to make a spreadsheet look attractive.
nodes.response: Spreadsheet formatting is used to make information clearer but is also important to ensure data values such as currency are formatted correctly.

nodes.misconception: A spreadsheet can only be used to explore the costs of the event after it has happened.
nodes.response: A spreadsheet model can be used to predict and model the costs of the event before it happens to help the organisers make decisions about income and expenditure.

nodes.misconception: The COUNTIF function is the same as the COUNT function.
nodes.response: A COUNTIF function returns the total number of cells based on a set criterion, whereas the COUNT function returns the number of cells that contain a number in a range.

nodes.misconception: Past participles with 'être' don't change, just like past participles with 'avoir'.
nodes.response: Past participles with 'être' always agree in gender and number with the subject. Add 'e' to agree a feminine past participle and 's' to agree a plural past participle.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will tire during the latter phases of a 100m sprint race and may withdraw their effort because fatigue is setting in and they expected to perform at maximal throughout.
nodes.response: Fatigue will always feature in the final stages if the athlete is giving it their best. Recognising this by remaining determined to finish and maintaining technique will result in the best possible time.

nodes.misconception: It is too tiring to sprint the whole course.
nodes.response: Strategise and plan who will take on what role and when to spread more difficult actions/moments among the team.

nodes.misconception: At the beginning of a sprint performance, pupils will rise up into an upright position as soon as possible.
nodes.response: An effective drive phase of sprinting sees the body gradually rise up over the first 20m before assuming an upright position. Trying to get upright too soon after starting will hinder acceleration.

nodes.misconception: When applying their acceleration skills to a race, pupils false start in an attempt to win.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that they need to start fast, reacting quickly to the start command, however, too many false starts can result in being disqualified.

nodes.misconception: Pupils slow down before the end of the race/ sprint, preparing to stop directly at the finish line.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that they should not begin to slow down until they have crossed the finish line as it will allow other runners to catch them up and potentially overtake them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils transition aburptly from a lower body position leaning forwards to running upright, which causes them to slow down and lose their rhythm.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to transition smoothly as they accelerate towards top speed as doing this too quickly can cause a loss of speed. Allow opportunities for pupils to practise this and address the misconception when observed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think power comes from just the size and strength of muscles.
nodes.response: Strength is important to generate power but so are speed, timing, coordination and the combination of levers to transfer power up from the ground.

nodes.misconception: You can delete data from a database using an SQL command without any consideration.
nodes.response: You should delete data using SQL commands carefully as data may be linked to other tables in the database.

nodes.misconception: Using SELECT * is always the best method for returning data from a database table.
nodes.response: You should only use the SELECT * query when all fields are needed. Including unnecessary data can be frustrating for the person viewing and working with the results.

nodes.misconception: Students think that all numbers are square numbers as you can square any integer.
nodes.response: A square is the product of 2 repeated integers.

nodes.misconception: The root of an integer is half of the integer.
nodes.response: The square root is the inverse of a square number. A square is the product of 2 repeated integers.

nodes.misconception: Snowball isn't to blame for the failed revolution.
nodes.response: How many examples can you find where Snowball supports hierarchical ideas that go against the ideals of equality?

nodes.misconception: St Bernadette's visions were believed by everyone at the time.
nodes.response: Many, including her family and Church authorities, questioned her mental state, and her visions were only accepted by the Church as genuine following investigation.

nodes.misconception: William I often used the Chapel of St John for his own private worship.
nodes.response: Although this was the plan, William died before the chapel was finished.

nodes.misconception: It is widely believed that St Patrick brought Christianity to Ireland.
nodes.response: Christianity had reached Ireland through contact with Roman Britain and as a result some Irish people converted to the religion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often tuck their thumbs under fingers or stick them out.
nodes.response: Pupils should lock thumbs around the outside of their fist to adopt the correct guard stance.

nodes.misconception: Using standardised components limit creativity and originality in design.
nodes.response: Standardised components can actually enhance innovation by allowing designers to focus on customisation, functionality, and efficiency while reducing costs and production time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak too quietly and find it hard to speak in full sentences.
nodes.response: Display the visuals for successful speaking and listening in your classroom. Ensure pupils are confident in what they are going to say - they could practise their show and tell at home or with a teacher prior to delivering it in front of the class.

nodes.misconception: Requirement to keep checking location to ensure on track. Regular stopping and time wasting as a result of re-orientating the map.
nodes.response: Thumbing the map means tracing your route as you move along the map to represent where you are on the map at any given time.

nodes.misconception: The Sun is not a star.
nodes.response: Make it clear that the only reason the Sun looks different to the stars in the night sky is because it is so much closer to Earth. Use visual examples to show what the Sun and/or other stars would look like at greater distances.

nodes.misconception: Manifestos are always communicated through text.
nodes.response: In art, manifestos don’t need to be written but can be multidisciplinary in their approach.

nodes.misconception: You cannot prevent things from going wrong in a project.
nodes.response: Things can be done to prevent negative things happening during a project - these are called mitigations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that substances need to be at their boiling point temperature to evaporate.
nodes.response: Use plenty of real life examples of liquids evaporating in situations where pupils know that the liquid is not above its boiling point but still evaporates.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the particles within the liquid will have melted or boiled rather than remain the same size and shape, i.e. atoms do not have bulk properties like melting and boiling points.
nodes.response: Ensure that you specifically say that the particles themselves will not melt or boil.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to know the difference between facts and opinions.
nodes.response: Provide lots of examples and opportunities for pupils to share different opinions about things they are familiar with like TV programmes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to know when a command ends in an exclamation mark and when it doesn't.
nodes.response: Choose clear examples that model strong emotion and calm emotion and use tone and intonation to support understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that both positive and negative charges can move when objects are charged by rubbing.
nodes.response: Emphasise that only electrons can move, explaining that they are found on the outer part of atoms. Use this to explain how a positive charge is created by the removal of electrons.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that ‘negative’ refers to a neutral material, that there is only one type of charge, and that friction creates charge.
nodes.response: Pupils need a secure understanding of the particle model of matter before being introduced to atomic structure. Using dynamic models to help pupils visualise what happens to negative charge can support their progression in understanding.

nodes.misconception: The word 'population' always refers to the entire population of a country or the world.
nodes.response: The population in a given context is defined by the entire set of people/creatures/items that are being considered.

nodes.misconception: You always need to start the axis of a scatter graph at (0,0).
nodes.response: The axis of a scatter graph should use a scale that makes the points as clear to see as possible, without distorting the shape of the data.

nodes.misconception: The findings for a data investigation using a sample can always be generalised to the population.
nodes.response: The generalisability of results can depend on how representative the sample is of the population which it is being compared to.

nodes.misconception: Either the mean, median or mode could be used as an average in any situation.
nodes.response: The choice of average can depend on the type of data. For example, in a list of colours, you can find the mode but not the mean.

nodes.misconception: Spreadsheets should always be used for data analysis as they are perfect.
nodes.response: Spreadsheet software is incredibly powerful but care should be taken as human error can lead to incorrect results.

nodes.misconception: Students often talk about Marley and Marley's Ghost as if they are the exact same character.
nodes.response: Marley in life held very different beliefs from Marley's ghost; his ghost acts as Scrooge's redeemer and represents something different.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Scrooge keeps his money to himself so that he can spend it on himself.
nodes.response: Scrooge's frugality also extends to his own existence: Scrooge refuses to spend money even on himself, choosing to live a meagre lifestyle.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Scrooge hates Christmas because it marks the anniversary of Marley's death.
nodes.response: Scrooge hates Christmas because he views it as a crime against oneself. He resents that people spend money they don't have at Christmas.

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Belle was never interested in having any money.
nodes.response: Belle was interested in having money - she just wanted to earn it with Scrooge over time.

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Dickens harshly condemns the wealthy.
nodes.response: Dickens only condemns people with money, who choose not to share it with those in need. This is exemplified in the character of Fezziwig.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Scrooge is selfish and miserable because he is a wicked person.
nodes.response: Scrooge's miserliness comes from his deep-rooted fear of being poor.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Dickens' message about Christmas is focused solely on the importance of charity.
nodes.response: Dickens uses the many Christmas scenes in this section of the novella to emphasise the importance of community and human connection.

nodes.misconception: Students tend to struggle to understand how Scrooge has metaphorically fathered Ignorance and Want.
nodes.response: By being ignorant, Scrooge has neglected his social responsibility and nurtured inequality and injustice - the two children represent this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Fred making fun of Scrooge is mean.
nodes.response: Fred is shown to have a great sense of humour and this is what he's expressing when talking about his uncle. It is this sense of humour that enables him to remain optimistic despite financial struggle.

nodes.misconception: Students often believe that Bob Cratchit represents the most poor group of people in society.
nodes.response: Whilst Bob Cratchit certainly struggles for money and has to be resourceful to feed his family, he still has a job and a home.

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Father Christmas was always pictured wearing red.
nodes.response: Victorian depictions of Father Christmas show him wearing green, with a wreath of holly around his head.

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Dickens only offers a condemnation of the immorality exhibited by Mrs. Dilber.
nodes.response: Dickens, though he doesn't condone the character's behaviour, does empathise with her, and illustrates that she is the product of injustice.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Dickens is solely emphasising the value of human life.
nodes.response: Dickens is also emphasising the importance of what we do with our lives - how we use them to enrich other people's human experience.

nodes.misconception: Students think that, in Stave 4, Scrooge is frightened of dying.
nodes.response: Scrooge is not frightened of death. He is frightened of dying without leaving a legacy because he has not contributed anything to society.

nodes.misconception: Students believe that the ghost shows Scrooge his future and that this will be Scrooge's fate.
nodes.response: The ghost shows Scrooge the "shadows of things that may be". The word "may" is vital, as he suggests that it is never too late to change.

nodes.misconception: Students fail to recognise that Scrooge doesn't just buy the Cratchits any old turkey.
nodes.response: Scrooge buys the Cratchits the "prize" (or most expensive) turkey. This shows that he is truly generous, as he goes above and beyond.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that activities for fitness are always solo tasks that don't encourage social interaction.
nodes.response: Being active with others can have lots of benefits, e.g. increased motivation, encouragement from others, and confidence. All these benefits combined, can encourage individuals to be more active, more often, resulting in increased activity levels.

nodes.misconception: Being seen as ‘healthy’ or ‘unhealthy’ is linked to personal attributes as well as physical attributes (such as regarding an unhealthy character as lazy or untidy).
nodes.response: Reminders that there are simple measures that a human can take to help them to lead a healthy life, such as having a healthy diet, having good personal hygiene and exercising regularly.

nodes.misconception: All industrial cities decline once their factories close.
nodes.response: Some cities, like Sheffield, adapt by developing new industries, services, and cultural attractions after industrial decline.

nodes.misconception: Stars just exist and do not change over time.
nodes.response: Explain the cause and effect of changes in stars and support pupils in explaining these ideas in their own words.

nodes.misconception: Adult stem cells don't exist or can differentiate in the same way as embryonic stem cells.
nodes.response: Give examples of adult stem cells and the types of cells they will differentiate into, using examples that pupils might be familiar with.

nodes.misconception: To communicate spray paint we rush around the room, making hissing noises.
nodes.response: To communicate the idea of using spray paint we need to perform smooth and flowing actions using control, balance and coordination.

nodes.misconception: All stories can be unambiguously plotted on a Freytag's Pyramid. It is clear which element is which.
nodes.response: Complex stories, like Jekyll and Hyde, are open to interpretation as to how each element can be plotted on the pyramid.

nodes.misconception: The Bible and the Qur’an say that people are in charge so they can do what they like with the world.
nodes.response: Most Christians, Jews and Muslims believe they have a responsibility to care for the world.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that there is only one interpretation of Genesis passages linked to creation.
nodes.response: Genesis passages can be interpreted to argue for either dominion or stewardship. Most Christians in the UK today take a stewardship interpretation.

nodes.misconception: Worship always involves talking or music.
nodes.response: Worship can be silent.

nodes.misconception: Stitches are just used to join materials together.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that while stitches can be used to join materials together, they are also used in a skilled and decorative way through embroidery.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to include thinking distance in the overall stopping distance, or imagine that thinking distance is too short to matter.
nodes.response: Model a situation in which a child steps out from behind a parked car 10 m in front of a driver. At 20 mph the thinking distance is about 6 m and braking distance 6 m; at 30 mph these are 9 m and 14 m.

nodes.misconception: Pupils take their eyes off of the ball when they approach it, as they look to see where they are going to throw it.
nodes.response: When pupils take their eyes off the ball, they increase the chances of misfielding it. Ensure pupils track the ball into their hands, before looking up to decide where to throw it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not understand clearly what is meant by stopping time and cannot explain why longer stopping times result in smaller forces.
nodes.response: Describe stopping time as the time it takes to stop ‘during which a force is acting’, and provide examples of smaller forces stopping moving objects over longer periods of time than larger forces.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to include thinking distance in the overall stopping distance, or imagine that thinking distance is too short to matter.
nodes.response: Model a situation in which a child steps out from behind a parked car 10 m in front of a driver. At 20 mph the thinking distance is about 6 m and braking distance 6 m; at 30 mph these are 9 m and 14 m.

nodes.misconception: Stories are just told for fun.
nodes.response: Many stories have a deeper meaning that contains a message about life.

nodes.misconception: Some children might think that militant tactics are a good way for them to get the things that they want to.
nodes.response: The Suffragettes used extreme tactics because they felt that it was their only option. Going on hunger strike is dangerous. For the issues that children might face, there are many safer and less harmful ways to make a change.

nodes.misconception: Dynamics describes how fast an action is performed.
nodes.response: Dynamics involves both speed and force. Some words do mean speed, e.g. quick, whereas others only talk about force, e.g. strong. However some words might mean both, e.g. explosive would be both fast and strong.

nodes.misconception: I have to know every word in a story in order to understand it.
nodes.response: To understand a story which contains a few unfamiliar words, you can use the surrounding words that you do know to work out the probable meanings of unfamiliar words. There may be other visual cues as well.

nodes.misconception: Similar to English, you can pronounce the last consonant of a word in French.
nodes.response: The final consonant of a word is often silent in French: le petit chat. The letters c, r, f and l are exceptions to this rule: le sac neuf.

nodes.misconception: 'You’ in German is just one word.
nodes.response: German has four different words for 'you', depending on who you're talking to: 'du' – informal, singular; 'ihr' - informal, plural; 'Sie' - formal, singular; 'man' - people in general, one.

nodes.misconception: Songs are written based on the beliefs and experiences of the person writing or singing.
nodes.response: Songs have been used for so many purposes from preserving history, sharing family history, entertaining people, to protesting, sharing political messages and to tell a huge range of stories both factual and fiction.

nodes.misconception: Bottom-up strategies can fully solve urban problems on their own.
nodes.response: Bottom-up strategies are valuable because they reflect community needs, improve trust, and lead to long-term change. However, they usually require support from NGOs or the government, such as funding, land rights, or technical help to be sustainable.

nodes.misconception: Top-down strategies always benefit everyone equally.
nodes.response: Top-down strategies often improve infrastructure at a large scale, but they do not always reach all areas fairly. Wealthier areas tend to benefit first, while poorer communities may lack reliable water, waste collection, or transport access.

nodes.misconception: Provision only includes funding or money.
nodes.response: Increasing provision can also include improving facilities, time, coaching and equipment.

nodes.misconception: Dams and reservoirs guarantee a reliable water supply for many years into the future.
nodes.response: Although dams and reservoirs do provide a reliable and easily-controllable source of water, this supply is not guaranteed. Over time, sediment will build up and reduce the capacity of the reservoir. Also, reservoirs can dry up during droughts.

nodes.misconception: Fairtrade is small-scale and mostly based in the UK.
nodes.response: The Fairtrade movement involves the trade in 300 different commodities and global networks of consumers as well as producers.

nodes.misconception: The development of new jobs in industry occurs at a large scale, involving huge factories and investment by a transnational corporation.
nodes.response: Microfinance loans can also support the development of new jobs in industry, at a smaller scale.

nodes.misconception: Development is always driven by governments and big international organisations.
nodes.response: While governments and organisations play a big role, development often happens through smaller, community-led projects where local people take charge.

nodes.misconception: Pupils rely on copying others to get the steps right rather than learning the steps themselves.
nodes.response: Exaplain to pupils the importance of showing resilience and rehearsing to become more familiar with the actions, directions and patterns.

nodes.misconception: Stratified sampling is biased and therefore produces a bad sample.
nodes.response: Stratified sampling is used to take a representative sample from the population. Selecting from within the strata can be done using a simple random sample.

nodes.misconception: Longer written tasks do not require careful planning and structuring.
nodes.response: It is essential to carefully plan and structure longer written tasks to avoid students writing off the topic and their work becoming unwieldy. The use of the acronym BORDER helps students to plan and review a relevant response.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not recognise the existence of a drag force on an object moving through air.
nodes.response: Demonstrate the effect of drag forces by dropping pieces or paper (folded and unfolded) and show they reach the ground at different times.

nodes.misconception: Street art is primarily an illegal activity or act of vandalism.
nodes.response: Street art is a legitimate and powerful form of artistic expression that addresses important social issues.

nodes.misconception: Street Pastors only support the people they directly encounter.
nodes.response: The work of Street Pastors improves the overall safety of local communities.

nodes.misconception: Digital ammeters are always accurate to the smallest amount they display.
nodes.response: Show pupils a copy of the specifications of the ammeters they are using that show how accurate they really are.

nodes.misconception: Weight training is only for people wanting to improve muscular strength.
nodes.response: Weight training improves strength, muscular endurance, power and speed, as well as increasing bone density and joint stability while reducing the risk of injury.

nodes.misconception: Being strong is about having big muscles.
nodes.response: Being physically strong relates to how our bodies are able to overcome the forces placed upon them. Strong muscles are essential for humans to complete everyday tasks and also help our joints to work effectively which helps to avoid injury and pain.

nodes.misconception: Packaging can only be reinforced from the inside.
nodes.response: Packaging can be reinforced on the inside and/or the outside using different methods.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think they need to write out their whole presention before they deliver it.
nodes.response: It can be much more effective to verbally plan and practice presentations without writing it in full. Approaching the tasks verbally can increase pupil confidence in articulating ideas out loud.

nodes.misconception: The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 was a legally binding agreement that could prevent all future wars.
nodes.response: The pact lacked enforcement mechanisms and relied on goodwill, making it more symbolic than practical.

nodes.misconception: Mental preparation is just for elite athletes.
nodes.response: Students should understand that everyone can benefit from mental preparation techniques and that performers in many fields of work practice them. They too could benefit in their own pursuits.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the bigger the spring constant, the more a spring stretches for a given force.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to apply understanding that the spring constant describes the stiffness of a spring. The bigger the spring constant, the harder it is to stretch (or compress) the spring.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the bigger the spring constant, the more a spring stretches for a given force.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to apply understanding that the spring constant describes the stiffness of a spring. The bigger the spring constant, the harder it is to stretch (or compress) the spring.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the bigger the spring constant, the more a spring stretches for a given force.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to apply understanding that the spring constant describes the stiffness of a spring. The bigger the spring constant, the harder it is to stretch (or compress) the spring.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the bigger the spring constant, the more a spring stretches for a given force.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to apply understanding that the spring constant describes the stiffness of a spring. The bigger the spring constant, the harder it is to stretch (or compress) the spring.

nodes.misconception: Extension is the extra amount the spring has stretched when a bigger force is applied.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils fully remove each hanging mass between measurements so they see the extension of the spring from its original length each time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it challenging to link the shape of a line graph with physical change in the real world.
nodes.response: Compare two sections of the graph, using the amount of extra stretch per newton as a measure of how easy the rubber band is to stretch.

nodes.misconception: The length of the spring is equal to the extension of the spring.
nodes.response: Focus on the fact that forces cause the length of the spring to change and pupils are measuring the size of that change.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not think that when you stretch some materials, they go back to the shape they were (and some snap).
nodes.response: Examples of different materials, some that stretch and return to their previous length, some that stretch and do not return to their previous length, and some materials that do not stretch and may snap if stretched.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to combine both power and accuracy, often focusing on just one.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that both power and accuracy are needed. Pupils should aim their hit and then think about the power when swinging through.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that every strike requires maximum power to be good.
nodes.response: Explain that different situations need different amounts of power, such as a shorter strike. Encourage pupils to also think about technique as well as power.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find when they move to throw/strike the ball, it goes somewhere different to where they had intended.
nodes.response: Encourage the striker/thrower to turn their body, as well as their head and shoulders towards the space they would like the ball to go.

nodes.misconception: Pupils underestimate the importance of following through with their racket when pushing/ striking the ball.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the follow through is important for accuracy and getting the right amount of power.

nodes.misconception: Pupils aim to strike the ball with a lot of power which can lead to missed timed strikes and no contact being made.
nodes.response: Power can range from the small amount of power needed to make contact, to a lot of power to make the ball travel further.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not move their feet when striking the ball, leading to mistimed and awkward shots.
nodes.response: Almost every shot requires some foot movement and the players stance should allow for this by being on the balls of feet and with knees slightly bent. Practising footwork using a batting tee will make applying footwork to a moving ball easier.

nodes.misconception: Pupils swing back and forwards quickly to hit the ball with power but take their eyes off of the ball, causing them to miss it.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of keeping eyes on the ball to ensure pupils make good contact when hitting it.

nodes.misconception: When hitting the ball, pupils focus on power and hitting it as hard as they can, neglecting the need for technique and accuracy.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the importance of aiming and using the correct technique for the best accuracy. It is best to master this before attempting to add more power.

nodes.misconception: Operations in programs can only be performed on numbers.
nodes.response: Operations can be performed on different types of data. What the operator does can change depending on the data type it is being used with.

nodes.misconception: The random module will only generate random numbers.
nodes.response: The random module can generate random characters as well as numbers.

nodes.misconception: We need to sing loudly for it to be heard or for it to be 'good'.
nodes.response: Learning to sing using a range of dynamics is a key aspect of conveying the mood of a song. Pupils can explore what quality singing feels like, and the effect it can have, using a range of dynamics to suit the song.

nodes.misconception: Larger magnets are always stronger than smaller magnets.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching  as well as opportunities for children to explore different size magnets and their strengths.

nodes.misconception: That structural choices happen accidentally.
nodes.response: Structural choices are consciously made by the poet in order to influence the meaning of the poem.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find understanding the difference between 'general' and 'specific' facts challenging.
nodes.response: When reading aloud the model introduction, highlight the general facts. When reading sections one and two, highlight the specific facts.

nodes.misconception: Lots of students do not realise that this novel was actually inspired by an earlier, 19th century novel called 'Coral Island' by Ballantyne.
nodes.response: Golding uses the established genre and subverts its conventions to create a horrifying exploration of what evil truly is and where it comes from.

nodes.misconception: Mixing up the different body systems and terminology used for each (for example not realising the cardio-respiratory system refers to the heart and lungs).
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that muscular means muscles, skeletal means bones, cardio means heart, vascular means blood vessels and respiratory means lungs.

nodes.misconception: The alap - gat - jhala structure is just about changes in tempo from slow, to medium to fast.
nodes.response: While the tempo does change, the bigger changes are around melody. The alap explores the raga freely, the gat is more structured and the jhala is heavily improvised and virtuosic.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all plants look the same/similar with the same style petals and leaves.
nodes.response: Provide examples of flowering plants with leaves and petals of different shapes, sizes and colour.

nodes.misconception: There can be confusion between the role of ligaments and tendons.
nodes.response: Ligaments connect bone to bone to stabilise a joint whereas tendons attach muscle to bone to enable movement.

nodes.misconception: Children may not realise that trees are plants.
nodes.response: Explanation that trees are a type of plant.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to appreciate the relative scales between each layer and features of the mantle.
nodes.response: Use common models (boiled egg or an orange) to stress the relative sizes and use multiple demonstrations to model features of the mantle.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that intermolecular forces exist within a molecule, unaware of the significant difference in strength between chemical bonds within atoms and the forces between molecules.
nodes.response: Help students to make the link between the structure of the polymer and its property by using models. Point out where the intermolecular forces occur and compare this to where the chemical bonds are.

nodes.misconception: Which side of the heart is the left when you look at the body and which side is oxygenated versus deoxygenated.
nodes.response: The left side of the heart is nearest to your left armpit and carries oxygenated blood, the right side of the heart has deoxygenated blood (remember: LORD - left, oxygenated and right, deogygenated).

nodes.misconception: A program must run line by line from top to bottom.
nodes.response: A subrotuine is an 'out of line' block of code, which is typcially written at the top of a program and then called upon within the main program.

nodes.misconception: A program must run line by line from top to bottom.
nodes.response: A subprogram is an 'out of line' block of code, which is typcially written at the top of a program and then called upon within the main program.

nodes.misconception: Only the first question matters when you are thinking about ordering the questions in your branching database.
nodes.response: The first question is really important but you also need to think carefully about the order of the other questions so that the branching database works properly and all objects can be identified.

nodes.misconception: Hyperbole and exaggeration are the same thing.
nodes.response: Exaggeration is a broad term for overstating something beyond the truth, while hyperbole is a specific type of exaggeration used deliberately for emphasis or effect, often in a dramatic or humorous way.

nodes.misconception: Students may feel that their viewpoint needs to be established in the very first line or so.
nodes.response: Viewpoint can be alluded to in the first few lines and firmly established at the end of the first paragraph or section.

nodes.misconception: Planning each paragraph to describe a different aspect of the scene will always create an engaging description.
nodes.response: Describing something different in each paragraph does not necessarily lead to an interesting description - it is the way in which the paragraphs link and build curiosity and tension that can make it more engaging.

nodes.misconception: I can guess the meaning of the words I don't know just by looking at them.
nodes.response: Guessing the meaning is not a reliable strategy for most words in Spanish as it may lead to misunderstanding, especially for tricky or abstract vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: When comparing the modal class for two datasets, pupils may think that the dataset with the greatest modal class is the one which has the greatest frequency for its modal class
nodes.response: Use the frequency to identify the modal class for each dataset, but then compare the values within each class to determine which dataset has the greatest modal class.

nodes.misconception: One trend line appearing higher on a graph than a different trend line means the higher line shows more change over time.
nodes.response: It is the gradient of a trend line that informs how quickly something is changing with respect to time.

nodes.misconception: Reliance on counting strategies. Not recognising combinations of smaller quantities within 5
nodes.response: Play games involving dice outside of the lesson to encourage subitising of more familiar arrangements. Then, look at those unfamiliar, such as the way a group of cubes appears when dropped onto a table. 'I can see ___ and ___. I can see ___!'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think any group of words following a verb is an object.
nodes.response: A noun, noun phrase or pronoun that directly follows a verb can be an object.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that a passive sentence always contains the old subject of the active sentence.
nodes.response: Sometimes the old subject is removed completely like in this example: 'We passed the ball.' > 'The ball was passed.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe using a co-ordinating conjunction always creates a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Using a co-ordinating conjunction only creates a compound sentence if the conjunction is joining main clauses.

nodes.misconception: Some subordination joining words can join the same sentences as others e.g. 'because', 'so', 'when'.
nodes.response: Discuss this with pupils if it arises in the lesson and explain that they have different purposes within the sentence but can both function.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not recognise that different subordinating conjunctions have different meanings and uses.
nodes.response: Each subordinating conjunction has a specific meaning. Each subordinating conjunction is useful for different sentence contexts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an idea starting with 'because' makes complete sense on its own.
nodes.response: Make sure that 'because' always begins the second idea so that pupils can hear that the idea does not make complete sense by itself.

nodes.misconception: It can be difficult to think of sentences with 'so' and 'that'.
nodes.response: Provide lots of examples before expecting pupils to do this for themselves.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an idea starting with 'when' or 'if' makes complete sense on its own.
nodes.response: Make sure 'when' and 'if' are always presented as part of the second idea so that pupils can hear the idea does not make complete sense.

nodes.misconception: Children might struggle with the idea that two fractions, each with the same numerator and denominator but different numbers, can be equivalent. For example, four-fourths is equal to ten-tenths.
nodes.response: Use a fraction wall to help with this. Compare the rows and establish that the whole is the same so they are equivalent. Ask the children to list as many as they can which will help build confidence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with exponents especially which value to square when variables have coefficients
nodes.response: Reminder of priority of operations and the exponent acts on the value it is directly preceded by.

nodes.misconception: Indexing starts at 1 as that is the location of the first element.
nodes.response: In Python, and many other programming languages, indexing starts at 0.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often try to use a written method/algorithm which they know gives an accurate answer but don't understand why it works.
nodes.response: Encourage the pupils to be brave and remind them that this is about mental subtraction so, with practice, will be quicker than any written methods.

nodes.misconception: Children will often reverse the minuend and subtrahend because they don't always appear in the order that they would in an expression.
nodes.response: Give time to ensure that the children understand the bar model representation and encourage them to discuss which number is the minuend and which is the subtrahend before engaging in a strategy for mental subtraction.

nodes.misconception: Trying to subtract 3 from 2 for example without regrouping and seeing the difference as 1
nodes.response: Continually acknowledge the whole and the parts in each 'column' so that children know what we have and what is being subtracted.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that a smaller mixed number cannot be subtracted from a greater one if its fractional part is greater. E.g. five and three-quarters cannot be subtracted from six and one-quarter.
nodes.response: If the mixed numbers are close to each other, try to ‘find the difference’ by counting forwards on a number line from the part to the whole.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often try to use a written method/algorithm which they know gives an accurate answer but don't understand why it works.
nodes.response: Encourage the pupils to be brave and remind them that this is about mental subtraction so, with practice, will be quicker than any written methods.

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand that a one can be exchanged from a whole and the fraction rewritten. E.g. four can be rewritten as three and five-fifths to add subtraction of an amount of fifths.
nodes.response: Use of rods or drawings will support children to understand this exchange. Four is the same as three and one; one is the same as five fifths so four is the same and three and five fifths.

nodes.misconception: Children may think the multiple of ten before 43 is 30, or partition the subtrahend incorrectly when bridging, meaning they do not use the most efficient strategy.
nodes.response: Display and use the stem sentences to support articulation of how to find the previous multiple of ten. Use ten frames, number lines and one hundred squares to support with appropriate partitioning of numbers.

nodes.misconception: Children often find it difficult to understand the idea that any whole can be represented by a fraction with the same numerator and denominator.
nodes.response: You might want to list down some different real life examples such as slices of pizza or pie, complete sets of sticker pages, full packs of pens/pencils. Label each example with fraction notation so the children get a firmer understanding.

nodes.misconception: Children will rush to subtract both the numerator and the denominator when performing a subtraction of fractions with either structure in the lesson.
nodes.response: Reinforce the concept of the unit being the fraction which is denoted by the denominator. Get children to perform subtractions using real life objects before moving them onto using fractions instead, perhaps using unit fractions to begin with.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand column subtraction. They may use regrouping without grasping the reasoning behind the algorithm.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand the purpose of regrouping and the value of the numbers when they are using column subtraction. Spend more time using base ten blocks with regrouping if pupils are not ready to progress onto the formal algorithm.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to regroup in the ones and tens when the tens digit is zero.
nodes.response: Explain that pupils may need to regroup from the hundreds first, and then regroup in the ones. They still need to start with the numbers with the smallest place value. When crossing out, pupils need to cross out the '10' tens and replace with 9

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with the language of unitising.
nodes.response: Encourage children to read aloud and spot what they notice - which known fact can they see - what is the same/different?

nodes.misconception: Children may automatically count back in tens to subtract a multiple of ten.
nodes.response: Discuss efficiency and compare different methods. Use practical equipment to draw attention to the relationship between adding multiples of ten in two-digit numbers and the known facts they already possess.

nodes.misconception: Children may spot a pattern and be able to continue it based on noticing numbers simply increasing or decreasing without making the generalisations needed to understand why this happens.
nodes.response: Encourage children to articulate not only the pattern, but also why it has occurred, at first using practical equipment to prove it, then mentally visualising and manipulating the numbers involved.

nodes.misconception: When subtracting numbers in standard form, pupils can also add the exponents of 10.
nodes.response: The use of the place value chart shows how the magnitude does not change to the sum of the powers of 10. The place value chart can support pupils to make the correct addition or subtraction of large or small numbers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly partition the subtrahend.
nodes.response: Partition the subtrahend to count back to ten or a tens number. Use number pairs that total ten to help subtract whatever is left.

nodes.misconception: Difference can only be found by counting back.
nodes.response: Difference can be calculated by subtracting the subtrahend from the minuend or by counting between the subtrahend and the minuend.

nodes.misconception: When there's more than one subtrahend, the order cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Subtrahends can be subtracted from the minuend in any order. They can also be added together before being subtracted.

nodes.misconception: Minus and a minus make a plus, 2 negatives make a positive, double negative makes a positive, etc.
nodes.response: The use of additive inverses should avoid this common misconception.  Be aware that pupils maybe already be familiar with this statement.

nodes.misconception: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway; using highlighters can help to visualise this pathway.

nodes.misconception: If we show compassion, we can eliminate suffering entirely.
nodes.response: While compassion can help reduce suffering, it doesn’t always eliminate it, as some suffering may be inevitable or necessary for personal growth and moral development.

nodes.misconception: Children may want to take their pencil off before forming the suffix as they see it as separate to the root word.
nodes.response: Encourage children by modelling and emphasising that the pencil only comes off the page once the letter string is complete. Getting them to identify the last letter before starting can help to remind them of this.

nodes.misconception: The lead out for the letter r can be challenging for children.
nodes.response: When introducing the suffix -er and its formation, take time to allow the students to investigate and practise the 'dip down' for the lead out.

nodes.misconception: The cursive formation of the letter f, with the lead in and lead out loop, can be challenging for students.
nodes.response: When modelling, ensure to include examples of words with the letter f at the beginning of the word and in the middle. Remind pupils that the letter f is the only letter in the alphabet with an ascender and a descender, therefore two loops.

nodes.misconception: Some children will lift their pencil before the letter string has completed.
nodes.response: Remind the children that the letters want to hold hands and if they lift their pencil then the connection is broken. Speaking out loud, while modelling, to highlight this will support the children to apply it in their practice.

nodes.misconception: Sufism is a branch of Islam, like Sunni and Shi'ism.
nodes.response: Sufis can be either Sunni or Shi'a, athough the majority are Sunni.

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Clear explanation of how properties of materials make them suitable or unsuitable for a particular purpose.

nodes.misconception: 'Everyone is entitled to their own opinion', therefore there is no need to justify our opinions.
