nodes.response: Although we are all entitled to our opinion, justifying your opinion allows people to trust and listen to your opinion more carefully.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that 'Suleiman the Lawgiver' and 'Suleiman the Magnificent' are different people.
nodes.response: Explain that these are different names used for the same person to remember different elements of his time as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the failure to capture Vienna meant Suleiman was a failure.
nodes.response: Emphasise that setbacks are normal and Suleiman was still able to extend the Ottoman Empire to its greatest ever reach.

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the buildings commissioned by Suleiman are not used or in existence today.
nodes.response: Many of them still exist 500 years later and can be seen today, particularly the mosques and religious buildings which have been continually renovated over time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think self-assessment is similar to being assessed in something.
nodes.response: Self-assessment is an opportunity to reflect and does not count towards any assessment. It is positive. Leaders are able to grow from self-assessments as they recognise strengths, but more importantly, identify keys areas of improvement.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the purposes of the different sections of the story.
nodes.response: Each section serves a different purpose for the reader or viewer. One section may intend to set a scene whilst another may increase tension.

nodes.misconception: The mean is the most meaningful average.
nodes.response: Looking at bimodal data, trimodal data or data with extreme outliers. Context may be relevant.

nodes.misconception: We can only find out information that is written in the text.
nodes.response: You can infer greater meaning about a person or event by looking for clues within the text.

nodes.misconception: Children might think that the story is only about a pebble being found and its story.
nodes.response: The author conveys the deeper meaning that everything that exists has a story to tell and builds our understanding of the world.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to draw out the most significant moments when summarising.
nodes.response: Model eliciting the key parts of Walter's life - using the contents page to support. Have these accessible during the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.

nodes.misconception: The sounds spelling correspondence [h] is pronounced as it is in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, to pronounce words starting with [h], we ignore it and pronounce the vowel that follows.

nodes.misconception: -AR verbs have the same ending for the 'I' form of the present and preterite tense.
nodes.response: In the present tense, the 1st person singular ends in '-o' and in the preterite, the 1st person singular ends in '-é'.

nodes.misconception: Use the simple present to translate future plans from German into English, e.g., 'Nächstes Jahr spiele ich Tennis.' - 'Next year I play tennis.'.
nodes.response: Use the present continuous in English when translating future plans (that are expressed in the present tense) from German, e.g., 'Nächstes Jahr spiele ich Tennis.' - 'Next year I am going to play tennis.'.

nodes.misconception: We swap the verb and subject around to ask a closed, yes/no question as in English, e.g. 'Are we going to go on holiday?'
nodes.response: All closed questions in Spanish have the same word order as the equivalent statement, e.g.'Vamos a ir de vacaciones' ('We are going to go on holiday') → '¿Vamos a ir de vacaciones?' ('Are we going to go on holiday?').

nodes.misconception: The spellings 'ss' and 'ß' make different sounds.
nodes.response: The spellings 'ss' and 'ß' make the same sound, but write 'ss' after a short vowel, 'ß' after a long vowel.

nodes.misconception: To say 'I'm eating pizza' in French it's 'je mange pizza'.
nodes.response: In English we often leave out the article, but in French we must use the partitive article when referring to an unspecified amount of food or drink. So we would say: 'Je mange de la pizza' because 'pizza' is feminine.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may over generalise and think that the sum of all possible events sum to 1. E.g. when rolling a standard six-sided dice, P(multiple of 6) + P(factor of 6) = 1.
nodes.response: Emphasise that probabilities sum to 1 when the events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. E.g. in the calculation P(multiple of 6) + P(factor of 6), the outcome '6' is counted twice.

nodes.misconception: A tall shape is only achieved by stretching both arms upwards.
nodes.response: Whilst stretching both arms upwards is an example of a tall shape, there are many others. These might include twists, tilts, balances etc. By encouraging the pupils beyond their initial response they will think more deeply and creatively.

nodes.misconception: The supply chain starts from where the product is processed.
nodes.response: The supply chain starts from the extraction of the raw materials.

nodes.misconception: Large-scale protests must mean that most people are against something.
nodes.response: A majority of people rarely, if ever, get involved in public protests, so we cannot draw absolute conclusions about what the majority thinks.

nodes.misconception: If you can't see the outcome of your performance, you are unable to learn how to improve.
nodes.response: Receiving feedback from teammates and other pupils about your performance will enable you to learn and make progress.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often struggle with combining the different phases of the triple jump in the correct sequence.
nodes.response: Build up to the full performance gradually, without an approach to begin with and gradually introducing one at walking pace and then jogging pace. Have a partner coach the performer to check their coordination and technique to quickly correct errors.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the mean rate of reaction with the instantaneous rate of reaction, thinking they are the same or not understanding the distinction between the two.
nodes.response: The tasks give pupils s the opportunity to distinguish between mean and instantaneous rate of reaction by calculating both from the same set of data.

nodes.misconception: That a larger surface area produces a larger volume/mass of product.
nodes.response: The experiment should help pupils realise they produce the same mass of carbon dioxide when using the same mass of calcium carbonate chips and powder.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the slant length (which is needed to find the curved surface area of the cone or frustum) with the perpendicular (or vertical) height.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to clearly label their diagrams, indicating the perpendicular height with a right-angle symbol. They may need to use Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry to calculate the slant length.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not subtract overlapping faces from their surface area calculation.
nodes.response: Ask the pupils to visualise turning around/rotating the compound solid, and consider which faces of the component solids would always be hidden.

nodes.misconception: Any arrangement of 6 square-faces will result in the net of a cube.
nodes.response: Some arrangements of 6 squares will result in some of them overlapping when the shape is folded into 3D, resulting in an incomplete cube.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may overlook whether they have been given the diameter or radius of the circles.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to always write down the radius before any calculation of the surface area is started.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to avoid sketching of nets or faces and in turn miss information.
nodes.response: Reassure pupils that a sketch does not need to be perfect and just needs to convey the key information.

nodes.misconception: Adding too many decorations will make the mask too busy or overwhelming.
nodes.response: It’s important to find balance in the mask’s design. Decoration can enhance the mask and highlight specific areas, such as the eyes or mouth, without overcrowding the mask’s overall look. Less can be more in some areas.

nodes.misconception: Timbers need a varnish to protect them.
nodes.response: There are many different options to finish the surface of timber and these are chosen depending on the type of timber, intended use, planned aesthetics etc.

nodes.misconception: When cutting complex shapes, we move the scissors rather than the paper.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to move the paper, rather than the scissors when cutting, with their thumbs facing upwards towards the ceiling.

nodes.misconception: I am not a qualified first aider so I can't help someone in need.
nodes.response: Basic knowledge can allow you to help with minor injuries. Knowing what to do in certain circumstances means that you can support and hopefully make a difference for any more major situations.

nodes.misconception: Building a more sustainable future is just the responsibility of governments.
nodes.response: Building a more sustainable future takes action from all levels of society, inidviudals, community and government.

nodes.misconception: Accents don't affect how we pronounce Spanish words.
nodes.response: Accents are very important and can differentiate between past and present. When we pronounce words with accents, we must remember to stress that syllable. For example, the verb 'caminó' means 'he, she, it walked' while 'camino' means 'I walk'.

nodes.misconception: In the preterite tense, er and -ir verbs have different endings.
nodes.response: -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the preterite: -í for 'I', -iste for 'you' and -ió for 'she, he, it'.

nodes.misconception: Critiquing is negative and criticising.
nodes.response: Critiquing involves looking at the positive and negative aspects of a product.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that all buildings are the same and don’t understand why some materials are better for the environment.
nodes.response: Some buildings waste energy, while others are designed to protect nature.

nodes.misconception: Sustainability is only about protecting the environment.
nodes.response: Sustainability also includes improving people’s lives and meeting their needs fairly.

nodes.misconception: Fabrics are always joined by stitching.
nodes.response: Fabrics can be joined using stitching, adhesives and mechanical fixings.

nodes.misconception: Customer decisions don’t make a difference to global fish populations.
nodes.response: Eating fish from well-managed fisheries helps prevent overfishing, protects marine biodiversity, and ensures fish populations remain healthy for future generations.

nodes.misconception: Sustainable buildings have to be buildings that are new.
nodes.response: Sustainable buildings can reuse materials from old buildings or be older buildings that have been redesigned.

nodes.misconception: Public transport is less convenient and more expensive that private transport.
nodes.response: Well-designed public transport systems can be faster, cheaper, and more reliable than driving, especially in urban areas with congestion and parking costs.

nodes.misconception: Only large global organisations, like the United Nations or Greenpeace, are responsible for protecting rainforests, and that local communities have little impact on sustainability efforts.
nodes.response: Both global and local actions are vital for rainforest sustainability. While global efforts fund and advocate, local communities protect forests through reforestation, sustainable farming, and ecotourism.

nodes.misconception: The only problem with using fossil fuels to generate electricity is that burning them produces greenhouse gases.
nodes.response: The lesson will explore additional concerns including the finite supply of fossil fuels and the fact that burning them causes air pollution.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all food is produced in the same way.
nodes.response: Explanation of how foods can be produced and harvested in different ways with differing environmental impacts.

nodes.misconception: Sustainable development is all about the environment.
nodes.response: One pillar of sustainable development is the environment but sustainable development is only achieved when social and economic aspects are also considered.

nodes.misconception: Wood is (always) a renewable resource.
nodes.response: Discuss with the pupils the different ways in which we can obtain and regenerate (or not) the wood we use. Highlight that trees do not necessarily replace all the wood we take from them, and even if they do, it may take many years of growing.

nodes.misconception: 'Grey' water includes the reuse of water already used to flush the toilet - yuck!
nodes.response: ‘Grey’ water does not include water that has been used to flush toilets as that water is too contaminated to be used again without treatment. However, one of the possible uses for ‘grey’ water from baths, showers, sinks etc is to flush toilets.

nodes.misconception: Cold water shock only occurs in the winter.
nodes.response: Cold water shock can occur all year round in waters around the UK.

nodes.misconception: All switches have to be pressed to work.
nodes.response: Switches control the flow of electricity in a circuit and can be pushed, slid, twisted or pulled.

nodes.misconception: All electrical appliances and circuits use the same type of switch.
nodes.response: Children will be introduced to a wide range of switches.

nodes.misconception: I have to translate 'didn't' into French.
nodes.response: There is no direct translation for 'didn't' in French. Using 'ne ... pas' with the perfect tense expresses the equivalent of  'didn't' in French.

nodes.misconception: The closed [eu] and the open [eu/œu] sounds are the same.
nodes.response: There are open vowel sounds and closed vowel sounds in French. The closed [eu] sound is like the [eu] in 'peu', it is short and sharp. The open [eu/oœu] sound is a longer sound like the [œu] in 'sœur'.

nodes.misconception: You need to look at the floor to avoid the swords.
nodes.response: If working carefully, it is possible to remember where the 'sword' markings are and avoid them. This skill takes a great deal of practice.

nodes.misconception: There are no common symbols across literature.
nodes.response: There are many common symbols across literature which writers use knowing that many of their readers will know what they mean. For example, a crown to symbolise power. A rose to symbolise love. Birds to symbolise freedom.

nodes.misconception: A symbol has only one meaning for everyone.
nodes.response: Symbols can mean different things in different cultures or to different people.

nodes.misconception: Students think the novella's title was chosen simply to reflect the festive period it covers.
nodes.response: The title is more symbolic of Dickens' intentions - he intended for the message from this text to be spread far and wide, much like a carol.

nodes.misconception: That the animals feel negatively towards the rituals and ideas put forward by the pigs.
nodes.response: Think about the response to Beasts of England. Is this same atmosphere created by Napoleon's parade? Why are the pigs' rituals different?

nodes.misconception: If you are in solitude, you feel lonely.
nodes.response: Solitude can be a pleasant state, one that lots of people seek out. It is different from feeling lonely or isolated.

nodes.misconception: Students often do not understand the depth of meaning that symbolism can provide.
nodes.response: Symbols communicate hidden or deeper meanings to the reader, so that they can better understand the characters or themes of the text.

nodes.misconception: Words are the only way of explaining things.
nodes.response: People express thoughts and feelings in lots of different ways.

nodes.misconception: All symbols are religious.
nodes.response: Some symbols represent a faith or belief, though not all members will choose these. There are many other symbols which are not religious and represent other groups or information.

nodes.misconception: Pupils create 1 balance idea and think they are finished, instead of trying a range of ideas. Pupils only work on one part of the apparatus and fail to try a range of apparatus to create their ideas.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that they must try out multiple ideas and use a range of apparatus in order to be successful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget the line of symmetry in their balances. Pupils always mirror their partner when creating symmetrical balances and always want to connect to their partner using the same body parts.
nodes.response: The content in cycle 3 will help with this but pupils will need lots of model examples to see how symmetrical balances can still be created without always mirroring their partner.

nodes.misconception: Improvisation in music is only done on instruments and not the voice.
nodes.response: Scat singing, from jazz music is one type of vocal improvisation. Other types include the sargams of Hindustani and Carnatic music from India, freestyle rap, even yodelling!

nodes.misconception: Beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Whilst syncopated rhythms are connected to the offbeats, this does not mean they are the same thing. Beats occur at regularly spaced intervals, with the rhythm the pattern that fits inside and inbetween these.

nodes.misconception: Syncopated rhythms are really complicated.
nodes.response: In its simplest form, syncopation is just rhythmic patterns that emphasise the offbeat. They can be simple rhythms, but the emphasis on the offbeat can create an interesting, but not necessarily difficult, sound to recreate.

nodes.misconception: Once we've performed, we don't need to keep thinking about the learning.
nodes.response: Reflecting on our performance is a valuable tool not only to feel a sense of pride in the skills we've developed, but also to see which areas of our musical learning need more focus.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe all words have an antonym e.g. chicken/duck; tree/plant.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that these are not strictly opposites - they are just different! Most antonyms are nouns and verbs.

nodes.misconception: The same words act as prepositions and adverbs or as prepositions and subordinating conjunctions.
nodes.response: Prepositions are followed by nouns; subordinating conjunctions are in clauses; adverbs modify verbs and adjectives.

nodes.misconception: There can be confusion between the role of ligaments and tendons.
nodes.response: Ligaments connect bone to bone to stabilise a joint whereas tendons attach muscle to bone to enable movement.

nodes.misconception: Misunderstanding the meaning of acoustic because the lesson examples are played on an iPad/computer.
nodes.response: Make it clear that the iPad/computer is imitating acoustic sound.

nodes.misconception: Systems are simple with just one input, process and output.
nodes.response: Systems can be complex with multiple inputs, processes and outputs, feedback and variables.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a scrum and line out in T1 rugby are contested and they push to get the ball.
nodes.response: T1 rugby is a non contact game therefore the scrum and lineouts are both uncontested. They are used to draw players into an area to create space on the pitch following a restart.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that performance is only determined by how many tries you scored.
nodes.response: A player can have a strong impact without getting a try by helping their team keep possession, organise defence or create space for others.

nodes.misconception: Computational thinking means writing code for everything.
nodes.response: While coding is a way to implement solutions, computational thinking can be applied to problems that don't require coding at all and should be seen as a set of processes that help people solve problems.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the wrong hand which leads to fouls and ineffective tackles, or they dive into the tackle, allowing attackers to easily sidestep away.
nodes.response: Always use the nearest hand to flick the ball away. Stay balanced when tackling, moving your feet quickly and timing the tackle properly.

nodes.misconception: Pupil think that if they go in to tackle at the legs they will get kicked in the face.
nodes.response: If you tackle low, with your head to the side and wrap their legs with your arms, they’ll go down safely and you won’t get kicked.

nodes.misconception: Running up quickly to tackle the ball carrier is always the best thing to do.
nodes.response: Moving up quickly to tackle the ball carrier is only the right thing to do if the rest of your defensive line is with you, as you can leave gaps which makes it easy for the ball carrier to stop you and break up the pitch to score a try.

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget that after making a tackle, they need to get back onside in a straight line.
nodes.response: Response: after a tackle, the whole defensive line need to be back onside 10m from the play of the ball. If you are not moving as a flat line, you leave gaps for attackers to break through.

nodes.misconception: It's only the defenders that need to be good at tackling.
nodes.response: Tackling is a crucial skill for all players, not just defenders. Midfielders need to win possession and disrupt attacks, while forwards use tackling to press high up the pitch and regain the ball in attacking areas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that defending to mainly important when playing a defensive position or during set pieces.
nodes.response: Defence starts from the striker position and works all the back to the GK. Defending well as an individual leads to collective marking and reduction of attacking space and opportunities.

nodes.misconception: Children might be under the impression that all agricultural crops are grown for human consumption.
nodes.response: In fact the vast majority of European cereal crop production is used to feed animals (and create biofuels, rather than feeding people.

nodes.misconception: Charitable giving will solve poverty.
nodes.response: While charity helps, long-term solutions require addressing the root causes of poverty, such as unfair wages, corruption and climate change.

nodes.misconception: All the elements have to be achieved perfectly in order to produce a successful taiko performance.
nodes.response: There is a lot to consider when putting the performance together. Focus on playing and moving together with repeated ideas to start with. Working as a team and getting the count in and stance right is important to support the rest of the performance.

nodes.misconception: Mixing up the dongo and doko strikes and comfortably swapping from one to the other.
nodes.response: The dongo is a shuffle feel, whilst the doko and kara are even beats. Practise alternating from one to the other so pupils can recognise them easily and can comfortably swap from one to the other in a performance.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that anything found outside is natural, even if it is actually human-made. For example, bricks, fences, playground equipment, or painted surfaces.
nodes.response: Remind children that natural means it comes from nature and wasn’t made by people. Human-made means humans designed or built it, even if you find it outside.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may hold the camera or device in a  landscape grip instead of portrait.
nodes.response: Pupils should hold their device/camera with a portrait grip.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that there is a very clear distinction between poetry and music lyrics.
nodes.response: Encourage students to consider what the poetry and song lyrics have in common. For example the use of verses and refrains, as well as the use of figurative language, often crosses over.

nodes.misconception: Every idea must be innovative and interdisciplinary.
nodes.response: Sometimes taking ideas and inspiration from others or following a tried and tested path moves you forward.

nodes.misconception: I still need to use the subject pronoun even if I am using a name or a noun before the verb form.
nodes.response: A noun or name can replace a subject pronoun. So 'ils chantent ensemble' could be changed to 'les garçons chantent ensemble' or 'David, Robert et Jacques chantent ensemble'.

nodes.misconception: There is just one way of saying 'you' in French like in English.
nodes.response: There are two ways of saying 'you' in French. We use 'tu' for 'you singular' and 'vous' for 'you plural'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it is always necessary to give advice when someone shares their feelings.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider that they may not be well-placed to advise in some situations; it can be absolutely fine to just show that you understand the person's feelings and that you will support them.

nodes.misconception: Artists only talk about their work to promote it in galleries and museums.
nodes.response: Artists might talk about their work for engagement and promotion, in a variety of contexts.

nodes.misconception: 'Haben' is a weak verb.
nodes.response: 'Haben' is an irregular verb because it does not follow a regular pattern of changes in the same way a weak verb does, even if the 'ich', 'wir' and 'sie' (they) forms look like weak verbs.

nodes.misconception: 'I am doing' is translated as 'Ich bin machen'.
nodes.response: There is no present continuous ('-ing' form) tense in German, and therefore no use of the verb 'sein'. Use a time adverb to express what you are doing right now in German, e.g., 'Ich mache jetzt ...'.

nodes.misconception: tan(60°) is double tan(30°).
nodes.response: The values of tan of an angle do not scale linearly. From the unit circle, we see that an angle of 30° meets a tangent to the circle at a height of approx. 0.58 units, whilst an angle of 60° meets the same tangent at a height of approx. 1.73 units.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have stereotypical views about what Tanzania is like and may not be aware of its geographical diversity.
nodes.response: Additional photographs of Tanzania could be found online to further emphasise the geographical diversity of this country.

nodes.misconception: Pupils serve towards the middle of the court which is easy to return.
nodes.response: Aiming their serve to force a defensive shot from their opponent is a much stronger way to start the point.

nodes.misconception: Sunni Muslims do not believe in the justice of Allah (adalat) because it is not mentioned in the six articles of faith.
nodes.response: Al-Adl ('the Just') is one of the 99 names of Allah and is important to Sunni Muslims as well as Shia Muslims. While it isn't in the six articles of faith, it may be seen as part of a belief in tawhid - the oneness of God.

nodes.misconception: That Muslims believe Allah is a different 'god' to the God of Christianity and Judaism.
nodes.response: Allah is Arabic for 'The God' and the Qur'an teaches that Allah is the God of the Abrahamic faiths. Moses/Abraham/Jesus and others are all significant prophets in Islam, and known through Arabic spellings of their names; they are the same prophets.

nodes.misconception: Pupils attack one end of the court similar to all other invasion games focused on territory and seek to tackle/intercept passes between the opposition.
nodes.response: Tchoukball is a unique game where both teams can score at both ends by throwing the ball into the rebound net and not being caught by the opposition. You are not allowed to tackle with the opposition while they are in possession of the ball.

nodes.misconception: You can pronounce the 's' in plural adjectives: contents.
nodes.response: The 's' is often silent at the end of a word, it is an SFC. The 's' in plural adjectives is silent.

nodes.misconception: Many pupils do not consider how adaptations and conditions can make games more enjoyable for different people, preferring to play the full version of a game even when it might be a struggle.
nodes.response: Helping pupils to be conscious of other people's motivations and understand how adaptations can make the game more accessible and enjoyable.

nodes.misconception: Teammates are so busy running away from taggers that they forget to look carefully and collide with others.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to avoid collisions, they must look ahead and dodge others by changing direction and slowing down.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they must be standing up to create letter shapes. When creating words, pairs make their letter shapes in the wrong order, or facing the wrong way, so that the whole word is not seen.
nodes.response: Letter shapes can be formed standing or lying down. Encourage teams to imagine that they are another team looking at their word, are all letters in the correct order and facing the same direction?

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't realise it's their turn to move.
nodes.response: Players stand on a 'next player' floor marker to help them to know who's turn it is next.  Remind pupils to encourage each other with kind words when it's their turn.

nodes.misconception: Pupils shout loudly thinking this will improve communication. Pupils high 5 with too much force.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of good sentences spoken at a normal talking volume. Be explicit about using gentle high 5s and ask pupils to imagine how a butterfly would high 5 their friend.

nodes.misconception: Pupils throw the ball up too high or throw overarm and then blame their partner for being unable to catch it.
nodes.response: Encourage underarm throwing, using gentle passes so the ball makes a rainbow shape in the air. Remind pupils that teamwork requires all individuals to work together and encouraging others.

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't concentrate, so they don't realise when it is their turn. Other team members shout at them to take their turn.
nodes.response: Encourage players to pay attention to their team so they know when it's their turn. Other team members can kindly prompt them if they miss their turn.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that only the selected pupil performing in the event needs to focus on it.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand that the whole team has a part to play in each event. Helping with tactics, motivating and encouraging each other are ways they can all be involved.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think balance is only a static position, such as standing on one leg, and is only really needed in sports like gymnastics.
nodes.response: The ability to balance whilst static is essential in sport and in life, be that on one leg or two, but it is important to highlight the kinaesthetic awareness that unlocks success is also required in dynamic balances (i.e. while on the move).

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a position in volleyball is determined by their physical location on the court.
nodes.response: Rotations do occur based on court location but players are also assigned positions, with an assigned role, which they can move into directly after the serve.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to get into an effective defensive position.
nodes.response: A quick transition out of a set position will reduce the chance of this occuring.

nodes.misconception: Pupils always use the same type of throw for passing and shooting (i.e. overarm with a focus on power and a direct route to the rebound frame).
nodes.response: It is easy to defend a square shot or an obvious attack angle at the rebound frame. To outwit the opposition, look to vary the type, angle and pace of shots as well as utilising fakes (e.g. a switch).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may argue about decisions, particularly close calls such as run outs. This can often lead to the decision going in the favour of the more dominant or boisterous pupils.
nodes.response: Pupils should experience the umpire role to practise making fair decisions and develop empathy, helping them understand not to challenge calls.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to recognise the right movement to execute different strategies, which results in losing possession or missed opportunities.
nodes.response: Break down the games so you can focus on good decision making. Stop game play when a poor is decision made to ask pupils to identify and resolve the problem.

nodes.misconception: Alliteration and onomatopoeia are devices used only in fiction writing (e.g. stories).
nodes.response: Alliteration and onomatopoeia are both types of aural device because they link to how writers use sounds. This means they are particularly useful for speeches because they are delivered aloud (as opposed to read).

nodes.misconception: Students often place the vanishing point too low or high, or forget to use it consistently, which causes the drawing to look distorted or unrealistic.
nodes.response: Remember: the vanishing point sits on the horizon line, which is your eye level. All diagonal lines must meet at the vanishing point—even if it’s off the paper!

nodes.misconception: Technical drawings created in CAD are always correct and error-free.
nodes.response: Using CAD reduces human error; however, users must add correct and relevant dimensions. Incorrect constraints can also result in errors.

nodes.misconception: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’, as in English.
nodes.response: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils (and teachers and even textbooks) suggest that plate movement is due solely to convection currents.
nodes.response: Stress that the understanding of what drives of tectonic plate moment is still developing; using demonstrations to reinforce the current understanding of slab pull and ridge push are helpful. Avoid any demos that reinforce ideas the mantle is liquid.

nodes.misconception: Utilitarianism does not argue that any action is acceptable as long as it makes the majority happy.
nodes.response: Utilitarianism considers both the positive and the negative outcomes to determine which action produces the best overall consequences for the greatest number of people.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes forget to move the hour hand when showing quarter to or quarter past, instead leaving it pointing to the o'clock time.
nodes.response: This is covered in Cycle 2 of the lesson. Continual access to a geared clock allows this idea to be revisited both in and beyond the lesson. Plan opportunities for children to see the positions of both hands at quarter past and quarter to.

nodes.misconception: Because the representation of numbers 1 to 3 bear a resemblance to tallies, pupils may be tempted to continue in this fashion, for example writing 4 in Roman numerals as IIII
nodes.response: Discuss with pupils the idea of Roman numerals being based around a small number of 'rules', which are never broken. One such rule is that the same letter is never used more than three times in a row. Spend time really focusing on IV and IX.

nodes.misconception: The 10 on a clock is unusual as when the minute hand is pointing to 10, it is 10 minutes to the next hour. Pupils may overgeneralise, thinking, for example, when it points to 9, it is 9 minutes to.
nodes.response: As with many mathematical ideas, regular exploration and practise outside of the lesson is key to truly understanding them. Take frequent opportunities to count in five-minute intervals on a clock using minutes past and minutes to.

nodes.misconception: The lesson deals with the idea of minutes past the hour to 5 minutes past. Pupils may overgeneralise and say that when sixty minutes have gone past the hour we say sixty minutes past.
nodes.response: Ensure plenty of time is spent dealing with this concept and that pupils are comfortable with the idea that when the minute hand is pointing to 12, it is an o'clock time with no minutes having gone past the hour.

nodes.misconception: When showing times on clocks (for example drawing hands onto blank clock faces or manipulating mini-clocks with movable hands) pupils may not consider the position of the hour hand.
nodes.response: Frequent exposure to both examples and non-examples (such as those in the slide deck) will help pupils to see that the hour hand will not be in an 'o'clock' position if it is ___ minutes to ___.

nodes.misconception: When representing the time, pupils do not always remember that both the minute and the hour hand have a role to play when showing any given time - often leaving the hour hand in the o'clock position.
nodes.response: Lots of examples and non-examples are shown in Cycle 2 of the slide deck to tackle this misconception. However, practice makes perfect. Give frequent quickfire opportunities outside of the Maths lesson for pupils to show times on mini clocks.

nodes.misconception: The left hand side of the clock can cause pupils problems when reading the clock to the half hour. For example, because half past nine is between nine and ten, pupils might read it as half past ten.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on the word ‘past’ - which number has it gone past?

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often mix the hour hand and the minute hand, labelling each as the other.
nodes.response: The lesson presents two stem sentences which run through each cycle. The use of these stem sentences, alongside frequent opportunities to practise interpreting clocks, outside of the lesson will help pupils to secure the learning.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see the minute hand as the hour hand, treating wherever the minute hand is pointing to as o'clock.
nodes.response: The lesson deliberately chooses to present clocks featuring just an hour hand to really focus in on its purpose. O'clock times with the hour hand and minute hand feature later in the unit. Explain to pupils that clocks do not only have an hour hand.

nodes.misconception: Some students think pitching means just reading out facts about the design.
nodes.response: A strong pitch is more than just facts. It’s a story with a clear beginning, middle and end that shows your idea solves a problem and stands out from the rest.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult or forget to switch from a character voice to a narrator voice when they have finished saying the speech and they are saying the reporting clause.
nodes.response: Print a copy of the speech section of the story that shows the speech and reporting clause in different colours to support children in their oral rehearsal for different character's voices.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that water cannot exist in a gas state because they cannot see it. They may also think that evaporation only occurs at high temperatures.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain the existence of water vapour, even though it is invisible. By investigation, children observe and measure that evaporation occurs at all temperatures.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that water cannot exist in a gas state because they cannot see it.  They may also think that evaporation only occurs at high temperatures.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain the existence of water vapour, even though it is invisible.  By investigation, children observe and measure that evaporation occurs at all temperatures.

nodes.misconception: Increasing the temperature increases the rate product is formed, and therefore think a faster reaction produces more product.
nodes.response: Increasing the temperature will make the reaction proceed faster but will not change the amount of product formed. The reactants are the limiting factor, not the temperature.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the higher the level of coloured liquid on a thermometer, the higher the temperature.
nodes.response: Explore plenty of examples of thermometers with different scales so that children can see that they need to look at the scale in order to compare two temperatures and not just the height of the coloured liquid.

nodes.misconception: The Ten Commandments were only relevant at the time, or to people who follow an Abrahamic religion.
nodes.response: The Ten Commandments and other religious rules have influenced many laws still in place, including things such as Sunday trading laws in modern Britain.

nodes.misconception: Shi'a Muslims do not perform the Five Pillars.
nodes.response: Salah, sawm, zakah and Hajj are all part of the Ten Obligatory Acts. The Shahadah is also said by Shi'a Muslims, but as a statement of faith upon which the Obligatory Acts rest.

nodes.misconception: A diminished seventh chord is just like any other extended chord - a triad with added notes.
nodes.response: A diminished seventh chord is quite unique as every interval is the same size (three semitones). It is different from extended chords that add notes to a triad. It has been used for centuries as a tense, dramatic chord, including in silent movies.

nodes.misconception: From the 1950s onwards, the USSR's human rights record continually improve.
nodes.response: Under Khrushchev, more respect was shown for political and social freedoms but these restrictions were tightened again once Brezhnev took power in 1964.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that as air resistance increases, a falling object decelerates (slows down).
nodes.response: Analyse footage of a falling object played back in slow motion, or frame–by–frame, to show that the speed of a falling object increases, up to a maximum speed, and at no time does it slow down.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that as air resistance increases, a falling object decelerates (slows down).
nodes.response: Analyse footage of a falling object played back in slow motion, or frame–by–frame, to show that the speed of a falling object increases, up to a maximum speed, and at no time does it slow down.

nodes.misconception: All terrorists are religious or act because of religion
nodes.response: While some terrorists misuse religion, not all terrorism is religiously motivated. There are political, racial and ideological causes too (e.g. Oklahoma City bombing, KKK, white supremacist attacks). Religious usually terrorism and promote peace.

nodes.misconception: Completed vehicles are finished and therefore will not need any changes or alterations neeeded to them.
nodes.response: Testing and feedback is a good way to spot any problems with the vehicles and therefore time to correct, adapt and alter specific parts of the finished product and demonstrates that products always need reviewing and adapting to make them work.

nodes.misconception: Finished products cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Adaptations can be made to individual components in a product to improve effectiveness.

nodes.misconception: Evaluating is one person's opinion.
nodes.response: Evaluating is most effective if it involves more than one person's opinion and data gathered from testing.

nodes.misconception: Feedback and testing can only be completed once the object is made and finished.
nodes.response: Testing and feedback can be a continuous process through the making and designing process. Pupils may reflect on the positives and negatives of any changes made in their final evaluation and feedback.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly.
nodes.response: The imperfect is used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly, but it has other uses in different contexts. For example, it can be used to set the scene in a narrative account or story, and to describe general situations in the past.

nodes.misconception: Programs should only be tested when they are finished.
nodes.response: Programs should be tested often to check for mistakes. Fixing mistakes as the program develops makes sure that these mistakes don't cause bigger issues later on and affect other parts of the program.

nodes.misconception: You only need to test your program when you have finished writing it.
nodes.response: Test your program often, especially after you finish a section.

nodes.misconception: Once a final product is complete, no further iterations or improvements are needed.
nodes.response: Designers constantly seek to improve and develop their designs and products, no product is ever perfect.

nodes.misconception: A test plan should only include data that will cause a program to not work.
nodes.response: A test plan should contain a range of test data, including normal, erroneous and boundary.

nodes.misconception: Penetration testing is illegal or the same as hacking.
nodes.response: Penetration testing is legal and ethical when done with permission. It's a form of ethical hacking used to help organisations find and fix security weaknesses before real hackers exploit them.

nodes.misconception: Testing only happens at the end of the making process.
nodes.response: Testing should happen throughout the making process. This allows the designers and engineers to change / alter and improve any aspects as they move through the making process.

nodes.misconception: Data always involves numbers.
nodes.response: Data is information and can be recorded using both numbers and words.

nodes.misconception: All products made for use in or around water need to be waterproof.
nodes.response: Clothing used for swimming ie, trunks, costumes, shorts and wetsuits, are not waterproof.

nodes.misconception: Absorbent materials hold water on their surface.
nodes.response: Absorbency involves the liquid being drawn into the material.

nodes.misconception: Testing is something you only do at the end of a project.
nodes.response: Testing is carried out throughout the development process. There are also specific stages and methods of testing that can be adopted. An overall approach to testing should be agreed and planned depending on the requirements of the system.

nodes.misconception: Models need to work first time.
nodes.response: Through testing and repeat testing, models can be tried and adapted to work.

nodes.misconception: Hardness testing is destructive.
nodes.response: Although an indentation is left in the test piece, hardness testing is less destructive than many other working property tests, such as tensile testing.

nodes.misconception: Testing only happens when the final prototype has been made.
nodes.response: Testing should happen throughout the iterative journey, so that design decisions are made to meet design requirements and produce a successful design solution.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes on method, results confusion, and poor descriptions using inaccurate terminology.
nodes.response: Methods and results are described, demonstrated and tested throughout, and methods tried by pupils with results gathered and analysed. Repeated review of results occurs throughout the lesson, and methods and results are applied to novel questions.

nodes.misconception: Might not recognise that the arrangement is still the same when it has been rotated or flipped.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunity to explore practically and model rotating, flipping and comparing arrangements.

nodes.misconception: The same text entered into two separate text files will always result in the same file size.
nodes.response: How the text has been encoded will affect the file size of a text file. ASCII uses 8 bits per character whereas Unicode uses up to 32 bits. Therefore the choice of character encoding affects the overall file size of the same text.

nodes.misconception: The same text entered into two separate text files will always result in the same file size.
nodes.response: How the text has been encoded will affect the file size of a text file. ASCII uses 7 bits per character whereas Unicode uses up to 32 bits. Therefore the choice of character encoding affects the overall file size of the same text.

nodes.misconception: Each period had a single defining texture (e.g. Baroque = polyphonic).
nodes.response: There were typical uses of texture for each period. For example, Baroque composers often used polyphonic textures, much more than Classical composers. However, within each period, there were examples of all textures being used and lots of variety.

nodes.misconception: The description thick texture relates to the number of people performing and loud dynamics.
nodes.response: Texture is more complex than thick/thin. Use good examples early on to show that texture is related to the different layers in the music and not neccesarily the number of performers. Show how lots of performers could be performing in a thin texture.

nodes.misconception: Changing the voicing of a chord is the same as changing the chord inversion.
nodes.response: They are not the same thing. The inversion of the chord is determined by which note is at the bottom (the root or a different note). The voicing is how the notes are spread above this - whether they are close together or far apart.

nodes.misconception: Texture is only a visual quality, it doesn't add meaning to your work.
nodes.response: Texture is one of the tools artists use as a visual language to communicate.

nodes.misconception: Texture describes something rough, bumpy or hard to touch.
nodes.response: Remind students that textures can be rough, hard and bumpy but they can also be smooth, soft and fuzzy.

nodes.misconception: Art should be something we instantly recognise and physically last a long time.
nodes.response: Art may not be a recognisable image and may exist only in a specific timeframe.

nodes.misconception: Only the USSR made compromises during the crisis.
nodes.response: Both superpowers agreed to compromises in order to avoid war and resolve the crisis. Soviet missiles were withdrawn from Cuba whilst the US promised not to invade Cuba and to withdraw its own missiles from Turkey.

nodes.misconception: The 1807 Slave Trade Act freed all enslaved people in the British Empire.
nodes.response: The 1807 Slave Trade Act did not free all enslaved people in the British Empire, but did ban the buying, selling and transportation of enslaved individuals from that point forward.

nodes.misconception: Tsunamis are just big waves.
nodes.response: Tsunamis are caused by displacement of the ocean, not wind blowing over the surface. Tsunami waves don’t break, they come as a fast-moving wall of water, which can be far bigger and faster than a normal wave. They can also flood kilometres inland.

nodes.misconception: If someone survives and is not injured during the earthquake, they are then safe.
nodes.response: Since many survivors had to stay in crowded shelters or sleep outside, the risk of diseases increased. In addition, strong aftershocks hit the area, damaging buildings that were already unstable.

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Reminders of the difference between the object, what it is used for, and the material it is made of. Use of real-life objects for children to explore to aid this understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that compost is just dirt or mud, or is no different from soil.
nodes.response: Explain that compost has a different composition to soil, and is full of nutrients that are beneficial to growing plants.

nodes.misconception: Christians only follow Jesus' teachings because of their belief in judgement.
nodes.response: Although the Bible makes it clear that there are consequences in the afterlife for actions in this life, for many Christians, the desire to live a good life is rooted in love for God and faith in Jesus as the saviour, not a fear of judgement.

nodes.misconception: Christians believe that Jesus will be the only person to be resurrected.
nodes.response: Many Christians believe that Jesus' resurrection is proof that resurrection is possible for ordinary people in the afterlife.

nodes.misconception: Students assume the Agricultural Revolution was predominantly facilitated by changes in technology.
nodes.response: Farming tech in common use didn't change much. Improvements in agriculture occurred mainly because of the use of new farming methods.

nodes.misconception: All punishments try to achieve the same thing.
nodes.response: Different punishments have different aims: some focus on changing the offender (like reformation), while others aim to protect society, discourage crime or deliver justice.

nodes.misconception: Students may aassume William Beveridge was a member of the Labour Party.
nodes.response: William Beveridge was actually a member of the Liberal Party.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may conflate the alternate segment theorem with alternate angles on parallel lines, thinking that the chord that meets the tangent is a transversal between two equal angles.
nodes.response: Alternate angles are only equal when the transversal is between parallel lines. In many of the examples for the alternate segment theorem, the tangent is not parallel to a chord.

nodes.misconception: The Declaration of Independence was signed after the settlers defeated the British in the Revolutionary War.
nodes.response: The Declaration of Independence was signed early on in the Revolutionary War and the US Constitution was signed after the war had concluded.

nodes.misconception: That Olympia and Mount Olympus are either the same thing or in the same place.
nodes.response: There are approximately 200 miles between the locations of Olympia and Mount Olympus. Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece, whereas Olympia was a large flat plain. Mount Olympus was the mythical home of the 12 major gods, Olympia was not.

nodes.misconception: When faced with a quadrilateral which has three vertices on a circle and one vertex at the centre, pupils may think that the interior angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
nodes.response: The two angles need to be subtended by the same arc for this circle theorem to apply. Therefore, it is the reflex angle at the centre of the circle which is twice the angle at the circumference.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may over-generalise the circle theorem by assume that all triangles that are inscribed in a circle are right-angled.
nodes.response: The triangle is only right-angled if one of its angles is subtended by the diameter. This also means that if the triangle is right-angled, then its hypotenuse is the diameter of the circle.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may reason that two angles are the same size, as they are subtended by the same chord.
nodes.response: Angles are equal, if they are in the same segment, subtended by the same arc, as well as subtended by the same chord.

nodes.misconception: Medieval and modern Church power is equivalent.
nodes.response: Explicitly outline the Church's organisational power: land ownership, clergy social status, and spiritual authority.

nodes.misconception: The power of the Church in the medieval and modern period is equivalent.
nodes.response: The medieval Church was a very powerful institution, it was involved in governing Anglo-Saxon England (as bishops served as advisors to kings) and it was a very wealthy landholder. The modern-day Church in England has less powers.

nodes.misconception: Church leaders had no role in how Anglo-Saxon England was governed.
nodes.response: Archbishops, bishops and other Church leaders could be part of the Witan, and that meant they were involved in advising the monarch about the government of Anglo-Saxon England.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that dividing England was a clever move for Alfred to make.
nodes.response: Alfred divided England and allowed the Vikings to control some areas. Alfred knew he could not get the Vikings to leave Britain as too many had already settled.

nodes.misconception: Anglo-Saxon monarchs had to be great warriors to be made king.
nodes.response: In fact some monarchs, such as Edward the Confessor, were not warriors but instead very religious men whose faith inspired others.

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxons are called that because only Angles and Saxons came to Britain.
nodes.response: 'Anglo-Saxon' is a term historians use to describe all the groups of tribes who came to Britain from Europe around this time.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that rocks are all just called 'rock' and they don't have different appearances and different names.
nodes.response: Make sure the rock samples you give them are not actual objects, e.g. an ornament, so they are not able to use usage as a way to classify. Use a wide range of rocks that are very different so the children can identify them correctly.

nodes.misconception: In emergency situations people often swim without assessing the situation first.
nodes.response: Floating for 60 seconds in a star float and then treading water to identify the most appropriate action is best for assessing a survival situation.

nodes.misconception: All Norman castles were built to the same design.
nodes.response: In fact, although we learn about the classic motte-and-bailey castle (and maybe even make models of them in school), there was a very wide variety of castle designs in England and in Normandy.

nodes.misconception: Animals in the Arctic are camouflaged with white fur all year round.
nodes.response: The Arctic fox is camouflaged with white fur in winter and brown fur in summer.

nodes.misconception: Using any two side lengths for the sine formula.
nodes.response: It must be two side lengths and the angle between them. So any two side lengths of the triangle can be used so long as you also use the angle between them.

nodes.misconception: No one challenged the Portuguese when they began buying enslaved people to take to the Americas.
nodes.response: Many rulers and local people in West Africa were opposed to the trading of enslaved people from the very beginning.

nodes.misconception: The Black Death only affected Europe.
nodes.response: European records from the time are numerous and detailed, so we have a very clear idea about the impact of the Black Death on Europe. However, the Black Death affected a large geographic area, including places without detailed records of the impact.

nodes.misconception: Europeans were more powerful than other states and social groups in the 17th century.
nodes.response: Although European groups like the EIC were powerful, the Mughal Emperors retained greater power in the 17th century. Aurangzeb comprehensively defeated the EIC's military challenged during Child's War.

nodes.misconception: The Vikings were nothing but brutal savages.
nodes.response: Whilst the Viking aptitude for battle is well known, they were also exceptional explorers and traders. Raiding was simply another way for them to gain wealth as opposed to their only way of life.

nodes.misconception: Art is only drawings or paintings.
nodes.response: Look at lots of different examples of ancient art, such as sculpture, textiles, jewellery, decorated household objects, weapons and armour.

nodes.misconception: Critical analysis in art is just about writing facts about artists.
nodes.response: Critical analysis goes beyond facts; it involves interpreting the artwork, understanding its context, and evaluating its impact and meaning.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that what archaeologists learn from artefacts is definitive knowledge.
nodes.response: Archaeologists carefully study artefacts to learn how people lived in specific times and places. New knowledge can be discovered and can change their understanding of how people lived.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they are not permitted to jump on a free throw.
nodes.response: There is no rule stating a jump is not permitted, however the feet can not pass the free throw line so players chose to keep their feet planted on the ground.

nodes.misconception: There are certain spelling exceptions to the general rules taught in this lesson.
nodes.response: Explicitly teach some of these exceptions ('crayon') and explain the addition of suffixes to root words ('playing' or 'rained').

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Elizabeth was born a queen.
nodes.response: There was already a king and queen in throne. There cannot be more than one king and queen at a time.

nodes.misconception: All Enlightenment philosophers were atheists and rejected religion entirely.
nodes.response: Enlightenment philosophers wanted to reshape and redefine the role religion and the Church played in society.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that many of the ideas of the Renaissance were new to science, literature and art.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the Renaissance was a period during which knowledge lost in Western Europe was rediscovered, rather than created for the first time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils avoid hitting a backhand if they find it too difficult which disrupts their balance and positioning. Pupils may face the net rather than rotating their body when hitting the shuttlecock.
nodes.response: Spend time focusing on just the backhand shot to develop pupils' confidence so they will use the shot in a rally. Remind pupils to shift from the ready position, to then rotate their body to hit the shuttlecock so they can generate more power.

nodes.misconception: All Baroque music is contrapuntal / polyphonic.
nodes.response: Textures are varied in the Baroque period, but use of contrapuntal/polyphonic textures was very common and contrasts with the later Classical period. This is a typical texture of the period, but not the only one.

nodes.misconception: Melody and accompaniment is not a homophonic texture.
nodes.response: There are different kinds of homophonic texture. A chordal homophonic texture is one in which all parts play the same rhythm. Melody and accompaniment is also called melody-dominated homophony, where there is a homophonic texture with a melody above.

nodes.misconception: Different animals need different things in order to stay alive.
nodes.response: Examples of different types of animals and how they need the same things to stay alive e.g. different foods they eat.

nodes.misconception: That the Bayeux Tapestry is a 'biased' source and therefore not useful to historians.
nodes.response: Although all sources were produced in a particular context, historians can ask careful questions of them to learn about the past.

nodes.misconception: The shield wall was not a very sophisticated or effective military tactic.
nodes.response: In fact, the shield wall proved effective in holding off the Norman attacks for many hours.

nodes.misconception: It took many weeks to travel from the south to the north of England in medieval times.
nodes.response: Harold and his housecarls were able to cover 185 miles in just four days in 1066: an amazing achievement.

nodes.misconception: The Bay of Pigs Invasion directly involved US combat forces.
nodes.response: JFK refused to involve US ground troops or air support in the invasion whcih relied upon a small group of Cuban exiles.

nodes.misconception: That Celts and Iron Age people were two different things and there was a Celtic Era.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that the Celtic people lived during the Iron Age.

nodes.misconception: People decide for themselves what religious beliefs they hold.
nodes.response: For much of English history, people had to believe what the monarch told them to believe, else they would be killed. This insistence upon belief became more relaxed only in the relatively recent past.

nodes.misconception: All broadleaf trees shed their leaves (are deciduous).
nodes.response: Some broadleaf trees are evergreen like the native holly tree. Broadleaf just means the trees have broad, flat leaves.

nodes.misconception: The modern republic of Benin and the kingdom of Benin are the same place.
nodes.response: The modern republic of Benin has no historical relation to the kingdom of Benin.

nodes.misconception: The German Democratic Republic (GDR) was West Germany.
nodes.response: The GDR was East Germany - the Democratic part of the name is confusing as it was not democratic in the Western sense of being able to choose freely between different political parties.

nodes.misconception: The German Democratic Republic (GDR) was West Germany.
nodes.response: The GDR was East Germany - the Democratic part of the name is confusing as it was not democratic in the Western sense of being able to choose freely between different political parties.

nodes.misconception: That there has only ever been one type of human.
nodes.response: Explain there was more than one type of early human but they are all extinct now. All modern humans are Homo sapiens.

nodes.misconception: Monarchs need to secure their positions by imprisoning or killing any claimants to the throne.
nodes.response: Although many monarchs have acted in this way, there are countless examples of monarchs who tolerated the freedom of strong claimants to the throne in order to not appear despotic. William III of Orange is a good example.

nodes.misconception: The physical geography of China doesn't vary across the country.
nodes.response: China is a huge country with diverse landscapes and a range of biomes including desert, grassland, tropical forests and temperate forests.

nodes.misconception: The physical geography of India doesn't vary across the country.
nodes.response: Use GIS or atlases to investigate how India's phyiscal geography varies across the country.

nodes.misconception: When describing patterns of distribution from maps pupils can make the mistake of including information not available on the map itself and get tempted to explain patterns.
nodes.response: Use only the available information to write a description of what you see on the map including the general pattern and specific details provided by the legend, labels, compass rose and scale.

nodes.misconception: There were no effective responses to the Black Death.
nodes.response: No effective treatments existed in the medieval period but some preventative methods, such as quarantines, could help protect people from plague.

nodes.misconception: The words for 'the' and 'a' are always the same after prepositions.
nodes.response: Prepositions take a specific case, e.g., 'durch' always takes the accusative. Some prepositions take different cases to create different meanings, e.g., 'in' and 'auf' can take the accusative, to show movement to, or the dative, to show location.

nodes.misconception: The perfect tense in German is always formed with a part of 'haben' to express what someone has done.
nodes.response: Some verbs require a part of 'sein' to form the perfect tense, often with verbs of movement to a destination.

nodes.misconception: Malcolm X founded the Black Panther Party.
nodes.response: The ideas of Malcolm X in his later life would inspire the Black Power movement; this in turn inspired the Black Panther Party in the year after his death. The party was founded by Bobby Seale and Huey Newton.

nodes.misconception: All Hindus see truth in the same way.
nodes.response: The Hindu worldview is pluralist, which means there are many paths to truth.

nodes.misconception: The C blues scale can use any of the black notes (flattened notes) on the keyboard.
nodes.response: The blues scale uses specific flattened notes - 3rd, 5th and 7th. It's important for pupils to practise finding these notes and getting used to how the scale sounds.

nodes.misconception: The Bolsheviks revolutionary background meant that they were completely different to the tsar.
nodes.response: The Bolsheviks treated opposition similarly to the tsar, using a secret police and re-introducing censorship.

nodes.misconception: That the story of Esther takes place in ancient Israel.
nodes.response: The story of Esther takes place in Susa, an important city in the Persian Empire.

nodes.misconception: Evergreen and coniferous trees are the same.
nodes.response: Coniferous trees produce cones and are normally evergreen (don't lose their leaves in autumn). Some evergreen trees are not coniferous, e.g. holly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistake another note for F when changing position.  Brass instruments can only be identified by pitch.
nodes.response: Reinforce that F is to the left of the three black keys; this has to be correct for the finger prompts to work. The ranges of the brass instruments overlap, so it's important to emphasise that the timbre of each instrument is slightly different.

nodes.misconception: All communist states fell under complete Soviet control because of the Brezhnev Doctrine.
nodes.response: Some states such as China, Yugoslavia, Romania and Albania became less trusting of the USSR and made increased efforts to develop their own independent relations to protect themselves against it.

nodes.misconception: Britain ruled over large areas of Africa throughout the 19th century.
nodes.response: British colonies were mainly confined to coastal areas in the first half of the 19th century. It was only later that British rule extended into the African interior.

nodes.misconception: All parts of the British Empire were always governed directly by the British government.
nodes.response: In the first half of the 19th century, India was ruled by the British East India Company, not by the British Government.

nodes.misconception: Governor Grant's reforms after the Morant Bay Rebellion reduced the problem of poverty for Black Jamaicans.
nodes.response: Grant tackled discrimination and other issues but did not provide the financial assistance needed to help many Black Jamaicans escape poverty.

nodes.misconception: Knowing that the Brownings were married to each other is an important piece of contextual information.
nodes.response: Although it is relevant to know they were married, it is in linking their own unconventional marriage to the subversive presentation of love and relationships in their poems that the best contextual points can be found.

nodes.misconception: Devotees worship the Buddharupa.
nodes.response: The Buddharupa is a focal point and reminder of the Buddha's great qualities and ability to attain enlightenment.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Hadrian's Wall was not very high, as the remaining stretches have been damaged.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that Hadrian's Wall is over a thousand years old, and any sections still standing were much taller in the past.

nodes.misconception: The Normans invented Romanesque architecture.
nodes.response: The Normans were enthusiastic adopters of Romanesque building style, but it was developed in northern Italy and France, combining Roman features with elements of Byzantine design.

nodes.misconception: The story of Abraham is only relevant to Jews.
nodes.response: Christians remember this story and learn from it.

nodes.misconception: Middle English is the same as Old English. Both are general terms, and mean the same thing.
nodes.response: Middle English was spoken from about 1100-1500. Old English was spoken before 1100. Both are technical terms and have a specific meaning.

nodes.misconception: Carbon atoms can be created or destroyed.
nodes.response: Focus teaching on the carbon cycle as a closed system in which the total amount of carbon is constant. Discuss the processes of how carbon is transferred from one place to another, rather than processes of how carbon is lost or gained.

nodes.misconception: The ba-dum of the heart beat represents the left then right side contracting.
nodes.response: The heart relaxes (diastole) to fill with blood then first phase of contraction squeezes blood from the top two atria down into the ventricles before the valves close off and then the second phase of contraction squeezes blood out of the ventricles.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that only oxygenated blood is transported around the body.
nodes.response: The body's cardiovascular system includes a group of organs and muscles that manage oxgenated blood and deoxygenated blood.

nodes.misconception: Earthquakes are random events.
nodes.response: Earthquakes are not random events, but are a consequence of tectonic plate movement.

nodes.misconception: Flooding is only caused by physical factors such as heavy rainfall.
nodes.response: Human factors can lead to flooding too, such as deforestation.

nodes.misconception: Parliament in the 17th century was similarly superior to the monarch as it is today
nodes.response: Parliament was there to assist the monarch but they could rule without it and did not consider it an equal to themselves

nodes.misconception: The only reason why crusaders went on the First Crusade was to capture Jerusalem for Christianity.
nodes.response: People went on crusade for a wide variety of reasons; for some people, capturing Jerusalem from the Muslims was important, but it was almost certainly not the reason why the First Crusade was called in the first place.

nodes.misconception: All the peoples who revolted in Saint-Domingue were enslaved people.
nodes.response: The revolutionaries of Saint-Domingue were comprised of a combination of enslaved people, free people of African descent and free indigenous people.

nodes.misconception: That the main aim of the rebels in the Peasants' Revolt was to overthrow the king.
nodes.response: In fact the rebels' grievances were against local officials and the king's advisers, who they believed were misleading the king into acting against the interests of his people.

nodes.misconception: Festivals are always serious and solemn.
nodes.response: The festival of Holi is full of fun and mischief.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that daughter cells have different DNA to the parent cell.
nodes.response: Slides repeatedly address the concept that DNA is copied and that daughter cells are genetically identical.

nodes.misconception: Chromosomes are halved when the cell splits.
nodes.response: Slides repeatedly address the concept that chromosomes are copied.

nodes.misconception: All people belong to some form of religion.
nodes.response: According to the 2021 Census in England and Wales, there are an increasing number of individuals who have no religion.

nodes.misconception: All religion is declining in the UK.
nodes.response: Christianity has declined in the UK, whilst other religions have increased. There are differences in different geographical contexts.

nodes.misconception: All Christians have the same view about the role of women in the church.
nodes.response: There is diversity of opinion across different Christian denominations. Even within denominations there are different perspectives.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that people in the past used phones and tablets to take photographs.
nodes.response: Show pupils the various devices that have been used in the past to take photographs and how they have evolved.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all aspects of religion, or all aspects of buildings changed.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that within an area of study that we define, there can be elements of both change and continuity.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe prevailing wind is the direction of wind on any particular day.
nodes.response: The prevailing wind is the most frequent wind direction that a location experiences.

nodes.misconception: All UK Christmas traditions are linked to the nativity.
nodes.response: There are many traditions associated with Christmas that come from outside of the nativity story, for example having a Christmas tree, santa and spending family time together.

nodes.misconception: As a result of legal changes, there was significant progress for all black Americans by 1960.
nodes.response: Legal changes led to some change for black Americans, although a significant amount of opposition from within and outside the government led to limited change for most black Americans.

nodes.misconception: Students might not realise that women as well as men were conscripted during WW2.
nodes.response: In 1940, single women aged 20-30, and widowed women without children, were conscripted into war work.

nodes.misconception: Women's suffrage led to a rapid increase in the number of female MPs in Parliament.
nodes.response: By 1931, there were only 15 female MPs in Parliament; however, women's suffrage meant that MPs were more likely to support new laws that had a positive impact on the lives of women.

nodes.misconception: The Big Bang was an explosion in which existing matter blew up.
nodes.response: Describe the Big Bang as an expansion of space combined with the creation of all matter in the universe.

nodes.misconception: Brod contrasts Enid in every way.
nodes.response: Brod and Enid clash over education, Jamaica and England, but they also have many commonalities: their past and their migration.

nodes.misconception: Oberon's commands, status and dominance in the dialogue mean he can only be interpreted as powerful.
nodes.response: There is much to suggest Oberon's power in this scene, but dialogue can be interpreted in many ways, and performance can affect how we perceive a character. There is no single reading of the play.

nodes.misconception: There is one interpretation of Puck (either malevolent or mischievous) and you have to work out which one is correct.
nodes.response: A play, and its characters, can be interpreted in many different ways. Different performances will draw out particular interpretations.

nodes.misconception: DNA is living and not necessarily a chemical.
nodes.response: Discussing that DNA is a chemical molecule and showing how it is made up of smaller chemical groups, and then modelling this chemical structure.

nodes.misconception: Arabia has always been Muslim.
nodes.response: Arabia was inhabited by Christians, Jews and people who had polytheistic beliefs before the time of Prophet Muhammad.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that serious topics need serious text types such as articles or speeches.
nodes.response: Encourage students to consider why a writer might choose to use a poem to write about a serious topic and take a stand.

nodes.misconception: Lady Macbeth doesn't value loyalty.
nodes.response: Lady Macbeth does value loyalty, but loyalty to herself and her ambitions, not the chivalric code.

nodes.misconception: Christianity is a Western religion.
nodes.response: Christianity originated in the Middle East and quickly spread across various regions, including Africa.

nodes.misconception: Christianity is a western European religion and looks the same everywhere.
nodes.response: Christianity has spread to many parts of the world. In these places it has adapted alongside the culture it is in.

nodes.misconception: All churches share exactly the same beliefs and history.
nodes.response: The Christian Church shares many similar beliefs but also has different beliefs and practices which have developed in different areas over time.

nodes.misconception: All churches share exactly the same beliefs and history.
