nodes.response: Role-play answers should be kept relatively brief, whereas conversations present the opportunity to develop answers.

nodes.misconception: Tone is always achieved through pressure.
nodes.response: Remind children that tone can be achieved through adding pressure, but layers of material can also be built up or removed to vary tone.

nodes.misconception: Artists can only use one material to create tone in an artwork.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can use a range of materials within one artwork to show tone. This is called a mixed-media artwork.

nodes.misconception: If music has a key, it must be diatonic.
nodes.response: Not necessarily. A piece of music can have a key, but use notes from outside of it. This would be chromatic. It could also have a key, but use some microtones as well, meaning it is microtonal.

nodes.misconception: Shading just means colouring in darker.
nodes.response: Tonal shading uses a range of light to dark tones to show how light hits different surfaces.

nodes.misconception: Hue and colour mean the same thing.
nodes.response: Colour is the overarching name for what we see but it is made up of hues and tones.

nodes.misconception: Practice using the tools is not needed when working with polymers and timbers as they are easy to cut.
nodes.response: Practice is needed when using tools to cut all materials. Polymers and timbers are easy to cut, but complete control can be lost if cut too quickly. It can be challenging to keep on the line, so practice is needed.

nodes.misconception: Synchronous communication tools are better than asynchronous communication tools.
nodes.response: Neither type of communication can be deemed better than the other overall. Some forms of communication will suit different tasks better than others.

nodes.misconception: Gantt charts are more effective than Kanban boards because they show project dependencies.
nodes.response: Neither tool can be deemed more effective overall. A business should decide which of the tools will work well for them based on the needs of the project.

nodes.misconception: When delivering a presentation you should read the slides out word for word.
nodes.response: Simply reading out the slides can disengage the audience and mean that your message can become lost.

nodes.misconception: Gantt charts are better than PERT charts.
nodes.response: Gantt charts may be deemed better than PERT charts in some instances, but not all. The choice of chart can depend on the project and what the team prefers to use.

nodes.misconception: The 'global shift' of manufacturing industries from developed to emerging and/or developing countries was a one-off movement of jobs.
nodes.response: TNCs continue to seek locations with the lowest wages, meaning the loss of manufacturing jobs from emerging countries is possible; so some of the benefits of FDI may only be short-term.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they should hit the ball with a flat racket face to generate topspin.
nodes.response: To create topspin, you need to angle the racket slightly downward and brush up the back of the ball.

nodes.misconception: To be a tourist you have to go abroad.
nodes.response: You can be a tourist abroad or in your home country.

nodes.misconception: Confusion between the country of Australia and the continent of Oceania.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring a map of Oceania and identifying the different countries and dependencies that make up this continent.

nodes.misconception: Pupils blame each other and lose focus rather than remaining positive and regrouping.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the balanced teams mean everyone should have an equal chance of winning. Hence it is the pair who gel the best and work hard to win as many points as possible across all their matches that will win.

nodes.misconception: All tournaments must focus solely on the outcome/winner of competition.
nodes.response: In order for all participants to feel included, tournaments can take many forms and be adapted so that everyone can enjoy an appropriate level of challenge.

nodes.misconception: Toussaint L'Ouverture was fighting against the French during the entirety of the Haitian Revolution.
nodes.response: He first fought Saint-Domingue's ruling French elites and slave-owners. He then fought Spanish troops after invading Spain's territory on the island. He then defeated a British invasion and became Haiti's official governor until France betrayed him.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all people in Roman Britain lived in Roman towns.
nodes.response: Make it clear to pupils that although many people came to the towns, Britain remained largely rural, with lots of small Celtic settlements.

nodes.misconception: Using trace tables guarantees correct logic and code.
nodes.response: Trace tables can be subject to human error and can be impractical to use for complex algorithms.

nodes.misconception: Hortense is the main protagonist.
nodes.response: Look at how many scenes other characters are in and the importance of their journeys. Why might Levy choose to have multiple protagonists? Think back to her original intentions.

nodes.misconception: Orwell offers a solution to the problems he explores.
nodes.response: Explore the idea of "resolution" in terms of 'Animal Farm'. Does Orwell offer any resolutions? Does the story feel finished?

nodes.misconception: That Hortense is only motivated by heartbreak.
nodes.response: How does Hortense view herself, even from a young age? She does at times view herself as superior. Furthermore, she has lived in the house for a long time and has perhaps internalised the moral and religious standards that Mr. Philip holds.

nodes.misconception: That all people in the medieval period completed the same type of work as one another.
nodes.response: Remind students that a wide range of different jobs and industries existed in medieval Norwich, even after it focused more on wools.

nodes.misconception: The Ghana Empire was located in the modern-day country of Ghana.
nodes.response: The Ghana Empire was located in the Sahel, north of the Niger River, which is nowhere near the modern-day country of Ghana.

nodes.misconception: Once you've learnt a word once, it will stay in your memory forever.
nodes.response: If you learn a word once and don't revisit it, it is unlikely to stay in your long-term memory. It is important to revisit prior learning regularly to retain knowledge in the long-term memory.

nodes.misconception: All computers can do everything equally well.
nodes.response: General-purpose computers can run many programs, but single-purpose computers are designed to do one task very efficiently.

nodes.misconception: Moves have to be performed in a specifc order to be effective.
nodes.response: After learning a few moves, we can ask the pupils which to perform and how many. This enables them to develop their choreographic skills of selecting and sequencing actions effectively.

nodes.misconception: 'Damit' always means 'with it' or 'with them'.
nodes.response: 'Damit' has a double identity! It can be used as a conjunction meaning 'so that' as well as a da-compound meaning 'with it' or 'with them'.

nodes.misconception: Adjectival nouns do not require a capital letter because they come from adjectives.
nodes.response: Adjectival nouns require a capital letter, just like all nouns in German.

nodes.misconception: Use 'mehr' with adjectives and adverbs to make comparisons.
nodes.response: Use the comparative form of adjectives and adverbs to make comparisons, e.g., 'interessanter als', not 'mehr interessant als'.

nodes.misconception: All verbs in German are followed by the accusative case, apart from 'sein' which takes the nominative case.
nodes.response: A number of verbs are followed by the dative case. These must be learnt and carefully identified when translating into German.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that fast running throughout will be the best pace to use in trail running.
nodes.response: Using smart pacing means the pupils can use variable speeds, across different terrain, to keep safe, save engery and complete the run.

nodes.misconception: More training makes a perfect model.
nodes.response: Not neccessarily - models can become too specialised and fail on new data.

nodes.misconception: If you get off the mat before the bar falls it will still count as a successful jump.
nodes.response: If the bar falls then the jump does not count, even if the jumper has left the mat. Every attempt should be made to clear the bar rather than rushing the landing and clearing the mat quickly.

nodes.misconception: Strength and power are more important than technique when throwing a javelin far.
nodes.response: While strength and power are both important, too much strength and not enough time focusing on technique, can impact the accuracy of the throw. A well executed throw will travel further than just force alone.

nodes.misconception: A common mistake in the triple jump is the athlete collapses the middle 'step phase' rather than getting equal height and distance from every phase.
nodes.response: Emphasis on all phases of the jump should be practised, especially the step phase, with height and efficiency.  All phases of the triple jump should contribute to an equal proportion of distance e.g. 2m x2m x2m

nodes.misconception: To get faster at running middle distance you always have to train at race pace.
nodes.response: Improvements in speed and fitness for middle distance running can also come from running easy efforts. This builds aerobic fitness and gives the individual a strong base where over time the same effort will be maintained but at a faster pace.

nodes.misconception: You throw a shot in the shot put.
nodes.response: The shot put does not require any rotation around a joint. It is pushed from under the chin and touching the neck. A throw action will likely lead to injury due to the weight of the shot. However, "throw" is standard terminology for this event.

nodes.misconception: Everyone's sprinting technique should look the same.
nodes.response: Everyone will have their own natural style of running. Forcing pupils to be too upright for example may be sub optimal for some. Pupils should find their natural position which may include a slight lean.

nodes.misconception: Each sport/activity has only one specific type of training suited to it.
nodes.response: Performers in many activities can benefit from a variety of training types. For example, a marathon runner will mostly benefit from continuous training, however weight training could help to condition their muscles and avoid injury.

nodes.misconception: Training seasons align with seasons of the year.
nodes.response: They are very different. Training seasons will align with the type of sport and their competition period. For example, the football season is currently a different time period to the netball super league and hence their seasons will be set by this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the relationship between rest and workouts, believing that more training, equals more progress.
nodes.response: Help pupils to understand the requirement for sufficient rest and recovery time if the body is to make adaptations and improve.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe twisting on the vertical axis is pointless as they are keen to do tricks which are often completed around the horizontal axis.
nodes.response: Learning to twist is fundamental to overcome possible anxiety when in motion and not being able to see the cross. In addition, more challenging techniques include a twist at the start or the end, so the motor programme is required to build on this.

nodes.misconception: God as transcendent means that God is not involved with or close to creation.
nodes.response: God is both transcendent (beyond the universe) and immanent (close to creation) at the same time. God's immanence is demonstrated through Jesus, the Holy Spirit, miracles and the revelation of the Bible.

nodes.misconception: Energy can be used up.
nodes.response: Describe the mechanisms that transfer energy from one object to another, or to a system, as the energy in the original object decreases – or vice versa.

nodes.misconception: Data travels in one large piece across the network.
nodes.response: Data is split into smaller packets, which travel separately and are reassembled at the destination.

nodes.misconception: A misconception that is often seen is that there is a build up of biomass along a food chain.
nodes.response: The lesson outlines how biomass is actually lost between trophic levels through life processes.

nodes.misconception: The Indian and Jamaican rebellions triggered complete change in those colonies.
nodes.response: Major changes were introduced after these rebellions although little was changed to address the problem of poverty in either Jamaica or India.

nodes.misconception: Students may confuse reflections and rotations depending on the object.
nodes.response: A reflection is the only transformation that changes the sense of the object, so check that first.

nodes.misconception: The size of the current in the primary coil controls the size of current in the secondary coil.
nodes.response: Explain how the p.d. across and resistance of the secondary circuit determines the secondary p.d. and therefore current, and how the current adjusts to ensure that the power input is equal to the power output.

nodes.misconception: For the combined transformation $$3$$f$$(x-2)$$ order does not matter so pupils may assume that order never matters.
nodes.response: For $$3$$f$$(x-2)$$ the $$3$$ affects the output, the $$y$$ value, and the $$-2$$ affects the input, the $$x$$ value. Model to show that these can happen in either order. Then point out that $$3$$f$$(x)-2$$ is two effects on the output.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse 'stretch' transformations. Many transformations of the form $$y=a$$f$$(x)$$ have the appearance of a compression towards the $$y$$-axis rather than a 'stretch' in the $$y$$-direction.
nodes.response: Interpreting the notation is key. $$y=a$$f$$(x)$$ is the output of f$$(x)$$ being multiplied by $$a$$. Which coordinate is the output? The $$y$$ coordinates change by a scale factor of $$a$$ so this must be a stretch in the $$y$$-direction.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse 'stretch' transformations. Does the transformation $$y=$$f$$(ax)$$ affect the $$x$$ or $$y$$ coordinates?
nodes.response: Interpreting the notation is key. $$y=$$f$$(ax)$$ is the input of f$$(x)$$ being multiplied by $$a$$. Which coordinate is the input?

nodes.misconception: Pupils can get confused between $$-$$f$$(x)$$ and f$$(-x)$$, which one is a reflection in the $$x$$-axis and which is a reflection in the $$y$$-axis?
nodes.response: Interpreting the notation is key. Remind pupils that $$-$$f$$(x)$$ is the output of f$$(x)$$ being multiplied by $$-1$$. Which coordinate is the output? The $$y$$ coordinates are altered from positive to negative, that is a reflection in which axis?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the vertical translation depending on the function used to show the effect of $$a$$.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils consider a range of functions so that they can see the movement of the graph.

nodes.misconception: f$$(x)+5$$ is a translation of $$+5$$ in the $$y$$-direction so pupils may assume that f$$(x+5)$$ is a translation of $$+5$$ in the $$x$$-direction.
nodes.response: Visually showing pupils, using graphing technology, that f$$(x+5)$$ is not a translation to the right will help. Showing them a comparison of the two tables of values for both functions shows them why this happens.

nodes.misconception: Pupils mix-up $$-$$f$$(x)$$ and f$$(-x)$$. Which is a reflection in the $$x$$-axis? Which is in the $$y$$-axis?
nodes.response: f$$(-x)$$ is the input being multiplied by $$-1$$ before the function is applied. Which coordinate is the input? The $$x$$ coordinates change from positive to negative so this must be a reflection in the $$y$$ axis.

nodes.misconception: Memories are always accurate and unchanging.
nodes.response: A common misconception about memories is that they are perfect and unchanging when in reality, memories can be inaccurate, influenced by emotions and change over time.

nodes.misconception: Transitions mean adding a travelling option as you move from one skill to another. Gymnastics lessons always need lots of apparatus and take too long to set up.
nodes.response: Reinforce the concept of transitions as the smooth transfer of one skill moving straight into another one. Gymnastics lessons can be taught using just mats and benches, that do not take long to set up.

nodes.misconception: Pupils get frustrated when they lose possession and fail to carry out their defensive tactics.
nodes.response: Remind pupils how important it is to defend and try and stop the attack. If we give up, it's likely our opponents will score.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the opposite team to the scoring team take the following center pass.
nodes.response: The center pass is alternated throughout the game regardless of which team scores.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all metals react vigorously with water, and may believe all transition metals form only one type of ion, and might think that all metals are equally good catalysts.
nodes.response: Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals react slowly with water or not at all. Transition metals can form ions with different charges, leading to compounds with varying properties and colours. Each reaction will be catalysed best by one catalyst.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all metals react vigorously with water, and may believe all transition metals form only one type of ion, and might think that all metals are equally good catalysts.
nodes.response: Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals react slowly with water or not at all. Transition metals can form ions with different charges, leading to compounds with varying properties and colours. Each reaction will be catalysed best by one catalyst.

nodes.misconception: Students may think all metals react vigorously with water, and may believe all transition metals form only one type of ion, and might think that all metals are equally good catalysts.
nodes.response: Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals react slowly with water or not at all. Transition metals can form ions with different charges, leading to compounds with varying properties and colours. Each reaction will be catalysed best by one catalyst.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might mistakenly alter the shape or size of the polygon during translation, thinking the process involves resizing or reshaping.
nodes.response: Emphasise that translation is a "sliding" motion that moves the shape without changing its size or orientation. Demonstrate this with cut-out shapes that can be physically moved on a grid, showing that the shape remains identical after translation.

nodes.misconception: Students may translate vertically before horizontally.
nodes.response: Remind the students that the column vectors work in the same way as coordinates.

nodes.misconception: TNCs sell the same products in different countries.
nodes.response: TNCs can sell different products in different countries.

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials children may rely purely on observation rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Opportunities to test each material to check if their thinking was correct.

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials children may rely purely on observation rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Ensure children have been able to test materials and generate a set of results.

nodes.misconception: Students get confused between transport in the xylem (water and minerals) and the phloem (sugars).
nodes.response: These sections are covered in separate lessons, each with clear explanations and reinforcing tasks to support learning.

nodes.misconception: If students fail to understand that water only enters the plant at the roots, and not through the leaves, then the process of transpiration will be very muddled and confused.
nodes.response: The lesson reinforces the pathway that water takes through the plant, clearly stating that water enters at the roots, and showing several times how it moves up through xylem.

nodes.misconception: A displacement-distance graph is a picture of a wave, with 1:1 vertical and horizontal scaling.
nodes.response: Interpret and sketch graphs of waves that are compared to pictures of each wave.

nodes.misconception: Que can be used in a subject relative clause e.g. le prof que s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.
nodes.response: When the relative clause introduces a verb to describe a subject, 'qui' must be used and not 'que'. E.g. le prof qui s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish the verb endings rarely change depending on who the verb refers to, like in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish verb endings always change depending on who the verb refers to. For -ar verbs, 'I' ends in -o, 'you' ends in -as, 'she, he, it' ends in -a, 'we' ends in -amos, and 'they' ends in -an.

nodes.misconception: All journeys start in GMT.
nodes.response: This lesson only uses journeys that begin in GMT. This is to avoid any that start in the western hemisphere, cross the Prime Meridian and end in the eastern hemisphere, which are more complicated for KS2 pupils to understand using time zone maps.

nodes.misconception: Both 'conocer' and 'saber' mean 'to know, knowing'.
nodes.response: They both mean 'to know, knowing' but 'conocer' is used for knowing facts and information, while 'saber' is used to say that you are familiar or become familiar with a place, a person or a thing.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives always come after the noun in Spanish.
nodes.response: In Spanish, adjectives generally come after the noun; however, certain prenominal adjectives come before the noun, e.g. 'último', 'mismo', 'propio', 'primero', 'segundo', 'tercero'.

nodes.misconception: Words ending in -c (like historic) also end in -c in French.
nodes.response: Words ending in -c in English often end in -que in French: historique.

nodes.misconception: There is only one translation of a French infinitive into English.
nodes.response: An infinitive can be translated into English using the -ing form or 'to ...': conduire - to drive, driving.

nodes.misconception: The 'she, he, it' form of -ar verbs and the 'they' form have the same ending.
nodes.response: The 'she, he, it' form of -ar verbs ends in -a, but the 'they' form ends in -an.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that travel writing needs to be about far away places.
nodes.response: Draw their attention to the social messages implied in the titles 'Down and Out in Paris and London' and 'Travels with Charley: In Search of America'.

nodes.misconception: Representing the journey of a train or bus must include mimed actions such as pretending to turn a steering wheel.
nodes.response: Whilst pupils may wish to include such gestures, our focus is on the journey rather than the mode of transport so there is not a requirement to include the use of mime.

nodes.misconception: When considering description, students often focus on the external effect.
nodes.response: Ask how things might look different depending on your personality or circumstances? Offer examples e.g. how a town might be described differently by someone who enjoys living there and someone who dislikes living there.

nodes.misconception: Incorrect hand placement when performing vaults can lead to poor balance and coordination.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils perform with the correct hand position, using one hand for the lazy vault and opposite hand to foot with the step vault. Perform the vaults slowly to build confidence.

nodes.misconception: Sound needs gaps through which it moves in order to enter a room or space. At the same time, most pupils can state that sound can't travel in a vacuum but the majority cannot correctly explain why.
nodes.response: An alarm can still be heard in a sealed container that has no gaps (e.g. kilner jar). Provide lots of experiences and examples of sound travelling through gases, liquids and solids and struggling to travel through a partial vacuum.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that sound is a material substance, or involves particles of some kind (e.g. of air, or 'of sound') travelling or being blown out from a source.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring and modelling how vibrating objects set particles vibrating, how vibrating particles will collide into neighbouring particles to set them vibrating too, and how patterns of vibrations produce the 'pulses' of a sound wave.

nodes.misconception: The only way to communicate about past events in German is by using the 2-verb perfect tense, e.g., 'Ich bin nach Deutschland gefahren. Ich habe dort einen Strandurlaub gemacht.'.
nodes.response: We also use the single verb imperfect tense - 'war', 'hatte' and 'es gab', and imperfect modal forms - 'musste', 'konnte', 'wollte', with a 2nd (infinitive) verb, to talk about events in the past.

nodes.misconception: The poor always accepted their position in medieval society.
nodes.response: The poor challenged the social order in Norwich violently in 1381 and had to be actively managed by the elites.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think trenches were dug like long, straight ditches.
nodes.response: Trenches were dug in a zig zag shape for better protection.

nodes.misconception: Rapid urban growth in Jakarta has improved living conditions for everyone, reducing inequality between rich and poor.
nodes.response: Rapid urban growth in Jakarta has not improved life for everyone. While some benefit from new jobs and development, many poor migrants face rising living costs, limited job security and end up in squatter settlements.

nodes.misconception: A trial is where people are judged to see who makes the cut and who doesn't.
nodes.response: A trial is an opportunity for everyone to show what they can do and also learn where they could focus on as priority areas for improvement.

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [ou] and [u] make the same sound in French.
nodes.response: The SSCs [ou] and [u] are similar but make different sounds in French. [ou] is pronounced as in 'nous' and [u] is pronounced as in 'tu'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often fail to get enough distance in the middle step phase of the triple jump and it is much shorter then the other two phases causing them to lose distance.
nodes.response: Help pupils to understand that ideally the distance covered in each phase will be similar. It might seem counterintuitive but the short step is often due to the hop stage being too long and we need to seek balance between all three stages.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that rainforests are only found in tropical regions.
nodes.response: Rainforests can be found in tropical and temperate regions.

nodes.misconception: Weather and climate are the same.
nodes.response: Weather is the day to day changes in the atmosphere. Climate is the long term weather for an area.

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms can form over land.
nodes.response: Tropical storms form over warm ocean waters where they can draw energy from the heat and moisture. Once over land, they lose their energy source and weaken.

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms only affect coastal areas.
nodes.response: Explain that tropical storms can impact inland areas as well due to heavy rainfall and flooding.

nodes.misconception: Immediate responses only happen during the tropical storm.
nodes.response: Immediate responses happen before, during and immediately after the storm.

nodes.misconception: Misconceptions associated with incomplete circuits: one wire to battery; connections to the same end of the battery; wires the wrong way round; not connecting clips to metal.
nodes.response: Children will be taught how to troubleshoot circuits which are not working to address these misconceptions.

nodes.misconception: When truncating, pupils are tempted to round. Also, when truncating, they cut off the number without thinking about the magnitude.
nodes.response: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value when truncating.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may only think about speaking in relation to communication.
nodes.response: Information can be communicated in lots of different ways including signals, gestures, sounds, pictures and words. Receiving, interpreting and acting on the information sent is also half the process of communication.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to trust others to have their back.
nodes.response: Trust is a two-way process and something that needs to be earned and then not taken advantage of.

nodes.misconception: A truth table can only have the column headings of single inputs like A, B, or X.
nodes.response: A truth table can have column headings that calculate the value of the expression, for example (A OR B).

nodes.misconception: Revolutions always involve the execution of the previous leaders of government.
nodes.response: Although there was violence during the February Revolution, Tsar Nicholas II agreed to abdicate.

nodes.misconception: In French, there is a separate word for 'would'.
nodes.response: The conditional verb form expresses the idea of 'would + verb' in its spelling. Students should be encouraged to used the conditional form of verbs instead of being over reliant on 'vouloir' in the conditional.

nodes.misconception: Governments and societies have generally been sympathetic to people in extreme poverty who may have been reduced to begging.
nodes.response: Throughout much of history, there has been little sympathy for people in extreme poverty from the majority of governments and societies, even when the circumstances that drove people into poverty are clearly out of their own control.

nodes.misconception: Once encrypted, a message cannot be decrypted.
nodes.response: A message can be encrypted and decrypted multiple times, this happens frequently during digital communications.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that all nouns are a person, place or thing that you can touch.
nodes.response: Show a range of different nouns, including common and abstract nouns. Show that they can be described with an adjective.

nodes.misconception: Contrast is the same as opposite.
nodes.response: Opposite is an example of contrast. For example, a contrast for travelling forwards is backwards. But contrast can also mean different. For example, travelling around a bend or turning on the spot are different so would also demonstrate contrast.

nodes.misconception: The turning effect is a force (it is often wrongly called a turning force).
nodes.response: Correct any use of the erroneous term ‘turning force’ and use examples of the turning effect caused by force with a lever.

nodes.misconception: Writing essays is not like creative writing, it doesn't matter how you write things so much.
nodes.response: Not writing clearly and accurately can mean excellent ideas can be lost once written down.

nodes.misconception: Children mix up the vowel spellings in the words 'desperate' and 'separate'.
nodes.response: Saying the words slowly how they are spelt can help: sep-ar-ate, des-per-ate.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may spell words with -ize, how the suffix sounds and in the American spelling.
nodes.response: Discuss the difference between the American and British spelling of the suffix -ise.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that turning points in a narrative only have negative consequences.
nodes.response: Note other examples of turning points in recently read narratives that have a range of positive and negative consequences. Pupils may wish to share examples from their own texts.

nodes.misconception: During Task A, pupils may not find an example of each of the tension-building techniques.
nodes.response: Different techniques may be used on each page. You could share examples for the three double-page spreads after the task.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a character's emotions have to change drastically throughout a chapter.
nodes.response: In some chapters and with some characters, there will be less change as events that happen to them may not affect their emotions. You can explore this through the use of an emotions graph.

nodes.misconception: Students can think that all water is the same, or can mix up saltwater (seawater) and freshwater and where these are found.
nodes.response: Water on Earth is either saltwater or freshwater. Saltwater is found in seas and oceans, freshwater is found in rivers and streams. Only salt tolerant plants and animal species can survive in saltwater.

nodes.misconception: Analysing language features is enough.
nodes.response: The best analysis - with the richest commentary - will also spend time focusing on structural decisions a writer makes.

nodes.misconception: If pupils do not cut a parallelogram from vertex to opposite vertex, they will end up with either two non-congruent shapes or two congruent quadrilaterals.
nodes.response: Modelling is key and this is a useful time to revisit the concept of a shape's diagonal, that is, a line connecting vertex to a non-adjacent vertex.

nodes.misconception: The two Commandments form part of the Ten Commandments given to Moses by God on Mount Sinai.
nodes.response: The two Commandments are taught by Jesus.

nodes.misconception: Languages don't change; they have a fixed number of words in them.
nodes.response: Languages are not fixed; they are changing all the time, adopting new words to reflect how people live and speak.

nodes.misconception: When singing in parts we need to stand away from other parts, so that we can concentrate on our part.
nodes.response: Understanding how parts fit together, hearing texture, structure and harmony, and feeling the steady pulse together are all important elements of learning to sing in parts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think verbs can only show 'doing'.
nodes.response: Verbs can show 'being' and 'having' as well as 'doing'. These are sometimes 'hidden' in contractions (I'm, she's, they've, we've).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that relative and adverbial clauses are two types of subordinate clause.
nodes.response: Emphasise that relative and adverbial clauses are both subordinate, but they are differentiated by their starting word and use in sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that using 'before' and 'after' always creates an adverbial complex sentence.
nodes.response: These words often create phrases, rather than adverbial clauses; a clause requires a verb.

nodes.misconception: Type 1 diabetes is caused by lifestyle, particularly poor diet.
nodes.response: The slide deck states that type 1 diabetes is caused by genes or environmental factors and there is a question in task A to assess this. In contrast there is a big focus on lifestyle and obesity being linked to developing type 2 diabetes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that primary data means data they collect first hand (and no one else can collect it).
nodes.response: Primary data refers to data that are directly collected for specific use in an investigation. This means that a team of researchers could collect the data for you for your investigation and this is still primary data.

nodes.misconception: Types of feedback are often confused with types of guidance from the previous lesson.
nodes.response: Ensure students can differentiate between guidance being information needed to understand how to perform a skill, and feedback being information about how well it is being performed.

nodes.misconception: Types of feedback are often confused with types of guidance.
nodes.response: Ensure students are able to differentiate between guidance, which is infomation needed to understand how to perform a skill, and feedback which is information about how well it is being performed.

nodes.misconception: Foods are either 'good' or 'bad' for you.
nodes.response: Explanation of different nutrients in foods and how they can be beneficial to our health.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that only one type of guidance can be used at any time.
nodes.response: Combinations of guidance can be very effective and are common in good coaching. For example, visual demonstrations are often combined with verbal explanations.

nodes.misconception: A count-controlled loop repeats forever.
nodes.response: An infinite loop repeats forever, unless the program is stopped.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused with the different names of fast/ slow and type I/ type II muscle fibres.
nodes.response: The word slow has an O in it and these fibres use oxygen to contract slowly and aerobically. They are our body's first choice of muscle fibre due to fatigue resistance, hence type I.

nodes.misconception: A muscle will always change length when it contracts.
nodes.response: A muscle pulls on a bone to create movement. However, occasionally, if the movement is static, the muscle is still contracting and under tension but not changing length. This is known as isometric muscle contraction.

nodes.misconception: All devices in a network do the same thing, they just send and receive data.
nodes.response: In a client–server network, devices have different roles. Servers provide services like file storage or email. Clients request and use those services, rather than providing them.

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of rain; it is all the same.
nodes.response: Students will be exposed to the three different types of rainfall: relief, convectional, frontal.

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes focus on one feature to classify rocks as one type or another.
nodes.response: Stress that the rock classification system is gradual - show examples of various metamorphic rocks, highlighting similarities / differences.

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of strength which we usually associate with lifting heavy weights.
nodes.response: There are four types of strength: maximal, dynamic, static and explosive.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all teeth are the same shape and size, and that different teeth do not have different names. They often do not know that our teeth are already in our jaw when we are born.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities for children to feel and look at their own teeth for differences in shape and size.

nodes.misconception: Each sport or activity has only one type of training suited to it.
nodes.response: Performers in most activities can benefit from a range of training types. A marathon runner would benefit most from continuous training; however, weight training and static stretching would also help with conditioning and avoiding injury.

nodes.misconception: Each sport or activity has only one training method suited to it.
nodes.response: Perfomers in most activities can benefit from the use of multiple trianing types. For example, a marathon runner would most benefit from continuous training; however, weight training could also be used to help condition the muscles and avoid injury.

nodes.misconception: Lava and magma can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Magma is molten rock underground, whereas lava is molten rock above Earth's surface.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can mix up population distribution and population density.
nodes.response: Population density is a spatial pattern of population whereas population density is the ratio of people to a defined space.

nodes.misconception: Children who have not used digital maps before may be confused by the scales used.
nodes.response: Spend time demonstrating the zoom function so children don't get 'lost' in their digital maps.

nodes.misconception: Upland areas in the UK were created by glaciers.
nodes.response: Glaciers shaped many upland landscapes during the last Ice Age, but the original formation of mountains like those in Scotland and the Lake District was caused by tectonic activity millions of years ago.

nodes.misconception: Plantations are large cash-crop farms found in the Americas.
nodes.response: Cash-crop plantations can be found all over the world, but the first plantations were established in Ireland. Protestants loyal to the monarch were 'planted' in Irish Catholic lands to help establish control of the area.

nodes.misconception: Ultrasonic sensors work like cameras and detect objects visually.
nodes.response: Ultrasonic sensors use sound not light to detect objects.

nodes.misconception: Ultrasound may be harmful to the human body (similar to X–rays).
nodes.response: Ultrasound is essentially the same thing as sound (longitudinal waves). It consists of vibrations of matter, rather than an additional entity or 'ray' that interacts strongly with matter. Compare sound of 19 999 Hz with ultrasound of 20 001 Hz.

nodes.misconception: There are only three types of regular verbs and they form their past participles in the same way.
nodes.response: There are distinct groups of 'ir' and 're' verbs which form their past participles differently from the regular pattern (-i, -u). Students will find it beneficial to learn these verbs together as a group.

nodes.misconception: There are only three types of regular verbs and they form their past participles in the same way.
nodes.response: There are distinct groups of 'ir' and 're' verbs which form their past participles differently from the regular pattern (-i, -u). Students will find it beneficial to learn these verbs together as a group.

nodes.misconception: It is acceptable to only give short answers in the conversation element of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: Students should focus on giving answers in conversation that include at least three verb clauses. They should also regularly practise developing their answers with different verb tenses, subjects, opinions and reasons.

nodes.misconception: It is acceptable to only give short answers in the conversation element of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: Students should focus on giving answers in conversation that include at least three verb clauses. They should also regularly practise developing their answers with different verb tenses, subjects, opinions and reasons.

nodes.misconception: The present continous in English has a direct translation in French.
nodes.response: Students need to take care to translate both the simple present and the present continous with the present tense in French e.g. I listen and I am listening are translated exactly the same way: j'écoute.

nodes.misconception: The present continous in English has a direct translation in French.
nodes.response: Students need to take care to translate both the simple present and the present continous with the present tense in French e.g. I listen and I am listening are translated exactly the same way: j'écoute.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives only have one possible translation.
nodes.response: In French, adjectives can be used as a noun. When preceded by a definite article, they are often translated as the (adjective) one e.g. le bleu is translated as the blue one, not blue or the blue.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, subject pronouns are never necessary as verb endings indicate who is doing the action.
nodes.response: We can use subject pronouns 'tú' (you, sing) and 'vosotros/as' (you all) to give emphasis or to present a contrast.

nodes.misconception: Add an -s to any Spanish noun to make it plural.
nodes.response: Add an -s to Spanish nouns ending in a vowel to make them plural. Add -es to Spanish nouns ending in a consonant to make them plural.

nodes.misconception: 'Tu' is both the subject pronoun 'you' and the possessive adjective 'your'.
nodes.response: 'Tu' without an accent is a possessive adjective: you; 'tú' with an accent is a subject pronoun: you.

nodes.misconception: You can just learn set sentences by heart and produce them mechanically when requested.
nodes.response: Both writing and speaking must be adapted to the question and have a level of personalisation and spontaneity.

nodes.misconception: French object pronouns go after the verb in place of the object, just as in English. e.g. The museum interests me.
nodes.response: French object pronouns go before the verb.  e.g. Le musée m'intéresse.  When speaking and writing French we have to take care to use the correct word, especially for object pronouns.

nodes.misconception: When forming yes/no questions, we need to translate the English 'do' or 'does' into French.
nodes.response: There is no equivalent to 'do' or 'does' in French. Use inversion, intonation or 'est-ce que' to form yes/no questions.

nodes.misconception: Word order in questions is the same in Spanish and English.
nodes.response: Prepositions appear at the start of Spanish questions. They usually appear at the end of English questions.

nodes.misconception: The ideas 'to', 'in', 'of' always have the same translation in French.
nodes.response: Prepositions are tricky to master in another language. Students should be given plenty of practice of 'à', 'en' and 'de' to see how their use varies according to context.

nodes.misconception: Add -e to all adjectives to make them feminine.
nodes.response: Some adjectives follow different patterns. 'Heureux' changes to 'heureuse' and 'naturel' changes to 'naturelle'.

nodes.misconception: Direct object pronouns can be used with verbs followed by 'à' like 'demander' and 'donner'.
nodes.response: Indirect object pronouns should be used with these verbs because you ask 'of' and give 'to' someone in French. In English, the 'to' is often dropped with these kinds of verbs e.g. 'je lui donne un cadeau' I give (to) him, her a present.

nodes.misconception: There is only one word in French to translate 'mine', 'yours', 'his', 'hers'.
nodes.response: In French, possessive pronouns match the gender and number of the noun they replace in a sentence. They are formed of the definite article and the pronoun, for example: 'les chocolats, ce sont les miens,' meaning 'the chocolates, they are mine'.

nodes.misconception: All similar looking French and English words have the same meaning.
nodes.response: Often, French words have multiple meanings and it is important to choose the right one for the given context e.g. 'durable' means durable and sustainable.

nodes.misconception: 'El que' and 'el cual' are completely interchangeable.
nodes.response: 'El cual' tends to appear in more formal contexts than 'el que'.

nodes.misconception: The simple future stem of 'aller' is its infinitive, like most -er verbs.
nodes.response: 'Aller' is an irregular verb and its stem in the simple future is ir-. The normal simple future endings are added to this stem.

nodes.misconception: 'Devoir' (must) and 'pouvoir' (can) do not require the second verb to be in the infinitive form because an infinitive is not required in English.
nodes.response: 'Devoir' means to have (to) and 'pouvoir' means to be able. Therefore, when followed by a second verb, this verb must always be in the infinitive form.

nodes.misconception: 'More than' is always translated as 'más que'.
nodes.response: 'More than' can be translated as 'más que' or 'más de'. 'Más de' is followed by numbers.

nodes.misconception: Cognates are words that look and sound like English.
nodes.response: Cognates may look very similar to English but sound quite different so attention must be paid to pronunciation.

nodes.misconception: The ending -ió is always used with -er and -ir verbs to refer to she, he or it in the preterite tense.
nodes.response: For -er and -ir verbs whose stem ends in a vowel, add -yó to refer to 'he', 'she' or 'it in the preterite tense.

nodes.misconception: Command/request verbs are always followed by an infinitive, as in English, e.g. 'I want you to go', 'I'm asking you to leave'.
nodes.response: When the sentence refers to only one person, these verbs are followed by an infinitive, but if the sentence mentions two people, the command/request verbs are followed by a subjunctive.

nodes.misconception: The relative pronouns 'que', 'donde' and 'cuando' have a written accent.
nodes.response: The relative pronouns 'que' (who/that), 'donde' (where) and 'cuando' (when) do not have a written accent. However, the question words 'qué' (what), 'dónde' (where) and 'cuándo' (when) do have a written accent.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, all masculine nouns end in -o and all feminine nouns end in -a.
nodes.response: This is often the case, but it is not a blanket rule. For example, words ending in -ista, -ente and -ante can be masculine or feminine depending on the context.

nodes.misconception: The only translation of 'fuimos' is 'we went'.
nodes.response: 'fuimos' can mean 'we went' or 'we were' depending on the context. The verbs 'ser' and 'ir' are identical in the preterite tense.

nodes.misconception: It is always necessary to use subject pronouns before Spanish verbs.
nodes.response: It is not usually necessary to use subject pronouns before Spanish verbs as the verb ending shows the subject. However, they can be used to emphasise a change of subject.

nodes.misconception: Their is only one way to say 'your' in Spanish.
nodes.response: There are six ways to say 'your' in Spanish depending on the gender and number of the following noun, and whether the owner is singular or plural: tu, tus, vuestro, vuestra, vuestros and vuestras

nodes.misconception: The only Spanish translation of 'in' is 'en'.
nodes.response: There are several Spanish words for 'in' depending on the context. For example, the phrase 'por la tarde' means 'in the afternoon'.

nodes.misconception: To describe the past we can use both the preterite and the imperfect interchangeably.
nodes.response: We use the imperfect to set the scene, to give background information and to describe onling states. And we use the preterite to express completed actions that move the plot forward.

nodes.misconception: 'Lo que' can refer to a specific noun or a person.
nodes.response: 'Lo que' means 'what' or 'the thing that'. It refers to a general idea, rather than a specific noun or person.

nodes.misconception: There is not much I can do to prepare for the listening exam.
nodes.response: You can prepare for the listening exam by revising vocabulary and being ready to listen out for synonyms and distractors.

nodes.misconception: There is not much I can do to prepare for the listening exam.
nodes.response: You can prepare for the listening exam by revising vocabulary and being ready to listen out for synonyms and distractors.

nodes.misconception: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.
nodes.response: Verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' can’t always be translated word-for-word - they don’t work the same way as English verbs. You need to choose the most idiomatic or natural-sounding translation based on the context.

nodes.misconception: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.
nodes.response: Verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' can’t always be translated word-for-word - they don’t work the same way as English verbs. You need to choose the most idiomatic or natural-sounding translation based on the context.

nodes.misconception: I should keep my answers to the follow-up questions after the photo description short without extra detail.
nodes.response: You need to try and develop your answers to the follow-up questions with at least 3 verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: I should keep my answers to the follow-up questions after the photo description short without extra detail.
nodes.response: You need to try and develop your answers to the follow-up questions with at least 3 verb clauses.

nodes.misconception: If I decide to use BORDER I will apply it once for the whole writing.
nodes.response: If you choose to use BORDER, apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

nodes.misconception: Translating word-for-word is an effective strategy when tackling translation tasks.
nodes.response: Effective translation requires more than direct word-for-word substitution. Applying knowledge of grammar and using proofing strategies, such as the VAN check (Verbs, Adjectives, Nouns), can significantly improve accuracy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils rarely consider the choice of equipment and its link to the accuracy of the data they collect in a practical.
nodes.response: Highlight that equipment with smaller resolution provides more precise measurements, which can decrease the uncertainty of a calculated mean.

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold the racket like a frying pan and squat lower and lower to hit overhead clears.
nodes.response: A shake hand grip and sideways stance is required to get power and accuracy into shots, but you also need to know when it is necessary to hit underarm rather than trying to hit everything above the head.

nodes.misconception: When in a game situation and trying to beat an opponent, pupils focus on throwing with more power and speed, rather than focusing on using the correct throwing technique.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that using the correct technique will produce better accuracy and eventually the speed and power of throws will increase.

nodes.misconception: Children may write the addends in any order when representing addition as an increase in quantity.
nodes.response: Present and discuss errors, focusing on what each number in an equation represents.

nodes.misconception: Two unrelated units of measure are called 'pounds' - the money version and the mass version. Pupils may confuse one for the other.
nodes.response: In this lesson, the word pounds (as in mass) is used with the abbreviation lb in brackets. It is recommended that you use both of these until pupils reach a point where they can automatically read lb as pounds and and record it as such.

nodes.misconception: A fast heart rate and feeling of nausea is dangerous and you should stop exercising.
nodes.response: This is quite normal and a sign that we are challenging our fitness. It is important to get used to the way our body feels when we start to exercise. Seek guidance if this concerns you.

nodes.misconception: Children may find the ‘then’ part of the story, where the amount changes, difficult to identify.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the change, talking about it as a decrease.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that addends must be represented in a certain order.
nodes.response: Ensure parts are seen alongside objects and pictures presented in different ways so the visual always matches the given expression.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will most likely understand that different shapes can and most often do have different perimeters. They may not realise that the perimeters can potentially be the same.
nodes.response: Allowing pupils to recreate perimeters using string or number rods and rearranging themselves to make a new shape is a powerful way of showing that different shapes can have equal perimeters.

nodes.misconception: One-tenth times the size may be a confusing phrase to use because pupils are used to seeing an increase when using '___ times as many'.
nodes.response: Ensure that children understand that a one is one-tenth times the size of a ten. Base 10 is an excellent resource for this. Then gradually increase the ones and the corresponding tens.

nodes.misconception: 10 times the size and 10 times as many are achieved through the same operation but they are different.
nodes.response: Use sticky-tack or plasticine. Create 10 blobs that are equal in length to 1 blob that has been stretched. Encourage the children to see that the value of their length is the same but one is made of countable objects whereas the other is stretched.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may overgeneralise and assume all perimeters can be calculated by multiplying one side length by the number of sides in the polygon.
nodes.response: 'Noticing' is a key mathematical skill. Encourage pupils to take their time to notice whether the shape is regular or irregular, if that information is not already explicitly given.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it more difficult to understand equations that start with the whole (e.g. 20 = 50 - 30)
nodes.response: Emphasise the need for balance in equations. To be equal, both sides must have the same value.

nodes.misconception: The terms minuend, subtrahend and difference may be difficult if only used occasionally.
nodes.response: Ensure the terms are used by the teacher throughout lessons and encourage children to use them when explaining their thinking.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe the equal sign must always be placed at the end of the equation.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities to rearrange equations, initially where both addends are presented as one unit which balances the sum.

nodes.misconception: The -ent ending of the 3rd person plural of the verb is pronounced.
nodes.response: The -ent ending of the 3rd person plural of the verb is not pronounced. It is therefore difficult to tell the difference between the 'il/elle' form and the 'ils/elles' form of verbs when spoken.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may reorder the numbers but forget to reorder the operations too.
nodes.response: Model the problems using tens frames and number lines, ensuring that pupils understand that both the numbers and operations need to be reordered.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the wife receives two letters.
nodes.response: The wife receives a telegram and a letter. Both the irony and the tragedy are in the fact that, due to the quick nature of telegrams, the wife receives news of her husband's death before she receives his letter.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that it is always best to buy a 'deal' as deals are always a good thing.
nodes.response: Throughout the lesson it is demonstrated that a deal or promotion may not always be right for every customer. Is a deal worth it if you don't need to buy that much?

nodes.misconception: Students often think that Larkin must have had a hostile relationship with his family because of this poem and some of his other poems.
nodes.response: Larkin didn't have a hostile relationship with his parents - he was just a cynical man who held quite bleak views. This doesn't mean he hated his parents - he just recognised that people are products of their own parents.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may often write the range as '3 to 10' or '10 - 3' rather than a single value.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the range is a single value which describes how far apart the extreme values are.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to remember the order in which the steps happen.
nodes.response: Review the steps in order lots of times together before completing the ordering board.

nodes.misconception: Sometimes students think that a focused summary requires analysis of language.
nodes.response: Analysis requires you to zoom in and comment in detail about language choices. Why might this not be useful for a summary, where the aim is to be succinct and give a brief overview of a text?

nodes.misconception: An Alberti bass is the notes of the triad played in any order.
nodes.response: An Alberti bass has a specfic, distinctive pattern which uses the lowest note, highest note, middle note, highest note of the triad in that order.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that using any verb that is associated with people makes good quality personification.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a choices of verbs, including incongruous ones, to allow them to identify high quality personification.

nodes.misconception: C position is thumb on C in the left hand.
nodes.response: The C position is when the hand is placed in a position to play C up to G. With the right hand, this would be the thumb on C, finger 2 on D etc. With the left hand, the C position is when the little finger is on C, finger 4 is on D etc.

nodes.misconception: The speaker explains how having children ruined her mother's life.
nodes.response: While Duffy does explore how motherhood has contributed to her mother's loss of confidence and freedom, the final stanza of the poem shows them both having fun together so it is evident that there are many positive aspects to motherhood as well.

nodes.misconception: That Caliban and Prospero always have a negative relationship.
nodes.response: When Prospero first arrived, Caliban showed Prospero how to survive on the island so it began as a positive relationship.

nodes.misconception: Confusion between the terms capacity and volume.
nodes.response: Capacity is the whole amount of liquid that a container can hold. Volume is the actual amount of liquid in the container.

nodes.misconception: This poem is entirely autobiographical, written about Clarke's experiences of motherhood.
nodes.response: This poem was written just after the birth of Clarke's fist daughter so does reflect on her experiences of motherhood but the later scenes of a older child playing out are necessarily fictional.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to identify character traits for Plop for the inside of the owl template.
nodes.response: Reread specific pages aloud to the children and discuss Plop's actions and what this tells us about his character e.g. when he hears noises he goes down from his tree to explore - this tells us he is curious.

nodes.misconception: In Task A, pupils may place character traits both on the inside and outside of the outline.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that inner emotions and feelings remain inside, attributes that other characters can see go on the outside.

nodes.misconception: The speaker is actually climbing a mountain.
nodes.response: The speaker compares the experience of climbing up his Grandfather's body as a child to climbing up a mountain.

nodes.misconception: During tasks, pupils may use a ruler to draw or check whether points are equidistant from a centre.
nodes.response: While the tasks could be completed with a ruler, it may be quicker, easier and more accurate to use a pair of compasses.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that there is only 'one right interpretation' of a poem.
nodes.response: Students are shown in this lesson that poetry can be read in several different ways and that any interpretation is valid. Students should be encouraged to explore multiple interpretations when discussing poetry.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the dying soldier was already dead when he was thrown into the wagon.
nodes.response: It is important that students understand that the soldier was still half-alive when he was tossed, dying, into the body wagon. This needs to be understood for students to grasp the brutality of war and the lack of respect soldiers were shown.

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of accent.
nodes.response: The regular accent is the most common, but composers often indicate more specific articulation by using other accents such as marcato and sforzando. These can be difficult to distinguish by ear, but as a performer you should be familiar with them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistake dystopia and utopia as the words are similar
nodes.response: Explicitly explain the difference between the two and explain that they are antonyms

nodes.misconception: Eden Rock is a real place.
nodes.response: Eden Rock is a fictional place, devised by the poet Charles Causley. Causley confirms this but does suggest that he based the location on the Cornish landscape where he grew up.

nodes.misconception: This poem is an autobiographical account of one of Heaney's childhood memories.
nodes.response: This collection, 'Death of Naturalist', is semi-autobiographical since it reflects on aspects of Heaney's childhood, growing up in a rural Irish farming community, but the poet has never confirmed that this particular memory is from his childhood.

nodes.misconception: Mrs Birling is a woman and therefore she automatically shares the same struggles as Eva Smith.
nodes.response: While both are women, Mrs Birling's high class gives her power to uphold societal norms, whereas Eva, from a lower class, is oppressed by them.

nodes.misconception: Music for dance must have a regular pulse (in 2, 3 or 4).
nodes.response: While most Western dance music has a regular time signature, in other parts of the world it is common to dance to music with irregular time signatures, such as 5/8 and 7/8.

nodes.misconception: A ground bass pattern should finish on the tonic as it 'sounds' finished.
nodes.response: The final bar of the piece should finish on the tonic note, but until that bar, the pattern wants to repeat. Finishing on the dominant or the leading note naturally helps the music return to the first note of the pattern, which should be the tonic.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Hughes wrote this poem about fascist dictators like Hitler.
nodes.response: Hughes stated that this was not his intention. Though the poem can be interpreted in this way, this was not what Hughes set out to convey - he wanted to convey the power of nature.

nodes.misconception: That a home is just a set of bricks and mortar.
nodes.response: A home offers us a place of refuge and safety - without a home we feel lost and unsure.

nodes.misconception: Typically, literature presents the idea of a simple life as dull and monotonous.
nodes.response: Literary movements such as the Romantics presented an idealised view of a simple, rural existence.

nodes.misconception: You cannot be both respected and feared.
nodes.response: The Romantic sublime was the concept that we should feel awe towards nature - a mixture of both fear and respect.

nodes.misconception: Art is always meant to be beautiful.
nodes.response: Art can be a means of sparking discussion, representing political views, or addressing problems in society.

nodes.misconception: That an economic migrant and a refugee are the same thing.
nodes.response: A refugee is someone who has been forced to leave their country in order to escape war, persecution or natural disaster.

nodes.misconception: AI image generators create completely original artwork from scratch.
nodes.response: AI image generators create new images by learning from and combining patterns found in millions of existing images. They don’t “imagine” or invent things like a human artist; they remix data they were trained on.

nodes.misconception: That all war poetry is designed to dissuade people from fighting.
nodes.response: Pro-war poetry is designed to encourage people to volunteer to fight.

nodes.misconception: 'Leave Taking' is either universal, or about specific experiences and characters.
nodes.response: Like with many texts, we must hold both the idea of Leave Taking's universal themes with the specific experiences of its characters.

nodes.misconception: The poem is about a long-distance romantic relationship.
nodes.response: The relationship between the speaker and the man who sends her letters is ambiguous; it could be platonic, romantic or familial.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to develop 'show and tell' ideas without stating the emotion.
nodes.response: Act out different feelings to encourage children to consider what happens in their bodies when they feel that emotion.E.g. What do you think or physically feel when you experience frustration? Answers could include 'chest tightens' or 'jaw clenches'.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Dharker is critical of the structures in the slums.
nodes.response: Though Dharker portrays how dangerous these buildings are, she also shows great admiration of the slum community's resourcefulness in building theses structures - she celebrates their fortitude and resilience in the face of adversity.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that, because society was very religious in the 18th century, that Blake must have been a devout Christian too.
nodes.response: Blake was extremely opposed to mass worship and hated the fact that religion was allied with the Government - he felt this gave institutions the ability to control and oppress people.

nodes.misconception: Shelley was a Romantic poet which meant all of his poems were love poems.
nodes.response: Romantic poetry did sometimes focus on themes associated with love, but not exclusively. Romantic poetry is instead characterised by its dramatic approach to exploring abstract and emotional concepts such as a love, nature or the supernatural.

nodes.misconception: Students often make the mistake of thinking that, like many of the other war poems, this poem was written by a soldier at the time of the war.
nodes.response: This poem is not a personal account; Sheers wrote this poem in 2005. He wanted to raise awareness about the loss of Welsh lives in Mametz Wood and illustrate how destructive war is.

nodes.misconception: Compound time signatures create more complex sounding music and aren't used often.
nodes.response: This isn't strictly true. Compound time signatures are extremely common, including in popular music styles. While the theory of them is slightly more complex than simple time signatures, to compose or play using them is not particularly difficult.

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that women were completely powerless in Shakespeare's time.
nodes.response: While there were legal restrictions and social pressures on women in Shakespeare's time, there were some women who had power and influence.

nodes.misconception: This poem is written in the form of a sonnet: it has 14 lines and a regular rhyme scheme.
nodes.response: This poem does not strictly follow the sonnet form but does use many of its conventions. It contains 15, not 14 lines and doesn't use a regular rhyme scheme. It does however end with a rhyming couplet and uses iambic pentameter in places.

nodes.misconception: The poem is set by a pond where a couple are walking.
nodes.response: The poem is set in the present day (for the speaker) and the speaker is looking back on the memory of walking around a pond with their ex-partner.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any word can replace an unknown word.
nodes.response: Replacement words should be based on contextual clues, which can be supported through inferring and reading around a word.

nodes.misconception: When using part-part-whole models, children may put counters in the parts and whole simultaneously.
nodes.response: Work practically, moving counters to show we can partition the whole into parts and recombine the parts to make the whole again.

nodes.misconception: Students may associate war poetry with soldiers of the first world war and not consider other perspectives.
nodes.response: Many other people were affected by war in less obvious ways than the soldiers themselves.

nodes.misconception: That planning is not something that needs to be practiced.
nodes.response: What are the benefits of practising planning over writing whole essay responses? Not only is planning a very important part of the writing process, but an efficient way to practise essay writing.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that this poem was written from one lover to another.
nodes.response: This poem is about Lord Byron's first encounter with his cousin's wife - as far as we know, he doesn't interact with her or pursue her - he merely observes her beauty from afar.

nodes.misconception: That ecosystems are made up of plants and animals only.
nodes.response: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with one another and with non-living components of their environment, such as soil and climate.

nodes.misconception: In this poem, the speaker mourns for their lover after they have died.
nodes.response: This could be a valid interpretation but there is no evidence to suggest the lover is definitely dead. In fact, the volta in L.9 has the speaker demand he return which implies that there is a chance they could be reunited with one another.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that this sonnet was written whilst Barrett Browning was married.
nodes.response: This poem was written before the pair were married. Barrett Browning knew of her father's disapproval, but loved Robert Browning very much.

nodes.misconception: That you should take imagery at face value.
nodes.response: Imagery in poetry is often metaphorical and symbolises a deeper meaning.

nodes.misconception: Homophonic and melody and accompaniment textures are the same thing.
nodes.response: Melody and accompaniment is a specific type of homophonic texture, often called melody-dominated homophony. This is different to a chordal homophonic texture. To avoid confusion, it is easiest to treat melody and accompaniment as a separate texture.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the plot confusing, particularly the idea that Ryder 'framed' Horner.
nodes.response: Model your own 'reader talk', talking through the process of how you connected up information to work out what has happened in the story.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that some sources have a greater inherent value than others.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a source's value rests entirely upon the enquiry for which it is used and the questions asked of it. No source has inherent value unless used as part of an enquiry.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that all Muslim women wear a hijab or struggle to understand why some do and some don't.
nodes.response: Expand upon the cultural and religious significance of the hijab as well as individual choice.

nodes.misconception: The centre of rotation is always in the centre of an object.
nodes.response: The centre of rotation can be anywhere. If it's outside the shape, imagine it like a pole in the ground, attached to the object by a rope.

nodes.misconception: That our feelings towards characters must be consistent.
nodes.response: Our feelings towards characters can change depending on what is happening during the plot.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the adverbial clause always comes second in an adverbial complex sentence.
nodes.response: The position of the adverbial clause can swap. The adverbial clause can come first or second in an adverbial complex sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise non-fiction texts in picturebook form.
nodes.response: Non-fiction can take many different forms. If possible, have a range of non-fiction texts accessible in the book area or school library for children to explore and compare.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the author's life experience with those of the protagonist.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 draws explicit comparisons and discussion around the similarities between the two.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe this is a non-fiction text because it is about Vikings.
nodes.response: Give clear explanations that this is a made-up narrative set in the context of a fictional Viking community.

nodes.misconception: Shakespeare's plays are too difficult to understand or inaccessible due to the language used.
nodes.response: Many of Shakespeare's themes, emotions and characters resonate universally across time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to place the time period in which the poem is set.
nodes.response: Explicit discussion of features of the 18th Century and visual representations on a timeline will help pupils' understanding.

nodes.misconception: Fashion illustrators make finished garments.
nodes.response: Fashion illustrators draw designs and ideas. They help fashion designers show what clothes will look like before they are made.

nodes.misconception: All speeches must include all of the features included in this lesson.
nodes.response: A good speech may include some of these features but it is not essential that all are used.

nodes.misconception: If a play is a comedy, it won't have any moments of sadness in it.
nodes.response: When thinking about genre, we consider the overall tone, plot and features of a play. However, many comedies have moments of sadness, just as many tragedies have moments of humour.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the difference between stories within the genre of folklore.
nodes.response: Explore the differences between folktales and fairytales. For example, fairytales are more likely to involve magical or enchanting elements whereas folktales tend to reflect real-world settings and events.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the difference between stories within the genre of folklore.
nodes.response: Explore the differences between legends and fairytales. For example, fairytales are more likely to involve magical or enchanting elements whereas legends tend to reflect some true element of history and focus on human actions and behaviours.

nodes.misconception: That only soldiers from England fought for Britain in WW1.
nodes.response: Soldiers from all over the British Empire fought for Britain.

nodes.misconception: Students may find the idea of house as a metaphor for the self challenging.
nodes.response: Draw their attention to their own ideas around houses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to see the distinction between the overall story structure and the structure of the mini-stories.
nodes.response: As pupils will be writing events from only one mini-story in this unit, focus on the idea of each of these as a complete, resolved story in itself. The larger, overall structure is less significant for our writing in this unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils who are Christian may find it hard to connect their faith to the one depicted here.
nodes.response: Explain to children that religions evolve over time and that beliefs are not always fixed.

nodes.misconception: Authors write books for anyone to read.
nodes.response: Authors design and write their texts in order to reach certain audiences.

nodes.misconception: Students often fail to appreciate the significance of the speaker being the soldier's wife.
nodes.response: The perspective the poem is written from is deeply significant. Perhaps Armitage chose to write the poem from the perspective of the wife because the soldier is too traumatised to speak of his own experiences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the position of the median with the median's actual value.
nodes.response: Choose data where the position number would not be a reasonable median value and ensure pupils sense check their answers every time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand what feature of a data set they're trying to find when identifying a mode
nodes.response: Phrase the question as 'What is the modal colour?' for instance, rather than just 'What is the mode?'

nodes.misconception: All French cartoons are complimentary of Napoleon and all British cartoons are critical of Napoleon.
nodes.response: Many French cartoons were critical of Napoleon and many British cartoons were critical of the British government's response to his actions.

nodes.misconception: That being an outsider is always a negative thing.
nodes.response: Sometimes people are considered outsiders because they don't fit society's expectations of normal and that's not necessarily negative.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to understand the plot due to all the nonsense words.
