nodes.misconception: South Vietnam needed US troops because they didn't have much of an army of their own.
nodes.response: The South Vietnamese Army was one of the largest in the world. What they lacked was modern equipment and training.

nodes.misconception: Art must be created with the hands.
nodes.response: Art is for everyone whatever their circumstances and is not always created through using hands. Artists can create art in innovative ways without using hands.  Art is a way for all of humanity to express their viewpoints and diverse experiences.

nodes.misconception: Hate crimes always involve physical violence.
nodes.response: Hate crimes can include verbal abuse, threats, harassment or damage to property, not just physical violence. They cause harm in many forms and can deeply affect both individuals and communities even without violence.

nodes.misconception: Rehabilitation and reform mean the same thing.
nodes.response: Rehabilitation focuses on helping offenders change through support like education and therapy, while reform is the wider goal of changing behaviour and becoming a better person. Rehabilitation is one way to achieve reform.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that archaeologists only dig up bones, like dinosaurs or extinct creatures.
nodes.response: Archaeologists work with all sorts of objects from the past, many of the items in museums have been dug up by an archaeologist.

nodes.misconception: All villages in northern Italy are the same.
nodes.response: Villages in northern Italy have different climates, architecture and culture.

nodes.misconception: Use the present tense after 'si' and before the conditional to say what you would do.
nodes.response: French uses the combination of 'si' + imperfect + conditional to express what would happen if a certain condition occurred e.g. If I won the lottery, I would move to France.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often read four figure grid references the wrong way round.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they find the easting first by reading along the corridor, then read the northing by going up the stairs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that yoga is always slow and steady, and is only for relaxation.
nodes.response: Yoga can be both calming and energising, depending on the style and intention of the practice.

nodes.misconception: Righteous anger always leads to violent protest.
nodes.response: Many Christians and humanists believe righteous anger can be shown through peaceful actions like marches, speeches, or campaigns. Violence is only considered by some, and only in rare cases when all peaceful options have failed.

nodes.misconception: Vipassana meditation is primarily about relaxation or stress relief.
nodes.response: Vipassana meditation is aimed at cultivating insight into the nature of reality, specifically the impermanent, unsatisfactory, and non-self characteristics of all phenomena, known in Buddhism as the three marks of existence.

nodes.misconception: Fashion designers only design clothes.
nodes.response: Fashion designers can also design accessories, such as hats. Some fashion designers, such as milliners, specialise in one area.

nodes.misconception: Testing must always be done using a physical control system.
nodes.response: Testing a control system can be done using a physical control system and a multimeter or using a CAD simulation.

nodes.misconception: Real images always or only form on screens, or a screen is necessary to observe a real image.
nodes.response: Be clear that real images can form on screens, but can also be observed without a screen. Demonstrate looking through a convex lens (e.g. a magnifying glass) at a diminished, inverted real image of a distant object.

nodes.misconception: Real images always or only form on screens, or a screen is necessary to observe a real image.
nodes.response: Be clear that real images can form on screens, but can also be observed without a screen. Demonstrate looking through a convex lens  (e.g. a magnifying glass) at a diminished, inverted real image of a a distant object.

nodes.misconception: Real images always or only form on screens, or a screen is necessary to observe a real image.
nodes.response: Be clear that real images can form on screens, but can also be observed without a screen. Demonstrate looking through a convex lens (e.g. a magnifying glass) at a diminished, inverted real image of a distant object.

nodes.misconception: Virtue ethics is just about being nice or kind, so it doesn't require much thought or effort.
nodes.response: Virtue ethics is about developing a well-rounded character through reflection and experience, not just being kind, and requires practising virtues like courage and honesty to achieve flourishing (eudaimonia).

nodes.misconception: The only translation of 'the best' in Spanish is 'el mejor'.
nodes.response: The superlative 'el mejor' must agree with the noun it describes in number and gender. Its other forms are 'la mejor', 'los mejores' and 'las mejores'.

nodes.misconception: The Spanish translation of 'I've broken my arm' is 'me he roto mi brazo'. You use the possessive adjective for body parts.
nodes.response: When referring to body parts, Spanish speakers replace possessive adjectives with definite articles, e.g. 'me he roto el brazo'.

nodes.misconception: Most people from the UK go on holiday to France, if they go abroad.
nodes.response: The most common destination is in fact Spain.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that to communicate an idea we have to show a picture.
nodes.response: We can communicate ideas through our dance actions.

nodes.misconception: The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas visualised during meditation are merely imaginary or symbolic constructs rather than meaningful presences with deeper significance.
nodes.response: In Mahayana schools of Buddhism, visualising Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is seen as a method for connecting with enlightened qualities, purifying the mind, and realising one's own buddha-nature.

nodes.misconception: The type of chart you select doesn't matter, all charts will represent data effectively.
nodes.response: Different types of chart present different types of data effectively. For example, a pie chart is used to represent data that makes up a whole part or 100%.

nodes.misconception: All verbs in French can be used before an infinitive without a preposition.
nodes.response: Certain verbs require 'à' or 'de' before a an infinitive. Learning which verbs this applies to is helpful. Teachers might like to point out the more frequently occurring verbs of this type to help students develop their confidence in using them.

nodes.misconception: You can only use single paragraph outlines to plan analytical writing.
nodes.response: We structure so much of our writing using paragraphs. All paragraphs, whether creative or analytical or something else, require a clear and carefully planned structure.

nodes.misconception: Fashion design only considers the aesthetic qualities of clothing and accessories.
nodes.response: Fashion designers must balance form and function when designing clothing and accessories.

nodes.misconception: Female voices are always higher pitched than male voices.
nodes.response: While this is mostly true, alto and tenor ranges overlap. A low alto voice can be as low as a tenor. Alongside this, men can use the falsetto technique to sing much higher than their normal range, in some cases higher than female voices.

nodes.misconception: Writing a vocal melody is the same as writing an instrumental melody.
nodes.response: Many of the same principles apply, such as phrase structure and using notes from the chords and the key. However, a vocal melody has to fit the natural rhythms and mood of the words well - we don't have to consider this with instrumental melodies.

nodes.misconception: Teental is in 4/4.
nodes.response: Teental sounds to us like it could be in 4/4, but this is just a coincidence. North Indian classical musicians don't think of time signature in the same way that we do - the tala is what structures the time and they can be many different lengths.

nodes.misconception: Lava is the only dangerous aspect to a volcanic eruption and you can just run out of the way.
nodes.response: Ash, lahars and pyroclastic flows are all extremely dangerous volcanic hazards. Pyroclastic flows can reach speeds of 435 mph, which is faster than a car.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often say volcanoes 'explode' rather than erupt.
nodes.response: Ensure that as 'good geographers' correct vocabulary for features and processes is always used and that pupils appreciate why.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often swing their racket at the ball generating too much power when hitting a volley. Pupils hit the volley with their feet square to the net rather than side on.
nodes.response: The volley technique involves blocking the ball rather than swinging the racket back to hit the volley. Pupils should step into the volley so their bodies turn to the side when they hit a volley.

nodes.misconception: Pupils use a big swing for volleys and consequently regularly miss the ball or hit it out.
nodes.response: When playing close to the net, you don't need to apply much swing and instead should use the power already in the ball, combined with a step into the shot, to apply power with more of a short punching action to block the ball back.

nodes.misconception: Voltage in a parallel circuit is shared out between each branch of the circuit.
nodes.response: Provide opportunity for pupils to measure voltage across each branch of a range of parallel circuits to give evidence for the correct rule.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to explain the difference between capacity and volume.
nodes.response: Look at examples of different containers containing different amounts of liquid and use these stem sentences to support their learning. 'The volume of liquid in A is _ than the volume of liquid in B.' 'The capacity of A is _ than the capacity of B.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that if you cut the height of the cone in a half, the resulting frustrum will have half the volume of the original cone.
nodes.response: The frustrum is actually seven eighths of the volume of the original cone; the small cone that was removed to create the frustrum is one eighth the volume of the original cone if the frustrum and the small cone have the same height.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only using given measures in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required for substitution into a volume formula.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to show how the are breaking down a compound/composite shape. Pupils should label the diagram with any new lengths needed. They may need to use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find these new lengths.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may multiply the length and radius before squaring.
nodes.response: Remind students of the order of operations and link to the volume of a prism formula: finding the area of the cross-section first.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may multiply all lengths on the diagram rather than find the area of the cross-section.
nodes.response: Draw the cross-sectional polygon out, find the area and then multiply by the length of the prism.

nodes.misconception: Muscles can pull and push.
nodes.response: Muscles are only able to pull, they work in antagonistic pairs so one muscle can contract to create a movement whilst the other relaxes in opposition and then their roles are reversed to move back.

nodes.misconception: I have to understand every single word in a text in order to understand its general meaning.
nodes.response: It is difficult to know all of the words in any given language! Use the words you do know and other contextual and linguistic clues to help you decipher the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: The word 'gefallen' always means 'fell'.
nodes.response: The past participle of 'fallen' ('to fall') is 'gefallen', as is the past participle of 'gefallen' ('to please'). The difference is that the auxiliary verb 'haben' is used with 'gefallen' (to please), but 'sein' is used with 'fallen' (to fall).

nodes.misconception: 'Vor' and 'bevor' and 'nach' and 'nachdem' are interchangeable because they mean 'before' and 'after'.
nodes.response: 'Vor' and 'nach' are prepositions and are followed by a noun, 'bevor' and 'nachdem' are conjunctions which link clauses and trigger word order 3.

nodes.misconception: English verbs followed by prepositions can be directly translated into German.
nodes.response: Whilst many of the same verbs are followed by prepositions in both languages, different prepositions are often used, so these must be learnt.

nodes.misconception: Mixing up STV and AV as both involve ranking candidates from favourite to least.
nodes.response: With STV, excess votes from the winning candidates are also reassigned.

nodes.misconception: Auden is saying suffering is unimportant.
nodes.response: Auden presents extreme suffering, but he is exploring how, inevitably, when something terrible is happening, something ordinary is happening at the same time too.

nodes.misconception: That life was the same 750 years ago as it is today.
nodes.response: Explain to children that lots of things were very different 750 years ago. For example, there were no cars, planes or trains and it would have taken Owain a long time to travel to Scotland and London. People would have travelled by horse or walked.

nodes.misconception: The use of adjectives is a simple technique, so there isn't much point analysing a writer's use of them, or planning for them in your own writing.
nodes.response: Adjectives are a wonderful way to express tone, nuanced meaning and atmosphere. As such, they can be rich for analysis, and have a powerful effect on your own descriptive writing.

nodes.misconception: Environmental activism and protest is primarily a European concern.
nodes.response: Wangari Maathai blended her Catholic and Kikuyu beliefs to argue for environmental justice in Kenya. She framed this through a distinctively African theological lens.

nodes.misconception: You need to conjugate the verb following a modal verb.
nodes.response: The second verb following a modal verb must be in the infinitive form.

nodes.misconception: Historically the contribution of colonial troops to the war effort has been overlooked.
nodes.response: Colonial troops made significant contributions to the war, both within Europe and across the world.

nodes.misconception: Swapping comfortably and accurately from one rhythm to another with the overall structure.
nodes.response: This is quite tricky as the strucutre is complex. Break it down for pupils so they learn each section comfortably and encourage them to practise going from one rhythm to the next and think about strategies for remembering the rhythms.

nodes.misconception: Improvisation means making something up from nothing
nodes.response: You can use typical rhythms or features of the style as a basis oof any improvisation. This might mean using an establisehd idea such as a prepared triplet or syncopated rhtyhm and then extending the idea with something made up in the moment.

nodes.misconception: Stretching is the first part of a warm up routine.
nodes.response: Before a muscle can be stretched, it needs to have an increase in temperature and pliability. Therefore, before stretching, an individual should do a pulse raiser to increase blood flow to the muscles.

nodes.misconception: Stretching is the first part of a warm up routine.
nodes.response: Before a muscle can be stretched it needs to have an increase in temperature and pliability. Therefore, before stretching, an individual should do a pulse raiser to increase blood flow to the muscles.

nodes.misconception: 'Können' and 'dürfen' both translate as 'can' in English.
nodes.response: 'Können' and 'dürfen' are often used incorrectly in both German and English. 'Dürfen' refers to permission - 'may I/am I allowed to?'. 'Können' refers to the ability to do something - 'can I/am I able to?', whether or not permission is given.

nodes.misconception: We need to use the present continuous in German when describing photos.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in German. The present continuous in German is the same as the simple present, so 'sie essen' means 'they eat' and 'they are eating'. When translating English present continuous sentences, use the simple present.

nodes.misconception: The verb 'mögen' takes regular verb endings.
nodes.response: The verb 'mögen' is irregular in the singular present tense forms, and the first and third person singular are identical: 'ich mag', 'er mag'.

nodes.misconception: Historians all study the same things in history.
nodes.response: There is a large and ever-growing variety of themes that historians look at in history that shape the way we view the past, e.g. military history, economic history, women's history and many more.

nodes.misconception: When developing a conversation about future plans, it is important to consistently use the future time frame in answers.
nodes.response: Whilst it is important to be able to refer to the future confidently, it is also helpful to add in different time frames to give more detail and to develop your sentences.

nodes.misconception: Being seen as ‘healthy’ or ‘unhealthy’ is linked to personal attributes as well as physical attributes (such as regarding an unhealthy character as lazy or untidy).
nodes.response: Explanation that everyone can take steps to be healthy and that good hygiene is an important part of being healthy.

nodes.misconception: Recycling is the most effective way reducing the amount of waste we throw away.
nodes.response: Highlight the understanding that reusing and reducing what is used is more effective and that recycling should be seen as a last resort. Repairing and repurposing can also help to reduce waste.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils think that 'wastewater' is the same as 'sewage' and/or that anything found in a sewer is 'sewage'.
nodes.response: Stress that wastewater is any used water that has been affected by domestic, industrial and agricultural processes; sewage is a part of waste water, but specifically that which is contaminated by with faeces and urine.

nodes.misconception: The same tools and methods are used for both small-scale and industrial manufacturing.
nodes.response: The scale of production heavily influences tool choice, speed, accuracy, and repeatability.

nodes.misconception: Cutting is the only form of removing material.
nodes.response: Removing material can include cutting, drilling and the use of abrasive papers and tools.

nodes.misconception: The Pathé news clips are just old videos used as a backdrop and don’t add meaning to the play.
nodes.response: The Pathé clips set the historical context and show a biased view of the British Empire. They contrast with the characters’ real experiences, deepening our understanding of the story’s themes.

nodes.misconception: There isn’t any humour in plays like 'Small Island' because the subject matter is too serious.
nodes.response: Humour is used in 'Small Island' to make the characters more relatable and to provide moments of relief during tense scenes. It helps the audience connect with the story while still exploring serious issues.

nodes.misconception: A flawed character is someone who is always unlikeable or hard to relate to.
nodes.response: In reality, flawed characters often have human weaknesses that make them more believable or even sympathetic, much like the character of Hortense.

nodes.misconception: The fixed setting in Act 2 means the play is less interesting or creative.
nodes.response: The fixed setting in Act 2 shows how the characters feel trapped or confined by their situations, which makes the story more powerful and emotional.

nodes.misconception: Gilbert shouting at Hortense shows he doesn’t respect her or care about their relationship
nodes.response: Gilbert’s anger reflects his frustration and the pressures he faces in a racist society. His harsh words mask his deep care and protectiveness, and the scene later shows their developing understanding and connection.

nodes.misconception: Because Gilbert jokes and is confident, it means he isn’t really affected by racism or hardship.
nodes.response: Gilbert uses humour to hide pain. Arguably, his confidence masks his struggle, making his experience more powerful and real. Consider this when you watch the perfomance.

nodes.misconception: The best endings are always neat and fully resolved, tying up every storyline.
nodes.response: While neat endings can feel satisfying, 'Small Island' shows powerful endings often include uncertainty. Edmundson says the play balances hope and love with an unclear future, making it realistic and thought-provoking.

nodes.misconception: That everyone, all around the world, can easily access clean fresh water whenever they need it.
nodes.response: In the UK, it is easy to take water for granted because it comes out of the tap. This isn't possible in all communities. In some places, water is very scarce. People may have to travel miles to reach water as they do not have taps in their homes.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that water wheels and water turbines cause water to move when they spin.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that water wheels and water turbines harness the energy of water to do work for us or to generate electricity.

nodes.misconception: That water enters a building in multiple places, or that whenever there is a tap water enters at that point.
nodes.response: All buildings have at least one stopcock. This is the only point of entry for water into a building. In the event of a flood or burst pipe, the stopcock can be turned off to stop any more water entering the building.

nodes.misconception: That there is nothing we can do to help with water supply problems.
nodes.response: Water is a precious resource everywhere in the world, in all countries. We can all do our bit by using water more carefully and encouraging other people to do the same.

nodes.misconception: That water originates from pipes or taps.
nodes.response: All water is a natural resource and originates from bodies of water such as rivers, lakes, reservoirs.

nodes.misconception: That water which comes out of the tap is a free resource.
nodes.response: Water is a utility, just like gas and electricity. We need utilities to run our homes and do everyday tasks. The money we pay for water goes to the company that provides our water pipes, drains, sewers and recycles our water so we can use it again.

nodes.misconception: All objects experience the same amount of water resistance, regardless of their size or shape.
nodes.response: Discussion and explicit teaching. The investigation they carry out will show them that this is not true.

nodes.misconception: All objects experience the same amount of water resistance, regardless of their size or shape.
nodes.response: Discussion and explicit teaching. The investigation they plan will, in the next lesson, show them that this is not true.

nodes.misconception: In LICs and NEEs there is a general lack of safe drinking water.
nodes.response: There is unequal access to safe drinking water in LICs and some NEEs, rather than a general lack. Investment in infrastructure often lags behind population growth. Wealthier people buy bottled water or expensive home purification technology.

nodes.misconception: Our wastewater is treated and sent straight to our taps, to drink.
nodes.response: Few water systems link wastewater treatment plants to the supply system, with treated water going into covered reservoirs before the clean water network. Most release treated wastewater into rivers; from where it is abstracted downstream, later on.

nodes.misconception: Many pupils think that if you fall in to water you should start swimming as quickly as possible.
nodes.response: But we need to teach them that if you fall into water, you should float on your back to regain your breath and calm yourself down, before assessing the situation.

nodes.misconception: All water is the same.
nodes.response: The dissolved solid content of water samples is affected by the environment from which it was obtained.

nodes.misconception: All water samples boil at 100°C.
nodes.response: If a water sample is impure, the boiling point of water increases. The greater the amount of impurities in a water sample, the larger the temperature range over which it boils.

nodes.misconception: All water samples are neutral (i.e. pH of 7).
nodes.response: The acidity / alkalinity of water samples is affected by the dissolved substances in each sample.

nodes.misconception: That aquifers are soaking wet and we can see or feel them.
nodes.response: Aquifers are areas of porous rock deep underground, we can not see or feel them from the surface. Rocks, like cliff faces or outcrops that we can see are not soaking wet because the water is found far deeper within the aquifer.

nodes.misconception: Water moves forwards with a water wave.
nodes.response: Show pupils animations depicting how transverse waves are created in water (and on ropes) by patterns of oscillation. Explicitly draw their attention to how the wave shape / wave pattern travels forwards without any material travelling forwards.

nodes.misconception: Artists always make artwork by themselves.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can choose to work by themselves, but they can also plan and make work collaboratively.

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Importance of testing each material to check if we are correct and not to rely on what we think we already know. Scientists ask questions and test their ideas.

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials children may rely purely on observation rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Opportunity to use real-life results to answer questions and draw conclusions.

nodes.misconception: That waves and tides are the same thing, or that tides are the cause of waves, or that wind causes both waves and tides.
nodes.response: Waves are caused by the wind blowing across the sea, not by the tide. The tide is the regular rise and fall of the sea level regardless of whether there are waves or if the sea is calm.

nodes.misconception: When soloing the ball, pupils don't flick their toe upwards causing the ball to travel in front of them. When passing, pupils throw the ball, forgetting the correct open or closed hand passing action.
nodes.response: When the foot impacts the ball, flick your toes up so the ball travels back into the hands. Pupils should spend a lot of time repeating their hand passing skills to avoid throwing the ball when under pressure.

nodes.misconception: All weapons of mass destruction are completely illegal under international law.
nodes.response: While chemical and biological weapons are fully banned, nuclear weapons are not completely illegal. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty aims to limit their spread and promote disarmament, but it does not ban their possession by certain countries.

nodes.misconception: Weather forecasts are only seen on apps and on the TV. Weather forecasts just use symbols.
nodes.response: Students will explore synoptic charts, used by meteorologists, to interpret the weather.

nodes.misconception: Climate and weather are the same thing.
nodes.response: Explain that weather tells you what clothes to wear that day. Climate tells you what sort of clothes you need to have in your wardrobe.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that weather and climate are the same.
nodes.response: Pupils will explore that weather is the short term changes in the atmosphere whereas climate is long term changes in the atmospheric patterns of a place.

nodes.misconception: All trees have leaves that change colour.
nodes.response: Evergreen trees are green all year round and do not shed their leaves. Only deciduous trees have leaves that change colour in autumn and eventually lose them in winter.

nodes.misconception: When flowers bloom and it's sunny, some children might mistake this for summer.
nodes.response: Spring falls in the months of March, April and May. In spring, the days start to get warmer and there are more hours of daylight, but temperatures are not the hottest and the hours of daylight are not the longest.

nodes.misconception: In summer it's always hot.
nodes.response: Even though the days are hottest in summer, there are still days that may be wet and cold.

nodes.misconception: It is always snowing in winter.
nodes.response: If conditions are right and it is cold enough then it will snow during the winter months. There are some days in winter that are mild and not cold.

nodes.misconception: That dance performances do not include repetition of ideas.
nodes.response: Repeating movement material in a dance is similar to the use of a chorus in a song, it emphasises the main idea and prevents the audience from being overwhelmed. Repetitions are usually varied or developed in some way to maintain interest.

nodes.misconception: In dance we are pretending to 'be' the subject we are creating a dance about.
nodes.response: In dance we use the subject to help us think of movements that show what it is like. Pretending to be something is a drama skill that is used in some, but not all dance.

nodes.misconception: The UK has a moderate climate and doesn't experience weather hazards.
nodes.response: The UK experiences a range of different weather hazards which can have serious impacts.

nodes.misconception: In French 'il fait' always means 'he does, makes'.
nodes.response: In French 'il fait' often means 'he does, makes' but when referring to the weather it means 'it is' e.g. 'Il fait froid.' (It is cold.).

nodes.misconception: Pupils associate different seasons with activities, rather than physical characteristics like the weather.
nodes.response: Explanation of different weathers that the pupils may experience in different seasons.

nodes.misconception: We use 'ser' to describe the weather in Spanish.
nodes.response: In English we use the verb 'to be' for the weather (e.g. 'it is cold'), but in Spanish the verb 'hacer' is used. For example, to say 'it is sunny' you would say 'hace sol'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may associate different seasons with activities, rather than physical characteristics like the weather.
nodes.response: Explanation of different weathers that pupils may experience in different seasons.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that it is always sunny in summer.
nodes.response: Explanation that there are different types of weather in summer but the temperature is generally warmer than during other seasons.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may associate sunny weather with summer and not winter.
nodes.response: Explanation that there are different types of weather in winter, but the temperature is generally cooler than during other seasons.

nodes.misconception: Children use the word weathering and erosion interchangeably to mean the same thing.
nodes.response: Explain the difference between these two processes, that are closely linked, through clear definitions, images and examples of where they are happening.

nodes.misconception: Weathering and erosion are the same process.
nodes.response: Students will be informed that erosion is the process of Earth’s surface, e.g. rock or soil, being worn away and transported from its original site, whereas weathering is the process of wearing or being worn by long exposure to the atmosphere.

nodes.misconception: Context must be included in every paragraph.
nodes.response: Context must be included in essays, but where it is relevant and develops your analysis - not as a tick box exercise for each paragraph.

nodes.misconception: Looms cannot be made from everyday objects.
nodes.response: Remind children that looms can be made on a wide variety of frames, including found sticks or paper plates.

nodes.misconception: I don’t need a wireframe or site map, I can just start coding.
nodes.response: Planning is a key step in web development. A wireframe helps you decide where things go before writing any code, and a site map ensures you know how pages connect. Skipping planning often leads to messy code and confusing navigation.

nodes.misconception: JavaScript only works after everything is perfect, I’ll fix it all at the end.
nodes.response: JavaScript is best written and tested in small steps. Writing a little, testing it, and debugging as you go helps avoid big problems later.

nodes.misconception: The header of a web page is the title.
nodes.response: The header is a section of the web page where the title is normally located but includes information that describes features of a web page but that is not actually part of the web page itself.

nodes.misconception: Web page divisions all need to have unique labels. They can't be the same.
nodes.response: When designing divisions of a web page the same formatting may need to be applied to multiple divisions. In this case the labels would  need to be the same.

nodes.misconception: Search engines instantly know every website and search live each time you type in a query.
nodes.response: Search engines don’t search the web in real time. They use crawlers to index content in advance. When you search, they quickly scan this index to return the most relevant results.

nodes.misconception: Closing tags are optional and are just used to make the code easier to read.
nodes.response: Most tags need to be closed and require the use of a forward slash. This marks the beginning and the end of the content that the HTML tag should be applied to.

nodes.misconception: It is fine to use the infinitive next to the subject pronoun.
nodes.response: The infinitive is the dictionary form of the verb but verbs change ending to match their subject (I, you, she, he etc.). Regular -er verbs always add the same set of endings.

nodes.misconception: If you use inversion and add a question word, you don't need to change your intonation.
nodes.response: Even when using inversion and/or question words, still raise your voice at the end of a sentence in French when asking a question.

nodes.misconception: 'Los' and 'las' always mean 'the'.
nodes.response: 'Los' and 'las' mean 'the' in front of a plural noun but 'them' when they come before a verb.

nodes.misconception: When 'de' appears before 'el' it becomes 'de el'.
nodes.response: When 'de' appears before a singular masculine noun with the definite article 'el' it merges with it to form 'del', e.g. 'la jugadora está fuera del estadio' - 'the player is outside the stadium'.

nodes.misconception: The indirect object pronoun 'le' changes to 'la' to match the gender of the person receiving the action.
nodes.response: 'Le' means 'to him', 'to her' or 'to it' regardless of the person receiving the action, e.g. 'le doy un regalo a Lucía' or 'le doy un regalo a Daniel'.

nodes.misconception: That for all situations the weightings are subjective.
nodes.response: There are situations in which a subjective decision is made about weightings but there are also situations where the multipliers used are dictated by the context in a logical way. An example of this is combining groups and combining their means.

nodes.misconception: Weimar Germany was a completely free and modernist society.
nodes.response: While it was a hub of cultural experimentation, it was also deeply divided, with strong conservative resistance and widespread political unrest. Many Germans viewed the cultural changes as dangerous and sought to restore traditional values.

nodes.misconception: Every family looks the same.
nodes.response: All families look different.

nodes.misconception: Only Hindu boys have their Mundan haircut.
nodes.response: Both boys and girls can have their Mundan first haircut as part of this special tradition.

nodes.misconception: Every family does everything the same way.
nodes.response: Families might welcome children in many different ways depending on their worldview

nodes.misconception: Every family welcomes new life in the same way.
nodes.response: Understand that people welcome new life in different ways.

nodes.misconception: The Welsh resistance was always a unified movement.
nodes.response: Many Welsh princes cooperated with Edward's Welsh campaign in 1277. Edward’s army also included 9000 Welsh soldiers.

nodes.misconception: The present continuous in German is different to the simple present.
nodes.response: The present continuous in German is the same as the simple present, so 'sie essen' means 'they eat' and 'they are eating'.

nodes.misconception: Use 'würd-' whenever you want to say 'would'.
nodes.response: 'Würd-' works for very many cases and is easy to remember because it sounds like the English 'would'. But 'haben' and 'sein' are important exceptions, especially in spoken German. 'Hätte' means 'I would have' and 'wäre' means 'I would be'.

nodes.misconception: German forms the present continuous tense by using sein with a verb e.g. "ich bin spielen" to say "I am playing".
nodes.response: German only has one present tense and does not use sein with a verb.

nodes.misconception: Climate change is just a natural part of Earth’s cycles, and humans aren't responsible for it.
nodes.response: While Earth’s climate has naturally changed in the past, the IPCC shows that the current rapid warming is mainly caused by human activities, like burning fossil fuels and deforestation.

nodes.misconception: All animals eat the same food.
nodes.response: Examples of animals that eat different types of food.

nodes.misconception: Women could not hold positions of power in the Shang Dynasty.
nodes.response: The tomb of Fu Hao tells us that she was a powerful queen and one of the most successful and important army generals of her time.

nodes.misconception: That changemakers are connected or influential people with lots of resources.
nodes.response: Anyone can be a changemaker. It depends on the ability of the person to bring people along with them and build a cause people believe in.

nodes.misconception: All communities are diverse.
nodes.response: Communities are different depending on where they are located and the people they contain. However, in some places, communities have not seen much migration and are not diverse as a result.

nodes.misconception: Representative democracies take away the choices of citizens because the representatives make all the decisions on their behalf.
nodes.response: In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf, but they can also influence policies through voting in elections, contacting their representatives and sometimes even through referendums.

nodes.misconception: Humanitarian problems are just conflicts.
nodes.response: Humanitarian problems can be a range of issues, including conflicts. It could be a natural disaster such as an earthquake or it could be other events which lead to a refugee crisis. Conflicts are one example of humantiarian problems.

nodes.misconception: It is the role of the police to make laws.
nodes.response: Laws are created by Parliament. The police do not make the law, they enforce it.

nodes.misconception: Local councils have full control of their spending so can make all decisions themselves.
nodes.response: Part of their funding comes from national government so they sometimes have to priorities government led initiatives over local need.

nodes.misconception: You have no protection after 30 days of purchasing goods and services.
nodes.response: After 30 days, a replacement, repair or credit can be given (except for food items like milk). A discount or a refund could also still be given. There is some level of protection up to six months after you purchased something with no extra guarantee.

nodes.misconception: Pressure groups are always fringe groups with little influence on the Government.
nodes.response: Pressure groups vary in size and influence. They can be insider groups which already support the Government in writing policies.

nodes.misconception: Referendums are only about national issues.
nodes.response: Referendums are held for a wide range of reasons. They might be national, (like the UK's relationship with Europe), or they might be regional, (like Scottish independence). Sometimes, a referendum can be local too.

nodes.misconception: The rule of law applies only to ordinary citizens, not leaders or those in power.
nodes.response: A key feature of the rule of law is that everyone, including those in power, are subject to the law.

nodes.misconception: Police are just authority figures who punish people.
nodes.response: Police protect communities, prevent crime, and ensure safety, not just enforce punishment. They also help in emergencies.

nodes.misconception: An uncodified constitution means there are no rules or limitations on government power.
nodes.response: There are rules and limitations on government power in an uncodified constitution, e.g. the UK’s uncodified constitution is made up of various sources, including statute law and common law. Rule of law is a key principle that guides Parliament.

nodes.misconception: Both chambers in the UK's bicameral system have equal power and roles.
nodes.response: The House of Commons holds more legislative power, while the House of Lords primarily acts as a revising chamber, providing scrutiny and suggesting amendments, rather than making final decisions.

nodes.misconception: Immigration control means stopping all immigration.
nodes.response: Immigration control does not mean stopping all immigration. It means managing who can come, when and why, using systems like visas, border checks and rules. The aim is to make immigration fair, safe and planned, not to block everyone from entering.

nodes.misconception: Devolved governments can make laws and policies on any issue in their devolved region.
nodes.response: The powers of devolved governments are limited to specific policy areas defined by devolution agreements. Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales have some executive and legislative powers. English regional governments only have some executive powers.

nodes.misconception: Becuase both countries are democracies, the UK and the US political systems are the same.
nodes.response: Both countries are democracies but they differ: for example, the UK has a parliamentary system where only the House of Commons is elected, while the US has a presidential system where voters elect both houses of Congress and the President separately.

nodes.misconception: Only direct action campaign methods such as protests can make change happen.
nodes.response: Direct action, like protests, can create change, but indirect methods are also powerful. Petitions, social media, education, and lobbying influence opinions and decisions over time. Successful campaigns often use both to make a lasting impact.

nodes.misconception: Discrimination only affects someone in the moment it happens.
nodes.response: The effects can be long-lasting and deeply personal. Discrimination can lead to emotional distress, loss of confidence and reduced life opportunities. Even if an incident seems small to others, it can be big to the person being discriminated against.

nodes.misconception: Local government has no control over their finances because the Government controls the Budget.
nodes.response: Devolution of the economy means that the Government have given local government more control over their local community spending.

nodes.misconception: Borrowing money is always a dangerous thing to do.
nodes.response: In our lives it is sometimes necessary to borrow money, e.g., when we buy a house most people have to get a mortgage. However, this can be part of budgeting sensibly and learning to be financially responsible by always paying loans back on time.

nodes.misconception: Laws are made the same way in both the UK and the US.
nodes.response: The process of creating laws is different. The UK has a parliamentary system whereas the US follows a presidential system.

nodes.misconception: Voting is the only way citizens can make a difference in global humanitarian issues.
nodes.response: There are numerous things citizens can do, for example, they can also take part in demonstrations, volunteer schemes, and other actions that raise awareness and provide direct support, all of which contribute to making a difference.

nodes.misconception: Only the police can prevent crime.
nodes.response: Communities can also play a key role by using strategies like education, situational changes and deterrents to reduce crime and promote safety.

nodes.misconception: Effective change only happens through large, dramatic actions or protests and smaller efforts don't make a difference.
nodes.response: Effective change can happen in many ways. While protests like those led by the women's suffrage movement can bring attention to important issues, smaller actions, like community policing can also lead to significant and lasting change.

nodes.misconception: Active citizenship campaigns are not part of democracy.
nodes.response: If you work together effectively, active citizen campaign tasks are an important form of taking part in democracy.

nodes.misconception: We are powerless to protect the rights of others until we are adults.
nodes.response: Children can protect the rights of others by using active citizenship methods.

nodes.misconception: Fairness is only about following the law; if something is legal, then it must be fair.
nodes.response: While laws set important standards, fairness also depends on how people treat each other every day. Sometimes, unfairness happens even when no laws are broken. True fairness requires respectful actions, understanding and challenging unfair attitudes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that carbon dioxide is inherently harmful due to the way information about climate change is often presented.
nodes.response: Explain that carbon dioxide is not necessarily harmful; it is in the air we breathe and it is vital for the survival of plants. It can, however, become problematic as levels in the atmosphere increase and cause a warming effect.

nodes.misconception: Protests always lead to immediate change.
nodes.response: Change brought by protests can take time and often requires persistence and widespread support. While some protests have led to quick reforms, others have taken years or even decades to achieve their goals.

nodes.misconception: There is a single, clear British identity that everyone shares.
nodes.response: British identity is diverse and multi-faceted, with different people valuing different aspects depending on their background and experience.

nodes.misconception: Algorithms only show people what they want to see, they don’t really affect how people vote.
nodes.response: Algorithms can reinforce existing beliefs and limit exposure to different views. The UK Undercover Voters project showed that targeted content could influence opinions and spread misinformation, which could affect voting behaviour.

nodes.misconception: Verbs form their past participles by sandwiching the verb stem with 'ge-' and '-t' or '-en'.
nodes.response: Not all verbs form past participles in the same way. For instance, verbs that start with inseparable prefixes or end '-ieren' do not add 'ge-'. Some groups of verbs have a vowel change in the stem, e.g., 'finden', 'gefunden'.

nodes.misconception: Community groups, charities and NGOs do not make much of a difference in local communities.
nodes.response: Charities, groups and NGOs make a huge difference and have a measurable impact on local communities and their success.

nodes.misconception: Councils only deal with minor issues, like park maintenance.
nodes.response: Local councils play a crucial role in many significant areas, including urban and housing planning, public health, education and community services. They have a say in local regulations, budgets and initiatives that greatly impact quality of life.

nodes.misconception: MPs only work in Parliament.
nodes.response: MPs spend a lot of time helping constituents, attending local events and managing casework.

nodes.misconception: Only governments can protect and enforce human rights.
nodes.response: NGOs also play a vital role by raising awareness, supporting victims and pressuring governments to uphold human rights worldwide.

nodes.misconception: Political parties are all either left wing or right wing.
nodes.response: Many parties mix both views or focus on specific issues, like regional concerns. Some parties are centrist or have ideas that don’t fit neatly into either side.

nodes.misconception: To make a verb negative in Spanish, you have to add an additional verb, like 'do not' or 'does not', like in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, no extra verb is necessary. You just add 'no' before the verb. This works for any verb and person.

nodes.misconception: It is not necessary for campaigners to have any financial skills.
nodes.response: Financial skills are really important in active citizenship campaigns. There are often budgets to stick to, risks to manage and financial reporting to complete.

nodes.misconception: The first person singular form of 'hacer' is 'haco'.
nodes.response: The first person singular form of 'hacer' is irregular. To mean 'I' with the verb 'hacer', use 'hago'.

nodes.misconception: 'Hacer' only means 'to do'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, 'hacer' is used for 'to do' and 'to make', there is no specific verb for either.

nodes.misconception: Cuál is used as in English, followed by a noun.
nodes.response: In Spanish, cuál is never followed by a noun.

nodes.misconception: The 'e' at the end of a word in French is pronounced.
nodes.response: The 'e' at the end of a word in French is silent, it is an SFe (silent final 'e'), e.g. 'timide'.

nodes.misconception: There is one word for 'some' for both masculine and feminine nouns.
nodes.response: In Spanish, there are two words for some. For masculine plural nouns, use 'unos'. For feminine plural nouns, use 'unas'.

nodes.misconception: 'Nicht' is always used to make negative statements in German.
nodes.response: There are two ways of making negative statements: 'nicht' and 'kein'. It is not always obvious when 'kein' should be used to translate negative English statements, e.g., 'I don't have a car' is 'ich habe kein Auto'.

nodes.misconception: The verbs 'ver' and 'visitar' are used in the same way regardless of who or what you are visiting.
nodes.response: When seeing or visiting a person or a pet, you need to add in the preposition 'a' after the verb.

nodes.misconception: Crime prevention strategies only work if they catch criminals.
nodes.response: Crime prevention strategies are about stopping crime before it happens. For example, strategies like educating young people, improving public spaces and changing attitudes can help reduce the chances of crime occurring in the first place.

nodes.misconception: Fairness always means treating everybody the same.
nodes.response: Fairness may involve treating people differently based on their individual circumstances in order to achieve equitable outcomes.

nodes.misconception: Some people believe that you can only have one identity.
nodes.response: People can have multiple identities because they can belong to different groups at the same time.

nodes.misconception: That a person can only be part of one community.
nodes.response: We can belong to multiple communities, such as our family, school, faith or clubs.

nodes.misconception: Democracy is just about voting.
nodes.response: Democracy is about more than just voting. Democratic values include freedom of speech, the right to protest and freedom to assemble etc.

nodes.misconception: That national government can impact local government, but that local government has no impact on national.
nodes.response: Local governments can play a crucial role in shaping the work and direction of national government.

nodes.misconception: Political decisions don’t really affect the population, people just move or live longer naturally.
nodes.response: Government policies (like immigration laws or public health measures) directly shape who lives in the country, how many people come or go and how long people live.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives in Spanish appear before the noun as they do in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, many adjectives appear after the noun and agree with the number and gender of the noun they describe.

nodes.misconception: Numbers change their spelling depending on gender of the noun.
nodes.response: Numbers do not change their spelling for gender.

nodes.misconception: The Civil Service is a political body.
nodes.response: The Civil Service is designed to be impartial, serving the Government of the day. Civil servants are expected to provide objective advice and implement policy without political bias. This allows for continuity even when political leadership changes.

nodes.misconception: The Government have full control of driving and impacting the economy.
nodes.response: Although the Government play a key role in the UK's economy, it is also impacted by external factors, and when this happens, the Government have to make poltical decisions to protect the economy.

nodes.misconception: The judiciary always protects and strengthens human rights, no matter what.
nodes.response: The judiciary plays a key role in defending rights, but it does not always act quickly or strongly enough. Judges often follow the law as it is written, and sometimes they decide that Parliament, not the courts, should make the final decision.

nodes.misconception: Campaigning doesn't really make a difference to the law.
nodes.response: Campaigning has played a key role in major legal changes, like women's right to vote and LGBTQ+ equality laws.

nodes.misconception: The media always tells the full truth about immigration.
nodes.response: Media can be biased; some reports may exaggerate or misrepresent immigration, influencing public opinion unfairly.

nodes.misconception: Everyone gets an education.
nodes.response: Some children do not have access to their right to education.

nodes.misconception: The Supreme Court has the same powers throughout the UK.
nodes.response: While the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal for most cases in the UK, its role in Scotland differs as Scotland has its own distinct legal system. In Scotland, the High Court of Justiciary is the highest court of appeal for criminal cases.

nodes.misconception: There are no advantages to having a zero-hour contract and they are illegal in the UK.
nodes.response: Zero-hour contracts are legal in the UK and can benefit some workers who want flexible hours or less commitment than signing a permanent contract.

nodes.misconception: A moving object has force that keeps it moving, and which runs out when it comes to rest.
nodes.response: Forces come from other objects. Forces change the motion of objects. Objects slow when forces act opposite to the direction of motion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a limited view of what constitutes a fossil, such as only things that resemble skeletons or ammonite shells, and not recognise things like coprolites or plant imprints as fossils too.
nodes.response: Use the range of examples used in the lesson to make it clear to pupils that there are a wide range of different types of fossil and different types of organisms that become fossils.

nodes.misconception: All rights and obligations are legal requirements.
nodes.response: Not all of our obligations are legal, some of them are moral, for example to be part of a community and support the community is a moral obligation rather than a legal one.

nodes.misconception: That the Ancient Greeks could go up Mount Olympus to find the gods or see the gods and talk to them there.
nodes.response: Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece, reaching almost 10,000 ft. There were no paths and there was no climbing equipment like we have today. Climbing the rough, rocky terrain was so dangerous it could cost the life of anyone who tried.

nodes.misconception: The party that wins the most seats will form the Government and have all the power.
nodes.response: If a party does not have the majority of seats (50%+1) in Parliament, they may not be able to form a government. They might have to form a formal coalition or a voting agreement with a smaller party to get the majority. Power may have to be shared.

nodes.misconception: The media always tells the truth, so we can trust everything we see during elections.
nodes.response: The media is not always completely unbiased or accurate. Different media outlets may have their own political leanings or agendas. Stories can be exaggerated or focus on sensational aspects, rather than providing balanced, factual information.

nodes.misconception: Most people in the UK identify only as British.
nodes.response: The UK is a multicultural society and many people identify as more than one nationality.

nodes.misconception: That archaeologists and historians are always right. That information about the past is always factual.
nodes.response: Explain that archaeologists and historians use clues to piece together what they think the past was like. These views and opinions can change over time as more sources or information is discovered.

nodes.misconception: To turn a statement into a question in Spanish you need to alter the order of the words as in English.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to alter word order when forming questions in Spanish. To turn a statement into a question, you can raise your voice at the end.

nodes.misconception: As in English, there is one way to say 'I am' in Spanish.
nodes.response: There are two ways to say 'I am' in Spanish. These are 'estoy' (for location, mood and temporary state) and 'soy' (for general traits).

nodes.misconception: The [l] and [ll] sounds are pronounced the same in Spanish.
nodes.response: The [l] and [ll] sounds are pronounced differently in Spanish; the [ll] sound is pronounced as in 'amarillo' and 'llamar'.

nodes.misconception: I can use 'avoir' as it is with any pronoun to mean 'have' or 'has' in French.
nodes.response: You have to use the different forms of 'avoir' depending on who you are talking about. For I have it is 'j'ai', for he has it is 'il a' for she has it is 'elle a'.

nodes.misconception: German [st] and [sp] sound the same as in English, wherever they appear in the word.
nodes.response: At the start of words, German [sp-] and [st-] are pronounced 'schp-' and 'scht-'. If [sp] and [st] occur in the middle or end of a word, pronounce them as in English, except for compound nouns and separable verbs, which are also 'schp-' and 'scht-'.

nodes.misconception: The sound [z] is pronounced the same in every Spanish-speaking country.
nodes.response: The sound [z] is pronounced differently in parts of Spain and in other parts of the world.

nodes.misconception: [v] is pronounced like the English 'v'.
nodes.response: [v] is pronounced like an English 'f'. [w] sounds like an English 'v'.

nodes.misconception: In word order 2, all the words in a sentence change position from word order 1.
nodes.response: The verb remains in the same position in word order 2 as in word order 1. If emphasis is on the adverb, the adverb and subject swap position.

nodes.misconception: The present continuous, e.g., ‘He is doing’ is translated as ‘Er ist machen’.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in German. ‘Er macht’ = ‘He does / He is doing’.

nodes.misconception: When we conjugate the verb we just add the ending to the infinitive.
nodes.response: In Spanish when we conjugate a verb, first, we remove the -ar ending and then add the correct ending depending on who is doing the action of the verb.

nodes.misconception: English and Spanish sound-spelling links are the same.
nodes.response: Sound-symbol correspondence [ce] is different in Spanish and English and reading aloud Spanish words with [ce] leads to more secure knowledge.

nodes.misconception: When there are two verbs together, we must conjugate both.
nodes.response: When we have two verbs together, we must conjugate the first one and use the infinitive for the second verb, i.e., 'Debo ayudar con las tareas en mi casa.'

nodes.misconception: The word 'si' means both 'yes' and 'if'.
nodes.response: In Spanish there is a difference between them: 'sí' with an accent means 'yes', and 'si' without an accent means 'if'.

nodes.misconception: When applying dynamics, fast actions are always strong.
nodes.response: We often tend to combine fast actions with strength and slow actions with softness but this isn't always the case. Slow and strong could suggest great effort against resistence, and fast and light actions communicate fluidity and ease.

nodes.misconception: Word order in German remains the same as English after ‘weil’ ('because').
nodes.response: When using ‘weil’ to give a reason, the verb moves to the end of the clause, e.g., ‘ich spiele gern Fußball, weil es Spaß macht'.

nodes.misconception: The endings for -er verbs change in the same way that they do for -ar verbs.
nodes.response: Whilst the 'I' form changes to -o for both -ar and -er verbs, for 'she, he, it' the endings are different - it is -a for -ar verbs and -e for -er verbs.

nodes.misconception: Two words are needed to express 'would like', as in English.
nodes.response: 'Möcht-' is a form of the verb 'mögen' and is used to mean 'would like'. 'Möcht-' can be used as part of a 2-verb structure to say what you would like to do. The second (infinitive) verb moves to the end of the sentence.

nodes.misconception: Local media is less important than national media in influencing public opinion.
nodes.response: Both are vital. Local media engages communities directly, while national media impacts the broader public and sets key agendas. They complement each other.

nodes.misconception: Crimes can only be committed by adults.
nodes.response: Anyone can commit a crime. In England, once you reach the age of ten, you can be held criminally responsible for your actions. This means that if a person aged ten or older breaks the law, they can face legal consequences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an opinion has to include 'my' or 'I'.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that an opinion is a view or belief that a person has. 'Tennis is the best sport' is an opinion because it is not a fact. Someone else may think differently.

nodes.misconception: Democracy is just about voting for leaders and making decisions by majority rule.
nodes.response: Democracy is about fairness, equality and everyone having a voice in how their society is run.

nodes.misconception: There are no rules in debating. It is just another way to argue or have an argument and does not need preparation.
nodes.response: Formal debating is an important part of society and allows important issues to be discussed in a constructuve way. It takes consideration and preparation to be involved in an effective debate.

nodes.misconception: Media outlets are always factual and not bias.
nodes.response: Media outlets strive to report factual information. However, they can still exhbit media bias that can be linked to political affiliations and concentration of media ownership.

nodes.misconception: Small political parties can’t make difference in the UK as they never win enough seats in Parliament.
nodes.response: Small parties can influence the Government by: raising important issues that main parties may ignore impacting election outcomes by taking votes away from larger parties; helping to shape policies; pushing their ideas into the national conversation.

nodes.misconception: Portraits must always show the person directly.
nodes.response: A portrait can also include symbolic representations, like objects that reflect the person’s personality or even something as unique as a sample of their DNA.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to speak correctly in the past tense, particularly with irregular verbs (e.g. saying 'sawed' or 'seed' for saw).
nodes.response: Use this lesson as an opportunity for as much oral rehearsal as possible to support children's errors in the moment. Repeat and re-model sentences back to them. Model incorrectly and ask the children to spot your mistakes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the points being used to justify an opinion in a speech.
nodes.response: At the start of LC1, watch the speech together and pause to identify the following: 1. the main opinion or argument 2. the points being used to justify. Focus on how information is used to persuade.

nodes.misconception: Once a video is recorded it cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Video footage can be edited using specialist software. The tools of such software allow overlays, adjustments and revmoval of content.

nodes.misconception: Active citizens are always high-profile people.
nodes.response: Anyone can be an active citizen. Active citizenship projects can be at a local, national or international level; the key purpose is to make a positive difference in society.

nodes.misconception: Citizenship is only about legal status.
nodes.response: Citizenship is all about being part of a society and being an active citizen.

nodes.misconception: An action is only considered a crime if it's seen as morally wrong.
nodes.response: In reality, a crime is defined by breaking the law, regardless of whether it seems unethical to the individual.

nodes.misconception: Democracy works exactly the same way in every country.
nodes.response: Democracy takes different forms across the world, for example, direct, full, flawed democracies and hybrid regimes.

nodes.misconception: Digital citizenship just means knowing how to use technology.
nodes.response: Digital citizenship includes understanding how to behave responsibly online, respect others, protect your privacy, think critically about information, and participate in digital spaces in ethical and constructive ways.

nodes.misconception: That all media types are regulated in the same way.
nodes.response: Although traditional media has consistent, central regulation, digital media sets its own guidelines and these can vary between platforms. Although anyone can be charged with defamation laws, regardless of media type.

nodes.misconception: All democratic countries are governed in the same way.
nodes.response: Democracy takes many different forms including direct democracy and representative democracy. Some representative democracies even include forms of direct democracy.

nodes.misconception: Positive stereotypes don’t cause any harm because they seem complimentary.
nodes.response: Positive stereotypes can be damaging because they create pressure for individuals to meet unrealistic expectations; ignore individuality and reinforce limiting roles and ideas about what people should be like.

nodes.misconception: Social media news posts are always accurate.
nodes.response: There is misinformation within all media, but even more so with social media due to a lack of regulation.

nodes.misconception: Changing intonation doesn't affect meaning.
nodes.response: If you raise your voice at the end, you can turn a statement into a question.

nodes.misconception: Infinitives are always verbs.
nodes.response: Many infinitives can be used as nouns. In German, infinitive nouns start with a capital letter, are always neuter, can be used with or without 'das' & are typically translated into English with the gerund -ing, e.g., '(das) Schwimmen' - 'swimmming'.

nodes.misconception: All two-verb structures with an infinitive use 'zu' before the infinitive.
nodes.response: Some two-verb structures with an infinitive use 'zu' before the verb, but not all. It depends on the verb in the sentence; 'zu' is not needed following modal verbs or 'werden' meaning 'will', but is needed after the structure 'es ist' + adjective.

nodes.misconception: 'Es' is the only word used to translate 'it' in German.
nodes.response: 'Es' is for neuter nouns or abstract ideas. Use the correct subject or object pronouns according to the grammatical gender of the noun they replace.

nodes.misconception: Inclusive design and accessible design are the same thing.
nodes.response: Accessible design is about making sure people with disabilities can use something. Inclusive design is about making sure everyone can use it, by thinking about all kinds of differences, including mental health and wellbeing.

nodes.misconception: The 't' in c'est is always a silent-final consonant.
nodes.response: The 't' in c'est is pronounced if it is followed by a word beginning with a vowel like 'un' or 'une'.

nodes.misconception: Once you've learnt a new word, you remember it forever.
nodes.response: New vocabulary has to be practised regularly or you might forget it.

nodes.misconception: 'Wie' always means 'how'.
nodes.response: 'Wie?' has two meanings: 1. 'How?' (e.g., 'Wie geht's?' - How's it going? / How are you?_; 2. 'What?' (e.g., 'Wie ist [der Gast]?' - What is [the guest] like?). Encourage pupils to learn both meanings and specific examples.

nodes.misconception: All adjectives come after the noun they describe in French.
nodes.response: Most adjectives follow the noun they describe, but not adjectives of beauty, age, goodness and size, which come before like English adjectives.

nodes.misconception: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender. If a word is feminine we think of it as female, if it is masculine we think of it as male.
nodes.response: Grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender. All French nouns are either masculine or feminine, whether they name people, places or things.

nodes.misconception: [ll] is pronounced the same in Spanish and English.
nodes.response: [ll] is pronounced differently in Spanish and English. It is important to recognise and pronounce sound-spelling links correctly to understand and be understood by other Spanish speakers.

nodes.misconception: All German verbs end in -en.
nodes.response: Verbs have different forms (endings) depending on the subject. Long form ends in -en and short form ends in -t.

nodes.misconception: Being involved in a community means only participating in big events or formal groups.
nodes.response: Community involvement can also be about smaller, everyday actions, like helping a neighbour or being part of a social group. It does not always require big events or formal organisations.

nodes.misconception: All members of political parties share the same views.
nodes.response: Political parties generally align with core values and principles but will have varying opinions on certain issues.

nodes.misconception: Young people have little or no power to influence political systems or decisions because they are too young, not eligible to vote, or lack resources and authority.
nodes.response: Individuals, including young people can be influential as they are still able to lobby MPs, liaise with the police, engage with media and take part in campaigns.

nodes.misconception: The media can print or publish what they like due to free press.
nodes.response: They must still follow regulations so that the public can trust what is being published.

nodes.misconception: Judges and magistrates have complete freedom in deciding sentences.
nodes.response: Parliament sets the laws that determine maximum and minimum sentences, and the Sentencing Council provides guidelines that judges and magistrates must follow.

nodes.misconception: Social action art must always make tangible improvements to an issue.
nodes.response: Social action art might make tangible improvements to an issue but might focus instead on sparking conversation or raising awareness.

nodes.misconception: Only famous people or those in power can speak truth to power and challenge injustice to make a difference.
nodes.response: Anyone, including young people, can speak truth to power and challenge injustice. Powerful speeches and actions have come from ordinary individuals who spoke out with courage and clarity.

nodes.misconception: Syncopation means only playing on (or emphasising) the ‘weak beats’ as in emphasising the 2nd and 4th beat of a 4-beat bar, instead of the 1st and 3rd.
nodes.response: Whilst emphasising the ‘2’ and the ‘4’ is common in pop music (often called backbeat) we can also create syncopation by holding notes, missing beats, and playing what is called ‘offbeat syncopation’.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to say 'a' in French.
nodes.response: All nouns have a gender in French. We use 'un' for all masculine nouns and 'une' for all feminine nouns.

nodes.misconception: Children under the age of 10 have no consequences for their actions.
nodes.response: Whilst the age of criminal responsbility in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is 10, this does not mean children under this age will face no conseqences if they break the law. They may still face other forms of intervention.

nodes.misconception: Banks and ethics don't mix. You cannot bank ethically.
nodes.response: There are ways to ethically bank in the UK that use the money you invest in responsible ways, such as funding community projects, supporting sustainable businesses, or avoiding investments in harmful industries like fossil fuels or weapons.

nodes.misconception: Criminal law and civil law are always handled in the same courts.
nodes.response: Criminal cases are typically heard in criminal courts, while civil cases are dealt with in civil courts; each have different procedures and purposes.

nodes.misconception: Non-democratic governments do not provide any rights or benefits to their people.
nodes.response: Non-democratic governments might limit political freedom and participation. However, they may still provide rights and benefits to their people.

nodes.misconception: The EU and the EC do the same thing.
nodes.response: The European Union is governed by the European Parliament which has directly elected represnetatives. These are called MEPs. The European Council has representatives from Member States who are their country's leaders.

nodes.misconception: That government is the same thing as parliament.
nodes.response: Parliament is the law-making branch, made up of elected MPs. The Government, including the Cabinet, is in charge of running the country and implementing those laws. It is led by the Prime Minister. Parliament scrutinises Government actions/decisions.

nodes.misconception: Equality means treating everyone the same, so that’s the fairest thing to do.
nodes.response: Treating everyone the same is not always fair. Equality gives the same to all, but equity gives people what they need to have the same chance and opportunities. Equality is about meeting different needs, not pretending everyone is the same.

nodes.misconception: Digital media is more diverse than traditional media because anyone can create content.
nodes.response: Digital media is still often controlled by a few large corporations, limiting true diversity.

nodes.misconception: We all get our news and information from the same place.
nodes.response: People get their news and information from a range of different media sources which can result in people believing very different stories.

nodes.misconception: Punishment is the only purpose of sentencing.
nodes.response: To try and change behaviour, rehabilitation is also needed. This aims to reduce further crime being committed.

nodes.misconception: Anyone forced to leave their home because of a risk to life is automatically recognised as a refugee and protected by international law.
nodes.response: People who migrate due to environmental reasons are not currently recognised as refugees under the 1951 Refugee Convention. That law only protects people fleeing persecution based on, for example, race, religion, nationality, political opinion.

nodes.misconception: People can protest anytime and anywhere without any restrictions.
nodes.response: While the right to protest is fundamental in a democracy, it is subject to certain limitations. Protests must comply with laws regarding public safety and order, and respect the rights of others.

nodes.misconception: All countries are in the International Criminal Court and therefore it is effective at enforcing humanitarian laws.
nodes.response: Not all nations are part of the ICC, for example, the USA and Russia are not. The ICC attempts to enforce humanitarian laws anyway and members can bring cases against non-members.

nodes.misconception: NGOs don’t get any government funding because they are non-governmental.
nodes.response: NGOs are independent of government control but can still receive government funding to help carry out important work.

nodes.misconception: Local councillors are the same as MPs.
nodes.response: MPs represent local areas on a national level. Councillors represent residents in the city/county. Councillors do not get a say in making laws, like MPs do. Councillors get an allowance, while MPs are paid a much higher salary.

nodes.misconception: The media doesn’t play a role in democracy and simply reports what the Government tells it.
nodes.response: The media has an important role in democracy. It sets the agenda by choosing which issues to focus on, helping inform and educate the public. This means the media, not the Government, decides which stories are highlighted and discussed.

nodes.misconception: The Government are able to control the media.
nodes.response: The media is separate from the Government and this is an important feature of a democracy.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think journalism is the same everywhere and not understand the risks faced by journalists in countries with limited press freedom.
nodes.response: Journalism is not the same everywhere. Due to a lack of press freedom laws in some countries, journalists are putting their lives at risk by investigating and reporting about key issues.

nodes.misconception: The police make up the whole of the justice system.
nodes.response: The police are part of the justice system. There are three layers to the justice system: laws, courts and the police.

nodes.misconception: Countries only respond to conflicts by sending soldiers to fight.
nodes.response: While military intervention is one option, countries often respond to conflicts through diplomacy, economic sanctions, and financial or arms support. These methods can be used to influence or support other nations without direct military involvement.

nodes.misconception: Climate change is a slow moving threat with limited impact on humanity so far.
nodes.response: Climate change is costing countries billions of dollars a year. There is already a cost to human life due to extreme weather events. Equally, governments are facing huge challenges to become more resillient to climate change.

nodes.misconception: Digital media can only be good or bad in relation to community cohesion.
nodes.response: Digital media can both unite and divide communities.

nodes.misconception: International organisations like NATO or the UN control the UK Government and make all its decisions.
nodes.response: International organisations can influence the UK, but they do not have power to make decisions for the UK Government.
