nodes.misconception: International laws are not enforceable.
nodes.response: International laws are enforceable by courts if the nation has signed up to it. For example, the UK has agreed to the ICC and funds it. The USA has not agreed to the ICC so should follow international law but it is harder to enforce it.

nodes.misconception: NATO is just an alliance between countries.
nodes.response: NATO is more than just an alliance. It is an international organisation with a command structure, a shared budget, and agreed aims. Like the UN, it sets goals and carries out missions agreed by its Member States.

nodes.misconception: The Commonwealth is just the British Empire with another name.
nodes.response: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association where countries choose to work together toward shared goals. Unlike the British Empire, which often involved control over other nations, Commonwealth members join freely and are treated as equals.

nodes.misconception: The UN can force countries to follow its decisions.
nodes.response: Most UN decisions are not legally binding. Only Security Council resolutions are, and even these can be blocked by a permanent member’s veto.

nodes.misconception: The WTO deals with what we buy and sell other nations. It acts as a regulator.
nodes.response: The WTO does not control specific goods or services we trade. It oversees the rules, policies and agreements that guide trade between countries, ensuring fairness and transparency, and works to prevent conflicts.

nodes.misconception: The sounds [ge] and [gi] are pronounced just like in English.
nodes.response: Both sounds are pronounced like an 'h' followed by 'e' for [ge] and followed by 'i' for [gi]

nodes.misconception: When negating, change any articles to 'de/d''.
nodes.response: Change indefinite articles to 'de/d'' when negating but keep the definite articles the same and keep the indefinite articles when using 'être'.

nodes.misconception: Using 'ne' before the verb makes verbs negative, like 'don't' in English.
nodes.response: In French, there are two parts to negation, 'ne' before the verb and 'pas' after.

nodes.misconception: Use the indefinite article after 'il n'y a pas' like you would with 'il y a'.
nodes.response: After 'il n'y a pas' always use 'de' (or 'd'' before words starting with vowels or silent 'h'), regardless of gender or number.

nodes.misconception: Only adults or famous people can be changemakers.
nodes.response: Anyone can be a changemaker, including children and young people.

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go before the noun in French, as in English: 'a grey bike'.
nodes.response: Most adjectives go after the noun in French: 'un vélo gris'. These are postnominal adjectives.

nodes.misconception: In ancient times, being Roman meant being from the city of Rome.
nodes.response: Initially, being Roman meant being from the city of Rome but later it included people who followed Roman ideology all over the Roman world.

nodes.misconception: That magistrates or JPs have a legal background and carry out the role in a paid capacity like crown court judges.
nodes.response: Magistrates and JPs carry out the role on a volunteer basis as part of their civic responsibility.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to include every one of these features in their speech.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a speech does not need to contain all of these features. Encourage pupils to choose three features to include.

nodes.misconception: Verbs are always verbs and nouns are always nouns.
nodes.response: Sometimes words of one type can be used as another type. For example, 'ich mag das Schwimmen' (I like swimming) is the verb 'schwimmen' used as a noun. When used as nouns, verbs have a gender (neuter), the article 'das' and a capital letter.

nodes.misconception: For communities to work together successfully everyone has to always agree.
nodes.response: Individuals can recognise and co-exist with beliefs, opinions and values that are different to their own. This allows people to peacefully live with others who we might disagree with, as long as they do not harm anyone through their choices.

nodes.misconception: Words which look the same in English and German will have the same meaning.
nodes.response: There are many false friends in German. These are words that look exactly the same but do not have the same meaning: for example, 'bald' means 'soon'.

nodes.misconception: The UK is a small nation and has limited impact around the world.
nodes.response: The UK is a small nation so has to use as much of its influence as possible to make a difference. It can use its hard power through work with organisations like NATO. It can also use soft power with diplomacy.

nodes.misconception: Cognates are always exactly the same in both languages.
nodes.response: Cognates might be written and/or pronounced differently. It is usually easier to recognise a cognate in the written form.

nodes.misconception: The sounds ‘t’ and [th] make the same sound in English as they do in German.
nodes.response: The sounds ‘t’ and [th] sound the same in German. Even though many words with these spellings come from English, German pronounces 't' and [th] in the same way.

nodes.misconception: You need to conjugate the verb following the modal verb.
nodes.response: The second verb following the modal verb, must be in the infinitive form.

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter whether we use 'ser' or 'estar' in Spanish as they both mean 'to be, being.'
nodes.response: Both verbs mean 'to be, being' but 'ser' is used to describe permanent traits and 'estar' to describe temporary states.

nodes.misconception: To say 'they are' it does not matter which verb 'to be' we use.
nodes.response: In Spanish there are two verbs 'to be'; we say 'son' (they are) to describe permanent traits, and 'están' (they are) to describe temporary states.

nodes.misconception: We put the 'ne ... pas' together after the main verb to form a negative sentence.
nodes.response: The 'ne ... pas' is in two separate parts and must be placed either side of the main (1st) verb in the sentence.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'c' always makes the same sound in French.
nodes.response: The letter 'c' is naturally soft (sounds like 's') before 'e' or 'i'. It is hard (sounds like k) before 'a', 'o' or 'u'. The 'c' is sometimes softened before 'a', 'o' or 'u' with a cedilla: 'ç'.

nodes.misconception: Using 'ne'/'n' makes verbs negatives in French, like 'not' in English.
nodes.response: French negation has two parts, 'ne' before the verb and 'pas' after, to say what there isn't.

nodes.misconception: The simple present tense in Spanish is only for habitual actions, e.g. 'every week I do my homework'.
nodes.response: The simple present in Spanish is used for habitual actions and immediate plans. '¿Qué haces hoy?' means 'What are you doing today?' and 'hoy hago mis deberes' means 'today I am doing my homework'. English uses the present continuous here instead.

nodes.misconception: -ar, -er, and -ir verbs all share the same endings in the present tense for 'she, he, it' and 'they' forms.
nodes.response: -er and -ir verbs share the same endings for 'she, he, it' and 'they' forms, but -ar verbs have a different ending.

nodes.misconception: 'En' always means 'in'.
nodes.response: Many words in French have more than one meaning. 'En' means 'in' and 'by'.

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' always means 'to do' or 'to make'.
nodes.response: 'Faire' has multiple meanings. 'To do' and 'to make' are the most common, but it can also mean 'to go' and 'to have', and it has other meanings in different verbal phrases.

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' always means 'to do' or 'to make'.
nodes.response: 'Faire' has multiple meanings. 'To do' and 'to make' are the most common, but it can also mean 'to go' and 'to have', and it has other meanings in different verbal phrases.

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' always means 'to do' or 'to make'.
nodes.response: 'Faire' has lots of different meanings, including 'to go, going'.

nodes.misconception: Use the infinitive with 'je'.
nodes.response: The long form of the verb (infinitive) means -to or -ing so it needs changing for the correct subject pronoun.

nodes.misconception: There is always a liaison when an 's' is followed by a vowel.
nodes.response: The liaison between a verb and an article (nous avons un chien) is in fact optional. An optional liaison is often used in a more formal setting, for example when reading aloud a prepared speech rather than in a more formal conversation.

nodes.misconception: The 's' in the liaison of 'ils ont' and 'elles ont' is pronounced like an English 's'.
nodes.response: The 's' in the liaison of 'ils ont' and 'elles ont' is pronounced like an English 'z'. This is distinguishable to 'ils sont' and 'elles sont' which have the pronounciation of an English 's' (no liaison).

nodes.misconception: The indefinite article 'ein' always refers to a masculine noun.
nodes.response: 'Ein' could refer to a masculine or a neuter noun. Learn noun genders and look for other clues about a noun's gender. Only masculine nouns use 'einen' after forms of 'haben' and most other verbs, except 'sein'.

nodes.misconception: Names (e.g., Alex) and pronouns (e.g., 'er') are not interchangeable and need different verb endings.
nodes.response: Names and pronouns are interchangeable and use the same verb endings.

nodes.misconception: There is just one word for 'some' in Spanish.
nodes.response: There are two words for 'some' in Spanish, just as there are two words for 'a/an'. 'Unos' is 'some' for plural masculine nouns.  'Unas' is 'some' for plural feminine nouns.

nodes.misconception: The sounds [ci], [si] and [z] are pronounced the same in all the Spanish-speaking countries.
nodes.response: In Latin America, parts of southern Spain and the Canary Island, [ci], [si] and [z] are pronounced the same. In the rest of Spain, [ci], [si] and [z] have different pronunciation.

nodes.misconception: To say 'I have', 'you have', 'she, he, it has' you need the words for 'I', 'you' and 'she, he, it'.
nodes.response: The verbs 'tengo', 'tienes' and 'tiene' mean 'I have', 'you have' and 'she, he, it has'. You do not need to use separate pronouns 'I', 'you', 'she, he, it'.

nodes.misconception: All numbers from 13 to 19 begin with 'dieci-'.
nodes.response: Numbers 16 to 19 begin with 'dieci-' + number, e.g. 'dieciséis', 'diecisiete', but numbers 13 to 15 do not follow the same pattern, e.g. 'trece', 'catorce', 'quince'.

nodes.misconception: German [ie] is pronounced as in English 'die'.
nodes.response: German [ie] is pronounced as in the German 'Liebe'.

nodes.misconception: To say 'not a' in German, say 'nicht ein'.
nodes.response: Use 'kein' to say what you do not have.

nodes.misconception: French infinitive verbs can only be translated by the 'to - ' structure in English.
nodes.response: The infinitive verb can be translated as 'to -' or '-ing' e.g. 'to do' or 'doing'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the need to use a second plant in their investigation that has all of its needs met, as they will be able to observe changes in the plant from which they are removing a requirement.
nodes.response: Explain that we need an additional plant with all of its needs met so that we can make direct comparisons between this plant and the one we are depriving of something.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they should evaluate their investigation based on things like the neatness of their writing or how quickly they finished, rather than how they planned and carried out the enquiry.
nodes.response: Explain that scientists evaluate their investigations based on how they planned and carried them out, not on how neatly they presented their work or how quick they were to finish because this helps them to plan better investigations in the future.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not consider plants to be living things because they do not move from place to place or have ‘babies’ in the way that many animals do.
nodes.response: Explain that plants are living things; we know this because they can move, grow and reproduce like other living things can.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants are able to grow in any conditions and will simply adapt to their surroundings.
nodes.response: Explain that plants have certain requirements to survive and grow well, and will be unhealthy and likely die without these requirements. Results from pupils' enquiries will back this up and help them to see this first-hand.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know how to remove only one growing condition in order to compare plants.
nodes.response: Explain that a plant without water will still require warmth and light, and discuss group A, B and C's options as a whole class.

nodes.misconception: Only "bad people" commit crimes.
nodes.response: Criminal behaviour can be influenced by various factors like their environment, the people around them, or their mental state.

nodes.misconception: The media can report whatever they like, there are no consequences.
nodes.response: There are consequences for the media breaking the rules and not fulfilling their responsibilities. They have to abide by a strict code of conduct and ethics.

nodes.misconception: We only have rights when we are adults.
nodes.response: We have rights as children as well as adults. Some of these are different but they are all designed to allow everyone to live a safe and happy life.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that rights solely lie with the victim of crime, as they are the ones who have been wronged in some way.
nodes.response: Our legal system is based on justice, a key aspect of this is to ensure rights for both defendants and victims of crime; this ensures a fair trial and allows justice to be served.

nodes.misconception: The economy is entirely controlled by the UK Government and that individuals have little to no influence over it.
nodes.response: While the Government plays a significant role through policies, taxation and public spending, individual citizens also shape the economy through their financial decisions, employment and consumer behaviour.

nodes.misconception: Schools have very little to do with the local community.
nodes.response: Schools are often at the centre of local communities, offering opportunities, facilities and events to people in the community as well as educating the young people who live in the community.

nodes.misconception: If a petition gets over 100,000 signatures and is debated in Parliament, it means the law will definitely change.
nodes.response: In the UK, Parliament agrees to debate any petition that gets over 100,000 signatures, but the decision to change a policy or create a new law is still up to the Government.

nodes.misconception: Civil society, NGOs and charities are all the same thing.
nodes.response: They are interlinked and might have common goals but work and run in different ways.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that soil is any dirt on the ground, or that soil was created when Earth was created. They may also think that plants make soil.
nodes.response: The activity to separate layers of soil in water allows children to make their own observations of what soil is made from.

nodes.misconception: The singular forms of the verb 'faire' are spelled the same way because they are pronounced the same way.
nodes.response: The singular forms of the verb 'faire' are spelled differently, but sound the same because the 's' and 't' are silent final consonants (SFC).

nodes.misconception: The verb 'faire' only has a single definition.
nodes.response: The verb 'faire' is used to translate two key verbs in English, both 'to do' and 'to make'.

nodes.misconception: Spanish verbs always need pronouns, like in English ,to convey the person doing the action.
nodes.response: Spanish verbs don't always need pronouns. When 'tiene' follows a name or noun it just means 'has'. Otherwise 'tiene' refers to the 'she', 'he' or 'it' that is the subject of the sentence and means 'she, he, it has'.

nodes.misconception: The adverbs 'normalmente' and 'siempre' always follow the English order when in a sentence.
nodes.response: In Spanish, adverbs tend to go at the start or end of the sentence.

nodes.misconception: 'Avoir' only means 'to have' in English.
nodes.response: 'Avoir' can be translated both as 'to have' or 'having'.

nodes.misconception: All British sources on imperial expansion were positive.
nodes.response: Not all British sources on imperial expansion were positive. There was nuance due to British awareness of the realities of empire. However, British sources are more likely to be positive in outlook regarding British imperial expansion.

nodes.misconception: Only asylum seekers need support when they move to a new country.
nodes.response: All migrants may need support. Refugees often flee danger and need urgent help, but even those who move for work, study or family benefit from language classes, job advice and community events to settle in and feel part of their new home.

nodes.misconception: Students may think the Wars of the Roses ended with the victory of Henry VII at Bosworth and that all historians agree with this interpretation.
nodes.response: Explain that Henry VII also faced rebellions at the start of his reign and, although the Tudors are well-known for their rule of England, few expected them to last long as a result of the rebellions and the prior decades of instability.

nodes.misconception: 'Hay' is pronounced as the English 'hi' and means there is.  There is another word for 'there are'.
nodes.response: The 'h' is not pronounced in 'hay' and it means both 'there is' and 'there are'.

nodes.misconception: All German-speakers speak the same way. There aren't different accents, unlike in the United Kingdom.
nodes.response: There are both different accents and different dialects in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. This means there are different ways of saying sounds, and different vocabulary. ‘Standard German’ is the version of German taught in schools.

nodes.misconception: Governments always protect human rights fairly and equally for everyone.
nodes.response: While governments are duty bearers, they don’t always protect everyone’s rights. In some cases, they may ignore, limit, or even violate rights, which is why human rights defenders are important because they hold duty bearers to account.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives work the same way in German as in English and do not change their spelling.
nodes.response: German adjectives change their ending when placed before the noun, depending on the case needed, and the gender of the noun they describe.

nodes.misconception: Article 50 means the UK left the EU.
nodes.response: Article 50 is the start of the process to leave the EU. A Member State must trigger this to begin negotiations to leave the EU.

nodes.misconception: You have to use an indefinite article when using 'sein' and a profession noun.
nodes.response: Do not use an indefinite article when using 'sein' and a profession noun, e.g., 'Ich bin Sänger'.

nodes.misconception: That everything we read about the past is always true.
nodes.response: Historians try to tell as accurate a story about the past as possible by carefully investigating and studying evidence. Sometimes though, historians do not always agree with each other especially about finer details, and so make generalisations.

nodes.misconception: Vote Leave only focused on immigration and didn’t really care about the economy or national identity.
nodes.response: While immigration was a key issue, Vote Leave also argued that leaving the EU would give the UK more control over its economy, laws, and national identity. These issues were central to their campaign, not just immigration.

nodes.misconception: Leaving the EU would make the UK stronger because we wouldn’t have to follow EU rules anymore.
nodes.response: This is too simplistic a viewpoint. While the UK wouldn’t need to follow EU rules, it would still need to establish new agreements with the EU and other countries.

nodes.misconception: The Brexit result was overwhelmingly in favour of Brexit.
nodes.response: The result was very close which is not typical of referendums. Many factors played a part including age, region and education.

nodes.misconception: Nouns in German have capital letters in the same situations as English nouns.
nodes.response: German nouns are always capitalised, no matter where or how they are used in a sentence.

nodes.misconception: A bilingual dictionary lists words from A-Z in one long list.
nodes.response: A bilingual dictionary is split into two sections. These is German to English, and English to German. Each section lists words from A-Z. To find the English meaning of a German word, look for it in the German to English section, and vice versa.

nodes.misconception: 'Sie' always refer to feminine 'it' when used as a subject pronoun.
nodes.response: 'Sie' means 'it' in the feminine form and 'they' in the plural form. 'Sie' is used for all plural forms.

nodes.misconception: French adjectives never change form.
nodes.response: French adjectives do change; this is called adjective agreement. One change is to match the gender of the person described.

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [an/en] make different sounds.
nodes.response: The SSCs [an/en] make the same sound.

nodes.misconception: Ne ... pas goes around both verbs in a two-verb sentence.
nodes.response: Ne ... pas surrounds the first verb in a two-verb sentence. If a sentence contains a modal verb and an infinitive, it will surround the conjugated modal verb.

nodes.misconception: There is one verb for 'can' in French like in English.
nodes.response: The verb for 'can' changes depending on whether you need specific skills/knowledge to be able to do it. If not, use 'pouvoir', if it does, use 'savoir'.

nodes.misconception: All German past participles have the prefix ge-.
nodes.response: German verbs starting with be-, ver- and er- do not have the prefix ge- added for the past participle, e.g., 'besucht' - 'visited' or 'verdient' - 'earnt'.

nodes.misconception: Giving the time as half past the hour works the same in German as it does in English, e.g., ‘halb neun’ is 'half past nine'.
nodes.response: In German, half past is expressed as half of the next hour, so 'half past nine' is 'halb zehn', or 'half way to ten', the next hour.

nodes.misconception: [ch] is pronounced as in the English 'cheese'.
nodes.response: [ch] is soft in German after [i] or [e]. It is hard after [a] [o] or [u]. This is because [a] [o] and [u] are pronounced with a more open mouth whilst [i] and [e] have a more closed mouth.

nodes.misconception: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’ as in English.
nodes.response: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.

nodes.misconception: I only need to know the gender of the noun to choose the right spelling for the possessive adjective.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives change spelling to match the gender of the noun, but they also change to match the required case. Verbs and prepositions affect the case that is needed for possessive adjectives.

nodes.misconception: All verbs in the 'nous' form end in -ons.
nodes.response: Some verbs like 'manger' behave a little differently. The 'nous' form of 'manger' is 'mangeons' so that the g sound remains soft.

nodes.misconception: Préféré(e) is often spelt wrong, with not enough, or indeed too many accents!
nodes.response: 'Préféré' is favourite in its masculine form. The e that is added in the feminine form does not have an accent; 'préférée'.

nodes.misconception: You have to include the word for 'do' in Spanish intonation questions.
nodes.response: Spanish intonation (yes/no questions) can be made simply by raising the tone of voice at the end of any statement. There is no equivalent of the word 'do' in Spanish intonation questions.

nodes.misconception: All past participles are formed the same way.
nodes.response: Weak verbs form their past participles by sandwiching 'ge-' and '-t' around the verb stem. Strong verbs sandwich 'ge-' and '-en' around the verb stem, but verbs with prefixes 'be-', 'ver-', 'er-', or ending '-ieren', do not add 'ge-'.

nodes.misconception: The German 'Ich will' means 'I will'.
nodes.response: The German 'will' comes from 'wollen' and means 'want'. Do not confuse this with the future tense. 'Ich werde' means 'I will'.

nodes.misconception: Only cars have wheels and axles.
nodes.response: Highlight that many vehicles, including bicycles and toy cars, use wheels and axles.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume some shapes have a larger area than others by comparison of a certain dimension. In this lesson, pattern blocks can be arranged to create shapes with very different dimensions.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to rearrange the composing shapes to prove that the compound shapes have the same area. This can be done effectively with tangrams or pattern blocks, both of which feature heavily in this lesson.

nodes.misconception: To say where someone goes, only 'a la/al' goes before the place.
nodes.response: If the place is a city or a country, 'a' goes before the place.

nodes.misconception: 'Jugar' and 'hacer' are interchangeable as they often are in English - I play football, I do football.
nodes.response: In Spanish, you can't use 'hacer' for all activities you do in your free time. If it is a ball sport or a game, use 'jugar'. If it is an activity, non-ball sport, task or something that you're making, use 'hacer'.

nodes.misconception: To express the date I use 'de' for 'of' so 2nd January would be 'le deux de janvier'.
nodes.response: There is no need to translate 'of' into French to express the date. For example 2nd January would be 'le deux janvier'.

nodes.misconception: Word order with adverbs is the same in French and English.
nodes.response: Word order with adverbs is sometimes the same and sometimes different in French and English. Think about whether the adverb is a how/how often or a where/when adverb to know where to place it in French.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that after agreeing a tactic, the team will be able to perform this tactic accurately every time and that when they do, it will always be successful.
nodes.response: Even when we make a great dodge into space and use a tactic, our opponents will react with a tactic of their own: this means that a tactic isn't guarenteed to be successful every time we use it.

nodes.misconception: To say 'my' in Spanish we use 'mi'.
nodes.response: There are two ways of saying 'my' in Spanish. 'Mi' is for singular nouns (masculine or feminine) e.g. 'mi madre' (my mother) and 'mis' is for plural nouns e.g. 'mis padres' (my parents).

nodes.misconception: 'Auf' always means 'on' or 'onto'.
nodes.response: 'Auf' sometimes means ‘at’ or ‘to’, especially with events or open spaces.

nodes.misconception: It is necessary to use pronouns with Spanish verbs.
nodes.response: In most cases, it is not necessary to use pronouns with Spanish verbs. The verb itself communicates the action and the subject.

nodes.misconception: Investments all carry the same level of financial risk.
nodes.response: There are many different types of investments and they all provide different risks. For example, cryptocurrency is very risky, whereas investing in funds provides more financial security.

nodes.misconception: When talking about travel, where and how you went can be given in any order, as is the case in English.
nodes.response: When using adverbs to say where and how you went in the same sentence, manner (how) always comes before place (where).

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister (PM) holds all of the power in the UK.
nodes.response: The PM is only in their position because of the electorate, and many decisions are made by the Cabinet, who are appointed by the PM to make decisions on behalf of the country. The media, other decision-makers and the public also hold power in the UK.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that fossils can be found anywhere on Earth and in any type of rock.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain how and why fossils are mainly found in sedimentary rock and the common locations these tend to be, such as cliffs, hillsides and quarries.

nodes.misconception: To talk about the past using the perfect tense, we always use the present tense of ‘haben’ with a past participle.
nodes.response: Some verbs require the present tense of ‘sein’ with a past participle when forming the past perfect tense. These are mostly verbs of movement to a destination, e.g., ‘fahren’ to travel, ‘fliegen’ to fly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are all uncomfortable with physical contact.
nodes.response: Contact must involve respect. Care should be taken to ensure any touch is appropriate. Most pupils are sensitive to this and respond appropriately. Teachers can guide this by identifying how contact should be made, e.g. touch toe to toe.

nodes.misconception: The sound 's' is always pronounced the same in French.
nodes.response: There are two 's' sounds, the hard 's' sound which sounds like a 'z', found between two vowels, including in liaisons and the soft 's' found in other words, often at the beginning, of words, between consonants and as a double 's'.

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused with what some materials are called when they look at where these materials come from, e.g. paper that makes books is processed after originally coming from trees.
nodes.response: Ensure a clear distinction between the natural materials that are used to make our man-made materials, e.g. a bookshelf is made from wood and a magazine is made from paper.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, after adverbs of position we always use 'del'
nodes.response: In Spanish, after adverbs of position we use 'de', 'del' or 'de la'. 'De' when what follows is a person or place name, 'del' when what follows is a masculine noun and 'de la' when what follows is a feminine noun.

nodes.misconception: Spanish has only one way to say 'you are,' like English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the form of 'you are' changes depending on who you're talking to. To say ‘you are’ to one person, use ‘eres’. To say ‘you are’ to two or more people, use ‘sois’.

nodes.misconception: When I combine 'à' with a plural noun with 'les', it becomes 'à les'.
nodes.response: When using 'à' with a plural noun to express 'to (the)' in French, it becomes 'aux'.

nodes.misconception: All words ending in -n or -s need an accent.
nodes.response: Words ending in -n, -s or a vowel generally have penultimate syllable stress and no accent. Words ending in -n, -s or a vowel with final syllable stress have an accent on the final vowel. Note the difference: 'canción', 'canciones'.

nodes.misconception: All Spanish adverbs are made by simply adding -mente to any adjective form.
nodes.response: When an adjective has masculine -o and feminine -a forms, you must use the -a form before adding -mente, e.g. 'rápido' - 'rápida' - 'rápidamente'.

nodes.misconception: I need Spanish words for 'do' and 'are' to ask yes/no questions, just like in English, e.g. 'Do you go to town?', 'Are you going to the park?'.
nodes.response: Spanish yes/no questions use the same words in the same order as Spanish statements.  To make a statement into a spoken question, use raised intonation. Written questions use two question marks; the one at the start is upside down.

nodes.misconception: All nouns ending in 'a' are feminine.
nodes.response: There are exceptions to this, like 'problema' or 'día', that's why it is important to learn the article and the noun together.

nodes.misconception: 'Zu' always means 'to'.
nodes.response: 'Zu' can also mean 'too', 'closed', 'off' and 'shut'! Context is important when translating into English.

nodes.misconception: To translate 'to' into French we just use 'à'.
nodes.response: There are several ways to express 'to' and 'at' in French and we need to carefully learn them to speak and write accurately.

nodes.misconception: The word 'coche' means 'coach'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the word 'coche' means 'car'. 'Coach' is 'autobús'.

nodes.misconception: [en] and [an] are different sounds.
nodes.response: [en] and [an] sound exactly the same as in 'enfant'.

nodes.misconception: The sounds [e] and [i] are pronounced the same as in English.
nodes.response: The sound [e] is pronounced as in 'elefante' and the sound [i] is pronounced as in 'idea'.

nodes.misconception: To greet German speakers, use either ‘hallo’ or ‘guten Tag’.
nodes.response: Greetings in German-speaking countries vary depending on time of day, country/region and level of formality, e.g., ‘hallo’ in Germany but ‘servus’ in Austria and ‘hoi’ in Switzerland.

nodes.misconception: That solicitors only work in the community and it is just barristers that work on criminal cases that end up in the court room.
nodes.response: Solicitors prepare the criminal case and advise the defendant prior to the case going to court, they appoint the barristers to represent their client (the defendant) in court.

nodes.misconception: As women now have the same voting rights as men in the UK, they are equally represented in the Government and Parliament.
nodes.response: This is not the case in the UK. However, as of the 2024 General Election, 40.5% of MPs in the House of Commons are female, which is the highest number ever recorded of female MPs.

nodes.misconception: A loop will always run at least once.
nodes.response: A loop only runs if the condition allows it. If the condition isn’t met initially, the code inside won’t run at all.

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxon Church was old-fashioned and corrupt.
nodes.response: The Normans were keen to present the Anglo-Saxon Church that way, but Edward the Confessor had kept up with reforms from the rest of Europe.

nodes.misconception: There are relatively few sources for Norman England, so historians have less to say about this period than later periods of English history.
nodes.response: Historians have plenty to say about Norman England because they are able to interpret the sources available in many different ways to support many different theories.

nodes.misconception: Migration is a new event, in the past people stayed where they lived.
nodes.response: Migration has always existed. Britain has benefited from many centuries of migration from Europe and the wider world.

nodes.misconception: Word order tells you if a sentence is a question or a statement.
nodes.response: Use clues such as intonation and vocabulary meanings to help you decide if a sentence is a question or a statement, as the word order in questions is similar to word order 2.

nodes.misconception: 'La' always means 'her' or 'it'.
nodes.response: 'La' means 'the' in front of a noun but 'her' or 'it' when it comes before a verb.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, like English, the object always goes after the verb.
nodes.response: In Spanish, unlike English, the object can go before or after the verb.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, like in English, the object always goes after the verb.
nodes.response: In Spanish, unlike in English, the object can go before or after the verb. In object-first sentences, we add the object pronouns lo (masculine) or la (feminine) before the verb.

nodes.misconception: Only the police enforce the law.
nodes.response: The police play a key role in enforcing the law, however, they are not the only ones involved. Other groups, like magistrates, judges, the CPS, and lawyers, all have important roles in making sure laws are followed and justice is served.

nodes.misconception: 'Wer' means 'where' in English because it sounds the same.
nodes.response: 'Wer' means 'who' in English. Words that sound identical but have different meanings are called false friends and we should be aware of them.

nodes.misconception: The verb 'avoir' in 'tu as' and 'il, elle a' and the verb 'être' in 'tu es' and 'il, elle est' sound the same and so must be spelt the same.
nodes.response: It is important to understand that they don't sound the same and are not spelt the same. Some forms of avoir sound the same due to SFCs. These singular forms of 'avoir' and 'être' should be learnt off by heart as they are extremely frequent.

nodes.misconception: I will just remember the new French words I learn.
nodes.response: When learning a new language, it is important to practise vocabulary regularly to strengthen your memory.  It's hardest to remember the words we learnt some time ago, so we need to practise them often.

nodes.misconception: Pupils should 'count' the music.
nodes.response: Whilst some pupils can count music accurately, it can be an additional level of challenge for others and divert them from the task in hand. Most pupils will naturally 'feel' the music and be able to respond to the tempo and rhythm appropriately.

nodes.misconception: Not accepting the first action that a pupil offers is likely to put them off.
nodes.response: Challenging pupils to generate more than one response, or to find ways to refine their actions, before making their final selection, enables pupils to develop their creativity and understanding of choreographic and performance skills.

nodes.misconception: When performing a 'pulling' counterbalance, pupils should hold hands.
nodes.response: There are many ways to perform 'pulling' counterbalances other than using hands, but if doing so, pupils should clasp one another's wrists to make a more secure connection.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are likely to focus on people who are famous.
nodes.response: It is entirely possible that pupils are naturally drawn to people who are famous, but it is still feasible to identify the qualities and behaviours that have made them successful such as hard work, determination or courage.

nodes.misconception: Migrants do not bring benefits to the country they have moved to.
nodes.response: Migrants help fill important skills shortages in the country, bringing valuable talents and expertise that keep essential services and industries running smoothly.

nodes.misconception: Asylum seekers and refugees are the same thing.
nodes.response: Asylum seekers are seeking safety but not yet granted leave to remain. Refugees were asylum seekers but have been allowed to remain in a country by the government as their claim has been assessed as credible.

nodes.misconception: Estás means she, he, it is.
nodes.response: Estás means you are. Está means she, he, it is.

nodes.misconception: The Government has absolute power and the media is just a neutral source of information.
nodes.response: The Government is powerful but must follow laws and face elections. The media influences opinion but can also mislead people.

nodes.misconception: The 'k' in [kn] is silent.
nodes.response: Both sounds in [kn] must be pronounced. This is different from English. Compare English 'knee' and German 'Knie'. Remember to pronounce the 'k' in German words containing [kn].

nodes.misconception: 'Des' always means 'some'.
nodes.response: 'Des' is the word for 'some' but is also a form of the preposition 'de' before plural nouns.

nodes.misconception: Always use 'müssen' in negative sentences to translate the idea of 'must not' in English.
nodes.response: English often uses 'must not' in lieu of 'don't have to', 'not allowed to' and 'should not'. However, you should use the correct modal verb in German to express these ideas, e.g. 'du musst nicht', 'du darfst nicht', 'du sollst nicht'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all these ancient civilisations existed at separate times.
nodes.response: Although beginning thousands of years apart, by the time of the Shang Dynasty, the Ancient Sumerian, Ancient Egyptian and Indus Valley civilisations were still going!

nodes.misconception: 'Wer?' means 'Where?'.
nodes.response: 'Wer?' means 'Who?'. A good way to remember its meaning is to think of a ‘hoover’: 'Who Wer?'.

nodes.misconception: Benjamin is a minor character in 'Animal Farm' and doesn't represent much.
nodes.response: Could Benjamin make a difference? Could he have used his intelligence? Benjamin's apathy has a key role in the pigs' reign.

nodes.misconception: 'Mi' and 'tu' changes according to whether the noun is feminine or masculine.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the possessive adjectives do not change according to whether the noun is feminine or masculine. They stay the same.

nodes.misconception: Alexander 'The Great' was the title that Alexander had when he was a living ruler.
nodes.response: 'The Great' is not a title. It is a type of nickname called an epithet. Epithets are only used to refer to people that have died and they tell us more about something significant the person did or what the person was like.

nodes.misconception: Possible outcome design fixation limits context exploration. Product analysis leads to copying.
nodes.response: Product analysis identifies successful features and those which can be improved.

nodes.misconception: Students who have less awareness of deepfakes may believe that anything they can see or hear within digital media is true.
nodes.response: Emphasise the sophistication of deepfakes and consider using the teacher tip to further demonstrate this point.

nodes.misconception: Only politicians and people in important jobs can contribute to a select committee.
nodes.response: Anyone can submit evidence to a select committee, including pupils.

nodes.misconception: You can take legal action if your human rights are abused by anyone.
nodes.response: You cannot take legal action for violations by private individuals, like a friend. You can only take action against a public authority if they’ve breached your human rights.

nodes.misconception: The Benin Bronzes were created for trade with Europeans.
nodes.response: The Benin Bronzes were created to serve as significant cultural and religious artefacts within the Benin Kingdom and made from the manilla used as payment for goods.

nodes.misconception: Atoms react because they 'want' to gain a fuller outer shell of electrons – atoms don't have feelings. Monatomic means one atom and may be confused with the term element, which means one type of atom.
nodes.response: Take care with language and avoid personifying the atoms. Make sure that definitions and terms are used correctly.

nodes.misconception: Atoms react because they 'want' to gain a fuller outer shell of electrons – atoms don't have feelings! Monatomic means one atom and may be confused with the term element, which means one type of atom.
nodes.response: Take care with language and avoid personifying the atoms. Make sure that definitions and terms are used correctly.

nodes.misconception: Very few changemakers make lasting change.
nodes.response: There are many examples, both throughout history and modern day society, where changemakers have made a positive impact and lasting change.

nodes.misconception: Computers use binary for data and instructions but they can use other number systems just as easily.
nodes.response: Computers have to use binary as they are powered by electrical circuits which contain transistors which can be switched on and off using electricity. Using other number systems would require more complex circuitry.

nodes.misconception: That crime is only committed by specific groups of people.
nodes.response: Crime is complex and there are social, economic, psychological and environmental factors which can all impact the likelihood of crime.

nodes.misconception: Migration only happens when people are escaping danger, like war or natural disasters.
nodes.response: Many people are forced to migrate because of danger, but others choose to move for different reasons, like better jobs, studying or a different lifestyle. Migration is not always about escaping something bad, but about moving toward something better.

nodes.misconception: Power is separated, therefore, each branch does not link together.
nodes.response: While power is separated, the branches are still linked and work together. Each branch has its own responsibilities but also checks and balances the others to ensure no one branch becomes too powerful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that criminal law deals with serious crime and civil law deals with less serious crime.
nodes.response: Criminal law and civil law are seperate. Within both, there is a range of severity.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Prime Minister and their government make the laws in the UK, single handidly.
nodes.response: Although the Government have mandate to drive their manifesto intentions, laws still pass through the whole of Parliament.

nodes.misconception: Times have changed: everyone is already treated equally, so we do not really need equality laws anymore.
nodes.response: While progress has been made, unfair treatment still happens. Equality laws are there to protect people and make sure everyone gets a fair chance, especially those who might otherwise be left out or discriminated against.

nodes.misconception: Rules are the same for everyone.
nodes.response: Rules may be different in different settings and situations, for example, you may have different rules at school and home. Laws are the same for everyone.

nodes.misconception: All people who are eligible will vote in general elections.
nodes.response: Just because someone is eligible, it doesn't mean they will vote. In the UK 2024 general election, voter turnout was 59.7%. This was the lowest turnout at a general election since 2001.

nodes.misconception: Fracking shale gas is more environmentally friendly than other gas and fossil fuels.
nodes.response: Whilst shale gas releases less CO2 than other gases and fossil fuels, it is still not a renewable energy and has several other negative environment impacts, such as wasting huge amounts of water.

nodes.misconception: If you have a particular opinion or viewpoint on an issue, everyone in your group will think the same.
nodes.response: This might not be the case, as diverse perspectives exist. This is why it's important to test this during primary research to discover whether your identified issue is shared by others.

nodes.misconception: That royalty do not have to follow the same laws as citizens or would not be subjected to the legal system in the same way.
nodes.response: Rule of law states all citizens must obey the law, this includes the Royal Family.

nodes.misconception: The media should always be neutral.
nodes.response: Media freedom does not require journalists to be entirely neutral. It allows for a range of perspectives, such as investigative journalism and opinion pieces, as long as they are reported accurately.

nodes.misconception: There’s no way an individual or national organisation can make a difference to tackling global poverty.
nodes.response: There are many NGOs, global organisations and communities that are working hard to make a difference to global poverty.

nodes.misconception: That primary research simple involves finding out what people think about your project.
nodes.response: Primary research does much more than this, it provides first hand accounts to help you be persuasive, it informs you whether or not your project is likely to be successful and it provides data that might not already be known to you.

nodes.misconception: Everyone automatically gets a chance to vote in a UK election.
nodes.response: Not all residents are eligible to vote or are registered to vote. Some may miss out on elections if they don’t register in time or are unaware of the process.

nodes.misconception: All secondary research has the same value.
nodes.response: Secondary research is the most vauable and useful whe it is valid, reliable, accurate, current and free from bias.

nodes.misconception: The view that it was the work women did to support the war effort which gained them the right to vote.
nodes.response: Many people were convinced women should be entitled to vote before 1914; however, the violence of the suffragettes and the interruption of WW1 delayed this.

nodes.misconception: All migrants move by choice. For example, for work or a better life, rather than because they are forced to leave.
nodes.response: Not all migrants move by choice. Some, like refugees and asylum seekers, are forced to flee due to war or persecution.

nodes.misconception: Everyone pays the same percentage of Income Tax.
nodes.response: Income Tax is on a progressive scale so the percentage of income tax you pay depends on how much you earn.

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that the Sun appears to move across the sky because the Sun moves around Earth
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities for children to use models to see that it is Earth rotating that makes it look like the Sun is moving.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that the Vikings came to Britain for different reasons over a long period of time.
nodes.response: The Vikings first came to Britain to raid monasteries; they then invaded and settled in some Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. Finally, they tried to capture all of Britain but were unsuccessful. However, they were able to stay and control the Danelaw.

nodes.misconception: To answer the question 'why' you have to use 'weil' or 'denn', which mean 'because'.
nodes.response: The structure 'um ... zu' followed by an infinitive verb means 'in order to' and can be used to give a reason or say why something is done. This structure is the same for any tense.

nodes.misconception: The EU is the same as the EEC.
nodes.response: The European Economic Community was formed first and is separate from the EU. The EU is the larger union of countries who cooperate on social, economic and security issues. The EEC is mostly focused on the economy of member states.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that we have night when the Earth is facing the Moon or the Sun goes behind clouds.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities for pupils to use models to show the Earth rotating on its axis, next to a bright torch or lamp for the Sun.

nodes.misconception: Activity is about being sporty, being active.
nodes.response: Activity is all the things we do and movements we make, not only sports. It includes sports, but also reading, sleeping and watching TV.

nodes.misconception: Pupils show balances instead of movements on the apparatus. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to be well-behaved. Pointed toes mean lifting toes towards the knees.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to travel or change their movements, not just hold still. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to show good control. Pointed toes mean pushing the toes away from the legs, making their legs look longer.

nodes.misconception: All working class men gained the right to vote due to the 1867 and 1884 Reform Acts.
nodes.response: As property qualifications remained in place, a significant proportion of working class adult men remained unable to vote even after 1884.

nodes.misconception: The word 'laut' always means 'loud' or 'loudly'.
nodes.response: As an adjective, 'laut' means 'loud', and as an adverb it means 'loudly'. However, when used as a preposition followed by the dative case, it means 'according to'.

nodes.misconception: Always leave out the subject pronoun when using the imperative.
nodes.response: The 'du' and 'ihr' forms of the imperative omit the subject pronoun, but the 'Sie' form retains it.

nodes.misconception: I should use word order two after phrases of opinion.
nodes.response: Use word order two after 'meiner Meinung nach' and word order three after 'ich denke, dass' and 'ich glaube, dass'.

nodes.misconception: The time-manner-place rule means that all sentences must have time before manner before place.
nodes.response: German sentences can start with any adverb to emphasise that element. The TMP order is then retained for any other adverbs in that sentence. For example, 'Mit dem Zug (M) werden wir morgen (T) nach Wien (P) fahren.'.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all plants have been planted by humans.
nodes.response: Clear explanation that plants can grow in the wild without need for human intervention or support.

nodes.misconception: Ekphrastic poems are poems inspired by someone or something.
nodes.response: Ekphrastic poems are poems inspired by a piece of art, and they describe that piece of art in the poem.

nodes.misconception: Williams didn't use any methods in his poem because he is just describing a painting.
nodes.response: Every word in a poem is carefully selected. Williams could have made any number of choices about what he depicted in terms of focus, structure, tone and language. We can explore these methods, and add layers of meaning to the painting.

nodes.misconception: Correcting Galen's mistakes led to immediate improvements in medical practices.
nodes.response: Despite Harvey's theory suggesting bloodletting would be dangerous, most physicians continued to recommend the procedure as a common form of treatment.

nodes.misconception: The one-dimensional view of William as a violent conqueror.
nodes.response: In fact, William was very pious and he repented some of the atrocities he had committed during his reign and insisted his treasures should be used to rebuild some of the areas he had harried.

nodes.misconception: Students may think James had a clear view on the existence of God.
nodes.response: James' investigtions led him to be agnostic and open to the idea of God rather than to be a believer.

nodes.misconception: William the Conqueror was hostile towards all Anglo-Saxons from the start.
nodes.response: Some Anglo-Saxons, if they had not fought against William at Hastings, were allowed to keep their land.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that creating actions that communicate wind involves running fast for strong wind and walking slow for a light breeze.
nodes.response: We can create actions using changes in size, levels and direction including travelling and creating shapes to communicate wind.

nodes.misconception: Wind farms are best located as remotely as possible.
nodes.response: Wind farms should be located far from densely populated areas but close to the electricity grid. If they are too remote, the cost of connecting them to the grid will be high.

nodes.misconception: The Windrush generation entered Britain illegally.
nodes.response: Those coming from the British Commonwealth were considered citizens.

nodes.misconception: The play is only about the past or historical events.
nodes.response: Pinnock emphasises that the play connects past and present. It explores immigrant experiences, cultural identity, and family relationships, showing issues that are still relevant today.

nodes.misconception: Enid and other immigrants came to Britain fully aware of the challenges and were prepared for discrimination.
nodes.response: Pinnock explains that many, like Enid, saw themselves as British subjects and expected a “homecoming”, so the hostility and racism they faced were a shock.

nodes.misconception: 'Leave Taking' was written about the Windrush scandal.
nodes.response: Pinnock explains that she wrote 'Leave Taking' decades before the Windrush scandal, but some themes, like the precarious position of immigrants, happened to resonate with contemporary events when the play was revived.

nodes.misconception: Use the partitive article with all uncountable nouns, even negatives.
nodes.response: After quantities and negatives use 'de/d' instead of the partitive article. E.g Il y a beaucoup de riz. Il n'y a pas de riz.

nodes.misconception: If we see a reflexive pronoun, e.g., 'uns' or 'sich', this always means the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the verb are the same.
nodes.response: Some plural reflexive verbs are reciprocal or two-way, meaning the action of the verb is done 'to each other' rather than to oneself. Use context to work out whether reflexive or reciprocal meaning is intended.

nodes.misconception: Bandwidth is the speed of data being transmitted across a network. The higher the bandwidth, the faster data can be transferred between points in a network.
nodes.response: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can be transmitted at a time, not the time it takes to reach from one point to another. Higher bandwidth reduces the total transfer time of data but this is only noticable when there is a lot to transfer.

nodes.misconception: All wired networks use the same type of cable.
nodes.response: Copper Ethernet and fibre optic cables have different speeds, distances and uses. For example, copper Ethernet is fine for short distances, but fibre optic is better for fast, long-distance connections.

nodes.misconception: Wireless networks are always better than wired ones because they don’t use cables.
nodes.response: Wireless is more convenient, but it can be slower, less secure and more prone to interference. Wired connections are often better for speed, stability and data heavy tasks.

nodes.misconception: [ß] is a capital B and sounds like [b].
nodes.response: [ß] sounds the same as [ss]. [ß] is used after long vowels, [ss] after short vowels. In words with 's' as the final sound, the spelling [-s] or [ß] needs to be learnt; for example, 'Glas' or 'Spaß'.

nodes.misconception: The majority of women worked in factories throughout this period.
nodes.response: The work women did and whether they worked at all was largely determined by class. From the mid-19th century, legislation placed restrictions on the type and amount of work women were able to do and the number of women working in factories decreased.

nodes.misconception: Medieval women completed no work other than housework and looking after children.
nodes.response: Although they were responsible for housework and childcare and did not have the same opportunities to work as men, women in the medieval period completed a range of other work; the type of work they completed was determined by where they lived.

nodes.misconception: All women in medieval Norwich had the same experience as one another.
nodes.response: Female experiences were varied, especially by wealth and social class. Those from wealthier backgrounds were more likely to be literate.

nodes.misconception: All women opposed Nazi policies.
nodes.response: Women's experiences under Nazi rule varied: some embraced traditional roles and rewards, while others resisted and faced punishment, showing a complex, not uniform, response to Nazi policies.

nodes.misconception: Sikh women are not as involved as men in religious and community life.
nodes.response: Sikh women have always played an active and important role, historically, as activists and modern day professionals.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only women from Britain served in the armed forces.
nodes.response: Highlight how thousands of women from across the British Empire at the time joined organisations like the ATS to help the British war effort.

nodes.misconception: That Paul's letters always oppose the leadership of women in Christianity.
nodes.response: Some letters can suggest this, but others commend women in various leadership positions in the Church.

nodes.misconception: Wood is only useful for the construction industry.
nodes.response: Wood has multiple everyday and industrial uses.

nodes.misconception: Force and pressure are needed to saw through wood.
nodes.response: Correct technique and posture allows the blade to work efficiently without force.

nodes.misconception: All hardwoods are hard and all softwoods are soft.
nodes.response: Balsa is very soft and light but it is a deciduous hardwood. Yew is heavy and hard but it is a coniferous softwood.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see adverbs as doing more than saying 'how' verbs are done.
nodes.response: Adverbs modify verbs by saying when, where, how or to what extent they are done - encourage pupils to look for words that modify the verb.

nodes.misconception: Children can sometimes see the word ending as a separate word and lift their pencil which disconnects the letter string.
nodes.response: Remind the children to look and read the word before writing it. Get them feeling confident that this is one word and the flow needs to continue until the last letter in the letter string.

nodes.misconception: Words don’t matter that much — it’s the drawing that tells the story.
nodes.response: Words can express things a face alone might not show — like beliefs, experiences, or emotions. The style of the text also adds meaning.

nodes.misconception: Poor people in medieval England survived by eating potatoes.
nodes.response: Potatoes were unknown in Europe until the 16th century.

nodes.misconception: In Spanish the ending for 'you singular' and 'you plural' for -ar verbs is the same.
nodes.response: To refer to 'you' for one person with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -as, e.g. 'buscas'; to refer to 'you' for two or more people with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -áis, e.g. 'buscáis'.

nodes.misconception: A present tense verb can be used on its own to talk about the future.
nodes.response: When using the present tense to talk about the future, it is essential to include a temporal adverb (such as 'mañana', 'la próxima semana', 'el lunes', etc.) to make the future meaning clear.

nodes.misconception: Everyone benefited from Nazi economic policies.
nodes.response: Reinforce that benefits were selective, often dependent on loyalty, and many gains were cancelled out by longer hours and lost freedoms.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the terms force, energy, and work done and use them interchangeably.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the three terms need to be used appropriately, e.g. in describing energy transfers for pushing (force) a crate (doing work) along a level surface (energy transferred).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the terms force, energy, and work done and use them interchangeably.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the three terms need to be used appropriately, e.g. in describing energy transfers for pushing (force) a crate (doing work) along a level surface (energy transferred).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the terms force, energy, and work done and use them interchangeably.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the three terms need to be used appropriately, e.g. in describing energy transfers for pushing (force) a crate (doing work) along a level surface (energy transferred).

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the terms force, energy, and work done and use them interchangeably.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the three terms need to be used appropriately, e.g. in describing energy transfers for pushing (force) a crate (doing work) along a level surface (energy transferred).

nodes.misconception: [ou] and [u] are both the same 'u' sound.
nodes.response: Be careful not to mix up the similar but not identical sounds, people may not understand you or you could be saying a different word to the one you mean.

nodes.misconception: All modal verbs follow the same pattern in the 3rd person plural.
nodes.response: 'Devoir' and 'pouvoir' are formed the same way, 'vouloir' is the same with the addition of an 'l' instead of a 'v' and 'savoir' is different; it follows the same pattern as the 'nous'/'vous' forms.

nodes.misconception: German [d] is always pronounced as English [d].
nodes.response: German [d] at the beginning of a word or syllable sounds like English 'd'; [d] at the end of a syllable sounds like -t. For example, the sentence 'die Landschaft in Deutschland ist wunderschön' contains examples of both [d] sounds.

nodes.misconception: Thinking the heart rate and breathing rate are zero when at rest.
nodes.response: Our body needs the energy from the oxygen we breathe in order to maintain basic living functions, hence why our heart rate is always raised above 0.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think they have to rely on others to include them and that there isn't anything they can or need to do in order to be included.
nodes.response: There are things that you can do to increase your involvement in a challenge and play a role in a team such as sharing ideas and supporting and encouraging others.

nodes.misconception: A GS is a static position.
nodes.response: The GS can move out of the goal circle to create space for the GA to drive in and receive the ball. A shooter position requires dynamic movements such as power to jump for a rebound.

nodes.misconception: Jesus' death on the cross ended the need for reconciliation.
nodes.response: Reconciliation is still important for many Christians; many Christians believe that the duty to promote reconciliation extends to Christians today.

nodes.misconception: Pupils choose to play with one player at the net and their partner at the back of the court.
nodes.response: Splitting front and back leaves a huge gap diagonally through your court that the opposition can exploit.

nodes.misconception: Working in politics is only about becoming an elected official, like an MP.
nodes.response: There are many other important roles, such as civil servants, journalists, and NGO workers, that also contribute to shaping policies and creating change.

nodes.misconception: This lesson talks a lot about tourism and traditional occupations. Some children may believe these are the only jobs for people living in the Lake District.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that although tourism is the main source of income, people also need access to other services such as healthcare and the emergency services. Therefore, there will be lots of other occupations including doctors, teachers and police.

nodes.misconception: Once a print is made, it’s finished, and no further changes can be made.
nodes.response: Prints can be developed further using mixed media and physical alterations like cutting. The process of refining a print is an important step to enhance visual interest and highlight specific areas, creativity doesn't stop after the initial print!

nodes.misconception: Bass parts are normally simple and just play the lowest notes from the chords.
nodes.response: In some cases this is true, but in many cases bass lines are interesting patterns and can often be defining features of songs. This is true for both Under Pressure and Feel Good Inc.

nodes.misconception: Physical properties and working properties are the same thing.
nodes.response: Physical properties describe inherent features (like density, colour, or conductivity), whereas working properties describe how a material behaves under stress (like flexibility, toughness, or hardness).

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that successful strategies need to be very complicated.
nodes.response: Simple strategies are usually most successful because everyone on the team can be clear about what they have to do and can do their part very easily and quickly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that if someone has been designated to a team, this means they have been included.
nodes.response: People can feel excluded even when they're part of a team if they are ignored or not included in the decisions being made. There are many things that you can do to help your teammates to feel included and valued in the team.

nodes.misconception: As long as I am being quiet, I am listening.
nodes.response: Although being quiet is an effective way to show you are listening, there are many other things to consider to ensure you are 'actively listening'.

nodes.misconception: You need to email a file to share it.
nodes.response: Shared links and cloud storage allow others to open the same file directly.

nodes.misconception: Jobs which use the results of science are science jobs.  Electrical engineers and electricians are both scientists because they use the results of science in their work.
nodes.response: Children will be taught the difference between doing and using science within the context of a range of jobs.

nodes.misconception: You can connect a motor directly to a microcontroller and it will work fine.
nodes.response: Microcontrollers send control signals, not power. Motor drivers act like electronic switches to take a signal and safely drive the motors with their own power supply.

nodes.misconception: Grouping objects is permanent.
nodes.response: Grouping objects can be reversed using ungroup. Combining objects is harder to reverse; only undo fixes combining.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often take user input for numerical values and then cannot perform arithmetic calculations on the data as the value is automatically stored as a string.
nodes.response: The int() function is used to convert a user's input to an integer so that calculations can then be performed. For example, age = int(input()) would allow a user to input their age in to a program.

nodes.misconception: It is always colder at the coast because it is near water.
nodes.response: Students will understand that, in winter, coastal areas tend to be warmer because water takes longer to heat up.

nodes.misconception: Difficulty in understanding how different causes overlap to cause hunger.
nodes.response: A consequence chain (see Lesson 5) could be used to investigate the potential impacts of different causes of hunger.

nodes.misconception: Trench warfare was fighting characterised by intense and constant action.
nodes.response: Trench warfare was characterised by intense periods of action, but also long periods of inaction which could be demoralising, boring and harrowing.

nodes.misconception: Bread is only made from wheat (flour).
nodes.response: Other plants can be used to make flour such as maize, rye and chickpeas.

nodes.misconception: Not everyone has a worldview and someone's worldview is entirely their own choice.
nodes.response: We may not be conscious of having a worldview but everyone stands somewhere and our worldview is influenced by many external factors.

nodes.misconception: The Bible is only used for reading and recitation during Christian worship.
nodes.response: Reading and reciting Biblical passages can be an important part of Christian worship, but this is not the only use of the Bible during worship. Many Christians interact and engage with the Bible through private reflection or group discussion.

nodes.misconception: My sculpture needs to show action or be realistic.
nodes.response: Our sculpture can be still, soft, or bulky. It doesn't need to move or look like a real person to hold meaning. Wrapping and shaping can show something inside you, a memory, a feeling or a story, without using words.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may explain the relationship with multiples of 10 as 'adding a zero' (e.g. 37 x 10 = 370).
nodes.response: Pupils should be discouraged from doing this. Instead, explore place value, reminding pupils that each 100 represents 10 lots of ten.

nodes.misconception: A design brief should be very specific and identify a product that will be designed and manufactured.
nodes.response: To avoid design fixation, a design brief should be non-specific and open. A design brief should focus on the context and the problem, and not name a product that will be designed and made.

nodes.misconception: The articles le/la/l'/les and un/une can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use the definite article (le/la/l'/les) for specific nouns and the indefinite article (un/une) for non-specific nouns.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to say 'it' in French.
nodes.response: In French, the word for 'it' changes depending on the grammatical gender of the noun it is replacing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might confuse the x-axis and y-axis, leading them to count along the wrong axis.
nodes.response: Reiterate that the x-axis runs horizontally (left to right) and the y-axis runs vertically (up and down). Use visual aids, like arrows or labels, to clearly mark the axes on the grid.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to apply their knowledge of adverbs.
nodes.response: Adapt outcomes or increase the scaffolds where necessary. Word banks should assist in generating the vocabulary, but if necessary, remove the expectation of adverb use, such as "Paddington is a kind, friendly bear." to describe his personality.

nodes.misconception: That using tentative language makes your argument seem less convincing.
nodes.response: Using tentative language acknowledges that we are exploring poets' intentions and that there are many valid interpretations of a text.

nodes.misconception: Effective analysis writing explores the attitudes in the first text and then, in another paragraph, explores the attitudes in the second text.
nodes.response: The most effective comparative analysis writing will weave comparisons of both texts together. The response will ideally move between examples from each text, weighing up and evaluating the writer's choices in each.

nodes.misconception: An introduction can be written without thoughtful planning
nodes.response: To make an introduction worthwhile, and for it to effectively introduce an essay, it requires thoughtful planning

nodes.misconception: Students often think that they need exciting experiences to write in a compelling manner.
nodes.response: Stress how the quality of writing is more important than the topic being written about.

nodes.misconception: Students might be used to writing their memories as a stream of consciousness, without stopping to consider craft.
nodes.response: Writing memories as a stream of consciousness is a good place to start. However, once one thinks about publishing work, editing and conscious crafting is necessary.

nodes.misconception: Discourse around teenagers in the 1950s and 60s would be entirely different to discourse around teenagers nowadays.
nodes.response: There are some strong similarities between the media portrayal of teenagers from decades ago and now e.g. their ability to shape trends.

nodes.misconception: All sensory imagery is equally effective.
nodes.response: The best sensory imagery employs precise language to achieve specific atmospheres.

nodes.misconception: You do not need to check your work after writing it.
nodes.response: Show pupils the value of checking and editing their work - show the transformation from first draft to final draft.

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.

nodes.misconception: All geographical questions make good fieldwork enquiry questions.
nodes.response: Fieldwork enquiry questions have to be answerable within the practical realms of data collection. Therefore some brilliant geographical questions might not be good fieldwork enquiry questions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that free verse poems must not contain any poetic techniques such as rhyming words.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that although free verse poems do not follow set poetic structures and rules, they may still contain a range of poetic techniques. Allow the pupils to choose which techniques they want to include in their free verse poem.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get stuck on trying to make every line rhyme.
nodes.response: Explain that free verse poems may use rhyme, but it's usually irregular and doesn't follow a particular pattern. Encourage pupils to include two rhyming words if they wish, but not to make this a focus of the poem.

nodes.misconception: Free verse allows for entirely random writing without any consideration for form or craft.
nodes.response: Successful free verse poetry involves deliberate choices regarding line breaks, rhythms and imagery to create a meaningful poem.

nodes.misconception: The focus should be on finding rhyming words.
nodes.response: Poets should aim for natural and purposeful rhymes that complement the poem's intent rather than forcing words to fit a specific pattern.

nodes.misconception: Once you have used an image or idea in a piece of writing, you can't reuse it in the same piece.
nodes.response: Sometimes repeating an idea or image throughout a piece can help give it a sense of structure. You might change certain details, but you can repeat them.

nodes.misconception: You can't repeat any ideas in creative writing. Once you have used them once, you must create new ideas in every successive paragraph.
nodes.response: Repetition of certain ideas or images can give your writing a sense of structure. This is particularly true in your final paragraph where repeating ideas from your first paragraph can alert your reader to the idea that you are about to finish.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it is acceptable to use the same letter for all expressions.
nodes.response: It may be acceptable for the letter to be the same but that depends on what the letter is representing.

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that that some people are just naturally funny and that being funny can't be taught.
nodes.response: Explain that humour is a skill that can be developed and practised by using words and phrases deliberately.

nodes.misconception: All planning should be in note form.
nodes.response: Foundations of your essay - thesis and topic sentences - should be written in full so you know they are powerful, precise and purposeful.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to structure the content of their letter.
nodes.response: Provide a model or structure for the pupils to follow.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that Sassoon's style of open letter is the only way to write an open letter.
nodes.response: Open letters can have a range of purposes. Those that will never be read by the recipient or where the writer doesn't expect to create change (e.g. open letter to Mondays) will typically involve more humour.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have a clear understanding of sentence types.
nodes.response: This is explicitly taught in Learning Cycle 1 and pupils are tasked with finding each type of complex sentence in a model opening.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse speech punctuation rules when writing speech first and speech second in a narrative.
nodes.response: At the end of speech first, a full stop must not be used. At the end of speech second, a full stop can be used.

nodes.misconception: Plot is the most important part of a narrative.
nodes.response: Voice is equally important to plot when writing a narrative. Ask students: if there was a resolution to the story but no distinct voice, how would the story change? Would it be effective, enjoyable?

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to embed a relative clause and they may forgot the necessary commas needed to demarcate a relative clause.
nodes.response: Ensure there is a model of a relative complex sentence where the relative clause follows the main clause and one where the relative clause is embedded. Write the relative clause and commas in a different colour to make them visually stand out.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find creating their own repeated phrase during Task A challenging.
nodes.response: Adults may wish to provide a scaffold for pupils with some example lines.
