nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to come up with imagery to describe their individual settings.
nodes.response: It would be useful to have a word bank with specific words or phrases to describe some key settings (for example, city, rural and coastal).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to generate rhyming words associated with the heat.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in partners, or as a whole class, to create a list of rhyming words.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to generate rhyming words associated with rain.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in partners, or as a whole class, to create a list of rhyming words.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find counting syllables challenging.
nodes.response: Adults can model appropriate methods for syllable counting (including clapping, humming, tapping wrist).

nodes.misconception: Angelou's poem is unstructured - the stanzas are uneven and she talks about lots of different things.
nodes.response: Every piece of writing has a structure - even a shopping list. Structure is about the how a text is put together - at its most simple, beginning, middle and end. But we can also look for other structural features. In this case, stanzas and a refrain.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be secure in listing nouns correctly.
nodes.response: The model includes an adjective before each listed noun (e.g. green park). If necessary, model with or without the adjective to simplify the skill and ensure pupils meet the outcome. Go back to previous lessons where adjectives have been generated.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate descriptions or facts.
nodes.response: Refer back to the setting description lesson and have pupils use their word banks and senses maps to help join ideas together. Facts are 'drip-fed' throughout the lesson. Keep referring back to them and tell pupils that they can choose one of these.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it is acceptable to use the same letter for all expressions.
nodes.response: It may be acceptable for the letter to be the same but that depends on what the letter is representing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils make think that fronted adverbials of time can be used in any order.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that while some fronted adverbials of time are interchangable, there are still many others which must be carefully positioned within a piece of writing e.g. First, Finally.

nodes.misconception: Students may think that concluding sentences are a repetition of topic sentences.
nodes.response: Concluding sentences focus on the writer's intentions and link to but do not repeat topic sentences.

nodes.misconception: You must stick to a single interpretation or approach throughout your essay to make a strong argument.
nodes.response: Whilst you should have an overarching argument, embracing nuance by exploring multiple interpretations deepens your analysis. This approach strengthens your argument by showing the text’s complexity and layers.

nodes.misconception: Analysing a text is an individual exercise.
nodes.response: Having discussions around a text can help us build on our ideas and reconsider different ways of interpreting the text.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the first attempt at their response is the finished version.
nodes.response: Redrafting your work has many benefits and the second attempt is always superior. Taking time to reflect on  your work and identify areas for improvements allows you to recognise any lack of clarity in your explanations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that apostrophes for possession are only used for physical nouns.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that nouns such as skills or senses can also be possessed, or owned. E.g. a bat's eyesight.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use viewpoint fronted adverbials inaccurately by selecting the wrong intensity. For example, using 'shockingly' before a piece of information that isn't shocking.
nodes.response: Teach children to accurately guage the intensity of a statement or fact and then choose the right viewpoint fronted adverbial to match.  You could turn this into a game they play in pairs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a joining word can be used at the start of a sentence.
nodes.response: Teach that the joining word acts as the link between two simple sentences and so no full stop is needed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the joining words used in compound sentences can also be used in complex sentences.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there are only certain joining words that can be used to join subordinate ideas to main ideas. Remind pupils that a compound sentence is made up of two ideas that make complete sense.

nodes.misconception: Children may accidentally develop rhetorical questions in present tense or first person when imagining what Arrietty is thinking. E.g. instead of "Was she safe?" they might write "Am I safe?"
nodes.response: Gather ideas from students about what Arriety might have been thinking and model turning these into third person and past tense. Provide examples in a shared bank for children to refer to while writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use repetitive language choices.
nodes.response: Exposing pupils to a range of synonyms and ambitious vocabulary in the teacher model will support with language variation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils write their facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write their facts in an incoherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use apostrophes incorrectly when indicating possession.
nodes.response: Supplement the content in Learning Cycle One with further teaching of the rules associated with using apostrophes for singular and plural possession.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify or develop appropriate prepositions to precisely describe details about nouns within the setting.
nodes.response: After revealing the prepositions 'beneath' and 'towards', brainstorm a range of helpful prepositions as a class and create a shared bank that the children can use.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write relative complex sentences where the relative clause does not describe the noun preceding it.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 explicitly models ensuring that the relative clause adds a relevant fact to the noun before it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that speeches do not need to follow a particular structure.
nodes.response: Following a structure, such as PEPS, can help a speech to flow and make it easier to follow for an audience.

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to change the order of the devices in the poem.
nodes.response: Joseph Coelho originally intends people to follow the set structure, but then you can allow pupils to play around with the structure of their poem and move things if they want to.

nodes.misconception: Including any statistics is enough to make your argument more convincing.
nodes.response: In order to be convincing, statistics have to be credible.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will modify their code to provide input directly in to the input() function, for example, user = input("Aisha"), rather than typing when asked as the program runs.
nodes.response: The computer follows the instructions of a program. Input that a user has to type in should only be entered when the program runs. This allows different users to provide different inputs without changing the program in any way.

nodes.misconception: That you should quote entire sentences of text in order to prove your point.
nodes.response: Often, individual words and short quotes are more effective in analytical writing.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to generate individual sentences per event.
nodes.response: Refer to the story mountain that the children made in a previous lesson and make that available. When retelling and reading the story, refer back to the model story mountain to refer to those points. Explain that each picture is one sentence.

nodes.misconception: That you should always select quotes with the most linguistic features to talk about.
nodes.response: You should select the quote that best matches the point of the sentence.

nodes.misconception: Students may think context should be mentioned separately at the end of their paragraphs, rather than integrated throughout their analysis.
nodes.response: Context should be woven into your analysis to enrich your interpretation e.g. 'Nagra's depiction of family duties versus personal desires draws from his British-Indian experience, showcasing challenges faced by second-generation immigrants.'

nodes.misconception: Students can forget to use the sources provided, and instead simply rely on their own knowledge.
nodes.response: The historical environment questions are mainly source-based and therefore students should base their answers on the sources, using their knowledge to explain what is in the sources and to judge the utility of the sources.

nodes.misconception: Students do not embed their quotations.
nodes.response: If students don't embed their quotations, the response is not as concise as it could be. Being concise makes your response sophisticated.

nodes.misconception: Students tend to 'bolt' irrelevant context onto the end of analytical paragraphs.
nodes.response: Context should be integrated into students' responses and should enhance or support their arguments.

nodes.misconception: Students think that the writer's method is just similes/metaphors etc.
nodes.response: The writer's method is anything that they do consciously - it's any conscious choice that they make.

nodes.misconception: Poetic language does not exist in everyday life.
nodes.response: Poetic language is everywhere since we use metaphors and comparisons in everyday speech all the time.

nodes.misconception: That an answer should include all of the interesting details about a text.
nodes.response: An answer should only include details that are relevant to the question.

nodes.misconception: Children may have already thought about a different aspiration (e.g. footballer, singer etc.)
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to choose a different job if they have requested and work with them to find a suitable adjective, such as 'unstoppable footballer' instead of 'helpful footballer'. The purpose of the task is about aspiration, so any job is suitable.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think they have to come up with new ideas for each essay question they attempt.
nodes.response: Highlight similarities between the modelled plan on 'hypocrisy' and their own ideas relationing to 'duality'.

nodes.misconception: That quotes in essays need to be long and are difficult to remember.
nodes.response: Can you remember anything Boxer says? How about words used to describe characters? Any of the commandments? These are all key quotes.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that linguistic devices should be used as often as possible.
nodes.response: Encourage them to use linguistic devices judiciously. Overuse can be as as much of a problem as underuse.

nodes.misconception: Memorising a presentation, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
nodes.response: An effective presentation will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing presentation.

nodes.misconception: An artist statement has to be a long, formal piece of writing full of complicated words.
nodes.response: Artist statements can be short and simple, written in clear and honest language, and can also take other formats such as bullet points, spoken word, visual mind maps, captions, or short videos.

nodes.misconception: That just identifying a method in a quotation is effective.
nodes.response: To be effective, you need to analyse the effect of the method in the quotation.

nodes.misconception: Analytical paragraphs should lead by comparing how the writers use language, form and/or structure.
nodes.response: The best comparative analytical writing begins by exploring connections between the key ideas or attitudes in a poem, supported by analysis of how writers use language, form and/or structure to convey these ideas or attitudes.

nodes.misconception: Students do not understand that an argument should build in complexity.
nodes.response: Students should consider the structure of their argument. Which ideas need to come first in order to foreground other ideas?

nodes.misconception: Analytical paragraphs should lead by identifying how a writer uses language, form and/or structure.
nodes.response: The best analytical writing begins by exploring how key ideas or attitudes in a text link to the question focus, supported by analysis of how the writer uses language, form and/or structure to convey these ideas or attitudes.

nodes.misconception: Analytical paragraphs should lead by identifying how a writer uses language, form and/or structure.
nodes.response: The best analytical writing begins by exploring how key ideas or attitudes in a poem link to the question focus, supported by analysis of how the writer uses language, form and/or structure to convey these ideas or attitudes.

nodes.misconception: Adding an alternative interpretation weakens your argument.
nodes.response: Showing how you can reach the same conclusion about a text through multiple interpretations strengthens your argument.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to sequence their instructions.
nodes.response: Complete lesson 8 first as this breaks down how to write commands needed for the lesson. Allow pupils to then use their instructions to present and add to their information page.

nodes.misconception: Not everyone can write a good melody.
nodes.response: Writing a melody is just like writing a paragraph. Break it into small chunks (phrases). If you are finding it difficult to create a phrase, keep it simple and start by just improvising using 2 or 3 notes.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that they have to write from their own perspective - that the 'voice' in the article has to be their own.
nodes.response: Students can create a voice. For example, they could write the article from the perspective of a teacher or a parent. This is still voice.

nodes.misconception: An effective essay includes all of your thoughts on the subject.
nodes.response: An effective essay is structured cohesively rather than including every thought.

nodes.misconception: You should write all the code before testing.
nodes.response: Test small parts frequently to catch errors early. It is easier to fix a few errors at a time than all of them at once.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of what a noun is and so, unable to understand their caption is a noun.
nodes.response: Teach the 'Year 1 Word Class Grammar Unit' at the same time as this so the children can have explicit teaching of nouns and word class.

nodes.misconception: That you should use definitive, authoritative language in your analytical writing to prove to the reader that you are right.
nodes.response: You should use tentative language because we can never be truly sure of the writer's intentions - you should use evidence and clear explanations to prove your idea to the reader.

nodes.misconception: Children may lift their pencil in the middle of the letter string to 'dot' the letter i or put the 'cross' on the letter t.
nodes.response: Model to the children that you wait until the end of the letter string before adding the 'cross' or the 'dot'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to evaluate composite functions by working from left to right.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they cannot do this as each function needs an input and with composite functions the input needs to be evaluated before it can be used.

nodes.misconception: Students think that they need to describe everything in a setting.
nodes.response: Ask students to 'bounce' around a scene, only describing the most influential and important aspects of it.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to develop appropriate similes for their special item.
nodes.response: Model examples for a range of colours and powerful nouns they could be compared to. E.g. Green items could be compared to elements of a meadow or a tree.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use 'and' repeatedly, creating a long sentence.
nodes.response: Give the children  an 'and' card. Tell them to keep it in their pockets and emphasise they only have one 'and' per sentence, so they have to decide when they have used it. Once they have used it for the sentence, they have to give it back!

nodes.misconception: Children may not write or speak in the past tense.
nodes.response: Consistently use sentence stems for the children to build their descriptive sentences from that are always in the past tense.

nodes.misconception: A comparative essay should deal with each poem separately in the body of the essay.
nodes.response: While one method of comparison might be to deal with each poem separately, you might also consider comparing the poems throughout the essay and instead splitting up the essay thematically or by methods.

nodes.misconception: Students often believe that longer sentences are more sophisticated.
nodes.response: Great writing needs to be concise. Students should be aiming for precision, rather than sophistication.

nodes.misconception: Figurative language such as similes belongs in fictional writing rather than non-fiction.
nodes.response: Non-fiction writing is all about informing, persuading or educating the reader and therefore similes can be a very useful device to explain ideas to the reader.

nodes.misconception: When $$x : y$$ are in the ratio 1 : 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$
nodes.response: The bar models shown in this lesson can help to support pupils with this.

nodes.misconception: Students often think all the characters are hypocritical because they are all keeping secrets.
nodes.response: Keep drawing their attention back to the keywords and their definitions.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that they need to 'zoom in' on every word when analysing a quotation.
nodes.response: Often, it can be useful to discuss the 'bigger' method that the poet is using e.g. their use of personification. By thinking about bigger methods, the students may be more focused on the themes of the poem and the poet's intentions.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that describing something's overall appearance makes a good description.
nodes.response: Description is about making your reader imagine what you are imagining. You have to give really specific details about a person or setting.

nodes.misconception: You should analyse one poem and then analyse the second, making your comparisons at this point.
nodes.response: The best analysis writing weaves comparisons throughout. A great way to practise this is by beginning each paragraph with a topic sentence that uses correlative conjunctions (e.g. both ... and ...).

nodes.misconception: Students think that they need to write an 'exciting' story which includes lots of action.
nodes.response: A genuinely engaging story allows the reader to empathise with the character(s) and experience the same emotions as them, at the same time.

nodes.misconception: Inference and analysis are the same thing.
nodes.response: Inference is about reading between the lines. Analysis focuses on unpicking writer's methods and explores their effects.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to find two similar facts.
nodes.response: Start by generating as many facts as you can about Floella; as you are receiving facts from pupils, model the thought process by saying 'Those two are linked because ...'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to present their information independently.
nodes.response: Create page layouts with boxes and lines for the children to use in order for presentation and handwriting to stay at their expected level. This may mean their reports go across multiple pages or use larger paper.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to write the exact same sentence from the non-fiction text.
nodes.response: In the first learning cycle, when repeating what they have learnt, re-phrase it into simple sentences that they could write in the next learning cycle. You could provide pictures linked to the facts to guide them towards specific ideas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often don't see the value in editing work and think once the first draft is finished, the work on it is done.
nodes.response: Writing is a process that involves multiple stages. Revising and editing are crucial steps to refine your work, enhance clarity, and improve overall quality. Even professional writers revise their drafts several times before publishing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to choose appropriate cohesive devices to connect ideas.
nodes.response: Give pupils access to the Cohesive Devices Bank throughout their writing.

nodes.misconception: Children will sometimes lift their pencils part way through the letter string.
nodes.response: Model to the children that they should look at the word first and plan for when they will be lifting their pencil: usually at the end of the word or after a break letter. Model writing the word, emphasising the flow as the letters connect.

nodes.misconception: When writing an extended piece of fiction or non-fiction, you should include every single method you know.
nodes.response: Different texts are read for different reasons and by different audiences. It is your job, as the writer, to consider which are the best methods for your particular text. Just because you know how to use a method, doesn't mean you have to include it.

nodes.misconception: That the subject of a sentence is always the person in the sentence.
nodes.response: A subject is the person, place, or thing that is performing the action of the sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may order the instructions incorrectly.
nodes.response: Children would benefit from having had some experience of following instructions to make a pizza in advance. Model how to follow a plan carefully to ensure the order of instructions is correct.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recall what they have written so far.
nodes.response: Spend time in the lesson re-reading what they have written so far. Then, refer back to when you made the sandwiches to sequence the final instructions.

nodes.misconception: When writing a list of nouns, pupils may keep extending it or repeatedly use 'and'.
nodes.response: Tell the children to focus on three nouns only and explicitly model that 'and' is used before the last noun and the comma is used in between the others.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can incorrectly write a number in standard form or use a number in incorrect standard form whereby the number A does not satisfy 1 ≤ A < 10 or pupils use division of positive powers of 10.
nodes.response: Standard form represents a multiplicative relationship, so there should always be a multiplication. Embedding the understanding that negative exponents refer to 1/10^n is important. Using the place value chart with fractional and exponent form helps.

nodes.misconception: That creative writing should be in present tense.
nodes.response: Because diaries are records of events that have happened, they should be written in past tense.

nodes.misconception: Children may try to use the same join for every connection.
nodes.response: Ensure the children are given plenty of reminders about the four joins and how the join used depends on the letters joining. Use the CFU's within this lesson to help explain this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often want to write their speech down word for word.
nodes.response: There often isn't time to write a speech word for word when preparing for a debate. Therefore, notes should be used instead.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that all exam questions need unique ideas and responses.
nodes.response: When looking at the question in the first learning cycle, ask pupils if they can use ideas/arguments from previous 'Macbeth' essays.

nodes.misconception: The most important thing in a poem is the words.
nodes.response: Structure is important, it can help tell your story. Not considering the structure of your poem is like an author not considering the beginning, middle and end of a novel.

nodes.misconception: Internal thoughts are rhetorical questions only.
nodes.response: Internal thoughts can be questions and statements. Ensure pupils use their plans with ideas for Paikea's internal thoughts and model how to write these in the third person.

nodes.misconception: Children may think the only way to convey Scrooge's thoughts is to use the phrase 'Scrooge thought'. They may struggle to incorporate different ways to incorporate his inner thoughts.
nodes.response: Highlight the different examples that convey Scrooge's internal thoughts and ask the children to spot the different verbs used instead of 'thought'. Other examples are 'considered', 'wondered', 'told himself'.

nodes.misconception: Internal thoughts are always written from the first person perspective of the character.
nodes.response: In this piece, pupils will not switch between the third person and the first person perspective. Ensure pupils use their plan with ideas for Paikea's internal thoughts and model how to write these in the third person.

nodes.misconception: The examples given for fronted adverbials of manner are adverbs ending in 'ly'. Children may assume this is the only way to write a fronted adverbial of manner.
nodes.response: Provide additional examples of fronted adverbials of manner that are phrases rather than individual words. E.g. 'With a grave expression on his face,...'.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with switching the order of the clauses in an adverbial complex sentence and remembering the comma rule.
nodes.response: Provide a model of an adverbial complex sentence. Example: 'Her heart raced as she tumbled backwards.' Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause in order to switch the clauses.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with switching the order of the clauses in an adverbial complex sentence and remembering the comma rule.
nodes.response: Provide a model of an adverbial complex sentence. Example: 'Her heart raced as she tumbled backwards.' Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause in order to switch the clauses.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with developing an appropriate rhetorical question and writing it in the correct tense. E.g. 'Will she make it?'
nodes.response: Model appropriate examples in the past tense and highlight the ways in which it sounds like Lila is asking the question herself (despite the use of the 'she' pronoun). E.g. She decided to brave the heat. After all, wasn't she used to fire anyway?

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that any mention of character speech is direct speech, because that has been the focus of their learning.
nodes.response: Model how speech can still be indirectly reported within the climax alongside direct speech. E.g. 'Lila pleaded for Razvani to help her.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include details and information that should be kept for the second part of the main body.
nodes.response: Pupils' planning documents clearly outline which key events should be described in part one. The planning document is re-visited and shared in learning cycle two.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use veiled threat as a persuasive technique, but they may use it clumsily or inappropriately.
nodes.response: The scaffolding and modelling of what appropriate veiled threat looks and sounds like is explicit in the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to convert notes into complete sentences.
nodes.response: Provide lots of time for oral rehearsal at each stage of the lesson and ensure children have access to vocabulary and plans used earlier in the unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may over-use one type of sentence, leading to poor text cohesion.
nodes.response: The range of sentence types are reviewed in learning cycle one with relative and non-finite complex sentences reviewed in detail. Encourage pupils to vary the placement of the subordinate clause in their complex sentences to enhance text cohesion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not back up their points or arguments using evidence.
nodes.response: Learning cycle one reiterates the importance of writing credibility and how using evidence can enhance the credibility of the argument.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might be confused by the crossover between a fronted adverbial of manner or time and a non-finite or adverbial clause, for example, 'Hunching over,...' or 'As soon as they had spoken, ...'.
nodes.response: Whenever a fronted adverbial of manner is also an adverbial or non-finite clause, make this explicit. For example, in slide 19, you could say 'Leaning towards her sisters,' is a fronted adverbial of manner, but it is also a non-finite clause.

nodes.misconception: Students should avoid short or one-word sentences in favour of longer, complex sentences.
nodes.response: If used correctly, shorter sentences can be great for amending pace and giving emphasis to particular parts of a speech.

nodes.misconception: Students commonly forget the comma after fronted adverbials.
nodes.response: Model sentences including fronted adverbials missing the comma and ask students to spot the punctuation error.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the progressive and perfect tenses as both use an auxiliary verb.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the progressive uses 'being' auxiliary verbs and the perfect uses 'having' auxiliary verbs.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spot progressive tenses in negative forms like 'won't be waiting'.
nodes.response: Highlight that we still have an auxiliary verb and an -ing verb even when a negative interrupts like in 'were not watching/aren't looking'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe all verbs in a sentence are always in the same tense.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the lesson to draw out the point that to maintain sense, we sometimes vary the tense of verbs in a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to spell more complex adjectives or nouns, such as soldier or ambulance.
nodes.response: Provide a word bank for more complex words to encourage pupils to use if necessary. Provide sentence stems and scaffolds if necessary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils can incorrectly write a number in standard form or use a number in incorrect standard form whereby the number A does not satisfy 1 ≤ A < 10 or pupils use division of positive powers of 10.
nodes.response: Standard form represents a multiplicative relationship, so there should always be a multiplication. Embedding the understanding that negative exponents refer to 1/10^n is important. Using the place value chart with fractional and exponent form helps.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with generating an introductory sentence for each section.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to think about the main point of the paragraph, e.g. What is most obvious about the penguins' appearance? Are penguins well-adapted? If so, to what?

nodes.misconception: Pupils start a speech by directly addressing the audience and explaining the purpose of the speech.
nodes.response: Ask pupils if the best method of getting your own way is by stating what you want straight away.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget the second bracket after parenthesis.
nodes.response: Teacher explicitly models making this mistake and correcting it when re-reading the final written outcome at the end of the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to answer questions.
nodes.response: Previous lessons in the unit have had similar sentence structures and stems. Refer back to these to help the children to make links and develop their own sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may just use 'and' to add on another word or phrase rather than another sentence.
nodes.response: Show two different sentences as two complete ideas. Ensure pupils understand that each sentence needs to make sense on its own.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may just use 'and' to add on another word or phrase rather than another sentence.
nodes.response: Show two different sentences as two complete ideas. Ensure pupils understand that each sentence needs to make sense on its own.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with the spelling of certain words.
nodes.response: Where possible, encourage the children to use phonics strategies to create phonetically plausible spellings. For other words, create a word bank for children to refer to. 'Decided', 'countryside' and 'adventure' would be useful words to include.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to generate individual sentences per event.
nodes.response: Refer to the story mountain that the children made in a previous lesson and make that available. When retelling and reading the story, refer back to the model story mountain. Explain that each picture is one sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with how to apply the comma rule in a relative complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of a relative complex sentence. Ask children to identify the relative pronoun that begins the relative clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place in the opening, climax or resolution.
nodes.response: The build-up follows a clear, chronological order that includes the three key moments from pupils' plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all fronted adverbials of time do the same job.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that different fronted adverbials of time can have different impacts on the writing. In parituclar, to speed up or slow down the action.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use inaccurate fronted adverbials of time.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the different fronted adverbials of time can control the speed of the action being described. Model them being used incorrectly and ask children to spot the errors.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place later in the narrative.
nodes.response: The first part of the build-up follows a clear, chronological order that includes the three key moments from pupils' plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to remember the comma rule in a complex sentence.
nodes.response: Commas are only needed in a complex sentence when the subordinate clause comes first. Remind pupils that if the subordinate clause comes second, they do not need a comma before the subordinating conjunction.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with how to apply the comma rule in a relative complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of a relative complex sentence. Ask children to identify the relative pronoun that begins the relative clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with switching the order of the clauses in an adverbial complex sentence and remembering the comma rule.
nodes.response: Provide a model of an adverbial complex sentence. Example: 'His pulse raced as he sprinted home.' Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause in order to switch the clauses. Ask them where the comma goes.

nodes.misconception: Children may not notice the subtle shifts in intensity and suspense at different points, e.g. how emotions may have shifted when the farmers waited and the Iron Man didn't arrive.
nodes.response: Ask children to imagine or act out how they would have felt as the farmers at each point to support them in incorporating the appropriate 'show and tell' throughout.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to come up with internal thoughts for a character.
nodes.response: Play a game of 'freeze frame' for different parts of the build-up and encourage children to share their thoughts and feelings, to support all children with ideas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to write ideas for Scrooge's inner thoughts in this lesson.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have a plan to use with ideas for Scrooge's inner thoughts and model how to write these.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with remembering the punctuation rules in speech second sentences.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of the speech second punctuation rules. Encourage pupils to use this when writing direct speech.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place in the opening, build-up or resolution.
nodes.response: The climax follows a clear, chronological order that includes the three key moments from pupils' plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may choose inappropriate fronted adverbials of manner, which do not describe the verb in the most effective way.
nodes.response: Give children printed sentences and printed fronted adverbials of manner and allow them to choose the most appropriate one to start each sentence. Children work in pairs and then compare with another pair.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss out the joining word 'and' when writing compound sentences.
nodes.response: Show pupils some examples of sentences missing the word 'and' and ask them to spot what is missing and where it should go. Encourage pupils to read back through their writing to check every sentence makes sense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with remembering the different punctuation rules in speech first and speech second sentences.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of the speech first and speech second punctuation rules. Encourage pupils to use this when writing direct speech.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that any mention of character speech is direct speech because that has been the focus of their learning.
nodes.response: Model how speech is still indirectly reported within the climax alongside direct speech. E.g. 'Hogarth opposed hurting the Iron Man and he told the farmers he had a plan to protect everyone.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not use a range of sentence types and structures, leading to a lack of cohesion.
nodes.response: Success criteria, shared writing and modelled writing explicitly prompt and model use of a range of sentence types. You could also use visual scaffolds and checklists for each sentence type to remind pupils with.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused when writing some sentences in present tense and some in future tense.
nodes.response: Teacher models must make use of both the present and the future tenses. This must be explicitly explained when scaffolding the writing task.

nodes.misconception: Students may find it hard to understand how different tenses can be used in one sentence.
nodes.response: Analyse example e.g. "Currently, forensic officers are examining the crime scene and they have sent off pieces of evidence for testing."

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have negative attitudes towards editing their work.
nodes.response: Encourage a growth mindset, modelling the idea that all work can be improved and avoiding negative responses to mistakes.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: A conclusion does not introduce new information. Its purpose is to summarise the key points made previously throughout the text.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: A conclusion does not introduce new information. Its purpose is to summarise the key points made previously through the text.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to repeat facts that were included earlier in the report.
nodes.response: Detailed facts about a balanced diet, exercise and sleep come in the earlier themed sections.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: It should not introduce new information that wasn't previously stated in the sections before it. Its purpose is to summarise the key points.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: A conclusion does not introduce new information. Its purpose is to summarise the key points made previously through the text.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to take plans written in note form and construct sentences.
nodes.response: Lesson gives the opportunity to explicitly model the thinking process when turning notes into full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use a semi-colon in an incorrect position.
nodes.response: What is either side of the semi-colon must be capable of being a complete sentence; the two parts must be closely-related to each other in meaning and content.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a conclusion is for summarising the key information from the report. Give children a range of sentences and ask them to sort into those you would or would not find in a conclusion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: A conclusion does not introduce new information. Its purpose is to summarise the key points made previously through the text.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the conclusion should review every detail of the digestive process.
nodes.response: It is important not to repeat the explanation, but to highlight the key parts by reviewing the most important subject-specific vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that every single verb in a past or present tense paragraph has to stick to that tense.
nodes.response: We're writing from a present or a past tense perspective, but the way that language works means that not every verb will be in the same tense in a paragraph. Encourage the children to think about what 'sounds right' and to orally rehearse sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will have been taught that exclamation sentences must contain a verb, as in 'What a mess there is!'
nodes.response: We use the term exclamative to include verbless construction like 'How cool!' alongside 'proper' exclamation sentences like 'How warm it is!'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils include relative clauses that include information that is not relevant to the main clause.
nodes.response: Task A and the quizzes specifically address the issue of relevance when selecting a relative clause.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to structure questions.
nodes.response: Spend time in the lesson modelling examples of questions using different sentence stems and emphasise this using your voice to show you are asking something. Refer to the Year 1: simple sentences Grammar unit for a Grammar lesson to teach alongside.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to end every sentence with an exclamation mark.
nodes.response: Emphasise that exclamation marks show shock or surprise and lose impact if overused. Give pupils a paper exclamation mark to trade in when used, ensuring they use only one in this piece of writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may tick their success criteria without checking and correcting.
nodes.response: When you are modelling your write, continuously refer back to the success criteria yourself. Adapt the success criteria accordingly to help pupils experience success.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse when to use an adjective or verb.
nodes.response: Scaffold this for pupils using sentence stems throughout the lesson. Support pupils' grammar knowledge by referring to Lessons 3 and 6 in the 'Word class' unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may tick their success criteria without checking and correcting.
nodes.response: When you are modelling your write, continuously refer back to the success criteria yourself. Adapt the success criteria accordingly to help pupils experience success.

nodes.misconception: Children might struggle to identify how to transition into the present tense smoothly in a way that supports text flow.
nodes.response: Highlight the use of the compound sentence using 'but' to contrast between past and present emotions. Encourage children to orally rehearse a similar sentence as their transition point to the present tense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to show elements of Maggie's story that are gratuitously graphic or violent.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that we are talking about real people and that we should consider how Addie reacted to this in the story.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use fronted adverbials inaccurately by getting the 'and' and 'but' adverbials mixed up.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to say their sentences out loud so they can hear if the fronted adverbial they've chosen to use sounds right.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the distinction between hyperbole and metaphors.
nodes.response: Explain that hyperbole always uses exaggeration and doesn't need to be metaphorical. E.g. 'That is the best news I have ever heard.' Metaphors can involve exaggeration but do not need to. E.g. 'That is music to my ears.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to maintain a consistent tense in their writing. Usually, this is moving betwen past and present tense.
nodes.response: Teach children that words such as 'was' and 'had' can change the tense of verbs to the past tense. Play a game where children have to change present tense verbs into past tense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect ideas together using cohesive devices.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of time for oral rehearsal using the bank of cohesive devices and model selecting different options for connecting ideas together.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to choose appropriate cohesive devices to connect ideas.
nodes.response: Emphasise that often, we can choose from a wide range of cohesive devices that serve the same purpose; it is simply the writer's choice. Allow plenty of time for oral rehearsal before writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to use the full range of cohesive devices and punctuation expected from them.
nodes.response: Our Y6 Grammar 'Revision' unit covers the full range of cohesive devices and punctuation expected of pupils in Year 6. You might wish to use these lessons to remind pupils of certain features they may wish to include.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to convert notes into complete sentences.
nodes.response: Provide lots of time for oral rehearsal at each stage of the lesson and ensure children have access to vocabulary and plans used earlier in the unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect ideas with appropriate linguistic features.
nodes.response: When completing shared writing, show how the same ideas can be connected in different ways; focus on looking at the relationship between the ideas being connected.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect ideas using a range of cohesive devices.
nodes.response: Lessons about all the relevant cohesive devices can be found in our KS2 Grammar curriculum; you could select slides to pre-teach particular concepts if needed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be accustomed to teacher modelling of written work.
nodes.response: Ensure plenty of time for oral rehearsal and encourage pupils to constantly refer back to their plan.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that their oral rehearsal has to be perfect or excessively detailed.
nodes.response: The oral rehearsal is a first attempt; it may not be perfect. It reduces the cognitive load when writing, allowing extra details to be added more easily.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be tempted to over-use short sentences in their writing.
nodes.response: Show in your shared writing that short sentences are impactful **because** they contrast with the longer or more complex sentences we tend to use in formal narrative writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to use all the cohesive devices listed in the lesson.
nodes.response: All these cohesive devices are covered in our Year 5 Grammar curriculum; some children may benefit from additional input using selected slides from that content.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may shift into writing from the third person perspective.
nodes.response: Pause at regular intervals during the writing process and have pupils read back and check for consistent use of the first person.

nodes.misconception: Children may try to include too many persuasive linguistic techniques in one sentence.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that their sentences still need to make sense, so focus on one linguistic technique per sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to use a colon to explain correctly.
nodes.response: Explain that there must be what could be a complete sentence on either side of the colon and the section after the colon must explain what comes before the colon.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may shift into writing from the third person perspective.
nodes.response: Pause at regular intervals during the writing process and have pupils read back and check for use of the first person.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to choose appropriate cohesive devices to connect ideas.
nodes.response: Emphasise that often, we can choose from a wide range of cohesive devices that serve the same purpose; it is simply the writer's choice. Allow plenty of time for oral rehearsal before writing and give access to the bank of cohesive devices.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use repetitive language choices.
nodes.response: Exposure to a range of compound adjectives and synonyms in the teacher model will support with language variation.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse co-ordinating and subordinating conjunctions.
nodes.response: Ensure that both conjunctions are taught within the context of full compound and complex sentences to avoid confusion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include fronted adverbials which are more suited to fiction writing e.g. In a heartbeat.
nodes.response: Explicitly teach the children that fronted adverbials in a report should be formal and give them plenty of examples.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that take place inside the hive.
nodes.response: This section explains the first two steps of the honey-making process that take place outside the hive.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that come in section 2 of the explanation text.
nodes.response: This section explains the first three steps of the mummification process, up to where the body was covered in natron salt.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include information about food travelling into the intestines.
nodes.response: This section explains the process of food entering the body, moving through the oesophagus and to the stomach.

nodes.misconception: Children may find the use of subordination more difficult in their writing, especially finding ways to use subordinating conjunctions other than 'when'.
nodes.response: Focus more heavily on subordination than coordination during teaching. It is appropriate to focus on the subordinating conjunction 'when' as this is the most valuable for the text's purpose, but model the use of other subordinating conjunctions too.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse this first person writing with internal monologue and focus only on Addie's thoughts.
nodes.response: Here, we haven't used the term 'internal monologue' because we are describing events and observations from Addie's perspective and not just thoughts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to select which facts to connect using cohesive devices.
nodes.response: Give pupils plenty of time to orally rehearse grouping information together using different cohesive devices.

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include subject-specific information in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include subject-specific information in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Children may write detailed information and facts about nocturnal animals in their introduction.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the introduction gives general information. Give examples of general vs specific information for children to identify

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: Emphasise that an introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Children may want to copy the teacher model and teacher plan.
nodes.response: Incorporate opportunities for paired talk and suggest a range of possible vocabulary choices to support pupils in using their own ideas.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they can place the sender's and recipient's address wherever they like.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there are strict rules to follow in terms of the layout of a formal letter.  Provide pupils with a range of examples of formal letters for them to explore in groups.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to use too many persuasive techniques all at once in the introduction.
nodes.response: Explain that evidence and veiled threat are not appropriate to include in the introduction because they are too specific.

nodes.misconception: Children may write detailed information and facts about the fire in their introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction plays a key role in a report and entices the reader to keep reading. It should only include brief, general facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: Emphasise that an introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: Emphasise that an introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect ideas with cohesive devices.
nodes.response: Model the idea that there are often many appropriate ways to link the same ideas; refer to the Cohesive Devices Bank for more ideas and give pupils access to it during writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may tick their success criteria without checking and correcting.
nodes.response: When you are modelling your write, continuously refer back to the success criteria yourself. Adapt the success criteria accordingly to help pupils experience success.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use an exclamation mark for every sentence or overuse them.
nodes.response: When you introduce exclamation marks, 'give' each child one exclamation mark to put in their pockets. Tell them they can only have one, so they should only get it out of their pocket when they think it is the best place to use it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate vocabulary about places or people.
nodes.response: Refer back to the previous lessons in the unit where you have generated vocabulary and consider how you could use the vocabulary to describe your own experiences. Model the process of going back through the previous lesson's writing and word banks.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be daunted by the quantity they are expected to write.
nodes.response: Spend time emphasising the repeated aspects to show pupils that once they have written one sentence, the following sentences are very similar.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use an exclamation mark for every sentence or overuse them.
nodes.response: When you introduce exclamation marks, 'give' each child one exclamation mark to put in their pockets. Tell them they can only have one, so they should only get it out of their pocket when they think it is the best place to use it.

nodes.misconception: That pathetic fallacy is only about using the weather to express emotions.
nodes.response: Pathetic fallacy is a type of personification where emotions are given to a setting, an object or the weather.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to punctuate direct speech correctly.
nodes.response: You may wish to select a few slides from our KS2 Grammar lessons on speech if appropriate to remind children of the punctuation rules.

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that any mention of character speech is direct speech, because that has been the focus in the lesson.
nodes.response: Model how speech can still be indirectly reported within the opening alongside direct speech. E.g. 'Scrooge muttered insults at all those he passed.'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include facts and details that are too specific for the opening paragraph.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 and the success criteria explicitly reinforce the importance of keeping information in the opening general.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to turn a simple past tense sentence into a perfect present tense sentence, especially when this involves changing the main verb.
nodes.response: Explore simple past tense examples where the main verb needs changing as well. E.g. 'It was' becomes 'It has been'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include facts that are too specific for the opening.
nodes.response: Make explicit and repeated reference to only including general information. Use the 5 Ws (who, what, where, when, why) to help embed this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include facts that are too specific for the opening.
nodes.response: Make explicit and repeated reference to only including general information. Use the 5 Ws (who, what, where, when, why) to help embed this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with using accurate punctuation in direct speech sentences.
nodes.response: Give pupils an opportunity to practise writing speech on mini-whiteboards and provide a visual scaffold to support them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place in the build-up, climax or resolution.
nodes.response: The opening follows a clear, chronological order that includes the three key moments from pupils' plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to describe the setting and the reader may struggle to picture it in detail.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that describing the setting using expanded noun phrases will help to add detail. Refer back to Lesson 2 where children will have created a sensory map of the setting.

nodes.misconception: Details of a crime can be reported in any part of an article.
nodes.response: Explain to students that more and more information is revealed as an article develops.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may just copy out the words from their plans.
nodes.response: Explicitly model reading your plan and turning those notes into full sentences. This will also be modelled in Learning Cycle 1 where the children orally rehearse their sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place later in the narrative.
nodes.response: The first part of the opening follows a clear, chronological order that includes the three key moments from pupils' plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find it challenging when writing in the irregular past tense.
nodes.response: Refer to the Year 3 unit 'Tense forms: simple, progressive and perfect' for opportunities for further discrete grammar teaching around tense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with remembering the comma rule in an adverbial complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of an adverbial complex sentence. Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.

nodes.misconception: Children may forget to refer to the Iron Man using a variety of nouns.
nodes.response: Ask children to brainstorm a variety of different nouns for the Iron Man. They can use their plan to help them with this. Create a shared bank for children to refer to during writing. Examples: figure, creature, lifeform.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that non-finite clauses always come at the start of sentences.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that non-finite clauses can vary their position in a sentence and model a non-finite clause in both positions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place later in the narrative.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know to focus on the three key moments from their plans from the previous lesson.

nodes.misconception: The words exchanged between characters are the most effective way to convey the relationship between them.
nodes.response: Often, the most effective dialogue comes from considering body language and the balance of the lines.

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.

nodes.misconception: Children might think that a valuable witness must be able to provide details about the event.
nodes.response: Explain that sometimes quotes from witnesses are used to gain an understanding of impact and can be primarily about emotions or feelings.

nodes.misconception: Some students might think that the use of a fronted adverbial phrase forms a complex sentence.
nodes.response: Model examples and non examples to demonstrate that a phrase doesn't contain a verb but a clause does.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to use accurate punctuation when writing direct speech that is part of a complex sentence.
nodes.response: Refer to the Year 4 Grammar unit 'Apostrophes and speech punctuation' to support pupils with writing direct speech correctly. Remind pupils to start a new line each time there is a new speaker.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place in the opening, build-up or climax.
nodes.response: The resolution follows a clear, chronological order that includes the three key moments from pupils' plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with how to apply the comma rule in a relative complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of a relative complex sentence. Ask children to identify the relative pronoun that begins the relative clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to determine which suffix or word to use to form superlatives.
nodes.response: Encourage children to orally rehearse the superlative forms of adjectives to check that they sound correct.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not write about all the key moments from the resolution.
nodes.response: The resolution follows a chronological order that includes four key moments that are detailed in pupils' plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may become confused and try to use a conditional clause without a main clause.
nodes.response: Use the visuals of the superheroes to help emphasise that the conditional clause needs the main clause to make the sentence make sense.

nodes.misconception: Children may include elements of Chulak's interaction with Lalchand in their recount because they know this as the reader but Lila only knows what Chulak tells her.
nodes.response: The diary is written from Lila's perspective. From her perspective, Chulak said he would visit her father and she doesn't find out anything about the interaction until he returns.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may inaccurately use an apostrophe for contraction by not removing letters and just putting the words together with an apostrophe.
nodes.response: Teach them that the apostrophe indicates where letters have been omitted. Give children examples and non-examples to sort and explain why they are right/wrong.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that a relative clause can only be placed in the middle of a sentence.
nodes.response: Relative clauses can be placed after any noun or noun phrase that they refer to, including at the end of a sentence.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to integrate direct and reported speech into a paragraph that also contains factual information.
nodes.response: During shared writing, model how we can switch between direct and reported speech.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to cover the 'events' of the story while focusing on descriptive and emotive details.
nodes.response: Ensure that you emphasise the need to move the action forwards and that you model this in oral rehearsal.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to convert notes into complete sentences.
nodes.response: Provide lots of time for oral rehearsal at each stage of the lesson and ensure children have access to vocabulary and plans used earlier in the unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only include the information in their research notes and not draw ideas together into a conclusion.
nodes.response: While shared writing this section, constantly refer back to the essay question to ensure the conclusion addresses it head-on.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to switch between tenses in the final paragraph.
nodes.response: Ensure you share your thoughts as a writer as you do the shared writing for this paragraph, showing that it is normal to switch tenses in this way when we are describing present emotions with a retelling of past events.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to convert their plan into complete sentences.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils have plenty of time to orally rehearse using their plans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect ideas with appropriate cohesive devices.
nodes.response: When completing shared writing, model considering and rejecting different ways of combining or connecting ideas; there is almost always more than one 'right' way and it is up to us to decide which we want to use.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to integrate techniques for increasing pace into their writing.
nodes.response: Model during oral rehearsal and shared writing how we can do this. For instance, ask pupils to consider what characters might be thinking at different points to generate rhetorical questions.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to punctuate direct speech correctly.
nodes.response: Complete lessons on punctuating direct speech can be found in our Year 5 Grammar curriculum; you may wish to briefly review a couple of these slides based on your assessment of pupils' work in the previous lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to switch fluently between tenses.
nodes.response: Practise saying sentences aloud to check tense is used accurately.

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with using a formal fronted adverbial to contrast appropriately.
nodes.response: Model a formal fronted adverbial of contrast used incorrectly (reiterate same point in main clause). Ask children to analyse and correct it.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to add parenthesis to a sentence in the correct position.
nodes.response: Parenthesis often follows a noun to add extra information; it can be removed and the sentence will still make sense.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may shift into writing from the third person perspective.
nodes.response: Pupils are going to be writing a persuasive letter written from the first person perspective of the red crayon in ‘The Day the Crayons Quit’. Ensure that pupils have a word bank or display with 'I', 'me', 'my', 'we', 'us' and 'our' prompts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may need support with punctuating direct speech in different forms.
nodes.response: Visual structures to support punctuating direct speech can be found in our KS2 Grammar lessons.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify the types of complex sentences.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle focuses on reviewing the three types of complex sentence previously learnt in the unit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may link sentences incorrectly with formal fronted adverbials that are unsuitable.
nodes.response: Focus on understanding the 'and' and 'but' categories of formal fronted adverbials and say the sentences out loud to hear if they make sense

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that take place outside of the hive.
nodes.response: This section explains the final three steps of the honey-making process that take place inside the hive.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that come in section 1 of the explanation text.
nodes.response: This section explains the final three steps of the mummification process, starting from when the body was covered in oil.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps in the process from when the food arrives in the mouth.
nodes.response: This section of the explanation text is about what happens after the food leaves the stomach.

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate and include the different types of fronted adverbials.
nodes.response: Create a shared bank of fronted adverbials that are appropriate for the text type and make sure these are available for children to support them in their writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use a lot of subject-specific vocabulary without clearly explaining its meaning to the reader.
nodes.response: Pupils should be taught how to use parenthesis demarcated using brackets to add additional information to sentences. Brackets are a great tool with which to explain meaning of tricky vocabulary to the reader.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to sequence their sequencing language.
nodes.response: Either provide a word bank of sequencing words 'First,', 'Then,' etc. or encourage children who struggle with this to only sequence using numbers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only include direct speech sentences from their plans.
nodes.response: One of the elements of the success criteria directs pupils to use adverbial detail and subordination in each reporting clause. This helps pupils remember to stretch their initial ideas in their plans when independently writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a recipe would not require an introduction.
nodes.response: Show pupils some examples of recipes that include introductions and let them analyse them. Teach pupils that an introduction can be effective in making the reader want to follow the instructions.

nodes.misconception: You can write integers directly to a CSV file using file.write(number).
nodes.response: All data must be converted to strings before writing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use an exclamation mark at the end of every sentence.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to read their writing back with expression and discuss the role of the exclamation mark here.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may tick their success criteria without checking and correcting.
nodes.response: Emphasise correcting mistakes to develop a growth mindset and model how you would like them to correct in terms of presentation.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives and adverbs are confused.
nodes.response: Explain adjectives describe nouns and adverbs describe a verb. Make sure to give sufficient examples before expecting the children to write.

nodes.misconception: You have to create a new write() line for each line you want to add to a file.
nodes.response: You can write mutiple lines in one write() statement. But if you want the text to appear on separate lines, you must use the new line character.

nodes.misconception: As children start to focus on adding emphasis, they can forget some of the routine handwriting expectations like lead-ins and lead-outs.
nodes.response: Remind the children before they start to look carefully at the sentence. Having a visual check-list, which includes handwriting prompts like lead-ins, lead-outs and the size of letters can help.

nodes.misconception: Children might forget the silent letter when forming the words in Tasks B and C.
nodes.response: Remind children that the purpose of the task is to write words with silent letters. Ask them to look back and ensure they have included the silent letter.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to think of imaginative ideas.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in pairs or small groups to generate ideas for their poems. You may also wish to do some further work on adjectives to describe and come up with a class word bank of adjectives to refer to.

nodes.misconception: A newspaper article can be written in the same style as a story retelling.
nodes.response: Newspaper articles must have different elements to show they are an article - interview quotes and a concise way of writing things are key.

nodes.misconception: Only one interpretation of Iago is relevant since he is clearly a villain.
nodes.response: Even villains can be looked at through multiple lenses. Doing this can elevate your response as you say what others may not consider.

nodes.misconception: Topic sentences are not worth spending much time on, the discussion of techniques is more important.
nodes.response: To make a paragraph even more effective, a topic sentence can be elevated in many ways to make writing clear and specific with a firm voice.

nodes.misconception: Use 'würde' whenever you want to say 'would'.
nodes.response: 'Würde' works in most cases, but for the conditional with 'haben' and 'sein', we usually use 'hätte' ('I would have') and 'wäre' ('I would be').

nodes.misconception: Objects can only be grouped in one way.
nodes.response: Objects can be grouped in multiple ways using different attributes to create groups.

nodes.misconception: Product design, particulary functional furniture, does not the impact the wellbeing of society.
nodes.response: Design that is uplifting, inclusive and accessible can benefit society in a positive way.

nodes.misconception: To form any verb in the conditional, add a conditional ending to the infinitive.
nodes.response: Not all verbs are regular in the conditional and some don't follow this pattern. Some verbs have irregular stems in the conditional, e.g. 'tener' ('tendr-') and 'poder' ('podr-').

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think York was only strategically important because the rivers acted as a natural defence.
nodes.response: York was strategically important because the rivers were a natural defence, but they were also key routes for trade.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all offspring resemble their parents.
nodes.response: Examples of offspring that resemble their parents and of those who do not.

nodes.misconception: Students may think all youth blindly accepted Nazi ideas.
nodes.response: While many participated, some - like Sophie Scholl - resisted. Peer pressure, fear, and excitement all played a role.

nodes.misconception: Feeling disappointed if some fitness test results fall below national average.
nodes.response: We all have different strengths and weaknesses and this is why we train to improve our areas of weakness.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that benchmarking times represent their fixed ability and that their times won’t change.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to understand that benchmarking is a snapshot in time - a starting point that effort and hard work can improve (growth mindset).

nodes.misconception: Form closed questions in German by adding 'do you ...' or 'are you ...', as in English.
nodes.response: Swap only the position of the subject and verb in a German statement to form a closed question.

nodes.misconception: The working class are the social class most likely to commit crime.
nodes.response: What types of crime are more likely to be committed by the wealthy? Why might they be less likely to be punished?

nodes.misconception: All designers, architects and engineers sketch in 3D.
nodes.response: Designers, architects and engineers often use elevations to show different 2D views of 3D objects from the side, front and plan.

nodes.misconception: Zakah and khums are voluntary donations to charity.
nodes.response: Zakah is obligatory in Sunni Islam and both zakah and khums are obligatory in Shi'a Islam. Additional voluntary donations can be made to charity as well and is known as sadaqah.

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not perform quality actions because they don't point their toes. They either pull their toes towards their body, so their ankle is 90 degrees, or their foot is in a relaxed position.
nodes.response: Some pupils will need to be taught how to point their toes. Remind them to push their feet away, making their legs look longer. Practice with everyone at the beginning of the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils only stand on 1 leg when asked to add a balance, or perform a straight jump off apparatus.
nodes.response: Encourage creativity by suggesting balances on different body parts or at different levels and remind them of a variety of jumps. Celebrate creativity.

nodes.misconception: That you should consider the bigger picture of a text rather than minute detail.
nodes.response: Zooming in on individual words is a powerful analytical tool that allows you to see patterns in meaning.

nodes.misconception: Nouns created from verbs are always formed from the infinitive and are always neuter.
nodes.response: Nouns can be formed from the infintive and those nouns are always neuter. However, other nouns can be formed from the verb stem rather than the infinitive. Nouns ending in the suffix '-ung' are always feminine.

nodes.misconception: Protestantism is a single unified religion.
nodes.response: There are, today, thousands of different Christian denominations that can be considered versions of Protestantism. Almost from its very inception, Protestantism split into a variety of competing belief systems.
